artigo.texto: San Antonio City Council votes to toughen data center rules amid resident concerns SAN ANTONIO — The debate over data centers in San Antonio is divisive, with some residents pushing for stricter regulations and others highlighting the financial benefits these facilities bring. On Thursday, San Antonio City Council voted 9-2 to approve District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan's plan for tougher data center zoning. The new rules require each proposed data center to go through a specific-use authorization process and receive council review before moving forward. Ahead of the vote, a small group gathered at City Hall to protest. One woman said, "Everything that is going on in city council tomorrow with the vote on the Unified Development Code is absolutely necessary. It's about time that the city of San Antonio protect residents from this enormous growth of data centers that has happened and continues to happen." The issue was last discussed at the Oct. 15 meeting, when city staff presented two options. The first would have allowed data centers in San Antonio automatically, as long as they followed certain rules: limiting them to commercial and industrial areas, keeping them at least 500 feet from buildings, homes and landscaping, and banning them from the Edwards Research Recharge zone. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones described a recent visit to a center, saying, "There you see in the picture, those are diesel generators in the back there, and we were all of 650 ft from a playground." The second option, which the council ultimately approved, included all the same guidelines but required each project to come before council for approval. Galvan said, "It's been critical for my community and for myself to make sure that we are pushing on policies that can ensure that residents have the ability to communicate directly with the developers, ask the question they want to get to know, make sure they get the concessions they're looking for and the community benefits they're looking for and finally, making sure that council has their back." Online data shows 89 data centers already operate in San Antonio. Galvan said the push for new regulations comes because "there hasn't been an opportunity before." District 10 Councilman Marc Whyte said he supports responsible policy that protects residents but also recognizes the economic impact of data centers. "I think we need to look at responsible policy again that protects our people and says to the data centers, if you can meet 'a, b, c, d, e' qualifications. If you're willing to abide by these rules and we're willing to talk about you being here within our city," Whyte said. He added, "The jobs that they create for our city, the revenue that they create for our city cannot be overlooked. I hope my colleagues take that into account [Thursday]." Galavan said in a statement, "The approved regulations make progress toward addressing longstanding concerns from residents, particularly in District 6 on San Antonio’s far Northwest side, where a majority of the city’s data centers currently operate. Efforts to address the rapid growth of data centers in San Antonio began with a Council Consideration Request in 2025 that examined the industry’s potential impacts on the city’s natural resources, infrastructure, and quality of life for surrounding residential neighborhoods." “When one of the largest and wealthiest industries in the world has the potential to negatively impact San Antonio’s water sources, energy usage, neighborhoods, and quality of life, the residents of San Antonio deserve to have a say. We understand the role data center development plays in increasing San Antonio’s economic and energy future, but growth must come with responsibility. Development cannot come at the expense of the working-class families who call San Antonio home. We must make sure residents are protected, developers are held to clear standards for worker benefits, and community concerns are considered before decisions are made — not after the fact. I will continue working to ensure San Antonio grows responsibly, protects its natural resources, and puts the health and integrity of working families first." “Today’s action is an important step in an ongoing effort to modernize the City’s development policies and respond to the concerns of local San Antonians. As implementation moves forward, continued oversight and public engagement will be essential to ensuring the adopted regulations deliver meaningful protections for neighborhoods across the city.” Councilwoman Misty Spears opposed requiring City Council approval for new data centers, saying the process could discourage investment and hurt San Antonio’s competitiveness. She said in a statement “San Antonio should welcome responsible investment with clear, consistent rules that businesses can rely on,” she said. “Requiring another Council vote creates uncertainty, even for companies willing to meet our development standards. These companies have choices, and unnecessary uncertainty can send investment, construction jobs and tax revenue elsewhere.” “I supported the more balanced approach recommended by the Zoning Commission, which combined development standards with a predictable approval path in heavier industrial districts." “The Zoning Commission recommended responsible, common-sense regulations that addressed community concerns while giving businesses clear requirements. Companies should know what is expected before investing significant time and money. Uniform standards provide that certainty." “Data centers support businesses, hospitals, financial institutions, military operations and cybersecurity while creating opportunities for local contractors and expanding the commercial tax base,” Spears said. The new zoning plan aims to balance community concerns with the city's economic needs as San Antonio continues to grow.

artigo.texto: My local grocery store in rural Virginia now has a blinking, beeping robot that rolls up and down the aisles, scanning inventory to let someone in charge know when they’re low on stock. Sentara Health, the Norfolk-based chain that opens hospitals across Virginia and North Carolina, now uses artificial intelligence programs to monitor patients and discharge timelines to make sure whatever services a patient needs after discharge (such as rehab or at-home care) is lined up. My email provider now automatically provides an “AI inbox” to summarize email. I didn’t ask for it. I don’t want it. I’m quite capable of reading my own emails, but there it is anyway. The connection for all these three otherwise unrelated events runs through “the cloud,” which is not really a cloud but a collection of data centers somewhere. One of the unexpected developments in this year’s congressional campaigns has been the emergence of data centers as an issue — with Democrats being the ones most likely to push the issue. Tom Perriello, the Democratic candidate in the 5th District, opened his campaign with an ad in which he appears to smash a hammer against a wall that says, among other things, “data centers.” Beth Macy, the Democratic candidate in the 6th District, has made a data center moratorium a central part of her campaign. So has Joy Powers, the Democratic candidate in the 9th District. Across Virginia, we see some localities already taking their own actions to restrict data centers. Suffolk and the town of Front Royal have enacted outright bans. Chesapeake and Virginia Beach have passed temporary moratoriums. At least six other localities have taken different actions to make it more difficult to build a data center. Whether the opposition to data centers is well-founded is a matter of political opinion, but there’s no doubt that the opposition is quite real. Now, here’s the problem: Any restrictions on data centers are treating the symptom, not the problem. The problem is that we keep creating data that requires data centers. A state moratorium, as some want, would simply send data centers elsewhere. That might solve our problems with increased energy and water demands, but in practice, it only transfers it elsewhere — most likely Texas. A national moratorium, as some want, would simply send that data overseas, which raises the question of whether you’re comfortable with your financial records or medical records sitting in some other country. I explored those questions in a previous column. Plot twist: Those records might already be overseas anyway. For all the political clamor over data centers, there has been surprisingly little political push to ban, regulate or otherwise restrict the data-creation forces fueling them. To do so would require legislators to reach further into the business world than even the most regulation-happy politician has ever proposed. There are some efforts underway. At the federal level, both Sen. Mark Warner, D-Virginia, and Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Prince William County, have proposed to ban “surveillance pricing,” the practice of using computer data to charge some customers more than others. (That makes it a more personalized cousin of dynamic pricing, which relies on general market signals to change prices, such as hotels raising prices when there’s a big college football game in town). At the state level, state Sen. Russet Perry, D-Loudoun County, has also introduced a bill to ban surveillance pricing. As a practical matter, hers probably stands a better chance because almost every bill in Richmond actually gets acted on in some way, while bills in Congress are often little more than press releases until party leaders decide to do something with them. Here’s how a statement from Perry describes the practice: “Companies now collect detailed information on their customers, including shopping history, browsing activity, location, and the device they shop on. Increasingly, businesses use that data to estimate how much each person is willing to pay and set prices accordingly. The practice, known as surveillance pricing, means a customer can be charged more simply because a company’s algorithm predicts they can afford it or won’t shop around.” However, the bill doesn’t propose to ban companies from collecting and storing that data — just using it or combining it with other data “to raise or change the underlying price of a product,” Perry’s statement says. The reality is that so much of our economy — and our personal lives — is digitized that little can be done to stop the demand for more data centers. All of our online banking, our direct deposits of paychecks, our online shopping, our social media activity — all of it requires data centers, and every day we create more data that has to be stored somewhere. In a previous column, I used estimates from one data center company to calculate that we each make use of anywhere from 58 to 87 different data centers every day. That’s because data is typically not stored in a single site; there are copies stored in multiple locations for redundancy. Fun fact: A few weeks ago, the company that Cardinal contracts with for our web hosting sent out a notice that its data center in the Dallas-Fort Worth area had cooling problems and was overheating, but not to worry, because “we maintain a real-time copy of each site across multiple data centers for redundancy” and operations were being temporarily shifted to those other locations. This did not appear to affect us; the vendor, which works with lots of online news sites, said it keeps “the main version of your site in the region closest to you,” with copies elsewhere. That means you’re probably reading this from a server somewhere in Ashburn in Loudoun County. However, the company has 28 data centers around the world — North America, South America, Europe, Africa and Asia. artigo.texto: No ranking internacional, Tóquio aparece como o mercado mais caro para construir data centers, com US$ 18,28 por watt INFRAESTRUTURA DIGITAL São Paulo tem custo de R$ 62 por watt para construção de data centers e atrai investidores globais Por Redação A cidade de São Paulo ocupa a 30ª posição em um ranking global de custos para construção de data centers, com investimento médio de US$ 11,66 (R$ 62,12) por watt de capacidade instalada. O levantamento, realizado pela consultoria internacional Turner & Townsend, coloca a capital paulista em posição competitiva para atrair projetos de infraestrutura digital, especialmente aqueles ligados à inteligência artificial (IA) e aos serviços de computação em nuvem. O custo registrado em São Paulo é inferior ao de importantes centros tecnológicos internacionais, como o Vale do Silício, nos Estados Unidos, onde a construção chega a US$ 15,01 por watt. No Rio de Janeiro, que ocupa a 20ª colocação, o valor alcança US$ 12,59 (R$ 67,05). O indicador considera os investimentos em construção por watt de capacidade elétrica instalada, sem incluir o consumo de energia durante a operação. O estudo aponta que a disponibilidade de fontes diversificadas de energia e a crescente demanda por processamento de dados contribuem para fortalecer o Brasil como destino de investimentos internacionais. O avanço da inteligência artificial também deve intensificar a expansão do setor nos próximos anos. Segundo a pesquisa, 52% dos especialistas consultados acreditam que, até 2027, a maioria dos novos projetos globais de data centers será direcionada a aplicações de inteligência artificial. Entretanto, a expansão enfrenta obstáculos relacionados à infraestrutura energética e à disponibilidade de profissionais especializados. A oferta de energia foi classificada como um desafio crítico por 56% dos participantes do levantamento. Além disso, 81% relataram dificuldades moderadas ou graves para contratar mão de obra qualificada. Os processos de aprovação e conexão à rede elétrica também representam entraves, podendo ultrapassar dois anos. No ranking internacional, Tóquio aparece como o mercado mais caro para construir data centers, com US$ 18,28 por watt, seguida por Osaka, com US$ 17,15, e Zurique, com US$ 15,93. Apesar dos desafios, a Turner & Townsend avalia que o crescimento da demanda por infraestrutura digital abre oportunidades para o Brasil ampliar sua participação no mercado global, desde que avance na oferta de energia, na eficiência dos recursos e na qualificação profissional.

artigo.texto: Delta Capacity has reached financial close on two battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Finland: Karppio BESS, a 125 MW/300 MWh project in Teuva in partnership with Strioga Family Foundation, and AKKU One, a 125 MW/300 MWh project in Lapinlahti in partnership with COVENERGO. With a combined capacity of 250 MW/600 MWh, AKKU One and Karppio are among the largest BESS developments in Finland to enter construction. Both partners bring extensive experience in developing and investing in energy projects of this kind. As the majority owner of AKKU One, COVENERGO contributes its expertise in renewable energy development, project financing, and investment structuring, drawing on its experience across six countries. Strioga Family Foundation brings its experience as an investor in BESS projects across five other European markets. Société Générale is the sole senior lender to both projects, providing long-term financing and acting as agent, security agent, and hedge provider. Finnvera provides a counter-guarantee in support of one of the facilities arranged by Société Générale. Key supply and offtake contracts with Sungrow and Centrica Energy have been executed, construction has started, and commercial operations are targeted for 4Q27. Delta Capacity acts as the construction and long-term asset manager for both projects. Financial close demonstrates Delta Capacity’s integrated model: developing battery storage facilities and bringing together the commercial, financial, and execution partners needed to build, finance, and take BESS projects to commercial operation. A key part of this model is Delta Capacity’s work with Centrica Energy, with partial tolling agreements already in place for both assets. The tolling structure gives the projects secured revenues while maintaining merchant upside, and builds on Centrica Energy’s role as optimiser of Delta Capacity’s 70 MW/160 MWh Ånge BESS in Sweden, which has been in operation since June 2026. Marc Weisser, CFO & CIO of Delta Capacity, commented: “Achieving financial close on both Karppio and AKKU One represents a significant milestone for Delta Capacity and our partners, COVENERGO and Strioga Family Foundation. The backing of Société Générale and Finnvera underscores the strength of these projects, the quality of our partnerships, and the confidence in our development and investment strategy. With construction already underway, our focus now turns to delivering both projects and bringing them into operation in 2027.” Christophe Hadjal, Head of Energy, Mining and Industries Finance, Europe at Société Générale, noted: “The development of BESS solutions is becoming an increasingly important part of the energy transition, enabling greater integration of renewable energy sources and supporting the resilience of power grids. As energy markets continue to evolve, new business models and emerging players are developing across this growing segment of the energy value chain. We are pleased to support this evolution and the companies contributing to it, such as Delta Capacity.” František Kalivoda, CEO of COVENERGO, responded: “Reaching financial close for AKKU One is a major milestone for COVENERGO and an important step in our expansion into the Nordic energy market. Together with Delta Capacity and our financing partners, we have brought the project into its next phase. With construction already underway, our focus is now on delivering a high-quality battery storage asset that will support the flexibility and resilience of Finland’s energy system.” Gediminas Uloza, CEO of Strioga Family Foundation, concluded: “Reaching financial close on Karppio BESS less than four months after our investment reflects the strength of the partnership with Delta Capacity and the professionalism of the full project team. Strioga Family Foundation is committed to supporting the European energy transition, and we see battery storage as central to integrating the continent’s growing renewable capacity.” ICECAPITAL acted as Debt Adviser on the financing. Castrén & Snellman and Cobalt acted as Legal Counsel to the borrowers and sponsors. HPP and Addleshaw Goddard acted as Legal Counsel to the lenders. AFRY acted as Technical Adviser and Aurora Energy Research provided market advice. Finland’s power system continues to see rapid growth in renewable generation, particularly wind power. Once operational, Karppio and AKKU One will provide flexibility to the Finnish grid, supporting frequency regulation, balancing, and the continued integration of renewable energy. artigo.texto: BYD's Blade Battery Supply Crunch Meets a Pivotal Earnings Test Published on 10/29/2026 at 11:31 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD has told investors that models fitted with its second-generation Blade Battery and fast-charging technology remain in short supply, with the company working to lift delivery capacity. The disclosure, posted Friday on an investor platform, lands just as the automaker's third-quarter and nine-month 2026 figures go before the board for review and approval — a reminder that demand signals only matter once they convert into shipped vehicles and healthy margins. Chairman Wang Chuanfu put the workforce at more than 1.02 million people, including as many as 120,000 research and development engineers, in remarks at the annual conference of the China Society of Automotive Engineers. That headcount frames the central question for shareholders: whether this vast apparatus of engineers and factory capacity can be turned into profitable growth rather than simply scale for its own sake. Headcount alone says nothing about productivity or earnings power. A product calendar running at full tilt The pipeline has been busy. On Tuesday, BYD launched the third generation of the Qin PLUS DM-i in China at limited-time prices ranging from RMB 76,900 to RMB 97,900. The plug-in hybrid offers up to 220 kilometers of electric range under China's CLTC test standard — figures that give a concrete read on the offering, though the promotional pricing is explicitly time-limited and the range figure is tied to that specific standard. The same day brought word that Yangwang, BYD's premium marque, has named its flagship sedan the Dingyao, carrying the English name YANGWANG ALTIOR. A naming announcement is not a sales launch, and investors would do well to keep the two apart: the Qin Plus represents a completed market debut, while Yangwang has so far only put a label on its halo model. Overseas, the company is advancing on several fronts at once. On October 15 it signed a letter of intent with Inokom Corporation, a subsidiary of Sime Darby, naming the Malaysian firm as partner for planned vehicle assembly — a partnership for a project, not yet running production. Six days later, on October 21, BYD and Truckman agreed to collaborate on approved accessories for the SHARK pickup in the UK. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? Safety credentials and a staged European rollout The SHARK DMO earned a five-star Euro-NCAP safety rating, announced October 15. Sales were slated to begin in selected markets within three months, with a broader European rollout planned for the first half of 2027. Each of these developments sits at a different stage of execution, and distinguishing completed launches from partnership agreements and still-planned sales steps is essential to reading the news flow correctly. Reuters reported Friday that BYD is seeking approvals to double annual capacity at its Brazilian plant to 600,000 vehicles. The executive overseeing Brazil also cited a target of 25,000 vehicles per month by the end of 2026. The two figures describe different things: the capacity expansion hinges on permits, while the monthly output number is an aspiration rather than achieved production. What the numbers must prove The bull case is straightforward enough. If BYD can ease the reported shortages and serve existing demand, new technology would move beyond generating headlines and reach customers at scale, with development and manufacturing feeding off each other. Capacity additions, paired with sufficient demand, would help supply the market instead of merely raising the theoretical production ceiling. The risk runs the other way: building out organization and manufacturing faster than the economics can justify. A large R&D payroll is not evidence of inefficiency, but neither does it guarantee an adequate return on the spending. And the pricing of new models adds a further test — the Qin Plus tariffs alone reveal nothing about margins, yet they sharpen the question of whether fresh offerings can win buyers while contributing meaningfully to earnings. Sales carried mainly by unattractive terms would leave growth lagging profitability expectations. The reported scarcity cuts both ways as well. Until delivery capacity catches up, potential demand is not realized revenue, and a delayed ramp-up could cap the very opportunity the new technology creates. A Chinese market calendar points to October 30 as the expected disclosure date, with today's board session set to review and approve the unaudited results. Whether those figures underpin the operational expansion economically is the yardstick that matters. Until then, the quality of BYD's growth — not its visible size — remains the deciding factor for investors. Ad BYD Stock: New Analysis - 29 October Fresh BYD information released. artigo.texto: New Jersey voters are evenly split over data center development nationally, but opposition grows considerably when proposed facilities move closer to home, according to the latest poll from the William J. Hughes Center for Public Policy at Stockton University. Voters are evenly split on the construction of data centers in the United States, with 40% in support and 40% opposed. When asked about data center development in New Jersey, opposition rises to 52% compared with 29% support, and when it comes to construction in their own town, nearly two-thirds (65%) oppose development while just 18% support it. One in five New Jersey voters (19%) support data center developments nationally but oppose one in their own town. That accounts for nearly half of all voters who support them nationally. “Not-in-my-backyard sentiment is real, but it isn’t the whole story,” said Alyssa Maurice, assistant director of the Hughes Center for Public Policy. “Twice as many voters oppose data centers at any proximity, so there is a broader ideological pushback at play.” Firm views lean toward opposition. Thirty-nine percent of voters oppose data centers at the national, state and local level, while just 17% support them at all levels. Voters who say they know more about data centers are also more likely to oppose local development. Among those who say they know at least a fair amount, 73% oppose a data center in their town, compared with 55% of those who say they know little to nothing. About one in five voters say a data center has been built or proposed in or near their town. Among this group, 68% strongly oppose a data center in their own town, compared with 52% of those who report no nearby development. Also, among this group, 68% say data centers harm communities, compared with 48% of those who report none nearby. “Towns facing proposals are likely to have more organized opposition or local news coverage,” Maurice said. “Once these projects move from an abstract policy debate to something happening in their own community, concerns about costs and quality of life become much more concrete.” Republicans are the most supportive group, but even they are more likely to oppose a data center in their town (44%) than to support one (36%). Among Democrats, 72% oppose a local data center. Democrats are also more than twice as likely as Republicans to say data centers harm communities (56% vs. 24%). Women are more likely than men to oppose data centers at every level (43% vs. 32%). Men are about twice as likely to support them at every level (24% vs. 11%). Nearly half of voters (47%) believe data centers harm the communities where they are located, compared with just 10% who believe they benefit their communities. Another 18% say they have little impact either way, and 24% are unsure. Among consistent supporters, as in those who back data centers at every level, a plurality (42%) say they have little impact either way on host communities. Asked to identify their biggest concerns about data centers, voters most frequently selected higher electricity bills (45%) and effects on the water supply (43%). Other concerns included artificial intelligence (24%), a lack of transparency (22%) and insufficient government oversight (22%). Respondents could select up to three concerns. Voters were also asked to identify any upsides. The most commonly cited benefits were good-paying jobs (33%), increased property tax revenue for the town (29%) and helping New Jersey compete in the technology economy (27%). One in five (20%) say data centers bring no benefits at all. The poll of 667 registered voters was sponsored and conducted by the William J. Hughes Center for Public Policy at Stockton University, and it has a margin of error of +/- 3.8 percentage points. The poll of New Jersey voters was sponsored and conducted by the Stockton Polling Institute of the William J. Hughes Center for Public Policy at Stockton University. Data collection took place from Oct. 13-19, 2026, using a N.J. voter list sample. A total of 667 New Jersey registered voters were interviewed.

artigo.texto: CHENNAI: After detailed discussions, the state cabinet approved the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Policy 2026 on Thursday. The policy targeting 1 MW and above projects aims to speed up the installation of BESS across power generation and transmission networks, improve the utilisation of renewable energy and reduce the wastage of power (curtailment) generated from renewable sources. The policy, accessed by TNIE, covers two categories of battery storage systems - standalone BESS and co-located BESS. Standalone BESS refers to independent battery storage systems with a capacity of more than 1 MW. These systems can be connected to transmission or distribution networks or private consumer networks. They will be eligible for a 100% waiver of applicable transmission and wheeling charges. These standalone BESS can be used to meet peak-hour demand, support grid operations and provide other approved services. Co-located BESS refers to battery storage systems integrated with solar, solar-hybrid or other renewable energy projects with a capacity of more than 1 MW. These systems store electricity generated by the associated renewable energy plants and supply it during peak-demand hours or when required. Co-located BESS projects in existing or new solar, wind or hybrid projects will be eligible for a 100% waiver of applicable transmission and wheeling charges. The policy will apply to all BESS projects for which applications are submitted on or after the date of notification, as well as projects commissioned on or after April 1, 2027.

artigo.texto: Shoto (Shuangdeng Group) and ACME Group have completed the commissioning of a 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Rajasthan, India, marking another development in the country’s expanding grid-scale energy storage sector. The project is designed to support renewable energy integration and strengthen grid stability as India increases its solar and wind power capacity. According to Shoto, the project incorporates a customized battery energy storage solution developed to meet India’s grid requirements and operate under Rajasthan’s challenging climatic conditions. The system has a four-hour storage duration, enabling it to deliver electricity during periods of high demand and support more effective management of renewable energy generation. The project has reportedly secured financing through a non-recourse syndicated loan involving Indian financial institutions, including State Bank of India (SBI), ICICI Bank, and local green finance institutions. This financing arrangement highlights the growing role of institutional funding in supporting large-scale energy storage infrastructure in India. The collaboration between Shoto and ACME brings together battery storage technology and renewable energy project development capabilities. The installation is expected to contribute to improved grid flexibility, reduced renewable energy curtailment, and more reliable electricity supply by storing excess generation for use when required. The commissioning comes as India accelerates the deployment of battery energy storage systems to address the intermittency of renewable power generation and support its clean energy transition. Shoto has positioned the project as a potential reference for future energy storage developments across India and other South Asian markets, where demand for flexible and reliable power infrastructure continues to grow. artigo.texto: As Forças Armadas dos Estados Unidos proibiram a entrada de veículos da montadora chinesa BYD na base aérea de Kadena, na ilha de Okinawa, no Japão. A decisão entrou em vigor nesta semana e foi justificada por possíveis riscos à segurança dos militares e das operações estadunidense. A restrição vale para todos os veículos da marca, independentemente do tipo ou da finalidade: carros particulares de militares e funcionários, veículos de empresas contratadas, táxis, entregas e veículos comerciais. Segundo a imprensa sul-coreana, que noticiou a medida primeiro, a base afirmou que não haverá exceções. Kadena fica no arquipélago de Okinawa, perto do Mar da China Oriental, numa das regiões com maior concentração de forças militares norte-americanas na Ásia. Segundo a agência Reuters, a porta-voz da base, tenente-coronel Alli Stormer, afirmou que os veículos representam um risco “inaceitável e impossível de mitigar” para os militares e suas operações. Ela não detalhou quais características dos carros motivaram a decisão nem apresentou evidências de alguma vulnerabilidade específica. Leia também - GM quer usar IA para desenvolver novos carros em apenas dois anos - Europa faz o oposto do Brasil e limita carros chineses; modelo pode servir ao País Preocupação seria com câmeras e sensores A base não explicou o motivo exato da proibição. Segundo a imprensa sul-coreana, a medida busca evitar que câmeras e sensores instalados nos carros captem e transmitam informações sobre as operações militares, os aviões, os radares e as munições mantidos em Kadena. Não há, porém, nenhuma evidência pública de que veículos da BYD tenham coletado ou enviado dados de bases militares estadunidense. A proibição tem caráter preventivo. BYD já havia sido incluída em lista do Pentágono A medida ocorre quatro meses depois de o Departamento de Defesa dos EUA incluir a BYD numa lista de empresas que, segundo o governo estadunidense, apoiam as Forças Armadas chinesas. A relação, divulgada em junho, também inclui Alibaba, Baidu e a fabricante de elétricos NIO. Na ocasião, a BYD rejeitou a classificação e informou que buscaria medidas administrativas e judiciais para defender seus interesses. A inclusão na lista não significa, por si só, que os veículos da fabricante tenham sido usados para espionagem ou tenham falhas de segurança comprovadas. China também restringiu carros da Tesla A preocupação com a segurança de veículos conectados não é exclusiva dos EUA. Em 2021, o governo chinês restringiu a entrada de carros da Tesla em algumas instalações governamentais, alegando preocupação com as câmeras dos veículos. A restrição foi retirada em 2024, depois que a fabricante norte-americana recebeu avaliação favorável da principal associação da indústria automotiva chinesa quanto às exigências locais de segurança de dados. O episódio mostra que carros equipados com câmeras, sensores e sistemas de comunicação passaram a fazer parte das discussões sobre proteção de dados em instalações estratégicas. Proibição acontece durante expansão internacional da BYD A medida chega num momento de expansão da fabricante chinesa fora de seu mercado doméstico. Em 2025, a BYD ultrapassou a Tesla e se tornou a maior vendedora mundial de veículos totalmente elétricos. A empresa também tenta crescer no Japão, mercado historicamente dominado por fabricantes locais como Toyota, Honda e Nissan. Em julho de 2026, lançou no país o Racco, um minicarro elétrico para disputar o segmento de compactos. Segundo a Reuters, não há informações sobre medidas semelhantes em outras bases estadunidense nem sobre restrições aos carros da BYD no mercado civil japonês. A imprensa sul-coreana, porém, relata que, dentro das forças norte-americanas, já se especula que a proibição possa ser estendida a outras instalações, como a base de Futenma, também em Okinawa, e a bases dos EUA na Coreia do Sul. Carregando ofertas...

artigo.texto: Top Portable Power Station Manufacturer Qingdao Chenyang Expands Energy Storage Solutions QINGDAO, SHANDONG, CHINA, October 29, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- As demand for flexible power supply and renewable energy storage continues to develop across residential, commercial, and outdoor markets, Qingdao Chenyang Electrical Technology Co., Ltd. is expanding its presence in the energy storage sector. Based in Qingdao, Shandong Province, China, the company focuses on the research, development, manufacturing, and sales of lithium-ion energy storage products. Its portfolio includes portable power stations, commercial and industrial battery energy storage systems, solar inverter chargers, and customized power battery packs. By combining energy storage technology with established manufacturing capabilities in metal processing and precision machining, the company is positioned to serve customers seeking integrated power solutions for a range of applications. The portable power station market has developed alongside growing interest in outdoor activities, mobile work, emergency preparedness, and renewable energy. Consumers and businesses increasingly require power sources that can operate beyond conventional wall outlets, while commercial users may need dependable electricity for temporary worksites, remote operations, and backup applications. These requirements have encouraged manufacturers to develop products that combine rechargeable batteries, power conversion systems, monitoring functions, and multiple output options in compact or transportable formats. For manufacturers, meeting these requirements involves more than assembling battery cells into an enclosure. Product development must consider energy capacity, output power, charging methods, battery management, thermal performance, mechanical protection, and the intended operating environment. These factors influence whether a power station is suitable for camping, mobile work, recreational vehicles, or emergency backup. Qingdao Chenyang Electrical Technology Co., Ltd. has established a product range intended to address several of these application areas, including outdoor portable energy storage and home backup power. Portable Power Stations for Outdoor and Backup Applications Portable power stations provide stored electrical energy for devices and equipment when grid electricity is unavailable or inconvenient. Depending on their specifications, they may supply power to lighting, communication equipment, laptops, small appliances, and other compatible loads. Outdoor users may value portability and flexible recharging, while households may prioritize backup capacity and the ability to support essential equipment during a temporary outage. Qingdao Chenyang Electrical Technology Co., Ltd. presents portable power station products for outdoor, camping, and emergency power scenarios. Its published product portfolio includes portable charging stations for recreational vehicles, outdoor portable power stations, emergency portable power stations, and other energy storage configurations. The company also lists products designed for home backup applications, reflecting the range of situations in which portable or compact energy storage may be useful. Battery chemistry is an important consideration when evaluating these products. The company's website identifies lithium iron phosphate, commonly known as LiFePO4 or LFP, cells in several portable power station listings. LFP batteries are widely used in energy storage because of their thermal stability and potential for long cycle life under appropriate operating conditions. Actual performance, however, depends on cell quality, battery management, charging and discharging conditions, temperature, and the design of the complete system. For buyers, nominal battery capacity and continuous output power should be considered separately. Capacity, usually expressed in watt-hours, indicates how much energy a battery can store, while output power, measured in watts, indicates how much electrical power the system can provide at a given time. A station with a high capacity may support a device for longer, but it must also have sufficient rated output to operate that device. Buyers should therefore compare rated capacity, continuous and peak output, available connectors, charging time, weight, and the manufacturer's operating recommendations before selecting a product. Charging flexibility is another factor in portable power station design. Depending on the model, energy may be replenished through a household electrical outlet, compatible solar panels, or other supported charging sources. Solar charging can be particularly relevant for camping, fieldwork, and remote locations where grid access is limited. The practical charging rate depends on the power station's input limits, solar panel output, sunlight conditions, and other system characteristics. Solar Energy Storage System Solutions Beyond portable products, integrated storage systems are becoming an important part of residential and commercial renewable energy projects. Solar photovoltaic panels generate electricity when sunlight is available, but generation and consumption do not always occur at the same time. Battery storage can retain some of the generated electricity for later use, while power conversion equipment helps manage the flow of energy between panels, batteries, loads, and the grid where the system supports grid interaction. Qingdao Chenyang Electrical Technology Co., Ltd. includes Solar Energy Storage System products in its portfolio. Its website also identifies commercial and industrial battery energy storage systems, outdoor energy storage cabinets, and other configurations intended for applications such as backup power, microgrids, and solar-storage projects. artigo.texto: BYD lança pistas de teste públicas para promover cultura automobilística na China Construção dos centros de experiência é um projeto prioritário do CEO da montadora Por Nikkei Asia — Guangzhou Atualizado A BYD, líder chinesa em veículos elétricos, está construindo pistas de teste em todo o país com o objetivo de fortalecer sua marca, permitindo que os motoristas experimentem dirigir em diversos tipos de terreno. O Centro de Experiências da Cultura Automotiva de Shaoxing, na província de Zhejiang, conta com uma pista de 1,6 quilômetro com cinco curvas e um trecho reto de aceleração de 550 metros. O local também possui outras cinco pistas. Uma delas é de baixa aderência, onde a água é adicionada ao solo coberto por cerca de 30 mil blocos de basalto completamente nivelados. Isso permite que iniciantes experimentem o drifting, onde os pneus deslizam lateralmente durante a condução. Outra pista apresenta uma inclinação acentuada de 28 graus que simula uma duna de areia, para que o motorista possa ter a sensação de dirigir em terrenos off-road. O centro de experiências, que iniciou suas operações em agosto, foi aberto à imprensa estrangeira há uma semana. Os visitantes podem escolher entre cursos para iniciantes, intermediários ou avançados e receber apoio de instrutores. Os veículos oferecidos são limitados aos modelos da BYD, incluindo o carro esportivo premium Yangwang e a marca Fangchengbao, focada em off-road. O preço do curso para iniciantes é de 599 yuans (US$ 90) por hora. A BYD inaugurou outros dois circuitos automotivos nas cidades de Zhengzhou e Hefei e planeja construir mais em outras regiões. A construção dos centros de experiência é um projeto prioritário do executivo-chefe (CEO) da BYD, Wang Chuanfu. Em um evento realizado em 2024, Wang afirmou que a empresa investiria 5 bilhões de yuans na construção de um circuito onde as pessoas pudessem testar veículos elétricos e outros veículos de novas energias. "Para se tornar uma marca global, tecnologia inovadora, valorização pelo mercado e o soft power da cultura automotiva são essenciais", disse Wang. Em outras palavras, uma cultura só pode ser cultivada tornando a tecnologia da empresa conhecida por um grande número de consumidores, segundo Wang. O volume de vendas da BYD aumentou onze vezes desde 2020, atingindo 4,6 milhões de unidades em 2025. Ao capturar a demanda por veículos de novas energias, a empresa subiu para o sexto lugar globalmente. Agora, a BYD parece estar se esforçando para ultrapassar a maior montadora em volume de vendas, a Toyota, que vende mais de 10 milhões de veículos por ano. O desafio da empresa chinesa reside na força de sua marca. O valor da marca BYD ficou em 11º lugar globalmente, de acordo com o relatório de 2026 da empresa de pesquisa britânica Brand Finance. Embora isso represente uma melhora em relação ao 12º lugar do ano passado, as 10 principais empresas são dominadas pelo Japão, Europa, Estados Unidos e Coreia do Sul. A diferença entre essas empresas e a BYD permanece significativa. A estratégia da BYD de usar pistas de corrida para fortalecer o valor de sua marca remete à história do Japão. A cultura das corridas e dos autódromos teve origem na Europa e nos Estados Unidos, mas começou a ganhar força no Japão com o crescimento das vendas de automóveis na década de 1960. A Honda concluiu o Circuito de Suzuka em 1962. O fundador da empresa, Soichiro Honda, buscava criar um autódromo "onde a direção em alta velocidade pudesse ser feita com segurança". O Autódromo Internacional de Fuji foi inaugurado posteriormente, em 1966. O Circuito de Suzuka e o Autódromo Internacional de Fuji sempre abriram suas instalações para iniciantes e entusiastas, incentivando-os a desfrutar da direção. Ao mesmo tempo, ambos os autódromos sediam corridas nacionais e internacionais, nas quais fabricantes de automóveis competem. Ao ampliar a base de fãs que apreciam automóveis e compreendem sua tecnologia e qualidade, os dois autódromos contribuíram para a construção da marca.

artigo.texto: Crux has facilitated construction-to-term loan financing for an 8 MW/40 MWh battery energy storage project being developed by EnerSmart Storage at the University of California, San Diego (UC San Diego), in a move aimed at strengthening campus energy resilience and reducing electricity costs. Announced on October 29, 2026, the financing involves a senior secured construction-to-term loan facility arranged by Crux. Crux is a capital platform specializing in clean energy and critical infrastructure. The battery energy storage system (BESS) will connect directly to the UC San Diego’s microgrid and is supported by a 10-year resource adequacy contract. The project is designed to improve the UC San Diego’s ability to manage electricity demand. It will also support reliable power supply and reduce peak-demand costs. Its 40 MWh storage capacity will also allow it to store electricity and discharge it when needed. This will help balance campus demand and supporting the wider electricity grid. UC San Diego battery storage project: Financing structure and development Crux arranged the financing through a targeted capital-raising process. The capital platform secured then competitive debt and preferred equity proposals within three weeks. Transaction closed six weeks after the term sheet was signed. This goes to demonstrate how tailored financing arrangements can help move energy infrastructure projects towards construction. The financing structure was also adjusted to accommodate changing project requirements. Crux worked with EnerSmart, the lender and legal counsel to increase the facility size and help bridge an equity grant. They also worked to absorb equipment cost increases associated with tariffs. The arrangement also highlights the importance of flexible project financing in the battery storage sector. This is because equipment prices, grant funding and project requirements often change during battery storage development. Combining construction financing with longer-term debt arrangements can also help developers manage the transition from construction into operations. According to Drew Venkatraman, Managing Director of Debt Capital Markets at Crux, the transaction demonstrates the value of flexible financing in bringing critical energy infrastructure to market. EnerSmart Chief Operating Officer Skyler Tennis also highlighted the contributions of UC San Diego. The California Energy Commission and other public- and private-sector partners were also noted for bringing together financing, grant support and energy-market programs. UC San Diego’s investment in campus energy resilience The battery storage project in UC San Diego also builds on long-standing efforts to strengthen the campus’ microgrid and advance energy storage deployment. In September 2024, the university announced a California Energy Commission award of approximately US$7.15 million to support a major campus battery installation planned at 10 MW/40 MWh. The initiative was set to improve energy reliability and support renewable energy integration. It was also intended to contribute to California’s electricity grid stability. However, the financing and ownership arrangements for the EnerSmart project have evolved. A California Energy Commission meeting transcript from February 2026 describes revisions to the earlier funding agreement. Some of the revisions include a third-party ownership arrangement for the first 10 years. According to the transcript, UC San Diego shares operational responsibilities before subsequently assuming ownership and operation. Financing to support universities green transition The newly announced EnerSmart financing is significant in two main ways. One, storage capacity; and two, the way public funding, private ownership and debt financing can be combined to support university energy infrastructure. Other universities, including University of Wisconsin, Platteville and New Mexico State University are also taking steps to make their grids greener. Both campuses Fact sheet for EnerSmart battery energy storage project at UC San Diego Location: University of California, San Diego, California Power capacity: 8 MW Energy storage capacity: 40 MWh Financing: Senior secured construction-to-term loan facility Financing arranger: Crux Project developer: EnerSmart Storage Offtake/revenue support: 10-year resource adequacy contract Grid connection: UC San Diego’s advanced campus microgrid Primary objectives: Campus energy resilience, peak-demand cost reduction and electricity-system support. Financing announcement: October 29, 2026 Who is involved in the UC San Diego battery storage project Crux – Arranged the construction-to-term debt financing and coordinated the capital-raising process. EnerSmart Storage – Battery storage project developer, owner and operator. University of California, San Diego – Campus partner and operator of the university’s advanced microgrid. California Energy Commission (CEC) – Public-sector funding partner. Also associated with the UC San Diego’s battery energy storage program.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- on Oct. 27, CATL addressed investor queries on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange's interactive platform regarding the progress of its Hefei sulfide solid-state pilot base. The battery giant remains firmly committed to all-solid-state technology — which it describes as industry-leading — and expects small-scale production by 2027. That timeline tracks with earlier disclosures: small-scale trial production in 2027, followed by mass production around 2030. Image credit: CATL On the technology front, CATL is betting heavily on the sulfide route. It has built a 10Ah-level verification platform and moved its sulfide solid-state battery into 20Ah sample prototyping, targeting an energy density of roughly 500Wh/kg. The company's 2025 annual report shows R&D spending of 22.147 billion yuan — a 19.02% annual jump — with the solid-state R&D team swelling to over 1,000 people. Even so, Chairman Zeng Yuqun struck a cautious note at the Summer Davos Forum. If technology maturity is scored on a 1-to-9 scale, he said, solid-state batteries are currently only at level 4. Commercialization still faces steep engineering and cost hurdles. CATL isn't alone in eyeing 2027. Samsung SDI has pegged its mass-production target for the second half of that year, while Toyota's sulfide-route preparations point to the same window. BYD, for its part, has explicitly targeted 2027 for small-scale output. With top players from China, Japan, and South Korea converging on the same rollout timeline, the engineering race for next-generation battery technology has entered a critical phase.

artigo.texto: Estonian renewable energy developer Sunly has commissioned a 21 MW/48 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at its Raba hybrid park in Põhja-Pärnumaa, Estonia. The facility complements a 45 MW solar plant completed in 2024, generating approximately 47 GWh annually, equivalent to 13,000 households' consumption. Connected to Elering's 110 kV network, the battery stores daytime solar electricity for evening supply. Developed with Metsagrupp OÜ and financed by Luminor Bank, the project underwent network testing by Smartecon. Sunly is also developing an 8 MW/20 MWh battery facility at Nurme, scheduled for completion in November, further expanding its Estonian storage portfolio. artigo.texto: Estimated read time: 5-6 minutes - A study by EmPower Analytics estimates Stratos data center emissions could cause 45 deaths annually. - Kevin O'Leary's team disputes the study, stating it uses unselected equipment assumptions. - The study highlights potential health costs and pollution impacts across northern Utah and beyond. SALT LAKE CITY — A new analysis of the proposed Stratos data center campus in Box Elder County estimates its emissions could contribute to as many as 45 premature deaths annually and hundreds of millions of dollars in health-related costs, but a representative for celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary and the project reject the study's conclusions. The report, released this week by EmPower Analytics Group, examines potential air quality impacts from the artificial intelligence-focused data center campus. Researchers said they wanted to evaluate possible public health consequences before major decisions about the facility are made. "The Stratos data center, if completed, would be one of the largest data center complexes in the world and one of the largest to be powered fully by methane gas," said Dr. Michael Cork, CEO and founder of EmPower Analytics Group. The analysis estimates emissions from the project could lead to between five and 45 additional premature deaths per year, along with illness, such as increased asthma cases, hospital admissions and heart attacks. Researchers also projected annual health-related costs ranging up to $690 million. Dr. Logan Mitchell, a climate scientist with Utah Clean Energy who partnered with the Natural Resource Defense Council, which commissioned the report, said the research found impacts would extend well beyond Box Elder County. "One of the things that really stood out to me is how far this pollution would travel," Mitchell said. "It's going to affect all of northern Utah and actually into Idaho and Wyoming and Colorado and states even further afield." He said the study found there would be more pollution in the air than normal. He pointed to winter months when inversion traps the pollutants in our valleys. "After we've done all of this work to reduce our pollution, it's really taking us several steps backwards," Mitchell said. Related: Mitchell defended the inputs and methods used in the report. "The tools that they use to produce this are really robust atmospheric modeling tools," he said. "They're really widely used." The study is not peer-reviewed, but Cork said it draws on peer-reviewed science. "Multiple reviewers examined our scientific assumptions," he said. "Decisions on this facility are being made now. So we've documented our methods and assumptions in the technical appendix and welcome scrutiny and feedback." Cork said the report modeled two plausible power-generation scenarios for the facility, based on technology being used in other data centers. "The lower emitting scenario is using it as a modern combined cycle gas plant, which is how many large power plants are built in the United States," he said. "The other is these gas engines, which in the report we call RICE engines, and these engines have been used to power facilities such as the Joule Partners data Center in Utah and represent a higher emitting scenario of how you might power a data center with methane gas." Stratos has not publicly specified how it plans to power the campus. "They're not necessarily the only two options," Cork said in response. "And in fact, it could be a combination of both. But they represent really plausible and realistic options of how you might power a data center the size of Stratos." Cork also said the estimates could change once more information about the project is released. "We evaluated this project (at) a three gigawatt and nine gigawatt scenario," he said. "Newer water applications now describe 7.5 GW. Holding the other assumptions fixed, that would reduce our estimates by roughly 17%." Stratos representatives strongly disputed the findings. Spokesperson Paul Palandjian sent this response to KSL. "Protecting public health and air quality is a core responsibility in developing Stratos, and everything we build will meet state and federal air-quality standards. That is not optional. The report models scenarios built on assumptions about generating equipment that Stratos has not selected, and its authors acknowledge that the scenarios are not predictions of what will be built. Its higher-impact scenario scales the permitted emissions of a different Utah facility, including that facility's diesel backup generators, which is not our design. Presenting those estimates as established health outcomes from Stratos overstates what the analysis shows. On electricity: Stratos generates its own power on site, behind the meter. It adds no load to the Utah grid and no cost to Utah ratepayers, so comparing it to statewide grid demand conflates two different things. Full build-out is phased, and as the project grows we will evaluate renewable sources as part of the generation mix. On the current plan: the generation design uses turbines for primary power and reciprocating engines for backup and bridging, with emissions reduction and heat capture engineered in from the start. Specific equipment models have not been selected. The plant will be permitted under Utah and federal rules, including best available control technology for new gas-fired generation, which for modern plants means heat capture, low-NOx combustion, selective catalytic reduction, oxidation catalysts and continuous emissions monitoring. Air permitting requires dispersion modeling of the actual equipment, and that modeling will be made public. We will continue to evaluate lower-emission options as the design advances. We take the concerns raised seriously. But publishing modeled assumptions as if they were Stratos's confirmed health impacts is irresponsible, and it fuels alarm the analysis doesn't support based on assumptions that are simply not true of Stratos." artigo.texto: Key points: Gotion’s Solid-State Roadmap: Materials, Cells, and Validation in Parallel - Materials: Watch Anqing’s 300-ton lithium sulfide pilot line for scale-up data and cost reductions (from RMB 1.3M/t toward RMB 500k/t). - Cells & Validation: While G-Yuan’s 12 GWh capacity is built, actual deliveries await customer on-vehicle testing. The Jinshi 2 GWh line is delayed, lacking formal equipment tendering. - Timeline: 2026 focuses on engineering and sample delivery, with volume installation likely pushed to 2027. The most important thing to watch in Gotion’s current solid-state layout is not any single energy-density figure, but the fact that it has compressed materials (lithium sulfide + sulfide electrolytes), cells (semi-solid batteries + solid-state batteries) and customer validation onto roughly the same timetable. Many Chinese battery makers are working on solid-state technology, but Gotion is the most advanced in being willing to enter lithium sulfide—an expensive and hard-to-handle segment—itself, with capacity planning directly pushed to the 10,000-ton scale. Another company that makes both ternary and LFP cathode materials is rumored to have a 10,000-ton electrolyte layout, but it has not reached the level of public confirmation, so I will not elaborate here. The timeline is roughly as follows: in 2026, 300 tons of lithium sulfide and 2,000 tons of electrolyte will be in place, and the Anqing 10,000-ton project will complete pilot testing by year-end; G-Yuan’s 12 GWh capacity will be completed and ready for mass production, with batch deliveries to start within the year; the Jinshi 2 GWh line will complete design and enter construction, while the 0.2 GWh pilot line continues on-vehicle road testing. In 2027, 20,000 tons of lithium sulfide and 10,000 tons of electrolyte will enter scale-up, and the Anqing project will be in full mass production; Jinshi will begin small-batch on-vehicle testing. In 2030, lithium sulfide capacity will reach 50,000 tons and electrolyte capacity 100,000 tons, corresponding to demand at the 150 GWh and 100 GWh levels; Jinshi will enter full mass production, with a cost target of RMB 1/Wh. Many Chinese battery makers are working on solid-state technology, but Gotion is the most advanced in being willing to enter lithium sulfide—the most “dangerous” and most expensive segment—itself, with capacity planning directly pulled to the 10,000-ton scale. There is also a rumor that another company making both ternary and LFP cathode materials has a 10,000-ton electrolyte layout. Gotion has placed its solid-state battery layout entirely in Anhui. Anhui is also home to Changxin Technology, which became a leader immediately after listing; Gotion previously invested heavily in LMFP batteries, but the results fell short of expectations. This article attempts to analyze whether Gotion can also achieve a “become king upon listing” position in the solid-state battery sector. I. Lithium Sulfide: A Formidable Player in Gotion’s Solid-State Battery Game Why lithium sulfide cannot be avoided: Gotion itself lays out the arithmetic bluntly—in the cost of sulfide solid-state batteries, solid electrolytes account for 70%–80%, and within electrolyte costs, another 70%–80% is concentrated in lithium sulfide. In other words, the price curve of lithium sulfide essentially sets the opening and closing rhythm of the commercialization window for all-solid-state batteries. According to SMM data, as of October 2026, the market price of battery-grade lithium sulfide was still around RMB 1.3 million/t, while Gotion’s target cost is RMB 500,000/t; the corresponding target at the electrolyte end is RMB 300,000/t. Only when both numbers are achieved can cell material costs be expected to approach RMB 1/Wh. This gap cannot be papered over by process optimization; it must be closed through scale. SMM predicts that the RMB 1/Wh threshold will emerge around 2031. 1.1 Gotion’s lithium sulfide pace is being laid out quickly: the 300-ton pilot line is in the equipment selection and procurement stage (as of the end of October 2026). The 300 t/y lithium sulfide pilot line to be located in Anqing in 2026 is led by Qianyuan Technology under Gotion Holdings, with total investment of RMB 620 million. It is planned to complete pilot-line construction by year-end and conduct three years of full-process testing. The core task is to validate process parameters for a 10,000-ton line. The 10,000-ton high-purity lithium sulfide mass-production line, launched on July 21, 2026, is also located in Anqing and is planned to be fully completed in 2027. On the capacity ladder: 300 tons in 2026, 20,000 tons in 2027 and 50,000 tons in 2030, corresponding to solid-state battery demand at the 150 GWh level (according to SMM estimates, for each GWh of 60 Ah sulfide solid-state batteries, sulfide electrolyte unit consumption is 0.7 t; within LPSC651 sulfide electrolyte, lithium sulfide unit consumption is 0.4; each GWh of solid-state battery consumes 280 kg of lithium sulfide). 1.2 Lithium sulfide process: gas–liquid–solid three-phase reaction method On process, Gotion is betting on the “gas–liquid–solid three-phase reaction method,” claiming a 3x improvement in reaction efficiency and a 40% reduction in energy consumption, with pilot products at 99.99% purity and particle size below 3 μm. SMM believes that if this route can maintain batch consistency and continuous operation stability under inert atmosphere during pilot-scale amplification, the 20,000-ton plan for 2027 will have a basis for implementation; but if scale-up effects emerge during pilot testing, the commissioning node for the 10,000-ton line will be passively pushed back, which would directly constrain the installation pace of Jinshi batteries in 2027–2028. 4N purity is not so easy to achieve. artigo.texto: Oro Valley is prepared to adopt zoning code amendments regulating data centers, to include a prohibition of all “large-scale” data centers using 20MW of power or more. If adopted, Oro Valley “will be the only jurisdiction” among 13 researched in Arizona “to prohibit large-scale data centers,” according to a staff report from Bayer Vella, Oro Valley’s town planner. The language was scheduled to go before the Oro Valley Planning and Zoning Commission on Tuesday, Oct. 27. The Oro Valley Town Council scheduled a special meeting and public hearing to consider regulatory code language Wednesday, Oct. 28, at 6 p.m. on the town campus. Vice Mayor and Mayor-elect Melanie Barrett initiated the discussion at the end of council’s Oct. 7 meeting. She realized “there could potentially be loopholes” in Oro Valley’s zoning code “that would allow for data centers in multiple zoning districts, and there were people potentially interested in moving forward with those. “I want to act as expeditiously as possible to eliminate that,” Barrett said that evening. She requested a code amendment “making clear data centers are not allowed by right in any zoning district in Oro Valley.” Further, Barrett asked that new code language address the issues of noise, water, energy and other concerns associated with data centers. And, while new code is being considered, “to the degree possible, there shall be a moratorium” on any data centers, she said. Currently, data centers could be developed on properties within Oro Valley’s Commercial and Technical Park zoning districts. Technical Park zoning applies within Oro Valley’s Innovation Park, as well as on lands on either side of the Honeywell complex immediately east of Oracle Road. Commercial zones that would be affected by new code language are primarily along Oracle Road, near Tangerine and Rancho Vistoso, and along La Cholla and La Canada south of Naranja. Code now considers data centers as a “technical services” use. “However, large-scale data centers that require significant amounts of power and water to support modern technologies and AI (artificial intelligence) were not the intended use for technical services,” Vella writes. Draft language would allow “ancillary data centers with limitations” in those zones, according to the staff report. Ancillary data centers are defined as “generally server rooms commonly used by major employers,” such as Roche Tissue Diagnostics, or the town itself. They “must be housed within an existing building on the site,” Vella writes. Oro Valley has not received a request to build a large-scale data center, he continues. “However, there are potential sites” that could accommodate one, Vella’s report said. “It is critical to have standards in place to evaluate data centers” in zones where they could be developed. The code amendment would require a council-approved conditional use permit for any proposed data center. Staff researched data centers and reviewed the zoning codes from 13 Arizona jurisdictions “to identify the necessary review tools” for Oro Valley consideration. It determined energy and water use are “critical areas to regulate.” Large-scale data centers require a minimum of 40 megawatts of electric power. One megawatt hour of energy can power approximately 1,000 average homes, or one grocery store, according to the staff report. Tucson and Pima County classify large-scale data centers as those using a minimum of 20 megawatts. Along with its prohibition of all data centers using 20 megawatts or more of power, Oro Valley’s proposed code amendment would require applicants to report estimated energy needs at the time of application submittal, and to do so annually for five years after a certificate of occupancy is issued by the town. Data center water use “is difficult to ascertain because neither data centers nor water providers disclose this information,” the report said. “Consumption is reportedly extreme,” with some media reports suggesting data centers use millions of gallons of water per day. As proposed, Oro Valley would require data center applicants to submit a water use and conservation plan, disclosing the amount of water they would need, and what type of cooling system they would use. Oro Valley Water Utility Director Peter Abraham has recommended the town initiate a code amendment to regulate “large water users,” to include any data centers, as well as manufacturers of microchips, solar panels, and batteries, which also use large volumes of water. Lastly, the code amendment includes parameters to address noise, location, design, and parking issues associated with data centers. “The industry is evolving at a rapid pace,” Vella concludes. “The town should re-evaluate and update these parameters as needed or in five years.” The Town Council’s special meeting and public hearing on the subject is set for 6 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28, in council chambers, 11000 N. La Canada.

artigo.texto: News Release: NLR Joins New DOE Consortium To Advance Battery Manufacturing and Strengthen US Competitiveness Battery Manufacturing Accelerator Will Integrate Super Intelligence and Automation With Manufacturing To Bring Energy Storage Innovations From Lab to Market The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) is joining the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator (BattMan) consortium, a national collaboration to address critical manufacturing barriers impeding the scale-up and market deployment of new battery technologies. The BattMan consortium will focus on lowering manufacturing costs, shortening development timelines, and establishing U.S. manufacturing leadership in advanced energy storage solutions for the electric grid, digital infrastructure, electric mobility, and national security. BattMan will also support critical mineral supply chains by helping make new battery designs using abundant domestic materials a reality. BattMan is led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and includes Argonne National Laboratory and Oak Ridge National Laboratory as well as founding university partners including the University of Washington, Binghamton University, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and University of Michigan-Dearborn. The consortium will also work closely with domestic companies across the battery and materials sector to test and validate manufacturing processes for commercially viable production. “Alignment across battery manufacturing processes is critical to boost U.S. competitiveness and bring energy storage innovations to market,” said Donal Finegan, an NLR senior scientist. “Our researchers bring extensive experience in material qualification, advanced characterization, and electrode design to support the integrated approach of the BattMan consortium.” In the near term, BattMan will implement high-throughput experimentation, automated synthesis and characterization, and digital manufacturing tools with the goal of improving data quality, reproducibility, and process consistency across partner institutions. Ultimately, the consortium aims to develop self-optimizing manufacturing systems using real-time data, automated feedback, and digital twin models that link virtual and real systems to identify opportunities to improve performance. Accelerating Materials Qualification for Better-Performing Batteries Before new battery materials can be used in commercial applications, they must undergo an extensive and time-consuming qualification process to ensure the final product performs consistently and safely across a full range of complex operational environments. “Small changes in material behavior can have big system-level consequences,” said Katie Harrison, NLR battery materials group manager. “Our work uses physics-based insights to gain a better understanding of how the physical properties of electrode materials relate to cell performance in the field. Improved diagnostic processes can reveal failure pathways early and increase the speed from discovery to production.” NLR researchers will establish physics-based machine learning models to analyze how specific defects and heterogeneities might impact cell performance years into the future, generating reliable data earlier in the development cycle. In addition, NLR will help guide validation workflows and metrics to quantify and record data to measure uniformity during manufacturing quality control. These materials qualification improvements could help give industry the confidence needed to adopt new materials and manufacturing processes, reducing risk and accelerating the introduction of battery innovations that improve energy density, lifetime, or cost. Leveraging Super Intelligence To Improve Quality Control and Characterization The highest-performing battery designs are carefully engineered, from atomic-scale chemistry to electrode manufacturing, coating, and assembly. Microscale batch variations in particle size, porosity, binder distribution, or interface morphology can dramatically affect battery behavior. Unfortunately, manufacturers lack the capabilities needed to measure critical defects effectively at the micrometer and sub-micrometer scale. This limits their ability to scale production and ensure consistent output. By pairing super intelligence with advanced imaging and characterization techniques, NLR could turn microscale measurements into statistically representative insights that apply to entire batches of manufactured material. This means manufacturers could use NLR findings to assess the quality of their final products, without specialized equipment. “Our work will focus on developing accessible, low-cost, high-throughput techniques and processes that unlock key information about the performance of manufactured materials, enabling both in-line and off-line quality control checks,” Finegan said. “These capabilities could help manufacturers improve quantitative insights to catch material defects and optimize processes.” Digital Cell Design and Smart Manufacturing Advanced computing techniques, such as digital cell design and “smart” manufacturing, have the potential to significantly alter modern battery manufacturing processes by evaluating how different electrode architecture decisions might affect cell performance before building a prototype. NLR’s long history in battery electrode design and multiphysics modeling will bring necessary expertise to help guide the consortium toward proven solutions. “Modeling is key to achieving first-time-right manufacturing, where we can digitally evaluate a wide range of battery electrode architectures faster and more efficiently,” said Andrew Colcasure, an NLR senior scientist. “NLR models could start with the ideal operational profile based and work backwards to help design electrode particle shaping, size distributions, and coating conditions.” Supported by DOE’s Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office in the Cri
