artigo.texto: ______________ OPINION By Denis Tukahikaho PhD|CLE| Far fewer flights could face delays or cancellations as the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) accelerates the global implementation of Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) — a move that could also reduce unnecessary fuel burn and aviation emissions. The push comes as the international aviation sector faces growing pressure to improve operational efficiency while cutting carbon emissions and, at the same time, a separate policy dispute is emerging over how those emissions should be regulated and offset. With ICAO's global Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) increasingly coming into tension with the European Union's Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), the recent airspace closures and severe weather events have highlighted the vulnerability of air services to disruption, and meanwhile, the introduction of new aviation technologies is adding to the complexity of flight operations. With global air traffic expected to continue growing, ICAO is accelerating ATFM as a comprehensive international approach to improving the efficiency, reliability and resilience of the aviation system. ATFM combines air navigation technologies with new operational procedures to improve the predictability of air services while reducing unnecessary fuel consumption and emissions. Under the system, airlines, airports and air navigation service providers can coordinate flights and operational constraints across national borders before aircraft take off. The objective is to match traffic demand with available airspace and airport capacity while reducing unnecessary holding, congestion and inefficient flight paths. One of the key procedures is Airport Collaborative Decision Making (A-CDM), which shall enable airlines, airports and air traffic controllers to exchange real-time information and coordinate decisions on when and how aircraft depart and arrive. The approach can improve the reliability and efficiency of flight operations. The concept of Total Airport Management extends this coordination across a wider range of airport activities, including baggage handling, aircraft refuelling and passenger movements. ATFM is also intended to make better use of available airspace. The gradual adoption of free route airspace will allow pilots to select more direct and efficient flight paths rather than being restricted to pre-established routes. Under the ATFM principle of flexible use of airspace, portions of controlled airspace can also be dynamically allocated according to traffic requirements, allowing available capacity to be used more efficiently. The Aviation operational reforms are significant because aviation's climate challenge is not limited to the carbon credits and emissions allowances used by regulatory systems, but cutting unnecessary flight time, efficient routing and de-congestion can reduce fuel consumption at source. But even as ICAO promotes operational measures to make flying more efficient, the organisation is facing a growing disagreement with the European Union over the regulatory treatment of aviation emissions. As we all know, ICAO's CORSIA is the global market-based measure established specifically to address CO₂ emissions from international aviation, and under CORSIA, qualifying airlines meet offsetting requirements by cancelling emission units that have been approved under ICAO's eligibility framework. But still, ICAO maintains a specific process for determining which emissions-unit programmes can supply credits for CORSIA, and the system has been designed to address issues including environmental integrity, eligibility and the avoidance of double counting. The European Union, however, operates the EU ETS, which places a carbon cost on covered aviation emissions through the European carbon market, and the EU currently applies stronger measures to intra-European flights and incorporates CORSIA for certain extra-European routes. In July, ICAO publicly expressed concern about a European Commission proposal to expand the geographical scope of the EU ETS for aviation from 2029, and ICAO urged that the proposed expansion could undermine CORSIA as the globally harmonised market-based measure for international aviation and could result in duplicative measures. As the European Commission takes a different approach, its current framework provides for a review of CORSIA in 2026 to assess whether the global scheme is sufficiently effective and adequately aligned with the goals of the Paris Agreement and, depending on the outcome, the Commission proposed extending the EU ETS to additional departing flights. This creates a significant policy question for international aviation: should airlines operating across borders primarily comply with one globally harmonised carbon mechanism, or should regional systems such as the EU ETS impose additional requirements where governments believe the global system does not go far enough? CORSIA relies on a defined pool of ICAO-eligible emissions units rather than allowing airlines to use any carbon credit available in the voluntary carbon market. ICAO evaluates emissions-unit programs against specific eligibility criteria before they can supply credits for CORSIA. For the 2024–2026 first phase, ICAO approved eight emissions-unit programs while four programs have been approved for the 2027–2029 second phase. ICAO also requires attention to host-country authorisation and the avoidance of double claiming in relevant circumstances, but the EU's rules similarly place conditions on the use of credits under CORSIA, including requirements related to participation in the Paris Agreement and CORSIA’s safeguards against double counting. artigo.texto: Have CATL's fundamentals changed? CATL has found itself in a rather delicate situation recently. Recently, CATL released its 2026 Q3 financial report, with both revenue and profit continuing to grow. In the first three quarters of this year, its daily net profit exceeded 230 million yuan, showing an astonishing cash absorption capacity. However, the day after the financial report was released, CATL's intraday drop once exceeded 10%. Prior to that, its stock price had fallen for consecutive months, dropping from the historical intraday high of 467.35 yuan in May to 227.9 yuan as of the writing date, which was almost cut in half. The biggest concern of the market is the "de-CATL trend". Automakers hope to reduce their dependence on CATL, and second-tier battery manufacturers hope to seize more orders. Since September, a number of new energy vehicle makers including Li Auto, XPeng, Xiaomi and Leapmotor have officially announced their self-developed battery progress one after another, and reached closer cooperation with second-tier battery manufacturers such as CALB, Sunwoda and Honeycomb Energy. CATL still leads the industry, but the market is worried about its future and has begun to vote with its feet. When the era dividend of power batteries fades away, where will CATL's next "era" start? 01 Warning lights on performance In the third quarter, CATL delivered a mixed report card. The good news is that CATL's revenue scale is still incredibly strong. In the first three quarters of 2026, CATL achieved a revenue of 442.137 billion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 56.19%; the net profit attributable to shareholders reached 64.53 billion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 31.6%. Among them, the revenue in the third quarter reached 165.221 billion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 58.58%, hitting a record high; the net profit attributable to shareholders was 21.246 billion yuan, a year-on-year increase of 14.54%. The concern is that while CATL's revenue is rising, its profit has not kept pace. From the first to the third quarter of this year, CATL's single-quarter revenue growth rates were 52.46%, 56.9% and 58.58% respectively; however, its net profit growth rate kept sliding, reaching 48.55%, 36.4% and 14.54% respectively. The scissors gap between the company's revenue and profit growth rate has expanded from less than 4 percentage points in the first quarter to more than 44 percentage points in the third quarter. The company's comprehensive gross profit margin also dropped all the way from 24.82% in the first quarter to 20.69% in the third quarter, and the pressure on the cost side is clearly visible. Policy changes are the most direct influencing factor. Starting from September 1, 2026, the consumption tax on lithium batteries has been levied, with a current tax rate of 2%, and it will be levied at 4% from September 2027; the export tax rebate for batteries has been reduced from 9% to 6% since April 1, 2026, and will be completely cancelled from January 2027. However, the current automobile price war has reached a white-hot stage. According to data from the China Automobile Dealers Association, from January to August this year, the revenue of the automobile industry was 7.0062 trillion yuan, with a year-on-year increase of only 2.9%, while the profit dropped by 16% year-on-year. Against this background, it is difficult for CATL to fully pass on this part of the tax cost to downstream automakers, and it may even encounter reverse price pressure from automakers on battery costs due to profit contraction. External pressure is also reshaping CATL's product structure. The domestic automobile market is under pressure, and the energy storage business has become the main incremental driver. CATL disclosed that the total sales of power and energy storage batteries in the third quarter exceeded 260 GWh, with energy storage accounting for about a quarter, and the sales growth rate was close to 60%, far higher than that of power batteries. However, although the gross profit margin of CATL's energy storage business is slightly higher than that of power batteries, it is a business with low unit price, long service cycle and low profit elasticity. In the long run, its marginal contribution to profit is far lower than that of power batteries of the same volume. The sharp drop in lithium carbonate prices is also impacting the selling price of power batteries. Since May this year, the spot price of lithium carbonate has dropped by more than 40% cumulatively, and the battery cost has decreased. However, the drop in lithium price has led to a reduction in battery selling price, and the profit difference may not remain in the company's accounts, and may even reduce customers' stocking expectation in the fourth quarter. In addition, CATL is also actively "increasing costs". In the third quarter, in response to industry initiatives, the company voluntarily shortened the upstream account period and increased prepayments, resulting in a 47.78% year-on-year increase in accounts receivable compared with the beginning of the year, and the inventory reached a record high of 144.77 billion yuan. Under internal and external pressures, although CATL sold more batteries, it barely made more money. In response, CATL said that it is mainly affected by short-term product changes and tax policies, and does not represent the long-term direction. However, the capital market may not hold the same view. 02 The truth of the "de-CATL trend" As early as a few months ago, the capital market had already cast a "bearish vote" on CATL — "de-CATL" has changed from a slogan to a collective action of some brands. In 2022, Zeng Qinghong, Chairman of GAC Group, said "I am working for CATL", which uncovered the undercurrent between automakers and CATL: power batteries account for 40%-60% of the total vehicle cost. artigo.texto: 36Kr Exclusive | The "shovel seller" in the solid-state battery industry has secured investments from Hongrong Capital, Matrix Partners China and other institutions, and has completed deliveries of dozens of tons. Source / Enterprise This article contains approximately 3500 words, with an estimated reading time of 9 minutes Author | Ou Xue Editor | Yuan Silai Hard Krypton learned that Sichuan All-Solid New Materials Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Sichuan All-Solid"), a manufacturer of lithium sulfide which is the key raw material for all-solid-state batteries, has completed tens of millions of yuan in Series A financing. This round of financing is led by Hongrong Capital and Mingshi Venture Capital, with follow-on investment from Tianhong Investment, Xingxiang Kechuang, and existing shareholder Inno Angel. Tuoshen Capital and Qichen Capital served as financial advisors, and Beijing Zhuohui Law Firm served as legal counsel. The funds will be mainly used for equipment upgrading and production capacity expansion of the hundred-ton-level production line, construction of the Changsha R&D center, and team building. On the eve of the industrialization of all-solid-state batteries, this startup founded in 2024 is trying to break through the top end of the lithium battery industry chain where giants gather. Lithium sulfide is not a new substance. As early as 2015, Yu Qingyan, the founder of Sichuan All-Solid, first came into contact with this material at the commission of a Japanese client. At that time, domestic all-solid-state batteries were still in the basic physical and chemical property research stage in laboratories, with very little market demand. But what Yu Qingyan valued was the early layout value of cutting-edge materials. Years of experience in market work gave him a systematic understanding of the applications and solutions of materials such as infrared optics, photovoltaics, semiconductor doping, and optical communications, and he gradually accumulated resources of early domestic scholars engaged in material R&D and electrolyte enterprises — which laid the groundwork for entering the lithium sulfide track in the future. The reason why lithium sulfide is so critical is that it is an indispensable raw material for sulfide solid electrolytes. Whether it is the Li₂S-P₂S₅ binary system, or the Li₁₀GeP₂S₁₂ and Li₆PS₅X ternary systems, lithium sulfide is the core prerequisite material. According to the calculation of the Orient Securities Research Institute, lithium sulfide accounts for as high as 60% of the cost of sulfide electrolytes. "Some people have tried to technically bypass lithium sulfide and replace it with other raw materials, but after more than ten years of verification, it is basically not feasible in academia," Huang Xiao, CTO of Sichuan All-Solid, told Hard Krypton. Different from materials such as phosphorus pentasulfide and lithium chloride that already have ten-thousand-ton-level industrial applications, lithium sulfide has almost no other industrial uses in history, and its supply chain has been missing for a long time — which just gives startups the tolerance space to build a process system from 0 to 1. At present, the preparation process route of lithium sulfide has not been completely finalized. The mainstream path in the industry mostly takes lithium hydroxide as the anchor point. To produce one kilogram of lithium sulfide, about two kilograms of lithium hydroxide are consumed, and the long-term cost is about twice the price of lithium hydroxide, which is not competitive compared with liquid battery materials. Sichuan All-Solid chose to bypass this path. The company has independently developed a variety of lithium sulfide preparation processes, among which the "one-step synthesis method" has achieved a breakthrough — solving the problem of disordered exothermic reaction, the reaction conversion rate is nearly 100%, and the energy-intensive and high fixed-asset investment purification link is eliminated. According to the company's disclosure, its mass production process has room to further reduce the cost to less than 100,000 yuan per ton in the long run. "The core reason why we choose this current technical route is to support the long-term realization of the same cost for solid-state and liquid-state all-solid-state batteries," Huang Xiao said. At present, the price of sulfide electrolyte is as high as several million yuan per ton. If the cost of lithium sulfide cannot be greatly reduced, the price competitiveness of all-solid-state batteries at the cell level will be out of the question. In terms of intellectual property rights, the company has published 10 patents, with more than ten other patents under review, and has simultaneously deployed a complete set of solutions for solid electrolyte precursor materials such as sulfides, oxides, selenides, and iodides. Among them, selenides are regarded as the next-generation potential material within the company because they do not generate gas on the positive electrode side and can significantly improve safety performance. At present, the laboratory development has been completed, and the construction of the pilot production line is nearly completed. In terms of commercial progress, Sichuan All-Solid has delivered dozens of tons of lithium sulfide so far. Its customers cover leading domestic sulfide electrolyte enterprises and some OEMs, and it has also established cooperation with overseas customers in South Korea, Japan, the United States and other countries. According to the company, the delivery volume in the first three quarters of 2026 has reached three times that of the whole of last year, and the annual revenue is expected to exceed 20 million yuan. In addition, according to statistics from Pursuit New Energy, Sichuan All-Solid ranked second among lithium sulfide suppliers in 2025. artigo.texto: Recognition covers next-generation battery material internalization and high-safety battery development Samsung SDI said Thursday it received a prime minister's commendation and a Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy minister's commendation at the sixth Battery Industry Day, observed Sunday. Battery Industry Day was established in 2021 to celebrate the achievements of South Korea's battery industry and promote its development. This year's ceremony was held Sunday afternoon at Joseon Palace Seoul Gangnam. Kim Young-ki, a researcher at Samsung SDI's research institute, received the prime minister's commendation in recognition of more than a decade of dedication to cathode material research and development and contributions to advancing the competitiveness of domestic battery material technology. Kim was honored particularly for internalizing lithium cobalt oxide material for prismatic batteries and developing lithium iron phosphate material for ESS applications. Yoo Hee-eun, group leader of the medium- and large-format business division, received the minister's commendation for leading the development of a high-safety battery that significantly reduces the risk of ignition even under physical damage, as well as a battery electrode with the industry's highest energy density — work recognized as a key contribution to securing next-generation battery technology competitiveness. The high-energy prismatic battery incorporating the record-energy-density electrode that Yoo led to development won the InterBattery 2026 Awards earlier this year, demonstrating its technological edge. "It is deeply meaningful that the achievements of our employees, who have worked tirelessly to drive technological innovation on the front lines of next-generation battery material and product development, have been recognized," a Samsung SDI official said. "We will continue to contribute to the advancement of South Korea's battery industry and the strengthening of its global competitiveness, backed by our differentiated technological capabilities." Meanwhile, Samsung SDI reported consolidated third-quarter sales of 4.69 trillion won ($3.51 billion), operating profit of 407.8 billion won and net profit for the period of 342.2 billion won. Sales rose 52.6 percent from a year earlier, while operating profit swung to a gain from a loss in the same period last year. Operating profit was roughly double the previous quarter's 203.8 billion won and the highest since the third quarter of 2023, when it reached 496 billion won. likehyo85@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: Pohang high-nickel line to convert for LFP; supply to begin early next year Companies to jointly develop next-generation materials including sodium-ion battery components Posco Future M said Friday it has signed a "future cooperation MOU" with LG Energy Solution to expand their partnership to include lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials and artificial graphite anode materials, as the two companies seek to jointly navigate the rapidly shifting electric vehicle (EV), energy storage system (ESS) and global trade environment. Under the agreement, Posco Future M is expected to supply a total of 720,000 tons of cathode and anode materials to LG Energy Solution over seven years from 2027 to 2033. The two companies plan to finalize a formal contract by year-end, with a concrete product diversification and supply roadmap for both material types. The MOU covers the supply and joint technology development of next-generation products, including LFP cathode materials, artificial graphite anode materials, ultra-high-nickel cathode materials, sodium-ion battery materials and silicon anode materials. For the nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) ternary cathode materials Posco Future M has long supplied to LG Energy Solution, the company plans to gradually increase the use of recovered metals extracted from spent batteries to improve cost competitiveness. The partnership will also extend to LFP cathode materials, demand for which is rising on the back of expanding AI data center capacity and growing sales of affordable electric vehicles. As a first step, Posco Future M will convert a high-nickel ternary cathode production line at its Pohang factory to an LFP cathode line, with full-scale supply to LG Energy Solution set to begin in early 2027. The company then plans to develop a new production process using lithium from the Posco Group's brine deposits in Argentina to supply next-generation LFP cathode materials with improved cost competitiveness and quality. Artificial graphite anode materials — which offer advantages for fast-charging performance and battery longevity — will be produced in South Korea and Vietnam for supply to LG Energy Solution. The two companies will also cooperate on technology development and supply of future battery materials, including materials for sodium-ion batteries (SIB), ultra-high-nickel cathode materials and silicon anode materials. They also agreed to jointly develop responses should global supply chain issues arise or be anticipated, such as the introduction of the US Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) requirements or the announcement of Europe's Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA). In July, Posco Group unveiled its future growth strategy, presenting a vision to build a "Triple-core" framework spanning steel as an industrial resource, lithium, cathode and anode materials, and rare earths as strategic resources, and LNG and renewable energy as energy resources — positioning the group as a national-champion supplier of core resources. Posco Future M said it will strengthen its competitiveness in the cathode and anode materials business by leveraging the group's internal value chain — including lithium brine deposits and graphite mines — to cement its standing as the Posco Group's key strategic-resource company. eyre@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: ESS orders top 60 GWh in US Production volume secured through 2028 LFP battery mass production begins in US Two additional lines to launch in first half of next year Solid-state battery samples supplied for humanoid robots Robots and aerospace targeted for 10%-plus revenue share by 2028 Samsung SDI has secured more than 60 gigawatt-hours of ESS battery orders this year, locking in enough work to run its US and Ulsan production lines at full capacity through 2028. The company is also accelerating development of solid-state batteries for humanoid robots — a next-generation growth driver — with commercialization targeted for the second half of next year after beginning performance evaluations with customers. Samsung SDI disclosed the plans Thursday during a conference call for its third-quarter earnings results. Cho Yong-hwi, executive vice president and head of Samsung SDI's ESS business team, said the company had secured more than 60 GWh in ESS orders through October, centered on the US utility-scale market. "Based on current order volume, our StarPlus Energy facility in the US and our Ulsan line have enough work to run at full capacity through 2028," Cho said, adding that the company is now focused on securing production volume for 2029 and beyond. To keep pace with growing orders, Samsung SDI is expanding its US manufacturing capacity. Earlier this month, the company began mass-producing prismatic lithium iron phosphate batteries for ESS at its StarPlus Energy factory in Indiana. Battery cells began shipping in mid-October, and completed Samsung Battery Box units are scheduled for delivery to customers starting in December, following module and battery box assembly. Cho said the company is converting and bringing online two additional lines to expand LFP production capacity next year, with a phased launch planned from the first half of next year. "Orders for the new lines have already been finalized, so we will prepare for mass production in line with the scheduled delivery timetable," Cho said. Samsung SDI also plans to use its Synergy Cells factory in the US as an ESS battery production hub. The facility, originally designed for electric vehicle battery manufacturing, is being converted to produce high-capacity LFP batteries for ESS applications. Cho said the company is working through an optimized design process to adapt the existing EV battery factory for ESS mass production, projecting a production launch between the second half of 2028 and early 2029. Production lines will then be added in stages to expand supply volume. Samsung SDI is also preparing for the gradual phase-down of the US Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit beginning in 2030. The company is negotiating supply prices that reflect the reduced subsidy with key customers, while planning to cut manufacturing costs through improvements in battery energy density and productivity. The company plans to commercialize solid-state batteries for humanoid robots in the second half of next year. Cho Han-jae, executive vice president and head of Samsung SDI's strategy and marketing division, said the company began supplying solid-state battery cell and pack samples for humanoid applications in September and that customers are currently conducting performance evaluations. "We are repeatedly refining and verifying performance to meet customer requirements, and are at the stage of finalizing product specifications for mass production next year," Cho Han-jae said. Samsung SDI is simultaneously building a supply chain for key materials including cathode materials and solid electrolytes. The company is concentrating on related technology development, anticipating that battery safety will become an increasingly important competitive factor as the humanoid market expands from industrial to household applications. Beyond humanoid robots, the company has also secured new customers in the aerospace sector. Cho Han-jae said supply volume from new businesses including humanoid robots and aerospace is expected to grow gradually from next year, forecasting that by 2028 these segments will account for more than 10 percent of revenue within the cylindrical battery business and make a meaningful contribution to overall earnings. Samsung SDI is also cultivating the battery backup unit market, driven by the proliferation of AI data centers, as a new growth pillar. The company expects the BBU market to grow at an average annual rate of about 30 percent through 2030, noting that rising power consumption in servers is increasing the importance of high-capacity, high-output batteries. In particular, Samsung SDI sees growing adoption of a "sidecar" architecture, in which BBUs previously installed inside server racks are moved to separate racks to increase capacity. In response, the company plans to broaden its product lineup with high-output cylindrical batteries and LFP cells, and to expand supply to global cloud service providers. In the EV battery market, Samsung SDI expects regional demand divergence to persist. Europe is seeing a recovery in small and affordable EV sales, supported by high fuel prices and government subsidies in major markets, while the US is expected to see continued demand softness for now as automakers adjust their electrification strategies. Samsung SDI said it plans to sustain earnings improvement in the fourth quarter, led by its ESS and small battery businesses. Oh Jae-gyun, executive vice president overseeing management support at Samsung SDI, said fourth-quarter earnings are expected to maintain a company-wide profit trend on the back of steady growth in ESS and small batteries. "ESS revenue from utility-scale applications will increase significantly with the launch of the first LFP line at SPE in the US and expanded volume from existing NCA lines, and supply of UPS units to data centers will also grow," Oh said. Proceeds from the sale of Samsung Display shares will also be used to fund investment in expanding production

MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CLOU Electronics (SZ: 002121), a global energy storage systems manufacturer and subsidiary of Midea Energy, showcased its battery energy storage portfolio at All Energy Australia 2026, held at the Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre on 28–29 October (Stand SS101). The portfolio spans utility-scale, commercial and industrial (C&I) applications. CLOU also used the exhibition to seek distribution, EPC and developer partnerships across Australia and the wider Oceania region. Australia's 2026 Integrated System Plan highlights the need for significant new storage capacity, including four-to-twelve-hour solutions to support grid reliability. The country's high adoption of rooftop solar is also creating opportunities for residential storage. Against this backdrop, CLOU drew on its experience in energy storage system development, integration and project deployment to address Australia's evolving energy needs. "Australia's energy transition represents a significant opportunity, and CLOU is here to be a reliable part of it," said Anthony Wang, Director of Product Management at CLOU. "Our portfolio spans utility-scale, C&I and residential storage, and we are ready to work closely with local partners to deliver solutions matched to the real needs of Australia's grid and energy users." Proven Technology, Global Track Record CLOU brought to All Energy Australia a global track record of more than 23 GWh in contracted and delivered energy storage systems across more than 100 countries, including over 13 GWh deployed outside China. The company holds BloombergNEF Tier 1 status in both the energy storage system and PCS/inverter manufacturing categories. Its credentials also include a DNV Technology Review Report for its flagship utility-scale system and DEKRA MTBF certification. CLOU's Aqua-C series containerised energy storage products received an AS/NZS 3000 conformity report from TÜV Rheinland during the exhibition. AS/NZS 3000, known as the Wiring Rules, sets requirements for the design, installation and verification of electrical installations in Australia and New Zealand. For project developers, owners and EPC partners, the report provides a third-party technical reference for electrical safety assessment, installation planning and project delivery. As Australia moves towards larger-scale and longer-duration energy storage, CLOU showcased an integrated portfolio covering both DC- and AC-side solutions. Its in-house capabilities span power conversion systems (PCS), battery management systems (BMS), energy management systems (EMS) and system integration. Together, these capabilities support coordination between battery systems and AC-side controls, as well as project-specific grid connection and integration requirements. A key utility-scale solution in the portfolio is the Aqua-C2.5H, a 5 MWh liquid-cooled battery energy storage system. As of September 2026, cumulative global shipments of the Aqua-C2.5H series had reached 12 GWh. CLOU's bionic liquid cooling system is designed to keep inter-cell temperature variance within 2°C, while active cell balancing helps extend cycle life and preserve capacity over time. The system is available as a standalone DC battery container or as part of an integrated AC solution combining BESS, PCS and EMS in a single pre-commissioned package. The Aqua-C3.0 complements the C2.5H with a next-generation utility-scale design featuring 587 Ah LFP cells and 6.25 MWh per unit, delivering approximately 25% more energy per footprint. CLOU also showcased the Aqua-C3.0 Ultra, a liquid-cooled energy storage system designed to combine high energy density with a lightweight form. Housed in a 13-foot enclosure, it delivers 5.154 MWh per unit and weighs less than 39 tonnes. Its compact design can help reduce shipping and logistics costs, land requirements and civil works, while simplifying on-site installation. For commercial and industrial applications, the Aqua-E261 and Aqua-X261 series provide 261 kWh per unit in a modular architecture. The systems can be deployed across a range of settings, including mining microgrids, industrial parks, commercial buildings and integrated solar-storage-charging sites. CLOU's project experience also includes deployments in challenging environments relevant to some Australian applications. In Argentina's Catamarca province, the company delivered storage solutions for lithium mining operations at an altitude of 4,100 metres. In Chile's Atacama Desert, CLOU systems operated for more than 900 days without reported faults. The Aqua-C2.5H has also undergone seismic qualification in accordance with IEEE 693 high-seismic requirements and obtained UL 9540 energy storage system safety certification. These examples offer relevant experience for utility-scale, mining and remote-site projects, where altitude, heat and limited access can present additional operating challenges. CLOU has annual BESS production capacity of 20 GWh at its Yichun facility. The company is also expanding its international manufacturing footprint in phases in Indonesia, with long-term capacity targeted at 18 GWh. About CLOU CLOU Electronics Co., Ltd. (CLOU) is a global high-tech enterprise offering equipment and solutions for smart grid and renewable energy applications. Founded in 1996, it is part of Midea Group, a Fortune Global 500 company. CLOU operates in more than 100 countries and, as of 2026, has contracted and delivered more than 23 GWh of energy storage systems. Learn more at https://www.linkedin.com/company/clou-energy/ About Midea Energy Midea Energy is the energy business division of Midea Group (Fortune Global 500, #231). artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution Asks Labs Worldwide About the Batteries of the Future - Input - 2026-10-29 07:59:16 - Updated - 2026-10-29 07:59:16 [Financial News] LG Energy Solution is stepping up efforts to secure next-generation battery technologies by partnering with universities and research institutions around the world. It is breaking down research fields into areas including materials, cells, battery management systems (BMS) and artificial intelligence (AI), and seeking technologies that can be applied in its business. The strategy is to strengthen its technological competitiveness by building on a decade of experience in industry-academia joint research. LG Energy Solution said on the 29th that it will hold its global research call, the Battery Innovation Contest (BIC) 2026. Marking its 10th anniversary this year, BIC has expanded its research topics to the broadest range yet. Launched in 2017, BIC selects outstanding research projects from universities and research institutions around the world and provides funding. LG Energy Solution researchers take part directly, supporting technology development and assessing the potential for commercialization. This year’s call covers the full spectrum of battery technology, from materials and cells to BMS and AI. Key topics include analytical technologies for diagnosing cell conditions and identifying mechanisms to improve battery safety. Notably, R&D teams from LG Energy Solution’s major business divisions directly selected topics for which they are seeking joint research. The focus has shifted beyond technology proposals traditionally centered on academia to identifying technologies needed in real-world industrial settings. An LG Energy Solution official explained, “We identify research topics in-house and make them public to invite proposals. The goal is to accelerate growth in the battery business by producing results that can be applied in actual business operations.” Over the past 10 years, BIC has supported about 50 research projects and accumulated results in technology development. Research whose feasibility has been demonstrated can be expanded into the joint research center FRL (Frontier Research Laboratory), which LG Energy Solution operates with leading universities and research institutions in Korea and abroad. Projects transitioned to FRL receive additional research funding and specialist research staff to carry out in-depth studies. Last year, a patent application was pursued through BIC for a physics-based model designed to improve BMS processing speed. In 2019, research through an FRL into long-life all-solid-state batteries that operate at room temperature was published in the prestigious journal Science. This year’s call runs from today through December 6. All universities and research institutions in Korea and abroad can participate by applying through BRIDGE, BIC’s dedicated communication platform. Applicants will be selected after a comprehensive assessment that includes technology readiness and commercialization potential. LG Energy Solution also plans to use BRIDGE to improve research project management and the efficiency of collaboration between industry and academia. The online, two-way system will enable the systematic management of research records, protect collaborative technologies and reduce unnecessary offline work. Kim Je-young, LG Energy Solution’s chief technology officer (CTO) and executive vice president, said, “I expect that industry and academia can drive innovation in the battery industry if they join forces. LG Energy Solution will continue to accelerate growth in the battery market based on its differentiated technological competitiveness.” [email protected] Kim Dong-ho Reporter

artigo.texto: Parceiro institucional: (Adobe Stock/Divulgação) Colunista Publicado em 27 de outubro de 2026 às 11h00. O avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) impulsiona a construção de datacenters. A energia elétrica é um recurso essencial para eles. A Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) projeta que o consumo global de datacenters salte de 485 terawatts-hora (TWh) em 2025 para 950 TWh em 2030, cerca de 3% da eletricidade mundial. No Brasil, o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) prevê que a carga dos datacenters cresça cerca de 10 vezes entre 2026 e 2030. Um exemplo do impacto dos datacenters na rede está em Paulínia (SP). A CloudHQ implementou um conjunto de datacenters que poderá chegar a 288 megawatts (MW) quando concluído, o equivalente à demanda de 890 mil domicílios. Segundo a IEA, os datacenters de IA podem consumir tanta eletricidade quanto fundições de alumínio, mas são mais concentrados geograficamente. Nos EUA, quase metade da capacidade está em cinco polos regionais e, só em São Paulo, concentram-se 38% da demanda existente no Brasil, conforme dados do JLL. Essa carga é quase constante ao longo do dia. Assim, garantir potência firme, no ponto certo, a toda hora, é o desafio central. Diversos países já criaram regras para integrar essas cargas. A Argentina, pela Resolução 264/2026, exige que o grande consumidor contrate geração nova e comprove potência firme; a geração própria é uma das opções. A Irlanda, desde dezembro de 2025, condiciona as maiores conexões a geração ou armazenamento despachável equivalente à capacidade do datacenter. Outros recorrem a tarifas e ao planejamento. Em Ohio, a American Electric Power passou a cobrar de datacenters acima de 25 MW ao menos 85% da capacidade contratada por até 12 anos. O Texas exige que cargas a partir de 75 MW aceitem corte remoto em emergências. Na Europa, a ENTSO-E recomenda conexões flexíveis, inclusive com geração despachável própria, e a Espanha propôs exigir 1 MW de renovável nova para cada MW de nova demanda, com cobertura horária de 80%, incentivando também baterias. Os instrumentos variam e mostram a preocupação dos países em garantir firmeza no suprimento, ou a pagar um extra por ela. Um desafio é o possível descompasso de ritmo: datacenters costumam ficar prontos bem antes da geração e da transmissão que os atendem. Isso exige informação sobre prazos e demanda, transparência sobre a capacidade da rede, como mapeamentos da capacidade de integração destas tecnologias, e alocação que priorize projetos maduros, capazes de garantir o próprio suprimento. Um exemplo é a Alemanha, que adotou ações para substituir a fila de conexão por ordem de chegada por critérios mais rígidos, como controle do terreno, status da licença, maturidade técnica, capacidade financeira e organizacional do desenvolvedor e ganhos de dividir o ponto de conexão. A demanda que motiva essas regras não é passageira. Bem dimensionada, ela pode ancorar o financiamento e contribuir para maior previsibilidade de receita à geração. Mas, se mal dimensionada, pode ser um risco ao abastecimento e à operação dos sistemas elétricos.

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution is inviting research proposals on next-generation battery technologies from universities and research institutions in South Korea and overseas. This year, the company has expanded its research topics to cover materials, battery management systems (BMS) and artificial intelligence (AI). LG Energy Solution said on Oct. 29 that it is launching the Battery Innovation Contest (BIC) 2026, its global research proposal program. Applications will be accepted from Oct. 29 through Dec. 6. BIC is an industry-academia collaboration program through which LG Energy Solution selects research projects proposed by universities and research institutions and provides funding. Company researchers also participate in the projects to evaluate technology development and commercialization potential. Launched in 2017, BIC marks its 10th anniversary this year. LG Energy Solution has expanded the scope of research topics to its broadest level yet. Key areas include battery cell condition diagnostics and investigations into mechanisms for improving safety. Research and development (R&D) teams from each business division directly selected topics based on actual business needs. Over the past decade, LG Energy Solution has supported approximately 50 research projects through BIC. Projects that demonstrate technical feasibility are expanded into joint research centers (FRLs) operated with domestic and overseas universities and research institutions, with additional funding and personnel provided. Last year, the company pursued a patent application related to improving BMS processing speed. In 2019, research findings on long-life all-solid-state batteries operating at room temperature were published in the international scientific journal Science. All universities and research institutions in South Korea and overseas are eligible to participate. Applications can be submitted through BRIDGE, the dedicated BIC platform. LG Energy Solution will select projects for funding based on criteria including technological maturity and commercialization potential.

artigo.texto: Wondering how you can get carbon credits? You’re not alone. Many do – especially after seeing just how rapidly the industry has grown. There are many reasons carbon credits are booming: increased regulation, improved standards, and accessibility are just a few. So really, if you’re interested in getting carbon credits, it’s a great time to do so. First of all, what are carbon credits exactly? Carbon credits essentially represent metric tons of carbon. Simply put, one carbon credit allows or offsets one metric ton of carbon emissions. The carbon market is where carbon credits are bought and sold. There are two kinds of carbon markets: Compliance Carbon Markets (otherwise known as Regulatory Markets) and Voluntary Carbon Markets (VCM). Compliance Carbon Markets (Regulatory Carbon Markets) Compliance markets are government regulated. The largest carbon compliance markets are in the European Union, China, Australia, and Canada. With the compliance carbon market, the government tells various industries how much carbon they can emit. It’s then up to a company within that industry to stay under their allotted carbon amount. The problem is, for some companies, staying within their permitted carbon threshold is simply not possible. This doesn’t mean that they’re not committed to reducing their carbon emissions. It just means that they can’t. Perhaps the tech to reduce or eliminate emissions isn’t available yet, or the tech to reduce or eliminate emissions isn’t accessible (it is too expensive to utilize, at least for now). It could be as simple as the electricity in their country being largely provided by fossil fuels. That’s where carbon credits come in. For example, Company A emits 150 metric tons of carbon into the atmosphere, but its government only allows it to emit 50. So, company A must do something to neutralize those extra emissions. It purchases 100 carbon credits (1 carbon credit = 1 metric ton of carbon) to offset that carbon. Companies can purchase two different types of carbon credits on the compliance carbon market: - Permits to pollute; or - Project-based reduction credits. A permit to pollute essentially says, “Hey, we went over our emissions, so we’re paying a fee for every metric ton of carbon above what we were allowed.” It’s important to note that the fees can be pretty excessive, so this isn’t necessarily a get-out-of-jail-free card. The price for permits increases annually, and the permitted amount also shrinks each year to push industries to go green. The government aims to reduce carbon emissions – not for companies to continue emitting them. So, when companies must purchase permits to pollute, it isn’t exactly favorable for them to do so. Project-based reduction credits work differently. With a project-based carbon credit, a company offsets its carbon emissions by investing in environmental projects such as forestry and conservation, improved agriculture practices, and renewable energy. Take a look at the table listed below from Offsetsguide.org to get an idea of how carbon offset projects work: One metric ton of carbon is offset from the atmosphere through environmental projects for every project-based carbon credit purchased. Therefore, these types of carbon credits are also known as carbon offsets. This allows companies to do more than just buy permits to pollute. It enables them to do something positive to negate the extra emissions into the atmosphere. In other words, they’re becoming “carbon neutral.” The good news is that project-based reduction credits aren’t just available on the compliance carbon market. Carbon offsets are the sole credit offered on the voluntary carbon market. Voluntary Carbon Market (VCM) What’s great is that when it comes to VCM, it isn’t just limited to companies in regulated areas. Individuals and NGOs across the globe can purchase offsets too. That means that offsets are available to everyday consumers. The VCM works differently because it is entirely voluntary. So, no government regulation or government mandate causes companies (or individuals) to purchase credits on the VCM. They’re simply doing so because they want to. They see the value carbon credits and offsets can bring to their organization and lives by making them carbon neutral. Here is a chart from Climate Care that maps out the different carbon credits and market types. How are carbon credits and offsets verified? While carbon credits for the compliance market are government regulated, carbon offsets for the VCM are not. That doesn’t mean that they’re not vetted – simply that they’re just verified by third parties. Critics felt this process wasn’t stringent enough in the past, but verification methods have changed. It has become far more accurate due to new regulations agreed upon at COP26, standardized across the globe. Third-party entities are non-profit organizations that ensure that customers receive what they are paying for. They measure the amount of carbon offset through an environmental project and interpret the data, giving any offset project with their seal a green light for approval. Third-party verifications include the Verified Carbon Standard (managed by Verra), the Gold Standard, the American Carbon Registry (managed by Winrock), and Climate Action Reserve. They’re committed to ensuring that offset projects are high-quality, so that those purchasing offsets aren’t throwing their money into something that isn’t real. Below are some of their standards. Let’s look at Verra for a moment since many consider them to be the premier standard. Verra has a network of auditors on hand to follow up on all Verra-approved offset programs. They oversee all operational aspects, aligning them with stringent standards as set by Verra. More importantly, these auditors are assigned to projects that align with their area of expertise. Because of this process, to date, more than 1,775 certified VCS projects have collectively reduced or removed more than 865 million tons of emissions

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI's Kim Younggi and Yoo Heeeun Receive Prime Minister's and Minister's Commendations at 'Battery Industry Day' Kim Younggi recognized for bringing cathode materials in-house and developing LFP Yoo Heeeun recognized for developing high-safety battery technology 6th Battery Industry Day ceremony held at Josun Palace in Seoul Samsung SDI said on October 29 that it received the Prime Minister's Commendation and the Minister of Trade, Industry and Energy's Commendation at the 6th Battery Industry Day in recognition of its achievements in bringing next-generation battery materials in-house and developing high-safety batteries. Kim Younggi, a professional at Samsung SDI’s research center who received the Prime Minister’s Commendation, (left), and Yoo Heeeun, group leader of Samsung SDI’s Large-Capacity Battery Business Division, who received the Minister of Trade, Industry and Energy’s Commendation, at the 6th Battery Industry Day ceremony. Samsung SDI View original image The 6th Battery Industry Day ceremony was held that afternoon at Josun Palace in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. Battery Industry Day was established in 2021 to celebrate the achievements of Korea's battery industry and promote its development. The commemorative day is November 1. Kim Younggi, a professional at Samsung SDI's research institute, received the Prime Minister's Commendation in recognition of his contribution to enhancing the competitiveness of Korea's battery materials technology through more than 10 years of dedicated research and development (R&D) on cathode materials. In particular, he contributed to securing next-generation battery materials technologies, including bringing lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) materials for prismatic batteries in-house and developing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) materials for energy storage systems (ESS). Yoo Heeeun, group leader at Samsung SDI's Large and Medium-Sized Business Division, received the Minister of Trade, Industry and Energy's Commendation for leading the development of high-safety batteries that significantly reduce the risk of ignition even when physically damaged, as well as battery electrodes that deliver high energy density. High-energy prismatic batteries incorporating electrodes whose development was led by Yoo received recognition for their technological capabilities by winning an award at the InterBattery 2026 Awards early this year. artigo.texto: DuPont Commits to 83% Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Cut by 2035 as SBTi Validates Net-Zero Plan - Near-term targets: DuPont commits to cut absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions 83% and Scope 3 emissions 63% by 2035. - Net-zero goal: The company targets net-zero value-chain emissions by 2050, with 90% absolute cuts across all three scopes. - Progress to date: By 2025, DuPont had cut combined Scope 1 and 2 emissions 76% and Scope 3 emissions 59%. DuPont said the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) has validated its net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets. The core commitment is an 83% cut in absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2035, from 2019 levels. Scope 1 and 2 cover direct emissions and purchased energy. The validation covers both near- and long-term targets, including net zero across DuPont’s value chain by 2050. DuPont also commits to cut absolute Scope 3 emissions 63% by 2035 from a 2020 base year. Scope 3 covers indirect emissions across its value chain. By 2050, it targets 90% absolute cuts in all three scopes, using the same base years. The company did not disclose the investment, delivery plan or absolute emissions volumes behind these percentages. SBTi is a corporate climate action organization that develops standards, tools and guidance for setting emissions reduction targets. Those targets are designed to match what is needed to reach net zero by 2050. DuPont said the validation shows its climate commitment while supporting customers cutting emissions in their own value chains. “SBTi validation reinforces the rigor we place on our climate commitments and the progress we’re making to reduce emissions across our operations and value chain,” said Scott Collick, Chief Sustainability Officer at DuPont. “By advancing sustainable innovation, building more resilient operations and collaborating across our value chain, we can reduce our footprint while helping our customers advance their sustainability goals.” RELATED ARTICLE: DuPont Sustainable Solutions Unveils New Brand Name: dss+ What’s New The new goals are DuPont’s second set of near-term SBTi climate targets. They follow its previous SBTi-validated 2030 emissions reduction target, which the company achieved ahead of schedule. DuPont has already moved most of the way: in 2025, combined Scope 1 and 2 emissions were 76% below 2019. Meanwhile, Scope 3 emissions were 59% below the 2020 baseline. Why It Matters SBTi validation gives DuPont externally checked targets for its next decade of emissions cuts. Based on 2025 progress, it needs 7 more percentage points on Scope 1 and 2 and 4 on Scope 3. That positions DuPont to win supply contracts with customers cutting their own value-chain emissions, if Scope 3 cuts stay on track. artigo.texto: France's Renewable Energy Syndicate (Syndicat des énergies renouvelables, SER) has presented 27 proposals to accelerate the energy transition and reduce the country's dependence on fossil fuels, addressing candidates ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The document, titled L’énergie, socle d’une France souveraine, solidaire et prospère (Energy: The Foundation of a Sovereign, Inclusive and Prosperous France), outlines a transformation of the energy system combining renewable energy deployment with storage solutions, grid modernization, electrification and targeted financing mechanisms. The association argues that France has sufficient domestic resources to expand its energy production, but warns that administrative restrictions, insufficient coordination between infrastructure projects and financial barriers could limit their development. According to SER, fossil fuels still account for approximately 60% of France's final energy consumption, while electricity represents around 27%. The organization therefore calls for a strategy that goes beyond expanding generation capacity to include the electrification and decarbonization of industry, transport and buildings. A five-year strategy to accelerate battery storage and energy flexibility One of the central proposals is to establish a five-year energy flexibility plan to identify system requirements and accelerate technologies capable of managing variations in renewable electricity generation. SER proposes new tenders for pumped-storage hydropower, the hybridization of renewable energy facilities and the deployment of standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS), alongside greater coordination between energy networks. The association also calls for a dedicated regulatory framework for batteries to facilitate their deployment and enable the electricity system to make better use of periods of abundant generation. To illustrate the potential of these technologies, the document notes that 50 GW of storage capacity with a four-hour duration would provide 200 GWh of energy per full cycle, allowing electricity generation to be shifted to periods of higher demand. This figure is presented as a technical illustration rather than an official storage deployment target for France. The proposal also includes demand-side management measures and innovation in energy storage technologies and power electronics. Preferential financing and up to €10 billion from regulated savings On financing, SER proposes that the European Central Bank (ECB) consider preferential interest rates for investments supporting the energy transition. The association argues that solar and wind projects are particularly sensitive to financing costs because of their high upfront capital requirements. The document references a study covering 28 European countries, according to which a 0.25-percentage-point increase in interest rates is associated with a 3.2% reduction in installed onshore wind capacity and a 5.3% reduction in solar photovoltaic capacity. Another proposal involves creating an energy transition fund backed by private savings, potentially supported by an allocation of €5 billion to €10 billion from regulated savings instruments. The objective would be to mobilize additional financing for clean energy technologies and investments delivering broader economic and social benefits. SER also proposes that certain public investments in the energy transition receive special budgetary treatment and be excluded from the calculation of the European Union's 3%-of-GDP public deficit ceiling. Greater support for self-consumption, PPAs and corporate participation The roadmap includes measures to accelerate self-consumption and develop local energy communities and supply arrangements, encouraging electricity generation closer to consumers. It also proposes facilitating long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) for public entities and businesses. For companies, SER suggests reductions or exemptions from certain energy-related taxes when they enter into qualifying long-term renewable electricity supply contracts. The association argues that these instruments could improve electricity cost predictability, reduce exposure to price volatility and support new industrial investment. Energy planning through 2050 and stronger grid coordination SER is also calling for a long-term energy strategy extending to 2050, coordinating electricity demand, new generation capacity, energy storage and infrastructure expansion. One of the challenges identified is insufficient alignment between energy planning, electricity grid development and land availability. To address this, the association proposes stronger territorial coordination and greater involvement of regional and local authorities in energy decisions. At the European level, SER advocates expanding energy interconnections between EU member states to improve system resilience and facilitate cross-border energy exchanges during supply disruptions or other crises. European manufacturing and stronger cybersecurity requirements for inverters Industrial policy is another major component of the 27 proposals. SER supports a "Made in Europe" industrial strategy aimed at strengthening European manufacturing of equipment and components considered strategic to the energy transition. The association argues that reducing supply chain vulnerabilities will require industrial and commercial measures that encourage domestic and European production. At the same time, SER proposes strengthening cybersecurity requirements for renewable energy facilities, particularly regarding inverters and supervisory control systems. Suggested measures include stricter standards for supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, storing certain operational data on European cloud infrastructure and ensuring that operators retain control of their installations even if their relationship with equipment suppliers is interrupted. artigo.texto: The Maryland Public Service Commission has conditionally selected two large-scale energy storage projects totaling 440 megawatts as part of the state’s effort to expand energy storage capacity. The commission estimates the combined cost of the two awards would be 6.98 cents per month for a typical Maryland residential customer. The selected projects are the 400-megawatt Chalk Point Storage Project in Aquasco and the 40-megawatt Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in Barton. Both projects would provide four hours of energy storage under proposed 15-year award terms, subject to the commission’s conditions and further approvals. The awards are part of the first round of procurement under the Next Generation Energy Act, a law enacted in 2025 to expand large-scale energy storage in Maryland. The program is designed to help energy storage developers secure financing by providing a more predictable revenue stream, even when prices in the regional electricity market change. The Next Generation Energy Act directs the commission to hold at least two rounds of applications for energy storage projects, with a combined goal of 1,600 megawatts of capacity. The first round sought proposals totaling 800 megawatts and opened Dec. 24, 2025. Five applicants submitted proposals. With help from its consultant, Power Advisory LLC, the commission reviewed the applications and determined that all five were complete and eligible for consideration. The proposals were then evaluated and ranked based on several factors, including cost effectiveness and the potential impact on customers’ electric bills. After a public hearing on July 30 and additional hearings from Aug. 4-6, the Commission determined that Chalk Point Storage Project and Jade Meadow III were the strongest proposals. The Chalk Point Storage Project would be built at the site of the existing Chalk Point power plant in Prince George’s County. The Jade Meadow III Project would combine solar power and battery storage at a reclaimed coal mine in Western Maryland. One notable entry from this round of applications was the Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project in Harford County. The commission recognized that Oystercatcher’s location could benefit the electric grid and invited the applicant to consider submitting a proposal benefit during the second round. The commission also rejected a request to increase the Chalk Point Storage Project’s proposed capacity from 400 to 535 megawatts during the first round. The larger proposal was submitted after the application period closed and had not been reviewed through the competitive process. However, the applicant can submit the expanded proposal during the second round. “These awards are an important milestone for Maryland in our efforts to meet state energy policy goals set by legislature in recent years,” Commission Chair Kumar Barve said. “While we are disappointed that these awards are below our 800-megawatt target for Round 1, our Round 2 solicitation is expected to attract many more offers due to a pool of over 40 additional energy storage projects from PJM’s Cycle 1 interconnection process.” The two selected projects must still apply to the commission for construction approval. That process will include additional public hearings and reviews of issues such as safety, the proposed locations and potential environmental effects. The commission plans to issue a request for applications for the second round by Jan. 1, 2027, as it continues working towards the state's goal of securing 1,600 megawatts of energy storage capacity.

artigo.texto: Battery Manufacturing Accelerator Will Integrate Super Intelligence and Automation With Manufacturing To Bring Energy Storage Innovations From Lab to Market Golden, CO, Oct. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) is joining the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator (BattMan) consortium, a national collaboration to address critical manufacturing barriers impeding the scale-up and market deployment of new battery technologies. The BattMan consortium will focus on lowering manufacturing costs, shortening development timelines, and establishing U.S. manufacturing leadership in advanced energy storage solutions for the electric grid, digital infrastructure, electric mobility, and national security. BattMan will also support critical mineral supply chains by helping make new battery designs using abundant domestic materials a reality. BattMan is led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and includes Argonne National Laboratory and Oak Ridge National Laboratory as well as founding university partners including the University of Washington, Binghamton University, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and University of Michigan-Dearborn. The consortium will also work closely with domestic companies across the battery and materials sector to test and validate manufacturing processes for commercially viable production. "Alignment across battery manufacturing processes is critical to boost U.S. competitiveness and bring energy storage innovations to market,” said Donal Finegan, an NLR senior scientist. "Our researchers bring extensive experience in material qualification, advanced characterization, and electrode design to support the integrated approach of the BattMan consortium.” In the near term, BattMan will implement high-throughput experimentation, automated synthesis and characterization, and digital manufacturing tools with the goal of improving data quality, reproducibility, and process consistency across partner institutions. Ultimately, the consortium aims to develop self-optimizing manufacturing systems using real-time data, automated feedback, and digital twin models that link virtual and real systems to identify opportunities to improve performance. Accelerating Materials Qualification for Better-Performing Batteries Before new battery materials can be used in commercial applications, they must undergo an extensive and time-consuming qualification process to ensure the final product performs consistently and safely across a full range of complex operational environments. "Small changes in material behavior can have big system-level consequences,” said Katie Harrison, NLR battery materials group manager. "Our work uses physics-based insights to gain a better understanding of how the physical properties of electrode materials relate to cell performance in the field. Improved diagnostic processes can reveal failure pathways early and increase the speed from discovery to production.” NLR researchers will establish physics-based machine learning models to analyze how specific defects and heterogeneities might impact cell performance years into the future, generating reliable data earlier in the development cycle. In addition, NLR will help guide validation workflows and metrics to quantify and record data to measure uniformity during manufacturing quality control. These materials qualification improvements could help give industry the confidence needed to adopt new materials and manufacturing processes, reducing risk and accelerating the introduction of battery innovations that improve energy density, lifetime, or cost. Leveraging Super Intelligence To Improve Quality Control and Characterization The highest-performing battery designs are carefully engineered, from atomic-scale chemistry to electrode manufacturing, coating, and assembly. Microscale batch variations in particle size, porosity, binder distribution, or interface morphology can dramatically affect battery behavior. Unfortunately, manufacturers lack the capabilities needed to measure critical defects effectively at the micrometer and sub-micrometer scale. This limits their ability to scale production and ensure consistent output. By pairing super intelligence with advanced imaging and characterization techniques, NLR could turn microscale measurements into statistically representative insights that apply to entire batches of manufactured material. This means manufacturers could use NLR findings to assess the quality of their final products, without specialized equipment. "Our work will focus on developing accessible, low-cost, high-throughput techniques and processes that unlock key information about the performance of manufactured materials, enabling both in-line and off-line quality control checks,” Finegan said. "These capabilities could help manufacturers improve quantitative insights to catch material defects and optimize processes.” Digital Cell Design and Smart Manufacturing Advanced computing techniques, such as digital cell design and "smart” manufacturing, have the potential to significantly alter modern battery manufacturing processes by evaluating how different electrode architecture decisions might affect cell performance before building a prototype. NLR’s long history in battery electrode design and multiphysics modeling will bring necessary expertise to help guide the consortium toward proven solutions. artigo.texto: (Reuters) — Space companies have spoken with insurers about coverage for orbital AI data centers, a sign of early progress for an experimental industry backed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. The concept of data center satellites — designed to bypass Earth’s power constraints — has drawn growing attention since Mr. Musk described them as the future of artificial intelligence development ahead of SpaceX’s record-breaking public listing this month. Securing insurance is critical for companies trying to move orbital data centers from concept to reality. Without coverage for the costly hardware and risks involved, attracting the debt financing needed to scale such ventures would be difficult. Blue Origin and a host of space startups, including Orbital, Starcloud, Lonestar Data Holdings and Cowboy Space, have also signaled their intention to launch space-based data centers. Reuters spoke to four brokers and underwriters and three space firms who said talks had taken place about orbital data center coverage, although they remain preliminary. Insurance broker Marsh said several companies have approached insurers to understand what future coverage for orbital data centers might entail, without naming the firms. “We’re already starting to see companies that are focused on data centers and companies that are focused on digital infrastructure looking to the insurance community for support,” said Patton Kline, U.S. aviation and space practice leader at Marsh. Lonestar said it recently held a briefing at Marsh’s offices for insurance marketplace Lloyd’s of London, attended by about 25 insurers. SpaceX and Blue Origin did not respond to requests for comment. Insurers already cover launch failures, satellite malfunctions, orbital debris and space weather in a global space market that collects roughly $500 million in annual premiums, according to industry executives and insurance firm Axa XL, a division of Axa SA. But while insurers have decades of experience covering satellites, they have little data on orbital AI infrastructure. “The conversations in the market are focused on whether the risk can be modeled, rather than what the premium should be,” said Kasey Roh, U.S. head of Upstage AI, which develops AI tools for insurance companies. Part of the challenge is valuing rapidly advancing AI chips, which could be vulnerable to harsh conditions in space, said Orbital CEO Euwyn Poon. David Wade, space underwriter at Atrium, said venture-capital-backed startups would have to expand before there would be a major insurance market for orbital data centers. “Until we get past that early round of financing and start seeing some of these companies expand by raising debt, I think the insurance needs are very limited at the moment.”

artigo.texto: Large letters reading "Korea Institute of Materials Science (KIMS)" stood out on a black wall. Below them, advanced materials technologies supporting carbon neutrality were introduced side by side, ranging from battery manufacturing processes to refrigerant-free cooling and hydrogen production. At the "Smart Energy Plus (SMART ENERGY PLUS·SEP) 2026" event held on the 28th at Hall B of COEX in Seoul Samsung-dong, the Korea Institute of Materials Science showcased next-generation materials technologies aimed at improving energy efficiency and reducing environmental burden. The most eye-catching was dry electrode technology to be utilized in next-generation battery manufacturing processes. Existing battery electrodes are manufactured by mixing active materials and binders with a solvent, coating them onto metal foil, and then drying them. In contrast, dry electrodes can reduce or eliminate the use of solvents, thereby lowering energy consumption and environmental burden required for the drying process. The Korea Institute of Materials Science has secured fundamental technology for dry mixing processes and is developing materials and processes necessary for electrode manufacturing together. The exhibition panel introduced the dry electrode manufacturing process, from powder mixing to kneading, sheet production, and cutting, accompanied by photos. Functional binder and composite material technologies for realizing high-energy-density batteries were also exhibited. A binder is a material that binds active materials inside the battery and maintains the structure of the electrode. The institute is developing new binders for high-performance cathodes and composite materials that improve the capacity and performance of active materials. This technology can be utilized in electric vehicles, energy storage systems (ESS), urban air mobility (UAM), and more. Cooling technology utilizing solid-state materials instead of refrigerants was also introduced. "Solid-state cooling materials and systematization technology" utilizes the property of magnetic materials whose temperature changes when a magnetic field is applied. It is a method that transfers heat by utilizing the temperature change of solid-state materials, rather than using gaseous refrigerants employed in existing cooling devices. The institute is developing manganese (Mn) and lanthanum (La)-based solid-state cooling materials to replace gadolinium (Gd), a rare earth element. The exhibition panel presented graphs measuring the magnetocaloric effect of the materials and the design structure of the cooling system. In addition to material development, it is also researching performance verification and modularization technology for application in actual cooling devices. Materials technology aimed at lowering hydrogen production costs also drew attention. The institute introduced non-precious metal catalysts and membrane electrode assembly (MEA) manufacturing processes applicable to anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEM) technology, which produces hydrogen by electrolyzing water. The institute is developing catalysts that can ensure high performance and durability while reducing the use of expensive precious metals. It is expanding its research scope from mass production of catalysts and manufacturing of large-area electrodes to the fabrication and operational evaluation of water electrolysis stacks. The exhibition panel included various catalysts, electrode prototypes, and the structure of water electrolysis devices. However, all three technologies require additional verification before commercialization. The technology readiness level (TRL) presented by the institute was 4 out of 9 stages for battery and solid-state cooling technologies, while the water electrolysis technology was marked as 4 out of 7 stages in the exhibition materials. Beyond research to enhance material performance, proving mass production feasibility, long-term durability, and economic viability compared to existing technologies is a future challenge.

artigo.texto: Feston S.E.V promoted its ORA S4 and Ener X Pro ESSs at the show, targeting C&I use cases The former employs air cooling and the latter liquid cooling for thermal regulation at the cell level The company also showcased its 10 ft containerized Giron Edge and 20 ft container-based Giron Max with a storage capacity of 2 MWh and 5 MWh, respectively India-based energy storage system (ESS) maker Feston S.E.V promoted its ORA S4 and Ener X Pro ESSs at REI 2026 for C&I applications. The ORA S4 is built around eight battery units, each rated at 16 kWh, for a total storage capacity of 128 kWh in an IP54-rated cabinet. These units use 314 Ah lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) cells. In comparison, the Ener X Pro consists of four 60.08 kWh LFP battery packs, each rated IP67 and using 314 Ah cells, for a total capacity of 241 kWh. Both products are equipped with a hybrid bidirectional power conversion system (PCS) that facilitates direct connection of PV + diesel generator (DG) + storage with the grid. The ORA S4's PCS connects a PV array of up to 65 kW via multiple built-in MPPTs. The PCS is rated for a full-load power output of 50 kW (3-phase). This ESS uses air cooling for temperature control. The company specifies a battery life of more than 6,000 cycles. Ener X Pro's 125 kW PCS, featuring eight MPPTs (each rated at 40 A DC and a voltage range of 180 to 850 V), can connect with a PV input of up to 250 kW. It can also directly connect to an external DG set. It offers more than 8,000 cycles of battery life and uses liquid cooling for thermal regulation. The company claims this cooling method can keep the cell-to-cell temperature difference within 2°C. The company also promoted its Giron Edge and Giron Max battery energy storage system (BESS) for utility-scale use cases. The Edge is housed in a 10 ft container and consists of multiple battery packs (each uses 314 Ah cells) for a total storage capacity of 2 MWh. It has a rated operating voltage (DC) of 832 V and can charge or discharge up to 6,000 times at a 0.5C rate. The container has an IP55 rating, while its built-in battery packs have IP65-rated enclosures. The Max series offers 5 MWh of storage capacity in a larger 20 ft container. It has a higher operating voltage of 1,331.2 V but has the same battery life (6,000 cycles). Both BESS models use a circulating liquid coolant to absorb the operating heat from cold plates connected beneath each battery pack. TaiyangNews has recently published its "Balance of System (BoS) Components 2026" report, featuring inverters, storage and technology trends presented at SNEC and Intersolar Europe 2026.
