artigo.texto: ADS-TEC Energy Advances One of Europe’s Largest Battery Storage Projects as Building Permit Nears NÜRTINGEN, Germany & MARKGRÖNINGEN, Germany--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 28, 2026-- ADS-TEC Energy PLC (NASDAQ: ADSE), a specialist in battery-based energy storage and fast-charging solutions, today announced that the permitting authority has confirmed that all application documents for its battery energy storage power plant at the Pulverdingen substation are complete. The building permit is expected shortly. With a planned power output of approximately 1 gigawatt (GW) and storage capacity of 4 gigawatt hours (GWh), the facility is intended to become one of the largest battery storage systems in Europe. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261028048928/en/ ADS-TEC Energy Headquarter Nuertingen Power-plant scale One gigawatt is roughly equivalent to the output of a large coal-fired or nuclear power plant, or of 250 wind turbines. The battery power plant is designed to deliver this output for approximately four hours, which corresponds to the daily electricity consumption of around 400,000 single-family homes or 800,000 apartments. Investment in a facility of this scale typically ranges from the high hundreds of millions to around EUR 1 billion. Financial significance for ADS-TEC Energy From 2029 onwards, the facility has the potential to become a long-term value driver for ADS-TEC Energy in three ways: through the proprietary battery management technology deployed in the plant, through technical services over its operating life, and through a continuing stake in the project company. According to third-party market data, large-scale battery storage systems in Germany have recently achieved revenues of approximately EUR 150,000 to 250,000 per megawatt per year from wholesale trading and balancing markets. [1] Such revenues accrue at plant level and are shared among the owners of the project company. ADS-TEC Energy’s share will depend on the outcome of the investor process, the final partnership structure and future market conditions. These figures are not a forecast and do not constitute financial guidance. A flagship project for the region and for Germany as a business location The project is a flagship from the region, for the region and far beyond. Large-scale battery storage systems are in the overriding public interest and support the implementation of the German federal government’s electricity storage strategy. “A project of this size requires staying power. I am proud that we can build in Markgröningen, and above all of our team, which has spent years preparing this project. Energy is the foundation for everything we produce in Europe. Anyone who does not control the infrastructure for it gives up part of their ability to act. With our own technology and renowned European partners, we are demonstrating that Europe can plan, build and operate critical energy infrastructure on this scale on its own. We owe the fact that a storage power plant of this size and relevance can be built in Baden-Württemberg to the local landowners, the strong local community, the public authorities and the state government, as well as to our good cooperation with the grid operator,” said Thomas Speidel, founder and CEO of ADS-TEC Energy. European partners and full technology control From the outset, ADS-TEC Energy has developed this project with strong European partners. Renowned German companies and leading corporations are ready to supply batteries, electrical switchgear, transformers and extra-high-voltage equipment. The batteries will run on ADS-TEC Energy’s proven proprietary battery management systems, whose electronics and software the company has developed and deployed in-house for more than 15 years. This reduces reliance on battery management suppliers, which are typically based in Asia, and supports local control over software, IT security and associated data. Storage as the backbone of a renewable grid Battery storage power plants do not generate electricity; they make it available when it is needed. The facility will absorb power when generation exceeds demand, for example at midday when solar output peaks or during periods of strong wind, and release it within fractions of a second when supply tightens. In day-to-day operation, it will typically run at partial load and adapt dynamically to grid requirements. It will also stabilize grid frequency, absorb load peaks and can support grid restoration after a power outage. Today, surplus wind and solar power often has to be curtailed or exported at negative prices, only for supply to fall short a few hours later, when other power plants must step in. The storage system will shift this surplus into the hours when it is needed most. The result: less strain on the grid, fewer interventions by grid operators and a more robust and affordable power supply in Baden-Württemberg. Rising demand for flexibility Wind and solar generation is inherently variable, while electricity demand continues to grow, driven by electric vehicles, heat pumps and data centers, and fluctuates significantly throughout the day. Large-scale storage bridges this gap and makes a physical contribution to the stability of the power system. This role becomes ever more critical as the economy and everyday life increasingly depend on electricity. Critical infrastructure built to last The facility is designed to operate for decades. Beyond developing and building the plant, ADS-TEC Energy will provide technical services to ensure operational reliability and availability over the long term. The power plant is to be operated primarily together with partners from the European energy sector. artigo.texto: - The companies plan to deploy Tener Sodium energy storage systems in markets including Germany, Switzerland and Austria. - The agreement marks another step in CATL's European sodium-ion storage commercialization push, following partnerships with Alfen and Solarpro. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with German energy storage solutions provider Intilion to deploy 3 GWh of sodium-ion energy storage systems in Europe over the next 5 years. The world's largest battery supplier announced the partnership on Wednesday, saying the companies would introduce its Tener Sodium energy storage systems in markets including Germany, Switzerland and Austria for grid-scale, commercial and industrial applications. The agreement builds on CATL's push into European sodium-ion storage this year and extends its existing project partnership with Intilion to a new battery technology. The companies have deployed more than 30 energy storage projects in Germany since 2022 and will promote the large-scale adoption of multiple battery technologies, including sodium-ion and lithium-ion, in Europe, CATL said. Designed for Europe's harsh winter conditions, the Tener Sodium system offers a cycle life of more than 15,000 cycles and 25 years of stable operation, while maintaining high discharge power at -20°C (-4°F), according to CATL. These features can support frequency regulation on European power grids and the long-term stability of energy storage systems, the company said. CATL unveiled Tener Sodium on June 22, describing it as the world's first field-validated sodium-ion energy storage solution. The system has a modular design that allows storage duration to be configured to suit project requirements. The system is dimensionally compatible with lithium-ion batteries. CATL previously said the design gives customers greater flexibility in choosing battery technologies and reduces their exposure to lithium price volatility. Before the latest agreement, CATL signed an MOU in July with European new energy integrator Alfen N.V. to deploy 5 GWh of sodium-ion energy storage systems in Western European countries, including the Netherlands, starting in 2027. That same month, the company signed a 2 GWh Tener Sodium energy storage cooperation agreement with Eastern European renewable energy company Solarpro, further expanding its regional partnerships. In China, CATL signed a 3-year supply agreement in April with energy storage system provider HyperStrong for 60 GWh of sodium-ion batteries for energy storage. The partnerships come as Europe's energy storage market expands rapidly. European lithium-ion energy storage battery shipments reached 72.7 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 74% year-on-year, according to South Korean market research firm SNE Research. Over the same period, CATL's global lithium-ion energy storage battery shipments rose 81% year-on-year to 125.0 GWh, giving it the leading market share of 27.1%.

artigo.texto: A estimativa para a oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO) da Anthropic, protocolado na segunda-feira (26), revelou a dimensão dos gastos da companhia com chips de inteligência artificial e data centers. A empresa, que cresce rapidamente e já desembolsou mais de US$ 19 bilhões (R$ 101,36 bilhões) em infraestrutura de IA desde sua fundação, em 2021, já assinou contratos que somam mais de US$ 500 bilhões (R$ 2,67 trilhões) para os próximos 20 anos. Esses acordos incluem contratos com grandes empresas de computação em nuvem, como Amazon, Google e Microsoft, além das fabricantes de chips AMD, Broadcom e Nvidia. Há também contratos de capacidade computacional com a SpaceX, de Elon Musk, e uma série de operadoras de “neoclouds” e data centers, entre elas CoreWeave, Fluidstack — apoiada pelo Google —, Lambda — que tem apoio da Nvidia — e Nscale. Grande parte dessas parcerias já era de conhecimento público, mas, até agora, os valores dos contratos não haviam sido divulgados. Segundo a projeção, em junho, a Anthropic tinha compromissos de aproximadamente US$ 587 bilhões (R$ 3,13 trilhões) relacionados a chips e data centers até 2045. Nos quatro meses seguintes, a criadora do Claude assinou outros US$ 266 bilhões (R$ 1,42 trilhão) em contratos novos e revisados. Há ainda US$ 20 bilhões (R$ 106,69 bilhões) em capacidade computacional prevista da AMD e outros US$ 125 bilhões a US$ 150 bilhões (R$ 666,83 bilhões a R$ 800,19 bilhões) destinados à aquisição de mais chips desenvolvidos pelo Google. Isso significa que as obrigações da empresa podem chegar a aproximadamente US$ 1 trilhão (R$ 5,33 trilhões) até 2045 — o equivalente a 3% dos US$ 31,6 trilhões (R$ 168,57 trilhões) que a gigante de consultoria PwC estima que serão investidos na expansão global da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial até 2050. A OpenAI, principal rival da Anthropic, estaria planejando destinar US$ 750 bilhões (R$ 4 trilhões) à capacidade computacional até 2030. Números altos É um salto gigantesco em comparação com o que a Anthropic gastou em sua curta história. De janeiro de 2023 a junho de 2026, a companhia desembolsou US$ 19,2 bilhões (R$ 102,42 bilhões) em capacidade computacional e infraestrutura de IA, incluindo data centers, chips, equipamentos e softwares utilizados para gerenciar essas operações. No mesmo período, a empresa registrou US$ 21,3 bilhões (R$ 113,63 bilhões) em receitas. A maior parte desse faturamento, US$ 16,3 bilhões (R$ 86,95 bilhões), foi contabilizada apenas no primeiro semestre de 2026, uma alta de 1.300% na comparação anual, enquanto as despesas com computação e infraestrutura cresceram apenas 283%. A capacidade da Anthropic de continuar construindo e pagando por esses data centers e chips depende de seu crescimento de receita acompanhar o ritmo dos investimentos. Aproximadamente 80% do faturamento da companhia no primeiro semestre do ano veio de clientes que pagam de acordo com o consumo, ou seja, conforme a utilização dos serviços da empresa. O restante teve origem em assinaturas. Com a concorrência cada vez maior da OpenAI e de uma ampla variedade de modelos de pesos abertos mais baratos, pode se tornar difícil para a Anthropic manter seu ritmo acelerado de crescimento. “O futuro deles depende da capacidade de cobrar esses preços elevados por seu modelo mais recente”, afirma Stijn van Nieuwerburgh, economista da Columbia Business School. “Sempre haverá um próximo modelo de um concorrente que fará algo um pouco melhor. Isso fará com que esse negócio seja muito mais volátil.” Outro fator que torna a situação mais complexa é o fato de vários dos maiores contratos da Anthropic terem sido firmados com seus próprios investidores. “O financiamento circular está se tornando cada vez mais relevante”, afirma Chan Ahn, CEO e fundador da plataforma de mercados privados Tessera PE. “Há muitas participações interligadas. A probabilidade de empresas como Anthropic e OpenAI quebrarem é muito pequena, mas tudo depende do fato de elas continuarem crescendo.” Ampliando os horizontes A companhia possui um contrato de US$ 114,5 bilhões (R$ 610,81 bilhões) com o Google para serviços de computação em nuvem e chips; outro de US$ 110 bilhões (R$ 586,81 bilhões) com a Amazon para computação em nuvem; e um acordo de US$ 45 bilhões (R$ 240,06 bilhões) com a Microsoft para capacidade computacional e acesso aos sistemas da Nvidia. As três empresas possuem participações na Anthropic, embora nenhuma delas apareça na tabela de capitalização apresentada no formulário S-1. O maior contrato da Anthropic é um acordo de US$ 161 bilhões (R$ 858,87 bilhões) com a Broadcom para fornecimento de chips e infraestrutura. A fabricante de semicondutores também detém US$ 42 bilhões (R$ 224,05 bilhões) em notas conversíveis que podem ser transformadas em ações da Anthropic. Segundo o S-1, a companhia espera gastar mais de US$ 20 bilhões (R$ 106,69 bilhões) em chips da AMD, que concordou, em julho, em comprar até US$ 5 bilhões (R$ 26,67 bilhões) em ações ordinárias da Anthropic. A empresa também compra memória e armazenamento da Micron, Samsung e SK hynix, todas participantes da rodada de financiamento Série H realizada em maio, que avaliou a Anthropic em US$ 965 bilhões (R$ 5,15 trilhões). O S-1 não trouxe informações sobre o tamanho exato das participações dessas companhias na empresa. Outro contrato de grandes proporções é o acordo de US$ 120,5 bilhões (R$ 642,82 bilhões) para acessar chips GPU da Nvidia por meio da SpaceX, que acumulou esses processadores. Quando a empresa de Elon Musk entregar toda a capacidade contratada, o que está previsto para dezembro, o acordo custará à Anthropic US$ 3,1 bilhões (R$ 16,54 bilhões) por mês. O contrato ainda representa uma fonte de receita para a SpaceX: nos três primeiros meses de 2027, responderia por aproximadamente 25% do faturamento projetado da companhia para o primeiro trimestre. artigo.texto: CARBON is becoming an asset. Forests, mangroves, peatlands, renewable energy, methane capture and other activities that reduce or remove greenhouse-gas emissions can generate carbon credits with growing monetary value. For Malaysia, particularly forest-rich states such as Sarawak, this presents an attractive opportunity. Protecting nature may no longer be viewed solely as an environmental responsibility; done properly, it can also generate investment, income and employment. However, as Malaysia develops its carbon market, an important question is emerging: if carbon reductions are valuable, how much should we sell to others, and how much should we retain for ourselves? The issue has gained importance following Malaysia’s move towards a more structured national carbon market. In September, the Federal Government indicated that international transfers of Malaysian carbon assets would require safeguards, including eligibility criteria and dynamic limits, to ensure carbon exports do not undermine the country’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). The principle is straightforward. Malaysia has pledged to reduce its greenhouse-gas emissions. If reductions achieved domestically are transferred abroad and counted towards another country’s climate commitments, Malaysia must ensure it retains enough reductions to meet its own target. Carbon differs from many commodities traditionally exported. When a tonne of palm oil, natural gas or manufactured goods is sold, the transaction is largely complete. A tonne of carbon dioxide reduced or removed can have a wider significance because it may contribute to national climate accounting. Under the Paris Agreement, countries report progress towards their climate commitments, while international transfers under Article 6 follow accounting rules designed to prevent the same emission reduction being claimed twice. This makes the concept of a “corresponding adjustment” important. If a Malaysian project reduces one tonne of carbon dioxide and that reduction is authorised for transfer to another country, the purchasing country may use it towards its climate target. Malaysia generally cannot then count the same tonne towards its own target. In simple terms, the same environmental achievement cannot be sold while still being treated as entirely Malaysia’s. This does not mean Malaysia should avoid international carbon markets. They can channel finance into forest conservation, peatland restoration, mangrove rehabilitation, renewable energy, methane reduction and improved land management. For communities and landowners, carbon finance can also strengthen the economic case for protecting ecosystems rather than converting them to more immediately profitable uses. Sarawak has particular reason to pay attention. Its forests, peatlands and mangroves store vast amounts of carbon while supporting biodiversity, water regulation, coastal protection and livelihoods. Carbon finance can strengthen the economic case for conservation, particularly where alternative land uses have historically offered higher returns. However, valuable carbon assets do not mean maximising sales today is necessarily strategic. As Malaysia’s climate targets become more demanding, carbon reductions may become increasingly valuable domestically. Malaysia aims to peak greenhouse-gas emissions around 2030 and achieve absolute reductions by 2035. Meeting these targets will require reductions across energy, industry, transport, waste, agriculture and land use, with some measures becoming increasingly costly or technologically challenging. This creates something similar to a carbon budget. Malaysia may be able to reduce emissions cheaply today through forest protection, methane capture or other activities, while future reductions in heavy industry or transport could be far more expensive. If inexpensive reductions are transferred internationally, Malaysia may later face higher costs to meet its own targets. A carbon credit generating revenue today could therefore carry an opportunity cost tomorrow. Decisions on carbon exports should not be based solely on the immediate market price. Malaysia must also consider the future cost of replacing the mitigation sold. For example, selling a tonne of reduction for US$10 may appear attractive if replacing it later costs US$50. Carbon policy therefore requires both environmental science and careful economic planning. Malaysia’s National Carbon Market Policy recognises this challenge, emphasising high-integrity markets, international participation, avoiding double counting and alignment with national climate objectives. Carbon trading should therefore complement, not operate separately from, national decarbonisation planning. For Sarawak and other states, carbon markets require close state-federal coordination. Land and forests largely fall under state jurisdiction, while Malaysia’s Paris Agreement commitments are national. States need incentives to develop quality projects, attract investment, protect natural assets and secure fair economic returns. Meanwhile, the Federal Government must ensure international carbon transfers comply with Malaysia’s climate obligations. Clear responsibilities can allow carbon markets to support both state development and national climate policy. Uncertainty, however, could deter investors and delay valuable projects. A successful carbon market therefore requires both levels of government to work together. Generating a carbon credit is not the same as deciding how it should be used. Not every credit needs to be exported. Some may be sold internationally, while others could support domestic companies seeking to reduce or compensate for emissions. Some mitigation outcomes may be retained for Malaysia’s own climate targets. The challenge is therefore not simply to produce as many credits as possible, but to determine where each tonne creates the greatest long-term value. This requires reliable data. artigo.texto: A first of its kind for the region, the new battery energy storage system at Darwin’s Channel Island power station presented a unique engineering challenge. But it soon proved it could provide essential grid services traditionally supplied by a gas turbine. Soon after the Channel Island Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) was commissioned, an external network event caused two of the power station’s largest generators to trip offline. The event provided a significant real-world demonstration of the capability of the first grid-forming battery in the Darwin-Katherine Interconnected System (DKIS), the Northern Territory’s largest electricity network. The battery responded to the trip immediately, injecting power to stabilise it and prevent extended blackouts. “It responded exactly as it was expected to,” Boyd Hillebrand MIEAust CPEng, Principal Electrical Engineer at Territory Generation, explained. “In response to a major system event, the battery saved the day. So that was a very good test case.” This was a particularly important outcome as the DKIS is an island network, meaning it exists and operates independently of the national electricity grid. As an island network, the DKIS must maintain system stability without support from the national electricity grid. The BESS provides a new way of supporting essential grid services. Replicating essential grid services with batteries The Channel Island BESS project, delivered by Territory Generation in partnership with principal contractor Hitachi Energy, was awarded the Northern Project of the Year at the 2026 Engineers Australia Excellence Awards. Its main engineering objective was to provide essential grid services traditionally completed by an ageing industrial gas turbine. “The brief was to make this battery provide these essential grid services as well as, or better than, the existing gas turbine,” Boyd said. The project first required extensive modelling and tuning of the battery’s capabilities. Before construction began, a significant level of effort went into the modelling of the technology and into its responses to the constantly changing needs of the network. Working with Hitachi Energy, the project team used this modelling to inform how the BESS control system was configured. The control software allows the battery to function as a virtual synchronous machine, responding in a similar way to a traditional generator to help stabilise the network when conditions change. But the way it adds power to the network is of vital importance. Because they don’t have rotating parts, batteries don’t provide physical inertia. Instead, the virtual synchronous machine imitates the stabilising behaviour of a large, spinning generator. Engineers had to optimise this inertial response, enabling the battery – which is actually a collection of 192 individual battery racks – to inject power rapidly to correct the frequency. It had to respond rapidly enough to stabilise the system without creating instability in the other generators connected to the network. This required detailed power system modelling as part of the connection process to understand how the BESS would respond under different network conditions. That same modelling enabled engineers to analyse different operating scenarios and identify relevant control settings long before the battery was ever connected to the network. Getting those settings right was critical. “If the settings weren’t properly tuned, there was a risk of introducing instability into the network,” Hillebrand said. New technology, 40-year-old network While the modelling broke new ground, integrating the battery into a power station approaching 40 years old brought new challenges. Engineers had to repurpose an existing connection point, modifying a 132 kV switchyard and its electrical protection systems. The ageing infrastructure came with its own, unique problems. “With infrastructure that has been modified and upgraded over many years, it was important to verify the existing equipment and connections against the drawings,” Hillebrand said. The engineering team painstakingly verified existing equipment and connections, collaborating closely with the substation’s owner, Power and Water Corporation. “You really need to go through an as-building process to make sure everything functions the way that you expect it to,” he said. All of this happened within a live network, as the station continued to supply electricity to the Darwin-Katherine network. Modifying the battery connection point required temporarily disconnecting one of the station’s auxiliary power supplies, leaving just a single transformer operational. “We made sure that we had backups of backups for critical station power,” Hillebrand said. Lessons for the future Commissioning confirmed the accuracy of the modelling. The subsequent unexpected generator trip demonstrated the battery’s ability to stabilise the network in place of traditional gas-fired spinning reserve capacity. Beyond its considerable fuel savings – a primary driver for the battery technology – the battery now helps manage demand peaks by avoiding unnecessary turbine starts. Territory Generation is already applying the experience to future projects. “One of our biggest learnings was that the modelling time and effort is absolutely imperative. We are focusing on making sure that we’ve got the modelling side of things well understood.” Celebrate the outstanding projects driving the construction pipeline with the Engineers Australia Excellence Awards. artigo.texto: El Pelicano solar/BESS refinanced Actis has closed on the bond financing for the El Pelicano 110MW solar and 82MW four-hour duration storage project in La Higuera, Chile. The sponsor closed a US$129.5m unregistered offering of 7.5% senior secured notes due December 31, 2044, marking the first capital markets financing of a single-asset battery storage project in Chile. BNP Paribas acted as placement agent. The bonds refinanced a bridge loan with BNP Paribas that closed in July 2026. Proceeds will also be used to fund construction of the project's battery component. The solar scheme is operational. Clifford Chance advised the project sponsor and White & Case advised lenders. Actis acquired the El Pelicano solar project from development partners SunPower and Total in 2018 and it has been operating since November 2017. The project was originally financed with a US$222m debt package advised by Credit Agricole in 2016. SMBC arranged the deal, with MUFG and Korea Development Bank contributing to the senior loan. Banco BCI provided a VAT facility. Metro de Santiago will buy the power generated by the plant under a 15-year power purchase agreement.

artigo.texto: A U-Haul decked with a makeshift sign declaring “SPRINGDALE DATA CENTER IS NOT A DONE DEAL” sat across from the borough building Wednesday as protesters in fluorescent green T-shirts began to assemble. Speakers took turns denouncing the data center plans in prepared speeches, then a spirit of improv took over. One attendee who said she had driven to the Allegheny Valley town from Pittsburgh performed a song she’d written for the occasion on a three-quarter-sized acoustic guitar. Then the crowd broke into a chorus of “we don’t need your damn pollution” to the tune of Pink Floyd. The carnival-like protest came ahead of a county-led hearing on Dynamo DC’s plans to transform a former coal-fired power plant site into a mega data center campus. With borough approval already secured in December, opponents from Springdale and beyond see Allegheny County’s land development review as their last chance to halt the project. “Make your voice be heard, our lives depend on it,” said Cathy Mager of Springdale from the parking lot podium. Inside, a couple hundred people filled the borough gymnasium for a four-hour hearing punctuated by whoops and jeers. Concerns about noise and pollution from 124 proposed diesel generations dominated public comments, while building trades representatives promoting construction jobs drew boos. The Oct. 28 meeting was the second of two public hearings led by Allegheny County Economic Development, following a virtual session on Oct. 14. Dynamo DC’s initial plan submitted to the department in September generated 97 comments from the county. Those range from pointing out a lack of detail over the intended diesel generation to questions about tree canopies and ADA compliance. An engineer representing the developer said during the meeting they have responded to all of them in a letter addressed to the county. “All of the comments you saw outlined tonight are addressed in the letter,” she said. ‘Typically a boring process’ Allegheny County’s Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (SALDO) process, required in this case because Springdale lacks its own land development ordinance, allows residents across the county to attend hearings and register comments through Nov. 30. Allegheny County’s Springdale data center timeline - June 22: Allegheny DC Propco LLC submitted its application for preliminary land development approval and related documents. - Sept. 16: The county responded with 97 comments. - Oct. 14: The county held a virtual public meeting, including an updated presentation by the developer and public comment. - Oct. 28: The county held an in-person public meeting at the Springdale Borough Municipal Building. - Nov. 30: Deadline for written public comments, which can be submitted here - January 26, 2027: Deadline for decision by county on the application The plan and the public’s comments will be reviewed by the Planning Division of Allegheny County Economic Development and its engineering and legal consultants. They’ll evaluate it all against the county’s development standards, ACED Director Lauren Connelly wrote in an email. “The use itself has been approved by the Springdale Borough,” she added. Speaking Oct. 28, Anna Skipper Jewart, a lawyer with Babst Calland representing the developer, emphasized SALDO’s limitations. “This is typically a boring process,” Jewart said. “This is a technical review.” Generators a central concern Most of the more than 40 speakers expressed concerns about the project’s potential impacts, including the noise and pollution that its 124 proposed diesel generators could produce. “I don’t need a study to tell me that living close to 124 diesel generators that will be tested once a month will not be good for my health,” said Carole Reinert, a Springdale resident who spoke at the hearing. Other speakers cited safety concerns, a decline in property values, the center’s water usage and the 97 discrepancies the county cited in the application. “I’m not against progress, but progress should never come at the expense of people’s health, homes and peace of mind,” said resident Sharon Spirk. “Data centers can be moved, but we cannot move 120 years of memory, hope and dreams from the people of Springdale.” Springdale Borough by the numbers: – 3,319 residents – 52.3 years median age (vs. 40.6 in Allegheny County) – 97% white (vs. 76% countywide) – $65,893 median household income (vs. $78,548 countywide) – 4% in poverty (vs. 11.5% countywide) – 69% of housing units owner-occupied (vs. 65% countywide) – 53% voted for Donald Trump in 2024 (vs. 39% countywide) Source: American Community Survey data analyzed by Census Reporter and Allegheny County Elections Division Jewart said the majority of the generators would only operate in emergency situations, though they will be tested on a monthly basis. Under the terms of Springdale’s approval, Jewart said, generators can only be tested during normal business hours, and they can’t be tested all at once. The goal of the testing is to “limit both the emissions as well as the sound that’s coming from it at any given time,” said Jewart. Sandy Ransom, a 72-year Springdale resident, lives around six blocks from the site. Before the hearing, she said she’s mainly concerned with the generators, which she said will produce noise and carcinogens. “Springdale has been a dying community for a long time, and there are a lot of people in town that are really trying to build it up … I would hate to see the town ruined by a data center,” she said. She’s also skeptical of the developer’s promises of jobs and tax revenue. “People are saying we’re going to get big money,” she said. “But if it affects our health, is it worth it?” A few at the meeting spoke out in favor. Several building trade union representatives touted the promise of construction jobs and the wages that would be spent in Springdale. Almost all of their testimonies were largely drowned out by jeers from the audience. “This data race needs to be won here in America.

artigo.texto: How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio Candidates work to ease concerns as data centers become hot-button issue for Ohioans Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly. MT. ORAB, Ohio — The data center mystery in this rural exurb of Cincinnati has consumed Nick Owens. The lifelong Republican and self-described small-town attorney has spent countless hours trying to figure out what's going on with 1,000 acres of farmland and trees that property records show were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025. In a few spots, the data center property runs right up against beautiful two-story homes. "This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. This is the small town charm," he says. "Living in the rural area, but getting the benefits of a nice, lovely neighborhood." Some of the most coordinated opposition to data centers anywhere in the country grew out of what happened in secrecy in this village of 4,300 people, a short drive up a country road from Owens' home. Nondisclosure agreements have stymied Owens' efforts to learn more. But along his quest, he crossed paths with another local attorney and a real estate agent who were equally alarmed. Together, they mobilized a network of volunteers in nearly all 88 counties in the state. They are Democrats, Republicans and Independents. They called themselves Conserve Ohio. "We all share the same ethos and the same passion for preserving our way of life, preserving the future of Ohio, frankly, from the hyperscale data center invasion," says Owens. "It's really beautiful." This fall, the group is behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities that would amend local charters to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers — the kind used to power artificial intelligence. It's an effort that goes beyond the temporary pauses that hundreds of municipal and county governments have embraced. "All too often you hear from the politicians, 'Well, the community should have a say,'" says Owens. "We're going to find out in ten communities whether or not the communities want them." Meanwhile, the grassroots group is working on a more ambitious undertaking: a petition for an amendment to the state constitution that would ban large-scale data centers statewide. Their goal is to put that to Ohio's voters in 2027. Data centers bring economic benefits and angst It's been more than a decade since tech companies first came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. That combination paved the way for some of the fastest data center growth in the country. Now, despite the economic benefits — considerable tax revenue, money for schools, numerous construction jobs and a smaller number of permanent jobs — no one seems to want a computing campus in their backyard, especially one shrouded in secrecy. "Should the school have extra money or the local government have extra money so we have a constant hum and ridiculous amounts of emissions and pollution?" Owens says, pointing out that hyperscale data centers will require new power plants. "Our community is not for sale." Pressed to consider whether the state should forgo all opportunities, Owens says he'd entertain the idea of putting data centers on old industrial sites, where they'd be buffered from people. "If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places," he says, while acknowledging that it'd be cheaper and easier for a developer to build on pristine farmland than on an old coal site. "I don't know if there are enough brownfield sites, but shouldn't we start with those first?" A hot-button election issue In recent months, candidates running for statewide office in Ohio have been trying to convince voters that they hear their concerns — even as they stop short of backing the kind of sweeping moratorium data center opponents are seeking. Until recently, data center projects weren't all that controversial, in part because they were smaller and weren't being built for AI. But as the issue has gained traction, it's become a hot topic in the midterms, including in the tight race to fill a U.S. Senate seat. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has cast his opponent, the incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers." Brown has been reminding voters that as lieutenant governor, Husted welcomed tech companies to Ohio and championed their data center investments. Meanwhile, Husted has accused Brown of hypocrisy, pointing to Brown's past support for data centers. Husted has also introduced his own solution, pushing a bill in Congress aimed at getting data centers to pay for power grid upgrades and other costs associated with their massive energy use. Senate Democrats have blocked the bill, calling it toothless, prompting Husted to accuse the Democrats of not caring or helping. Unconvinced that politicians will help These political gestures have not persuaded Linda Moodie, an independent who's been volunteering with Conserve Ohio. She doesn't trust that any of the candidates running for statewide office "will do the right thing" if elected, which is to give the people a say in the data center buildout. "It's really something that I think a lot of us didn't see coming, and all of a sudden there's just an influx of them," she says. Between now and election day, she's seizing every opportunity to collect signatures to get the statewide ban on the ballot next year. On a recent evening, she set up a booth at the "Halloween on the Green" celebration in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. She handed out candy to kids and clipboards with the petition to parents. Both were enthusiastically received. "The closer it hits to home, the more people that are going to want to do something," says Moodie. A estratégia prevê aproveitar o potencial de geração de energia renovável do país para atrair empresas de tecnologia, ampliar a infraestrutura de processamento de dados e reduzir a dependência de soluções estrangeiras. LEIA: Missão Rede Bee ao Vale do Silício para profissionais de TI tem data marcada; participe! Energia renovável para atrair data centers Durante o discurso, Lula destacou a capacidade energética brasileira como diferencial para receber centros de dados, estruturas fundamentais para serviços de computação em nuvem e sistemas de inteligência artificial. “Temos que aproveitar o potencial energético de um país que talvez seja o que tenha mais capacidade de energia renovável para trazer os datacenters necessários para acumular dados no Brasil.” O plano de governo prevê contrapartidas para empresas que instalarem data centers no país, incluindo capacidade computacional destinada ao mercado brasileiro. Também estabelece investimentos em supercomputadores nacionais e expansão dos serviços de nuvem. A instalação dessas estruturas deverá considerar eficiência energética, uso progressivo de fontes 100% renováveis e impactos sobre o abastecimento de água, o sistema elétrico e as comunidades locais. Governo prevê desenvolvimento de IA brasileira Outra proposta é desenvolver sistemas nacionais de inteligência artificial para diminuir a dependência de tecnologias dos Estados Unidos e da China. Para isso, o presidente defendeu ampliar o ensino de disciplinas ligadas à ciência e à tecnologia. “Queremos ensinar mais matemática, mais engenharia porque não quero ficar dependendo de inteligência artificial chinesa e americana. Quero criar uma [inteligência artificial] brasileira”, afirmou. O plano prevê modelos de linguagem em português e em outras línguas, além de uma plataforma nacional de dados para treinamento e avaliação desses sistemas. artigo.texto: The U.S. Department of Energy’s National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) has joined the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator (BattMan) consortium, a national partnership working to overcome manufacturing challenges that are slowing the large-scale production and commercial adoption of next-generation battery technologies. Led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, BattMan brings together Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and several university partners, including the University of Washington, Binghamton University, the University of Alabama, Arizona State University and the University of Michigan-Dearborn. The consortium will also collaborate with US companies across the battery and materials sectors to test and validate manufacturing processes suitable for commercial production. The initiative aims to reduce manufacturing costs, speed up development timelines and strengthen US leadership in advanced energy storage technologies. These technologies have applications across electricity grids, digital infrastructure, electric vehicles and national security. BattMan will also support domestic critical mineral supply chains by helping bring battery designs based on widely available US materials closer to market. “Alignment across battery manufacturing processes is critical to boost U.S. competitiveness and bring energy storage innovations to market,” said Donal Finegan, an NLR senior scientist. Improving Materials Qualification and Quality Control A key focus for NLR will be accelerating the qualification of new battery materials. Before reaching commercial use, materials must undergo rigorous testing to ensure they can perform safely and consistently in demanding operating environments. “Small changes in material behavior can have big system-level consequences,” said Katie Harrison, NLR battery materials group manager. Researchers plan to use physics-based machine learning models to better understand how material defects could affect battery performance over time. The work is expected to generate reliable data earlier in the development process and improve manufacturing quality control through more effective validation methods. Driving Smart Manufacturing BattMan will also deploy automated synthesis, advanced characterisation tools and digital manufacturing technologies designed to improve consistency and reproducibility across partner organisations. The consortium’s longer-term ambition is to create self-optimising manufacturing systems that use real-time data, automated feedback and digital twin models to improve production performance. “Modeling is key to achieving first-time-right manufacturing, where we can digitally evaluate a wide range of battery electrode architectures faster and more efficiently,” said Andrew Colcasure, an NLR senior scientist. Supported by the DOE’s Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office, BattMan aims to combine super intelligence, materials science and advanced manufacturing to accelerate the delivery of safer, more reliable next-generation battery technologies. Image: From left to right, Donal Finegan, Bertan Özdoğru, and Bertrand Tremolet de Villers celebrate the successful demonstration of BatMan’s novel laser-patterning process, which alters the microstructure of battery electrode materials to improve battery performance. artigo.texto: Malawi and Switzerland have approved a clean cooking project that aims to generate nearly 1.8 million carbon credits by 2030. The project will help households switch from charcoal to electric cooking, funded by the international carbon market. Climate technology company ATEC Global plans to distribute 76,000 smart electric cookstoves to homes in Lilongwe and Blantyre, two districts in Malawi. The stoves will help families reduce their use of charcoal, which contributes to climate change, forest loss, and unhealthy indoor air. The project is part of a climate agreement between Malawi and Switzerland under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. This agreement allows countries to pay for emissions cuts made in other countries and count those cuts toward their climate targets. The deal shows how carbon finance can help bring cleaner cooking technology to more households while supporting efforts to reduce emissions. How Malawi and Switzerland Will Finance Emissions Cuts Malawi and Switzerland signed a climate cooperation agreement in 2022. Under the deal, Switzerland can buy approved emissions reductions from projects in Malawi. The Swiss KliK Foundation helps fund these projects by agreeing to buy the resulting carbon credits. This money can help pay for equipment, support households, and cover project costs. Each carbon credit represents one metric tonne of greenhouse gas emissions reduced or removed. The project aims to generate nearly 1.8 million credits by 2030, but this is a target, not a number of credits already issued. Before the credits can be transferred to Switzerland, the project must meet the agreed rules and show that it has reduced emissions. The two countries must also prevent double counting. This means Malawi cannot count the same emissions cuts toward its own climate target if Switzerland also claims them. The countries use a process called a corresponding adjustment to avoid this problem. 76,000 Electric Stoves to Replace Charcoal Many households in the target areas still use charcoal as their main cooking fuel. Making charcoal can contribute to forest loss, while burning it releases greenhouse gases and smoke. ATEC plans to provide 76,000 smart induction cookstoves to households that have access to the electricity grid. These stoves use electricity to heat pots and pans instead of burning charcoal. The change could bring several benefits. Families may use less charcoal, reduce smoke inside their homes, and put less pressure on nearby forests. The stoves also have built-in meters that record electricity use and send the data to a monitoring system. This helps project managers track how often households use the stoves and estimate the emissions they save. This data is important because the project must show real results before it can claim carbon credits. The number of credits will depend on verified emissions cuts, not simply on how many stoves are distributed. Carbon Payments Could Help Families Afford Electric Cooking Buying an electric stove can be expensive for families with limited incomes. Without financial support, many households may continue using charcoal even when cleaner options are available. The project uses a system called “Cook-to-Earn” to encourage households to use their new stoves. Under the scheme, families can receive payments based on verified stove use. The KliK Foundation says payments can reach up to $50 per household. Carbon finance also helps cover project costs and make the stoves more affordable. ATEC says the project would not be financially viable without this support. The model links funding to actual use. Instead of paying only to distribute the stoves, the project also rewards households for using them. This could help the programme reach more families and keep the stoves in regular use. However, results will depend on whether households can access reliable electricity and continue using the equipment. - RELATED: Verra Approves Rwanda’s 5.69 Million Article 6 Carbon Credits, A Major Boost for Clean Cooking Project Targets Cleaner Air, Forest Protection and Jobs The project aims to deliver benefits beyond lower emissions. Replacing charcoal stoves with electric cookers can reduce smoke inside homes. This may help protect health, especially for women and children who are often more exposed to cooking smoke. ATEC estimates that the project could save women around 8 to 10 hours each month by reducing time spent on cooking tasks. It also expects the programme to create about 300 jobs in stove distribution, sales, transport, and maintenance. Using less charcoal could also help reduce pressure on forests. These are expected benefits, and the project must be carried out successfully to deliver them. Access to electricity is also essential because the programme targets households connected to the power grid. Clean Cooking Credits Face Price Pressure Clean cooking is an established part of the voluntary carbon market. By August 2025, cookstove projects had issued more than 181 million carbon credits, according to an RMI analysis. However, oversupply has weighed on prices. The Clean Cooking Alliance reported that unsold credits reached 124.4 million in 2024, while average prices fell from about $12 per credit in early 2022 to around $5 in 2024. Major buyer sectors include energy, professional services, and financial services. Prices vary by credit quality and eligibility. MSCI reported in May 2026 that cookstove credits eligible for CORSIA, the international aviation offsetting scheme, traded above $14 per tonne, compared with about $4 for the broader clean cooking market. These figures show how quality standards can influence demand and prices. artigo.texto: [PRNewswire] CATL launches ultra-high capacity energy storage system MELBOURNE, Australia Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire=YONHAP/ -- Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited [https://www.catl.com/en/] (CATL) today unveiled TENER+ in a global launch at All Energy Australia 2026, where it also showcased TENER Sodium. The company signed memorandums of understanding (MoU) with Hitachi Energy [https://www.hitachienergy.com/company/company-profile/country-and-regional-information/australia], EPEC Group [https://epecgroup.com.au/] and UNSW Sydney [https://www.unsw.edu.au/] to strengthen the delivery and grid connection of utility-scale battery projects in Australia. TENER: Engineered for long-term performance and Australia's demanding grid connection requirements CATL's TENER+ and TENER Sodium energy storage systems are designed to deliver the reliability and long-term performance Australian utility-scale energy projects need. Engineered for harsh weather conditions, they are designed to support compliance with Australia's demanding grid connection requirements and give project financiers confidence in the reliability and long-term performance that underpin battery revenues. TENER+ is a 9MWh ultra-high capacity energy storage system that helps developers to achieve a longer-term project value and to maximise the storage capacity of their project, TENER+ reduces the number of containers needed by up to 40% and the project footprint by 12%, making this ideal for projects that are facing land constraints. Its intelligent thermal management system supports a higher round-trip efficiency and lower auxiliary power consumption. Multiple TENER+ batteries can be simultaneously commissioned with a single click to streamline project deployment. Designed for a 25-year lifespan, TENER+ features liquid cooling and protection for humid and coastal environments. Noise levels remain below 65 dBA at 1 metre. Its "no heat island" top-exhaust design directs hot air vertically upwards, away from adjacent units. This prevents horizontal heat discharge and minimises thermal impact on neighbouring PCS units, allowing them to operate at full rated power even in extreme summer conditions. TENER Sodium is the world's first mass-produced, field-validated sodium-ion battery energy storage system. It delivers more than 30MWh through its modular cabinet architecture. Built for Australia's heat, it operates in temperatures of up to 55°C and delivers more than 10,000 cycles at 45°C. It delivers 95% round-trip efficiency with an operating lifespan of more than 20 years. Together, these energy storage systems give developers and asset owners a choice of lithium-ion and sodium-ion chemistries. Sodium is far more abundant and geographically widespread than lithium and it delivers an additional pathway for battery supply chains. "A battery's value is measured over the entire lifespan of a project and not just on the day it's commissioned," said Zane Zhou, General Manager of CATL Australia and New Zealand. "Developers need confidence that their batteries can handle the expected cycling to trade in the National Electricity Market and to perform throughout the lifespan of batteries installed in a utility-scale project. That is what TENER+ and TENER Sodium are designed to deliver. We're offering both sodium-ion and lithium-ion technologies to give asset owners and developers the flexibility to choose the right technology for their success." CATL's local industry partnerships to advance Australia's clean energy transition TENER energy storage systems solve the challenges the Australia's grid is facing as more renewable energy powers the grid. Renewables supplied a record 44.3% of the National Electricity Market's (NEM) generation in the September quarter of 2026. Grid-scale batteries supplied 8% of evening peak generation, overtaking gas-powered generation for the first time according to the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO [https://www.aemo.com.au/newsroom/media-release/qed-q3-2026]). As coal-fired power stations retire, the grid increasingly needs energy storage systems with grid-forming capability to provide voltage and frequency support. To help deliver more storage in Australia, CATL's three MoUs aim to address the challenges of a renewables-driven grid through Australian expertise and innovation. CATL's DC battery products and Hitachi Energy's power conversion systems will form the basis of a proposed integrated offering in Australia and the Asia Pacific region. Through this partnership, the company's aim to improve compatibility, standardise project delivery and to reduce integration risk. In Australia, CATL will collaborate with EPEC Group and the Xiamen Energy Storage Validation Research Institute (ESVL) to combine its energy storage technology, with EPEC's grid integration and engineering delivery expertise, and ESVL's full-scale system validation. The parties aim to strengthen technical validation and accelerate the delivery of reliable, bankable and grid-compliant energy storage projects in Australia. artigo.texto: The union organizations of the CITUB in the "Maritsa-East" complex insist on Bulgaria developing a unified national position for the revision of the European Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The appeal is addressed to President Iliana Yotova and Prime Minister Rumen Radev. The reason for the request is also the increase in the price of carbon quotas. According to the unions, their price has reached 88.36 euros per ton of carbon dioxide, which represents an increase of about 17.2% since the beginning of the year. According to the Confederation of Bulgarian Trade Unions (CITUB), this increase in cost is hindering the economic activity of coal-fired power plants. “We insist on the development of a unified national position of Bulgaria for the revision of the European Union Emissions Trading System“, states the union organizations in their appeal. They want a change in the mechanism for pricing quotas, as well as special mechanisms and derogations for coal-fired power plants, which they believe are necessary for energy security. As an argument, the unions point to the role of the complex for employment and livelihoods in the region. According to them, “Maritsa-East“ provides production capacity and the ability to respond to accidents, low production from renewable sources and crises in the energy markets. The use of local lignite coal, according to the assessment of the Confederation of Bulgarian Trade Unions, reduces the country's dependence on imported fuels. Unions point to a decline in the region's economy The appeal cited Eurostat data, according to which the real gross domestic product of the Southeast region decreased by 20.5% between 2019 and 2024. Over the same period, the European Union economy grew by 5.6%. The CITUB defines the difference as an indicator of the economic consequences of the transition in regions dependent on coal energy. The organization insists that the president support the achievement of a national consensus, and that the prime minister commission the development of a position with the participation of state institutions, energy companies, unions, employers and the expert community. According to the CITUB, the Ministry of Energy must prepare an expert justification with quantitative estimates of the costs, risks and consequences of the different scenarios. The unions also call on Bulgaria to seek coordination with other EU countries that are interested in changes in the system. Miners are against structural reforms The unions insist that the pace of coal power reduction be consistent with the availability of replacement capacities that would guarantee the security of electricity supply. In early September, the chairman of the Company Trade Union Organization “Podkrepa“ in “Mini Maritsa-iztok“ Biser Binev and the chairman of the CITUB's Corporate Trade Union Organization, Georgi Gospodinov, announced that the miners are against the structural reforms and restructuring in the sector proposed by the Ministry of Energy. Now the trade unions are placing the issue of the European emissions trading system at the center of their demands and insisting that the state present a common position, supported by specific estimates of the impact on the energy sector and the region. Sources: bta.bg, bnrnews.bg

artigo.texto: Oposição a data centers cresce no Brasil e alerta setor A oposição a data centers cresce no Brasil e acende alerta em empresas. A rápida expansão de grandes data centers nos Estados Unidos tem transformado esses empreendimentos em alvos de protestos e da oposição de diferentes segmentos da sociedade. Pesquisas mostram que a maioria da população se opõe à construção dessas inf. O cenário brasileiro ainda não é de sinal vermelho, mas já exige cautela. Sinal amarelo para investimentos no setor “O cenário está mudando, e as empresas vão precisar ter uma nova abordagem a partir de agora. Não é um sinal vermelho como nos EUA, mas é um sinal amarelo. É bom porque nos obriga a avançar com mais cautela, mas há uma janela de oportunidade para investimentos”, diz Gutierrez. A declaração reflete a percepção de que o crescimento acelerado pode gerar atritos locais. Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), observa empresas do setor tentando se aproximar de comunidades locais para negociar benfeitorias junto com a implementação de projetos. Essa aproximação busca reduzir resistências e garantir apoio social aos empreendimentos. Exemplos de bloqueios nos EUA e no Brasil Nos Estados Unidos, pelo menos 106 projetos de data centers foram bloqueados ou adiados por oposição de comunidades locais no primeiro semestre de 2026, segundo a consultoria 10a Labs. O dado ilustra a dimensão do desafio enfrentado pelo setor em mercados maduros. No Brasil, uma ação parecida do Ministério Público Estadual afeta um projeto da Elea Data Center em Belém, ainda em desenvolvimento. A empresa afirma colaborar com o órgão e seguir todos os processos de licenciamento. A fonte não detalhou o andamento atual do caso. Crescimento acelerado e potencial brasileiro Mesmo pequeno, o setor brasileiro ficou seis vezes maior desde 2012, segundo a multinacional de serviços imobiliários JLL, e 2026 caminha para recorde de novas entregas, com investimentos previstos de US$ 8 bilhões. O tamanho do mercado consumidor, a demanda global puxada pela IA e a matriz elétrica majoritariamente limpa colocaram o Brasil como potencial polo de atração. O tema apareceu até no discurso de vitória do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, no domingo (25). A Brasscom, associação de empresas de tecnologia da informação, projeta que o mercado deve triplicar até 2031, com potencial de R$ 92 bilhões em investimentos. Esses números reforçam a importância econômica do segmento, mas também aumentam a pressão por infraestrutura e aceitação social. Disputa por energia e regras mais rígidas Os data centers já disputam espaço na rede com outras indústrias. No primeiro leilão da Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast), em outubro, três data centers em São Paulo levaram todos os 228 MW disponíveis. Tossi, da ABDC, atribui isso à expansão em meados da década de 2010, durante a crise hídrica em São Paulo, que concentra os empreendimentos no país. “O mercado americano é muito mais liberal, é uma realidade muito diferente do Brasil”, diz. Para ter acesso ao Redata, os projetos precisarão de eficiência hídrica igual ou inferior a 0,05 litro por kWh. A regulamentação também deve fixar um índice de eficiência energética, que pode variar conforme o clima de cada região. As associações também destacam que o Brasil é deficitário em serviços digitais e “importa” processamento de dados, o que levanta preocupações de soberania digital. O Redata prevê que as empresas beneficiadas destinem ao menos 10% do processamento de dados ao mercado interno. Perguntas Frequentes Por que a oposição a data centers está crescendo no Brasil? A oposição cresce devido à rápida expansão dos data centers, que gera preocupações com consumo de água, energia e impacto nas comunidades locais, levando a protestos e ações do Ministério Público, como no caso da Elea Data Center em Belém. Quantos projetos de data centers foram bloqueados ou adiados nos EUA por oposição local? Pelo menos 106 projetos de data centers foram bloqueados ou adiados por oposição de comunidades locais no primeiro semestre de 2026, segundo a consultoria 10a Labs. Qual é a projeção de investimentos em data centers no Brasil até 2031? A Brasscom projeta que o mercado deve triplicar até 2031, com potencial de R$ 92 bilhões em investimentos.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBM.resumo: O que é desperdício para uma indústria pode ser um tesouro para outra. Isso é certamente verdade em partes da Europa, onde o calor residual de data centers agora abastece redes de aquecimento urbano. Na Alemanha, por exemplo, os centros de dados convertem atualmente mais de 13 TWh de eletricidade por ano em calor. Esse montante é suficiente para suprir as necessidades elétricas de 3,7 milhões de residências, considerando um consumo médio anual de 3.500 kWh. Países como Dinamarca, Suécia e Países Baixos também estão explorando formas de os centros de dados contribuírem para a rede elétrica. Esses projetos ainda são a exceção, mas mostram que os data centers, assim como os produtores residenciais de energia solar, podem se tornar "prosumidores", ou seja, tanto fornecedores quanto consumidores. Essa é uma maneira de abordar o debate sobre a quantidade de energia que os data centers consomem. À medida que a inteligência artificial (IA) se dissemina, essas instalações figuram entre os consumidores de energia que mais crescem. A Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) estima que, até 2030, os data centers poderão dobrar seu atual consumo. A IEA também aponta preocupações crescentes da opinião pública em relação à acessibilidade de custos e ao meio ambiente, e que já estão entrando no debate público. Segundo a Goldman Sachs Research, o mundo precisará de mais capacidade de data centers ao longo dos próximos cinco anos, especificamente projetados para atender à demanda das empresas. Não apenas os data centers existentes precisam ser ampliados para suprir essa demanda, como também estão sendo planejados novos complexos que, em termos de complexidade operacional e a interdependência com as comunidades locais onde se situam, assemelham-se, cada vez mais, a instalações industriais de grande porte do que a instalações de TI convencionais. Assim como instalações industriais construídas em qualquer lugar, essas novas fábricas de IA de escala de gigawatts devem ser planejadas para gerar o maior impacto positivo possível nas regiões onde estão sediadas, e projetadas, desde o início, para serem boas vizinhas. Os data centers se conectam às redes locais de energia e de abastecimento de água. Por isso, sua localização e a estratégia de resfriamento das novas instalações devem ser compatíveis com as condições regionais antes que se tomem decisões finais de onde serão construídas. Isso significa que um projeto de escala gigawatt precisa demonstrar como se integra ao cenário local de energia e clima. Se a rede elétrica da região já opera próxima ao limite de sua capacidade e o ambiente local apresenta escassez de chuvas, esses fatores precisam ser considerados logo no início. Paralelamente, as autoridades locais precisam repensar a cadeia de valor, da produção à distribuição e à resposta. O setor já está investindo em soluções para contornar as filas de conexão à rede elétrica, com mais de 130 GW em recursos energéticos colocalizados anunciados nos EUA. O primeiro centro de dados subaquático alimentado por energia eólica offshore acaba de entrar em operação. Enquanto isso, em Manchester, no Reino Unido, empresas estão testando parcerias de deslocamento de carga responsivo, visando gerar receita adicional e, ao mesmo tempo, contribuir para a preservação do meio ambiente. Nesse contexto, faz todo sentido seguir o exemplo do setor de Engenharia, Suprimentos e Construção (EPC) que, há décadas, constrói as infraestruturas industriais mais complexas do mundo e sabe como realizar entregas em escalas monumentais, sob enormes pressões de prazo e custo. Os epecistas agora utilizam uma fórmula comprovada e escalável conhecida como gêmeo digital. Esse modelo virtual da instalação planejada opera a partir de uma espinha dorsal digital comum, que abrange todo o projeto, desde o design 3D até a montagem final e a operação. Na fase de planejamento, os engenheiros podem acessar gráficos, layouts e conectores pré-configurados, específicos para a indústria de data centers, em sistemas baseados no gêmeo digital, como um Centro de Operações Unificado. O conteúdo também pode ser personalizado, inclusive com o uso de IA de design generativo, capaz de gerar inúmeras opções de roteamento de tubulações e sistemas elétricos. Essas possibilidades podem, então, ser mapeadas em projetos detalhados dentro do gêmeo digital e sobrepostas ao histórico de dados climáticos locais e ao uso atual da rede elétrica em um único modelo. Assim, planejadores e operadores conseguem visualizar o funcionamento da nova instalação antes mesmo de o primeiro tijolo ser assentado. Todos têm acesso ao mesmo conjunto de dados, e equipes multidisciplinares podem testar layouts e estratégias de resfriamento para avaliar como a eficiência do uso de energia (PUE) ou a eficiência do uso de água (WUE) seriam afetadas caso a densidade computacional aumentasse mais rapidamente do que o previsto. Exemplo brasileiro E não se trata de teoria. A empresa brasileira de engenharia multidisciplinar AP Consultoria e Projetos utilizou um conjunto de tecnologias voltado a epecistas para acelerar a modelagem, o projeto e a construção de projetos de capital complexos. Ao combinar projetos em 3D, varreduras a laser e dados de engenharia em um ambiente digital compartilhado, as equipes conseguem identificar erros mais cedo e colaborar de forma mais eficiente. E média, o prazo de entrega foi reduzido pela metade (49%), com 29% menos retrabalho e até 90% menos visitas a campo. Em todo o setor, uma abordagem que prioriza o digital poderia reduzir drasticamente os prazos e os custos de construção em até 20% cada, diminuindo em até US$ 250 bilhões o gasto total de US$ 1,7 trilhão previsto até 2030, segundo a McKinsey. Mas enquanto grande parte da discussão sobre data centers se concentre em novos projetos, exige-se cada vez mais que as instalações existentes façam mais com menos. O setor de data centers enfrenta o mesmo ambiente de negócios que outros segmentos da economia. Choques geopolíticos e políticas imprevisíveis vieram para ficar, sendo que os custos de energia se revelaram a maior surpresa do ano, conforme aponta a pesquisa da PwC com CEOs globais realizada em meados do ano. Em um cenário em que a disrupção se tornou o novo normal, empresas altamente tecnorresilientes – aquelas que aliam planejamento estratégico de longo prazo a flexibilidade operacional e bases sólidas em IA – têm 66% mais probabilidade de relatar confiança em um alto crescimento de receita. No entanto, a resiliência começa com maior visibilidade e insights mais precisos: a inteligência industrial do dia a dia que capacita as equipes operacionais a tomarem decisões mais rápidas e fundamentadas, mesmo sob pressão. Ao visualizar para onde a energia e a água estão sendo realmente direcionadas, as equipes podem passar de ajustes periódicos para pequenos ajustes constantes. É possível, por exemplo, desativar um único chiller antes que ele precise de reparos, em vez de desligar toda a instalação. Da mesma forma, alertas sobre servidores ociosos permitem que sejam desativados regularmente, evitando que máquinas zumbis continuem consumindo energia e capacidade de refrigeração. Isso reduz as surpresas e permite que as instalações lidem melhor com aumentos repentinos nas cargas de trabalho de IA. O PayPal exemplifica como métricas em tempo real, incluindo o status de energia e a refrigeração, viabilizam a resiliência tecnológica. Desde que a gigante de pagamentos criou uma visão centralizada que integra três milhões de pontos de dados, atuais e históricos, provenientes de toda a sua operação, suas equipes têm conseguido monitorar cargas de servidores, dados de temperatura e problemas de refrigeração, além de prever quando a capacidade dos racks precisará ser reduzida ou aumentada. Desbloqueando a inteligência industrial em prol da comunidade Quando os data centers realizam otimizações em tempo real, eles utilizam menos recursos e reduzem os custos operacionais. Uma menor dependência de resfriadores superdimensionados resulta em menor consumo de energia, ao passo que um projeto de refrigeração mais eficiente pode reduzir o consumo de água e diminuir a emissão de calor para as ruas, que já estão mais quentes do que costumavam ser. Ao ser gerido dessa forma, o data center fortalece sua licença social para operar. Como um vizinho melhor, ele apoia a economia digital local e consome menos energia e água, recursos que, de outra forma, sobrecarregariam as redes locais. Ajustes de eficiência não substituem a expansão da capacidade, mas operações mais otimizadas podem prolongar a vida útil dos sistemas existentes e dar tempo para que investimentos maiores tramitem pelos processos de aprovação e licenciamento. Como aponta a IEA, os formuladores de políticas já dispõem de ferramentas para gerenciar a acessibilidade dos custos de eletricidade, seja por meio de uma melhor gestão da rede ou de exigências regulatórias. Apenas a IA, por exemplo, poderia economizar mais de 13 exajoules (EJ) de energia até 2035, ou cerca de 3% do consumo final global de energia, caso sejam superadas as barreiras para sua adoção em maior escala. No que diz respeito às regulamentações, o exemplo da Alemanha é ilustrativo: novos centros de dados em construção devem atingir um PUE de 1,2 ou inferior, embora as instalações já existentes disponham de mais tempo para se adequar. Em contrapartida, a média global de PUE do setor situa-se em 1,55. Talvez seja uma métrica difícil, mas é necessária e perfeitamente alcançável se as operações do data center forem estruturadas com base na inteligência industrial. Quando as equipes têm visibilidade em tempo real do comportamento do consumo de energia, da refrigeração e das cargas de trabalho de IA, elas podem operar a instalação de maneira a facilitar a convivência com a vizinhança. *Gary Wong é Líder Global do Segmento de Energia, Serviços Públicos e Infraestrutura da AVEVA

artigo.texto: Data center health worries animate midterm campaigns Page, Arizona — Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor — a proposed $10 billion mega data center — could imperil his health. "I'm a patriot, but I'm highly against the data center," Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads "No Data Centers." "There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise," he said. Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid desert studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction. The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections. The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona's 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state's attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building. Emerging research into data centers' possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who've broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes. It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds. "Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition," said Lee Hannah, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio. "That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending." The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power AI, with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn't been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend, an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists. Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies. Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California-Riverside. Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals, synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing. Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands. "We're just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers," said Alison Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. "By the time we have a substantial volume of research it's going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now." A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market — Virginia — found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts. "Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate," said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition. It cuts across politics Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Trump, who supports the facilities' construction as vital for economic growth. Two in 3 Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll. Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned. Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Mr. Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won. Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Mr. Trump's coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support. "This is where most of the data centers go," Hannah said. "They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they're all in." In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards. The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely, who won his primary with an endorsement from Mr. Trump. He says they are key to keeping up with China. Democratic opponent Amish Shah wants a pause on new constru
