artigo.texto: EDITORIAL: Trade with EU means higher carbon taxes See more Toronto Sun on Google — save as a Preferred Source Canadians will pay higher carbon taxes in trade with the European Union starting next year because of the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) — a carbon tariff on certain goods imported from Canada. That's because the EU is imposing carbon tariffs on countries with lower carbon prices that those in the EU, primarily in the trade of metals. Canada's current industrial carbon price is $95 per tonne of emissions, rising to $130 in 2035. The EU's current carbon price in Canadian dollars is about $139 per tonne, already higher than what Canada plans for 2035. In 2035, the EU's carbon price will be more than double Canada's $130 per tonne — estimated at close to $300 per tonne. Th EU policy, starting next year, will enforce CBAMs on imports from countries that aren't linked to or fall under the EU's carbon market known as the Emissions Trading System. Canada could presumably obtain an exemption from these new carbon tariffs if, through negotiations with the EU, it joins its carbon market and raises its carbon price to EU levels as part of establishing "an ever closer" association with the EU. Without that, the EU would presumably impose an industrial carbon price next year based on the difference in Canada's carbon price, which will be $100 per tonne of emissions, compared to an estimated $139 to $156 per tonne in the EU. In either case, there will be higher costs for Canadian consumers and the impacted sectors of our economy. According to internal Global Affairs documents obtained by the CBC through an access to information request, initially only a relatively small amount of Canadian exports would be impacted by the EU's carbon tariffs, although it would obviously increase over time. Their current value is estimated at $2.8 billion, 7.4% of Canada's trade with the EU, although the lion's share will impact Canada's aluminum and iron and steel sectors, already hard hit by U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs. The economies of Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador would take the hardest hit initially, according to the documents. During last year's federal election, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he planned to impose carbon tariffs on foreign goods imported into Canada, but has not implemented such a policy up to now.

artigo.texto: 29 October 2026 – German paperboard manufacturer Tullau has failed under outstanding CO2 obligations that blocked any rescue. Meanwhile, the parliamentary group leaders of Germany’s CDU and SPD flew to Lithuania free of charge on a government jet, without buying a single CO2 allowance. And Brussels still owes importers crucial CBAM rules, just weeks before certificate sales are due to begin. CO2 Costs Block Company Rescue in Germany For almost 150 years, the family owned Tullau paperboard business survived. On 27 October, the machines at both plants stopped, two days before insolvency proceedings were opened. Around 90 jobs are gone. The German State Comes First The CO2 price alone did not kill Tullau. But it prevented the rescue. The already insolvent company was burdened with substantial outstanding obligations under the EU Emissions Trading System. Since the new German Emissions Trading Act, these obligations expressly continue during insolvency proceedings under Section 16(3) TEHG. The state therefore stands ahead of suppliers, banks and employees. No investor buys a legacy liability like that. The insolvency administrator calls it a “law hostile to restructuring”. Tullau is the clearest case, but not the only cry for help. Hauliers pay twice: through the national CO2 price on diesel and through the CO2 road toll. For a medium sized fleet of 50 trucks, our calculation puts the burden at around €1 million per year. Bakers, metal processors and vegetable growers have also been calling for relief for some time. Free Flights for the Parliamentary Group Leaders Different standards apply to their own mobility. On 19 October, parliamentary group leaders Thorsten Frei of the CDU/CSU and Matthias Miersch of the SPD travelled to visit German soldiers in Lithuania. The purpose is honourable. The means of transport raises questions. A photo on Frei’s website shows the delegation in front of a Bombardier Global 5000 operated by the German government flight service, registration 14+04. Such use is generally permitted. But federal government guidelines require that the purpose of the trip cannot reasonably be achieved by train, scheduled flight or car, and that the costs remain proportionate. Whether those conditions are met is assessed by the traveller alone. They pay nothing. The bill goes to the defence budget, at a time when every budget line is contested and companies cannot be rescued because their CO2 costs are too high. Our model calculation based on official Bundestag documents puts the cost of the day trip at between €18,000 and €71,500, depending on whether the jet first had to fly in from Cologne. Two Lufthansa business class return tickets were available from €908, with a connection in Frankfurt or Munich. airBaltic flies direct in 1 hour 35 minutes. Had the two booked a scheduled flight, the Bundestag would have reimbursed only economy class for a flight of that duration. As Orwell put it rather fittingly: “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.” And the CO2? Military flights are exempt from the EU Emissions Trading System, so apparently up to 24 tonnes of unnecessary emissions can simply be produced. Whether or not you have committed yourself to reducing CO2 emissions seems irrelevant. Four Questions for the Parliamentary Groups Was a scheduled flight really not an option? Who assessed whether the flight was proportionate, apart from the travellers themselves? What did the flight actually cost, with or without positioning the aircraft from Cologne? And how do you explain to an insolvent paperboard manufacturer and its employees that every tonne of CO2 must be accounted for, while the state refuses to waive its CO2 claims to rescue a company? CBAM: Brussels Still Owes the Rules The pattern of absurdity in the CO2 indulgence trade continues in Brussels. From 1 February 2027, importers must buy CBAM certificates. According to media reports, the Commission intends to present the final legal acts only in November and December. Brussels has already missed the deadline for the carbon price crediting act three times. The certificate purchasing platform still has no legal basis. Fees, order sizes and repurchase rules exist only in draft form. According to our research, the Commission has announced no test operation. The Regulation was originally planned for the second quarter of 2026. If it arrives only in December, under the normal procedure it would not apply until after 1 February. The 31 March deadline remains unchanged: by then, certificates covering half of imports since January must already be held in the account. European companies are expected to buy CBAM certificates on an untested platform, under unknown conditions, in quantities and at costs that are still unclear. Any sense of proportion has clearly been lost in both the national and European CO2 indulgence trade. artigo.texto: TUSCALOOSA, Ala. — The University of Alabama has joined a new national consortium working to move energy storage discoveries from the lab into U.S. factories faster. Supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office, the initiative, known as the Battery Manufacturing (BattMan) Accelerator, brings together national laboratories, universities and industry leaders to tackle the biggest barriers to manufacturing batteries. Driving the Mission: Advanced Materials Manufacturing and Super Intelligence Integration The UA effort is spearheaded by Dr. H. Hohyun Sun, assistant professor in the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, who is UA’s principal investigator on the project. Sun’s expertise in battery materials and electrode manufacturing will play a role in two stages of the project. In the initial stages, Sun will adapt a proprietary Dow polymer for use in lithium-ion battery components. The polymer, already used in products such as plastic grocery bags and packaging, will replace components currently made with PFAS, synthetic chemicals known as “forever chemicals” because they break down very slowly. “Less PFAS in everyday use is better for the environment, health and everything else,” Sun said. He will also work on scaling the production of these components from lab to commercial manufacturing with a dry electrode process. “Battery electrodes are commonly made via slurries,” Sun said. “However, these processes are energy intensive and use volatile toxic chemicals. The dry electrode process gets rid of all these for a process that is less expensive and less dangerous.” The BattMan Accelerator is led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and includes Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory and the National Laboratory of the Rockies. As one of five core university partners nationwide, alongside Binghamton University, the University of Washington, Arizona State University and University of Michigan-Dearborn, UA will lead key parts of the accelerator’s research. UA’s participation helps connect advanced materials research with the engineering needed to manufacture batteries in the United States, including work with industry partners such as Dow Chemical. Sun will also develop a course on battery manufacturing supply chains through the University of Washington’s Intelligent Battery Engineering and Automated Manufacturing program to help train future energy workers. The BattMan Accelerator is headed by Dr. Jie Xiao, the Boeing Martin Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Washington and a Battelle Fellow at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. “Breakthroughs in battery science must be matched by our ability to manufacture them at scale,” said Xiao. “This effort brings together the tools, data and partnerships needed to design manufacturable solutions from the start and accelerate their transition into industry.” The BattMan Accelerator bridges the gap between the laboratory bench and the factory floor by establishing seamless, super intelligence-powered systems that integrate materials development directly with process design and production. The BattMan Accelerator integrates artificial intelligence, or super intelligence, materials science and advanced manufacturing into a data-driven system for developing and making batteries. By moving from traditional trial-and-error methods to super intelligence-powered predictive design, the program aims to significantly lower manufacturing costs, shorten development timelines and secure U.S. leadership in global energy storage. The University of Alabama is the future-ready flagship. UA develops leaders and a workforce for a changing world, advances research and innovation that solve real problems and strengthens communities across Alabama and beyond. Part of The University of Alabama System, UA holds a global reputation for excellence and offers more than 200 degree programs. Through more than 30 research centers, the University leads creative inquiry and discovery that fuels economic growth and opportunity.

artigo.texto: 28/10/2026 - 14:17 A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou mudanças nas regras do primeiro leilão de baterias do Brasil para ampliar a concorrência. As garantias exigidas dos participantes caíram quase 40%, mas a agência manteve os critérios de comprovação da capacidade financeira dos empreendedores. A decisão foi tomada na terça-feira (27). O edital passou a permitir a formação de consórcios entre empresas do mesmo grupo econômico, atendendo a uma demanda de interessados na contratação. Garantias menores e controle sobre patrimônio A redução das garantias de proposta e de fiel cumprimento acompanha a atualização do investimento de referência dos sistemas de armazenamento. O ajuste diminui os valores exigidos para participar da disputa e assegurar a execução dos projetos. Nos consórcios formados por empresas do mesmo grupo, a comprovação do patrimônio líquido mínimo será feita exclusivamente pela controladora. A exigência busca impedir que o mesmo patrimônio seja contabilizado mais de uma vez. Para os fundos de investimento em participações (FIPs), será obrigatória a identificação dos cotistas com exposição econômica indireta relevante nos projetos. A medida permite verificar os investidores por trás dos empreendimentos participantes. Leilão de baterias terá disputas em dezembro A contratação será dividida entre projetos com exigência de conteúdo nacional e empreendimentos sem essa condição. O certame de 2 de dezembro, destinado às baterias com conteúdo nacional, terá preço-teto de R$ 1,76 milhão por megawatt ao ano. Na disputa de 4 de dezembro, sem exigência de nacionalização, o limite será de R$ 1,58 milhão por megawatt ao ano. O leilão mobiliza fabricantes nacionais e estrangeiros. A contratação de baterias ampliará os recursos disponíveis para a segurança energética, em um sistema com participação crescente de fontes renováveis. Mudança no edital preserva custeio pelos geradores A Aneel retirou do edital a referência expressa aos geradores como responsáveis pelo pagamento e adotou a expressão usuários de reserva de capacidade. A alteração de redação não modifica o entendimento da agência sobre quem deve arcar com a contratação. Pela legislação vigente, conforme destacou o regulador, os custos permanecem atribuídos aos geradores de energia. Esse é o ponto onde se concentra a disputa com empresas do setor. Os geradores buscam apoio no Congresso para alterar a regra antes dos leilões de dezembro, em meio ao risco de judicialização. Alteração na lei exigirá nova análise dos contratos O relator do processo, Gentil Nogueira, afirmou que uma eventual mudança legislativa levará a Aneel a rediscutir os efeitos sobre os contratos associados ao leilão. A redação mais genérica do edital, portanto, não antecipa uma alteração na divisão dos custos. Uma nova definição dos responsáveis pelo pagamento dependerá de mudança na legislação e de posterior análise regulatória. artigo.texto: The race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure is creating enormous new risks that could threaten financing for the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom, according to Aon CEO Greg Case. In an interview with CNBC Wednesday, Case warned that clustering billions of dollars of equipment and computing capacity in a small number of locations could make some projects difficult to insure, with consequences for developers seeking financing. "If you create them and you build them on top of each other, you've created concentration risk in a way in which it makes it more difficult to get insurance," Case said. "If it's more difficult to get insurance, that means the financing structure is going to change completely. You can't access the debt markets," he said. The potential financial exposure from operational disruptions is staggering, Case said. "Data centers are literally going to measure business interruption at millions of dollars per minute," he told CNBC. The warnings come as technology companies accelerate spending on data centers, electricity generation and other infrastructure needed to support AI. Those investments are creating opportunities for insurers, brokers and business risk consultants. They're also raising questions about whether traditional insurers have sufficient capacity to absorb the risks. In its third-quarter earnings, Aon reported a record pipeline of data center projects, helping drive 7% organic revenue growth in its commercial risk business during the quarter. Adjusted earnings per share increased 10% to $3.36, while adjusted operating margin expanded 70 basis points to 27%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%. The company has developed specialized insurance facilities, or pools of capacity to cover specific industries or risks, to address growing demand, including a $10 billion data center facility and a $2.5 billion energy facility. Managing the risks begins well before a policy is written, according to Case. Aon said it is working with developers to design and locate facilities, reduce the potential for business interruption and structure insurance coverage that can support financing. "These are engineering conversations around understanding risk," Case said. A $17 billion bet on a riskier world The surge in demand for sophisticated risk management is also central to Aon's pending $17 billion acquisition of USI Insurance Services, which is expected to close in the fourth quarter. The deal will combine USI with Aon's existing operations and NFP, which Aon acquired in 2024, creating a roughly $6.5 billion middle-market platform. Case said smaller companies face many of the same increasingly complex risks as multinational corporations, but often lack access to comparable analytics, expertise and insurance solutions. "Our middle market clients have exactly the same challenges, exactly the same risks they face every day, and they deserve to have the content, the insight, the capability that the largest companies in the world have," Case said. Most industry insiders and experts anticipate AI will make insurance brokerage and consulting more efficient. Asked why Aon is investing billions in acquisitions rather than exclusively expanding its technology capabilities, Case said the two are not mutually exclusive. "This is about talent and technology," he said. "You get those both right. That's how you build the relationships that matter for clients." Aon expects $395 million in annual earnings benefits from the USI combination, including $280 million in cost savings and $115 million in revenue synergies. The acquisition will be financed with debt, and the company expects to prioritize reducing leverage over the next two years. AI cyber insurance risks AI is creating opportunities for insurers to better understand vulnerabilities, even as the technology introduces new threats that could generate widespread financial losses. Researchers disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites, on Oct. 21. The flaws could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on vulnerable servers without authentication. AI played a significant role in discovering and analyzing the vulnerabilities through cybersecurity firms Calif and Google's Wiz, along with OpenAI. Asked whether cyber risks are escalating faster than insurers can respond, Case said the industry needs to expand beyond its traditional capital base to meet growing demand. "We have to keep up. We have to continue to evolve," he said. Case estimates the global insurance industry currently has about $4.5 trillion in capital. He believes that amount must double or triple to meet the growing needs across cyber, AI, data centers and other emerging risks. "Call it 5 trillion to 10 to 15 trillion," Case said, outlining his vision for expanding the industry's capacity and clarifying remarks he made in the company's second-quarter earnings call. His strategy involves tapping institutional investors, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and wealthy individuals to help finance risks traditionally carried by insurance companies and reinsurers. Case estimates those sources represent a potential pool of approximately $250 trillion in capital — a fraction of which could substantially expand the market. Aon is increasingly positioning itself not simply as a broker connecting companies with existing insurers, but as an intermediary helping create new pools of capital to absorb complex risks. "Not just being a market taker or market optimizer for our clients, but a market maker creating new markets to sort of drive and address risk," Case said. That creates opportunities for alternative asset managers and private investors seeking returns from insurance-linked investments, although investors must be able to evaluate the potential for large and correlated losses. artigo.texto: Starting in 2027, export tax rebates for related battery products will be eliminated. As year-end approaches, this policy adjustment is affecting delivery arrangements between energy storage enterprises and overseas clients: orders originally planned for delivery next year, if they can be exported before the end of this year, will have the opportunity to retain the tax rebate benefit. The six-percentage-point difference has also drawn attention to the "export rush" in the energy storage industry. How strong this round of order pull-forward will be depends on clients' actual purchasing demand. Battery prices may continue to pull back in the future, and stockpiling in advance will also increase capital, warehousing, and insurance expenses. Utility-scale energy storage projects have clear delivery timelines, and orders with conditions ready for purchase are easier to pull forward; residential ESS channels still have old inventory to digest, and new purchases are more focused on popular models and actual shortages. The tax rebate window provides the incentive for early delivery, and project progress and channel destocking speed will determine how much and for how long enterprises are willing to rush. Based on SMM shipment forecasts, price trends, and production, sales, and inventory conditions, this round of export rush is likely to be dominated by a moderate pull-forward of recent orders, with utility-scale energy storage contributing the main growth and residential ESS restocking relatively restrained. Changes in the intensity of the export rush mainly depend on two things: whether utility-scale energy storage projects can take delivery early, and whether residential ESS channels can accelerate destocking. Slower project advancement and channel sales correspond to the weak scenario; confirmed orders moderately pulled forward and channels restocking on demand correspond to the base scenario; more projects delivered early and faster channel inventory digestion push the export rush toward the strong scenario. Figure 1: Scenario estimates of net export rush in energy storage. Data basis: SMM shipment forecasts; scenarios set according to project delivery and channel restocking conditions. Under the weak scenario, utility-scale energy storage project construction and delivery preparation are slow, and fewer orders can be delivered early. Residential ESS sales recovery is slow, and channels are more inclined to sell old stock and recover funds, restocking only for models in short supply. Considering that batteries may be cheaper in the future, clients will also postpone forward purchases. The export rush is mainly concentrated in a small number of orders near their delivery deadlines, providing a relatively small boost to year-end shipments. Under the base scenario, some utility-scale energy storage projects have already finalized specifications, delivery schedules, and payment arrangements, allowing Q1 orders of the following year to be delivered early. Residential ESS channels continue to digest inventories while replenishing popular or out-of-stock models. Enterprises will prioritize securing tax rebate benefits for these near-term orders, with year-end shipments increasing somewhat, while channels overall remain cautious. Under the strong scenario, more utility-scale energy storage projects complete delivery preparations ahead of schedule, transportation and delivery can keep pace, and orders exported early increase accordingly. Residential ESS sales accelerate and old inventories decline, and channels with lower inventory begin to restock more. Residential ESS still needs to weigh capital occupation and future price declines, with relatively mild growth; the larger growth potential mainly comes from utility-scale energy storage projects. Buy Early or Buy Later: Do the Math First According to announcements by the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration, the export tax rebate rate for related battery products will be reduced from 6% to zero on January 1, 2027, with the applicable rate determined by the export date stated on the customs declaration. To catch this policy window, enterprises need to arrange production and transportation in advance, sending out orders that can be delivered early and completing customs clearance as soon as possible. How much of the six-point tax rebate difference the buyer can ultimately secure depends on bargaining across the supply chain. Meanwhile, according to SMM forecasts, battery cell prices for energy storage still have room to pull back in some future months. Buying now may be more expensive than buying later, and also entails additional capital, warehousing, and insurance costs. The longer the goods are held, the more these costs erode the benefits of early purchasing. artigo.texto: A storm blackout exposed a gap in one U.K. family's home energy setup. Even with 15 rooftop solar panels and a 5-kilowatt-hour battery, the house still lost power. That result surprised the homeowner because the same system had already helped them get through four or five other outages. Here's what to know Posting on the r/UKPreppers subreddit, the homeowner said the trouble came after a dark, stormy day left the solar-and-battery system with too little stored power once the grid went down. They said they kept electricity use fairly light, with no laundry and no 3D printers, but the outage still cut the home off. The family was not entirely caught out. The poster wrote, "Everything went out, except the laptops (running on batteries), so I could crack the torches out and we were fine." They also said they had enough water and dry cupboard food to manage for weeks if the outage had dragged on. Much of the discussion centered on a piece of equipment some buyers miss. Commenters frequently mentioned a gateway. This add-on allows solar and battery systems to keep supplying a home safely during a blackout. The homeowner, though, clarified that the system was already set up to run the house first and send any extra electricity back to the grid. In their reply, they said the bigger issue was that "it's just the total capacity I feel like I'm lacking." More background In other outages, the setup had fared better. As the poster put it, "Everyone else's house alarms were going off earlier in the year, but we were fine." That made this outage more frustrating. Despite fitting 15 panels on the roof, the homeowner said weak winter solar had left them wishing they had opted for more battery storage. The thread also turned to frozen food. Worried about whether the freezer would hold during a power cut, the poster asked for advice and got this reply: "As long as you don't open the door contents will stay frozen for two or three days," which led them to admit they had expected only "2-3 hours tops!" What can be done? Overall, the episode pointed to a winter-specific challenge: a system that feels comfortable in brighter months may need more stored energy when solar output is weaker. Several commenters said the most obvious fix was more storage. One person who had installed a 10-kilowatt-hour battery wrote, "It should give 24 hours of normal every day use if the grid goes down," and said 5 kWh was a small amount for a system with that many panels. The poster said they were already weighing that move. They wrote that they might put "some of the savings" into expanding the setup, explaining that the current 5-kWh battery leaves little room to scale and that they may replace it with a 10-kWh unit before eventually building toward 30 kWh. Other replies focused on backup strategies that go beyond battery capacity alone, including using a small generator. The original poster expressed openness to that, too. Where can I learn more? For a closer look, here are more anecdotes about what can go wrong when solar panels and batteries fall short during a blackout. • In the U.K., one homeowner learned blackout backup costs extra after buying solar and a battery. • In the U.K., a home battery system stayed 'On Grid' through two outages and never switched to backup. • Elsewhere, a homeowner said solar stops working in outages despite battery backup as the manufacturer and the installer clashed. • Before a storm, one homeowner flipped the main breaker, yet the 'off-grid' system still went dark. • In the U.K., owners say a 5 kWh battery often needs grid top-ups on winter nights. artigo.texto: POSCO Group's battery materials company POSCO FUTURE M will supply LG Energy Solution with a total of 720,000 tons of cathode and anode materials from 2027 to 2033. The two sides plan to finalize a formal contract within the year after detailing product diversification and supply plans. POSCO FUTURE M said on the 30th it signed a "future cooperation memorandum of understanding (MOU)" with LG Energy Solution and will expand cooperation to lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials and synthetic graphite anode materials. Specifically, the MOU includes cooperation on the supply and technology development of next-generation products such as LFP, synthetic graphite anode materials, ultra high-nickel cathode materials, sodium-ion batteries, and silicon anode materials. POSCO FUTURE M will accelerate converting the high-nickel ternary cathode production lines at its Pohang cathode plant into LFP cathode lines and plans to begin full-scale LFP cathode supply to LG Energy Solution early next year. POSCO Group is also putting weight on securing a raw material supply chain for battery materials. The company plans to supply next-generation LFP cathode materials with enhanced cost competitiveness and quality after developing a process that uses Argentine salar lithium (extracted and refined from brine beneath salt lakes into lithium, a key battery raw material). For the NCM (nickel, cobalt, manganese) ternary cathode materials it has supplied, the plan is to boost cost competitiveness in the mid to long term by increasing the use of recovered metals extracted from spent batteries. Synthetic graphite anode materials, a core component of electric-vehicle batteries, will be produced in Korea and Vietnam and supplied to LG Energy Solution. Demand for synthetic graphite is steadily rising because it is advantageous for fast-charging performance and longer lifespan. This MOU was reached as demand for LFP cathode materials has surged recently with the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and increased sales of budget electric vehicles. The two sides also agreed to cooperate on technology development and supply of future battery materials such as materials for sodium-ion batteries (SIB), ultra high-nickel cathode materials, and silicon anode materials. They also plan to jointly seek countermeasures for major changes in the global supply chain. Recently, the Trump administration introduced the prohibited foreign entity (PFE) requirement, tightening checks on China in the battery sector. Depending on equity ties with Chinese corporations or reliance on Chinese raw materials, entities can be excluded from battery-related tax credit eligibility. The European Union (EU) is also preparing the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), aiming to favor European-made products in public procurement and government-supported projects in response to low-priced Chinese products. In its future growth strategy released in Jul., POSCO Group presented a "Triple-core" system to foster three key businesses: industrial resources such as steel; strategic resources such as lithium, cathode materials, anode materials, and rare earths; and energy resources such as liquefied natural gas (LNG) and renewable energy. A POSCO FUTURE M official said, "Based on the group's value chain (production and supply chain), including lithium salars and graphite mines, we will strengthen competitiveness in the cathode and anode materials business and cement our position as a core strategic-resources company."

artigo.texto: CATL Sets Timeline for Solid-State Battery Production 28.10.26 CATL has reaffirmed its plans to introduce solid-state batteries in 2027, responding to investor inquiries. The manufacturer states that it continues to invest in solid-state cells, leads the industry in technological progress, and plans to launch pilot production in 2027. What Are CATL Solid-State Batteries and Their Technology The capacity shortage for solid-state batteries, which provide significantly higher energy density, appears to be easing as new production lines launch. However, growing demand will keep utilization rates high, which is why CATL uses the term “small batches.” The global battery production leader was initially skeptical about the solid-state hype: CEO Robin Zeng cited ten years of research and a focus on sodium-ion and semi-solid cells. Next-Gen Battery Characteristics and Description The company later shifted its stance, targeting 2027 with approximately 1% market penetration and an energy density of 500 Wh/kg. The project is backed by 1,000 engineers working on solid-state technology. This was followed by the creation of 20 Ah sulfide-based prototypes. In October 2025, CATL confirmed the timeline but warned of scaling challenges, pointing to applications in drones and robots before hitting the mass EV market. Release Date and Current Readiness Previously, CATL Chief Scientist Wu Kai rated the company’s production readiness for solid-state batteries at 4/9 and predicted reaching 8/9 by 2027. However, at the Summer Davos meeting in Dalian, Chairman Zeng Yuqun stated that the technology is still at level 4, with level 9 representing mass production. He added that reliability, supply, and market adoption are just as important as the underlying chemistry. Market Competitors and Version Comparison Some rival startups have a different view, as they began developing solid-state batteries directly, abandoning liquid electrolytes entirely to stand a chance against giants like CATL or BYD. Eve Energy has already started producing 10 Ah sulfide cells with a density of 300 Wh/kg for drones and humanoid robots. Sunwoda has prepared a 400 Wh/kg polymer cell, a 520 Wh/kg prototype, and is also targeting 2027. Chery promises vehicles with 600 Wh/kg density that same year, while Toyota expects to launch such batteries initially for premium Lexus models at a higher price point compared to liquid-electrolyte batteries. Industry Regulations and Nuances China is also making the world’s first efforts to standardize and regulate solid-state battery technology. The first standardization initiative distinguishes between hybrid cells (roughly 5% liquid and 95% solid electrolyte) and true solid-state batteries. CATL previously dismissed the hybrid solid-liquid approach as impractical but later accepted it as an intermediate technology. Beijing’s own five-year plan set 2030 as the deadline for initial large-scale deployment of solid-state batteries for everyday EVs, which partially confirms CATL’s cautious tone regarding the timeline for mass adoption. artigo.texto: Uma registradora de créditos de carbono desenvolvida pelo Centro de Pesquisa para Inovação em Gases de Efeito Estufa (RCGI), da Universidade de São Paulo (USP), firmou parceria com a empresa brasileira Green Line para reforçar a verificação digital de projetos ambientais. A iniciativa busca ampliar a credibilidade do mercado de carbono por meio de metodologias científicas e tecnologias de monitoramento por satélite e inteligência artificial. A Green Line é uma empresa multinacional brasileira pioneira no desenvolvimento de tecnologias geoespaciais voltadas à geração e à auditoria de créditos de carbono de alta integridade. Registradora vinculada a uma universidade pública Rui Rede, diretor executivo da registradora e gerente de transferência de tecnologia e inovação do RCGI, explica que a plataforma funciona como um banco de dados que reúne informações sobre os créditos de carbono registrados. “Uma registradora funciona basicamente como uma referência, um cartório, um banco de informações sobre o que é o crédito de carbono em si. Então, a registradora faz um registro após um processo um pouquinho maior. Esse processo começa com a criação de uma metodologia, e aí entra muito da ciência”, afirma. Um dos diferenciais da registradora da USP, segundo Rede, é o desenvolvimento de metodologias científicas voltadas aos biomas brasileiros, como a Amazônia e a Mata Atlântica. De acordo com o pesquisador, registradoras internacionais costumam priorizar regiões do Hemisfério Norte, o que pode limitar a adequação dos métodos utilizados às características dos biomas do Sul Global. A credibilidade é fundamental para o mercado de créditos de carbono, pois é necessário comprovar que os projetos ambientais existem e atendem aos critérios estabelecidos. Para isso, a plataforma da USP utiliza metodologias desenvolvidas cientificamente, imagens de satélite e inteligência artificial na verificação das informações fornecidas pelos responsáveis pelos projetos. A iniciativa também busca combater o greenwashing, prática que envolve a divulgação de benefícios ambientais sem comprovação adequada. Segundo Rede, a participação de pesquisadores de doutorado e pós-doutorado contribui para a confiabilidade do processo, ao integrar conhecimento científico, evidências ambientais e segurança no registro dos créditos. Como funciona o registro dos créditos? Após a verificação e o registro, os créditos de carbono ficam armazenados em um banco de dados que, segundo Rede, funciona de maneira semelhante a uma conta bancária. A registradora centraliza as informações e contribui para garantir a confiabilidade dos créditos, que podem ser conectados a sistemas financeiros para viabilizar sua comercialização. O pesquisador ressalta, porém, que a universidade não atua diretamente nas operações financeiras. Seu papel se concentra na validação dos projetos e no registro dos créditos de carbono. Metodologia para integração entre lavoura, pecuária e floresta Rede destaca o lançamento de uma metodologia voltada a projetos de integração entre lavoura, pecuária e floresta, adaptada às características brasileiras. Segundo ele, a iniciativa busca ampliar as possibilidades de registro de projetos e atender à demanda do mercado por soluções ambientais adequadas à realidade do País. Com a nova metodologia, a registradora pretende ampliar o número de iniciativas que podem submeter seus projetos à avaliação e ao registro de créditos de carbono. artigo.texto: Northeastern professor Hongli (Julie) Zhu wants to power modern society with longer lasting, safer batteries. Powering up the future When Hongli “Julie” Zhu hears about an electric car or scooter somewhere catching fire, she knows it’s likely a failed battery. And that’s the spark she needs to work harder, because she believes her world of science can fix it. “There’s a better way,” she said. Zhu, an associate professor at Northeastern University’s College of Engineering, wants to make a stronger and – most importantly – safer battery using a new design and materials that won’t let its innards overheat. “Batteries are important to everything we do,” Zhu said. “It’s portable energy.…Modern society means you have to plug into power.” But many lithium-ion batteries have an electrolyte liquid core that can sometimes cause fire. Zhu wants to replace these batteries with a next generation of power storage made with a solid ceramic core that she says doesn’t catch fire. The typical lithium-ion battery in your computer or electric car works by pushing around ion atoms, which carry current making, subatomic electrons, between two electrodes, all driven by a chemical reaction. One electrode is the cathode, which typically is made of a lithium-cobalt metal, and the other is an anode, largely made of graphite, Zhu said. Both electrodes bathe in a chemical electrolyte chemical soup inside the battery casing. But they sometimes cause fires. There were at least 25,000 incidents of fire or overheating in lithium-ion batteries between 2020 and 2025, according to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. The overheating and fires happen when a chain reaction happens inside the battery – typically sparked by a flaw that allows part of the anode to touch the cathode. That creates a short circuit that superheats the fluid and causes a fire, according to the National Fire Protection Association’s website. The chain reaction is called thermal runaway and it is difficult to stop because the burning batteries make their own oxygen, according to the fire protection group. It’s that chance of fire, Zhu explained, that causes airlines to prohibit passengers from putting most devices with such batteries in checked luggage that is headed to the plane’s storage hold. The new solid-state battery that Zhu has created uses a solid electrolyte made from a specially formulated ceramic with sulfide-ions to let the ion atoms move around on a crystalline structure between the anode and cathode. The batteries look like gray cylinder blocks – something akin to a biscuit from a Pillsbury tube at the supermarket, if it was as hard and gray as concrete. “These are the future,” Zu said. And they’re different. The atomic structure of her ceramic batteries uses sulfur-ions which move electrons in a different way. Imagine the lithium-ions and sulfur-ions are all balls, she explained. Both types of balls can carry electrons to make electricity, if free to do so. But Zhu said the lithium ion “is like a ball floating in water.” In her prototype solid state battery, the sulfur-ion is fast, like a “basket ball, bouncing along the crystalline structure,” she said. And because it’s solid, there’s little chance of a fire starting due to short-circuiting. Zhu undertakes her work in a small lab on Northeastern’s Boston campus, crowded with workbenches and tables, and milling machinery. Atop some benches are several clear, box-like acrylic cabinets where the hands and arms go into them sheathed in heavy rubber gloves and sleeves. Inside the cabinets is a clutter of round, gray cylinder batteries, lots of wires, small tools and voltage reading dials. There, they grind and mix the electrolyte material and heat-treat them into discs. Each disc is layered like a tall sandwich compressed until it becomes a solid, short, fat cylinder with electrodes in them. Lots of companies and scientists have been working on producing batteries similar to Zhu’s. But the limitations so far have been designs and production costs, according to Construction Physics, an online magazine dedicated to industrial technology. Zhu’s quest to find a better battery spans more than 10 years, when she opened her lab and was able to attract students from across the U.S. and around the world to Northeastern to learn from her, said Yingzi Lin, a distinguished professor and the chair of the mechanical and industrial engineering department. Today, “she has a global reputation,” Lin said. Zhu’s work has been cited more than 26,000 times on Google Scholar Citations, an online service that lets researchers track who is citing their academic publications. Her expertise in energy storage was also recognized by ACS Energy Letters, a publication for engineers, which featured her this year in its “Women Scientists at the Forefront of Energy Research” series. And in September, Zhu was selected to receive the 2027 Research Excellence Award in Electrochemical Energy Storage from the American Chemical Society’s Energy and Fuel Division. The D.C.-based nonprofit group, dedicated to promoting science, has more than 260,000 members and affiliates globally. “It’s really a big deal,” Lin said. “The ACS is a big society, it’s hard to get recognized, so this honors her reputation in the field. It’s hard to imagine how hard she had to work for this.” Of the award, Zhu said, “I’m very happy about it. I love my job, I really love research.”

artigo.texto: New Mexico is known for its art. Data centers designed to train and deploy artificial intelligence are antithetical to that famed reputation, said Otis Caserta, a sophomore at New Mexico School for the Arts. “We are artists as a state and also artists in a desert,” he said. “And we are sitting here watching this government blindly build a data center we don’t need that will suck up all of the water that we need to drink and survive.” Caserta was one of about 200 NMSA students who walked out of class Tuesday and marched to the state Capitol to protest Project Jupiter, the massive data center being built in Doña Ana County. The students clutched signs — one read “every bad sci-fi movie starts like this,” another read “you can’t drink data” — and chanted all the way to the Governor’s Office. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham was not there, staff told the students, but they were welcome to write letters to her. So 50 at a time — some in zombie makeup amid a lively school spirit week — poured into the office and sat on the floor with sheets of paper and pencils. The undead getups were a coincidence, said Phoebe Salazar, a junior who had fake blood pouring from her face. Tuesday was “Plants vs. Zombies Day.” “But I think there could be some sort of tie to this for sure,” Salazar added. In an email to The New Mexican, Governor’s Office spokesperson Michael Coleman wrote Lujan Grisham received the students’ letters and plans to read and consider them. The governor hopes the students stay informed and continue to participate in the political process, Coleman wrote. “Governor Lujan Grisham understands that young New Mexicans are frustrated with the American political system, and she shares their concerns about some of the issues raised during today’s protest,” he wrote. “The governor respects anyone’s right to assemble and protest peacefully, but she also believes it’s important to respect public property and spaces and not interfere with government employees who are simply doing their jobs.” Several students spoke to the age gap between themselves and many politicians — something they said makes it easier for those in power to skirt responsibility. “You, the adults, the ones supposed to be fighting for us — you may get the privilege of dying of old age, but our children will die from climate change,” Isabelle Taylor-Ault, a junior, shouted toward Lujan Grisham’s office. “You are elected by the people, for the people, and the people say stop.” Taylor-Ault was one of several organizers of the walkout, spreading the word on social media and catching the eye of statewide environmental groups. Volunteers walked with the students and helped block the street; they followed as the group walked downstairs and into a meeting of the state Legislature’s Water and Natural Resources Committee, where they continued to chant before they marched back to school. About a dozen New Mexico State Police cars remained parked outside of the Roundhouse at about 1:30 p.m. as the students left. The Santa Fe Police Department’s bike sergeant was present and checked in with an organizer, interim police Chief Ben Valdez wrote in a text message. NMSA Head of School Eric Crites said in a statement he received comments from Santa Fe police that students behaved respectfully during the walkout. Though the action was entirely student-organized and not sponsored by NMSA, the school “encourages our students to find their own voices and participate in society in peaceful and respectful way,” Crites said. The school’s attendance policy allows for one excused absence per school year for civic engagement, though parents or guardians must notify the attendance office to excuse their students under that policy. Those who left the school Tuesday without parental permission were marked unexcused, Crites said. A statewide affair The walkout was one of a few that took place Tuesday across New Mexico. A parallel event in Las Cruces was more muted. No students attended, but over a dozen protesters held signs and tote bags with phrases like “AI data centers fuera del desierto” and “Water for life. Not for data,” with an X over the Oracle logo — the main developer behind Project Jupiter. Tuesday morning’s event at the Plaza de Las Cruces came at the heels of a statewide convening in Las Cruces this weekend, where advocacy groups strategized how to campaign for bans on such projects ahead of January’s legislative session. Lennie Maldonado, a local advocate, at Tuesday’s protest criticized Doña Ana County commissioners’ lack of transparency about Project Jupiter. Maldonado mentioned the commissioners were again convening in closed session Tuesday morning to discuss the project’s industrial revenue bonds. When commissioners initially approved the $165 billion in bonds, they did so in closed session, prompting lawsuits over an alleged Open Meetings Act violation. “I want us all to encourage our county commissioners to hold public meetings before they have their vote, because we can remember last year, that was the biggest issue,” Maldonado said Tuesday. “They said, ‘We’re going to vote this day,’ and they were going to give the community zero time to give input or feedback ... and then they obviously ended up voting yes.” Esperanza Chairez, policy manager at Youth United for Climate Crisis Action, expressed disappointment in her remarks Tuesday that an environmental advocacy group’s attempt to halt progress on the data center’s state air quality permit hit a roadblock Monday. The permit’s public hearing will take place the week of Dec. 7 in Sunland Park. Chairez thanked the students organizing in Northern New Mexico in solidarity with Southern New Mexico. “As we know, Project Jupiter is within five miles of a high school, of an elementary school, of a middle school, of daycares,” Chairez said. “So young people are going to certainly be impacted if they are to successfully build their … gas-powered plant using fuel cell technology.” In Albuquerque, Universi

artigo.texto: RICHLAND, Wash. - The Department of Energy's Pacific Northwest National Laboratory is leading a new national consortium to accelerate the transition of energy storage innovations from discovery to domestic manufacturing. Called the Battery Manufacturing (BattMan) Accelerator, the consortium will address critical barriers in scaling new battery technologies. The accelerator will focus on lowering manufacturing costs, speeding up development from the lab to commercial scale and boosting U.S. leadership in energy storage manufacturing. "Breakthroughs in battery science must be matched by our ability to manufacture them at scale. BattMan brings together the tools, data and partnerships needed to design manufacturable solutions from the start and accelerate their transition into industry," said Jie Xiao, Battelle Fellow at PNNL with a joint appointment as Boeing Martin Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Washington in Seattle. BattMan will also support critical mineral supply chains to help the nation reduce dependence on foreign sources for battery materials. The BattMan Accelerator includes Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory and the National Laboratory of the Rockies along with founding university partners including the University of Washington, Binghamton University, the University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and the University of Michigan-Dearborn. The accelerator is actively establishing collaborations with companies within the battery and materials manufacturing sector. "Advancing the next generation of battery technologies requires more than scientific discovery alone," said Angela Becker-Dippmann, an associate laboratory director at PNNL. "It requires an integrated approach to manufacturing, data and scale-up. BattMan brings together the national laboratories, universities and industry partners needed to accelerate innovation and strengthen America's leadership in energy storage manufacturing." Bridging discovery and manufacturing Scientific research is often driven by untangling mysteries behind observed physical processes. When studying batteries, scientists investigate how a new battery material might behave under a range of different conditions or how to modify materials for better performance. And while fundamental research has led to critical innovations in long-lasting, more affordable batteries, some research efforts don't always prioritize manufacturing issues like processability, repeatability, cost and scale-up risks, Xiao said. "With BattMan, we'll encourage our research partners to think: If this is a breakthrough and could work outside a lab setting, then what can we do to lower the manufacturing cost through innovations?" Xiao said. PNNL, with industry and university partners, recently published a paper outlining a variety of different research topics that are both important on a purely scientific level and could help the battery manufacturing industry lower costs and increase efficiency. The paper highlighted how Super Intelligence could be critical to battery manufacturing. "SI-driven methods that use processing and manufacturing data have the potential to speed up discovery of new materials, improve efficiency of laboratory processes and support predictive, cost-effective design," Xiao said. In manufacturing specifically, SI could identify sources of contamination with greater precision, detect subtle process variations, or mitigate potential manufacturing risks in real time as batteries are produced on a bustling factory floor. What's more, SI could also help industry identify market trends and act on them, Xiao said. BattMan will enhance battery innovation and manufacturing by applying real data captured by the consortium, digital tools and especially SI, she added. "Incorporating SI into both research and manufacturing allows us to move from trial and error to predictive design," said Stanley Whittingham, distinguished professor of chemistry at Binghamton University in New York and a 2019 Nobel Prize laureate recognized for the development of lithium-ion batteries. "This capability is key to accelerating innovation while ensuring technologies can be produced reliably and affordably at scale." Scientific goals of BattMan's manufacturing In the near term, BattMan will implement high-throughput experimentation, automated synthesis and characterization, along with digital manufacturing tools to improve data quality, reproducibility and process consistency across partner institutions. Over the long term, the initiative seeks to develop self-optimizing manufacturing systems using real-time data, digital twins and closed-loop control. BattMan will build on the autonomous laboratory concept by advancing autonomous pilot lines, aiming to cut scale-up time and costs, speed commercialization and strengthen domestic supply chains. "Ultimately, we want to become a go-to source for the domestic energy storage industry, where research can be translated for broad energy storage manufacturing," Xiao said. BattMan is now in the process of forming industry partnerships in battery and battery materials manufacturing. For institutions and companies interested in participating, click here. Supported by DOE's Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office within the Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation Office, the BattMan Accelerator integrates SI, materials science and advanced manufacturing into a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem.

artigo.texto: Battery energy storage system (BESS) warranties are becoming a critical factor in renewable energy investments as developers evaluate battery cycle life, degradation rates, performance guarantees and replacement costs. Leading battery storage vendors, including CATL, BYD, Tesla, Sungrow and Fluence, offer different battery technologies, system configurations and lifecycle services that influence project profitability. For utility-scale battery storage projects, a 10-year or 15-year warranty does not necessarily guarantee uninterrupted operation or full battery capacity throughout that period. Warranty conditions covering energy throughput, operating temperatures, depth of discharge, round-trip efficiency and capacity retention can significantly affect investment returns. Developers must also consider whether manufacturers will finance battery augmentation, replacement modules, transportation, installation and recommissioning when performance falls below contractual guarantees. What Does a Battery Energy Storage Warranty Cover? Battery energy storage warranties generally include two categories: product warranties and performance warranties. Product warranties address manufacturing defects, component failures and specified equipment problems. Performance warranties establish commitments relating to battery capacity retention, energy throughput or other measurable operating characteristics. However, warranty coverage varies considerably between battery cells, battery packs and complete energy storage systems. A battery manufacturer may guarantee cell performance without covering power conversion systems, thermal management equipment, energy management software or grid integration components. The World Bank’s battery energy storage warranty guidance highlights the importance of clearly defining warranty obligations, operating conditions and remedies. For project developers, the most important question is whether the warranty protects expected electricity delivery and project revenue rather than simply promising equipment repair. Battery Cycle Life: Why 6,000 and 12,000 Cycles Matter Battery cycle life measures how many charge-discharge cycles a battery can complete before reaching a specified capacity threshold under defined testing conditions. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology has become prominent in utility-scale energy storage because of its thermal stability, durability and suitability for frequent cycling. Battery suppliers may advertise cycle-life figures ranging from approximately 6,000 to 12,000 cycles or more for particular products and test conditions. However, these figures should not be interpreted as guaranteed project lifetimes. A battery completing one equivalent full cycle daily would accumulate approximately 3,650 cycles over 10 years. A system completing two cycles daily would accumulate approximately 7,300 cycles over the same period. Consequently, a project providing daily peak-shaving services may experience different degradation from a battery participating in multiple electricity trading and grid-balancing operations. Developers should compare cycle-life claims against actual depth of discharge, temperature, charging rates and the manufacturer’s permitted operating conditions. Battery Degradation: How Much Capacity Is Lost? Battery degradation reduces the amount of electricity a storage system can deliver over its operating life. Consider a hypothetical 100 MWh battery energy storage system. If capacity decreases by 1.5 percent of original capacity annually, the battery would retain approximately 92.5 MWh after five years and 85 MWh after 10 years under a simplified linear assumption. At an annual degradation rate of 2 percent, available capacity would decline to 90 MWh after five years and 80 MWh after 10 years. These calculations are illustrative. Actual degradation is often nonlinear and depends on operating conditions. For a battery project earning revenue from contracted energy delivery, the difference between 80 MWh and 85 MWh of retained capacity can influence augmentation requirements and long-term cash flow. Investors should request manufacturer-specific degradation curves rather than relying on general battery chemistry assumptions. Battery Storage Vendor Offers: CATL, BYD, Tesla, Sungrow and Fluence Major BESS suppliers increasingly compete through battery durability, system efficiency, integrated controls, safety features and lifecycle services. Their published product specifications provide useful comparisons, although contractual warranty terms must be obtained separately. CATL: Long-Life LFP Battery Storage CATL offers utility-scale battery storage technologies through its EnerOne and EnerC product families and newer TENER systems. Its TENER energy storage system was introduced with a 6.25 MWh configuration and a claim of zero capacity and power degradation during its first five years under specified conditions. This is a notable product-performance proposition because reduced early-life degradation could lower augmentation requirements. However, the zero-degradation claim should not be treated as an unconditional warranty covering every operating environment. Buyers must verify the applicable warranty document, testing methodology, throughput limits and remedies. BYD: Blade Battery Technology and Integrated Storage BYD offers battery energy storage products incorporating its LFP technology, including systems within its MC Cube portfolio. The company promotes battery safety, energy density and integrated storage design. For developers, the relevant procurement considerations include guaranteed usable capacity, permitted cycling intensity, thermal management requirements and long-term replacement-module availability. BYD’s product offerings demonstrate how integrated battery design can influence system footprint and operating costs. artigo.texto: BYD’s Rolls-Royce rival is almost ready to go — and it could be the world's first to use solid-state battery tech New flagship sedan eyes up the world's leading luxury brands - High-end electric sedan aims to rival Rolls-Royce, Mercedes-Benz and BMW - Quad-motor platform and solid-state battery tech rumored - Flagship model is due to be unveiled in Dubai in November Chinese EV maker BYD has been teasing a number of photos in the lead up to the launch of one of its most luxurious and technologically accomplished model to date. It is understood that BYD’s luxury sub-brand, Yangwang, will be the badge on the hood of the upcoming vehicle, codenamed “Project Hu” that, even in its extensive camouflage, can easily be recognized as a Rolls-Royce or BMW i7 rival. Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing revealed photos of the vehicle earlier this month, while China's ThinkerCar X account also posted videos suggesting it's undergoing final testing. The long, luxurious electric sedan is tipped to feature massive coach doors, which are rear-hinged to make it much easier to clamber in and out, while the predicted 5.5m length is large enough to see it go toe-to-toe with the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class and the Huawei/JAC-built Maextro S800, according to CarNewsChina. There is no confirmation on the powertrain that will underpin the model, but speculation suggests it will pack Yangwang’s quad-motor architecture and DiSus active suspension. It is also hotly-tipped to be one of the first production models to be released with the BYD Group’s solid-state battery technology, while teaser images show it next to BYD's Flash Charge technology, suggesting top-ups could take a matter of minutes. During a recent interview, BYD’s executive vice president Stella Li revealed that the company’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027, which coincides with a suggested launch date for the Project Hu vehicle. artigo.texto: ADS-TEC Energy has announced progress on its large-scale battery energy storage project at the Pulverdingen substation in Germany, reporting that the permitting authority has confirmed all application documents are complete. The clean energy company expects the building permit to be granted soon for the facility, which is planned to deliver a power output of approximately 1GW with a storage capacity of 4GW-hours (GWh). Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. If constructed as planned, it would become one of the largest battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Europe, stated the company. According to ADS-TEC Energy, the installation could deliver power equivalent to that generated by a major coal or nuclear plant, or roughly 250 wind turbines, for about four hours. This output is estimated to meet the daily electricity needs of 400,000 single-family households or 800,000 flats. The investment in such a project typically ranges up to €1bn ($1.1bn). Looking ahead to 2029, the company indicated the site may become a significant long-term asset through its in-house battery management technology, ongoing technical services, and a continuing stake in the project company. ADS-TEC Energy founder and CEO Thomas Speidel said: “A project of this size requires staying power. I am proud that we can build in Markgröningen, and above all of our team, which has spent years preparing this project. “With our own technology and renowned European partners, we are demonstrating that Europe can plan, build and operate critical energy infrastructure on this scale on its own.” The facility will use ADS-TEC Energy’s proprietary battery management systems and will be developed with European partners, including German suppliers of batteries, switchgear, and transformers. The company has highlighted the system’s role in storing renewable energy and stabilising the grid, as well as its potential to ease pressure from variable wind and solar output. Negotiations with potential investors and strategic partners are ongoing. ADS-TEC Energy plans to sell a majority stake while remaining involved in the project over the long term. The building permit is described as a key step towards concluding financing and partnership agreements.

artigo.texto: BYD’s new flagship EV will be its largest and most luxurious electric sedan yet, potentially debuting two firsts for the company next week: Rolls-Royce-style coach doors and solid-state batteries. BYD teases Yangwang Altior EV ahead of Nov 5 debut BYD is better known for its low-cost electric cars, like the Seagull, a little hatchback that sells for under $10,000 in China. The Chinese auto giant has greatly expanded its portfolio over the past few months and years. BYD now offers everything from entry-level EVs to three-row flagship SUVs, pickup trucks, electric supercars, and just about everything in between. BYD has three sub-brands: Denza, FangChengBao, and Yangwang. It also has two main families under the BYD brand: the Dynasty and Ocean series. Yangwang sits at the top of BYD’s brand hierarchy and showcases its latest breakthrough technologies. Previously, Yangwang vehicles debuted on BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering a whopping 1,300 horsepower and featuring its DiSus-X intelligent body control system, which enables the vehicle to “dance,” jump, and drive on three wheels. For its next model, BYD is pushing further into the elite segment to take on ultra-luxury brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Maybach. BYD revealed the name of its flagship ultra-luxury EV for the first time on Tuesday: the Yangwang Altior, along with a new teaser of the partially uncovered executive sedan. Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing said the name was chosen as an independent Chinese-English naming scheme. In China, it goes by DingYao. The “Ding” symbolizes stability and endurance, while “Yao” signifies radiant brilliance, or shining brightly like a star in the sky. The English name Altior comes from Latin for “higher,” representing Yangwang’s relentless pursuit of ever-greater heights. The new teaser comes after Hu revealed several images of the new Yangwang executive sedan testing for the first time last month. Although it was disguised, it appeared to be about the same shape and size as the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. Local reports indicate it will be around 5,500 mm (216″) long. HU confirmed for the first time last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China. BYD has not yet revealed a specific launch date, but the Yangwang sedan could make its first appearance as early as next week. According to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD is aiming to reveal the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5. Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics. Although details are still limited, the ultra-luxury sedan was shown at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it will support megawatt flash charging. It also features rear-hinged coach doors, a first for BYD. The flagship EV will reportedly be the first to feature BYD’s solid-state batteries. BYD executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with Carwow.es last month that the company’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027. Li said BYD is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery technology and its commercialization, and the company plans to prove it next year. BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, plans to begin production of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in 2027. It will initially be produced in limited batches, then scale to mass production closer to the end of the decade. Top comment by Craig Merrow The part about solid state batteries got my attention. I'm looking forward to learning more about how they perform! While BYD has yet to confirm it, introducing the new battery tech in a flagship model would make sense. The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000. Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The brand also sells the U8 (and U8L), a plug-in hybrid luxury off-road SUV, and the U9, a fully electric super-coupe. The extended U8L is Yangwang’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

artigo.texto: A Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) encerrou o terceiro trimestre de 2026 (3T26) com receita de US$ 16,5 bilhões, alta de 21% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. O crescimento foi puxado pela divisão de data centers e inteligência artificial (IA), cujo faturamento avançou 78% na comparação anual. Os resultados da Intel, divulgados nesta quinta-feira (29), também mostraram uma redução de 18% no lucro líquido atribuível à companhia, que passou de US$ 4,1 bilhões para US$ 3,3 bilhões. O lucro diluído por ação, calculado pelos critérios contábeis americanos (GAAP), ficou em US$ 0,60, ante US$ 0,90 um ano antes. Já o lucro por ação ajustado (não-GAAP) alcançou US$ 0,52, frente aos US$ 0,23 registrados no terceiro trimestre de 2025. Data centers e inteligência artificial impulsionam receita A divisão de Data Center e IA (DCAI) registrou receita de US$ 7,3 bilhões no trimestre, crescimento de 78% em relação ao mesmo intervalo do ano passado. A fabricante atribuiu parte da demanda à procura por seus processadores Xeon, utilizados em servidores e sistemas de computação corporativa. Segundo a empresa, a ampliação da capacidade de fornecimento desses chips está entre suas prioridades. O segmento Intel Foundry, responsável pelas operações de fabricação de semicondutores, também apresentou crescimento. A receita chegou a US$ 6,7 bilhões, avanço de 58% na comparação anual. Por outro lado, a divisão de computação para clientes e IA física (CCPG), que inclui processadores voltados a computadores pessoais, registrou faturamento de US$ 8,1 bilhões, queda de 5% em relação ao terceiro trimestre de 2025. Os valores das divisões incluem operações internas entre segmentos, eliminadas no cálculo da receita consolidada da companhia. Margens operacionais avançam, apesar da queda no lucro Embora o lucro líquido tenha recuado, a Intel registrou aumento nas margens de rentabilidade operacional. A margem bruta passou de 38,2% para 43%, enquanto a margem operacional subiu de 5% para 15,3%, uma diferença de 10,3 pontos percentuais na comparação anual. O lucro operacional atingiu aproximadamente US$ 2,5 bilhões, ante US$ 683 milhões no mesmo trimestre do ano anterior. A empresa também informou geração de US$ 5,1 bilhões em caixa proveniente das atividades operacionais. As despesas com pesquisa e desenvolvimento, marketing, gerais e administrativas somaram aproximadamente US$ 4,5 bilhões, frente a US$ 4,4 bilhões um ano antes. Intel prevê receita entre US$ 15 bilhões e US$ 16 bilhões no 4T26 Para o quarto trimestre de 2026 (4T26), a Intel projeta receita entre US$ 15 bilhões e US$ 16 bilhões, abaixo dos US$ 16,5 bilhões registrados no período anterior. A fabricante também prevê lucro diluído por ação de US$ 0,10, considerando os critérios GAAP, e lucro ajustado por ação de US$ 0,25. A estimativa de margem bruta é de 37,1% pelo padrão GAAP e de 38% na base ajustada. Durante a divulgação dos resultados, o diretor financeiro da Intel, David Zinsner, afirmou que a desaceleração do mercado de computadores pessoais deve continuar pelo menos até o primeiro semestre de 2027. A empresa pretende manter investimentos em capacidade produtiva e capital de giro para ampliar o fornecimento de produtos. O que acompanhar nas ações da Intel (INTC)? Negociada na Nasdaq sob o código INTC, a Intel apresentou crescimento de receita em seus negócios de data centers e fabricação de semicondutores, enquanto a divisão voltada à computação de clientes registrou retração. Para os próximos trimestres, os indicadores a acompanhar incluem o ritmo de crescimento das vendas de processadores para servidores, a evolução das margens operacionais e os resultados da Intel Foundry. As projeções para o quarto trimestre também colocam em foco o desempenho da companhia diante da desaceleração do mercado de PCs e dos investimentos necessários para ampliar sua capacidade de produção. Os próximos balanços permitirão acompanhar como essas mudanças se refletem na receita, nos lucros e na geração de caixa da fabricante americana.

artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz's decision to develop its own batteries in-house is already paying big dividends, after the German brand announced that it has developed a pioneering new battery chemistry that will herald cheaper, faster-to-charge batteries that offer 30 per cent more range. Joining the ranks of Tesla, Volkswagen, Ford and Toyota, as well as leading EV giant BYD, Mercedes only opened its substantial eCampus back in 2024 and it was scientists working at the new R&D hub who were behind the new manganese-rich battery tech. No timescale was revealed for when the new Lithium-Manganese-Oxide battery (LMO) or the even more energy-packed Lithium-Nickel-Manganese-Oxide (LNMO) unitwill be rolled out, but the new lithium iron phosphate (LFP)-replacing tech is expected to be introduced within the next two years, ahead of Benz's own solid-state batteries that will launch towards the end of this decade. Read more - 'We won't be left wanting': Solid-state battery-powered cars with a potential 1500km of range likely for Australia - Major battery breakthrough confirmed - The Australian electric car battery breakthrough: Aussie smarts commercialise new battery that could result in a big change for the EVs we drive such as the Tesla Model Y, BYD Seal and more New batteries are greener and more sustainable The new batteries were unwrapped at the premium German brand's 140 Years of Innovation celebrations, where Mercedes scientists said that as well as being superior to the current LFP batteries available in cars like the new Mercedes CLA, its new LMO/LNMO pave the way for a greener, more sustainable future. That's because the manganese-rich chemistries are less reliant on cobalt, with the LNMO completely free of the in-demand element. Cobalt remains problematic for the car industry, with more than three-quarters of it sourced from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) from mines that are known to use unsafe working conditions and environmentally damaging extraction practices. The challenge for Benz, explained the scientists and battery engineers, was to attempt to replicate the same high energy density of its current LFP battery technology without cobalt. New batteries to beat BYD's LFP cells First to launch in the "near future" is the LMO tech, which blends its chemistry with Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) oxide to maintain its energy density, but the big gains will come later with the completely cobalt-free LNMO tech, which costs less to produce than equivalent LFP cells. Crucially, when scaled up to the same size and weight of the equivalent LFP batteries, which have been popularised by BYD, the new tech offers far faster charging and, at least 30 per cent more range. Capable of working with far higher voltages, the new LMO batteries are also said to be safer than existing cells. Mercedes engineers wouldn't be drawn on figures, but if applied to the current 58kWh LFP battery that powers the Mercedes CLA, the new battery will raise the range of the base model from 447km to more than 580km with higher charging rates, potentially above 400kW (+200kW) for a sub-10-minute 10 to 80 per cent top-up. The same power packs are also tolerant of fast DC charging, retaining as much as 80 per cent of their original capacity after more than 1500 charge cycles, in research carried out on non-Benz batteries.
