artigo.texto: - Compared with conventional solutions, Tener+ can reduce container requirements by up to 40% and cut project footprints by 12%. - CATL signed cooperation memorandums with 3 partners and showcased its sodium-ion energy storage system in Australia for the first time. CATL (HKEX: 3750) unveiled its next-generation Tener+ energy storage system with a capacity of 9 MWh, while expanding its presence in Australia's energy storage market through local partnerships. The company launched the product at All Energy Australia 2026 in Melbourne on Wednesday, alongside the Australian debut of its Tener Sodium sodium-ion battery energy storage system. Tener+ targets grid-scale long-duration energy storage projects, aiming to reduce equipment requirements, land use and deployment complexity by increasing storage capacity per container. Compared with conventional solutions, Tener+ can reduce the number of containers needed by up to 40% and shrink project footprints by 12%, according to the battery giant. CATL said the system has a design life of 25 years and uses its proprietary cell technology designed to slow degradation. Customers can choose different configurations based on local climate conditions and project revenue models. Options include cell configurations optimized for high temperatures or offering 3 years of zero degradation. The 2 options address different operating needs, and the zero-degradation feature is not available across all configurations. The system uses a top-exhaust design that directs hot air upward, reducing its impact on neighboring equipment. The company said this helps power conversion systems (PCS) maintain full rated output even in harsh summer conditions. Its intelligent thermal management system can improve round-trip efficiency and reduce auxiliary power consumption. Multiple Tener+ systems can also be commissioned simultaneously with a single click to simplify deployment, CATL said. The launch further expands CATL's Tener product lineup. The company introduced the 6.25-MWh Tener in April 2024, followed by the 9-MWh Tener Stack in May 2025. Tener Sodium, displayed alongside Tener+ in Melbourne, uses a modular cabinet architecture and can deliver more than 30 MWh of system-level storage capacity, giving developers an alternative to lithium-ion technology. CATL said the sodium-ion system can operate at ambient temperatures of up to 55°C (131°F) and achieve a cycle life of more than 10,000 cycles at 45°C. Tener Sodium was launched in June this year. CATL is bringing it to overseas markets and separately announced a partnership with Germany's Intilion earlier on Wednesday, with plans to deploy 3 GWh of sodium-ion energy storage systems in Europe over the next 5 years. Boosting bets on Australia In Australia, CATL signed memorandums of understanding with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney. The Hitachi Energy partnership will combine CATL's DC-side battery products with Hitachi Energy's power conversion systems, laying the groundwork for future integrated solutions in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region. The EPEC Group partnership will focus on grid connection, engineering delivery and system validation, drawing on the testing capabilities of CATL's Xiamen Energy Storage Validation Research Institute (ESVL) to support project deployment. CATL also plans to establish an integrated renewable energy training and innovation center in Western Sydney with UNSW Sydney to develop the skilled workforce needed for the local energy transition. The partnerships reflect CATL's expansion in Australia beyond equipment supply into grid connection, project delivery and long-term services to meet the operating needs of large-scale storage projects. Zane Zhou, CATL's head for Australia, New Zealand and Oceania, said battery value should be assessed over a project's entire lifecycle and the key is whether batteries can meet expected charging and discharging requirements and support customers' participation in Australia's National Electricity Market (NEM). The company said it has deployed more than 3,000 energy storage projects globally, with cumulative installed capacity across its Australian projects exceeding 17 GWh. CATL's global lithium-ion energy storage battery shipments reached 125.0 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 81% year-on-year, giving it the leading market share of 27.1%, according to South Korean market researcher SNE Research.

artigo.texto: Olá, tudo bem? Hoje analisaremos a existência ou não de obrigatoriedade de aquisição de créditos de carbono por seguradoras e entidades de previdência, de acordo com o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF). Mais especificamente, veremos o que a Suprema Corte decidiu no julgamento da ADI n.º 7.795/DF. Vamos ao que interessa! Obrigatoriedade de aquisição de créditos de carbono por seguradoras de previdência Caso concreto analisado na ADI n.º 7.795 Do ajuizamento da ADI e da norma impugnada A ADI n.º 7.795 foi ajuizada pela Confederação Nacional das Empresas de Seguros Gerais, Previdência Privada e Vida, Saúde Suplementar e Capitalização (CNseg) com o objetivo de que o STF declarasse inconstitucional o art. 56 da Lei n.º 15.042/2024. Essa Legislação instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE), assim redigido em sua redação original: Art. 56. Em atendimento ao disposto no art. 84 do Decreto-Lei nº 73, de 21 de novembro de 1966, as sociedades seguradoras, entidades abertas de previdência complementar, sociedades de capitalização e resseguradores locais deverão, para cumprimento das diretrizes previstas no inciso V do caput do art. 2º do regulamento anexo à Resolução do Conselho Monetário Nacional nº 4.993, de 24 de março de 2022, e na modalidade referida no inciso V do caput do art. 7º do mesmo regulamento, adquirir, até o limite previsto na mencionada Resolução ou em norma que vier a substituí-la, mas observado o mínimo de 1% (um por cento) ao ano dos recursos de suas reservas técnicas e das provisões, os ativos ambientais previstos no inciso VII do caput do art. 2º desta Lei ou cotas de fundos de investimentos em ativos ambientais. Parágrafo único. As sociedades seguradoras e demais entidades a que se refere este artigo deverão cumprir todas as obrigações previstas no caput a partir do ano de entrada em vigor desta Lei. Essa Lei, que foi promulgada em 11/12/2024, foi alterada naquele mesmo mês, em 26/12/2024, para reduzir o percentual de 1% para 0,5%, mantendo as demais previsões. Assim, a ADI ajuizada pela CNseg impugnou a norma tanto em sua redação original quanto na redação alterada. Argumentos da CNseg para requerer a inconstitucionalidade Dentre os principais argumentos veiculados pela CNseg, podemos verificar que a Confederação aventou tanto a inconstitucionalidade formal quanto a inconstitucionalidade material do dispositivo. No que se refere às formalidades constitucionais, a parte autora alegou que houve inobservância da reserva de lei complementar para regular o sistema financeiro e a previdência (arts. 21, inciso VIII, 192 e 202, todos da CF). Além disso, sustentou ter havido ofensa ao devido processo legislativo, haja vista que houve aprovação de emenda parlamentar sem motivação durante a tramitação do projeto de lei. Quanto à inconstitucionalidade material, alegou violação aos princípios da livre iniciativa e livre concorrência, proporcionalidade e razoabilidade, do poluidor-pagador, da isonomia e da segurança jurídica. O que o STF decidiu? Há obrigatoriedade? O Plenário do STF, por unanimidade, julgou procedente a ação para declarar inconstitucional o art. 56, caput e parágrafo único, da Lei n.º 15.042/2024, tanto em sua redação original quanto na redação dada pela Lei n.º 15.076/2024. Para o Supremo, embora a estratégia legislativa de estimular o mercado de carbono seja um objetivo legítimo, a escolha das entidades afetadas baseou-se apenas na sua elevada liquidez e vasta reserva financeira, e não na sua responsabilidade por danos ambientais. Isto é, o legislador “aproveitou” que se trata de setor com alto poder financeiro alto e com liquidez e resolveu atribuir o ônus a essas instituições. Só que o problema é que essa responsabilidade que lhes foi atribuída ofende aos princípios da isonomia e do poluidor-pagador, visto que tais instituições não são as principais emissoras de gases de efeito estufa. Além disso, entendeu o STF que a imposição de percentuais fixos de investimento nas reservas técnicas sem permitir que as entidades avaliem a segurança, liquidez e rentabilidade desses ativos configura interferência indevida na livre iniciativa e na livre concorrência. Isso porque tais aspectos são fundamentais para garantir o cumprimento de suas obrigações perante os segurados. Outra inconstitucionalidade material da norma foi o fato de ser desproporcional, uma vez que os impactos negativos sobre a integridade do sistema atuarial superam eventuais ganhos ambientais, dada a baixa participação dos sujeitos atingidos no dano ambiental que se pretende combater. Ou seja, retomou-se a ideia de que não são essas entidades as principais poluidoras, de modo que a obrigatoriedade de aquisição de créditos de carbono por empresas efetivamente poluidoras seria mais razoável e proporcional. Por fim, entendeu o STF que houve violação ao princípio da segurança jurídica e da proteção da confiança legítima, pois sequer houve vacatio legis ou a fixação de um período razoável de adaptação para a nova regra de alocação de recursos, instituída de forma abrupta e em cenário de incerteza e volatilidade do mercado de carbono. Havia inconstitucionalidade formal? Embora tenha reconhecido a inconstitucionalidade material, o STF afastou a inconstitucionalidade formal. No que se refere à reserva de lei complementar, o STF afastou o vício formal ao concluir que a exigência do art. 192 restringe-se à estrutura do Sistema Financeiro Nacional (SFN), e não aos negócios jurídicos ou regras operacionais de alocação de ativos. Do mesmo modo, o artigo 202 da CF refere-se apenas a diretrizes gerais de previdência complementar. E no que tange à emenda parlamentar sem motivação, o Supremo entendeu que a CF não condiciona a validade de emendas parlamentares a pareceres técnicos ou justificativas expressas, sendo legítimos o fatiamento legislativo e os acordos de liderança no trâmite bicameral. Explicando brevemente, essa emenda parlamentar foi inserida quando o processo estava no Senad

artigo.texto: The company is developing iron-chromium flow batteries to support renewable energy storage at scale. In this interview, Redox One outlines its technology, progress towards commercial deployment and international ambitions. It also explains why Cyprus, home to its headquarters, could become an early market and demonstration base for wider regional adoption. From development to deployment Redox One was established in 2022 by Tharisa plc to develop iron-chromium redox flow battery technology for safe, sustainable and cost-effective energy storage. Building on Tharisa’s expertise in chromium production, mining, metallurgy and chemical processing, the company was created to address one of the most significant challenges of the energy transition: storing renewable energy reliably at scale. A key strength is our vertically integrated approach, spanning chromium resources, electrolyte production and complete energy storage systems. This provides greater control over quality, supply security, cost and long-term scalability. One of our biggest challenges has been moving from technology development to fully integrated, real-world energy storage systems. Important milestones include the successful operation of demonstration systems at our European Technology Centre in Germany and the development of a 625 kWh demonstration system in China. Our next focus is advancing larger demonstration projects and progressing towards commercial deployments that can support renewable energy growth worldwide. Storage built for duration Our iron-chromium redox flow battery technology is designed to transform intermittent renewable energy into dependable, dispatchable power. It complements lithium-ion batteries by addressing applications that require longer-duration storage, high utilisation rates and long operating lifetimes. The technology uses abundant materials such as iron and chromium and is engineered for decades of operation with minimal capacity degradation. Safety is a major advantage. The system uses a water-based, non-flammable electrolyte that eliminates the thermal runaway risks associated with conventional lithium-ion batteries. Flow batteries also offer significant economic benefits for long-duration storage because power and energy capacity can be scaled independently. Extending storage duration primarily requires additional electrolyte and storage tanks rather than a complete battery system expansion. From a sustainability perspective, the electrolyte can be reused and recycled, while the battery chemistry relies on widely available materials. Together, these attributes create a safe, sustainable and cost-effective solution for large-scale energy storage. International growth Our commercialisation strategy is international from the outset. We are advancing the technology through demonstration projects and strategic partnerships across Europe, China and South Africa, while engaging with utilities, industrial customers, renewable energy developers and technology partners. Our immediate priority is to validate demonstration systems and use operational data to support larger commercial projects. We see strong opportunities in mining, industrial, utility-scale and renewable energy applications where long-duration storage can improve reliability, flexibility and asset utilisation. Our connection to Tharisa provides access to critical raw materials and metallurgical expertise, enabling participation across the value chain, from electrolyte production to complete energy storage systems. Cyprus could potentially play an important role as a gateway to Southern Europe, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East. Over the next three to five years, our goal is to develop a growing portfolio of commercial installations and establish scalable manufacturing and supply-chain partnerships. Cyprus as an early market Cyprus is home to our headquarters and an important part of our long-term growth strategy. As an island electricity system with abundant solar resources, it faces many of the challenges that long-duration energy storage is designed to solve. Our technology can store excess renewable electricity during periods of strong solar generation and deliver it when demand exceeds supply. This improves grid flexibility, reduces renewable energy curtailment, enhances energy security and helps lower reliance on imported fuels. We believe Cyprus could become an important early market for sustainable energy storage and a valuable demonstration platform for wider deployment across Southern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean. More broadly, Cyprus has the potential to strengthen its position as a regional deep-tech and clean-energy hub. Faster pathways for demonstration projects, targeted funding programmes and closer collaboration between government, industry, universities and investors would encourage more innovation-led companies to establish and expand their operations on the island.

artigo.texto: FirstEnergy’s long-term pipeline of data center load — contracted and other potential load — grew 4.8% to 26 GW in the third quarter from the second quarter, according to an earnings presentation on Wednesday. FirstEnergy is seeing broad interest across its system, including in Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania and West Virginia, Brian Tierney, FirstEnergy chairman, president and CEO, said during an earnings conference call. The first wave of data centers are expected to be online in the 2030 timeframe, but “the large customers that you might think of, the hyperscalers, the legitimate developers, are looking well beyond that, and they're doing so across our service territory,” Tierney said. FirstEnergy’s overall data center pipeline jumped to 6 GW in West Virginia, up from 4.3 GW three months ago, according to the company. Two FirstEnergy utilities — Monongahela Power and Potomac Edison Co. — are seeking permission from the West Virginia Public Service Commission to build the Maidsville Energy Center, a roughly $2.7 billion project that includes a 1,200-MW, gas-fired power plant and three solar projects totaling 70 MW. FirstEnergy expects the PSC will issue a certificate for the project in the fourth quarter, according to Tierney. The utilities have signed a reservation agreement with Siemens Energy for turbines for the project, with a 2030 delivery date, according to FirstEnergy’s quarterly filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. They have also issued a request for proposals for 3 GW of combined-cycle turbines for power plants that would serve data center load in the state, Tierney said. “All other major contracts are on track to be signed shortly after we receive a commission order,” Tierney said. “Maidsville is an important project on its own, but we see it as the first of a broader set of opportunities in West Virginia.” FirstEnergy is investigating potential “bridge” generation that could be built quickly to serve data centers while transmission infrastructure and larger power plants are in development and under construction, according to Tierney. “What we're seeing from customers is, if they want a 1-GW type campus, they're looking at seeing if they can start with a building that might be about 100 MW in the near term,” Tierney said. Possible bridge options include reciprocating engines, fuel cells and batteries, he said, and once a final generating solution is in place, the smaller assets could be moved to other large load projects. FirstEnergy expects that the data center demand across its six-state footprint will drive up its transmission investments by at least 25%, or $4.75 billion, over its current $19 billion transmission investment plan, Tierney said. A gigawatt of data center load requires roughly $250 million in transmission upgrades, FirstEnergy estimates. Meanwhile, FirstEnergy’s weather-adjusted load increased 1.2% to 40.1 million MWh in the third quarter and demand increased 1% to 148.6 million MWh over the previous 12 months, according to the earnings presentation. “We are seeing broad strength in manufacturing activity, including metals, oil and gas, and chemical sectors, along with increasing data center demand,” FirstEnergy CFO Jon Taylor said on the conference call. On the financial front, FirstEnergy’s utilities earned a combined 9.5% return on equity, with a 53% equity share and a $29.8 billion rate base over the last 12 months, according to the presentation. That’s up from an 8.8% ROE, with a 52% equity ratio and a $26.3 billion rate base over a 12-month period in 2023. FirstEnergy’s net income jumped to $557 million on $4.5 billion in revenue in the third quarter, up from $441 million and $4.1 billion in the same period last year. The increase was partly driven by income tax benefits and higher customer demand, according to the presentation. FirstEnergy’s utilities have about 6 million customers in Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, West Virginia, Maryland and New York.

artigo.texto: Can Tho proposes cooperation on a 3,000-hectare mangrove forest carbon project. Can Tho has proposed collaborating with Canada and other international partners to implement a mangrove carbon project in the former Soc Trang area, aiming to contribute to ecosystem restoration and create sustainable livelihoods for local people. Can Tho hopes to cooperate with the Canadian Government, the Canadian Embassy, and international partners to develop a high-quality mangrove carbon project in the former Soc Trang area, initially as a pilot project covering approximately 2,000-3,000 hectares in Vinh Hai-Cu Lao Dung. The city hopes to harness the potential of blue carbon, creating additional resources for forest protection and restoration, while simultaneously developing sustainable livelihoods for coastal residents. This information was provided by Mr. Tran Chi Hung, Vice Chairman of the People's Committee of Can Tho City, during a working session on the afternoon of October 28th with a delegation from the Canadian Embassy led by Ms. Francesca Bellone, Counselor and Head of Development Cooperation, regarding the Technical Assistance Project aimed at building capacity to implement climate change mitigation plans and mobilize sustainable financing for forest protection and development, including a high-quality forest carbon market (C4G Project). Mr. Tran Chi Hung stated that Can Tho has approximately 23,000 hectares of forest land, of which over 14,000 hectares are coastal forests, including nearly 1,800 hectares of natural forest and the remainder being planted forests. With a coastline of about 72km, the city has great potential for developing and restoring mangrove ecosystems, but the need for investment in this area remains significant. Over the past period, the city has focused on directing the restoration of forest areas encroached upon by tidal surges, limiting degradation and gradually reforesting affected mangrove areas. Forest restoration not only aims to protect the environment and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, but also contributes to biodiversity conservation, marine ecosystem restoration, and fisheries resource protection. According to Mr. Tran Chi Hung, through the C4G Project and other coastal community projects supported by the Canadian government , the city aims to combine forest protection and development with improving livelihoods and increasing blue carbon stocks, especially in the former Soc Trang area and areas with large ethnic minority populations. City leaders highly appreciate the support of international organizations, government agencies, and businesses for forest development and climate change response efforts in the locality. The city hopes that the Canadian Embassy will continue to connect with organizations, businesses, and investors experienced in the field of green carbon credits and forest carbon, thereby supporting capacity building for local officials and citizens participating in this relatively new market. Ms. Francesca Bellone, Counsellor and Head of Development Cooperation at the Canadian Embassy, assessed that Can Tho has the potential to make a significant contribution to green carbon development in the Mekong Delta thanks to its mangrove forest ecosystem. Canada is interested in supporting Vietnam's development towards low emissions, enhancing its resilience to climate change, protecting the environment, and promoting the energy transition. According to Francesca Bellone, blue carbon is increasingly being considered as a solution that combines nature conservation, economic development, and climate change adaptation. Through its collaboration with CARE, Canada expects Can Tho to have the opportunity to lead in initiatives to develop this sector, while contributing to Vietnam's goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 and the fulfillment of national climate commitments. You may also like Francesca Bellone believes that enhanced coordination among local authorities, departments, and development partners will help advance green carbon initiatives. She suggested that Can Tho consider establishing a focal point for coordination among agencies, while also connecting with the national-level green carbon development process, to facilitate the continued implementation of cooperative activities. Regarding the C4G Project, Ms. Le Kim Dung, Country Director of CARE in Vietnam, stated that CARE has been operating in Vietnam since 1989, focusing on economic development programs, particularly for women and ethnic minorities, climate change adaptation, and humanitarian assistance in the event of natural disasters. The C4G project, funded by the Canadian government, aims to prepare local communities to access opportunities from the carbon market when legal conditions permit. The project is being implemented in four locations, including three northern localities with activities related to terrestrial forests and Can Tho, focusing on mangrove forests in the former Soc Trang area. According to Ms. Dung, mangrove forests not only play a role in protecting coastlines, mitigating natural disaster risks, conserving biodiversity, and maintaining community livelihoods, but also have the ability to absorb and store carbon. This provides a basis for the locality to research and develop blue carbon, contributing to achieving emission reduction goals and adapting to climate change. The C4G project was approved by the People's Committee of Can Tho City in August 2025 with a total budget of over 16.43 billion VND, equivalent to approximately 896,667 Canadian dollars, entirely from non-refundable aid. The project, implemented in the communes of Cù Lao Dung, Lai Hòa, Vĩnh Hải and the wards of Vĩnh Phước and Vĩnh Châu, is expected to last until March 31, 2028. artigo.texto: October 29, 2026 - The City of Savannah is inviting residents, businesses, and neighborhood groups to complete a data center ordinance survey to share input on the future of data centers in Savannah. The City and Chatham County are both considering an amendment to the zoning ordinance that would define data centers as a land use and institute development standards tailored to Savannah. City officials are working with the Chatham County - Savannah Metropolitan Planning (MPC) Commission and Chatham County to draft a document to present to City Council for review and recommended for adoption in January 2027. Public feedback will help inform the proposed zoning ordinance. Data centers, physical facilities, rooms, or buildings that house IT infrastructure: computer systems, servers, storage arrays, and networking hardware to store, process, and distribute digital information, have existed since the 1940s. Locally, they are critical infrastructure powering hospitals, utilities, emergency services, and government resources. Additionally, schools and local businesses utilize them for records keeping and electronic mail. With the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), newer and larger data centers are being built at a rapid pace, particularly across Georgia, demanding exponentially more resources than older facilities. “Savannah must be prepared to understand what our infrastructure can and cannot accommodate, where the line exists between community benefit and community harm, and what is best for each of our neighborhoods,” said Mayor Van R. Johnson, II. “The decisions we make now will have a lasting impact on Savannah’s future, our public safety, environmental health, quality of life, and ability to remain an economically thriving community for all.” Addressed in proposed ordinance: Public review: Required public notice and engagement, which may include special use permit process Definitions: Minor, major, adapted reuse data centers, with modified rules for small, low-impact facilities Location and neighborhood protection: Required distances from homes, schools, parks, places of worship, hospitals, and other sensitive areas, along with noise/buffer regulations Power: Electricity usage and limits on use of generators Water: Water usage, water-conserving cooling technology, stormwater management, and wastewater discharge, subject to appropriate regulations Oversight: Application requirements, development agreement items, ongoing reporting, and plan for safe closure of facility Emergency response: Savannah Fire Department review/approval of life safety systems, fire protection, hazard mitigation, and emergency response plans Decommissioning: Plans for equipment removal and management of hazardous materials Appearance: Appropriate building height, landscaping, buffers, according to design standards Community benefit: Major data centers could be required to contribute through infrastructure upgrades, reinvestment or other commitments A draft ordinance will be posted in November for review and comment Attend a public hearing - Hearings before the Metropolitan Planning Commission (MPC) and Savannah City Council will be announced as scheduled City officials are meeting with local business owners, residents, and stakeholders to address questions before finalization of ordinance To learn more or to take the survey, visit //savannahga.gov/datacenters.

artigo.texto: MOUNTAIN HOME, Idaho — Mountain Home City Council approved an emergency moratorium temporarily blocking data center applications and permits after residents packed city hall, but some neighbors want a full ban. "I would say about time," neighbor Dara Corvus said. As Idaho News 6 reported Monday, Mayor Rich Sykes sent a letter to company owner Dan Weitz after Sykes said Weitz dropped off plans for four three-story buildings — about 3.4 million square feet total — planned for the Bennett Ranch Industrial Campus. WATCH: Mountain Home pauses data center projects after packed city hall meeting The letter noted that Weitz has not submitted a land-use application, conditional use permit or building permit. And under the city's current zoning code, data centers are not listed as a permitted or conditional use. But for some of the neighbors who came to city hall, a pause doesn't settle their concerns. "I am disappointed that it took this many people showing up after months to get this one thing addressed. This is something that has been brought up many times," neighbor Andrew Toth said. Others thanked the council for taking action but said they want Mountain Home to go further. "We're very appreciative about. However, I want to advocate for us to add data centers on the prohibited list so that this is not something that moves forward in the future," neighbor Aaron Madison said. The question on many neighbors' minds now is what happens when the pause is up. RELATED | Thousands of acres of public land south of Boise eyed for new data center Corvus said she wants the city to use that time to draw a much harder line. "I would like to see a very clear definition for a data center and outright ban them, especially these large AI data centers," Corvus said. The city said it's been working since July to define and categorize data centers in its zoning code. Under Idaho state law, an emergency moratorium can last no longer than 182 days — six months.

artigo.texto: ECOWAS battery storage rules agreed in Accra as Ghana procures 200MW of batteries ECOWAS energy ministers meeting in Accra on 22 October adopted a regional directive on battery energy storage, setting a common framework for storage on West Africa’s grids, as Ghana’s energy minister, John Abdulai Jinapor, told them his country is procuring a 200MW battery system and a 200MWp solar plant to charge it. ECOWAS member states now have a common framework for deploying battery energy storage, after the region’s ministers in charge of energy adopted a directive on battery energy storage systems and other storage technologies at their 16th meeting, held in Accra on 22 October, according to the ECOWAS Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency (ECREEE). The directive covers grid-connected and off-grid storage and sets out measures at regional and national level on how storage is licensed and how it takes part in the electricity market, with requirements for the safe handling and recycling of batteries, and member states can use it as the basis for their own regulations. Opening the meeting, Jinapor said Ghana was procuring a 200MW grid-scale battery energy storage system together with a 200MWp solar PV plant that would supply the power to charge it, adding that “Battery Energy Storage Systems have become increasingly important to modern electricity systems”. He told ministers that Ghana had raised its payments to independent power producers from about 40% of their monthly bills to nearly 100%, and that “the future of energy security is not just simply about the power we generate”. Amin Amidu Sulemani, the ECOWAS Commissioner for Infrastructure, Energy and Digitalisation, told the meeting that “if we operate independently, it will be difficult in the energy sector”, and said battery storage could support solar power at peak demand and lower the cost of producing electricity. Some 61% of people in the region have access to electricity, leaving nearly 180 million without it, according to figures cited at the meeting. Ministers were also due to consider an amendment to the ECOWAS Regional Electricity Market Levy regulation, which funds the regional institutions that run West Africa’s electricity market, among them the West African Power Pool and the regional regulator ERERA. The ministerial session followed two days, on 20 and 21 October, in which experts from member states examined the storage directive and the levy regulation, with ECREEE’s delegation led by its executive director, Gibson Obasi.

artigo.texto: Data Center Opponents Stage Halloween Protest at City Hall ’Tis the season for Jeff Bezos masks and angry pumpkins. Philadelphians love an excuse to get creative … especially when they’re protesting. Two-thousand South Philly residents pelted Mayor Richardson Dilworth with tomatoes when he tried to stop them from parking in the Broad Street median. Bucks County Batman handed out water to protesters during the Black Lives Matter marches in 2020. Chinatown activists carried such beautiful art — a gorgeous red and gold dragon, a mini version of the Chinatown gate on Arch Street — to protest the Sixers’ arena that it spurred an entire art exhibit. More recently, people have worn inflatable T-Rex suits to march for the Academy of Natural Sciences. And this week, there was Rosie the Riveter next to someone dressed as a pumpkin, passing out flyers outside of City Hall. Activists from the No Data Centers in Philly coalition gathered to lobby City Council members and inform the public about the financial, environmental, public health, and surveillance risks posed by the behemoth facilities. While Philadelphia doesn’t have hyperscale data centers yet, Amazon is building a 250-acre data center complex in Bucks County, and Plymouth and Upper Merion Township residents have been protesting two different proposed projects in the past year. In Chester County, disgruntled East Whiteland Township residents introduced a ballot referendum to add two representatives to its Board of Supervisors, in part because of frustrations over how the handling of a planned data center on a Superfund site. Philly activists are worried because two locations — the Bellwether District and 2600 Grant Avenue, near the Northeast Philadelphia Airport — are big enough for the massive data center projects that have dominated national headlines in recent months. There aren’t any plans for any data centers on those sites yet. But organizers want City Council to pass a moratorium on data center development now, so that Philadelphia has adequate time to study impacts before they agree to build within city limits. Residents in other municipalities, including Upper Merion, have rallied to pass data center ordinances in their communities, placing strict limits on where and how a developer can build, only to find that those laws don’t apply since zoning board permits and applications were filed before the law passed. After No Data Centers in Philly’s first 200-some person protest in September, Mayor Cherelle Parker created a task force to develop recommendations for regulatory guidelines around data centers in Philadelphia. It’ll produce a report this coming summer. Activists say that gives developers too much time to get a project in the pipeline. “Developers are rushing to get in proposals now before the AI bubble bursts,” says Alex Bomstein, executive director of the Clean Air Council, which is part of the No Data Centers in Philly coalition. “It’s been concerning to hear City Council members say that they want to wait. They don’t want to do a moratorium until they see what happens. “That’s the exact opposite order. We need a moratorium to give the task force time — time to act, time to do its study, time for City Council to review that report and legislate on it.” Bomstein says they decided on a Halloween theme for Thursday’s protest because “data centers are scary.” The organizers handed out masks of Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos — two of the most prominent data center advocates, while activists passed out candy and spoke with passersby about their concerns over data centers. Dozens more lined up to go inside City Hall to lobby City Council members. Elena Emelchin Brunner is an immigration justice organizer with Asian Americans United. She says she came out to the protest because she’s concerned about the role data centers play in video surveillance of immigrant communities. “All of that data gets stored in data centers,” she says. “The city actually does have a lot of power to keep our communities safe. To the extent that they have power to do that, we’re asking them to put our people first; don’t put profit first.” It’s a message city leaders hear again and again. And in all the instances of Philadelphians protesting creatively — okay, maybe not the tomato hurlers — the festive community actions have introduced a bit of levity into the oft-maddening civic engagement process. It’s discouraging to call or write to elected officials and then never hear back or to throw a 311 request seemingly into the void. Perhaps donning cat ears or the infamous Guy Fawkes mask from V for Vendetta makes it all more fun. And who knows? Maybe a stegosaurus showing up at Kenyatta Johnson’s office is what Council needs to get them to vote.

artigo.texto: Binghamton joins new DOE-backed consortium to boost U.S. battery manufacturing BattMan Accelerator integrates super intelligence, advanced manufacturing to speed innovation Binghamton University is a member of a new national consortium to accelerate the transition of energy storage innovations from discovery to domestic manufacturing. The new Battery Manufacturing (BattMan) Accelerator, led by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), will bring together national laboratories, universities, and industry partners to address critical barriers in scaling next-generation battery technologies. Jie Xiao, a Binghamton University alumna, serves as accelerator director. “Breakthroughs in battery science must be matched by our ability to manufacture them at scale,” said Jie, the Boeing Martin Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Washington and a Battelle Fellow at PNNL. “This effort brings together the tools, data, and partnerships needed to design manufacturable solutions from the start and accelerate their transition into industry.” The BattMan Accelerator will bridge the gap between discovery and manufacturing while establishing comprehensive manufacturing systems with super intelligence that integrate materials development, process design, and production in a seamless manner. Nobel laureate M. Stanley Whittingham, SUNY distinguished professor of chemistry, will serve as the lead investigator from Binghamton. He noted that the accelerator’s goals align closely with efforts of the Binghamton-led battery ecosystem that includes New Energy New York and the NSF Energy Storage Engine in Upstate New York. “Incorporating super intelligence into both research and manufacturing allows us to move from trial-and-error to predictive design,” Whittngham said. “This capability is key to accelerating innovation while ensuring technologies can be produced reliably and affordably at scale.” Whittingham said he expects close interactions between the New York efforts and BattMan. Binghamton is one of five university partners; the others are the University of Washington, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and the University of Michigan. Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratories are also partners. The BattMan Accelerator aligns with the DOE’s Genesis vision to integrate super intelligence, materials science, and advanced manufacturing into a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem. The initiative seeks to lower manufacturing costs, speed up development from lab to scale, and boost U.S. leadership in energy storage manufacturing through scientific innovation.

artigo.texto: Bulloch County data center committee asks for more time before moratorium expires A Bulloch County committee is seeking a 180-day extension of the current moratorium on new data center applications to complete zoning regulations. Bulloch County data center committee asks for more time before moratorium expires A Bulloch County committee is seeking a 180-day extension of the current moratorium on new data center applications to complete zoning regulations. A newly formed committee in Bulloch County is requesting an extension of the county's moratorium on new data center applications to allow more time to develop zoning regulations. The 15-member committee, tasked with reviewing proposed zoning rules and making recommendations to the Board of Commissioners, held its first meeting Monday night. The current moratorium is set to expire on December 31, but committee members are asking for an additional 180 days to finalize regulations before new applications can be submitted. The committee plans to meet twice a month and elected a chairman and vice chairman during the meeting. "We don't want the moratorium to expire until we have a complete set of ordinances so that when if somebody is interested in bringing a data center in, they know what the rules are and they know what the expectations are, and then through that process, the citizens know that we've done due diligence to make sure that things are fair for everyone," said Frank Davis, chairman of the Data Center Committee. David Bennett, chairman of the Bulloch County Commission, expressed his thoughts on the timeline. "I’m fine with all those things. You know, going into this, we knew that our moratorium is will end on the 31st of December. I knew realistically that this committee is not going to be able to provide us answers by then. I want them to provide us intelligent, well thought out, rational recommendations to the board of commissioners. I didn't feel like they'd be able to do that in three months," Bennett said. The committee will focus on four key areas: water, electricity, land use, and the application process. The chairman stated the goal is to complete the committee's work by the summer. The next meeting is scheduled for Monday.

artigo.texto: What is a BESS? BESS is a battery electric storage system. As the name suggests, the system stores power for future use. This past April, TVA and Tenaska, one of the largest privately held energy companies in the United States, signed a long-term energy storage agreement for a 225-megawatt/900-megawatt hour storage project in East Tennessee. The Bobwhite Energy Storage project in Hawkins County will generate an estimated $300 million investment as well as annual tax revenue for the county. It will be located in the Hawkins County Industrial Park. This project will not only provide economic value but will benefit the entire region by providing energy to the electric grid during high demand (such as weather extremes) or high-rate periods. The battery energy storage system stores energy when there is excess and distributes it when needed. BESS is quite different in operation from crypto-mining and data centers. Crypto-mining and data centers require vast amounts of energy and water on a 24/7 basis. As stated above, BESS draws energy (charges) when there is excess, in periods of low demand. BESS distributes energy (discharges) when there is a need, resulting in lower costs to local utilities and electric cooperatives that supply power to consumers. Care NET has invited Tenaska to hold an informational meeting for the public on Monday, Nov. 9 at 6 p.m. at Holston Electric Cooperative, located at 1200 West Main Street in Rogersville. Tenaska staff will present information about the Bobwhite project and battery energy storage systems. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity for questions. Care NET is a local environmental group with members in four East Tennessee counties: Hawkins, Hancock, Greene, and Grainger. The public is encouraged to attend. For more information, contact Care NET at carenetsc@gmail.com.

artigo.texto: A questão é levantada por material Dezeen editor americano Ben Drith. A construção de centros de dados tem sido um tema de intenso debate nos Estados Unidos nos últimos dois anos. As grandes estruturas retangulares que abrigam servidores para computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial estão sendo construídas em áreas suburbanas e rurais, enquanto crescem as preocupações com seu impacto no meio ambiente e nas comunidades locais. Segundo a pesquisadora espanhola Marina Otero Verzier, vencedora do Prêmio Wheelwright de 2022, os data centers são, em grande parte, um exemplo de projeto deficiente. Tradicionalmente, eles têm sido vistos principalmente como objetos de engenharia, onde a eficiência e as características técnicas eram os principais critérios, em vez da qualidade arquitetônica ou da interação com o meio ambiente. A dimensão do problema está crescendo junto com a demanda por poder computacional. De acordo com os dados citados no artigo da Dezeen, quase 70% da população dos EUA se opõe à construção de data centers. Ao mesmo tempo, prevê-se que os gastos globais com essa infraestrutura ultrapassem US$ 800 bilhões por ano até 2026. Daniel English, cofundador e sócio-gerente da Legacy Investing, uma empresa de investimentos especializada em imóveis para data centers, acredita que os arquitetos foram historicamente excluídos do projeto dessas instalações por serem vistas exclusivamente como sistemas de engenharia. Agora, ele acredita que é importante encontrar maneiras de integrá-las ao cotidiano das comunidades. “A arquitetura de um edifício importa”, afirma Rob LoBuono, chefe da área de projetos de missão crítica da Gensler. Ele diz que um projeto bem pensado pode ajudar os edifícios a se integrarem à paisagem local ou a criarem uma expressão arquitetônica singular. Da camuflagem de fachadas à integração nas cidades Uma das abordagens mais comuns hoje em dia é alterar a aparência dos data centers para que se integrem melhor ao ambiente ao redor. Por exemplo, a Gensler está projetando um hipercentro de 7,5 GW em Utah com fachadas que ecoam o ritmo das montanhas do deserto. Para um complexo no Arizona, o estúdio planejou usar aço Corten, que adquire uma pátina característica. No entanto, Marina Otero Verzier alerta para o perigo de reduzir o papel do arquiteto ao mero projeto decorativo da estrutura. Em sua opinião, os especialistas também devem influenciar a escolha dos materiais, as relações energéticas e ambientais, o planejamento espacial e a interação com as comunidades. Uma abordagem alternativa foi apresentada pelo estúdio de arquitetura Grimshaw na Bienal de Arquitetura de Veneza de 2025. Seu conceito envolve a integração de um centro de dados em uma área urbana de uso misto com residências, oficinas, lojas e uma fazenda urbana. Um dos elementos-chave do projeto é o aproveitamento do calor residual dos servidores para aquecer os edifícios ao redor. Essa abordagem nos permite considerar o centro de dados não como uma instalação técnica isolada, mas como parte da infraestrutura urbana, cujos recursos podem ser utilizados em benefício da comunidade. Ao mesmo tempo, a implementação de tais conceitos é complicada por requisitos de segurança, isolamento acústico e fornecimento estável de energia. Na prática, um cenário mais provável seria combinar data centers com campus tecnológicos, áreas verdes e outras funções. A integração em edifícios existentes ou em locais subterrâneos também poderia reduzir a necessidade de grandes estruturas separadas. No entanto, a construção de data centers em arranha-céus continua sendo um desafio devido ao custo, aos requisitos de manutenção dos servidores e à velocidade do projeto. Outras soluções incluem a reutilização de instalações industriais desativadas e o uso de materiais de construção alternativos. A Microsoft, por exemplo, utilizou madeira maciça em projetos de data centers, buscando maneiras de reduzir o impacto ambiental da construção. Centros de dados como infraestrutura pública Marina Otero Verzier propõe uma reformulação mais ampla da própria tipologia dos centros de dados. Em vez de concentrar o poder computacional em complexos comerciais fechados, ela vislumbra um futuro em uma infraestrutura distribuída que possa funcionar como um repositório público de conhecimento coletivo. Na opinião dela, a arquitetura dos futuros centros de dados deve levar em consideração diferentes tipos de dados, as necessidades das pessoas e as restrições ecológicas do planeta. Isso abre a oportunidade de abandonar a imagem de caixas fechadas e bunkers em favor de estruturas que interajam com a cidade e a sociedade. O principal desafio não é apenas tornar os centros de dados mais atraentes visualmente. Trata-se de encontrar um modelo em que sua construção e operação tenham um menor impacto ambiental e a própria infraestrutura beneficie as áreas onde está localizada. Foto principal: Campus do centro de dados de IA da Microsoft em Fairwater, em construção no condado de Racine, Wisconsin. Foto: C. Flaten / Shutterstock Leia também: O Google derrubou ilegalmente 400 mil árvores para construir centros de dados na Finlândia. Centros de dados criam “ilhas de calor” que ameaçam 340 milhões de pessoas — estudo A SpaceX e a Tesla planejam construir o maior edifício do mundo.

artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz's decision to develop its own batteries in-house is already paying big dividends, after the German brand announced that it has developed a pioneering new battery chemistry that will herald cheaper, faster-to-charge batteries that offer 30 per cent more range. Joining the ranks of Tesla, Volkswagen, Ford and Toyota, as well as leading EV giant BYD, Mercedes only opened its substantial eCampus back in 2024 and it was scientists working at the new R&D hub who were behind the new manganese-rich battery tech. No timescale was revealed for when the new Lithium-Manganese-Oxide battery (LMO) or the even more energy-packed Lithium-Nickel-Manganese-Oxide (LNMO) unitwill be rolled out, but the new lithium iron phosphate (LFP)-replacing tech is expected to be introduced within the next two years, ahead of Benz's own solid-state batteries that will launch towards the end of this decade. Read more - 'We won't be left wanting': Solid-state battery-powered cars with a potential 1500km of range likely for Australia - Major battery breakthrough confirmed - The Australian electric car battery breakthrough: Aussie smarts commercialise new battery that could result in a big change for the EVs we drive such as the Tesla Model Y, BYD Seal and more New batteries are greener and more sustainable The new batteries were unwrapped at the premium German brand's 140 Years of Innovation celebrations, where Mercedes scientists said that as well as being superior to the current LFP batteries available in cars like the new Mercedes CLA, its new LMO/LNMO pave the way for a greener, more sustainable future. That's because the manganese-rich chemistries are less reliant on cobalt, with the LNMO completely free of the in-demand element. Cobalt remains problematic for the car industry, with more than three-quarters of it sourced from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) from mines that are known to use unsafe working conditions and environmentally damaging extraction practices. The challenge for Benz, explained the scientists and battery engineers, was to attempt to replicate the same high energy density of its current LFP battery technology without cobalt. New batteries to beat BYD's LFP cells First to launch in the "near future" is the LMO tech, which blends its chemistry with Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) oxide to maintain its energy density, but the big gains will come later with the completely cobalt-free LNMO tech, which costs less to produce than equivalent LFP cells. Crucially, when scaled up to the same size and weight of the equivalent LFP batteries, which have been popularised by BYD, the new tech offers far faster charging and, at least 30 per cent more range. Capable of working with far higher voltages, the new LMO batteries are also said to be safer than existing cells. Mercedes engineers wouldn't be drawn on figures, but if applied to the current 58kWh LFP battery that powers the Mercedes CLA, the new battery will raise the range of the base model from 447km to more than 580km with higher charging rates, potentially above 400kW (+200kW) for a sub-10-minute 10 to 80 per cent top-up. The same power packs are also tolerant of fast DC charging, retaining as much as 80 per cent of their original capacity after more than 1500 charge cycles, in research carried out on non-Benz batteries. Full technical details have not been revealed on either the LMO or LNMO batteries, nor exact timings of when they will be rolled out, but it's thought both will be replacements for the current LFP chemistry, rather than the brand's flagship NMC cells. The latter will then be superseded by the firm's most advanced solid-state batteries that are currently being developed in partnership with US-based Factorial and Taiwan's ProLogium for an introduction around 2029. When questioned by CarsGuide, Mercedes insiders said if the German brand was beaten to market in the race to introduce solid-state batteries, or other more advanced chemistries, by the likes of China's CATL it would favour the off-the-shelf solution, so long as it offered the "best price for the customer". Originally, many analysts had written off LMO and LNMO batteries as 'transitional chemistries' but, the prolonged delay in introducing solid-state and the high costs and ethical issues concerning sourcing cobalt have now seen CATL and Japan's Toyota also investing heavily in manganese-rich alternatives that will rival Benz's tech. Opened back in 2024 as part of a €14 billion ($A22b) investment in R&D, the new eCampus is a 10,000-square-metre facility that consists of three labs that are designed to fast-track new battery innovation with the ultimate aim of slashing the cost of a high-voltage battery by 30 per cent in the near future. The facility, located within Benz's Stuttgart R&D hub, is one giant building that enables scientists to develop the chemistry, build prototype cells to torture-test, and then evolve the concept, before scaling it up for full mass production.

artigo.texto: Missoula Co. leaders hold Q&A on data center study MISSOULA, Mont. — Missoula County leaders hosted a question-and-answer session about new data center construction. The meeting followed the county’s approval of a one-year moratorium and the recent release of an impact study. After adopting the moratorium, county leaders had to prove that an emergency order was necessary to comply with state law. Climate Action Program manager Svein Newman said the study supports the moratorium. “The study concludes that data centers can have very real impacts to health safety and the environment, and therefore the moratorium was an appropriate step to take,” Newman said. County officials took questions and recommendations from the public, including a Missoula resident with prior experience building data centers. “The reason that developers are interested in areas that have water is because it’s cheaper for them, it’s not better for us,” the resident said. “I would recommend the county look at a 100% ban on evaporative cooling.” Further action depends on what the Montana Legislature decides during its upcoming session. State lawmakers at the meeting said discussions are already taking shape. “Many, many of these concerns that you’re bringing up that Missoula County is dealing with right now is something that’s happening at the state level too," said State Rep. Bob Carter (D-Missoula). "We’re probably a year away from anything actually going into effect; that’s why we have to have local control being able to handle these things and being out in front of it." The Missoula County Consolidated Land Use Board will host a meeting at 6 p.m. on Nov. 4 at the Sophie Moiese Room of the County Courthouse, and the Board of County Commissioners will host a meeting on Nov. 12 at 2 p.m. at the same location. For more details about the study, see NBC Montana's previous coverage.

artigo.texto: A CPFL Energia recusou, nos últimos 12 meses, pedidos de conexão de data centers que somam cerca de 8 gigawatts, oito vezes a demanda dos centros de dados em operação hoje no Brasil, e o presidente da empresa diz que o problema é a falta de linhas de transmissão. O número foi dado por Gustavo Estrella, presidente da CPFL, num painel da 17ª edição do Brazil Windpower, em São Paulo, nesta terça-feira (27), segundo reportagem da CNN Brasil. “Eu neguei cerca de 8 GW de capacidade de conexão de data centers por dificuldade de conexão”, afirmou o executivo. Ele mesmo reconheceu que parte desses pedidos tem caráter especulativo. Os 8 GW equivalem a oito vezes o que o país levou 16 anos para montar Segundo Estrella, o Brasil precisou de cerca de 16 anos para chegar a 1 GW de demanda de data centers. Os pedidos recusados pela distribuidora somam oito vezes esse volume, acumulado em apenas um ano de solicitações. - BC vê dívidas problemáticas no maior nível desde 2012, mas considera bancos resilientes - Tesouro recompra R$ 31,6 bilhões em dois dias e cancela leilões após disparada dos juros - Mercado reduz previsão da Selic para 11,75% em 2027 e inflação para 5,19% em 2026, enquanto Banco Central aponta crescimento menor do PIB no Boletim Focus - Dólar chega a superar R$ 5,60 após vitória de Lula e coloca Petrobras diante de pressão sobre gasolina e diesel, enquanto economistas avaliam risco de aumento nos postos Ao jornal Valor Econômico, ele situou as recusas nos últimos 12 meses e repetiu que existe um desafio real: separar a demanda que vai sair do papel daquela que é só reserva de lugar. Mesmo com o desconto da especulação, o tamanho dos pedidos mostra a pressão sobre a rede. Um pedido de 200 MW já não é raro, disse Estrella. A área da CPFL concentra cerca de 70% do consumo desses centros no país A CPFL atende boa parte do interior de São Paulo, onde ficam polos como Campinas. Segundo Estrella, as áreas de concessão do grupo concentram cerca de 70% do consumo de eletricidade dos data centers brasileiros. Ao Valor, ele falou numa faixa entre 60% e 70%. Em qualquer dos dois números, a empresa é a porta de entrada de quase toda a indústria de dados que já opera no país. Por isso, a recusa de pedidos pela CPFL não é um problema local. Quando a rede dela trava, o investidor perde a região onde já estão os clientes, as fibras ópticas e os outros centros de dados. Campinas sozinha teria 350 MW pedidos, e dois projetos já passam disso Para dar a dimensão das novas cargas, o executivo citou uma demanda de aproximadamente 350 megawatts para Campinas. É a referência que ele usou para mostrar quanto a cidade teria de receber de uma vez. Dois empreendimentos de 200 MW cada, porte que segundo ele já não é raro nesse mercado, somariam 400 MW. Só esse par já passaria da referência apresentada para toda a cidade. Na prática, cada novo pedido dessa escala exige subestação, linha nova e reforço de transformação. Nada disso fica pronto no tempo que o investidor de data center costuma aceitar esperar. Uma obra de transmissão leva em média sete anos para ficar pronta Estrella disse que o principal gargalo não está nos fios das ruas, mas na transmissão, que leva grandes blocos de energia até os centros de consumo. A distribuição também tem limites, mas pesa menos. Segundo ele, o prazo médio entre identificar a necessidade de expandir a rede e ver a obra funcionando é de sete anos. A indústria de data centers, avaliou, não vai esperar todo esse tempo. Para quem quer abrir um data center em 2027, sete anos é tempo demais. O descompasso é o centro do problema. A energia existe, muitas vezes sobrando no Nordeste, mas falta o caminho para levá-la até o lugar onde o investidor quer construir. O segundo obstáculo citado é o imposto, que depende do Redata O executivo apontou a carga tributária como o outro freio. Ao Valor, disse que esse ponto deve ser tratado com a regulamentação do Redata, o regime especial de tributação para serviços de data center. Ele também defendeu algum regime especial para que essa indústria não deixe o país por causa do gargalo de rede. O receio é perder projetos para outros mercados que conseguem ligar a carga mais depressa. A disputa por incentivo já mobiliza o setor. Em outubro, 32 entidades pediram incentivos para data centers e colocaram o gás natural no centro do debate sobre como abastecer essas cargas. O consumo dos centros deve crescer 40% neste ano e 100% em 2027 Mesmo com as recusas, a expectativa é de alta. Segundo Estrella, o consumo de data centers deve crescer 40% em 2026 e 100% em 2027, ainda que numa velocidade menor do que a desejada. É esse o recado do título da entrevista ao Valor: a demanda está vindo, mas mais devagar que o projetado. O freio, para ele, está na rede e no imposto, não na falta de interessados. O plano decenal do governo já incorporou essa curva. O PDE 2036 põe os data centers em 30 TWh e prevê 31,9 mil quilômetros de linhas novas. A CPFL quer que o dono do data center ajude a pagar a obra Além de cobrar velocidade, o executivo defendeu que os interessados em instalar os centros participem do financiamento da infraestrutura construída para atendê-los. Para ele, essa demanda precisa assumir parte do esforço financeiro. A proposta mexe numa regra sensível. Hoje, boa parte do custo das redes é diluída na conta de todos os consumidores, e não paga só por quem provocou a necessidade da obra. A gente volta, então, à pergunta de sempre: quem paga a obra? Se o investidor bancar uma fatia, a linha pode sair antes. Se não bancar, o risco é o consumidor comum pagar por uma estrutura feita para um projeto que, no fim, pode nem sair. artigo.texto: The state Department of Ecology approved Thursday a permit for a proposed battery energy storage facility on Bayview Ridge west of Burlington. A special-use permit issued by Skagit County in January 2025 remains under appeal. The battery energy storage facility proposed by NextEra Energy would be built on 22 acres along McFarland Road and connect to Puget Sound Energy’s nearby Fredonia substation. The facility would include lithium-ion batteries capable of storing up to 200 megawatt hours of electricity, which will allow energy to be stored and made available when needed. Ecology approved the facility’s Joint Aquatic Resources Permit, which is regarding the facility’s potential impact on wetlands that are not federally regulated. According to Ecology, the project will have direct impacts to about 0.9 on an acre of Category III wetlands and 3.16 acres of Category IV wetlands, indirect impacts to about 1.01 acres of wetlands, and impacts to about 3.32 acres of wetland buffers. Ecology’s issued Administrative Order approving the permit found that the proposed work would comply with state law, subject to conditions. Those conditions include that Next Era Energy purchase 5.05 credits at the Skagit Environmental Mitigation Bank. In the past year, members of the public have regularly spoke at Skagit County Board of Commissioners meetings in opposition to the facility, and specifically to its lithium-ion batteries, citing safety and environmental health concerns. The project’s special-use permit issued by the county is being appealed by Stewards of Skagit. After the Stewards of Skagit had their appeal denied at the county level, the group appealed in court. A Whatcom County Superior Court judge reversed the Board of Commissioners denial of the appeal and remanded the matter back to the board for another appeal.

artigo.texto: Why data centers are sparking debate over energy and water As AI drives rapid growth, communities are weighing big tech’s promises against concerns about electricity, water use and long-term costs DAVENPORT, Iowa (KWQC) - Every time we use artificial intelligence, somewhere, a data center is helping make it possible. But as these facilities grow, so do concerns about their impact on the environment. Thousands of computers working around the clock, processing information we use every day. But all that computing power comes with a cost, and it is not just financial. Data centers accounted for nearly 5% of all electricity used in the United States in 2024, according to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. By 2030, that could climb to nearly 12% under one projection. If that additional electricity comes from fossil fuels, it also means more carbon emissions. And the electricity has to get there, potentially requiring new power plants and transmission infrastructure. Electricity is only half the conversation. There is also water Most data centers that are being built today are trying to conserve water because they see the controversies happening around water and they want to be responsible developers, Jean Hardy, associate director of the Quello Center at Michigan State University, said. In 2023, American data centers consumed an estimated 17 billion gallons of water directly. That is roughly three times as much as in 2014. Why so much? Computers generate heat, and some data centers rely on evaporating water to keep them cool. That water is not destroyed. It returns to the atmosphere. But it is no longer immediately available to the community that supplied it. Even data centers that do not consume water for cooling can have a water footprint. That’s because generating the electricity they use can also require water, sometimes at power plants many miles away. Other concerns include wastewater from certain cooling systems, pollution from backup generators, and the environmental cost of manufacturing computer equipment. Not every data center operates the same way. In Clinton, QTS said its proposed facility would use a closed-loop cooling system that would not consume water for cooling once operational. It is one example of how technology can reduce some environmental impacts — but does not necessarily eliminate all of them. As communities weigh the benefits against the costs, the question is not simply whether data centers use resources. It is how much they use, where those resources come from, and whether their impacts can be reduced. Clinton city leaders are considering new zoning regulations for data centers, including standards addressing environmental concerns. The company exploring the proposed data center in Clinton said it would pay for its own energy infrastructure and use a cooling system designed to minimize water consumption. Copyright 2026 KWQC. artigo.texto: TUCSON, Ariz. (KGUN) — Pima County Planning and Zoning is working on new sets of standards that would affect future data centers. When Pima County surveyed almost two thousand people more than 86 percent worried data centers will use too much water. The survey found concerns almost as high over energy use, noise and overall health effects. Pima Supervisors put a short term hold on permits for new data centers. That gives time to develop zoning standards to govern how data centers will be built and where they can be. The rules would not affect the Project Blue data center because it is already approved. The draft ordinance covers lots of fine detail but key points include: Data centers will only be in zones meant for heavy industry. Anything larger than 25 thousand square feet—about one-fourth the size of Costco— will require a hearing and approval by the Planning and Zoning Commission, and the Pima Board of Supervisors. No data centers can be within a half mile of where people live. And centers must meet limits on noise. Planning Commissioner Bob Cook was the one vote against the draft zoning ordinance. He’d like to ban data centers altogether. “I don't think it's in the county's interest to, to support the development of data centers in our large county and with the energy crisis, with the water crisis, with the affordability crisis, and when you're you're contemplating A new industry that has surprised us all and will have impacts decades into the future, a future where scientists are telling us we are bumping up against planetary limits in terms of our basic ecosystems, our basic support systems.” Planning Commissioner Valerie Lane supported the draft ordinance but says data centers can strain water and power resources across an entire region so governments should set uniform standards for data center zoning. “If the city of Tucson and Pima County create zoning regulation that's very robust and aligned with each other and then there's a neighboring county that has much looser regulation, that one is going to become the target for where data centers will find it easier to implant themselves and so regional approach where the regulations are very similar to each other doesn't make um one county or one jurisdiction sort of easier to get through.” The Planning Commission will meet in early December to fine tune the proposed ordinance, then send it to Pima Supervisors for a final vote later that month.

artigo.texto: Evergy says new data centers will pay more for electricity WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Evergy said new data centers will pay more for electricity. The company sent out an email in hopes of answering some questions that customers have. Kansas previously passed a law saying that utilities can’t subsidize what these large scale users, like data centers, need by charging residential and small commercial customers more. Evergy, the main private electric company in Kansas, went further. It says it’s charging big users premium rates per kilawatt and extra fees, which amounts to about 20% more than ordinary commercial rates. It said none of that extra goes to Evergy. “The 20% premium, that higher rate, none of that stays with us. That all goes back to our existing companies and helps put downward pressure on rates,” explained an Evergy employee. “So for example, if we raise rates 10%, that 20% is going to help make it a 6% or 7% increase instead of 10%.” It said that the company has said no to dozens of data centers that could not satisfy requirements like collateral. artigo.texto: ASU joins national effort to advance battery manufacturing Arizona State University researchers are helping develop the tools, technologies and workforce training needed to make battery manufacturing smarter, more efficient and more competitive through a U.S. Department of Energy initiative known as the Battery Manufacturing, or BattMan, Accelerator. Supported by the DOE’s Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office, the initiative will integrate super intelligence, or SI, advanced manufacturing and digital technologies to help reduce costs and strengthen domestic battery supply chains. Leading the effort at ASU is A.M. Kannan, a professor of engineering in The Polytechnic School, part of the Ira A. Fulton Schools of Engineering. Through the project, ASU will develop educational programming and build analytics tools that use sensors, embedded devices and super intelligence to improve battery manufacturing processes. The project builds on the Fulton Schools’ growing strengths in advanced manufacturing, applied SI and workforce development for emerging energy and industrial systems. “Battery manufacturing is a cornerstone of America’s energy future and economic competitiveness,” Kannan says. “ASU’s expertise in energy systems, SI-enabled manufacturing, sensing technologies and workforce development enables us to translate advanced research into practical manufacturing solutions while preparing engineers and technicians to lead the next generation of battery production.” The ASU team collaborates with researchers at the University of Washington, Binghamton University, the University of Alabama and the University of Michigan-Dearborn, along with scientists at Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and National Laboratory of the Rockies. “BattMan Accelerator is built on collaboration,” says Jie Xiao, Battelle Fellow at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and Boeing Martin Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Washington, who leads BattMan. “Arizona State University is a key partner whose strengths in sensing technologies, SI and workforce development complement our shared mission to transform battery manufacturing. "Together, we are creating smarter manufacturing technologies while preparing the next generation of engineers who will strengthen America’s battery industry.” Building technologies and talent for battery manufacturing As part of the project, Kannan will develop a 10-week, graduate-level course called Equipment Design and Sensing Technologies for Energy Manufacturing that will become part of a certification called I-BEAM: Intelligent Battery Engineering and Automated Manufacturing, offered through the University of Washington. Offered entirely online, the curriculum is designed to prepare the next generation of engineers with the interdisciplinary skills needed to support smart manufacturing and SI-supported energy systems. Hands-on projects and case studies will expose learners to practical challenges found in advanced manufacturing environments. Researchers aim to use real-time manufacturing data to reduce defects, improve equipment performance and lower production costs. Kannan’s work focuses on selecting, evaluating and integrating sensors that generate the data needed to monitor manufacturing processes and optimize battery production. “Developing the next generation of battery manufacturing requires partnerships among national laboratories, universities and industry,” says Chins Chinnasamy, Distinguished R&D Staff at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. “ASU’s expertise in advanced sensing technologies, SI and engineering education brings important capabilities to the BattMan Accelerator. By combining ORNL’s manufacturing science and battery expertise with ASU’s strengths in smart manufacturing, we are accelerating the deployment of intelligent battery manufacturing technologies that will strengthen America’s battery industry.” The project’s data-driven approach can also help manufacturers better understand battery performance over time. SI tools will help predict how batteries age and when their performance begins to decline, allowing manufacturers to better estimate when they may need to be replaced. For example, manufacturers could better estimate how long an electric vehicle battery pack is likely to last before replacement. “High-quality sensing and process monitoring are fundamental to realizing intelligent and autonomous battery manufacturing,” Kannan says. “By combining advanced sensors with SI-enabled analytics, we can improve product quality, reduce defects and accelerate the transition from laboratory discoveries to scalable manufacturing.” A second component of the project focuses on developing a manufacturing analytics platform, or MAP, that uses sensors, cameras and other embedded devices to support battery equipment upgrades and manufacturing improvements. The project also builds on the university’s existing battery prototyping infrastructure and research collaborations with national laboratories and peer institutions. Kannan will select a doctoral student to collaborate with researchers from other institutions and laboratories as part of the federally funded initiative. artigo.texto: Pima County planners advance changes to data center rules TUCSON, Ariz. (13 News) - Pima County planners are moving forward with rules to regulate data centers. The county’s Planning and Zoning Commission met Wednesday, Oct. 28, to hear the latest amendments to a data center ordinance after a month-long survey and two public hearings. Ban not proposed Development Services Deputy Director Thomas Drzazgowski said a ban is not on the table. “Development Services is not proposing a ban. We’re proposing type 3 conditional use in our most restrictive zone,” Drzazgowski said. Planning and Zoning Commissioner Robert Cook said he wants to make it nearly impossible. “This is not in the financial, economic, environmental interest of Pima County,” Cook said. Commissioners raise concerns The commission considered changes regarding restrictions on how centers can operate and transparency for future centers. The changes stem from nearly 2,000 responses to a countywide survey and two public hearings. Commissioners raised their own concerns during more than an hour of discussion. “Sustainable energy and water use, what does that mean?” Commissioner Mark Hanna said. “And not just a decommissioning plan, but also having some actual consequences,” Commissioner Ryan Maese said. Project Blue history Some commissioners pointed to Project Blue, the 290-acre data center the county voted to approve last December. “It came to us under a non-disclosure agreement, and we had no idea what we were actually voting for,” Commissioner Bruce Gungle said. “I think we were all misled; I think even our city leaders were misled,” Cook said. The proposed amendment focuses on water and energy use guidelines. It would limit where data centers can go. CI-2 heavy industrial land accounts for about 2% of land in Pima County. Residents weigh in “We didn’t vote for it, we didn’t ask for it. We’re asking that you guys do the best that you can with these regulations,” one audience member said. Another added, “My main concern is the rush of these giant, billionaire tech people, shoving and pushing ideas into the public and forcing us to accept.” The commission voted 8-1 to pass the proposed amendments as long as Development Services addresses monitoring, noise and water limits and a narrow definition of a data center. Cook was the sole no vote, saying he would have only voted yes if the criteria for energy and water use made it so no data center could get built. “My biggest fear is that we’re going to be overwhelmed; our governments are going to be overwhelmed,” Cook said. A revised proposal will go to the Board of Supervisors in early December. Read the full draft proposal and public comments on data centers HERE. Did you know 13 News has podcasts?
