artigo.texto: Each data center developer that wants to build in San Antonio will have to get a special permit from the city before it can begin construction. Council members approved new rules for data center development and chose stricter requirements, rather than allowing data centers to build by right. Council members approved the new policy in a 9-2 vote on Thursday. Councilman Ric Galvan (D6), who kicked off discussion about the issue last year, voted for the new rules, along with Sukh Kaur (D1), Jalen McKee-Rodriguez (D2), Phyllis Viagran (D3), Edward Mungia (D4), Teri Castillo (D5), Marina Alderete Gavito (D7), Ivalis Meza Gonzalez (D8) and Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones. Council members Misty Spears (D9) and Marc Whyte (D10) both voted no. City officials have been mulling land use rules for data centers since Galvan asked city staff to start writing regulations on Oct. 29, 2025. After meeting with community members and developers throughout the summer, the city’s Development Services Department put forward a series of rule proposals this fall. The choice included two extremes: Data centers could be allowed to be built by right when they met a list of requirements or they would need case-by-case approvals, also known as a specific use authorization, from the council. In the end, council members overwhelmingly approved a case-by-case approach. “Every single data center that is proposed to come to San Antonio must come to council … and make sure that there is clear coordination with the community and with council on how this data center will come to our city,” Galvan said. New rules explained The new rules will only allow the approved data centers in commercial or industrial zones. Galvan said council members will be able to unpack each proposal individually and ask questions about distance from neighbors, noise, water and energy use, lighting and a list of other concerns community members have presented. “Residents will be able to voice their opinion. It means that residents will be able to get their thoughts and feedback,” Galvan said. “Not only will they be able to ask those questions, council will have their back, too.” Galvan said he expects some questions around water, power and site plans to be asked consistently, but the policy is wide open. Residents will be able to raise whatever issues concern them about nearby projects. Council members also unanimously supported rules for the city’s UNESCO World Heritage Sites on the South Side. Data centers built near those sites would need to go in front of City Council for specific setback requirements. Four proposals Council members were considering four options entering the meeting. City staff recommended by-right development in commercial and industrial zones. The second option, which was approved, required case-by-case approvals. Mayor Jones put forward her own policy, which would have a list of requirements, including 1,000-foot setbacks, noise limits, water and energy use information and frequent public notifications from data centers. After meeting those requirements, data centers would still have to get a specific use authorization from council. Last week, the city’s Zoning Commission presented its own proposal, allowing by-right development in heavier industrial areas and case-by-case approvals in business parks or commercial zones. The by-right rules included downward facing lighting, 350 feet of separation between data centers and neighborhoods, and landscape buffers. Council members navigated a complex web of decisions and motions. Even city staff members were confused at times before council members landed on the blanket case-by-case policy. Jones pushed for her proposal hard this week, holding a news conference for it on Monday. She put the policy in front of council members Thursday, but it lost in a 6-5 vote. Galvan, McKee-Rodriguez, Castillo and Mungia all supported Jones’ proposal, while Kaur, Viagran, Alderete Gavito, Meza Gonzalez, Spears and Whyte voted it down. Whyte then pushed for the Zoning Commission policy, which he called a compromise between by-right and case-by-case approvals. Meza Gonzalez became the critical vote in the room, flipping sides to defeat that proposal 6-5. That cleared the way for case-by-case specific use authorizations, which a majority of council members decided to support. The night before the vote, a group gathered in front of City Hall to speak, chant and protest against data centers. Many wanted to go beyond limiting future data center development. “We need to start thinking about how to shut down the data centers that are already here,” Anayanse Garza told reporters. It’s a window into how invested community members have become in the issue. Throughout the Development Services Department’s regulatory process, residents have raised concerns about noise and light pollution, water and energy use and the impact on property values for those who live around data centers. “We cannot sell houses that are near brownfields, and that is exactly what they are — the air pollution, the noise pollution,” local real estate agent Nikki Rosas told council members on Thursday. “The community is not talking about what we are going to lose in value in homeownership.” Other public commenters raised concerns about air pollution and public health and a lack of transparency during development, advocating for specific use authorizations. Developers and construction workers have argued that data centers provide essential digital infrastructure while creating property tax revenue and good-paying jobs. They want consistent regulations to allow for predictable development and said the Zoning Commission proposal was the best way to get there. “Utilizing responsible data center development guidelines, as proposed by the Zoning Commission, will allow San Antonio to keep responsible data center development on track,” said Anthony Bolner, a San Antonio resident and founder of Stream Data Centers. artigo.texto: CATL globally launches ultra-high capacity energy storage system at All Energy 2026 and signs three Australian partnership MoUs MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) today unveiled TENER+ in a global launch at All Energy Australia 2026, where it also showcased TENER Sodium. The company signed memorandums of understanding (MoU) with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney to strengthen the delivery and grid connection of utility-scale battery projects in Australia. TENER: Engineered for long-term performance and Australia's demanding grid connection requirements CATL's TENER+ and TENER Sodium energy storage systems are designed to deliver the reliability and long-term performance Australian utility-scale energy projects need. Engineered for harsh weather conditions, they are designed to support compliance with Australia's demanding grid connection requirements and give project financiers confidence in the reliability and long-term performance that underpin battery revenues. TENER+ is a 9MWh ultra-high capacity energy storage system that helps developers to achieve a longer-term project value and to maximise the storage capacity of their project, TENER+ reduces the number of containers needed by up to 40% and the project footprint by 12%, making this ideal for projects that are facing land constraints. Its intelligent thermal management system supports a higher round-trip efficiency and lower auxiliary power consumption. Multiple TENER+ batteries can be simultaneously commissioned with a single click to streamline project deployment. Designed for a 25-year lifespan, TENER+ features liquid cooling and protection for humid and coastal environments. Noise levels remain below 65 dBA at 1 metre. Its "no heat island" top-exhaust design directs hot air vertically upwards, away from adjacent units. This prevents horizontal heat discharge and minimises thermal impact on neighbouring PCS units, allowing them to operate at full rated power even in extreme summer conditions. TENER Sodium is the world's first mass-produced, field-validated sodium-ion battery energy storage system. It delivers more than 30MWh through its modular cabinet architecture. It delivers 95% round-trip efficiency with an operating lifespan of more than 20 years. Together, these energy storage systems give developers and asset owners a choice of lithium-ion and sodium-ion chemistries. We're offering both sodium-ion and lithium-ion technologies to give asset owners and developers the flexibility to choose the right technology for their success." CATL's local industry partnerships to advance Australia's clean energy transition TENER energy storage systems solve the challenges the Australia's grid is facing as more renewable energy powers the grid. Grid-scale batteries supplied 8% of evening peak generation, overtaking gas-powered generation for the first time according to the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO). As coal-fired power stations retire, the grid increasingly needs energy storage systems with grid-forming capability to provide voltage and frequency support. CATL's DC battery products and Hitachi Energy's power conversion systems will form the basis of a proposed integrated offering in Australia and the Asia Pacific region. In Australia, CATL will collaborate with EPEC Group and the Xiamen Energy Storage Validation Research Institute (ESVL) to combine its energy storage technology, with EPEC's grid integration and engineering delivery expertise, and ESVL's full-scale system validation. The parties aim to strengthen technical validation and accelerate the delivery of reliable, bankable and grid-compliant energy storage projects in Australia. CATL and UNSW Sydney will also jointly develop the Centre for Integrated Renewable Energy Training and Innovation in Western Sydney, NSW. This renewable energy training and innovation centre will advance the skills and capabilities needed for Australia's clean energy transition. Zhou added, "CATL is working with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group, ESVL and UNSW Sydney to give our Australian customers greater confidence in how our technology is integrated, validated and supported throughout a project's life. artigo.texto: Graphene-enhanced batteries use graphene, a single-atom-thick sheet of carbon with outstanding electrical and thermal conductivity, to improve conventional battery chemistries. In most commercial products, small amounts of graphene are added to the electrodes or coated on current collectors of lithium-ion cells, helping them charge faster, run cooler, and last longer, while graphene is also used in lead-acid batteries and supercapacitors. IMARC values the global market at about USD 166.4 million in 2025 and expects it to reach USD 898.5 million by 2034, growing about 20% a year, with lithium-ion products and automotive uses leading. With India's electric vehicle and energy storage boom and incentives for local cell making, Graphene Battery Manufacturing Plant Setup in India is an emerging opportunity for technology-led investors. Investment depends mainly on whether the plant makes its own cells or assembles packs, annual capacity in gigawatt-hours, cell chemistry and format, how graphene is sourced and incorporated, the level of automation, dry room and formation capacity, and testing and R&D. The Graphene Battery Manufacturing Plant Cost ranges from about INR 30–60 crore for a pack assembly or graphene lead-acid unit, to INR 700–900 crore for an integrated plant of about 1 GWh making graphene-enhanced lithium-ion cells and packs, and INR 6,000–9,000 crore for gigafactories of 10 GWh or more. Materials make up most of operating cost, so sourcing and manufacturing yield decide competitiveness. For a well-run cell plant, a gross margin of 22 to 32% and a net margin of 7 to 12% are realistic once yields stabilise. This guide is written for investors exploring how to start a Graphene Battery manufacturing plant in India. It focuses on an integrated plant of about 1 GWh a year that makes LFP lithium-ion cells with graphene conductive additives and coated foils for faster charging and better heat handling, and assembles them into packs for electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, and energy storage, and also explains pack and lead-acid units and large gigafactories. It covers products and markets, the demand outlook, the production process flow, machinery and raw materials, location and infrastructure, a detailed cost and financial breakdown, certification and approvals, and how a DPR and financial model turn all of this into a bankable plan. The snapshot shows a small but fast-growing global niche within the much larger lithium-ion battery industry. Asia-Pacific leads demand, and India's incentives for advanced cell chemistry, together with rapid growth in electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, and storage, create room for differentiated, high-performance cells made locally. A site-specific Graphene Battery Feasibility Report narrows each of these assumptions to your chosen capacity, chemistry, location, and customers. Table of Contents Graphene is a form of carbon arranged in a flat honeycomb sheet one atom thick, which conducts electricity and heat far better than conventional carbon additives. In batteries it is mostly used as a conductive additive in cathodes and anodes, as a coating on aluminium and copper foils, or in composite anodes with silicon, where it helps electrons and heat move quickly, reduces internal resistance, and supports faster charging and longer cycle life. The underlying chemistry is usually still lithium-ion, lead-acid, or a supercapacitor, so graphene improves rather than replaces existing technology. Consistent graphene quality, dispersion, cell safety, and proven test data decide value. Commercially, products are sold to electric two-wheeler and three-wheeler makers, e-rickshaw and fleet operators, energy storage integrators for solar, telecom, and commercial buildings, makers of power tools, drones, and consumer devices, and defence and specialty users. A Graphene Battery Manufacturing Plant can serve all these customers by varying cell format, capacity, and pack design. Customers value verified fast-charge and cycle-life performance, safety certification, warranties, and reliable supply. The Main Products and Applications Choosing the product mix is the most important commercial decision, because it determines cell design, equipment, certification, and margins: These choices shape the whole project. Graphene-enhanced lithium-ion cells and packs for mobility and storage offer the largest market, while lead-acid products are a low-cost entry route for e-rickshaws and inverters, and supercapacitors serve niche high-power uses that need different equipment. artigo.texto: Laser launches semi solid state powerbanks in Australia Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today) Laser has launched a new ChargeCore powerbank range in Australia using semi solid state battery technology, with the products among the first of their type to reach local retail shelves. The Sydney-based consumer electronics group is introducing three models in the ChargeCore Everyday Semi Solid State Series, with capacities of 10,000mAh, 20,000mAh and 27,000mAh. Prices range from AUD $49.95 to AUD $99.95, placing the devices in the mainstream market. The range targets consumers concerned about battery safety in portable chargers. Laser has positioned semi solid state chemistry as the key point of difference, alongside built-in protections against overcharging, overcurrent, short circuits and overheating. The launch reflects a broader focus on battery design in portable consumer electronics, particularly as powerbanks have become a routine accessory for smartphones, tablets and other mobile devices. Safety has drawn greater attention across the category in recent years, with brands seeking to differentiate products through battery chemistry, charging control and thermal management. Laser described semi solid state technology as an evolution in battery chemistry that offers improved thermal stability and safety compared with conventional designs. It said the technology can also support stronger charging performance while allowing more power to be stored in a compact form factor. The three models offer either 20W or 35W USB-C PD charging, depending on capacity. Each includes a digital battery display and a carry-on-approved design. Range details At launch, the 10,000mAh model is priced at AUD $49.95 and the 20,000mAh version at AUD $69.95, both with 20W USB-C PD charging. The 27,000mAh model, with 35W USB-C PD charging, is listed at AUD $99.95. Black versions are available now, while some other colour options will follow across parts of the line-up. The Everyday Series will be offered in Black, Galactica, Grey and Dark Cherry, although availability varies by model. The products are being sold through Harvey Norman and Laser's online store. The launch gives the company a position in a powerbank segment where differentiation has often centred on capacity, charging speed and form factor rather than battery chemistry. Battery strategy Laser has sold powerbanks in Australia for 15 years and has been expanding the battery technologies used in the category. It says it launched an Australian range using LiFePO4 battery technology in 2025 and is now moving into semi solid state products as manufacturing developments make the chemistry more practical for smaller consumer devices. The business has operated for almost 40 years and says it develops its portfolio from its Sydney headquarters. Its broader product line spans home entertainment, portable power, personal audio, gaming and connectivity accessories. Chris Lau, Managing Director, Laser, linked the latest release to the company's focus on product safety. "We've been closely following semi solid state battery development for some time, since first visiting an EV factory several years ago, and advancements since that time mean that it can now move into smaller, more compact options. Simply put, I believe that Semi Solid State chemistry makes this the safest powerbank technology available in Australia today. We are focused on safety and peace of mind, and we know that it is a huge concern for Australian consumers these days when buying powerbanks," said Chris Lau, Managing Director, Laser. Laser also pointed to the testing behind the new range as it seeks to reassure buyers about reliability in everyday use. Portable chargers are regularly carried in bags, used in transit and exposed to repeated charging cycles, making durability and thermal management important selling points in the category. The company sees the new line as an everyday entry point for consumers interested in the technology rather than a niche premium experiment. By pricing the products below AUD $100, it is testing whether shoppers will pay attention to battery chemistry in the same way they already compare charging speed and capacity. "I've personally had the opportunity to see first-hand the testing that goes into the manufacturing of these semi solid state powerbanks, including the stress testing placed on the battery technology. It gives you an appreciation for just how much engineering, testing and development sits behind something consumers simply put in their bag and use every day," said Lau.

artigo.texto: Maryland plans to invest $200 million in battery storage and renewable energy development as officials try to add much-needed power supply, shore up a stressed grid, and respond to rising electricity costs driven by data-center demand. Here's what to know Under a new initiative called Megawatts for Maryland, the state will award grants over the next two years for battery storage and renewable energy projects. Maryland Energy Administration officials say the effort could support "several hundred megawatts" of power — enough for about 150,000 homes, according to the Baltimore Banner. Projects using battery storage can qualify, as can renewable technologies including solar, wind, geothermal, and certain biofuels. Democratic lawmakers authorized the program in 2025 through the Utility RELIEF Act, a sweeping state energy measure. Maryland Energy Administration Director Kelly Speakes-Backman said that the strategy is intended to address the state's supply problem as electricity demand rises. "This is simple economics," Speakes-Backman explained. "When high demand sends prices up, we need to bring more supply online." More background Officials announced the program as Maryland contends with shrinking in-state generation, rising electricity demand, and a clean energy rollout that hasn't kept up with its climate ambitions. Maryland has struggled to replace major coal and gas plants with renewable power quickly enough, the Banner reported. Local pushback has made that harder. In parts of Maryland, proposed wind, solar, and battery projects have drawn opposition, slowing renewable development as electricity demand continues to rise. Officials at the Maryland Energy Administration also point to federal actions as part of the problem. According to the Banner, the grants are partly meant to close financing gaps left by President Donald Trump's cuts to federal clean energy tax credits, while the administration's actions targeting offshore wind have further hindered Maryland's clean energy buildout. When supply lags and demand rises, energy becomes more expensive. In Maryland, officials are betting that expanding generation and storage can help stabilize a system already under strain. What's being done? Maryland's clean energy fund, financed through compliance payments from utility companies, will provide the grant money. Although that fund has expanded significantly, lawmakers and Gov. Wes Moore's administration have also tapped it extensively for energy rebates, clean energy projects, and budget balancing. Applicants seeking Megawatts for Maryland grants must meet multiple requirements before awards are made. Maryland Energy Administration spokesperson Erin Dempsey noted that projects must show financial solvency and already have applied for state permits and regional grid connections. They must also present public engagement plans, which can include potential community benefits agreements — an important condition in a state where local resistance has repeatedly delayed clean-energy projects. Even so, state law still requires auction awards to prioritize projects offering the lowest energy prices. That structure reflects the program's dual goal: adding cleaner power while trying to protect consumers from even higher costs. The tradeoff is timing — because grants will be administered over two years, any effect on household electric bills is likely to be gradual rather than immediate. Speakes-Backman asserted that Maryland's investment still matters even if the state cannot fully counter federal policy on its own. "We are one state within the entire nation. But I don't think it's a drop in the bucket, either." Where can I learn more? Maryland's push to add cleaner power is unfolding alongside a wider fight over utility costs. These stories cover the state's long-term solar deals, utility rate hikes, and customer refunds. • Maryland just locked in a 20-year solar deal that officials say could save $300 million. • Maryland regulators expect more utility rate hike requests even as RELIEF Act savings begin. • Maryland utility customers could still see $160 million back on bills after a court tax ruling. artigo.texto: NEO Battery Contracted by South Korean Defense Prime & Tier-1 Battery Pack Manufacturer to Develop Custom Batteries for Defense Program - Contracted by South Korean defense prime and tier-1 battery pack manufacturer to develop custom-built, high-performance batteries for defense project - A-sample phase development and production to validate prototype quality, with a defined path to B-sample pilot orders and volume production upon successful evaluation - Advances NEO's Korean Defense Integration Strategy as a flexible, domestic cell partner supplying qualified battery products to established defense contractors TORONTO , Oct. 27, 2026 /CNW/ -- NEO Battery Materials Ltd. ("NEO" or the "Company") (TSXV: NBM) (OTC: NBMFF), a low-cost, silicon-enhanced battery manufacturer enabling high-performance capabilities for drones, robotics, and physical AI, is pleased to announce that it has been contracted by a South Korean defense prime and tier-1 Korean battery pack company to develop and manufacture custom-built, high-performance batteries for an undisclosed defense project. Under the A-sample phase, NEO will supply initial battery prototypes for electrochemical and mechanical testing to verify performance and quality against the project's requirements. Upon successful evaluation of A-samples, the program is expected to progress to larger pilot orders with B-sample manufacturing and evaluation, followed by subsequent volume production. The contract advances NEO's Korean Defense Integration Strategy under which the Company serves as a flexible, high-performance cell partner to established defense integrators, supplying qualified, domestically manufactured batteries into packs and systems for Korean defense applications. "This contract reflects our continued progress in engaging larger organizations and converting them into customers," said Mr. Spencer Huh, President and CEO of NEO. "Working with a major defense prime and an established pack manufacturer has formed another pathway into the Korean defense supply chain. NEO's engineering and manufacturing team are focused on fulfilling the customers' validation requirements and supporting the program through its next phases as a potential anchor vendor." About NEO Battery Materials Ltd . NEO Battery Materials is a Canadian-South Korean battery technology company focused on developing and producing silicon-enhanced lithium-ion batteries in drones, robotics, physical AI, electric vehicles, and energy storage systems. With a patent-protected, low-cost silicon manufacturing process, NEO Battery enables longer-running and ultra-fast charging properties and provides end-to-end battery solutions from materials selection, cell architecture, and process optimization. The Company aims to be a globally-leading producer of high-performance lithium-ion batteries and materials, building a secure, robust battery supply chain for Western manufacturers. For more information, please visit the Company's website at: https://www.neobatterymaterials.com/. artigo.texto: NEO Battery Reports Fiscal Year 2027 Second Quarter Results TORONTO , Oct. 29, 2026 /CNW/ -- NEO Battery Materials Ltd. ("NEO" or the "Company") (TSXV: NBM) (OTC: NBMFF), a low-cost, silicon-enhanced battery manufacturer enabling high-performance capabilities for drones, robotics, and physical AI, today announced its financial and operational results for the second quarter ended August 31, 2026, and provided an update on its facility expansion, commercial pipeline, and growth initiatives. All amounts are in Canadian dollars unless otherwise specified. "The second quarter marked a continued increase in our pipeline with qualified leads, and now, we are converting the pipeline into active customers," stated Spencer Huh, President & CEO of NEO. "Since reporting the first quarter, we received our first direct order from the Republic of Korea Army, our largest foundry contract to date from a Fortune 500 automotive OEM, and a development contract from a South Korean defense prime. Outside Korea, we have established direct inroads into Ukraine for battery development and are serving key U.S. battery and defense players that can potentially translate into concrete commercial contracts. Each came to NEO for the same two reasons: battery performance their current suppliers cannot deliver, and a secure, non-Chinese supply source. With certified products and validated manufacturing, our priority is scaling production to meet this demand. As we do so, we will continue to evaluate partnerships and other opportunities that strengthen our position as a secure, high-performance battery supplier to Western and allied customers." FY2027 Q2 Financial and Recent Operational Highlights - Revenue of $203,566 for the three months endedAugust 31, 2026 , and revenue for the six months endedAugust 31, 2026 , was$382,530 . - Gross loss of $807,492 for the quarter, and gross loss for the six months endedAugust 31, 2026 , was$1,450,753 . Margins continue to reflect early-stage commercial production and the scale-up phase for the cell manufacturing expansion facility, where volumes have not yet reached the level required to absorb the fixed cost base. Data centers are popping up all over the world at stunning speed. But not everyone is rolling out the welcome mat. Countries have long housed power-hungry data centers—the facilities packed with computing infrastructure that underpins the internet as we know it. But their numbers have exploded amid the global artificial intelligence race, which requires massive computing power. That has led to the spread of even bigger data centers around the world, including the more controversial “hyperscale” facilities used by tech giants. Last year, data centers consumed more electricity than all but 10 countries, according to a United Nations University report, with even more to come. If data centers were their own country, BloombergNEF forecasted that they are set to gobble up so much energy by 2035 that they could rank among the top 5 countries in terms of electricity use. While governments have courted data centers due to their potential economic benefits, many local communities have resisted their development over concerns about the impact on jobs, energy bills, water usage, and the environment. From Chile to Scotland to Australia, opposition to the massive facilities has erupted around the entire world. “It’s a complicated moment,” said Boris Gamazaychikov, co-founder of the Sustainable AI Group, a research firm that focuses on AI’s environmental impacts. “The space is really polarized.” As data centers proliferate, Foreign Policy looked at what their global footprint looks like right now and how it might evolve in the coming years. To grasp the full scale and scope of these facilities’ global footprint, it’s important to first establish that it’s only the beginning of the boom. The world is still in the early stages of deploying data centers and AI, and significant growth is expected, according to Ashish Sethia, the global head of commodities at BloombergNEF. Here is what we know: In 2024, data centers accounted for about 1.5 percent of global electricity consumption. But that share is set to more than double by 2030—which means that data centers would consume as much electricity as Japan does today, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). For regions with big clusters of data centers, demand can be far more overwhelming. In some places, the facilities can account for as much as 25 or 30 percent of total electricity consumption—posing a big challenge for the local grid, said Siddharth Singh, an analyst at the IEA. “These data centers are coming up very, very quickly,” he said. About three quarters of the world’s data center capacity is concentrated in just three regions: the United States, China, and Western Europe, Singh said. The United States is the clear leader in the charge. With U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambitions of AI supremacy, more than 1,500 data centers are now in development, adding to the 3,000 that are already operational across the country. That expansion has been largely powered by natural gas: To secure more energy, and fast, many tech giants have turned away from the electric grid and instead resorted to building their own on-site natural gas plants. Yet the Trump administration’s push for a rapid data center buildout has faced fierce bipartisan backlash, and at least 15 states have weighed moratoriums. Trump has dismissed data center critics and said that they are playing into the interests of Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping “will take every data center that we don’t want,” Trump told reporters last month. “He would love to have every single one, because you know why? They’re smart.” China is indeed going all-in on data center construction in its bid for AI dominance, although it still lags behind the United States. Beijing’s operational data center computing capacity is still less than half of Washington’s, according to SemiAnalysis, a research firm. But Beijing has some key advantages in ensuring a swift expansion. Unlike the United States, public pushback is rare, and Chinese companies can build quickly. The country also has cheap land and abundant energy, with coal currently fueling the bulk of the country’s data center electricity supply, according to the IEA. The bigger constraints that Beijing faces are accessing advanced chips and the high-end IT equipment going into data centers, said Thomas Spencer, an analyst at the IEA. (U.S. export bans have limited Beijing’s access to powerful AI chips.) Western Europe, Japan, and South Korea also have sizable data center markets. But those booms have come with their own strains: Many of these advanced economies are grappling with stagnant electricity demand and older electricity networks, and community pushback has been forceful. Ireland, for example, developed so many data centers that they sucked up more energy than all the country’s urban homes combined—ultimately forcing the government to bar new data center construction. And across Europe, public backlash has delayed or canceled roughly $42 billion in data center investments. “There’s a combination of social pushback and infrastructural bottlenecks, which holds across developed markets as a sort of general trend,” Spencer said. With so much of the world’s data center capacity concentrated in just a handful of countries, emerging market economies are eager to attract data centers and see their own ecosystems grow. artigo.texto: China’s largest battery maker, CATL, is likely to expand Its Sodium energy storage system network in Europe over the next five years as it entered into an agreement with a German counterpart. A memorandum of understanding (MOU) was signed Monday between CATL and German energy storage solutions provider, Intilion, to install 3 GWh of sodium-ion energy storage systems in Europe by 2031. Under the latest agreement, these battery systems for grid-scale, commercial, and industrial applications would expand into the German, Swiss, and Austrian markets. Robust alternative in harsh winters Since 2022, the companies have deployed more than 30 energy storage projects in Germany, including lithium-ion batteries. Going forward, CATL aims to strengthen its existing project partnership with Intilion while scaling up adoption of new battery technologies this year. Tener Sodium, the world’s first field-validated sodium-ion energy storage solution, which is expected to enter the European market this year, was launched by the Chinese Energy company over four years ago in June. Sodium-ion batteries are viewed as a potential alternative because they maintain stronger performance in cold conditions. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, sodium-ion systems use sodium, a more abundant raw material than lithium. This could help diversify battery supply chains and reduce exposure to fluctuations in lithium prices. Their ability to operate in freezing conditions also makes them a potential fit for renewable energy storage, where reliable power delivery is essential. More from Energy See All “Built for Europe’s harsh winter climates, CATL TENER delivers over 15,000 charge cycles across a 25-year operational lifespan while maintaining high power discharge even at -20°C (-4 degrees Fahrenheit). This level of reliability helps stabilize local grids and strengthen regional power security,” said CATL in a social media post. Swappable packs These sodium-ion battery solutions have been built with dimensions compatible with lithium-ion batteries, the company said, offering flexibility to choose between these battery technologies, safeguarding the users against the global lithium price volatility. In June this year, CATL unveiled a new battery pack architecture that allows sodium-ion and lithium-ion batteries to be used inside the same enclosure, a move aimed at accelerating sodium-ion deployment in electric vehicles, battery-swapping networks, and energy storage systems. The announcement of the partnership comes as Europe’s energy storage market expands rapidly. According to South Korean market research firm SNE Research, European lithium-ion energy storage battery shipments reached 72.7 GWh in the first half of 2026, marking a year-on-year rise of 74 percent. Earlier in July 2026, the Chinese company signed an agreement with European energy integrator Alfen N.V. to deploy sodium-ion energy storage systems in Western Europe, including the Netherlands. The planned deployment capacity was 5 gigawatt-hours and would begin in 2027. The company also signed a 2 GWh cooperation agreement with Eastern European renewable energy company Solarpro in the same month. The latest announcements suggest China’s sodium-ion battery sector is moving beyond laboratory-scale development and into large-scale commercial deployment. With standardized pack designs, longer lifetimes, and expanding material production, manufacturers are positioning sodium-ion batteries as a complementary technology to lithium-ion systems rather than a direct replacement.

artigo.texto: CATL told investors it will start small-batch pilot production of solid-state cells in 2027, maintaining that its chemistry leads the industry, while its chairman warned the technology remains at readiness level 4 of 9. CATL will begin pilot production of solid-state batteries in 2027, the company told investors in a recent reply. The world’s largest EV battery manufacturer says it continues to invest in the technology and considers its approach industry-leading. The company expects initial penetration around 1% with energy density near 500 Wh/kg. CATL has assigned roughly 1,000 engineers to the project and produced 20 Ah sulfide samples. Pilot lines will start in 2027, though CATL describes the output as small batches because high demand will keep utilization rates elevated even as new capacity comes online. CATL first dismissed the solid-state push. CEO Robin Zeng pointed to a decade of research and urged adoption of sodium-ion and semi-solid cells instead. The company reversed course, setting the 2027 target and backing it with expanded engineering resources. In October 2025, CATL confirmed the 2027 window but warned that scale remains limited. Drones and humanoid robots will receive the cells before mass-market electric vehicles. Chief Scientist Wu Kai rated production readiness at 4 out of 9, predicting an 8 by 2027. At this year’s Summer Davos in Dalian, Chairman Zeng Yuqun said the technology has not advanced beyond level 4, where level 9 represents full mass production. He added that reliability, supply chains, and market acceptance matter as much as the chemistry itself. Rival startups are moving faster by skipping liquid electrolytes entirely. Eve Energy has started producing 10 Ah sulfide cells at 300 Wh/kg for drones and robots. Sunwoda offers a 400 Wh/kg polymer cell and a 520 Wh/kg prototype, also targeting 2027. Chery promises vehicles with 600 Wh/kg cells that same year, while Toyota aims to use the technology in premium Lexus models priced above liquid-electrolyte equivalents. China is drafting the world’s first regulatory framework for solid-state batteries. The initial standard separates hybrid cells containing about 5% liquid electrolyte and 95% solid electrolyte from true solid-state designs. CATL once rejected the hybrid solid-liquid approach as impractical but now embraces it as a bridge technology. Beijing’s five-year plan targets 2030 for initial mass-scale production of solid-state batteries in everyday electric vehicles. That timeline supports CATL’s cautious stance on widespread adoption. artigo.texto: Gaispi aprova proposta de data center de R$ 375 milhões para IA Projeto da EAF prevê infraestrutura para aplicações governamentais, com operação pela Telebras, e segue ao Conselho Diretor da Anatel. O Gaispi, grupo da Anatel presidido pelo conselheiro Edson Holanda e que supervisiona o cumprimento de obrigações do 5G, também aprovou nesta terça-feira, 27 de outubro, a proposta da Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz (EAF) para implantar um data center preparado para aplicações de inteligência artificial, com orçamento estimado de R$ 375 milhões. O projeto será submetido ao Conselho Diretor da Anatel e prevê utilizar recursos remanescentes do leilão do 5G para atender órgãos e instituições federais. Segundo a proposta, a infraestrutura deverá permitir o processamento de dados sensíveis, o treinamento e a inferência de modelos de IA e a hospedagem de serviços governamentais críticos. O arranjo recomendado é de titularidade da União e operação pela Telebras, com implantação a cargo da EAF. O prazo pretendido para implantação é de 12 meses, condicionado à disponibilidade de energia, ao licenciamento e aos prazos de fabricação e integração dos equipamentos. Dois módulos e 48 GPUs O cenário de referência prevê terreno de aproximadamente 5 mil metros quadrados e dois módulos externos. O primeiro será dedicado à infraestrutura de IA; o segundo, à infraestrutura física para serviços tradicionais de tecnologia da informação e colocalização. O módulo de IA contempla 20 racks de 42U, seis servidores com um total de 48 GPUs, nove servidores CPU, armazenamento all-flash e armazenamento de objetos. Já o módulo tradicional comportaria até dez racks de colocalização, sem aquisição de servidores na etapa inicial. A arquitetura prevê alimentação elétrica redundante, geração de emergência, resfriamento líquido no módulo de IA e conectividade redundante. A estimativa de carga inicial é de 2 MW para o módulo de IA, sendo 1 MW comissionado e 1 MW de reserva. Telebras na operação O grupo técnico recomenda que o data center seja estruturado como infraestrutura pública vinculada aos serviços e sistemas governamentais, em modelo igual ao da Rede Privativa de Comunicação da Administração Pública Federal. Ou seja, a titularidade será da União e a operação ficará a cargo da Telebras. A atuação da EAF ficará restrita à implantação. A análise financeira considera R$ 3,69 bilhões sob responsabilidade da EAF no fechamento do segundo trimestre de 2026. Desse total, propõe reservar aproximadamente R$ 2 bilhões para concluir os projetos originais do edital, incluindo margem de segurança de 10%. Com essa reserva, a disponibilidade estimada para projetos adicionais seria de R$ 1,69 bilhão. O data center consumiria R$ 375 milhões, restando cerca de R$ 1,32 bilhão que vão para a distribuição de conversores de TV 3.0.

artigo.texto: Australian startup MP Space raised an AUD $23M ($16.1M) seed round to expand its satellite battery manufacturing capacity, and begin building other pieces of satellite power systems, the company announced on Monday. Blackbird VC led the round, which included additional participation from Seraphim Space, Systemiq Capital, Speedinvest, and MFV Partners. Meet MP: MP Space was cofounded in 2024 by two ex-Tesla engineers—CEO Jay Manley and CCO Sam Paterson—with the aim of manufacturing low-cost, high-performing power systems for space applications. Manley explained that the company is trying to provide a new option to satellite operators who currently only have two choices: buying batteries and power systems from an expensive, slow-moving supply chain, or building them in-house. “We’re kind of becoming this third option,” Manley told Payload. “I can sell this product…about a fifth to a third below the market average while still making a profit, which basically brings it in line—or below—the cost to develop [batteries] in-house.” The market seems to be responding well to the pitch. MP Space’s batteries launched for the first time last week with an undisclosed customer on SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 mission, and already the company has orders to support 500+ spacecraft. To meet this demand, MP Space plans grow its manufacturing capacity and engineering team at its facility in Sydney, Australia. The goal, according to Manley, is to be able to produce “5,000 space widgets per year, by the end of next year.” Power training: MP Space will also use the new funds to grow its product line beyond small-sat batteries. The company aims to produce low-cost products for sat-power parts between the solar panels and the payload—including maximum power point trackers and chargers, power-conditioning and distribution units, and solar-array drive assemblies. The company is also looking ahead to products that can support larger, more power hungry satellites, since power demands are increasing as the industry prepares for SpaceX Starship to come online. Today, the company’s two batteries both weigh in at under 5 kg, but Manley told Payload power products for Starship will need to be ~10x bigger and more powerful. “We’re trying to go engineer a power backbone that would bring Starlink satellite-unit economics to everyone who’s not Starlink,” Manley said.

artigo.texto: Mountain Home adopts emergency moratorium on data centers Mountain Home, IDAHO (CBS2) — The city of Mountain Home is adopting an emergency moratorium on accepting applications and issuing permits for data centers. The Mayor and City Council moved to temporarily halt new data center proposals inside city limits after residents packed a City Council meeting Tuesday night to oppose a large project planned for the Bennett Ranch Industrial Complex. The proposed project from Weitz and Co. would have spanned 3.4 million square feet near West Fifth North Street, with four three-story buildings covering roughly 19.5 acres each. Mountain Home Mayor Rich Sykes said data centers are not a permitted nor conditional use in any zone within the city. Residents who spoke out at Tuesday night’s meeting urged the city to block such projects going forward. “I want to advocate for us to add data centers on the prohibited list so that this is not something that moves forward in the future,” Mountain Home resident, Aaron Summers said. “The whole data center project has many problems, these facilities have many problems which i think cannot be of benefit to our community,” Mountain Home resident, Rob Monastario added. Mayor Sykes said Weitz and Company has not submitted a formal land use application or building permit for the proposed data center.

artigo.texto: The Palm Beach County Commission knows that many residents do not want data centers but are divided on how they should create new rules to protect communities. Consultants are lining up to help them, and hiring one could cost taxpayers big money. The commissioners directed staff Thursday, Oct. 22, to bring back additional proposals from consultants to assist in establishing stricter data center regulations. The effort comes after the county imposed a one-year moratorium on related large-scale projects to allow time for developing new rules. The moratorium, however, exempts the controversial Project Tango site off Southern Blvd. near 20-Mile Bend. (See related story, page 1.) Commissioners at previous meetings were interested in creating a task force composed of local residents and experts to address these problems. Those plans were scrapped in September because officials were unsure if the committee could reasonably bring recommendations back in time before the moratorium ends, given that multiple meetings would have to be held and several areas of concern needed to be addressed. Staff suggested hiring a consultant to provide specialized expertise in data centers and local planning to develop the regulations. At the meeting, county staff members proposed hiring consulting firm VHB to advise officials throughout the process. “VHB is a highly qualified planning, engineering and environmental firm, with extensive experience in code of development, especially in emerging areas and an inherent understanding of large load data centers,” said Whitney Carroll, executive director of the Planning, Zoning & Building Department. The firm’s proposal would provide the county with research, technical recommendations, outreach support and assistance with regulatory documents. Staff said that since putting out a request for a consultant, they received six offers, which would cost anywhere from $200,000 to $2 million with a range of services. VHB’s proposal will cost $199,900 plus up to $25,000 for additional services if authorized — totaling $224,900. It was one of the lowest offers received. The consultant contract would include reviewing existing county conditions to identify gaps within it, researching the impact of data centers on multiple areas of interest and developing a regulatory framework for commissioners to adopt. If hired, VHB and county officials will also conduct up to eight targeted discussions with stakeholders, two public outreach events and three check-ins with the board. “From a staff perspective, we are asking for this assistance because we are limited in our capacity to do the work,” Carroll said. “We need the technical expertise. We need that assistance to help support our staff to get this done in a timely manner.” Earlier this year, the commissioners rejected a controversial plan to build an expanded 202-acre hyperscale AI data center near 20-Mile Bend called Project Tango. While that project was originally proposed at up to 1.8 million square feet of data center use, the site had previous approvals from 2016, which could still put up to 700,000 square feet of data center use there. This, along with receiving multiple data center applications, led the commissioners to pass the one-year moratorium — believing the county’s current code was not adequately equipped to regulate the rapidly advancing technology infrastructure. Public outcry against Project Tango and any data center in Palm Beach County is still running hot among residents. At the meeting, those who gave public comments questioned the need for the consultant, especially with taxpayer money being used to hire them. Many claimed that VHB has ties to data center developers. “VHB, the consultant that is being looked at today, I am not in favor of it because they obviously work for AI data centers,” said Ben Brown, an Arden resident who has been a leader in the fight against Project Tango. “You are putting the fox in the hen house.” VHB’s web site indicates that it does provide consulting services to help construct data centers and secure approvals. Carroll also confirmed that it does have private data center clients. The county’s moratorium ends in September 2027, and if new regulations are not put in place, any applications will have to abide only by already existing regulations. The moratorium can be extended under some specific circumstances. Given the need to create new rules by next year and for expert opinions on how to do so, Commissioner Joel Flores supported hiring VHB despite the expense. “I understand the hesitation about spending taxpayer dollars,” he said. “At the end of the day, we’re trying to protect our people, and the only way we can do that is with information.” Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter did not support hiring a consultant. She believed the county should revert to creating a community task force to deal with the issue. “We shouldn’t get a consultant,” Baxter said. “I believe it’s a waste of taxpayer dollars… When people work for data centers or have clients that work for data centers, they can have a persuaded opinion.” Commissioner Maria Sachs added that the board needs more information before making this type of decision. Commissioners did not receive much information on the firm’s background or have a chance to negotiate a price, she said. “I haven’t heard one positive opinion about this particular company, as opposed to others,” Sachs said. “I cannot professionally agree to a particular company, and to these amounts of money, without having a little more in front of me.” The board initially passed a motion to hire VHB as a consultant. However, Commissioner Bobby Powell requested a reconsideration vote to instead have staff bring back additional proposals from other consultants. The reconsideration narrowly passed, with commissioners subsequently approving a new motion for the board to consider other consultants for the matter.

artigo.texto: CATL hit another milestone in its solid-state battery development, advancing to 20 Ah cells. The world’s leading battery maker aims to begin small-scale production in 2027. CATL continues advancing solid-state EV batteries CATL remains the leading global EV battery manufacturer by a wide margin. According to SNE Research, CATL held a commanding 39.9% share of the global EV battery market through the first half of 2026. To stay ahead, the company is advancing several new battery chemistries, including solid-state and sodium-ion, promising to be safer, more efficient, and lower cost than traditional lithium-ion batteries. When investors asked about the progress of its solid-state battery program on Tuesday, CATL said it continues to invest heavily in all-solid-state batteries and expects to begin small-scale production in 2027. As it has stated before, output is expected to be limited at first as it scales up to mass production around 2030. Speaking at the Summer Davos Forum in June, CATL chairman and CEO Robin Zeng said that, on a scale of one to nine, all-solid-state batteries have only reached level four. All-solid-state batteries differ from semi-solid-state batteries in that they require a solid electrolyte to conduct lithium ions, rather than a liquid. The company uses a sulfide-based solid electrolyte system, which offers high ionic conductivity and deformability, but maintaining stable contact between solid components remains a hurdle. CATL said its sulfide-based batteries have now entered 20 Ah trial production as it aims to achieve an energy density of 500 Wh/kg. Trial production in 2027, reaching mass market in 2030 CATL’s 2027 timeline to begin small-scale production aligns with other automakers and battery manufacturers racing to introduce all-solid-state EV batteries. Toyota, which has been promising solid-state batteries for nearly a decade now, aims to launch the first all-solid-state battery-powered EV in 2027 or 2028. Using Sumitomo Metal Mining’s proprietary powder synthesis technology, Toyota claimed to have developed a “highly durable cathode material” for all-solid-state batteries last October. Toyota revealed a prototype last year, claiming it can deliver 745 miles (1,200 km) of range and charge in under 10 minutes. However, like CATL, Toyota expects production to be limited and will not reach the mass market until closer to the end of the decade. Samsung SDI, on the other hand, aims to begin mass production of its SolidStack all-solid-state batteries in the second half of 2027. BYD, which ranks second in global EV battery sales behind CATL, also plans to launch its first solid-state battery-powered vehicle in 2027. In an exclusive interview with Carwow.es last month, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD is in “the leading position” on solid-state batteries and will “prove that” next year. BYD’s battery division, FinDreams, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, ramping up to mass production by 2030. Electrek’s Take While solid-state batteries are often hailed the “holy grail” of battery tech, they are only one part of the equation. Top comment by AutoMotive Toyota is not to be trusted as their press briefings are misinformation over facts for the past 10 years. CATL has legitimacy and timeline is a maybe. Mass produced for ev is a huge under taking before applications for small electronics tools lawn mowers motorcycles. They need to crawl before they walk. CATL, BYD, and others continue advancing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and sodium-ion batteries, which will ultimately create more efficient, lower-cost options that offer various performance needs. BYD’s second-generation Blade LFP batteries already deliver over 1,000 km (621 miles) of CLTC range. What’s next? One thing is certain: New battery chemistries and evolving tech will only continue making EVs more efficient, unlocking longer driving ranges, faster charging speeds, and better performance. artigo.texto: - Four national labs, five founding universities on board, battery manufacturers next - AI models to flag process drift, contamination during production - Autonomous pilot lines with digital twins form long-term target Pacific Northwest National Laboratory has taken the helm of a battery manufacturing consortium that will use artificial intelligence to fast-track lab breakthroughs into domestic production, with backing from the Department of Energy’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation. The Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan, will work to lower production costs and reduce U.S. reliance on foreign battery materials, the laboratory said Wednesday. The Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office within that DOE office supports the consortium as the department works to link AI and advanced manufacturing research across national labs, universities and industry. “Breakthroughs in battery science must be matched by our ability to manufacture them at scale,” said Jie Xiao, a Battelle Fellow at PNNL who holds a joint appointment at the University of Washington. She added that BattMan intends to give partners shared data and tools so manufacturing constraints shape research from its earliest stages. Which Institutions Are Joining the BattMan Accelerator? Argonne, Oak Ridge and the National Laboratory of the Rockies join PNNL as the consortium’s national laboratory members. Its five founding universities are Arizona State University, Binghamton University, the University of Alabama, the University of Michigan-Dearborn and the University of Washington. Battery and battery materials manufacturers can apply to join through PNNL’s BattMan page as the consortium works to bring industry partners on board. Angela Becker-Dippmann, an associate laboratory director at PNNL, explained that combining labs, universities and companies is meant to tie scientific discovery to manufacturing, data and scale-up. How Does BattMan Plan to Use AI in Battery Manufacturing? According to Xiao, some laboratory research gives too little weight to cost, repeatability and scale-up risk. Under BattMan, partners will be asked to consider how a promising result could be produced affordably before it leaves the lab, she said. AI models trained on the consortium’s manufacturing data are intended to help factory teams catch process drift and contamination early and respond to production risks as they arise. Stanley Whittingham, a distinguished professor of chemistry at Binghamton University and a 2019 Nobel laureate recognized for developing lithium-ion batteries, described bringing AI into research and production as a shift from trial and error toward predictive design. “This capability is key to accelerating innovation while ensuring technologies can be produced reliably and affordably at scale,” he noted. What Are BattMan’s Manufacturing Goals? BattMan’s first phase will automate materials synthesis and testing and run high-volume experiments across partner sites, so each institution produces data the others can compare and reproduce. Over the longer term, the consortium aims to stand up autonomous pilot lines that adjust their own processes using digital twins, closed-loop control and real-time data. The launch coincided with DOE’s release of a national battery strategy that seeks a continuous domestic supply chain by 2030. Among its priorities, the strategy calls for building manufacturability into early-stage research and investing in AI-based quality control and digital twins for factories.

artigo.texto: Sioux County approves strict new rules for future data centers ORANGE CITY, Iowa (KTIV) — Leaders in Sioux County have approved changes to county ordinances that impact the future of data centers in the county. On Tuesday morning, the Sioux County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to approve the third and final reading of an amendment to County Ordinance One. The amendment adds strict regulations for data centers in unincorporated areas, including limiting the size of data centers and creating standards on where they can be built. It also addresses water usage, noise and light pollution, and requires a decommissioning plan in case a data center is abandoned after becoming obsolete. Officials note the vote was only on a change to the ordinance, and not on the creation of any data center. Want to get the latest news and weather from Siouxland’s News Source? Emerald Battery Labs Partners with City of Issaquah to Deliver Safe, Cost-Effective, Sustainable Battery Storage for Pickering Barn Resiliency Project Emerald Battery Labs, Inc. 5 min read Sodium-ion battery energy storage system to complete the Pickering Barn microgrid and strengthen a community Resilience Hub during grid outages Emerald Battery Labs Partners with City of Issaquah to Deliver Safe, Cost-Effective, Sustainable Battery Storage for Pickering Barn Resiliency Project SEATTLE, Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Emerald Battery Labs, a Seattle-based manufacturer of sodium-ion batteries, today announced a partnership with the City of Issaquah, Washington, to provide a safe, cost-effective and sustainable battery energy storage system (BESS) for the City's resiliency project at Pickering Barn. The project is supported, in part, by a $671,000 grant from TransAlta Centralia Generation LLC. Pickering Barn is a historic landmark in the heart of Issaquah and a designated Resilience Hub site under the City's Resilience Hub Initiative, providing warming and cooling centers, emergency services and community support during grid outages or natural disasters. "Issaquah is committed to investing in clean energy that also strengthens our community's resilience," said Issaquah Mayor Mark Mullet. "Pairing solar power with battery storage at Pickering Barn will help keep essential services available during power outages while advancing our climate goals." The City's Solar + Storage Microgrid Feasibility Study identified Pickering Barn as a priority site for a community resilience microgrid. Earlier this year, the City completed installation of a 64.9 kW-DC solar PV array as the first step. The next critical step, integration of a battery energy storage system, is required to let the facility "island" from the grid and support critical loads during extended outages. This grant funding will enable Emerald to develop and deploy a 60-kWh sodium-ion battery system to pair with the City's existing solar and hardware systems at Pickering Barn. "Emerald was founded to unlock the full potential of sodium-ion batteries," said David Bell, co-founder and CEO of Emerald Battery Labs. "Sodium-ion batteries are more sustainable than lead-acid, safer than lithium-ion, and can be produced from abundant, low-cost materials sourced in the United States. Pickering Barn is a real-world, public setting where we can show that sodium-ion battery systems can meet or exceed the safety, cost and performance standards required for municipal deployment." Sodium-ion chemistry offers significant advantages over lithium-ion alternatives for stationary storage, including improved thermal stability, improved safety, longer cycle life, and no cobalt or lithium dependency. A certified sodium-ion product at the community microgrid scale would open a new segment of the stationary storage market to sodium-ion technology, at a scale directly relevant to resilience hub, microgrid and backup power applications across the Pacific Northwest and beyond. The approach focuses Emerald's design work on sodium-ion integration, energy management and battery management system communication protocols, and system-level safety validation. Emerald will finalize the design of its sodium-ion BESS, achieve UL 9540, UL 9540A and UL 1973 certifications, and support the City through permitting and procurement for a deployment at the historic community venue. For more than 110 years, Pickering Barn has stood proudly as an icon of Issaquah. Merging the history of this farmland with present day community needs, The City of Issaquah has advanced multiple initiatives to move Pickering Barn into the future while preserving its unique charm, including installing heat pumps in 2025 and solar panels in 2026. These projects improve energy efficiency, generate clean electricity, help lower municipal energy costs, and serve as an educational resource for the Issaquah Community. As a public facility, it hosts a weekly Farmers Market from May through October and welcomes more than 37,000 visitors a year, including 264 events in 2025. In 2023, the U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC) awarded the City of Issaquah with LEED® Gold certification for its exceptional performance in fostering a sustainable, resilient and equitable community. Issaquah is the first city in Washington state to achieve LEED Gold certification – and one of only five LEED-certified communities statewide. About Emerald Battery Labs Based in Seattle, Emerald Battery Labs is a developer and manufacturer of sodium-ion batteries. Emerald targets applications where sodium-ion wins on longevity and cost today while building for the sodium-ion future. Its first products use sodium-ion's superior safety, cycle life and high- and low-temperature performance in 12V and 24V batteries for commercial vehicles, 48V stackable DC blocks for data center UPS and 60 kWh battery energy storage systems for commercial and industrial microgrids. Emerald is also developing proprietary anode materials and cell architecture designed to help sodium-ion batteries achieve an energy density of 400 Wh/L at a cost of less than $30/kWh. Emerald's advances will enable a fully domestic sodium-ion supply chain for electric vehicles and grid storage. More information is available at www.emeraldbatterylabs.com. About the City of Issaquah Issaquah, WA is a community of more than 40,000 and is conveniently located off the Interstate 90 corridor, just 16 miles east of Seattle. Nicknamed Trailhead City, the town is centered within the Issaquah Alps (Cougar, Squak and Tiger mountains) and is a destination for countless outdoor enthusiasts, including hikers and paragliders. Learn more at issaquahwa.gov

artigo.texto: A Galaxy Digital Inc. (NASDAQ:GLXY) reportou um lucro líquido de US$ 323 milhões para o terceiro trimestre encerrado em 30 de setembro de 2026, em comparação com um prejuízo líquido de US$ 85 milhões no trimestre anterior, devido ao aumento da receita e dos lucros ajustados provenientes de suas operações de data center. A empresa de infraestrutura de ativos digitais e data centers registrou EBITDA ajustado de US$ 455 milhões e lucro bruto ajustado de US$ 569 milhões no trimestre. O lucro diluído por ação atingiu US$ 0,66, enquanto o lucro ajustado por ação totalizou US$ 0,83. A Galaxy também reportou crescimento em seu balanço patrimonial, expandiu seu portfólio de desenvolvimento de data centers e anunciou uma nova autorização de recompra de ações no valor de US$ 200 milhões, após a conclusão de um programa anterior de recompra. Galaxy Digital volta a apresentar lucro trimestral A Galaxy Digital reportou um lucro líquido de US$ 323 milhões no terceiro trimestre, revertendo o prejuízo líquido de US$ 85 milhões registrado no segundo trimestre de 2026. O EBITDA ajustado totalizou US$ 455 milhões, enquanto o lucro bruto ajustado atingiu US$ 569 milhões. A empresa reportou lucro diluído por ação de US$ 0,66 e lucro ajustado por ação de US$ 0,83. O total de ativos aumentou 51% em relação ao trimestre anterior, atingindo US$ 16,4 bilhões em 30 de setembro de 2026. O patrimônio líquido total era de US$ 3,0 bilhões ao final do período analisado. Os resultados trimestrais refletiram as contribuições dos negócios de data center e ativos digitais da Galaxy, juntamente com mudanças na posição financeira da empresa. O segmento de data centers reporta lucros ajustados mais altos O segmento de Data Centers da Galaxy registrou lucro bruto ajustado de US$ 79 milhões durante o terceiro trimestre, em comparação com US$ 20 milhões no trimestre anterior. O EBITDA ajustado do segmento aumentou para US$ 69 milhões, ante US$ 11 milhões no segundo trimestre. Os resultados incluíram o primeiro trimestre completo de receita associada ao arrendamento da Fase I do Helios I. Nos termos do acordo, a Galaxy forneceu 133 megawatts de carga crítica de tecnologia da informação para a CoreWeave. A contribuição desse arrendamento foi um fator no aumento do lucro bruto ajustado e do EBITDA ajustado reportado pelo segmento de Data Centers. Galaxy garante financiamento de US$ 3,5 bilhões para expansão do Helios A Galaxy concluiu uma oferta de US$ 3,5 bilhões em títulos seniores garantidos para financiar a construção da Fase II do projeto Helios I. A empresa prevê que as entregas dos data centers associados à segunda fase comecem no segundo trimestre de 2027. O financiamento apoia a próxima etapa de desenvolvimento do centro de dados Helios, após a entrega da capacidade na fase inicial. A Galaxy também informou que sua capacidade total de geração de energia bruta agora ultrapassa 5,7 gigawatts. O número de projetos em desenvolvimento representa a capacidade de desenvolvimento divulgada pela empresa e deve ser diferenciado da infraestrutura que já foi concluída ou colocada em operação. O segmento de ativos digitais registra um crescimento de 9% no lucro bruto ajustado O segmento de Ativos Digitais da Galaxy reportou um lucro bruto ajustado de US$ 71 milhões no terceiro trimestre. O valor representou um aumento de 9% em comparação com o trimestre anterior. O total combinado de ativos sob gestão e ativos em risco atingiu US$ 10,4 bilhões, um aumento de 46% em relação ao trimestre anterior. Os números refletiram o crescimento dos ativos gerenciados ou suportados por meio de atividades de staking nas operações de ativos digitais da Galaxy. A empresa também anunciou um acordo com o objetivo de expandir seus serviços de infraestrutura de ativos digitais institucionais. Galaxy firma acordo plurianual de ativos digitais com o BNY A Galaxy firmou um acordo plurianual com o BNY para desenvolver infraestrutura de ativos digitais para mercados institucionais. O acordo inclui suporte para serviços de staking por meio da plataforma de Custódia de Ativos Digitais do BNY. O acordo tem como objetivo apoiar o acesso institucional à infraestrutura de ativos digitais e serviços relacionados. A Galaxy não divulgou o valor financeiro do acordo no comunicado fornecido. A parceria faz parte das atividades comerciais de ativos digitais da empresa, juntamente com a gestão de ativos e as operações de staking. Reservas em dinheiro, stablecoins e títulos do Tesouro atingem US$ 4,9 bilhões A Galaxy reportou possuir, em 30 de setembro de 2026, um total de US$ 4,9 bilhões em reservas combinadas de dinheiro, stablecoins e títulos do Tesouro dos EUA. O valor se compara aos US$ 2,5 bilhões registrados no final do segundo trimestre. O aumento representou um crescimento de aproximadamente 96% em relação ao trimestre anterior. A empresa também reportou ativos totais de US$ 16,4 bilhões e patrimônio líquido total de US$ 3,0 bilhões ao final do trimestre. Esses números fornecem informações sobre a situação financeira da Galaxy, à medida que a empresa continua desenvolvendo suas operações de data center e seus negócios de ativos digitais. Galaxy conclui programa de recompra de ações de US$ 200 milhões A Galaxy informou ter recomprado aproximadamente 9,8 milhões de ações durante 2026, no âmbito de um programa de recompra de ações de US$ 200 milhões. A empresa concluiu esse programa em 15 de outubro de 2026. Após a sua conclusão, o conselho de administração da Galaxy autorizou um novo programa de recompra de ações no valor de 200 milhões de dólares em 26 de outubro de 2026. A nova autorização permite à empresa realizar recompras adicionais de ações, sujeitas às suas decisões de alocação de capital e às condições aplicáveis. O comunicado não especificou o cronograma nem o volume de recompras no âmbito do programa recém-autorizado. Quais são os próximos desenvolvimentos para a Galaxy Digital? Os resultados do terceiro trimestre da Galaxy mostraram um retorno à lucratividad

artigo.texto: Texas' rapidly expanding data-center industry could threaten decades of progress in reducing air pollution, according to new research examining the enormous amounts of electricity the state's AI boom may need. A recent assessment published by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) modeled how different ways of meeting future data-center electricity demand could affect emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), sulfur dioxide, fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and carbon dioxide through 2031. The researchers found that the impact depends heavily on how the additional electricity is generated. Newsweek has contacted HARC for comment. The warning comes as data centers spread across Texas, with state records showing projects in Abilene, the Dallas-Fort Worth area, San Antonio, Austin and parts of West Texas. The Texas comptroller maintains registers of qualifying data centers and qualifying large data-center projects, including facilities associated with companies such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Oracle. The City of Abilene maintains a dedicated information page for data-center construction, including the Stargate project, while the City of Fort Worth reported in June that it already had four data centers comprising 10 buildings and about 3 million square feet, with additional projects proposed within the city and surrounding area. Pollution Could Reverse Years of Progress Texas has made substantial reductions in emissions over the past two decades. HARC found that between 2002 and 2024, NOx emissions from power generation declined by 67 percent, sulfur dioxide by 80 percent, VOCs by 37 percent, carbon dioxide by 52 percent and PM2.5 by 60 percent. But electricity demand from data centers could change that trajectory. Under HARC's scenario in which new data-center demand is supplied entirely by the Texas electricity grid, using the mixture of energy sources the grid is projected to have at that time, NOx emissions in 2031 would be 136 percent higher than HARC's projected no-data-center baseline, approaching volumes last recorded around 2004. VOC emissions would exceed their 2002 volume by 32 percent, while PM2.5 emissions would rise to about their 2006 level. Power sources make a pronounced difference. HARC found that nitrogen oxide emissions could be two to 10 times higher if data centers generate the additional power they need by burning fuel rather than relying on a combination of grid electricity, solar and wind. Even under the cleanest energy scenario studied, the research center found that data-center growth would still increase emissions because of the large amount of additional electricity the facilities require. Texas Data Center Demand Surges Separate figures from the state's electric-grid operator, Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), illustrate the scale of potential data center development. In August, Republican Governor Greg Abbott's office said ERCOT was considering more than 474 gigawatts of requests to connect to the grid and that about 90 percent were from data centers. Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to carry out an audit of data-center projects going through the interconnection process, including their electricity and water requirements and plans for on-site generation. The administration went further in September, when Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt permits sought by data centers until the ERCOT audit was completed, citing concerns such as grid reliability and natural resources. Newsweek has contacted TCEQ for comment. HARC said Texas' future emissions depend on decisions now being made about power supply, concluding that the projected data-center build-out could produce impacts ranging from relatively marginal increases to a reversal of much of the progress made over the past two decades. Newsweek's reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Shakeema Edwards.
