artigo.texto: The Prince George’s County Council approved legislation Tuesday that removes development privileges previously granted to data centers in the county. The bill removes an exemption, which was approved in 2021, that allowed data center developers to bypass a process called a detailed site plan review. A detailed site plan review is a step in the county’s permitting process for larger projects that includes an in-depth review and a public hearing. District 1 council member Thomas Dernoga, council chair Krystal Oriadha and at-large council member Wala Blegay first introduced the legislation in January, The Diamondback previously reported. During Tuesday’s meeting, District 5 council member Shayla Adams-Stafford said the legislation was created to ensure that data center applications will no longer be able to bypass the site plan review, as the now-shuttered Landover Mall site did. County residents started to raise concerns about the proposed $5 billion data center project, which is located in Adams-Stafford’s district, after it went through the fast-tracked review process. The council approved the site plan exemption in 2021 to make it easier and cheaper for data centers to move forward in the county. Oriadha, who represents District 7, said in a September council meeting she felt the exemption blindsided the community. [Voters to weigh in on fate of at-large Prince George’s County Council seats] “It created a process that would allow for data centers not to come before the council, it would allow them to go straight to permitting,” Oriadha said. “I think it was done intentionally to allow for the Landover site to get where it was in the dark of night.” The council is currently under a two-year moratorium it approved in July for the review and approval of new data center applications. Tuesday’s legislation does not end the current moratorium, but the pause would expire automatically in July 2028 if the council fails to implement zoning regulations. The council established a data center task force in April 2025 to assess the potential community impacts and economic prospects of data centers in the county. The county also approved a 180-day moratorium on reviewing and approving new data center proposals in September 2025. During the Tuesday meeting, District 2 council member Wanika Fisher proposed an amendment to the legislation that would have required data center proposals to come before the council for approval before they can move forward. The council approved the bill without Fisher’s amendment in a 10-0-1 vote, from which Fisher abstained. Fisher argued that the measure would help the council have a more involved role in controlling data center development once the countywide moratorium on their development expires. [Joan’s House details services to Prince George’s County amid nonprofit funding controversy] Adams-Stafford, Blegay and Oriadha all said they did not want to approve the amendment because it would require an additional public hearing due to the significance of the legislative change. The necessary public hearing would significantly delay the bill’s approval because there is not another council meeting until December. “If we want to create a regulation bill around data centers, we have to follow what the task force advises us to do,” Adams-Stafford said during the meeting. “Convene the public, convene experts and put forward real legislation.” During the vote, Blegay told the council she felt the legislation was important to pass now given the county’s opposition to data center development. In a Tuesday statement to The Diamondback, Adams-Stafford stood by her decision, writing that she is glad the bill was approved without the amendment. She also wrote that she is confident that the approved legislation is the best way to meet the community’s concerns about data centers. Blegay, Oriadha and Dernoga did not respond to The Diamondback’s request for comment in time for publication. Fisher declined to comment. The County Council’s approval came during its last legislative session before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Its next scheduled meeting is on Dec. 8 and will introduce the newly elected council. Contact staff writer Devon Armor at darmor@terpmail.umd.edu.

artigo.texto: Shopping de “De volta para o futuro” pode virar data center O shopping que inspirou o Twin Pines Mall do filme de 1985 pode dar lugar a uma instalação de 10 megawatts, mas a comunidade local se opõe à proposta O shopping Puente Hills Mall, localizado na cidade de Industry, no sul da Califórnia, é mais conhecido pelos fãs de "De volta para o futuro" como o Twin Pines Mall. Caso você não tenha assistido ao filme, é lá que Marty McFly e Doc Brown são perseguidos por terroristas insatisfeitos porque Doc havia roubado o plutônio deles. O local era um shopping de verdade quando o filme foi rodado. Mas, como tantos outros centros comerciais nos Estados Unidos, acabou vítima da pandemia e da ascensão das compras online. Em vez de fechar as portas, porém, os proprietários do imóvel esperam transformá-lo em um complexo com dois galpões logísticos, uma estação de transporte coletivo por ônibus e um data center de 10 megawatts. Considerando os data centers atuais, não se trata de uma instalação especialmente grande – as instalações de hiperescala podem chegar a mil megawatts. Ainda assim, o projeto é suficiente para provocar a reação contrária de moradores da região. Por enquanto, a proposta não passa disso. As autoridades municipais ainda não aprovaram a transformação do shopping, praticamente vazio, em um complexo de data centers. Na verdade, há duas propostas distintas para o imóvel. Uma prevê a construção de dois galpões, com a possibilidade de converter um deles em data center. A segunda combina empreendimentos industriais e comerciais, com a construção de um galpão ou de um galpão acompanhado de um data center, além de vários novos edifícios comerciais. O Puente Hills Mall foi usado nas cenas externas do fictício Twin Pines Mall no filme de 1985. Inaugurado originalmente na década de 1970, o shopping perdeu o brilho aos olhos dos consumidores. Embora ainda tenha entre 100 mil e 110 mil metros quadrados de área locável, hoje restam basicamente um cinema da AMC e o Round1, um espaço de entretenimento com jogos de fliperama e pistas de boliche. Apesar disso, o shopping continua atraindo visitantes graças à popularidade duradoura da trilogia "De volta para o futuro". O imóvel foi comprado há dois anos por US$ 115 milhões, segundo informações divulgadas na época. FORTE OPOSIÇÃO Um grupo de moradores organizou uma mobilização contra os planos de construir o data center, argumentando que a instalação vai piorar a qualidade do ar na cidade de Industry, aumentar a poluição sonora e elevar as contas de serviços públicos. Além disso, o grupo afirma que o shopping representa um importante terceiro espaço para a comunidade: um lugar onde as pessoas podem se reunir e socializar fora de casa, do trabalho ou da escola. “Conheci meu marido aqui em 2001”, contou a organizadora dos protestos, Falynn Love, à rádio KCRW-FM. “Ele estava aqui com um amigo para ir ao cinema e eu estava com minha prima, também para ir ao cinema.” Embora algumas cidades da Califórnia, como a vizinha Baldwin Park, tenham adotado moratórias temporárias para a construção de data centers, a cidade de Industry não é Hill Valley. Industry tem uma população muito menor que a de seus vizinhos e 92% de seu território está zoneado para uso industrial. Isso pode dificultar os esforços dos opositores para impedir a transformação do shopping. “Quem vive nas áreas não incorporadas do condado de Los Angeles vai acabar arcando com os impactos – os efeitos sobre a saúde pública e os danos ambientais –, sem nenhuma solução, possibilidade de recurso ou mecanismo de fiscalização neste momento”, afirmou Sam Brown-Vázquez, organizador do grupo No Data Centers San Gabriel Valley, segundo o site LAist. Leia mais: Expansão de data centers no Brasil pode multiplicar consumo de energia em 20 vezes até 2038 Mas as autoridades locais parecem menos sensíveis à oposição. Em fevereiro, o Conselho Municipal aprovou mudanças nas leis de zoneamento que, segundo os críticos, permitiriam a instalação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias e data centers em toda a cidade. Infelizmente para os opositores, não existe um DeLorean capaz de levar o shopping de volta aos seus dias de glória.

artigo.texto: Engetron apresenta soluções para eficiência energética e continuidade de data centers no DCD Connect Brasil 2026 Empresa levará ao evento seu mais recente lançamento, o menor UPS modular de 600kW do mundo, e baterias de lítio da Saft, além de realizar palestra sobre inovação em energia para operações críticas A Engetron, empresa brasileira líder em fabricação de UPS IoT, apresentará tecnologias para ampliar a eficiência e a continuidade energética dos data centers no DCD Connect Brasil 2026, que acontece nos dias 4 e 5 de novembro, em São Paulo (SP). Entre os destaques do estande da empresa (nº 25) estarão o DWTT Modular 600kW, o menor UPS modular de 600kW do mundo, e um banco de baterias de lítio da Saft, parceira da Engetron. No evento, os visitantes poderão conhecer as soluções de última geração da empresa, desenvolvidas para acompanhar a crescente demanda energética dos data centers, impulsionada pela expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) e do processamento de dados. O tema também será abordado por Aluízio Ábdom, Diretor Comercial e de Marketing da Engetron, em uma palestra sobre inovação em energia para missão crítica, na qual discutirá como as novas tecnologias de UPS podem contribuir para a evolução da infraestrutura elétrica desses ambientes. "O avanço da IA está mudando a forma como os data centers precisam planejar sua infraestrutura. Na Engetron, acreditamos que não basta apenas aumentar a potência disponível. É necessário pensar em como crescer de maneira sustentável, preservar a disponibilidade dos sistemas e aproveitar melhor os recursos existentes", afirma Ábdom. Segundo o executivo, a participação no DCD permite discutir essas tendências com profissionais do setor. "Queremos mostrar como a inovação em energia pode apoiar a expansão dos data centers, oferecendo mais flexibilidade para os investimentos e segurança para operações que não podem parar", diz. O DWTT Modular 600kW, que será apresentado pela empresa no evento, se destaca por reunir módulos de 100kW em um rack de apenas 600 milímetros de largura, possibilitando uma redução de até 50% na área ocupada em comparação com outras soluções. Sua arquitetura modular permite ampliar a potência instalada de forma gradual, evitando o superdimensionamento inicial da infraestrutura e adequando os investimentos ao crescimento do negócio. Com tecnologia hot-swap, os módulos podem ser incluídos ou substituídos sem interromper o fornecimento de energia. O equipamento também alcança até 97% de eficiência em dupla conversão, reduzindo perdas elétricas e custos operacionais, e incorpora Engetron IoT e Osciloscópio Virtual para monitoramento remoto e diagnóstico de ocorrências. Além disso, a solução da Engetron, aliada às baterias de lítio da Saft, contribui para uma infraestrutura mais resiliente diante de falhas no fornecimento elétrico. Com elevada vida útil e menor necessidade de substituições e manutenção, as baterias oferecem armazenamento de energia para sustentar cargas essenciais. A combinação das tecnologias proporciona maior segurança energética e pode reduzir os custos de manutenção ao longo da operação. Durante os dois dias do DCD Connect Brasil 2026, os especialistas da Engetron estarão disponíveis no estande da empresa para demonstrar os equipamentos e discutir aplicações para diferentes projetos de infraestrutura crítica. Para mais informações, acesse www.engetron.com.br. artigo.texto: Na Espanha, uma empresa quer utilizar a energia irradiada pelos data centers para aquecer as residências Em Odense, a Meta aquece milhares de lares com seus servidores; em Soria, uma startup quer fazer o mesmo com o centro de dados da Seguridade Social A startup espanhola Hotta quer transformar data centers em centrais térmicas para aquecer residências, aproveitando o calor residual dos servidores. A iniciativa se inspira no caso da Meta na Dinamarca, onde o ar quente das instalações é direcionado a serpentinas de água e aquecido por bombas até 75 °C, abastecendo cerca de 9.000 lares. Com a alta demanda por IA e eletricidade, o desperdício térmico contínuo desses centros surge como uma solução viável e econômica para o inverno. Um servidor é, para fins práticos, um radiador caríssimo que, além disso, realiza milhões de cálculos. Toda essa energia residual que não é aproveitada transforma-se em energia térmica (calor). Os centros de dados operam 24 horas por dia e são refrigerados ininterruptamente; por isso, grande parte da eletricidade que consomem acaba convertida em calor. Durante anos, isso foi um incômodo que precisava ser dissipado (usando turbinas, vapor, água, uma mistura diluída com propilenoglicol...). Mas, com a IA elevando o consumo e o inverno chegando, isso se tornou um atrativo comercial: aquecimento quase gratuito. Na Espanha, essa promessa tem nomes e sobrenomes. Aarón Molina e Gonzalo García, fundadores da Hotta, estabeleceram como desafio transformar centros de dados em centrais térmicas urbanas. Antes de verificar se a conta fecha, vale a pena olhar para a Dinamarca. Um radiador do tamanho de Odense O caso de referência é o centro de dados da Meta nessa cidade dinamarquesa. Segundo o OKDiario, ele fornece, a cada ano, 165.000 MWh de calor para a rede urbana gerenciada pela Fjernvarme Fyn. O documento publicado pela Meta em setembro de 2026 menciona o atendimento a cerca de 9.000 residências. Onde está o truque? A Meta explicou, em 2019, que direciona o ar quente dos servidores para serpentinas de água. Como essa água morna não é suficiente para uma residência, ela é enviada a uma central vizinha, equipada com bombas de calor elétricas, que eleva sua temperatura até os 70-75 °C ... Matérias relacionadas Apple responde às telas quebradas do iPhone Duo e, curiosamente, a culpa não é dos usuários

artigo.texto: Piedmont City Council voted Monday, Oct. 26, to advance plans for a second proposed data center as residents continued raising concerns about the developments. Council members approved an amended master design statement for Beltline Energy’s proposed 640-acre data center campus, which could include approximately 19 buildings. The council also voted to send the amended plan back to the Planning and Zoning Commission for further consideration. Council members requested a special meeting for Nov. 17 at 6 p.m. That decision does not give the developer final approval to begin construction. What about the Cloverleaf data center? The decision comes after the council approved an amended master design plan for a separate data center proposed by Cloverleaf Infrastructure on Oct. 22. MORE ON THE PROPOSAL: How a 4-1 City Council vote moved Piedmont’s data center plans forward That project covers approximately 633 acres and could include six data center buildings. Both developments are moving through the city’s approval process, but neither has received final construction approval. What are residents concerned about? During Monday’s meeting, residents voiced their opposition to the developments, raising concerns about noise, water consumption, infrastructure and the impact on nearby homes. WATCH THE FULL CITY COUNCIL MEETING HERE. Council members discussed additional requirements for Beltline’s proposal, including environmental studies, noise protections and landscaping. The council also postponed action on a proposed data center moratorium until November. What happens next for the proposed data centers? Both proposed data centers have additional steps in the city’s approval process. The next reported project-approval hearing for Cloverleaf Infrastructure is scheduled for Nov. 12, while Beltline Energy’s amended proposal is expected to return to the Planning and Zoning Commission for a special meeting on Nov. 17 at 6 p.m. Beltline’s proposal would then need to return to the City Council for further consideration. A date for a final council vote has not been confirmed. Residents will have additional opportunities to voice concerns as the projects move through the approval process. Neither project has received final construction approval.

artigo.texto: Voters in dozens of localities across 10 states will decide on 41 ballot measures related to data centers on Nov. 3, according to Ballotpedia. Seventeen of the measures call for prohibiting data center development, while eight would empower local governments to permit it. At least 49 local ballot measures related to data centers have been or will be on the ballot in 13 states in 2026, according to Ballotpedia. All six that have already been decided limit development. Voters in Clarksville, Arkansas, will decide whether to authorize bonds related to specific data centers on Dec. 1. More than half of the Nov. 3 ballot measures — 21 — are in Ohio, one of the fastest-growing hubs for data center investment with 257 data centers in the state. Eleven of the local ballot measures ask voters to prohibit data centers, and six call for zoning changes related to their development. At least 138 Ohio municipalities and townships have already placed moratoriums on data center development, and 23 communities in the state have effectively banned them, according to the Ohio Capital Journal. A grassroots effort to amend Ohio’s constitution to prohibit data centers with a peak load of more than 25 megawatts per month missed the deadline to get on the Nov. 3 ballot, the Capital Journal reported. Its backers are working to get it on the ballot next year. Local data center measures on Nov. 3 ballot “It’s not surprising that we have this many local ballot initiatives on data center moratoriums, and particularly in Ohio because of the higher concentration there,” Ishyan Veluppillai, who tracks state and local data center policy for energy companies and investors at investment advisor group Capstone, told Smart Cities Dive. “As communities across this calendar year have been trying to respond to projects that are being announced in their own backyards, this is one of the tools that some communities are using to properly regulate the industry and future projects.” As data center development accelerates rapidly to meet growing demand for AI compute, voters from both political parties are pushing back. Data centers have emerged as a central issue in the midterm elections, with more than $45 million spent on ads mentioning data centers in gubernatorial, House and Senate races between January and September, according to NPR. Spending on political ads discussing data centers increased 61% month-over-month in September, Marketing Brew reported. “The mutiny is about the way this technology is being introduced into people's lives, and I would argue that that has been pursued in a shoddier way than usual,” Mark Muro, a senior fellow at Brookings Metro, said during a webinar last week about data centers on the ballot in the 2026 midterms. “People may be worried about electricity costs, or water, or automation, or agents going rogue, but more broadly, they seem to feel they have little say in how AI is being rolled out.” “Depending on next week’s results, I think this momentum towards trying to get more community involvement will continue,” Veluppillai said. State officials could respond to the Nov. 3 election results by giving more autonomy to cities and counties over data center policy, he said. “For city and county officials, I think the biggest implication is in pre-filing windows for the 2027 state sessions,” he said. “As soon as the elections are complete and we know which way the wind’s blowing for data centers, I think you’ll start seeing a lot of legislation get introduced.”

artigo.texto: A California-based company has big plans in Eastern Oregon. A proposed battery storage facility could land near Irrigon, located in Morrow County, as part of an expansive push from Copia Power, which also recently proposed a data center near Hermiston. Morrow County has spent the past 15 years becoming a hub for energy-related infrastructure, beginning with the arrival of Amazon’s first data center in 2011. Now, the proposed standalone battery storage project — which would be the first of its kind in the county — could introduce another type of energy infrastructure as the region grapples with growing electricity demand and the challenges of powering its expanding industrial base. Large-scale battery parks are increasingly being tied to data centers around the globe as a way to store electricity when power is abundant, and then keep those data centers running during power outages or spikes in local electricity demand. City officials say this project could bring additional tax revenue, while residents say the only people benefiting from the project are the companies developing it. Copia Power declined to comment. Copia Power is a U.S. developer and operator that builds large-scale battery storage facilities and data center projects. Records obtained by OPB show Sawtooth DevCo LLC, a subsidiary of Copia Power, requested a pre-application meeting with the Morrow County Planning Department in December 2024 for a proposed 40-acre battery storage facility. However, records show the official application wasn’t submitted until late September 2026, which is still under review. The records also don’t establish the company’s relationship between the proposed battery facility and the 100-acre proposed data center in Hermiston — the first campus that would be on federal land in Oregon. In a phone interview, Morrow County Planning Director Tamra Mabbott said this standalone battery farm includes a 237-megawatt battery energy storage system, substation, switchgear, and a Gen-tie transmission line that would connect to the nearby Longhorn Substation in Boardman. Todd Olinsky-Paul, senior project director at Clean Energy States Alliance, a nonprofit that focuses on clean energy technologies, said battery storage could help data centers manage spikes in electricity demand. “If you want to make sure the data center isn’t burdening the grid during peak times and you don’t want to install new generation and want to shift when you have excess power or when you need it, then you use the battery storage,” Olinsky-Paul said. He said battery storage facilities can mitigate data centers’ added demand for electricity and the cost of that extra demand. The project is under consideration just weeks after Gov. Tina Kotek ordered the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality to pause air and water pollution permits until July 2027. DEQ spokesperson Carisma Sanchez said the agency has no current application record for the proposed Morrow County battery project and could not say whether it would be affected by the data center permitting pause. “As directed by Governor Tina Kotek, DEQ is continuing to work on permit applications for data centers up to the point where a draft permit is completed and ready for public comment. Once that stage is reached, DEQ will pause work until we receive further instructions from the Governor, or until July 1, 2027, whichever comes first,” Sanchez stated in an email. Mabbott said having a project like this near Irrigon will provide a new source of needed electricity. “We’re seeing a large amount of growth in the county and all the new energy generation that can come online helps support new growth, whether it be residential or data centers or other industrial or commercial development,” Mabbott said. But Irrigon resident and farmer Barrett Dash said the only people benefiting from these projects are the companies that build them. “They have swayed every bit of influence that they can with all the money,” Dash said. At the most recent Irrigon City Council meeting, he said, many residents expressed concerns about any potential data centers or battery farms in the area. Residents filled the room, Dash said, with at least half a dozen giving public comments, opposing any data centers or battery storage in Irrigon — surprising the council. “They said, ‘It’s great to see so many people here because normally it’s just us and a couple people telling jokes,’” he said. Mayor Michelle Patton said close to 30 people attended the meeting to express concerns about rumors swirling on social media that Amazon had proposed an Irrigon data center, she said. “At this point, no application from Amazon has been made,” Patton said. She said she wasn’t aware of Copia Power’s proposal near Irrigon until OPB reached out. She said she would need to do more research before commenting on the energy company’s project. Once Morrow County reviews the application, Mabbott said, it will send out a notice to property owners adjoining the project site, and to other public entities at local and federal levels that may have an interest or require oversight in the review of the application.

Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) shares fell 2% in overnight trading ahead of Friday's session amid a broad-based selloff in AI infrastructure stocks, driven by mixed reports from Intel (INTC) and Amazon (AMZN) and a report that the chipmaker was in talks to provide credit support to data center operator Nscale. Nvidia is in discussions to provide credit guarantees for an Nscale data center facility that Anthropic plans to use, Bloomberg reported late Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. UK-based Nscale is racing to get a series of large data centers online, including this flagship site in West Virginia. It is also pursuing an initial public offering, with some investors pushing back on its $30 billion IPO target. Nvidia's credit support, as an investor in Nscale and its GPU supplier, would help backstop the electricity and construction costs for an AI data center campus in West Virginia, according to the Bloomberg report. AI Selloff Chip and AI infrastructure were sharply lower in overnight trading, with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) down 6.4% and Micron (MU) down 3.4%. Intel plunged 23% after it forecast December quarter sales and profit below expectations and flagged persisting weakness in the PC market. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, noted that Intel's report and selloff have little bearing on Nvidia. "The $INTC (down 17% in after-hours) guide down should not be extrapolated on $NVDA(down 1.3%). Bottom line: Main issue is PC demand… Nvidia has been beating numbers despite high memory costs and Jensen was bullish last week at GTC Berlin. $SPCX, $META, $GOOG all said Capex in CY27 will be significantly higher than 2026," he said in an X post. Meanwhile, investor Jason Calacanis, a co-host of the All-In Podcast, bought shares of Nvidia and Alphabet on the dip, calling them "two exceptional companies with exceptional leadership and exceptional products." artigo.texto: O Banestes, banco estatal do Espírito Santo, contratou o Instituto de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação do Estado (Prodest) para hospedar seus dados no Data Center do Estado, localizado na sede da autarquia, em Vitória. O contrato tem duração de cinco anos e prevê a utilização do modelo de colocation, no qual equipamentos de TI são instalados em uma estrutura que oferece infraestrutura física, energia, refrigeração, segurança e conectividade. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Mercado global de colocation para data centers deve atingir US$ 223 bilhões até 2031 O acordo estabelece a necessidade de manter as informações do banco com disponibilidade próxima de 100%. Para atender a esse requisito, o data center conta com sistemas de detecção e combate a incêndio, além de mecanismos de proteção contra fumaça, água, vandalismo, pequenos desmoronamentos e roubos. A infraestrutura também dispõe de climatização para manter as condições adequadas de funcionamento dos servidores e de um sistema elétrico redundante, composto por subestação, geradores, transformadores e nobreaks. Esses recursos permitem manter a operação mesmo diante de falhas no fornecimento de energia. Modernização da infraestrutura O Prodest realizou um retrofit no Data Center do Estado para atualizar equipamentos e aprimorar os serviços de tecnologia da informação e comunicação (TIC) prestados aos órgãos públicos. Segundo a autarquia, a modernização elevou o nível de segurança operacional e reduziu em aproximadamente 20% o consumo de energia. “O retrofit foi uma atualização necessária para garantir que os dados das instituições públicas permaneçam seguros e sempre disponíveis. Com equipamentos mais modernos, ganhamos em confiabilidade e em eficiência energética”, afirmou o diretor-geral do Prodest, Marcelo Cornélio. Para o executivo, a contratação pelo Banestes também reforça a importância dos investimentos na infraestrutura tecnológica estadual. artigo.texto: CATL globally launches ultra-high capacity energy storage system at All Energy 2026 and signs three Australian partnership MoUs MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) today unveiled TENER+ in a global launch at All Energy Australia 2026, where it also showcased TENER Sodium. The company signed memorandums of understanding (MoU) with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney to strengthen the delivery and grid connection of utility-scale battery projects in Australia. TENER: Engineered for long-term performance and Australia's demanding grid connection requirements CATL's TENER+ and TENER Sodium energy storage systems are designed to deliver the reliability and long-term performance Australian utility-scale energy projects need. Engineered for harsh weather conditions, they are designed to support compliance with Australia's demanding grid connection requirements and give project financiers confidence in the reliability and long-term performance that underpin battery revenues. TENER+ is a 9MWh ultra-high capacity energy storage system that helps developers to achieve a longer-term project value and to maximise the storage capacity of their project, TENER+ reduces the number of containers needed by up to 40% and the project footprint by 12%, making this ideal for projects that are facing land constraints. artigo.texto: From Grid Constraint to AI Growth: Hitachi Vantara and Duraflow Transform Data Center Energy Management for Greater AI and Compute Capacity - Hitachi Vantara pilots one of the world's largest Phase Change Material installations in itsNetherlands data center, demonstrating how organizations can use up to 90% less electricity for thermal management - Implementation requires zero water for cooling, reducing the resources needed to support data center operations - This generates more computing capacity from existing power infrastructure, rather than diverting power to cooling ZALTBOMMEL, The Netherlands and SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As artificial intelligence (AI) accelerates demand for computing power, data centers face a growing challenge: how to increase AI and compute capacity when access to additional electricity is increasingly constrained. Hitachi Vantara , the data storage, infrastructure and hybrid cloud management subsidiary of Hitachi Ltd. (TSE: 6501), is demonstrating a new approach to address this challenge by showing how data centers can effectively use their power for AI and compute capacity rather than power and cooling. At its data center in the Netherlands, Hitachi Vantara has deployed one of the world's largest operational Phase Change Material (PCM) installations, using technology developed by Dutch thermal energy company Duraflow. For more information about Hitachi Vantara's approach to AI, please visit: https://www.hitachivantara.com/solutions/ai-analytics Depending on the application, PCM technology can help reduce electricity consumption related to thermal management by up to 90%, while requiring no water for cooling. By reducing the energy needed to manage power and cooling, a greater share of available electrical capacity can be used for computing – an increasingly important consideration as organizations deploy more energy-intensive AI workloads. Tackling the energy challenge behind AI Every watt consumed by AI ultimately becomes heat and managing that heat requires as much as 40% of a data center's total energy needs. At the same time, as AI workloads continue to grow, the ability to convert available electricity into useful computing capacity will increasingly determine how quickly digital infrastructure can expand. This creates a growing challenge for data center operators seeking to increase computing capacity within constrained power infrastructure. In regions where grid congestion or limited access to additional electricity can constrain data center expansion, improving infrastructure efficiency can help organizations make more computing capacity available within their existing power connection. Hitachi Vantara faced this challenge as demand for high-density computing and AI infrastructure increased. Rather than assuming that more computing required a greater amount of power, the company explored ways to make its existing electrical capacity work harder. The resulting deployment of Duraflow's PCM technology provides a real-world proof point for this approach at an operational scale. Real-world performance: 240 kW of cooling with low electrical consumption The installed system provides a total cooling capacity of 240 kW across two 120 kW PCM units. According to operational monitoring data, the two units collectively consume just 5–8 kW of electricity, depending on operating conditions. For comparison, a conventional DX cooling system delivering the same 240 kW cooling capacity would require an estimated 60–80 kW of compressor power. These operational figures illustrate how PCM-based thermal management can significantly reduce the electricity required for cooling, freeing up more of the data center's available power capacity for computing. "This project started with a very practical challenge: how do we grow our computing capacity when access to additional electricity is limited," saidSimon Ninan, Senior Vice President of Business Strategy, Hitachi Vantara. "We realized that if we could dramatically reduce the amount of power required for thermal management, we could make more of our existing electrical capacity available for computing. By partnering with Duraflow, we are demonstrating how smarter energy management can become an important enabler of AI growth." The approach also supports Hitachi Vantara's broader commitment to operating more efficiently and sustainably, including its goal of becoming carbon neutral in Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by FY2030. Building efficiency across the infrastructure stack The deployment is part of Hitachi Vantara's broader focus on helping organizations get more value from their infrastructure while managing the growing energy demands of digital workloads. That approach extends across the infrastructure stack. Hitachi Vantara's Virtual Storage Platform One (VSP One) Block includes a 4:1 Data Reduction Guarantee and features Dynamic Carbon Reduction technology, which reduces energy consumption by switching CPUs into eco-mode during periods of low activity. Its always-on compression capability allows the system to switch from inline data reduction to post processing, which further reduces energy consumption and helps reduce a CO2 footprint by as much as 40%. "Addressing the energy demands of AI isn't about optimizing one part of the business in isolation," said Courtney Hadden, Sustainability Director, Hitachi Digital. "It's about working in concert across the organization and with innovative ecosystem partners to find efficiencies at every stage – from the products we build, how we bring them to market, and everything in between. The answer cannot simply be to consume more power. We need to become smarter about how we use the power we already have." artigo.texto: Researchers at Cornell University have developed a method that cuts a critical stage of lithium-ion battery manufacturing by up to 60%, potentially saving large factories as much as $100 million in production costs. Developed in collaboration with New York-based battery company Charge CCCV (C4V), the approach uses real-time measurements to monitor chemical changes inside batteries during their initial charging and discharging cycles. The process, known as battery formation, creates protective layers inside a battery that influence its performance and lifespan. It is among the most expensive and time-consuming stages of lithium-ion cell production. According to the researchers, formation accounts for roughly one-third of battery production costs and occupies about a quarter of a manufacturing facility’s floor space. By accelerating this stage, manufacturers could reduce production bottlenecks, free up factory space and lower overall electricity consumption by an estimated 10% to 15%. Monitoring batteries in real time Battery formation typically involves repeated charging and discharging cycles under carefully controlled conditions. These cycles help establish protective interfaces between the electrodes and electrolyte. However, manufacturers have limited visibility into how these layers develop during the process. Determining whether a particular formation protocol will maintain long-term battery performance can require months or years of testing. More from Energy See All “Evaluating formation processes is typically very trial and error,” said Vibha Kalra, a professor of chemical engineering at Cornell and the study’s principal investigator. “It can take months to years to effectively evaluate long-term performance because you’re letting the battery run for thousands of cycles.” To address this limitation, the researchers combined two diagnostic techniques that observe batteries while they operate. Operando Raman spectroscopy tracks chemical changes occurring at electrode surfaces, while electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measures changes in electrical resistance. Together, the techniques allowed researchers to monitor the development of protective layers and identify when important chemical and electrical properties stabilized. The team found that slower charging helped create more uniform, inorganic-rich protective layers, which are important for maintaining stable battery performance. However, the discharge stage could be accelerated without compromising the formation process. Crucially, key resistance measurements stabilized after just 1.5 cycles, providing an early indication of how the protective interfaces were developing. Factory tests show savings Using these findings, the researchers developed two accelerated formation protocols and tested them at C4V’s battery manufacturing facility in Binghamton, New York. Both protocols maintained performance comparable to the company’s conventional process while reducing formation time by approximately 60%. The results suggest that manufacturers could shorten a costly production stage without sacrificing the battery performance measured during testing. “This work demonstrates why strong partnerships between research institutions and cell manufacturers are so important for moving the battery industry forward,” said Shalabh Gupta, system engineering manager at C4V. Formation also accounts for approximately one-quarter of a battery factory’s electricity consumption. Gupta estimated that reducing formation time by half or more could lower overall factory electricity use by 10% to 15%. For large-scale operations producing more than 10 gigawatt-hours of batteries annually, the approach could deliver up to $100 million in reduced formation costs. However, those savings remain projections rather than independently verified commercial results. The research was supported through the National Science Foundation’s Energy Storage Engine in Upstate New York, which brings together universities and industry partners to advance battery technology. The findings could help manufacturers increase battery production capacity without proportionally expanding factory space or energy consumption. The findings were published in the journal Energy Storage Materials.

artigo.texto: Strategic Value Partners Invests in NewEdge Power and Launches Utility-Scale Battery Storage Joint Venture The joint venture will launch with a seed portfolio targeting up to 1.2 GW of capacity in PJM; SVP's commitment will also support the expansion of NewEdge's platform. GREENWICH, Conn. and NEW YORK, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Strategic Value Partners, L.P. (together with its affiliates, "SVP"), a global alternative investment firm, and NewEdge Power ("NewEdge"), a utility-scale and distributed power development platform, today announced a partnership under which funds managed by SVP (the "SVP Funds") will make an initial capital commitment to establish a joint venture focused on utility-scale power and supporting the expansion of NewEdge's platform. The partnership builds on NewEdge's existing backing from SJF Ventures, which led its Series A financing in 2025, and from its initial investment partners, Segue Sustainable Infrastructure and North Sky Capital. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed. NewEdge's pipeline includes utility-scale battery storage and solar projects, as well as distributed power projects, across several U.S. power markets. The joint venture will launch with a seed portfolio targeting up to 1.2 GW of capacity in PJM, the grid operator serving 13 states and Washington, D.C. SVP's commitment will enable NewEdge to advance this portfolio and pursue additional opportunities in PJM and other U.S. markets. The partnership comes as PJM and other U.S. power markets face growing demand for electricity. Manufacturing, electrification and data center growth are increasing the need for new capacity that can come online quickly. Battery storage is one resource that can help meet that need on a tight timeline and cost effectively. "For decades, power availability was taken for granted as demand stayed flat. Today, with unprecedented demand growth driven by data centers and the reshoring of manufacturing, we're seeing a need for new resources to serve the market. Battery storage has emerged as a critical part of the solution that can be delivered quickly to meet this need," said Joe Nano, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of NewEdge. "SVP brings the scale, expertise and conviction to build on our platform's successful track record and expand our capabilities to serve the U.S. power market during this window of opportunity." "Power markets are being reshaped by rising electricity demand and the need to bring new capacity online at pace. However, power demand is only part of the story. In markets like PJM, securing well-located sites and a viable path to the grid is a significant part of the growing opportunity we are seeing," said Mike Ungari, Global Head of Real Estate at SVP. "This partnership combines NewEdge's expertise to identify and advance those sites with SVP's capabilities investing across power and infrastructure." NewEdge will lead development under the joint venture, with SVP funding select projects as they progress. SVP's platform investment in NewEdge will also be funded over the investment period to support and expand the company's development team and capabilities. "We've built NewEdge around securing high-quality sites and interconnection positions in the markets where new capacity is needed most," said Steve Barna, Chief Development Officer and Co-Founder of NewEdge. "With SVP's capital, we believe we can move our seed portfolio and pipeline through development at the pace this market requires." As part of the transaction, Andrew Shore, Managing Director, North American Investment Team at SVP, will join NewEdge's Board of Directors as an observer, alongside Joe Nano and Steve Barna of NewEdge, Dave Kirkpatrick and Alan Kelley of SJF Ventures, and independent director Brent Beerley. The board brings deep power-sector experience, including SJF Ventures' clean energy investments in Terabase Energy, Nextpower (NASDAQ: NXT, formerly Nextracker), Community Energy (sold to AES) and groSolar (sold to EDF), and Mr. Beerley's two renewable company exits, to Iberdrola Renewables and AES. Ackman-Ziff Real Estate Group LLC served as financial advisor to NewEdge on the transaction. Verdonck Partners LLC served as buy-side advisor to SVP. Amis, Patel & Brewer, LLP served as transaction counsel to NewEdge. Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP served as transaction counsel to SVP. About NewEdge Power NewEdge Power is a utility-scale and distributed power development platform active across several key U.S. power markets. The company develops utility-scale battery storage, utility-scale solar and distributed power projects. NewEdge's executive team has successfully created leading development platforms and independent power companies across both renewable and conventional power. Collectively, the team has worked on and delivered more than 48 GW of power projects across solar, battery storage, wind, geothermal, hydroelectric and conventional power. Follow NewEdge on LinkedIn or visit newedgepower.com. About SVP SVP is a global alternative investment firm that invests across the full range of opportunistic strategies - from performing and event driven debt to hybrid solutions, hard assets (infrastructure, real estate, power, airplanes) and special situations private equity. It has extensive resources to improve or transform companies, as well as hard assets with a team of in-house operating partners, and operating platforms in power, retail real estate and aviation. Today, SVP has approximately $22 billion in assets under management and, since inception in 2001, has invested more than $60 billion of capital. The firm, established by Victor Khosla, has over 200 employees, including over 100 investment professionals, across its main offices in Greenwich (CT), New York and London, and presences in Tokyo and Dubai. artigo.texto: DTE Energy and sonnen Launch Michigan's First Residential Battery Virtual Power Plant Pilot to Explore New Ways to Lower Energy Costs The two-year pilot is a first step toward how connected home batteries can reduce grid costs, improve reliability and support long-term affordability for Michiganders. ANN ARBOR, Mich. , Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DTE Energy and sonnen today announced the launch of Michigan's first residential battery virtual power plant (VPP) pilot at Veridian at County Farm, an innovative carbon-neutral community developed by Thrive Collaborative. The pilot is a first step toward showing how connected home batteries can be used to reduce energy costs, improve reliability and create a more flexible electric grid while delivering greater value for customers. Approved by the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC), the two-year pilot will virtually connect nearly 100 homes through sonnen battery systems and VPP technology. By coordinating individual residential batteries as an additional grid resource, DTE will evaluate how this approach could ultimately help meet growing energy demand while supporting reliability and affordability goals for customers. This approach aligns with recent MPSC recommendations encouraging greater use of distributed energy resources and existing assets to help lower energy costs for Michigan families. "Across Michigan, families are feeling the pressure of higher costs for groceries, housing, childcare and other everyday necessities, and we know affordability matters more than ever," said Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy. "That's why we're exploring innovative ways to make better use of energy resources. This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability. It's exactly the kind of forward-thinking approach that has the potential to help keep energy affordable for customers over the long term." Through the pilot, DTE will evaluate how residential VPPs could ultimately help lower costs, support high demand periods and create new opportunities to deliver customer value. Insights from the pilot will help determine how residential virtual power plants could support a more affordable and clean energy future in Michigan. "Veridian was designed from the outset around a fundamentally different approach to energy," said Matt Grocoff, founder of Thrive Collaborative. "This pilot marks a historic moment for Michigan as DTE's first VPP pilot project, and a defining moment for Veridian. We're incredibly proud that this community can serve as the place where this vision can move from concept to reality, and grateful to everyone involved for helping bring it to life." Veridian is located on 14 acres adjacent to County Farm Park, features 170 mixed-income homes and is built to be fossil fuel-free, with each home designed to operate as a resilient, self-balancing energy ecosystem. Every home is equipped with sonnen battery systems, and the community brings together geothermal energy, advanced electric heat pumps, EV-ready charging, all-electric appliances and rooftop solar arrays to create an integrated, all-electric model for sustainable living. The pilot represents the next chapter in Veridian's energy playbook. For several years, sonnen and Thrive Collaborative have been working toward a vision of making Veridian a model for community-based residential VPPs in Michigan. "The Veridian VPP pilot will be a true demonstration of the decentralized, digitalized and decarbonized energy system of the future," said Blake Richetta, chairman and chief executive officer of sonnen Inc. "By coordinating intelligent batteries across an entire community, we are turning individual home batteries into a pooled, grid-interactive resource that responds to grid needs in real time. We're proud to partner with DTE, a world-class utility and a pleasure to work with. Their innovative spirit and firm resolve are making Michigan's first grid-interactive VPP community a reality, and that is a major achievement." VPPs can help utilities meet energy needs by coordinating resources such as batteries and other smart technologies. As electricity demand increases, this approach has the potential to improve reliability, reduce system costs and create long-term affordability benefits for customers. This concept aligns with recent recommendations from the MPSC to maximize existing grid resources and expand opportunities for distributed energy participation as a way to lower energy costs for Michigan families. sonnen's VPP architecture continues to gain recognition for its role in advancing the capabilities of residential energy storage. The VPP at Veridian was nominated for the Michigan Energy Innovation Council's(EIBC) Project of the Year award, as part of its 14th Annual Michigan Energy Innovators Gala. sonnen was also recently named a 2026 POWER Awards finalist for its Wattsmart Battery Program with Rocky Mountain Power. About DTE Energy DTE Energy (NYSE:DTE) is a Detroit-based diversified energy company involved in the development and management of energy-related businesses and services nationwide. Its operating units include an electric company serving 2.3 million customers in Southeast Michigan and a natural gas company serving 1.4 million customers across Michigan. The DTE portfolio also includes energy businesses focused on custom energy solutions, renewable energy generation, and energy marketing and trading. DTE has continued to accelerate its carbon reduction goals to meet aggressive targets and is committed to serving with its energy through volunteerism, education and employment initiatives, philanthropy, emission reductions and economic progress. Information about DTE is available at dteenergy.com, empoweringmichigan.com, x.com/DTE_Energy and facebook.com/dteenergy. artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Engages Newmark to Arrange Non-Dilutive Long-Term Debt Financing for the Michigan AI Data Center LAS VEGAS , Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that Alliance Cloud Services, LLC ("ACS"), an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of Hyperscale Data, has engaged Newmark Group, Inc. ("Newmark")") to identify prospective lenders to provide non-dilutive long-term debt financing for the development and expansion of the Company's AI data center campus in Michigan (the "Michigan Campus"). The engagement supports the Company's strategy to fund the Michigan Campus on an institutional basis and reduce reliance on issuances of its common equity. Newmark is a world leading commercial real estate advisor and service provider with a dedicated data center and digital infrastructure capital markets practice. Newmark's publicly announced data center assignments include arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in 2025 for an AI data center project in Abilene, Texas, and arranging $975 million in financing in 2026 for a newly constructed data center in Northern Virginia. More generally, Newmark arranged for approximately $59 billion in investments and an additional $73 billion in debt placements during 2025. Hyperscale Data believes that specialized experience in data center financing will be valuable in presenting the Michigan Campus to prospective lenders and evaluating financing alternatives that address the project's requirements. "Hiring Newmark is an important step toward financing our Michigan Campus on an institutional, long-term basis," said Milton "Todd" Ault III, Executive Chairman of Hyperscale Data. "Successfully securing the debt financing we are pursuing would, once consummated, substantially reduce our need to raise additional equity capital for this project. We believe Newmark's significant experience and expertise can help us pursue a financing structure that reflects the scale of the Michigan Campus and its anticipated revenue profile. Our objective is to fund development responsibly while preserving more of the project's long-term value for our stockholders." William Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data, stated, "Long-term debt financing arranged with Newmark's assistance would reduce our reliance on outside equity and provide a stronger financial foundation for building and operating the Michigan Campus over the long term. We are interested in financing that supports the infrastructure needed for customer deployments and gives us a clear framework for funding the project as it develops. Our focus is on securing appropriate terms, managing the cost of capital and limiting dilution while maintaining the financial flexibility needed to execute." The Company's financing objective is to secure debt capital suited to the Michigan Campus' development requirements and anticipated operating cash flows. The process is intended to evaluate the availability of long-term funding, potential borrowing structures and repayment schedules appropriate for the Michigan Campus' expected progression from construction and commissioning into revenue-generating operations. Management believes that obtaining suitable institutional debt financing could improve the Company's ability to plan capital expenditures across successive development stages. The Company will evaluate potential financing based on its overall economic terms, including interest expense, repayment obligations, collateral requirements and covenants, and other terms or conditions that lenders may require. The Michigan Campus is operated by ACS. As previously announced, ACS entered into a master services agreement with a California-based neocloud provider (the "Customer") for colocation and related data center services supporting an initial 20 megawatts ("MW") of critical AI compute capacity. The agreement has an initial term of 10 years, with two five-year extension options exercisable by the Customer. It also provides the customer with a right of first offer for an additional 32 MW, if available, which could bring its total deployment to 52 MW of critical AI compute capacity. Additional capacity and extension periods remain subject to the applicable contractual provisions and development requirements. As previously disclosed, the Company expects the first 10 MW of critical AI compute capacity at the Michigan Campus to be energized in December 2026, with revenue-generating activities expected to begin in connection with that milestone. Achieving this timetable remains subject to completion of the necessary infrastructure and commissioning activities. The engagement of Newmark does not constitute a commitment to lend or confirmation that financing has been secured. Any financing will be subject to lender underwriting, due diligence, definitive agreements and applicable closing conditions. The amount, pricing, maturity and other terms of any financing have not been announced. There can be no assurance that financing will be obtained on terms acceptable to the Company, or at all, or that it will eliminate the need for additional equity capital. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA A Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) afirmou que os preços iniciais do leilão de baterias, marcado para ser realizado em dezembro, contribuem para a atratividade da disputa. Os valores, de R$ 1,76 milhão por MW/ano no certame com conteúdo nacional e de R$ 1,58 milhão no leilão sem essa exigência, foram fixados pelo MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) e constam no edital aprovado na terça-feira (27) pela ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica). Segundo a ABSAE, os preços vieram em linha com o que o mercado esperava e com as projeções discutidas ao longo da construção do leilão. “Os valores reconhecem a realidade de custos do armazenamento, tornam o leilão atrativo e deixam espaço para uma competição de verdade”, afirmou a entidade em nota nesta quarta-feira (28). A associação ainda avaliou que a autorização para participação de transmissoras, fundos de investimento em participações (FIPs) e entidades de previdência é positiva. “Mais participantes significa mais competição e, no fim, preços menores. […] Essas medidas aumentam a concorrência e fortalecem o financiamento dos projetos, o que é fundamental para o sucesso do primeiro leilão de baterias do país”, comentou. Outro avanço destacado pela Absae foi quanto às exigências de habilitação econômico-financeira e às garantias. Para a entidade, os ajustes na habilitação “dão segurança de que os projetos vencedores sairão do papel, sem criar barreiras desproporcionais para empresas qualificadas”. Já a redução das garantias, que acompanhou a revisão do investimento de referência para R$ 6 milhões por MW, foi classificada como acertada por ”filtrar aventureiros sem afastar quem tem condições reais de entregar”.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Despite trade barriers and project cost inflation, the U.S. is set to deploy 30% more energy storage capacity over the next 10 years than expected just six months ago, BloombergNEF said Thursday. BNEF forecasts cumulative U.S. deployments of 213.9 GW by 2030 and 434.4 GW by 2036, BNEF senior energy storage analyst Isshu Kikuma told Utility Dive. - The latest edition of the energy consultancy’s semiannual energy storage outlook sees global deployments reaching 3,098 GW/11,106 GWh in 2036, roughly 10 times today’s levels. In the U.S., near-term drivers include favorable economics for colocated storage and renewables and data centers’ growing appetite for both behind-the-meter and front-of-meter capacity, BNEF said. - BNEF’s report landed amid signs of continued momentum for the U.S. energy storage industry. On Thursday, Google said it would expand by a factor of 10 the battery-supported virtual power plant it plans to deploy with Voltus in the PJM Interconnection, to more than 1 GW. The same day, the sodium-ion battery manufacturer Peak Energy said it closed $108 million in financing from General Motors and other backers as it works to deploy nearly 5 GWh of capacity by 2030. Dive Insight: Energy storage deployments have far outpaced solar capacity additions in recent years, with the global cumulative installed solar-to-storage ratio falling from 94:1 in 2016 to 7:1 in 2026, BNEF said Thursday. BNEF sees the capacity ratio stabilizing at 4:1 in 2030, and annual deployments remaining steady at 3:1 thereafter, as the energy storage industry matures. Much of the new solar and storage capacity is colocated. The United States had installed 20.7 GW/66.4 GWh of energy storage projects colocated with 41.3 GW of solar by the end of 2025, about 30% of total colocated solar-plus-storage capacity, according to BNEF. Some 4 GW of storage was colocated with solar in the U.S. in the first nine months of 2026, the group said. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which extended federal tax credit eligibility for energy storage through 2035 while sunsetting solar eligibility later this decade, will support a pipeline of 83.7 GW/166.1 GWh of energy storage to be paired with 149.2 GW of solar, BNEF said. The robust U.S. pipeline comes despite the Trump administration imposing trade barriers BNEF characterized as world-leading, including import restrictions on foreign-made power conversion systems and recent broad limits on imports of bulk power system equipment. The combined duty on stationary storage batteries imported from mainland China is 40.9%, according to BNEF. “The US has been making the most aggressive [protectionist] efforts by favoring the domestic battery storage industry while restricting the use of supply chains involving mainland China through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other policy measures,” the report said. Though still a relatively small share of overall U.S. battery deployment, on-site data center energy storage is growing quickly, with 4.9 GW/7.4 GWh expected this year — up from 500 MW/1.4 GWh in 2025, BNEF said. The group sees on-site data center energy storage deployments reaching 6.3 GW/8.4GWh in 2027 and continuing through the decade thanks in part to large-scale deployments like the 2.6-GW battery array NextEra Energy plans to build alongside a 2-GW gas-fired power plant at a $100 billion proposed Brookfield Asset Management computing campus in Kentucky. Multiple battery suppliers have announced firm commitments from data center customers or utilities serving them this year, BNEF said. Fluence Energy inked a $300 million deal with a data center operator for behind-the-meter batteries earlier this year, while Canadian Solar subsidiary e-Storage said in March it would deliver 500 MW/2.5 GWh of energy storage to “a major U.S. utility” in 2027 to support data center grid infrastructure. Cumulative data center energy storage could reach 36 GW/66 GWh in 2036, much of it on grids overseen by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, PJM and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator. Data centers in PJM are more likely to use energy storage for load shifting than behind-the-meter gas due to tighter restrictions on power plant emissions in the region, BNEF said. Though lithium-iron-phosphate will remain the dominant chemistry for new energy storage deployments over the next 10 years, sodium-ion alternatives will begin to eat into its market share, reaching 9% penetration by 2036, BNEF said. Sodium-ion batteries can be passively cooled, reducing parasitic energy load, and may be more durable than lithium batteries over a 20-year service life, proponents say. Led by Google, data center operators are experimenting with alternative chemistries that can discharge power for longer than lithium- or sodium-based batteries, including a proposed 10 MW/100 MWh zinc battery in West Virginia and a 300 MW/30 GWh iron-air battery in Minnesota. But those efforts are too early to include in deployment forecasts, BNEF said.

artigo.texto: Check Point Secures AI-Scale Traffic for Neoclouds, Sovereign AI and the Enterprise with New Maestro Hyperscale Orchestrator Next-generation Maestro Hyperscale Orchestrator 200 quadruples hyperscale capacity with 400GbE ports, so organizations can secure AI traffic without slowing it down REDWOOD CITY, Calif. , Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Check Point Software Technologies Ltd. (NASDAQ: CHKP), a pioneer and global leader in cyber security solutions, today announced the next-generation Check Point Maestro Hyperscale Orchestrator (MHO) 200, helping neoclouds, telcos, governments and enterprises inspect fast-growing, largely encrypted AI traffic and other communications in the data center without trading security for speed. The launch is the next step in Check Point's mission to redefine network security for the agentic era. Earlier this year, Check Point introduced the AI Network Firewall, bringing AI security directly into the firewall to inspect AI traffic, protect AI applications and govern AI agents. It followed with Agentic Network Security Orchestration, which moves network security operations from intent to automation, and AI Data Center Security, which includes a collaboration with NVIDIA. Maestro now extends that protection to hyperscale, so organizations can secure AI traffic at the speed and volume AI infrastructure demands. AI is reshaping the network. For neoclouds and enterprises modernizing their data centers, both perimeter and east-west traffic are growing fast, and the need for constant uptime and resilience remains. A significant portion of this traffic is encrypted, and all of it needs inspection. Yet many organizations switch off advanced threat prevention to keep performance acceptable, or buy oversized appliances that leave capacity idle to absorb sudden spikes in throughput. "AI is forcing a rethink of network capacity planning. Training, inference and agentic workloads are driving east-west traffic inside the data center to levels most security architectures were not designed for, and much of it is encrypted," said Pete Finalle, Research Manager, Security and Trust at IDC. "Organizations should not have to choose between inspecting that traffic and keeping it moving. Security platforms that can scale threat prevention elastically, without overprovisioning hardware, will be essential for neoclouds, telcos and enterprises building AI infrastructure." Maestro is a hyperscale firewall orchestrator built for flexibility. Unlike chassis solutions tied to dedicated hardware, it combines firewalls of different models and generations into one system that grows with demand. You can also split that system into up to eight independent security groups (policy domains), each with its own rules, with no trade-off in advanced threat prevention. Enterprises modernizing their data centers, neoclouds and GPU-as-a-service providers, colocation operators, telcos protecting their backbone and government bodies building sovereign AI infrastructure all need to support higher network throughput, and 400GbE is becoming the new standard for high-end data centers and AI factories. The MHO 200 adds new 400GbE ports and delivers: - Four times the capacity: total fabric capacity rises to 12.8 Tbps, up from 3.2 Tbps on the MHO 175, in the same compact 1RU form factor - Four times the threat prevention: up to 4.5 Tbps of threat prevention throughput per Maestro system, up from 1.1 Tbps - Always-on resilience: sessions stay live through failures, with automatic failover across two sites for 99.999% uptime Maestro's single-object management lets teams run an entire multi-firewall system as one, while Agentic Network Security Orchestration automates policy tuning, health monitoring and compliance across it. Security at AI speed With the MHO 200, organizations can discover and secure every AI application, large language model, agent and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server directly from the firewall. For private and sovereign AI projects, Check Point's AI Factory Firewall integrates with NVIDIA BlueField data processing units. Live patching applies security updates on the fly, with no reboots or downtime. "AI is changing the scale at which networks need to be protected," Nataly Kremer, Chief Product Officer, Check Point Software Technologies. "We started by bringing AI security into the firewall, then added agentic automation to network operations. Now we are taking that protection to AI scale. Too many organizations are still forced to choose between performance and prevention. With the MHO 200, they can inspect all their traffic at AI speed, grow capacity as demand rises, and keep their operations running through failures." Every step in this journey builds on Check Point's prevention-first security. Check Point ranked first in the Miercom 2026 Hybrid Mesh Network Security Benchmark with 99.8% security effectiveness, the fourth consecutive year it has led the assessment. Availability MHO 200 is now available on the product catalog for all regions. Learn more at https://www.checkpoint.com/quantum/maestro-hyperscale-network-security/. Frequently asked questions What is the Check Point Maestro Hyperscale Orchestrator MHO 200? The next-generation Maestro hyperscale orchestrator. It delivers 12.8 Tbps of total fabric capacity and up to 4.5 Tbps of threat prevention throughput per Maestro system in a 1RU form factor, with 400GbE ports for AI-scale traffic. Who is the MHO 200 designed for? artigo.texto: Bartow County data center: Neighbors raise water, land concerns KINGSTON, Ga. - Community members packed a local restaurant to question developers over a massive data center proposed on more than 500 acres of rural Bartow County land. Kingston data center proposal What we know: New York City-based Thor Equities wants to build a data center along State Route 293 about two miles east of town. Organizers had to move a town-hall-style meeting from Kingston City Hall to a nearby restaurant because of high resident turnout. The developer holds a 561-acre site but plans to build on only half of the property. Developers told neighbors the site will run on a closed-loop water system to reduce municipal water consumption. Bartow County land debate What they're saying: Thor Equities Executive Vice President Raj Vohra defended the economic impact of the project during the meeting. "We're really hoping to do it in a way that will add net benefits to the community through new tax dollars," Vohra said. "We believe the community and the schools in the area can greatly benefit from [the revenue]." Vohra said. Some neighbors supported the potential financial windfall for the small town of under 1,000 residents. Resident Jody Hardin attended to verify his personal research. "I think it's good for Kingston." Hardin said. "For the revenue and everything, because we do need the revenue for improvements and everything like that here." Other neighbors voiced concerns about development swallowing rural green space. Paul Muir lives down the road from the proposed site. He says that elected leaders haven't been transparent about the zoning process. "I love farming, agriculture, conservation work, and the more development that comes to Kingston and Bartow County, the more the natural resources get pushed away," Muir said. He added: "You have economics to make money, and the forest usually loses. So my concern is the forest, my farm." Community development concerns What we don't know: Thor Equities confirmed that no client has signed a contract to occupy the planned data center facility. It remains unclear exactly which technology or enterprise companies might eventually operate on the site. Construction timing is also pending final local authorizations. If the project clears all required government reviews, construction will still take between two and four years to begin. City council permit decision What's next: The Kingston Unified Zoning Board approved a recommendation for a special use permit Monday in a 2-1 vote. The full Kingston City Council ultimately needs to approve the special use permit. The council's next meeting is scheduled for Monday, Nov. 2 at 7 p.m. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from FOX 5 Atlanta reporter Hernan Gutierrez, who attended the developer town hall and interviewed residents and company officials, as well as local zoning board records.

artigo.texto: Quer surfar o boom dos data centers nos Estados Unidos? Compre Gerdau. É essa a visão do UBS BB, que publicou um relatório elevando o preço-alvo da ação, aumentando suas projeções para o resultado e reiterando a recomendação de ‘compra’ para o papel, que é o top pick do banco no setor. A tese central do analista Caio Greiner é que o mercado pode estar subestimando o potencial de geração de caixa da siderúrgica nos EUA, onde a expansão dos data centers de inteligência artificial deve sustentar a demanda por aço e manter as margens em patamares elevados. Para ele, o mercado está excessivamente focado nos riscos do lado da oferta – com um potencial aumento da capacidade e das importações –, mas “o crescimento da demanda provavelmente continuará superando qualquer pressão sobre a oferta.” O analista disse que o segmento de vigas e barras comerciais (MBQ, na sigla em inglês) nos EUA está se beneficiando de tendências estruturais no mercado de construção não-residencial, e que a expectativa é que a demanda permaneça elevada nos próximos trimestres e anos. “O consumo aparente desses dois produtos cresceu cerca de 6,5% no acumulado do ano, apesar de uma queda de cerca de 1% nos gastos totais com construção não residencial. Essa divergência reflete, em parte, a força dos data centers, um segmento intensivo em aço longo, cujos gastos com construção nos Estados Unidos cresceram 75% na comparação anual em agosto,” escreveu o analista. “Embora os data centers representem apenas cerca de 5% dos gastos com construção não residencial nos EUA, os produtos da Gerdau têm maior exposição a esses segmentos de construção pesada.” O UBS disse ainda que espera que os investimentos dos grandes provedores de serviços em nuvem (hyperscalers) acelerem até 2027 – com o início de novas construções avançando cerca de 200% –, o que pode sustentar um crescimento adicional da demanda pelos produtos da Gerdau. “Na nossa visão, essa aceleração do consumo deve ser suficiente para absorver a entrada de nova capacidade e o aumento das importações, mantendo as margens da Gerdau em patamares elevados.” No relatório, o UBS elevou seu preço-alvo de R$ 31 para R$ 35 e ampliou suas projeções para o EBITDA deste ano e do ano que vem. Agora, o banco espera que a Gerdau faça um EBITDA de R$ 13,9 bilhões este ano, 3% a mais que a projeção anterior, e de R$ 15,2 bi em 2027, 8% a mais. A revisão reflete a perspectiva mais favorável para a operação na América do Norte, cuja margem EBITDA esperada para 2027 subiu de 24% para 26,4%. Após a reeleição de Lula, o banco também mudou sua premissa para o câmbio – e agora espera um dólar a R$ 5,40 – o que beneficia os resultados da Gerdau. Nas contas do UBS, a Gerdau negocia a 3,5x o EBITDA estimado para 2027, com um free cash flow yield de 14%. A companhia vale R$ 47,8 bilhões na B3, com a ação subindo 33% nos últimos doze meses. Hoje o papel sobe 6,5% em mais um dia de queda do Ibovespa.
