artigo.texto: Gov. Josh Shapiro says he’s reining in Pennsylvania’s data center development after previously promising to speed it up. His Aug. 18 executive order removed data centers from the state’s Permit Fast Track Program and put new conditions on how developers can move forward. It was a marked shift for a governor who had once celebrated the industry as an economic development win. As recently as June 2025, Shapiro was touting Amazon’s planned $20 billion investment in Pennsylvania cloud computing and AI campuses, promising jobs and new opportunities for local communities. The Fast Track permit program aimed to help accelerate that growth: Data centers accounted for more than half of the projects approved for expedited permitting. Data center development has since become a campaign issue. Shapiro, a Democrat, faces Republican Stacy Garrity in the Nov. 3 election. Public sentiment has shifted significantly since Fast Track launched in November 2024. Two-thirds of likely PA voters now oppose data center construction, according to an August poll conducted by The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times and Siena University. Nearly 74% of Pennsylvanians would oppose an AI data center in their community. The nine projects formerly listed in Fast Track show a mixed record. State officials credited their assistance with speeding an Amazon permit review. At least two projects, however, received no state environmental permits during their time in the program, according to Technical.ly and NewsWorks Lab’s review. Fast Track’s stated goal was to give businesses in Pennsylvania clearer timelines and greater certainty of obtaining permits necessary for construction and operations. By March of this year, data centers accounted for more than half of the projects listed on its dashboard, the Pittsburgh Media Partnership reported. The program didn’t guarantee approval or let developers bypass environmental laws and required local approvals. It did assign project managers to help speed the process. “What Fast Track did was put a coordinator in the room to keep agencies moving,” Kate Cooper, a lawyer at Pittsburgh-based law firm Babst Calland, told Technical.ly and NewsWorks Lab. “But in terms of a data center project, getting a state permit decision faster doesn’t mean that a project got delivered faster.” For Amazon’s Falls Township project in Bucks County, the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) processed an air permit in under four months, compared with the typical six-month review, PA Secretary Jessica Shirley boasted at an August 2025 event. Removing a data center from Fast Track doesn’t cancel its permits The nine data center projects are at different stages, from planning and permit reviews to construction. Their progress also depends on local decisions that Fast Track could not make for them. “One question I get a lot is: ‘Is removal from Fast Track like a revocation of permits?’ and that’s not the case,” said Cooper, of Babst Calland. “The difference is if they’re going to work with you before or after you get your local approval.” FAQ: Pennsylvania’s Permit Fast Track Program When did the Permit Fast Track Program launch? Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro launched the PA Permit Fast Track Program in November 2024 by signing Executive Order 2024-04. The initiative was designed to speed up state permitting and licensing decisions for major economic development and critical infrastructure proposals across the commonwealth. How does the Fast Track process work? The state coordinates interagency reviews and assigns dedicated project managers, but it does not waive regulatory requirements. The Governor’s Office of Transformation and Opportunity (OTO) convenes participating state agencies to identify required permits, establish milestones and resolve interagency disputes. Progress is monitored through a public online dashboard. The program expedites the state’s administrative review clock, but it does not guarantee permit approvals, override local zoning authority or accelerate physical construction and utility hookups. What projects qualify? Any public, private or public-private entity can apply for Fast Track consideration through OTO. The coordinating office evaluates applications based on project scale, capital investment, job creation, potential economic benefit and overall public impact. Which projects are currently on the Fast Track dashboard? At publication time, the state’s PA Permit Fast Track dashboard includes seven industrial and infrastructure developments: • The Bellwether District: A 1,300-acre innovation and logistics campus on the site of the former Philadelphia Energy Solutions refinery in South Philadelphia. • Project Tribeca: A planned $1 billion-plus Johnson & Johnson pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Montgomery County. • PennSTART: A specialized highway safety and autonomous vehicle testing facility in Westmoreland County (completed). • URBN Nuuly Bucks County: A roughly 975,000-square-foot fulfillment and laundry facility for Urban Outfitters’ clothing rental brand. • CrossRoads East Business Park (Phase 2): An industrial and commercial logistics park in Luzerne County. • Martinsburg Community Digester: An agricultural anaerobic digester project in Blair County designed to convert manure into biogas (on hold). • Century Development Industrial Park: A manufacturing and distribution facility in Lackawanna County (on hold). Which data centers were removed from Fast Track? Gov. Shapiro removed all data centers from the program in August 2026, under Executive Order 2026-05, making them permanently ineligible for Fast Track processing. Past data center project pages now redirect, but they can be found on the Wayback Machine. Data centers previously on the Fast Track include: Falls Township Data Center Development, Kline Township Data Center Development, Pennsylvania Digital 1 (PAX-1), Project Hazelnut, Project Hummingbird, Project Phoenix, QTS Salem, Salem Township Data Center

artigo.texto: Data center development continues to loom over many Michigan races ahead of the midterm elections with the growth of artificial intelligence and the expansion of big tech companies, as the Great Lakes state remains an ideal destination for large-scale data facilities. Opposition towards data center development has garnered bipartisan support with candidates on either side of aisle championing data center moratoriums and support for local control over development. 70% of Michigan residents oppose data center construction in their local communities, according to a recent Michigan State University Institute for Public Policy and Social Research survey. 52% are strongly opposed, whereas 18% are somewhat opposed. Michigan, which is home to 20% of the world’s surface freshwater, has become a hot commodity for big tech companies seeking the environmental resources necessary to sustain data center development. Data centers house servers that store, process and transmit digital information, although the supercomputers make websites, streaming and scientific research possible by supporting large-scale computing while simultaneously serving users. The infrastructure has existed for years, but gained a new reputation with the rising popularity of large language models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. In July of this year, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced six companies signed the Michigan Affordability and Responsible Growth Pledge, including Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and Verrus. Solstice Data later joined the pledge, signing the agreement a week later. The pledge ensures companies “will agree to invest in the electric grid, use clean energy, hire Michiganders, safeguard our natural resources, operate transparently, and bear the full cost of data center construction, operation and service,” according to the state of Michigan. Michigan operates under the new Enterprise Data Center Sales & Use Tax Exemptions, which went into effect on April 17, 2025 and are scheduled to run through Dec. 31, 2050. The exemption eliminates Michigan’s 6% sales and use tax on eligible data center construction and equipment purchases. Tax burdens for qualified entities that receive certification from the Michigan Strategic Fund are also significantly lowered, making Michigan a welcome home for data center developers. Regardless, nearly three out of four Michigan residents remain concerned that data center development is "very bad" or "somewhat bad" for the environment, according to the survey. Over half of the respondents said the same for the economy. Michigan residents' contempt for data centers became apparent in June, when Whitmer received political backlash for her appearance alongside OpenAI CEO Sam Altman at the formal groundbreaking of "The Barn" — a $16 billion AI data center for Oracle and OpenAI in Saline, Michigan. Apple brownie thank grand starter unhand bebe bronze tyra. Large-scale AI models, like The Barn, are housed in hyperscale data centers, which require massive amounts of freshwater and electricity to operate. This water is typically sourced from municipal supplies or groundwater, the same sources that supply drinking water. Data centers have the potential to use between five million gallons and 1.8 billion gallons of water per day. In comparison, East Lansing and Meridian Township collectively use 11.6 million gallons daily, according to East Lansing principal planner Landon Bartley. U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, and William Lawrence, the Democratic challenger for Michigan's 7th Congressional District, have clashed over the future of data center development in the Greater Lansing Area. Lawrence, who co-founded the national Sunrise Movement, an organization that focuses on environmental protection, has made data center opposition a core part of his campaign. “From the start of my campaign, I’ve stood alongside residents fighting to stop AI data centers because our land, air and water belong to our communities," Lawrence said in a statement to The State News. Barrett's campaign spokesperson Jason Cabel Roe said the congressman has worked to ensure residents have the final say on data centers in their communities. “That means full transparency so they can make informed decisions,” Roe said. Roe also said Barrett authored legislation to prohibit the federal government from overriding local decision-making and prohibiting public officials from signing non-disclosure agreements — although Barrett's vote in favor of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025 includes a section overriding local decisions over data center development. Support student media! Please consider donating to The State News and help fund the future of journalism. The City of East Lansing has a moratorium on all data centers until March 17, 2027. This gives the city time to craft an ordinance that will address concerns. East Lansing has a handful of smaller-scale data centers already, but residents worry about the hyperscale ones that take up thousands of acres, deplete natural resources and contribute to noise pollution. There are no current applications for AI data centers in East Lansing, but companies have shown interest, according to Bartley. artigo.texto: Nvidia, AMD Commit $4B to Meta AI Buildout Nvidia and AMD are deepening chip partnerships to secure long-term AI infrastructure business as Meta expands AI compute spending. Nvidia and AMD are investing a combined $4 billion in Meta as the chipmakers deepen their relationships with the hyperscaler and position themselves for a larger role in its expanding AI infrastructure footprint. Meta disclosed Monday, Oct. 26, that it plans to raise $97.5 billion through an equity offering to support its continued investment in AI infrastructure. Nvidia announced a $3 billion investment the same day, and AMD followed Tuesday with a $1 billion commitment. As part of the expanded partnership with Nvidia, Meta plans to deploy more Nvidia infrastructure, including its Vera Rubin platform and Vera CPUs for next-generation agents, as well as Spectrum-X Ethernet networking and BlueField-4 DPUs, the companies said. Nvidia and Meta also said they will deepen their collaboration on Meta’s Muse models and agents, which leverage Nvidia infrastructure. The companies are also considering additional work involving Nvidia OpenShell Reference Architecture to strengthen AI agent security. AMD, meanwhile, used its Tuesday announcement to highlight new milestones in its partnership with Meta. The chipmaker said initial AMD Helios rack-scale systems have been installed and are being tested by Meta ahead of a broader deployment. AMD also said Meta has deployed millions of Epyc processors and is a lead customer of its sixth-generation Epyc CPUs. According to AMD, Epyc chips support the dedicated computing environments behind Meta’s Muse personal AI agent. Meta is also using AMD Instinct GPUs for training, ranking, and recommendation workloads and plans to deploy a custom AMD Instinct GPU optimized for its own workloads, AMD said. Analysts said the investments reflect Nvidia’s and AMD’s efforts to secure long-term AI infrastructure business with major hyperscalers. “This continues AMD’s and Nvidia’s investments in strategic hyperscalers to drive greater adoption of their platforms,” said Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. Brendan Burke, research director at Futurum Group, said both Nvidia and AMD view Meta’s AI agent strategy as one of the more promising in AI. Meta’s recent progress in training models and advancing its personal AI agent strategy, he said, suggests it has become a viable frontier AI lab, underscoring why the company continues to increase compute spending. That gives both Nvidia and AMD a strong incentive to support Meta’s roadmap more aggressively, Burke said, with the potential payoff coming through future GPU and CPU purchases.

artigo.texto: Fim da escala 6 X 1 não compromete a produção, diz BYD Vice-presidente de montadora no Brasil afirmou que empresa manterá ritmo na fabricação de carros O vice-presidente da BYD do Brasil, Alexandre Baldy, disse nesta 5ª feira (29.out.2026) que o fim da escala de trabalho 6 X 1 não influenciará na produção de carros na fábrica de Camaçari, na Bahia. Ao Poder360, o executivo afirmou que a BYD se adaptará para respeitar a mudança na legislação. “O mercado, hoje, está acima da nossa capacidade produtiva, e nós vamos ajustar isso. Então, não há nada que vá impactar ou reduzir. [Vamos] gerar empregos e produzir aquilo que for necessário. Nós respeitamos a lei, seguimos a lei, e vamos investir de acordo com a legislação”, afirmou. O complexo industrial mantém 9.500 empregos diretos. A empresa é a 2ª maior empregadora no setor industrial da Bahia. A montadora chinesa difere da posição oficial da Fieb (Federação das Indústrias do Estado da Bahia) –que expressou ressalvas com a diminuição da escala de trabalho nacionalmente. Em comunicado publicado em 15 de outubro, a entidade declarou que “reconhece a importância” da redução da carga horária, mas que ela “pode comprometer avanços econômicos e sociais”. A BYD tem como meta produzir 600 mil carros por ano. Atualmente, a capacidade da montadora é de 150 mil veículos por ano. NACIONALIZAÇÃO A empresa passa por um processo de nacionalização dos veículos produzidos na Bahia, que deve entrar em fase de testes em novembro. Consiste em ampliar a produção local de componentes e reduzir a dependência de peças importadas. Desde que a fábrica de Camaçari foi inaugurada, em outubro de 2025, a BYD opera no modelo SKD (semi-knocked down): são importados da China kits parcialmente desmontados para a montagem no Brasil. Com a instalação de fábricas de estamparia, soldagem e pintura, a empresa passará a produzir etapas importantes da carroceria no Brasil, avançando além da montagem de veículos com peças importadas. A nacionalização também pode facilitar as exportações para o Mercosul. No caso das exportações de veículos para a Argentina, há exigências de conteúdo regional que podem chegar a 35%. artigo.texto: Data center de R$ 7,4 bilhões começa com 100 MW, e pelo número do Século Diário, 500 das 550 vagas são de obra, cargos que duram só enquanto a construção durar Baixo Guandu, no Noroeste do Espírito Santo, perto do Rio Doce, vai receber um data center de grande porte. Segundo o A Gazeta, o projeto custa R$ 7,4 bilhões e começa com 100 MW de capacidade. O complexo pode chegar a 1 GW se a demanda crescer. O projeto se chama Projeto Rubi e é da empresa capixaba Line Solution, segundo o Século Diário. O complexo ocupa cerca de 566 hectares. Inclui ainda condomínios logístico e industrial. A operação está prevista para 2031. Quem explica as etapas é o fundador e CEO da empresa, Mário Rodrigues. Quando as obras começam? Rodrigues diz que, em Baixo Guandu, a fase atual é de engenharia, licenças ambientais e aprovação de conexões de energia. Essas etapas levam de 24 a 36 meses. - Hyundai vai abrir 3.750 vagas em fábricas de carretas nos EUA, nos antigos terrenos da Caterpillar e da Lion Electric, e um terceiro turno sozinho somou 1.250 empregos ao plano - Fender manda aviso legal a 533 funcionários de fábrica em Corona, mas a empresa garante que a parada de fim de ano não tem demissão - Macaé tem 2,7 mil cursos gratuitos de qualificação, mas nenhum é de offshore: o ciclo desta vez tem só beleza e panificação, e as inscrições já fecharam - Porto-Ilha de Areia Branca: Intersal deu lancha no 1º turno, avisou que não daria no 2º, e a Justiça mandou levar 50 embarcados às urnas sob multa de R$ 5 mil por trabalhador impedido Antes das obras físicas, a intenção é fechar contratos de pré-locação de 20 anos, em dólar, com multinacionais de tecnologia. Quantas vagas, afinal? O número muda de uma reportagem para outra. O A Gazeta fala em 300 a 500 empregos diretos, na montagem e nas obras civis. O Século Diário e a Tribuna Online falam em até 550 vagas. Pela conta do Século Diário, 500 das 550 vagas (91%, conta nossa) são de obra. Esses empregos duram enquanto a construção durar. Na operação do data center, o A Gazeta projeta cerca de 10% do total, de 30 a 50 postos para técnicos e engenheiros de alta qualificação. Para quem busca empregos fixos em Baixo Guandu, o número é bem menor que o anunciado. Quanto a prefeitura ganha com o data center? Segundo o investidor, o faturamento anual previsto passa de R$ 1 bilhão. Com a alíquota de 5% do Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS), isso deve render entre R$ 50 milhões e R$ 60 milhões por ano para a Prefeitura de Baixo Guandu, segundo o A Gazeta. A conta bate: 5% de R$ 1 bilhão são R$ 50 milhões. A Tribuna Online cita também incentivos fiscais e a formação de condomínios logístico e industrial integrados ao data center. A água do Rio Doce entra na conta? O prefeito Lastênio Cardoso (MDB) disse ao Século Diário que a água viria de uma represa no Rio Doce. A energia já está ao lado, na Usina Hidrelétrica de Mascarenhas. Merci Fardin coordena o Observatório Capixaba da Água e do Meio Ambiente. Ele questiona o uso de água do projeto. E cobra que o data center seja avaliado junto com os outros empreendimentos anunciados para a região. Data centers usam água para resfriar servidores, e é por isso que o consumo hídrico entra na discussão. O empresário afirma, ao A Gazeta, que o resfriamento roda em circuito fechado, com a água recirculando. Ele diz que a perda por evaporação do bloco de 100 MW equivale ao consumo de três casas populares com quatro moradoras cada. Segundo ele, a água doce da região dispensa dessalinização do mar, e a proximidade com o Rio Doce pesou na escolha do local. Até o data center passar pelas licenças ambientais e pela conexão de energia, o número final de vagas e o consumo de água seguem como estimativas do investidor.

artigo.texto: O projeto fornece energia limpa para a fábrica de automóveis VinFast , a fábrica de baterias VinES e a joint venture de fabricação de baterias VG. Com uma capacidade total de até 22 MWp de energia solar e 45 MWh de sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), a VinEnergo garante um fornecimento de energia estável e econômico para seus parceiros, além de contribuir para a redução da sobrecarga na rede elétrica nacional. A VinEnergo opera um sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica em telhados, combinado com armazenamento em baterias. (Jornal Dan Tri) - No dia 28 de outubro, a VinEnergo Energy Joint Stock Company colocou em operação um sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica em telhado, combinado com armazenamento em baterias (BESS), na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang (província de Ha Tinh). O projeto de energia solar em telhados com sistema de armazenamento de baterias (BESS) na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang é o primeiro projeto operado pela VinEnergo sob o mecanismo de contrato direto de compra de energia (DPPA). Os primeiros clientes a beneficiarem da eletricidade limpa e da tecnologia avançada de armazenamento de energia da VinEnergo são a Future Production, Investment and Development Joint Stock Company (proprietária e operadora da fábrica de carros e motocicletas elétricas VinFast em Ha Tinh ) e a VinES Ha Tinh Energy Solutions Joint Stock Company (proprietária da fábrica de baterias VinES Ha Tinh). Além disso, o sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica instalado no telhado da VinEnergo também fornece eletricidade para a fábrica de baterias da joint venture VG, que também está localizada dentro do complexo de fabricação de baterias e veículos elétricos na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang. Segundo estimativas, em seu primeiro ano de operação, o sistema deverá gerar aproximadamente 39 milhões de kWh de energia limpa, contribuindo para a redução de mais de 25 mil toneladas de emissões de CO2 (o equivalente à absorção de mais de 1,13 milhão de árvores por ano). A transição para a energia limpa da VinEnergo também ajuda as unidades beneficiárias a reduzir a pressão sobre a rede elétrica e aumentar a autossuficiência energética, otimizando custos em cerca de 3,5 bilhões de VND por ano. O sucesso operacional e o fornecimento estável de energia às três usinas parceiras na fase inicial servem como base para que a VinEnergo continue desenvolvendo e promovendo a transição para energia verde nas fases subsequentes. Este modelo combina fontes de energia renováveis com um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) de grande escala, visando completar a infraestrutura de energia verde, a distribuição e a comercialização de eletricidade para os consumidores da região. A Sra. Nguyen Huong Giang, Vice-Diretora Geral Permanente da VinEnergo Company, afirmou: “Por meio deste projeto, a VinEnergo irá gradualmente completar um ecossistema energético abrangente, desde fontes renováveis, sistemas de armazenamento e mecanismos DPPA até infraestrutura de distribuição e varejo, capaz de atender à crescente demanda de eletricidade dos projetos industriais em desenvolvimento na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang, em particular, e em todo o país, em geral. Temos orgulho de usar nossos próprios produtos, capacidades tecnológicas e infraestrutura de fabricação no Vietnã para solucionar os desafios energéticos de nossos parceiros comerciais, ajudando a aumentar a competitividade e a proporção de energia verde no setor.” A VinEnergo tem fornecido soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) para muitos grandes projetos da Hanoi Power Corporation e da Northern Power Corporation, com uma escala total superior a 1,1 GWh, confirmando a capacidade das empresas vietnamitas de dominar tecnologias essenciais e implementar projetos de grande escala. No mercado internacional, a VinEnergo anunciou um portfólio de projetos de energia renovável totalizando 10 GW e está atualmente implementando seus primeiros projetos na Ásia e na Europa. Nos próximos três anos, a VinEnergo pretende desenvolver um portfólio de projetos com capacidade total de até 100 GW, tornando-se assim uma das empresas líderes mundiais em energias renováveis.

artigo.texto: Residents vent frustration after Aurora data center vote, tell city council "You failed us" Boos erupted inside the Aurora City Council chambers Monday night after a controversial vote left data center opponents feeling unheard and uncertain about what comes next. A motion to suspend council rules and reopen discussion on a proposed data center moratorium failed 6-5, falling one vote short of the seven needed to move forward. As the result was announced, residents shouted "shame" from the audience after what many viewed as one of their last opportunities to slow the rapid expansion of data centers across the city. "I'm scared for the water, I'm scared for the pollution, I'm scared for my air, I'm scared for my quality of life," one teenage resident told the council. "That's why I'm so disappointed in this." The frustration continued throughout hours of public comment. "We needed this moratorium, and you all failed us, and you failed yourselves," Aurora resident Gary Zimmerman said. One speaker accused the council of ignoring residents' concerns, while another delivered one of the night's sharpest rebukes. "These data centers, as they go up, if they do, they will be a monument to your stupidity," the man said. The five council members who voted against the motion were Rob Andrews, Francoise Bergan, Curtis Gardner, Stephanie Hancock, and Angela Lawson, which prompted immediate reactions from the crowd. Residents repeatedly argued the city should pause approvals until more protections are in place addressing concerns about water use, noise, energy consumption and proximity to neighborhoods. Councilwoman Amy Wiles, who first proposed a moratorium this summer, said she understands residents' disappointment but believes there has been confusion about what council actually voted on Monday night. She explained the vote was not on the moratorium itself; rather, council was deciding whether to suspend its rules and bring the proposal back for discussion. "A lot of people feel very blindsided about the data centers popping up, and so they don't feel heard," Wiles said. "Which I understand, and I understand their disappointment." Wiles said she shares many of the concerns she's heard from residents over the past several months and believes the city must continue working toward regulations that balance economic development with neighborhood impacts. At the same time, she's uncertain whether another attempt to advance a moratorium would be successful. Any moratorium proposed would need seven votes to pass because the effort previously failed. "I just don't know that we would ever get the seven votes to pass it," Wiles said. "And I worry that it would continually sort of give the community a little bit of false hope that it might happen, and then it doesn't happen." Still, Wiles urged residents not to view Monday night's outcome as the end of the discussion. "I don't want them to be discouraged because this didn't pass," she said. "The work is continuing; it's not stopping." While the moratorium effort appears stalled for now, city leaders are still considering a number of potential regulations for future projects. During Monday's study session, council members discussed measures including increased separation requirements between data centers and residential neighborhoods. Those proposals move next to the Planning and Zoning Commission before returning to city council for consideration.

artigo.texto: A proposed battery energy storage system in western Goleta divided the city’s Planning Commission and residents on Monday night. The commissioners voted 2-1 to recommend that the Goleta City Council defer a decision on the Greenbark 30 Battery Energy Storage System project. They noted potential fire risks and neighborhood incompatibility, and said the project needs more analysis. Commissioner Rita Serotkin was absent, and Anne Miller recused herself, citing a possible conflict of interest because of the proximity of her home to the project site. Developing Vacant Land on Viajero Drive Scale Microgrids LLC proposes installing 36 Tesla Megapack 2 XL battery units on a 2.1-acre site at an unaddressed location on Viajero Drive, which could provide up to 30 megawatts of stored power. The project has been in the works for about two years, according to project staff. The proposed system is expected to enhance the existing grid by storing power during peak generation. That power could then be discharged during peak demand or emergencies, according to city planner Travis Lee. The site is near the Ellwood Generating Station, Ellwood Elementary School and Westmont of Santa Barbara, a senior-living residential community formerly known as Mariposa at Ellwood Shores. “I support battery storage systems,” Commissioner Jennifer Fullerton said, “but I cannot support one in this location.” She called for a full environmental impact report, saying she was left with unanswered questions and that the project was incompatible with the area. “The location was selected because it’s the ideal location for a battery storage project in this area,” said Nelson Gould, an Environmental Resources Management Inc. project consultant. The project could “tap into” the Ellwood Generating Station’s Southern California Edison interconnection point and thus not need new development or transmission lines, Gould added. The project also would require a General Plan amendment to change the site’s zoning to office institutional to make way for the project, according to Lee. The proposed battery storage facility, however, is not adequate to serve the entire South Coast, and the ability to use that energy during power shutoffs depends on the ability to create islands with certain portions of the grid, according to Peter Imhof, Goleta’s planning and environmental review director. The project could provide power for four hours, enough power to support up to 30,000 homes within the greater Goleta area, according to Gould. Commissioner Cary Penniman agreed with Fullerton and advocated for further review. “I would like to bring the public up to speed on this. I would like to get up to speed. It’s super fascinating,” he said. “Let’s just not rush into it.” Goleta plans to analyze land use within the city to determine which areas would be appropriate for utility-scale battery storage, according to Imhof. Planning Commission members and some residents wanted the city to complete that study before making a final decision. “That is a little bit of a different time horizon than this project,” Imhof said. “We didn’t feel like we could hold up this project in order to complete that comprehensive planning effort.” A study found potentially significant environmental impacts associated with the facility’s construction and operation, but mitigation measures could reduce the impacts, Lee said. Goleta already has another battery energy storage system at 6864 Cortona Drive that was approved about five years ago, according to Mary Chang, a supervising city senior planner. Commissioner Katie Maynard said denying a recommendation of approval for the project would mean the city held the two projects to different standards. “I wish that we did have that more comprehensive assessment, but we didn’t ask the other battery storage project to wait,” she said. Commissioners Penniman and Fullerton voted to defer the decision, and Maynard opposed. The vote also carried a recommendation to postpone a General Plan amendment, ordinance amendment and development plan. Goleta Residents Divided in Stances A group of Goleta residents also pushed for approval of the project, citing its community benefits of renewable energy and electrical grid resilience. “I believe the Greenbark project will make the area safer, not riskier, while providing economic benefits and helping keep the power on for really critical needs,” said Katie Davis, a Sierra Club volunteer and Goleta resident. She added that she toured the larger Cortona Drive battery storage facility and noted it was “very quiet” and “three times closer” to homes. More than 20 local organizations and groups, including the Santa Barbara Unified School District, the nonprofit Clean Coalition and Mariposa at Ellwood Shores, the former name of the nearby senior-living community, are listed in a joint letter supporting the project. The batteries proposed for the vacant site are the “exact same” as those on various Santa Barbara Unified School District campuses, said Craig Lewis, Clean Coalition’s founder and executive director. He added that a battery fire is comparable to a house fire, citing nonfatal risks to human life unless someone is “in the fire.” “This is not something where people with pitchforks should be out here, screaming about this,” Lewis said. He also pointed to the fact that the project garnered the support of the nearby retirement home. However, one senior-living facility resident said otherwise. Westmont of Santa Barbara resident Jo Ann Winter said residents and facility management discussed the project but did not hear that management was in support. She said the 67 disabled and senior residents who live at Westmont of Santa Barbara and the Ellwood Elementary School community could be exposed to “toxic fumes” if a fire were to break out. artigo.texto: Word in Black With Election Day just a week away, the NAACP has launched a new electoral tracker dashboard focused on what could be a defining local issue for Black voters in the midterm elections: data centers. The dashboard tracks 1,728 data centers already online and another 1,042 that are either proposed, approved, or under construction across the country. It also highlights how close these typically massive projects are to Black communities, particularly in the South. The organization sent a questionnaire about data centers and other environmental issues to candidates in 17 different states. Voters can find answers on their local ballots by plugging their address into the dashboard. Abré Conner, director of the NAACP’s Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, said in a press release that voters “deserve to know where candidates stand on the climate and environmental issues shaping their communities.” “From data center development to clean energy laws, these decisions have real consequences for our health and our neighborhoods,” Conner said. “Climate on Your Ballot gives voters the information they need to hold candidates accountable and demand action on these issues.” The dashboard lets users see not only which data center projects are nearby, but also the stances on AI infrastructure development and other environmental issues of candidates running for local office. For example, if a user enters an address in Boxtown (the South Memphis neighborhood founded in 1863 by freedmen that’s at the heart of a local data center controversy), the dashboard shows Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 on a map. Elon Musk developed both facilities and wants permission from the city government to build a third. The tracker shows how many people live near data centers and how many are Black. In Boxtown, more than 38,000 people live within 2 miles of nearby data centers, and 73% are Black; zoom out to 5 miles, and the total population rises to more than 163,000 people, with 73% Black. Three candidates on the local Boxtown ballot have answered the NAACP’s questionnaire about data centers: Robert Jones, an independent candidate for the Senate; Misam Abidi, an independent candidate for governor; and Robert Vick, another independent running for governor. Although state Rep. Justin Pearson, the Democrat’s candidate for Congress, has been one of the most visible faces in the Memphis data center fight, he has yet to answer the questionnaire. In a kind of multiple-choice response, candidates can endorse pre-written NAACP answers or provide their own. On the question of air quality and emissions, Abidi said, in part, “Approval should require enforceable emissions limits, public reporting, and monitoring matched to the risks. Equipment approved for emergency backup should not quietly become a routine power source without further review.” Voters concerned about data centers can find similar information about projects in and around their communities and see questionnaire responses from candidates running in local and statewide races. The map function effectively shows the proximity of data center projects, some of which are far less high-profile than others. An address in Bessemer, Ala., for example, shows not only the proposed Project Marvel facility that has upended local government in the majority-Black city, but also another proposed 300-megawatt facility between Bessemer and Birmingham — and the up-and-running DC Blox data center in Birmingham. The dashboard will continue to be updated with questionnaire answers as more candidates respond. Election Day is Tuesday, November 3.

artigo.texto: Simplified: Hundreds of people filled Carnegie Town Hall for a more than three-hour public meeting on Tuesday night to talk about data centers and share concerns with elected officials from the Sioux Falls City Council and the Lincoln County Commission. But unlike the typical long line of public input – though that was still part of it – this meeting gave a full hour for public officials to chat in small groups with residents. Why it matters - Earlier this year, the Sioux Falls City Council voted unanimously to pave the way for a hyperscale data center in northeast Sioux Falls after four hours of public input – largely in opposition. - Since then, residents have turned up time and time again to speak out against data centers at public meetings, including a contentious joint city-county meeting in August at which point officials agreed to the public meeting held Tuesday night. - Tuesday's meeting was a unique format centered on civic engagement and listening to residents. Residents arranged themselves in groups of 10-15 people, and both councilors and commissioners moved from group to group listening and discussing unanswered questions on data centers, impacts on the community and what expertise officials should seek as they look to establish policy around these facilities. "It's very different to sit down one-on-one with people to talk compared to getting emails or hearing people at the dais," Councilor James Oppenheimer said, adding, "It’s a very clear message from the public that they are not in favor of having data centers in Sioux Falls." Tell me more Tuesday's meeting started with a presentation from Brent Van Aartsen, chief technology officer for Dakota State University, who spoke as a subject-matter expert on data centers. Van Aartsen outlined the types of data centers and the various ways in which they operate. - After that, planning officials from the city and county shared the existing zoning ordinances and where data centers might be permitted. Then – in a move atypical of local government – the meeting recessed for a full hour while officials spoke to small groups of residents to hear their specific questions and concerns. After that, councilors and commissioners shared their takeaways before opening up to another hour-plus of public input before recessing around 10:15 p.m. Takeaways from officials included acknowledging the overall agreement that people don't want hyperscale data centers in Sioux Falls. "It is so interesting in this country today, nobody gets along on anything except for data center opposition," Commissioner Joel Arends said. "The community is prioritizing quality fo life over the perceived or real benefits of a data center." Additionally, councilors and commissioners noted still-unanswered questions about how any rules they put into place now would impact the proposed Gemini data center in northeast Sioux Falls. What happens next? The Sioux Falls City Council has engaged its Regulatory Oversight Committee to look closer at potential ordinances related to data centers. That group's next meeting will be Nov. 9. Folks are also able to share feedback online. - Councilors also asked for feedback on whether the community would like to see more of these types of public meetings with space for residents to talk directly with elected officials.

artigo.texto: Amazon eyes expanding data center investment in Montgomery County Amazon announced it was exploring plans for additional data center facilities in Montgomery County. A company spokesperson said Amazon informed Montgomery County commissioners about the potential expansion during a public meeting last Thursday. Amazon said it would work with the county on future approvals and permits. The plans were still in an early phase, and the company had not yet acquired land for the potential expansion. Amazon previously announced a $10 billion data center investment in Montgomery County. The project was one of two major data center developments in the county, alongside Google's $15 billion project announced in May. Amazon previously said its data center project would create thousands of construction jobs and more than 400 full-time positions. The company had not announced additional details about the potential expansion.

artigo.texto: The AI boom has led to a gargantuan surge in energy demand across the country. Critics say this upswell in connections is enacting a stress test on America’s aging grid infrastructure. Worries abound that, in the short term, the energy crunch could lead to surging electrical bills and, in the long term, may eventually lead to outages or other technical problems. At TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this month, industry insiders tempered much of this criticism with optimism about how the flood of new energy connections could actually be opening the door for grid modernization. Apoorv Bhargava, founder and CEO of WeaveGrid, Tim Heidel, CEO of Veir, and Kristin Eberhard, VP of policy at Rewiring America, said that though the grid faces new challenges, there are also plenty of new opportunities as well. “It’s a very different electric grid, right?” said Bhargava. “We’re dealing with a ton of new variables, including renewable energy. We’re dealing with a ton of new load in the form of electric vehicles and data centers and heat pumps, and the ability to manage and orchestrate is fundamentally what utilities are now grappling with.” While all of those new connections are driving an ever larger amount of stress to the grid, Bhargava’s company hopes to provide the kind of load orchestration and management that helps utilities maximize the potential of the current system. WeaveGrid’s software can help organizations efficiently deploy energy while also optimizing connections to reduce utility payers’ bills, the founder said. Heidel, on the other hand, runs a company that is working to build out and expand the physical infrastructure of the grid, while also making it run much more efficiently. Veir sells superconductive power lines that promise to transfer energy at a much more efficient rate than traditional ones. Veir’s cables can carry power five times farther than traditional cables while also requiring 20 times less space, the company has said. Earlier this month the startup raised $110 million in a Series C funding round. “The scale of the investment in AI infrastructure is driving a tremendous amount of innovation,” said Heidel. “There’s a ton of new technologies that are coming off the shelves and starting to get to scale that, pulled together, can actually really make sure that data centers are the best community neighbors and citizens they can possibly be.” He added: “I think that we really need to look at ways that we can really adopt all of that as fast as possible to ease this next stage of growth.” Eberhard, whose organization advocates for household electrification, also said that while the surge in data center energy demand has spurred a new urgency to the modernization cause, it has also created an environment where industries are ready to try new things. “I feel like this era of AI and load growth is a very improv era,” Eberhard said. “There’s a lot of yes-and-ing going on. So yes, we need more transmission lines. Yes, we need more centralized power plants, and we also need to make sure that we’re taking advantage of all this other stuff that we had previously been leaving on the table when we didn’t have this urgency of the AI demand.”

artigo.texto: With the midterm elections approaching, data centers have become an increasingly popular political target. Politicians are raising alarms about their impact on communities, with some calling for construction moratoriums or outright bans. There's been plenty of fearmongering. But, the more Americans learn about data centers, and the more communities experience their benefits firsthand, the stronger the case for continued development becomes. Data centers have existed for decades, but the rapid growth of artificial intelligence has dramatically increased the demand for computing power. Americans understandably have questions about what this development means for electricity prices, water supplies, and their quality of life. Newer facilities are increasingly being designed with technologies that can address these concerns, including closed-loop cooling systems and quieter operations. DATA CENTERS COULD BE THE SLEEPER ISSUE OF THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS Yet much of the national debate overlooks what data centers are already delivering to communities across America. Take Ellendale, North Dakota, a town of 1,100 people. Before Applied Digital's new $11 billion data center development, the town collected roughly $400,000 annually in sales taxes. In the first seven months of 2026 alone, that figure jumped to $3.5 million. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS That revenue is helping the city repave its roads and renovate its senior center. A historic opera house is being restored. For a small town, this kind of investment can transform the community for generations. And Ellendale is far from alone. Schools across America are seeing enormous benefits from the data center boom. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, Meta's massive investment has helped fund an increase in annual teacher bonuses ranging from $10,000 to $50,000. Think about what that means for a working family. Teachers who have dedicated their careers to educating children are receiving a life-changing financial benefit, while the school district becomes an attractive destination for talented educators. It's hard to imagine a politician campaigning against higher teacher pay or better schools. Yet those are precisely the kinds of benefits communities stand to lose when development gets blocked. PROPOSAL WOULD PAY HOMEOWNERS 'DATA CENTER DIVIDENDS' TO COUNTER GROWING BACKLASH The benefits extend to homeowners struggling with the rising cost of living. In Loudoun County, Virginia, data centers generate 45 percent of county revenue. That enormous tax base has allowed local officials to cut homeowner property tax rates every year for a decade. TO BEAT CHINA IN AI, AMERICA MUST WORK WITH COMMUNITIES — NOT AROUND THEM In neighboring Henrico County, local leaders used data center revenue to fund a $60 million Affordable Housing Trust Fund, helping young families and first-time buyers purchase homes. At a time when housing affordability is dominating political conversations, building data centers is helping some communities make the American Dream a little easier to achieve. Electricity prices are another major concern, and understandably so. Families are already struggling with higher utility bills, and the arrival of a major new industrial customer can raise legitimate questions about who pays for new infrastructure. But the enormous, predictable electricity demand from data centers also creates opportunities to finance new generation and grid investments, spreading infrastructure costs across a larger customer base. In Georgia, agreements involving new large electricity customers, including OpenAI, are projected to lower residential power bills by $180 annually by 2029. With the right arrangements in place, the arrival of data centers can mean lower costs for the families already living in these communities. And the benefits extend well beyond tax revenue and household expenses. Trade unions have been among the most vocal supporters of data centers because of the good-paying jobs they create. Building these facilities requires years of work for skilled tradesmen, with new projects creating opportunities for the next generation of American workers. In Baltimore, Maryland, IBEW Local 24 expanded its membership by 50 percent alongside data center construction. In Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, IBEW Local 163 doubled its ranks following construction of an Amazon data center. Politicians have spent decades promising to bring back good-paying blue-collar jobs. Here is an industry creating enormous demand for exactly those workers. Of course, developers have a responsibility to work with residents and local governments to address legitimate concerns. Communities deserve clear answers about electricity costs and water use. They should also understand how the investments taking place in their backyards will benefit local families. But, when data centers are developed responsibly, the economic benefits can be enormous. Communities are rebuilding roads and improving schools. Homeowners are seeing lower tax burdens, and skilled workers are finding new opportunities. For decades, politicians have campaigned on championing the Forgotten Man and bringing economic opportunity back to communities that have struggled to attract investment. Now, data centers are delivering billions of dollars in private investment to many of those very places. We're watching a new industrial boom take shape across America, creating jobs and revitalizing communities that Washington has spent decades promising to help. Before politicians rush to stop it, they ought to take a serious look at what those communities are gaining. artigo.texto: Read this article in 中文 Français Deutsch Italiano Português Español HKL adds BESS units to rental fleet 28 October 2026 German rental company HKL Baumaschinen is offering battery energy storage systems for rental and sale nationally through a partnership with power specialist MobilHybrid. The MobilHybrid systems – the MH-36 unit is shown on HKL’s website - can be used as grid boosters, alongside diesel generators, or in combination with solar panels. MobilHybrid, which is based in Augsburg, close to Munich in Bavaria, said the units can reduce diesel consumption, generator runtime and associated emissions by up to 70%. The manufacturer said its BESS units use non-lithium-based battery technology, which makes them exempt from ADR regulations on transport and also robust for use on construction sites. “The energy storage systems can be transported between different construction sites without the hazardous goods transport regulations that apply to many lithium battery systems”, said MobilHybrid. “This simplifies logistics, reduces organizational effort, and enables flexible deployment. ” The supplier said customers can rent the units on a project-specific basis, test them under real construction site conditions, or purchase directly . MobilHybrid said it had also recently “significantly increased” the performance of its BESS units while keeping prices the same. The existing MH36 is now known as the MH-45, increasing the available power. In addition, the efficiency of the unit has been increased, with energy consumption during normal operation reduced by more than 50%, meaning that a larger proportion of the stored energy is available. MobilHybrid was founded in 2016 and has been selling internationally since 2022, with more than 200 BESS units in service.

artigo.texto: A traction battery is built from lithium-ion cells, each made by coating metal foils with cathode and anode materials, assembling them with a separator and electrolyte inside a sealed case, and charging them for the first time in a controlled formation process. The cells are then grouped into modules and packs with a battery management system, cooling, and a protective enclosure, ready to power two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses, and trucks. The battery is the most valuable part of an electric vehicle, accounting for roughly 35 to 45% of its cost. IMARC values the global market at about USD 74.92 billion in 2025 and expects it to reach USD 455.24 billion by 2034, while India sold about 2.45 million zero-emission vehicles in FY2026. With most cells still imported and the PLI scheme for advanced chemistry cells in place, Electric Vehicle Battery Manufacturing Plant Setup in India is one of the country's most strategic industrial opportunities. Investment depends mainly on whether the plant makes its own cells or assembles packs from bought-in cells, annual capacity in gigawatt-hours, cell chemistry and format, the level of automation, dry room and formation capacity, and in-house testing and engineering. The Electric Vehicle Battery Manufacturing Plant Cost ranges from about INR 40–80 crore for a pack assembly unit of 0.5 to 1 GWh a year using bought-in cells, to INR 1,200–1,600 crore for an integrated plant of about 2 GWh making LFP cells and packs, and INR 7,000–12,000 crore for gigafactories of 10 to 20 GWh. Cathode, anode, electrolyte, separator, and foils make up 70 to 80% of operating cost, so material sourcing and manufacturing yield decide competitiveness. IMARC estimates a gross margin of 20 to 30% and a net margin of 5 to 10% for a well-run plant. This guide is written for investors exploring how to start an Electric Vehicle Battery manufacturing plant in India. It focuses on an integrated plant of about 2 GWh a year making prismatic LFP cells and assembling them into modules and packs for two-wheeler, three-wheeler, and light commercial vehicle makers, with energy storage as a second market, and also explains pack assembly units and large gigafactories. It covers products and markets, the demand outlook, the production process flow, machinery and raw materials, location and infrastructure, a detailed cost and financial breakdown, certification and approvals, and how a DPR and financial model turn all of this into a bankable plan. The snapshot shows one of the fastest-growing industrial markets in the world, and an Indian market where vehicle demand is rising quickly but local cell production is still small. By the end of 2025, installed capacity under the PLI scheme was only about 2.5% of what had been awarded, so domestic supply is far behind demand and early movers with working technology have a clear opening. Indicative Project Cost in India (2026) These ranges provide a realistic frame for early planning, but actual returns depend on access to proven cell technology, manufacturing yield during ramp-up, prices of lithium and other materials, competition from imported cells, offtake contracts with vehicle makers, incentives under the PLI scheme, power costs, safety certification timelines, and the working capital needed for materials and long qualification cycles. A site-specific Electric Vehicle Battery Feasibility Report narrows each of these assumptions to your chosen capacity, location, chemistry, and buyers. Table of Contents Each lithium-ion cell holds a cathode, such as lithium iron phosphate or nickel manganese cobalt oxide coated on aluminium foil, a graphite anode coated on copper foil, a porous separator, and a liquid electrolyte, sealed in a cylindrical, prismatic, or pouch case. Lithium iron phosphate cells are safer, last longer, and avoid cobalt and nickel, which makes them the leading choice for two-wheelers, three-wheelers, buses, and storage in India, while nickel-rich cells give more range for cars. Packs add a battery management system, thermal management, wiring, and a strong enclosure. Energy density, cycle life, safety, charging speed, and cost per kWh decide value. Commercially, cells and packs are sold under supply agreements to two-wheeler, three-wheeler, car, bus, and truck makers, to battery swapping and fleet operators, to energy storage integrators and utilities, and to telecom and backup power users, with exports possible once quality is proven. An Electric Vehicle Battery Manufacturing Plant can serve all these buyers by offering cells in standard formats and packs designed with each customer. Buyers value safety, consistent performance, long warranties, competitive cost per kWh, and local engineering support. The Main Products and Applications Choosing the product mix is the most important commercial decision, because it determines chemistry, cell format, equipment, and customers: These choices shape the whole project. LFP prismatic cells and packs for two- and three-wheelers and storage give the most accessible entry point, while nickel-rich cells for cars need more advanced technology, tighter controls, and long qualification with vehicle makers. Key Growth Drivers in India and Export Markets Demand is supported by vehicle electrification, energy storage, and policy support: India-Specific Market Opportunity The strongest opportunity for new entrants lies in LFP cells and packs for two- and three-wheeler makers, in storage cells for the fast-growing grid market, and in long-term supply partnerships with vehicle makers seeking local sources. Producers that secure proven technology, high yields, and committed customers will be best placed to grow. Understanding the process helps you plan equipment, layout, and where cost and quality are decided. artigo.texto: Glendale approves major step to start construction on data center GLENDALE, AZ (AZFamily) — Another data center is on its way toward being built in the Valley. The Glendale City Council approved annexing and rezoning an area at Litchfield Road and Olive Avenue for the 160-acre Project Eagle, also known as Project Baccara, data center. It’s about 2 miles northwest of the front entrance of Luke Air Force Base. The $36 billion project is expected to include two data center buildings and about 700 megawatts of natural gas generators to supply power to the data center and help the regional power grid. That’s according to the City of Surprise, which has information about the project because it’s close to the city. Glendale Development Services Director Randy Huggins said the city worked with Luke Air Force Base to make sure the project would be compatible with nearby base operations. He said the project is expected to generate about 200 permanent jobs and more than $150 million in revenue for Glendale over the next 10 years. The developer must help pay for a new traffic signal and enter into an agreement to fund specialized hazardous materials and fire services before any work starts. The Glendale approval comes after the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors gave the green light for a military compatibility permit for developers in May. Only one supervisor voted no, and residents expressed their concerns about the project’s impact on groundwater, pollution and air quality. Construction is scheduled to start next month, with the first data center building set to open in 2028. See a spelling or grammatical error in our story? Please click here to report it. artigo.texto: O Sebrae no Rio Grande do Norte inaugura nesta quinta-feira (29), às 18h30, o segundo data center do Sistema Sebrae no Brasil. Instalada na sede da instituição, em Natal, a estrutura recebeu investimento de aproximadamente R$ 70 milhões e será responsável pelo armazenamento e processamento de dados de unidades do Sebrae em 12 estados das regiões Nordeste, Norte e Sudeste. O investimento reúne recursos do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais que utilizarão a infraestrutura. A iniciativa busca ampliar a segurança da informação, padronizar sistemas e aumentar a eficiência tecnológica da instituição. Estrutura terá nome de ex-presidente do conselho O data center receberá o nome de Senador Fernando Bezerra, primeiro presidente do Conselho Deliberativo do Sebrae-RN, na década de 1990. Ele também teve participação na aquisição do imóvel onde funciona a atual sede da instituição, em Natal. Com a inauguração, o Rio Grande do Norte será a segunda unidade do Sistema Sebrae a contar com um data center próprio, ao lado da estrutura já existente no Distrito Federal. Data center vai armazenar e processar dados de 12 estados Um data center, também chamado de centro de dados, reúne servidores, equipamentos de rede e sistemas de armazenamento que processam, gerenciam e protegem grandes volumes de informações. Segundo o Sebrae-RN, a nova estrutura atenderá unidades da instituição em 12 estados das regiões Nordeste, Norte e Sudeste. O projeto também busca padronizar a infraestrutura tecnológica do sistema, que atualmente utiliza diferentes sistemas e tecnologias, ampliando a complexidade das operações. Potencial energético do RN é apontado como diferencial De acordo com Franklin Maux, gerente de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação do Sebrae-RN, o potencial energético do estado contribuiu para a escolha do Rio Grande do Norte. A disponibilidade de fontes renováveis, segundo ele, pode favorecer a competitividade potiguar na atração de investimentos em infraestrutura tecnológica. A expectativa da instituição é que o empreendimento também estimule o mercado local de tecnologia e incentive a formação de profissionais especializados. “A ideia de termos esse Data Center no Rio Grande do Norte também é estimular que outros investimentos venham para o estado, aproveitando nossos recursos e, principalmente, a mão de obra local. Fazemos questão de fomentar a formação desses negócios”, afirmou Franklin Maux. Leia também: Câmara de Natal aprova pulseira de identificação para pessoas com Alzheimer

artigo.texto: Participants can earn up to $1,000 upfront and $600 a year for making stored power available during high-demand periods, while lowering bills for all customers SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FranklinWH Energy Storage Inc. today announced that homeowners with a FranklinWH System can enroll in Entergy Solutions, a new residential battery incentive program from Entergy Louisiana that compensates customers for making stored energy available during periods of high electricity demand. Under the program, Louisiana homeowners who install a new FranklinWH System and enroll in the program within one year of purchase will receive $75 for every kilowatt-hour of installed battery storage, up to $1,000. Both new and existing FranklinWH Systems enrolled in the program will also earn $125 for every average kilowatt discharged during program events, up to $600 per year. Solar panels are not required to participate. During high electricity demand periods, Entergy calls on participating systems to discharge stored energy to the grid. The system can provide approximately 80 percent of an enrolled aPower battery's available stored energy during an event. Dispatches are managed automatically through the FranklinWH App, so homeowners do not need to do anything when their systems are called upon. Entergy Louisiana will not draw customers' battery storage if a severe storm is forecast, so customers have full battery storage for backup power if needed. "We designed the FranklinWH System to give homeowners confidence during an outage, and Entergy Solutions extends that value in a new direction. Homeowners can now be compensated for helping meet overall demand while keeping the reserve power they count on," said FranklinWH global CEO, Ke Bi. "That is a meaningful evolution in the role of residential energy storage." Entergy projects that its virtual power plant (VPP) programs will provide 155 megawatts of dispatchable capacity by 2030. The utility says that capacity reduces its need for costlier new utility-scale generation, which in turn lowers bills for all customers. Entergy Solutions adds to FranklinWH's participation in utility-led VPP and demand-response programs across the United States. FranklinWH batteries are enrolled in more than 30 VPP programs nationwide, letting homeowners earn incentives for making stored energy available to support the grid. About FranklinWH FranklinWH Energy Storage Inc. is a global leader in whole-home energy management and battery storage, with systems that integrate solar, generator and grid power. Its systems are engineered and manufactured in Santa Clara, California, home to the company's U.S. Innovation Center, which leads product design, grid controls, testing and certification. FranklinWH systems participate in more than 30 utility-led virtual power plant (VPP) programs across the U.S., allowing homeowners to support the grid at peak times, receive program payments and retain backup power. Learn more at franklinwh.com. artigo.texto: Sungrow partners with ENGIE to expand Victoria BESS project This 150 MW/300 MWh Hazelwood BESS expansion will feature 66 units of Sungrow’s ST5015-UX BESS, part of the PowerTitan 2.0 series, alongside 33 units of SC6900UD-MV PCS inverters and Sungrow’s smart controller EMS3000. PV inverter and energy storage system provider Sungrow is partnering with ENGIE and Elecnor on the 150 MW/300 MWh Hazelwood BESS expansion (HBESS 2) in Victoria, Australia, with Sungrow Australia as the technology provider and Elecnor as the BOP contractor. This project will feature 66 units of Sungrow’s ST5015-UX battery energy storage system (BESS), part of the PowerTitan 2.0 series, alongside 33 units of SC6900UD-MV Power Conversion System (PCS) inverters and Sungrow’s smart controller EMS3000, Sungrow said. With commercial operations targeted for 2028, the Hazelwood BESS 2 project is expected to add significant battery storage capacity to Victoria’s energy infrastructure. Grid-forming technology will further enhance the project’s capabilities, helping strengthen network performance as renewable generation increases, Sungrow said. “The Hazelwood BESS 2 represents an important step in advancing grid-forming energy storage in Australia. Through our collaboration with ENGIE, we aim to bring advanced energy storage technology to support grid stability and enable greater integration of renewable energy,” said Thomas Hou, Managing Director at Sungrow Australia. “We look forward to contributing our expertise and supporting the continued development of a more resilient energy system in Victoria.”

The publication reported that these tailwinds are expected to outweigh a slowdown in the local market, where weaker-than-expected demand has pulled lithium-ion battery supply chain stock prices down by more than 46 per cent over the past six months. Lucas Zhang Liutong, director of Hong Kong-based consultancy WaterRock Energy Economics, said demand for battery energy storage system products had risen in the Middle East and Southeast Asia amid the war in the Middle East. He added that solar and wind projects relied on such storage systems and that Chinese companies dominated the market. The reported shift highlights how elevated fossil fuel prices tied to Middle East conflict are feeding through to demand for storage capacity in renewable projects across the Middle East and Southeast Asia, even as the domestic market remains soft. artigo.texto: Por Ana Beatryz Fernandes O Rio Grande do Norte passou a ocupar uma posição estratégica na infraestrutura tecnológica do Sistema Sebrae com a inauguração, nesta quinta-feira (29), do segundo Data Center da instituição no Brasil. Instalado na sede do Sebrae-RN, em Natal, o empreendimento recebeu investimento de aproximadamente R$ 70 milhões e será responsável por armazenar, processar e proteger informações de unidades do Sebrae em 12 estados das regiões Nordeste, Norte e Sudeste. A estrutura também aposta em soluções de energia renovável e segurança cibernética para modernizar os serviços digitais oferecidos aos empreendedores brasileiros. A inauguração ocorreu na noite desta quinta-feira (29). O equipamento recebeu o nome de Senador Fernando Bezerra, primeiro presidente do Conselho Deliberativo do Sebrae-RN, na década de 1990, que também contribuiu para viabilizar a aquisição do imóvel onde funciona a atual sede da instituição. Em entrevista ao Diário do RN, o gerente de Tecnologia da Informação do Sebrae-RN, Franklin Maux, destacou que a escolha do estado representa um reconhecimento da capacidade técnica local e das condições favoráveis à implantação de grandes projetos tecnológicos. “A escolha do Rio Grande do Norte para sediar o segundo Data Center do Sistema Sebrae representa uma conquista estratégica para o nosso estado e reforça seu protagonismo no cenário da inovação e da transformação digital”, afirmou. Segundo Maux, a infraestrutura tecnológica já existente na instituição, a qualificação da equipe técnica, a localização geográfica, as condições de conectividade e o potencial de geração de energias renováveis foram determinantes para a escolha de Natal. “Mais do que sediar uma estrutura de tecnologia, o Rio Grande do Norte assume um papel estratégico na modernização dos serviços digitais do Sistema Sebrae”, ressaltou. Estrutura reúne segurança e capacidade de armazenamento O investimento de aproximadamente R$ 70 milhões, realizado com recursos do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais participantes, contempla equipamentos de processamento e armazenamento de dados, sistemas de climatização, infraestrutura energética e soluções de segurança digital. Um dos principais diferenciais é a chamada Sala Segura, ambiente desenvolvido especialmente para proteger equipamentos contra incêndios, superaquecimento, poeira, água e acessos não autorizados. “Diferentemente de uma sala convencional de servidores, trata-se de um ambiente especialmente preparado para manter equipamentos essenciais funcionando em condições adequadas e com maior proteção”, explicou Franklin Maux. A estrutura também conta com um sistema de backup com capacidade inicial prevista de mais de 1 petabyte, equivalente a aproximadamente mil terabytes. A tecnologia inclui mecanismos de proteção contra ataques cibernéticos, como o ransomware, modalidade de crime digital em que informações são bloqueadas ou sequestradas. Entre os recursos previstos está o backup imutável, que permite preservar cópias dos dados contra alterações ou exclusões durante determinado período, facilitando a recuperação das informações em caso de incidentes. “É importante destacar que nenhuma estrutura tecnológica está completamente livre de riscos. Por isso, nosso objetivo não é apenas prevenir ataques, mas também estar preparados para responder rapidamente a eventuais incidentes, reduzir seus impactos e assegurar a continuidade dos serviços”, destacou o gerente. A proteção também envolve criptografia, controle de acesso e separação dos ambientes tecnológicos utilizados pelas unidades estaduais, de acordo com as diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). Energia renovável é diferencial do projeto Outro destaque do Data Center é a adoção de soluções voltadas à eficiência energética. O projeto prevê a integração da geração de energia solar já existente na sede do Sebrae-RN com um sistema de armazenamento em baterias, conhecido como BESS, com capacidade total prevista de 520 kWh. A tecnologia funciona como uma reserva de energia, permitindo manter os equipamentos em funcionamento durante determinadas interrupções no fornecimento elétrico, conforme a autonomia disponível. “Estamos aproveitando uma das principais vocações do Rio Grande do Norte para construir uma infraestrutura tecnológica mais sustentável, demonstrando que é possível conciliar inovação, segurança e responsabilidade ambiental”, afirmou Maux. O sistema também busca reduzir a dependência de geradores movidos a diesel, diminuindo emissões locais de poluentes, ruídos e riscos associados ao armazenamento de combustíveis. Além disso, a Sala Segura dispõe de climatização de precisão, responsável por controlar a temperatura dos equipamentos e direcionar o resfriamento às áreas necessárias, evitando desperdícios de energia. Para o gerente, a iniciativa demonstra que o potencial energético potiguar pode ser aproveitado não apenas na geração de eletricidade, mas também na atração e no desenvolvimento de empreendimentos tecnológicos. Integração deve beneficiar empreendedores de 12 estados Com a nova estrutura, unidades do Sebrae em 12 estados poderão compartilhar recursos tecnológicos de processamento, armazenamento e hospedagem de sistemas, sem a necessidade de manter individualmente toda a infraestrutura. A integração ocorrerá por conexões de rede seguras, preservando a separação das informações de cada unidade. Entre os resultados esperados estão a redução de custos operacionais, a padronização tecnológica e a melhoria do desempenho dos sistemas. “O grande diferencial é o conceito de compartilhamento. Em vez de cada unidade enfrentar isoladamente os desafios e os custos de manter uma infraestrutura tecnológica complexa, passamos a contar com um ambiente regional, estruturado para oferecer maior eficiência, segurança e capacidade de expansão”, explicou Franklin Maux. artigo.texto: Previously Published in The Messenger By Matt Meduri Perhaps one of the most salient topics in Suffolk over the last couple years has been that of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facilities. These facilities hold lithium batteries capable of harnessing energy and dispersing it to the grid in times of blackouts or grid strain due to high electricity usage, particularly during the summer months. The State has been keen to roll these facilities out, with proponents arguing they’re necessary for sustaining the grid while broader concerns are addressed. Opponents say the technology is too new and firefighting capabilities have not yet evolved to combat lithium fires. At present, there is no conventional method of extinguishing these fires. Letting them burn themselves out is the only option, and that process can take days or weeks depending on the size of the fire. A proposed site on Weeks Avenue in Manorville has caused Senators Anthony Palumbo (R-New Suffolk) and Dean Murray (R-East Patchogue) to urge Governor Kathy Hochul (D-Hamburg) to pause the plans on this facility. The proposed facility is a 150MW lithium-ion storage facility developed by Key Capture Energy (KCE) on a 4-acre portion of a 13-acre light industrial site. It’s adjacent to a LIPA switchyard. “When it comes to the question of safety at these BESS facilities, there are simply too many important questions that have yet to be answered and I’m not willing to move forward without those answers and gamble with the safety of my constituents,” said Senator Murray in a statement. “God forbid a fire does break out at this massive facility, our firefighters need more of a plan than “let it burn”, which is the state’s official policy for such fires.” Local officials have even more reason to call for the brakes on BESS facilities after a 5MW facility in Wainscott caught fire in 2023. Contamination of at least three wells has been linked to that fire. The County announced in early October that the developer of that facility, NextEra Energy, has suspended operations at two East End locations. “Following the battery energy storage system (BESS) fire in East Hampton and the subsequent contamination of the area’s drinking water, I believe it is prudent to pause further construction of battery storage facilities in Suffolk County,” said Senator Palumbo in a statement. “That pause should last until a thorough review is completed, and safety measures are strengthened to better protect the region’s drinking water and Long Islanders.” KCE is the same developer that pitched a 79MW facility in Hauppauge, which led to vocal opposition from the community, a Town Council-led ban on large-scale BESS facilities in the Town of Islip, and the ascension of the Hauppauge Fire Department to be a de facto regional leader on the issue. While KCE, based in Houston, Texas, is the developer behind the project, the State is involved in the project through funding and contracting. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) chose the Manorville project, while Governor Hochul selected this site as one of eight BESS projects as part of her initiative to deploy 6,000MW of energy storage across the state by 2030. The Town of Brookhaven has no blanket moratorium on BESS facilities. KCE is also behind a 50MW, LIPA-contracted facility in Shoreham on the grounds of the former nuclear site. A large-scale, 110MW plant in Holtsville (Savion Energy) continues to face zoning issues, while a separate, 79MW plant is also proposed in Holtsville (Rhynland). Savion Energy is also exploring large-scale facilities in the Setauket-Port Jefferson Station area. Another 1.9MW facility in Patchogue, developed by Agilitas Energy, is slated to come online by the end of this year or early next year. A 100MW Medford facility has also been proposed by AES. Seven towns – Babylon, Huntington, Islip, Riverhead, Smithtown, Southampton, and Southold – have extended their moratoria on these facilities until large concerns have been addressed.
