artigo.texto: Data Centers Decoded: Water and electricity usage put into context LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN) - The exact amount of water and electricity data centers use had been a mystery until data centers in Nebraska had to submit an annual report at the end of September. But comprehending the scale of use, especially what water usage looks like, has been more difficult to decode. 10/11 took these reported figures to experts to better understand how much water and electricity all six data centers in the state are using. Water Use In total, the six data centers reported using 779,557,504 gallons of water. But geologist at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Aaron Young says, it’s best to understand water use in inches. “780 million gallons of water works out to very similar to applying approximately 8.9 inches of irrigation water to about five sections of land,” Young said. “That’s about what it takes in a moderate to dry year to grow a section of corn.” For city folk- a section is a square mile. Each section is 640 acres. Young says 8.9 inches being the average is geographically dependent, it’s a little high for eastern Nebraska and low for the western part of the state. As for concerns that data centers are depleting the state’s Ogallala aquifer and causing groundwater to decline, Young says he’s found nothing to support that. “The CSD, Nebraska’s Geological Survey, has been looking into this for the last several months. I can say that as of mid-September, no data centers have applied for large water user permits to any of the NRDs (Natural Resource Districts.),” Young said. “So what that means is no data centers currently have large capacity wells to draw water for cooling. That water is currently coming from municipal systems.” 10/11 confirmed with Lincoln Transportation and Utilities that the Google Data Center in Lincoln is a customer. So where does blame belong for declining groundwater? 10/11 spoke with Director Jesse Bradley of the Department of Water, Energy and Environment this summer. He pointed to lack of snowpack feeding rivers in Nebraska and lack of rainfall. “Statewide, obviously, we’ve been kind of in a pesky persistent drought here for a few years kind of on and off,” Bradley said. “We would expect those declines to recover when we kind of get back to those above average and average years, that we will string those together again, I’m sure.” Electricity Use The six data centers reported electricity usage differently, so 10/11 spoke with Lincoln Electric System and John Krajewski, of JK Energy Consulting, LLC to get a better understanding of scale. According to Scott Benson, the director of Strategy and Innovation with LES, during peak electric demand, the Google Data Center in Lincoln used the same amount of electricity as 13,162.5 average Lincoln homes. He estimates it takes 250 homes to use 1 megawatt of electricity. “Certainly, the last three, four years what’s going on with data centers has been easily the most significant change I’ve been through,” Krajewski said. “This is clearly the most disruptive thing we’ve had to deal with in the utilities I work with.” Data centers reported in megawatts used during peak demand and megawatt-hours. “A megawatt is a million watts. That’s a measure of how much electricity a customer is using at a specific moment. Think of it like the speedometer in your car,” Krajewski said. “Megawatt-hour, that’s energy. Think of that like the odometer on your car. If you use one megawatt, the same amount for an hour, you will have used one megawatt-hour of energy.” Krajewski said a typical house in Nebraska uses probably a thousand kilowatt-hours a month. “One of these data centers can use basically what I use in a month in about three or four seconds,” he said. “And here I am running around the house, shutting my lights off to make sure that I... conserve energy and these data centers are just running full out.” 10/11 spoke with LES, who supplies the electricity to the data center in Lincoln. Benson said none of the site’s electricity usage is passed on to your residential bill. “We’re buying all the energy from the Southwest Power Pool to serve you at your house, just like we’re buying all the energy from the Southwest Power Pool to serve Google up at the interchange of I-80 and North 56th Street. What we do under that special rate is every week, when the Southwest Power Pool renders us a bill, they render us a bill for LES’s system without Google, and they render us a bill specific to the part that serves Google,” Benson said. “We take that bill and turn right around and pass it on to Google and they pay 100% of it. So the importance of that is, the Southwest Power Pool, their electricity price changes every five minutes. The price that we give you as a residential customer is a fixed price for an entire year.” Benson says setting a fixed rate for Google is placing “too many eggs in one basket,” but a fixed rate is a risk the utility is willing to take on for your bill. Additionally, Google funded the upgrades made to infrastructure to accommodate the data center coming to town. “We also have a series of contracts with them. Contracts that cover things like all the upgrades we have to make to the transmission system to be able to serve you, you have to pay for 100% of those,” Benson said. “What that means is the rate for all these individual, large customers ends up being specific to them because it depends on the underlying components of all those contracts and such.” Still, many say their electricity bill is rising, and it coincides with the arrival of the data center. Benson says that is likely due to inflation. “Google happened to come at a time when we’re experiencing rate increases because the pressures, most of them, the pressures out there in the world, just like everybody’s seeing the price of everything they’re dealing with going up these days. artigo.texto: Harmony planning commission approves draft data center ordinance Sixth draft of regulatory standards goes to city council after public hearing HARMONY, Minn. (KTTC) – The Harmony Planning and Zoning Commission approved a draft ordinance that would establish regulatory standards for potential data center development in the Fillmore County community. The ordinance now goes to the city council for consideration. The next council meeting is Nov. 10. Public hearing A public hearing took place before the commission’s Wednesday evening decision. About 50 people attended, and about 20 addressed the five-member commission. One community member supported the proposed ordinance. The other speakers expressed reservations about a data center taking shape in Harmony. Speakers raised quality of life issues, noise concerns and environmental impacts. Several speakers also questioned the city’s candidness about the process and asked that elected officials take more community input into account. What the ordinance says The ordinance is in its sixth draft. According to its language, it establishes clear regulatory standards for the development and operation of data center facilities within the city by protecting public health and safety while preserving Harmony’s rural character and environmental resources. Unlike the planned Google data center development in Pine Island, there has been no public announcement about a specific project in Harmony. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. artigo.texto: O impacto da instalação de Data Centers no Brasil e a influência da Inteligência Artificial no setor elétrico são temas da Coniben 2026 O encontro reunirá investidores, especialistas do Brasil, Portugal e da Espanha num encontro que antecipa o futuro do setor elétrico no país. Clique aqui e escute a matéria Tema central nas discussões de empresários, governos e diretores de instituições que cuida do gerenciamento do setor elétrico em nível global a instalação de Data Centers move tanto interesses de investidores interessado retorno desse novo negócio, como de ambientalistas preocupados com o consumo água para a refrigeração de seus parque de máquinas. E ele esteve entre os temas tratados pelo presidente Lula no seu discurso de agradecimento pela vitória eleitoral deste domingo (25), quando prometeu dar condições para que o Brasil seja um grande destino desses capitais, destacando a função estratégica para a segurança nacional. Faz sentido. Apenas no recorte dos grandes data centers, por exemplo, o consumo projetado passaria de aproximadamente 3 TWh em 2026 para 30 TWh em 2036. E impactaria o crescimento do consumo nacional em 3% em 2036, e a demanda em cerca de 10% no decênio. O Brasil, de fato, tem vantagens importantes para receber esses investimentos: uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, grande disponibilidade de recursos energéticos e uma extensa rede interligada. Além disso, o próprio Plano Decenal de Energia (PDE 2036) elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética projeta que 88,8% da geração elétrica permanecerá renovável em 2036, com cerca de 65 GW adicionais de solar e eólica, incluindo geração distribuída. Entretanto, para o planejamento, a abordagem disso não passa apenas por quanto esses empreendimentos vão consumir. E para o presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, localização, potência demandada, cronograma de implantação, perfil horário e exigência de confiabilidade são igualmente importantes. Um data center de grande porte conectado em um ponto com capacidade disponível produz um impacto muito diferente do que um que exija reforços significativos na rede. “Por isso, será necessário coordenar o crescimento dessas cargas com geração, transmissão e novas soluções de flexibilidade, como, por exemplo, resposta à demanda, autoprodução e armazenamento de forma isolada ou combinada”, adverte o executivo. Ele chama a atenção para outro aspecto: a forma de planejar e operar também se transforma. Se antes cenários de perda da maior central geradora ou da maior máquina são considerados nos estudos de confiabilidade, o desligamento de grandes cargas também deverá ser objeto de estudo, antevendo os seus efeitos e perturbações no sistema elétrico. “O desafio não é apenas produzir energia suficiente para os data centers; é garantir energia, potência, rede e confiabilidade no lugar e no momento em que essas novas cargas surgirem e passarem a operar continuamente na rede”, diz Thiago Prado. Sua análise está em linha com a Assessora Executiva da Diretoria de Planejamento do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), Sumara Ticom, ao revelar que o ONS vê a chegada dos data centers como parte de um movimento mais amplo, que a Agência Internacional de Energia chama de “Era da Eletricidade”, em que o consumo de eletricidade cresce bem mais rápido que o consumo total de energia. No Brasil, desta Sumara Ticom, esse movimento já é concreto. Lembrando que, com a abertura da primeira Temporada de Acesso, em junho de 2026, o ONS havia recebido 144 pedidos de conexão de data centers à rede de transmissão, que somam 17,5 GW de demanda. Cerca de 8 GW desse total, viabilizados ainda no modelo anterior de acesso, já têm contrato assinado ou viabilidade de conexão confirmada. Empreendimentos de grande porte e impactantes Mas não basta querer. O principal desafio é de tempo e de lugar, afinal um data center pode ser construído em dois ou três anos, enquanto linhas de transmissão e reforços de rede exigem prazos bem maiores. Além disso, esses empreendimentos tendem a se concentrar em poucos pontos da rede, com demandas de centenas de megawatts. “Sem planejamento, o consumo pode crescer mais rápido que a infraestrutura capaz de atendê-lo, criando gargalos de conexão”, adverte. Para Sumara Ticom, as ações necessárias seguem quatro frentes: A primeira é a expansão da rede. A EPE, responsável pelo planejamento da expansão da transmissão, vem incorporando aos seus estudos as regiões que concentram os maiores pedidos de conexão e indicando os reforços e as novas instalações necessários para atendê-las, em estreita articulação com o ONS. A segunda frente é a conexão planejada, com o objetivo de reduzir o descompasso entre o prazo de implantação das cargas e o da rede. A rede deve chegar aonde as cargas pretendem se instalar e as cargas também precisam ser orientadas para onde a rede já pode recebê-las, o que exige transparência sobre a capacidade disponível em cada ponto, destaca a analista. A terceira, da lista dela, é a definição de requisitos técnicos que assegurem o bom desempenho dessas cargas diante de distúrbios na rede e, finalmente, a quarta é a discussão de modalidades de conexão flexível, “que permitam à carga se conectar mais rapidamente sem transferir riscos aos demais consumidores”. Tudo muito bom, tudo muito bem, mas, como o órgão de planejamento de médio e longo prazo, o que a EPE define como as premissas para o suporte técnico que esse novo cliente exige? O presidente da EPE avalia que a primeira premissa é justamente que não podemos tratar grandes cargas apenas como um acréscimo agregado de consumo. O planejamento precisa saber onde a carga pretende se conectar, qual sua potência, quando entrará em operação, qual seu perfil de consumo e quais são seus requisitos de continuidade e qualidade do fornecimento. artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution (373220.KS) is holding a research competition aimed at securing a lead in next-generation battery technology. The company said on the 29th that it has opened the Battery Innovation Contest (BIC) 2026 and will accept submissions through Dec. 6. Launched in 2017, BIC is LG Energy Solution's flagship global research competition and is now in its 10th edition. The program selects promising research projects from universities and research institutes, funds the work, and assigns LG Energy Solution researchers to provide ongoing feedback so that academic ideas can reach commercialization. Applications are accepted through BRIDGE, the BIC communication program. LG Energy Solution selects recipients based on the technological maturity of the proposed research and its potential for commercialization. The company expanded this year's research themes to the largest scope yet. Designated topics include analytical techniques for diagnosing cell conditions and identifying mechanisms that improve safety, and span the full range of future battery technologies, including materials, cells, battery management systems (BMS) and artificial intelligence. Research and development teams across LG Energy Solution's main business divisions chose the topics they want to pursue jointly. The company said it expects the more granular themes to spur two-way collaboration between industry and academia. LG Energy Solution plans to advance next-generation battery technology by funding research projects through BIC. About 50 projects have received support since 2017. Those whose feasibility has been demonstrated are expanded into the Frontier Research Laboratory (FRL), a joint research center run with leading universities and research institutes in Korea and abroad. Projects that move to FRL receive additional funding and are staffed with LG Energy Solution researchers for in-depth work. Last year's BIC produced a patent application for a physics-based model that improves BMS computing speed. In 2019, FRL research on long-life all-solid-state batteries operating at room temperature was published in Science, one of the world's most prestigious academic journals. Kim Je-young, chief technology officer and executive vice president at LG Energy Solution, said that innovation in the battery industry can be achieved if industry and academia join forces, adding that the company will accelerate growth on the strength of differentiated technological competitiveness in the battery market.

Spain’s electricity system is expected to require substantial growth in energy storage capacity as the share of variable renewable generation increases. Battery energy storage systems can help balance differences between electricity production and demand, support grid stability and provide additional flexibility to the power system. The projects form part of Return Energy’s wider pipeline in the Basque Country, which exceeds 1,400 MWh of energy storage capacity and 352.6 MW of power capacity. “Energy storage is becoming an increasingly important part of Spain’s power system as renewable generation grows” said Brice Le Gallo, Brice Le Gallo, Vice-president and regional director for Southern Europe, MEA & LATAM, Energy Systems at DNV. “DNV’s Energy Transition Outlook for Spain shows that a more electrified, renewables-based energy system will require substantially more storage to provide flexibility and support grid stability. Projects reaching financial close are an important part of moving energy storage development from planning into deployment. Our role is to provide an independent view of the technology, design and technical risks so that the parties involved can make investment decisions with greater confidence.” Spain’s National Energy and Climate Plan foresees a substantial expansion of storage capacity by 2030: 22.5 GW, including 12.5 related to BESS. artigo.texto: Mexico Extends Battery Storage Registration Deadline to March Mexico’s Ministry of Energy has extended the BESS project registration deadline to March 1, 2027, giving private developers a vital operational runway. This strategic adjustment aims to synchronize deployment with CFE, mitigate midday solar oversupply risks, and support the nation's broader transmission and renewable energy expansion goals. Mexico’s Ministry of Energy (SENER) has officially extended the deadline for energy storage developers to register projects under its strategic generation and storage call to March 1, 2027. Announced through an administrative amendment signed by Minister of Energy Luz Elena González, this fourth adjustment to the regulatory roadmap provides private sector participants with crucial operational runway to refine technical proposals, optimize project financing structures, and synchronize deployment timelines with state utility Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE). Originally slated to close under earlier schedules, the extended application window specifically targets approximately 935 MW of standalone Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity intended to buffer intermittent renewable generation across key industrial load centers. The necessity for flexible storage infrastructure has become increasingly urgent as large-scale solar and wind portfolios advance nationwide. An unprecedented pipeline of solar photovoltaic generation coming online between 2026 and 2029 introduces significant risk of midday oversupply and subsequent evening net-demand steep ramps. Without adequate co-located or standalone storage to capture and redistribute excess solar generation, developers face potential curtailment and falling capacity revenues during critical operational hours. SENER’s deadline extension provides developers additional time to review technical interconnection studies issued by the National Energy Control Center (CENACE) and adapt their system engineering to mitigate these grid-wide effects. Long-term strategic planning mirrors the operational imperative for rapid storage integration across Mexico's power grid. IRENA highlights that national grid operations will require between 8GW and 9GW of operational energy storage capacity by the mid-2030s to effectively manage peak demand growth, alleviate persistent transmission bottlenecks, and maintain baseline stability across high-demand industrial manufacturing corridors. By granting developers until early 2027 to finalize their registration and study requirements, regulatory authorities aim to attract highly viable proposals that comply fully with the General Administrative Provisions for BESS integration established by the National Energy Commission (CNE). While storage systems provide localized flexibility, expanding and reinforcing the underlying transmission network remains paramount to secure reliable power delivery. CFE's 2026-2030 Expansion Plan encompasses 245 distinct infrastructure works split between 107 transmission lines and 138 electrical substations, alongside significant investments funded through mixed instruments such as Fibra E and financed public works schemes. Industry analysts emphasize that building utility-scale generation and battery assets without simultaneous transmission buildout leads to localized bottlenecks, underlining the critical need for synchronized execution between state entities and private engineering contractors. This regulatory evolution coincides with historic levels of private capital commitment toward Mexico's energy transition. The federal government's mixed development framework has advanced a substantial pipeline of renewable energy projects designed to integrate private capital under CFE off-take and Wholesale Electricity Market (WEM) participation, with finalized awards encompassing 37 renewable projects totaling 7,411MW. The extended BESS deadline represents a strategic window of opportunity. Aligning capital deployment with binding national energy planning, adhering to CENACE interconnection protocols, and leveraging CFE's co-investment framework will be essential for mitigating regulatory and financial risks through 2030. As these multi-billion-peso infrastructure initiatives progress from planning to physical execution, close coordination between public authorities and private developers will determine the long-term reliability, competitiveness, and sustainability of Mexico's National Electric System (SEN).

artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., Marisa Wanzeller e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA A área técnica da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) sugeriu abrir espaço no edital do leilão de baterias para eventuais mudanças no modelo de custeio da contratação. Atualmente, a legislação prevê que as despesas sejam divididas entre os geradores de energia. No entanto, há um projeto de lei no Congresso (PL 3.716/2026) que inclui os consumidores na conta. Segundo fontes, essa proposta deve contar com o apoio do governo para viabilizar o certame em dezembro deste ano. Conforme proposta das notas técnicas disponibilizadas na segunda-feira (26), para os certames de conteúdo nacional e geral, o edital pode ser alterado para atribuir o pagamento dos encargos a “usuários de reserva de capacidade” no lugar de “agentes de geração de energia elétrica”, como estava na proposição original. Agentes consultados pela Agência iNFRA viram a mudança como positiva por permitir que a legislação seja alterada a qualquer tempo sem impactar a segurança do contrato. Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), ressaltou que a entidade vinha pedindo o ajuste para evitar especificações no edital e contrato. “A ideia é que o contrato deve se referir ao usuário de reserva de capacidade, na forma da lei, podendo a lei a qualquer tempo ser alternada – sendo que não cabe a qualquer um de nós prever ou definir eventuais mudanças. E o usuário continuará sendo responsável pelo custeio, seja ele quem for nos termos da lei e da regulação”, disse Lima, que explicou ainda que todos os contratos regulados estão submetidos a mudanças da lei e da regulação. O diretor de Novos Negócios da Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), Marcello Cabral, diz que a alteração seria uma “boa vontade” da reguladora, para evitar a necessidade de futuras mudanças no edital caso o PL 3.716 seja aprovado no Congresso. “Apesar de a ANEEL ter criado uma mudança na referência que ela fazia aos agentes de geração, para usuários de reserva de capacidade, ela não está mudando a base pagante”, ressalta. O tema está pautado para reunião extraordinária de diretoria, convocada para esta terça-feira (27), a partir das 16h. Paralelamente à mudança de entendimento na ANEEL, fontes da Esplanada ouvidas pela reportagem afirmam que, passada a eleição, o governo deve ajudar na tramitação do PL das baterias. O projeto ainda não tem relator definido e já teve urgência aprovada. Baterias em usinas A área técnica também sugere a retirada da vedação para que usinas com contratos no ambiente regulado possam participar do certame, ofertando potência com baterias associadas aos seus empreendimentos. No entanto, o edital deve determinar que os contratos regulados não sejam prejudicados. Segundo os documentos, os agentes argumentaram que a proposta original da ANEEL era restritiva e que a medição individualizada e a independência operativa das baterias seriam suficientes para assegurar o cumprimento dos contratos regulados. A área técnica pondera que as usinas associadas às baterias compartilham o uso da rede, o que poderia afetar o ambiente regulado. Mas acata as sugestões da consulta, deixando a análise para cada caso. “Contudo, os contratos regulados dos agentes de geração e armazenamento têm prazos distintos, podendo levar a situações nas quais a sobreposição temporal de tais contratos seja pequena”, disse. Marcello Cabral, da Abeeólica, aponta que esse compartilhamento de rede, na verdade, otimiza o uso das conexões e pode tornar o leilão mais competitivo. Ele explica que, na associação com um gerador, as baterias podem contratar até cerca de 30% a menos de Must (Montante de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão). Assim, caso uma bateria com capacidade de até 30 MW (megawatts) se associe a uma usina de 100 MW, ela poderá contratar um montante de 100 MW para despacho, exemplificou o executivo. Garantia financeira Outra mudança que pode aumentar a competitividade do leilão é a redução da garantia financeira exigida dos participantes, conforme apontaram agentes ouvidos pela Agência iNFRA. Os documentos sugerem reduzir o aporte de R$ 9,8 milhões/MW para R$ 6 milhões/MW. As contribuições em consulta pública apontaram que o valor inicial baseava-se em premissas desatualizadas de custos de implantação de sistemas de baterias. Segundo os agentes, as referências mais recentes indicam custos de implantação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias. Inadimplência As notas técnicas também mudam o trecho sobre o risco de eventual inadimplência do recebimento do encargo – seja qual for a base pagadora. A versão inicial, na abertura da consulta, previa que o risco total pela falta do pagamento recairia sobre o agente. Agora, o agente ficaria com o “risco de insuficiência momentânea” de recursos na conta setorial, o que posteriormente seria regularizado com repasse do fundo de garantia atrelado à conta, pela CCEE (Câmara de Comercialização de Energia). Fabio Lima, da Absae, explica que o risco de não pagamento é baixo, uma vez que se trata de uma obrigação de os usuários pagarem encargos que lhes forem legalmente atribuídos. Assim, deixar de pagar gera penalizações, como possibilidade de desligamento da CCEE. Com o ajuste feito pela ANEEL, o agente acabaria recebendo de qualquer forma, seja por uma fonte ou outra. “Quem paga a bateria não é cada usuário, mas sim essa conta para a qual todos os usuários contribuem. E essa conta tem um fundo para inadimplência. Então, para o agente não ter a sua remuneração, teria que ser uma inadimplência massiva que ultrapasse a inadimplência média prevista”, explicou Lima, que destacou ainda que a lógica é a mesma de outras contas setoriais. Apesar de considerar o novo entendimento positivo, o diretor da Absae afirma que ele não precisaria estar detalhado no edital. “Se é um risco geral e inerente a toda conta setorial, como dá para se ler da nota técnica, não tem por que ele estar ex

artigo.texto: The Menifee Planning Commission unanimously approved plans for a third battery energy storage facility Wednesday, following discussions about fire safety and nearby residential development. The Seaflower Battery Energy Storage System would occupy approximately 3.7 acres near Matthews, McLaughlin and Menifee roads, with a storage capacity of up to 400 megawatt-hours. The facility would connect to Southern California Edison’s nearby Valley Substation and join the existing Nova Power Bank and previously approved Double Butte Battery Energy Storage System. Planning Manager Ryan Fowler outlined the project’s safety features, including fire and smoke detection systems, cooling equipment and remote monitoring. The plans also include landscaping and decorative walls, including a 14- to 18-foot wall facing future residential development. Commissioners questioned fire officials about inspection requirements and a recent battery storage incident in La Verne, where a lithium battery explosion and fire occurred last month. Fire Marshal Sonya Bu said the facility would undergo annual inspections. “I would say that that’s sufficient for an unoccupied site,” Bu said. “There is no changing of technologies. They’re standalone systems.” Fowler said a hazard mitigation analysis had also been prepared to evaluate potential risks, including battery overheating and electrical failures. Commissioners also raised concerns about the facility’s proximity to Menifee 37, a proposed 701-home development considered later in the meeting. Fowler said the distance between the battery equipment and proposed homes includes setbacks, Matthews Road, railroad tracks and a residential wall. “So, all in all, it adds up to about 250 feet, so approaching like a football field,” Fowler said. He added that noise and air quality studies found impacts below applicable thresholds. Fowler also confirmed that the city has negotiated a community benefit fee with the developer. The agreement will go to the City Council for approval, although the amount was not disclosed. Previous battery storage projects have included similar fees. Menifee received approximately $6.5 million for Nova Power Bank and is expected to receive approximately $4 million for Double Butte, according to previous Menifee 24/7 reporting. No members of the public spoke during the hearing. Commissioner Chris Thomas expressed support for the project’s location near the existing electrical substation. “It’s a good spot if you’re going to do it, sitting right next to the power station right there,” Thomas said. “So, I don’t see any problem with it.” City staff said no additional battery storage facility applications are currently being processed.

artigo.texto: Solar, Battery Storage Help Lower Power Prices in California, Texas: SEIA Rooftop solar generation increased by 4,137 GWh in California and 970 GWh in Texas October 30, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights California and Texas recorded an estimated wholesale electricity cost savings of $2.5 billion and $3.55 billion, respectively, between June and August 2026 compared with the corresponding period in 2021, according to an analysis by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA). The decline in wholesale electricity prices was attributed partly to increased solar generation and battery energy storage deployment. The analysis examined the weighted average hourly wholesale day-ahead electricity prices for June, July, and August 2021 and the same months in 2026. Both the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) and the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) saw weighted daily average prices drop over the period. After adjusting for inflation, CAISO prices declined 51% from $77.54/MWh to $38.32/MWh, while ERCOT prices declined 42% from $54.97/MWh to $31.77/MWh. During the same period, the generation component of residential electricity prices declined by 10% in California and 4% in Texas. However, increases in other cost components pushed overall residential electricity prices up by 22% in California and 3% in Texas. California Average hourly electricity prices during the three summer months were significantly higher in 2021 than in 2026. Solar power generation rose 90% over the five years in California, while installed battery storage capacity grew from 8.1 GWh in 2021 to 62 GWh by the end of the first half of 2026. According to SEIA, batteries now supply 6% to 7% of CAISO’s daily energy use. From June to August 2026, California’s electricity consumption was 2.5% higher than during the same period in 2021, while average wholesale electricity prices were 51% lower after adjusting for inflation. The decline in wholesale electricity prices saved the state an estimated $2.5 billion. While the generation component of residential electricity prices declined by 10%, transmission, distribution, and other costs, such as wildfire management, increased substantially. Texas During the three summer months, average hourly electricity prices in Texas were significantly higher in 2021 than in 2026. Over the five years, solar power generation in Texas increased 421%. Installed battery storage capacity grew from 1 GWh in 2021 to 33.1 GWh by the end of the first half of 2026. Battery storage now supplies over 1.3% of the state’s energy demand. From June to August 2026, Texas’ electricity consumption was 30.1% higher than in the same period in 2021, while average wholesale electricity prices were 42% lower after adjusting for inflation. The decline in wholesale electricity prices saved the state an estimated $3.55 billion. SEIA’s comparison of residential electricity price components across selected Texas utilities shows generation costs fell by 4%, while transmission and distribution costs rose by 17% and 23%, respectively. Other electricity costs declined by 5% Rooftop solar generation increased by 970 GWh in Texas and 4,137 GWh in California between the three-month periods of 2021 and 2026, helping meet rising electricity demand in both states. Rooftop solar and customer-sited battery energy storage reduce grid stress and the need for additional centralized generation assets. Texas and California face heightened permitting risks for solar and wind energy projects amid increased federal oversight, with potential delays to scheduled commercial operation dates. According to an analysis by Wood Mackenzie, projects in these states, along with Arizona, have some of the highest exposure to additional reviews under a U.S. Department of the Interior memorandum. The reviews could add uncertainty to project development timelines and investments. According to a September report by Wood Mackenzie and SEIA, the U.S. added 11.4 GW of solar capacity in the second quarter of 2026, a 45% year-over-year increase and a 43% quarter-over-quarter increase.

artigo.texto: Geminus has been selected by AFWERX for a SBIR Phase I contract focused on physics-informed AI for microgrid and battery optimisation to address the challenges in the Department of the Air Force (DAF) The award extends a platform already running across large-scale energy infrastructure into battery storage and grid management as a wave of new demand hits the grid. The Air Force Research Laboratory and AFWERX have partnered to streamline the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) process by accelerating the small business experience through faster proposal to award timelines, changing the pool of potential applicants by expanding opportunities to small business and eliminating bureaucratic overhead by implementing process improvement changes in contract execution. The DAF began offering the Open Topic SBIR/STTR programme in 2018, which expanded the range of innovations the DAF funded and now, Geminus will begin creating and providing innovative capabilities that will strengthen the national defence of the United States. Geminus is the AI orchestration layer for intelligent twins. Digital twins were bespoke projects that were built by hand, calibrated once, and were often out of date the moment the real system changed. Geminus can make digital twins repeatable, reliable, and rapid, grounded in physics, aware of their own certainty, and fast enough to optimise live operations, even on systems that age and change. Greg Fallon, CEO of Geminus, said, “Every digital twin used to be a bespoke project, so most industrial systems never got one. We made intelligent twins repeatable, reliable, and fast enough to act on in real time. Storage is where the grid’s biggest problem gets solved or gets stuck.” For the Air Force, Geminus is set to build and intelligent twin of a forward-deployed microgrid: diesel generators, lithium-ion batteries, and shifting mission loads. It hopes to achieve longer battery life, consume less fuel, and deliver reliable power where it is mission critical, with Phase I opening the door to a follow-on pilot. The views expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official policy or position of the Department of the Air Force, the Department of War, or the U.S. government.

artigo.texto: Who benefits when massive AI data centers come to town? The battle over data centers is hitting the ballot box. Brookings scholar Darrell West talks about how the backlash against the AI boom, flock cameras and tech companies is crossing party lines. TONYA MOSLEY, HOST: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Tonya Mosley. The AI boom has a problem. It has to be built somewhere, and to power it, tech companies are building massive data centers. They need land, enormous amounts of electricity, and in many cases, water. In exchange, they promise jobs and community investment. But people who live in these communities are demanding to know, what's this going to cost us? There's also another question, who gets to decide? In communities from Wisconsin to Louisiana, residents say local officials are negotiating data center deals without their input. This midterm election, voters in more than 40 cities and towns across eight states will decide ballot measures on data center bans, moratoriums and requirements that residents get a vote before one is built. And Democrats and Republicans are going after their opponents for what used to be a bragging right, the ability to bring billions of dollars in investment to town. My guest is Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. He and his colleague, Nicol Turner Lee, write about the backlash against AI data centers and how these local fights are becoming part of something much bigger, a challenge to the enormous power of the tech industry and who gets to decide what our future looks like. And, Darrell West, welcome to FRESH AIR. DARRELL WEST: Thank you, Tonya. It's nice to be with you. MOSLEY: Well, I actually want to start with a couple of political ads. And the first one is from Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown is challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted. And Brown accuses Husted of aggressively courting data centers and backing corporate tax breaks while residents face rising electricity bills. Let's listen. (SOUNDBITE OF POLITICAL AD, "THE FACE OF DATA CENTERS") UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #1: He's been called the face of data centers in Ohio. Why? Because Jon Husted spent years aggressively recruiting data centers to the state, cutting sweetheart tax deals and fast-tracking approvals while ordinary residents watch their electricity bills explode. UNIDENTIFIED JOURNALIST: We're here with Ohio Senator Jon Husted. You have a lot of experience with something called data centers. UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #1: Jon Husted, who's he really working for? SHERROD BROWN: I'm Sherrod Brown and I approve this message. MOSLEY: OK, now listen to this one. And it comes out of Wisconsin. Republican Tom Tiffany is running for governor against Democrat David Crowley. And Tiffany accuses Crowley of wanting to turn Wisconsin into a global data center hub at the expense of taxpayers and local communities. Let's listen. (SOUNDBITE OF POLITICAL AD, "DATA CENTER DAVID") UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #2: Meet Data Center David Crowley. DAVID CROWLEY: There's an opportunity for us to really become an AI and a data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe. UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #2: And he wants you to pay for it. Data Center David Crowley won't roll back data center tax incentives. Our lakes run dry, family farms paved over - why? - because Crowley's campaign is funded by the people building them. Data Center David Crowley; Big Tech wins, Wisconsin pays. MOSLEY: All right. So, Darrell, what's fascinating to me about these ads is you've got a Democrat from Ohio and a Republican in Wisconsin, and they're making practically the same attack. When did you realize this wasn't just a string of maybe local zoning fights anymore, that it really has become a national political story? WEST: Now, Tonya, you're completely right. It has become a national political story. And public opinion has changed dramatically just over the course of the last year. As you mentioned in your intro, a year ago, politicians of both parties were falling all over themselves trying to attract these economic development dollars into their local communities. They were basically providing tax breaks to these very wealthy tech companies in order to get the data centers built there. But over the last six to nine months, we've just seen this huge change where people either went from being mildly positive or at least neutral towards data centers, to today, 70% of Americans now say they have serious reservations about data centers. A recent survey showed 50% of Americans said they did not want to live next to a data center. And so these ads that you just showed basically demonstrate how that has changed. But it's not just Democrats versus Republicans. I mean, whoever has supported data centers in the past, whoever has supported tax breaks for data centers in the past, is now finding that policy position being used against them in this campaign. MOSLEY: Data centers, though, they've really been around for decades. So what's different about the enormous ones that are being built now for AI? WEST: The big difference is just the size of these new facilities. So you're right that data centers have been around for a long time. A lot of companies have facilities that house their computing equipment and their file servers just in order to run their internal operations. But the data centers that are being built today are huge in size. A number of them often take the space of two or three football fields, if not bigger. They are enormous in terms of the expenditures that are behind them. And as they have grown bigger, the public has started to grow more wary of them. Like, if you're living next to a data center, neighbors complain about noise. You mentioned the issues of energy, water and land use. People are worried about those aspects as well. And of course, people are just worried about the uses to which data centers are being put, which is to run AI, which also has become very contentious in recent months. MOSLEY: Yeah

artigo.texto: Edge AI May Give Telecoms a Seat at the Table Edge AI may give telecoms a bigger AI role, with metro sites, not towers, emerging as the clearest near-term opportunity. October 30, 2026 While the telecommunications industry has spent years absorbed in “the G’s” – 4G, 5G, and now 6G – the hyperscalers have been rewriting the broader narrative of computing. Telcos have fed every stage of that evolution through their pipes and platforms, yet by some measures they still end up cast as plumbers. More recently, the fanfare around generative AI has further eclipsed telecom’s own next act. Against the spectacle of large language models, GPU clusters, and hyperscale AI buildouts, 6G can look less like an imminent frontier than a contender stranded in an early round. Yet the next phase of AI may reopen the question of where telecoms fit in the digital infrastructure stack. As generative AI and agentic AI move into daily use, new opportunities are emerging through edge AI inference. Most of that work will still be done in hyperscale data centers. But latency, data gravity, and cost are likely to push parts of workloads toward the edge. That is where some observers see a new convergence taking shape – one that could place telecoms closer to the center of AI inference infrastructure. Nvidia has already signaled part of that opportunity. The company’s moves at the AI edge have been quieter than the daily procession of hyperscale megadeals, but the roots of convergence are visible in projects and partnerships involving AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica, T-Mobile, and others. Nvidia has placed particular emphasis on edge AI for factory and robotics use cases – often called “physical AI” – closely tied to AI-RAN. The GPU infrastructure connected to AI-RAN is also expected to help telecom operators improve their own efficiency through greater automation of network operations. Still, this emerging edge is by no means a monolithic thing. It is nuanced, layered, and still taking shape. How it develops is now a central question in both data center and telecom circles. The Physical Hurdles of Edge AI The edge holds real potential to offload some of the work now concentrated in hyperscaler facilities and to serve applications located far beyond regional data centers more efficiently. In practice, however, deploying AI beyond large regional facilities introduces a new set of infrastructure problems for telecom operators. David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, said the economics and engineering can become difficult very quickly. EnterpriseWeb, which develops an orchestration platform for mapping and automating agentic AI workflows, has participated in proof-of-concept projects with Intel, Dell, and others focused on applying generative AI and automation at the edge. As Duggal explained, one of the first challenges is definitional. The “telco edge” is not the same as the “customer edge.” One refers to radio towers, base stations, and network-adjacent facilities. The other may sit inside an enterprise campus, factory, warehouse, or other operational site. That distinction matters because deploying high-performance AI inference directly at a tower or cell site is far more difficult than placing it in a better-provisioned metro or enterprise facility. “Power and thermal concerns make AI on a tower or cell site a Catch-22 situation,” Duggal said. “That GPU requires a lot more power … and more power means more heat.” More heat, in turn, means more supporting infrastructure. GPUs are expensive, dense, and power-intensive, making it difficult to justify equipping every radio tower with advanced inference hardware. As Duggal and others point out, some emerging radio access network models instead push heavy AI inference workloads back toward the data center or another better-served aggregation layer. The Many Edges of AI Today’s AI inference buildout spans several tiers of infrastructure. Since the debut of ChatGPT, hyperscale clouds have handled the most intensive generative AI training and development workloads, often running across thousands of compute nodes per region. Beyond that central cloud lies a more varied edge continuum: - Metro edge: Central offices, regional hubs, and other aggregation facilities operated by large telcos or neutral hosts. These sites can support hundreds of nodes, consolidate data flows from both the cloud and the far edge, and offer a more practical setting for higher-density GPU deployments. - Far edge: Cell towers, base stations, and local on-premises cabinets serving highly time-sensitive tasks, including machine vision and localized telemetry. These environments are the natural focus of AI-RAN and O-RAN conversations, but they also face the toughest power, cooling, and space constraints. - Endpoint AI: Devices such as smartphones, vehicles, industrial controllers, telematics units, and IoT sensors. These systems handle some processing locally and pass data or decisions upstream to the far edge, metro edge, or cloud as needed. The point is that “the edge” is not one place. It is a gradient of infrastructure, with different economics and different technical realities at each tier. New Life for Old Switch Houses? US telecom operators also hold a less discussed asset: real estate. Central offices, network huts, and legacy switching facilities may not look like the future of AI infrastructure, but many could become useful sites for edge inference, particularly as community resistance complicates large greenfield data center development. That possibility is also showing up in standards work. Refurbishing brownfield facilities is only one part of a broader push at the Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) to define more unified practices for AI data center infrastructure. artigo.texto: John James says no new data centers until plan to protect communities BAY CITY, Mich. — U.S. Rep. John James, a Republican candidate for governor, toured Bay Plastics Machinery Company in Bay County while campaigning on Thursday, Oct. 29. TV5 was there and asked James about his position on data centers. James said, “No new data centers until we have a plan to protect our communities.” “We have to have local control. We have to protect our water, prevent our electricity bills from going up, prevent pollution. That means land, air, water, and noise pollution. And also prioritize our blighted brownfields over productive green farmland,” James said. James also said: “Don’t accept that affordability is the standard. Only accept that prosperity is your destiny.” James’ opponent, Democrat and current Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, calls data centers a top issue. She says she would place a moratorium on them as governor. In part, Benson says, “no data centers would be built unless there are rules in place that make them negotiate with communities in the open ... ban them from getting tax breaks and using up water, and require them to pay for their power.” Related Coverage: Governor’s race: Jocelyn Benson vs. John James James will be in West Branch tonight for a “Get Out the Vote” event. artigo.texto: A cidade de São Paulo está próxima da mediana no ranking de custos de regiões globais para construção de data centers elaborado pela Turner & Townsend, empresa global de gestão de projetos. O estudo aponta que São Paulo ocupa a 30ª posição, com um custo por watt de US$ 11,66, que representa R$ 62,12 por watt. Com isso, a capital paulista é uma alternativa competitiva em comparação com polos consolidados, como o Vale do Silício, nos Estados Unidos, onde o custo é de US$ 15,01 por watt (cerca de R$ 76,55 por watt), e o norte da Virgínia, também nos Estados Unidos, com US$ 11,80 por watt (cerca de R$ 60,18 por watt). A capital fluminense, por sua vez, tem um custo mais alto, de US$ 12,59 por watt (R$ 67,05). Segundo a Turner & Townsend, isso reflete a expansão da capacidade do Rio de Janeiro e a sua atratividade para novos investimentos. “A posição de São Paulo e do Rio de Janeiro no índice global reforça o Brasil como o principal polo de infraestrutura de data centers da América do Sul. Uma matriz energética diversificada, a crescente demanda por capacidade de computação em nuvem e a expansão da inteligência artificial mantêm o país atrativo para grandes investidores e empresas globais de hiperescala, conhecidas como hyperscalers”, analisa Henrique Cicchetto, diretor de Real Estate da Turner & Townsend no Brasil. No contexto do relatório, o indicador “custo por watt” (US$/W) corresponde ao custo médio de construção por watt de capacidade elétrica de um data center. Com isso, é possível comparar o custo de construção dessas instalações em diferentes localidades, independentemente do tamanho. O indicador não se refere ao custo da eletricidade consumida pelo data center, mas ao custo de construção da infraestrutura para cada watt de capacidade instalada. artigo.texto: Redata atrai investidores, mas não acelera obras de data centers Pesquisa do GRI mostra que apenas 4% apontam antecipação de projetos como principal efeito do incentivo O governo conseguiu aumentar a atratividade do Brasil para investimentos em data centers com a aprovação do Redata, mas ainda está longe de resolver um dos principais problemas enfrentados pelo setor: a demora para colocar os empreendimentos em operação. Um levantamento do GRI Institute mostra que apenas 4,08% dos participantes da pesquisa apontaram a antecipação dos cronogramas de projetos como o principal efeito esperado do novo regime de incentivos fiscais. O resultado evidencia uma distância entre a redução dos custos de investimento e a capacidade de acelerar a instalação dos centros de processamento de dados no país. A pesquisa, realizada em setembro durante um encontro do GRI que reuniu 239 participantes, entre executivos, investidores, financiadores e representantes do setor público, revela um contraste. Enquanto 53,06% apontaram o aumento da competitividade internacional do Brasil como principal efeito do Redata, a expectativa de antecipação dos empreendimentos ficou restrita a uma pequena parcela das respostas. O estudo captou as expectativas dos participantes no dia da sanção da lei, e não os resultados efetivos do programa. O obstáculo está principalmente na infraestrutura. Embora o Brasil tenha uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável e disponibilidade de energia para atrair grandes investimentos, a conexão dos empreendimentos à rede de transmissão esbarra em limitações de capacidade, obras de expansão e procedimentos regulatórios. Segundo o GRI, os prazos necessários para viabilizar essa infraestrutura podem ser incompatíveis com a velocidade de implantação exigida pelas empresas de tecnologia, sobretudo diante do avanço da inteligência artificial. A importância desse gargalo aparece em outro resultado do levantamento. A disponibilidade de infraestrutura de apoio, incluindo energia, conectividade e transporte, passou de 43,40% das menções em 2025 para 72,92% em 2026, tornando-se o principal fator apontado como capaz de impulsionar investimentos. Superou até mesmo a demanda por inteligência artificial, mencionada por 66,67% dos participantes. Já a proporção de respostas indicando apetite alto ou muito alto por investimentos no setor subiu de 76% para 83,78% no mesmo período. As limitações também dificultam uma das ambições do governo: distribuir os investimentos para além dos mercados tradicionais do Sul e Sudeste. Apesar dos incentivos diferenciados previstos para o Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, apenas 4,08% apontaram o redirecionamento regional dos projetos como principal efeito esperado do Redata. A escolha da localização continua condicionada à disponibilidade de infraestrutura elétrica, à conectividade e à proximidade dos principais centros consumidores. Sancionado em setembro, o Redata prevê benefícios tributários federais para a aquisição e importação de equipamentos destinados aos centros de processamento de dados, mas sua implementação ainda depende de regulamentação. O setor também cobra avanços na desoneração do ICMS, que exige articulação entre os estados. O diagnóstico do GRI indica que a política tributária pode ajudar o Brasil a conquistar investimentos, mas transformar esse interesse em projetos operacionais exigirá resolver obstáculos que os incentivos fiscais, isoladamente, não conseguem eliminar.

artigo.texto: A VinEnergo opera um sistema de energia solar combinado com armazenamento em baterias em Ha Tinh. No dia 28 de outubro, a VinEnergo colocou em operação um sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica em telhados, combinado com armazenamento em baterias (BESS), para fornecer eletricidade limpa à fábrica de veículos VinFast, à fábrica de baterias VinES e à joint venture de fabricação de baterias VG, na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang. Com uma capacidade total de até 22 MWp de energia solar e 45 MWh de sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), o sistema ajuda a VinEnergo a garantir um fornecimento de energia estável a custos otimizados para seus parceiros, além de contribuir para a redução da sobrecarga na rede elétrica nacional. O projeto de energia solar em telhados com sistema de armazenamento de baterias (BESS) na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang (Ha Tinh) é o primeiro projeto operado pela VinEnergo sob o mecanismo de contrato direto de compra de energia (DPPA). Os primeiros clientes a beneficiarem da eletricidade limpa e da tecnologia avançada de armazenamento de energia da VinEnergo são a Future Production, Investment and Development Joint Stock Company (proprietária e operadora da fábrica de carros e motocicletas elétricas VinFast em Ha Tinh ) e a VinES Ha Tinh Energy Solutions Joint Stock Company (proprietária da fábrica de baterias VinES Ha Tinh). Além disso, o sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica instalado no telhado da VinEnergo também fornece eletricidade para a fábrica de baterias da joint venture VG, que também está localizada dentro do complexo de fabricação de baterias e veículos elétricos na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang. Você também pode gostar Segundo estimativas, em seu primeiro ano de operação, o sistema deverá gerar aproximadamente 39 milhões de kWh de energia limpa, contribuindo para a redução de mais de 25.000 toneladas de emissões de CO2 (o equivalente à absorção de mais de 1,13 milhão de árvores por ano). Em particular, a transição para a energia limpa da VinEnergo ajudará as unidades beneficiárias a reduzir a pressão sobre a rede elétrica e aumentar a autossuficiência energética, otimizando custos em cerca de 3,5 bilhões de VND por ano. O sucesso operacional e o fornecimento estável de energia às três usinas parceiras na fase inicial servem como base para que a VinEnergo continue desenvolvendo e promovendo a transição para energia verde nas fases subsequentes. Este modelo combina fontes de energia renováveis com um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) de grande escala, visando completar a infraestrutura de energia verde, a distribuição e a comercialização de eletricidade para os consumidores da região. A Sra. Nguyen Huong Giang, Vice-Diretora Geral da VinEnergo, declarou: “Por meio deste projeto, a VinEnergo irá gradualmente completar um ecossistema energético abrangente, desde fontes renováveis, sistemas de armazenamento e mecanismos de DPPA até infraestrutura de distribuição e varejo, capaz de atender à crescente demanda de eletricidade de projetos industriais emergentes na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang, em particular, e em todo o país, em geral. Temos orgulho de utilizar nossos próprios produtos, capacidades tecnológicas e plataforma de fabricação no Vietnã para solucionar os desafios energéticos de nossos parceiros comerciais, contribuindo para o aumento da competitividade e da participação de energia verde no setor industrial.” Você também pode gostar Atualmente, a VinEnergo fornece soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) para diversos grandes projetos da Hanoi Power Corporation e da Northern Power Corporation, totalizando mais de 1,1 GWh, o que comprova a capacidade das empresas vietnamitas de dominar tecnologias essenciais e implementar projetos de grande escala. No mercado internacional, a VinEnergo anunciou um portfólio de projetos de energia renovável totalizando 10 GW e está atualmente implementando seus primeiros projetos na Ásia e na Europa. Nos próximos três anos, a VinEnergo pretende desenvolver um portfólio de projetos com capacidade total de até 100 GW, tornando-se assim uma das empresas líderes mundiais em energia renovável.

artigo.texto: Who benefits when massive AI data centers come to town? From Virginia to Kansas, the battle over data centers has reached the ballot box this midterm election. Communities are voting on whether to limit or ban the massive facilities being built to power AI – and the fight crosses party lines. Both Democrats and Republicans are accusing their opponents of being too eager to welcome billions of dollars in tech investment without considering the costs. Darrell West, a researcher at the Brookings Institution, has been studying the backlash. He says it's become something much bigger. "The data center fight is no longer just about data centers. It's about AI and its possible impact on people." Communities want to know what they'll have to give up, and who gets to decide. artigo.texto: A controversial Microsoft data center set to draw up to 1 GW of power from Consumers Energy’s grid could see “more progress” on local permitting after next week’s elections, CMS Energy CEO Garrick Rochow told investors and stock analysts on the company’s quarterly earnings call Tuesday. CMS Energy is the parent company of Consumers Energy, which operates regulated gas and electric utilities in Michigan. Rochow suggested that much of the opposition to data centers is being driven by political campaigns and could subside after the midterms. “Some of the spin that you see leading up to the election does not equal reality,” Rochow said. Without mentioning Microsoft by name, he said the data center — which Consumers announced an agreement to serve earlier this year — was “[continuing] to progress through zoning in multiple locations” after a permitting setback in April. Still, a “funnel” slide depicting Consumers’ multi-gigawatt large-load pipeline was conspicuously absent from CMS Energy’s third-quarter earnings presentation. Rochow said it was an intentional decision not to include the slide, which had appeared in the past several quarterly presentations. “It’s a little bit like watching [the University of] Michigan play football. You can spend a lot of time looking at the plays, but you’ve got to get it across the end zone,” he said. Rochow added that Consumers’ electric utility has energized about 450 MW of new large load in its territory out of a total of 745 MW of signed contracts in its five-year plan. Those contracts cover a “medium-sized data center” plus semiconductor, food processing and manufacturing facilities, but don’t include the Microsoft data center, he said. One gigawatt of incremental large load could drive $2 billion to $5 billion in capital investment for the utility, CMS Energy executive vice president and chief financial officer Sri Maddipati said. CMS Energy earned $0.39 per share in the third quarter of 2026, down from $0.92 per share in the third quarter of 2025. NorthStar Clean Energy update The company said the EPS results “reflect asset impairment and restructuring activities associated with NorthStar Clean Energy,” the non-regulated clean energy developer and independent power production subsidiary CMS plans to split apart in the coming quarters. CMS has agreed to or closed on sales for more than 35% of NorthStar’s assets, with the majority of the remainder in advanced negotiations with buyers as CMS works to wrap up the restructuring by the end of the year, the company said. CMS previously said it would retain some NorthStar assets in Michigan, including two gas-fired peaker plants, a 770-MW waste- and gas-fired cogeneration plant and about 500 MW of solar. The restructuring will allow CMS Energy to reallocate at least $500 million from NorthStar into its utility business, the company said this week. Maddipati said that estimate may be conservative. “I would be disappointed if we are not above the $500 million funding benefit,” Maddipati said. J.H. Campbell update Neither Rochow nor Maddipati on Tuesday mentioned the J.H. Campbell Generating Complex, a roughly 1,420-MW coal-fired power plant that Consumers has continued to run at the U.S. Department of Energy’s behest past its planned May 2025 retirement date. But in a required securities filing this week, CMS Energy said it has spent $303 million through the end of September to operate the plant under DOE’s Section 202(c) authority after accounting for $344 million in market revenues from the Midcontinent Independent System Operator. CMS said it plans to petition the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to recover the entire net cost to run Campbell. Requests to recover costs incurred during the first three 90-day order periods remain pending before the FERC, it said. In September, a federal appeals court invalidated DOE’s original emergency order on Campbell, saying it improperly usurped states’ regulatory authority. This week, CMS Energy said it expected DOE to appeal the ruling, which came in response to a suit brought by environmental groups and attorneys general for Michigan and two other MISO states. Pending rate case and planned system investments In a rate case pending before the Michigan Public Service Commission, Consumers Energy downwardly revised its requested revenue requirement from $456 million to $443 million. It is seeking a 51.75% equity ratio while keeping its requested return on equity steady at 10.25%. It expects a final order from the MPSC by early April 2027. In a separate investor presentation earlier this month, CMS Energy said it plans to invest more than $17 billion in its electric system and boost its companywide rate base for both gas and electric by about 10.5% annually over the next five years. Over the longer term, Consumers’ most recent integrated resource plan — filed this year — envisions adding nearly 16 GW of clean energy resources and 4.1 GW of batteries by 2040, putting the company on track to achieve Michigan’s energy law target of 100% clean energy by 2040, it said.

artigo.texto: Em 29 de outubro, a polícia finlandesa anunciou uma investigação sobre desmatamento e problemas de drenagem na área onde o Google está construindo um centro de dados perto da cidade de Muhos. Segundo as autoridades, a Tuike Finland, subsidiária da Alphabet (Google), é suspeita de cortar árvores e instalar um sistema de drenagem sem concluir as avaliações de impacto ambiental necessárias. A inspetora-chefe Kari Pakanen afirmou que a polícia está verificando se essas atividades violam as leis de recursos hídricos e causam danos ambientais. Caso seja constatada a violação, a empresa poderá ser multada. Inspeções preliminares revelaram diversas deficiências no sistema de drenagem e nas práticas de gestão de água na área do projeto. A investigação deverá continuar até 2027. Anteriormente, em 6 de outubro, a agência finlandesa de monitoramento (LVV) solicitou ao Google que suspendesse as atividades preparatórias que poderiam potencialmente alterar o meio ambiente em Muhos e em outro local. Um representante do Google afirmou que a empresa cooperará com a polícia e as autoridades competentes e prometeu cumprir as normas ambientais. O incidente ocorreu no mesmo dia em que o Google anunciou planos de investir US$ 15 bilhões em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial ( IA ) na Finlândia, incluindo centros de dados, melhorias na rede elétrica e desenvolvimento de energia limpa. A Finlândia está atraindo investimentos significativos em data centers graças ao seu clima frio e fontes de eletricidade de baixo carbono. No entanto, de acordo com a operadora da rede elétrica, Fingrid, a demanda de eletricidade do país poderá aumentar em até 40% nos próximos anos, caso todos os projetos que já concordaram em se conectar à rede sejam implementados.

artigo.texto: On Monday, Goleta’s Planning Commission voted to hit pause on a proposal to build a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at a site on Viajero Drive operated by Scale Microgrids, LLC, located across Hollister Avenue from Ellwood Mesa. Despite the project being green lit by Goleta city staff after the proposal passed an initial environmental review, the commission voted to delay the project until a citywide study on appropriate locations for utility-scale battery storage facilities is completed in April of 2027. The initial study for the proposal found that the Greenbark 30 Battery Energy Storage Project has no significant impact on “biological resources, cultural resources, geology and soils, hazards and hazardous materials, transportation, and noise,” said Goleta Staff Planner Travis Lee. As Goleta and other cities across the state make the switch to renewables, the issue becomes energy storage. Unlike coal, which can be stored until burned, renewable energy generated by wind and solar have to be stored in batteries so that it can be used when needed. Building battery centers, like the proposed Greenbark BESS, adds storage capacity to Goleta’s grid, and in turn, allows for more input from renewable sources. This proposal would add up to 120 megawatt hours of storage to the grid, helping Goleta reach its goal of powering the city with 100 percent renewable energy by 2030. The proposed 2.1-acre Greenbark BESS facility would house 36 Tesla Megapack 2 XL units, which have a combined output power of 30 megawatts and are able to store up to 120 megawatt-hours of electricity. In layman’s terms, the center is able to power 18,000 to 30,000 Goleta homes for four hours. The batteries within the Tesla Megapacks are made of lithium-iron phosphate, which is a battery chemistry that is more stable and has a higher ignition temperature than nickel manganese cobalt batteries used at older battery centers, like the Moss Landing BESS facility that has seen fires in 2025 and September 2026. “Nickel magnesium cobalt batteries have a much lower threshold for ignition at closer to 180 degrees, where the lithium ion is closer to 500 degrees,” said Santa Barbara County Fire Marshal Fred Tan. Each of the 36 liquid-cooled units are self-contained and equipped with “battery monitoring and automatic shutdown systems, infrared fire detection, ventilation, fire hydrants, and enclosures designed to limit fire spread,” said Staff Planner Lee. If a fire were to occur in one of the units, the entire system could be shut down in a matter of seconds. “The battery industry has progressed rapidly in recent years for battery safety, honing in on alterations to the battery chemistry itself, the design of the units, and the regulation and oversight imposed on battery sites,” Lee said. The facility would be connected to Goleta’s energy grid though Southern California Edison’s substation located inside the Ellwood Generating Station, which directly neighbors the proposed site on Viajero Drive. There would be no need to lay additional transmission lines since the substation is located so close to the site. But the proposal has raised concerns from community members due to the proximity of the site to Westmont of Santa Barbara Assisted Living Facility and Ellwood Elementary School, citing the Moss Landing BESS fires as the root of their worries. “There are 67 disabled very elderly seniors living here, who just experienced a fire nearby in the neighborhood that spread smoke through our building,” said Westmont resident Joanne Winter, referencing a fire that broke out along Highway 101 on September 22. Due to concerns of resident safety, Winter said “we oppose this.” This battery center would not be a first for Goleta. In December 2023, the GridStor BESS center, located on Cortona Drive behind the Hilton Garden Inn, flipped the switch and started operations at twice the amount of megawatts of the proposed Viajero site. That center utilizes 44 Tesla Megapack battery units and produces an output of 60 megawatts of electricity, enough to power over 30,000 Goleta homes daily during peak hours. There have been no reported fires at the Gridstor facility. “I’ve toured the existing Goleta Energy Storage Facility on Cortona Drive. It’s twice as big as this project and three times closer to residents,” said longtime Goleta resident and Sierra Club volunteer Katie Davis. “It has zero emissions and no complaints from residents. If I lived there, I would be more worried about the proximity to the freeway and known emissions and the dangers of living near a freeway.” Goleta’s Planning Environmental Review Department is currently conducting a study that will designate sites across Goleta as suitable for utility-scale battery storage facilities, which is set to be completed in April of 2027. “We didn’t feel that we could hold up this project in order to complete that comprehensive planning effort,” said Planning & Environmental Review Director Peter Imhof. The study currently being conducted “would look at many of the same things that are being considered in the context of this project individually.” Despite Director Imhof’s comments, Commissioners Cary Penniman and Jennifer Fullerton both voted to put a pause on the project, leaving Commissioner Katie Maynard as the only vote in favor of moving it forward. For now, the vacant lot at the end of Viajero Drive will remain vacant, only with a large white board describing the proposed Greenbark 30 Battery Energy Storage Project.

artigo.texto: Defiance voters to decide charter amendment limiting data center size Citizen-led proposal on the November ballot does not ban data centers outright TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG) - Defiance voters will decide in November on a citizen-led charter amendment that places limits on the size of data centers in the city. The proposed amendment does not ban data centers outright. People on both sides of the debate want a bright future for the community, but they differ on how to get there. What the amendment would do Sonya Mavis, a local business owner, is one of the people behind the amendment. “We collected nearly 500 signatures, when we only needed 235ish,” Mavis said. “It’s just banning data centers that are over 25 megawatts within city limits,” Mavis said. Residents’ concerns Mavis said residents she spoke with voiced concerns about increased water and energy bills, along with noise. “Because of that frequency, that vibration, the hum that comes off of data centers, they don’t want that in their community,” Mavis said. Mavis said her group is not against technology. She said she agrees data centers are needed, but their size needs to be regulated. “We don’t need a data center at 400 megawatts that can power Portland, Oregon,” Mavis said. Property owner opposes amendment A local business owner is looking to bring industrial development to his 340-acre property. Bryan Keller, CEO of Keller Logistics, said the property has natural gas, some power to get started and is already zoned industrial. “I think the highest and best use for this would be a data center,” Keller said. Keller said he is against the charter amendment. He listed potential revenue to the city near the top of his reasons. “They’re writing significant checks to the schools, they’re putting money into community development,” Keller said. His land has been annexed into the city of Defiance. “We don’t have an end user yet,” Keller said. The reporter asked the city whether it has received proposals from any developers. The city said it could not comment on any proposed development that may have legal implications. How to vote A “yes” vote is for the restriction, meaning the voter is against large-scale data centers. A “no” vote means the voter would like to allow large-scale data centers. Temporary ban in effect The Defiance City Council passed a temporary ban on data centers. The moratorium went into effect in September and will stay in place for six months. Council said it needed the time to study the impact a facility would have on the community. Statement from the city A city spokesperson released the following statement to 13 Action News: “The City recognizes the public interest in data center development and its potential impact on our community. Any proposed development is subject to the City’s applicable laws, zoning regulations, and established review and approval processes. The City’s role is to evaluate development proposals in accordance with applicable law and the City’s adopted regulations, while considering relevant land-use, infrastructure, public safety, and community welfare issues. Because certain matters involving proposed development may have legal implications, the City will not comment on specific proposals or related legal issues at this time. The City will continue to follow the appropriate legal and municipal processes as these matters are considered.” Latest Local News | First Alert Weather | Crime | National | 13abc Originals Copyright 2026 WTVG.
