artigo.texto: Lais Carregosa e Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA A diretoria da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) aprovou na terça-feira (27) os editais do leilão de baterias, marcado para ser realizado em duas sessões nos dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. No entanto, o diretor-geral da reguladora, Sandoval Feitosa, disse que o cronograma pode ser adiado caso o Congresso aprove uma alteração na lei que atribui o custeio das contratações aos geradores. Atualmente, há uma proposta em discussão para incluir os consumidores na conta. “Se o Congresso Nacional mudar a lei [antes do certame], nós vamos ter que republicar o edital e vamos ter que reprogramar a sessão pública do leilão”, afirmou o diretor-geral à imprensa após reunião extraordinária da diretoria. Segundo Sandoval, caso a alteração legislativa seja feita após o leilão, seria necessária uma diretriz na lei para o tratamento do certame que já ocorreu. Se uma mudança for feita depois da homologação e da adjudicação do resultado, Sandoval explicou que os contratos seriam atos jurídicos perfeitos por terem sido firmados na vigência da lei atual, com pagamento pelos geradores. Assim, uma mudança legislativa também deveria disciplinar esse tratamento. “Ou seja, em qualquer cenário, a única certeza que a gente tem é que a ANEEL vai cumprir a lei”, disse. Preços e garantias Antes da reunião da ANEEL, o MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) enviou ofício à reguladora definindo os preços iniciais do leilão. Os valores serão de R$ 1,76 milhão por MW/ano (megawatt/ano) para o certame do dia 2 de dezembro, voltado a soluções com conteúdo local; e de R$ 1,58 milhão por MW/ano no leilão geral, de 4 de dezembro. Já as garantias financeiras a serem aportadas pelos agentes, conforme recomendação da área técnica da ANEEL, serão menores que as que foram propostas inicialmente. A faixa de referência, que era de R$ 9,8 milhões/MW, caiu para R$ 6 milhões/MW. Editais Foram aprovados por unanimidade os dois editais. O relator, diretor Gentil Nogueira, seguiu as sugestões da área técnica, adotando no edital um termo mais genérico para o pagador do encargo de contratação das baterias, diante da possibilidade de mudanças na lei para incluir os consumidores no rateio. Sandoval Feitosa afirmou que é possível o edital ficar com essa definição em aberto. De acordo com ele, a decisão foi tomada para que o edital se torne aderente à norma em elaboração pela agência, sobre o rateio do encargo de custeio das baterias. No entanto, disse que essa especificação sobre qual será a base pagadora precisará estar no contrato a ser assinado pelos vencedores após o certame. “O edital pode ficar abstrato. Agora, o contrato não. É um contrato de adesão ou CRCAP [Contrato de Potência de Reserva de Capacidade], mas você não pode deixar indeterminado quem é o responsável pelo encargo. Tem que ficar específico quem deve pagar. E a escolha de quem deve pagar foi feita pelo Legislativo, uma lei que foi sancionada pela Presidência da República”, afirmou. Em seu voto, o relator também acolheu a recomendação de permitir a participação de usinas com contratos regulados em associação às baterias. O voto também autoriza as transmissoras a participar do certame, mas deixa o tratamento das obrigações da concessão para etapas posteriores. Em parecer, a Procuradoria Federal junto à ANEEL entendeu que as concessionárias podem participar do certame desde que revertam parte da receita para a modicidade tarifária. Gentil também apontou propostas de agentes para criação de excludentes de responsabilidade em caso de atraso na conexão dos projetos ao SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional). Ele rejeitou as sugestões, mas destacou que o cronograma da temporada de acesso ao sistema de 2027 prevê um mecanismo específico para os vencedores do leilão, encurtando o processo em pelo menos dois meses. Projeto no Congresso O setor tem articulado pela aprovação do Projeto de Lei 3.716/2026 no Congresso. O texto, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), inclui os consumidores como pagadores do encargo das baterias. A proposta já teve aprovada a tramitação no regime de urgência e aguarda a designação de relator pelo presidente da Câmara, deputado Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB). Fontes têm afirmado que o governo deve apoiar a aprovação do texto, após certa resistência durante a votação da urgência.

artigo.texto: Bloomfield's zoning rules prohibit data centers and battery energy storage facilities in every zoning district, affecting an informal proposal for a nearly 1-million-square-foot facility that had been floated for the town's northwest corner. The new rules bar data centers as a principal use, an accessory use, or as part of a mixed-use development in every zone townwide, and they also prohibit battery energy storage facilities outright, according to Hartford Business Journal. The vote comes more than a year after New York-based Atlas Capital Group made an informal presentation to the town in June 2025 for a data center at 132 Griffin Road North, on a vacant 44-acre former tobacco field. The project as described to Hartford Business Journal would have included roughly 900,000 square feet of data-center space and a 127,000-square-foot substation, though a separate description on the town's own civic-alerts page characterized the conceptual plan as a 1-million-square-foot facility — the two accounts differ on the exact scale of what was pitched. Scope of the Zoning Change The prohibition applies across Bloomfield's zoning districts. The rules apply to data centers as a principal or accessory use, as well as projects that would combine them with other uses. The amendments also prohibit battery energy storage facilities. Part of a Wider Connecticut Pushback Bloomfield isn't alone. Days earlier, East Lyme's zoning commission voted unanimously to prohibit both traditional and AI data centers, along with their accessory uses, with that ban taking effect Oct. 24, as WFSB reported. Unlike the temporary moratoriums many towns have adopted, East Lyme's ban is intended to be permanent, though the underlying zoning regulations could still be changed later if officials choose. That town's commission pointed to concerns about strain on the water supply, noise from the facilities, and impacts on nearby residents. The resistance is showing up at the state level too. Connecticut currently has no large-scale AI data centers operating within its borders, according to a report from CT Public, yet critics have already zeroed in on the industry's heavy water and electricity use, warning it could drive up utility rates for residents who live nearby. State Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff has said he intends to introduce legislation creating a statewide moratorium on AI data centers when the legislature convenes next year, telling the outlet, “We need to have new legislation in the state of Connecticut that puts a moratorium on AI data centers across the state of Connecticut.” In Groton, a proposed AI data center drew resident opposition over fears about local electric rates. Tax Breaks Still on the Books The regulatory crackdown comes even as older state incentives remain in place to lure data-center investment. Connecticut lawmakers created tax breaks in 2021 aimed at attracting such projects. Qualifying developments investing at least $200 million — or $50 million in certain designated economic-development zones — may receive sales and property tax exemptions. For now, Bloomfield has decided those potential tax benefits aren't worth the tradeoff. With the amendments in place, any future data-center pitch — however it's labeled — would have to clear a zoning code that no longer leaves room for it anywhere in town.

artigo.texto: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: October 29, 2026 CONTACT: Jarice Thompson, jarice@ourfinancialsecurity.org Private Equity is Fueling the Data Center Crisis Washington, D.C. — As data center backlash sparks across the country, private equity firms are playing a significant role in fueling this growing crisis. According to a new report, “Tracing the Money,” from Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, private equity now owns or backs an estimated 20 percent to 30 percent of existing data centers. The report documents not only private equity and private credit’s existing data center firms and facilities but also their planned expansion. “Data centers’ environmental health impacts, increased utility costs, water use, and climate effects have made them a net negative across the board for everyone, except the mega-corporations that profit. As Big Tech firms are increasingly moving the expenses required for this costly buildout off their books, private equity is happily stepping in,” said Dustin Duong, senior research associate at Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. “It’s important for communities on the ground to know who is behind the massive expansion and the private equity playbook as they continue to fight back across the country.” “As they spin up the AI Bubble, Big Tech firms are pushing for ever-increasing computing power, driving the sudden boom in data center development across the country,” said Iván Cazarin, senior policy coordinator at Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. “This first of its kind report details exactly where and how Big Tech and Wall Street are joining forces in this speculative overbuild that will drive up the cost of living for everyday people.” Other key findings: - Private equity firms own or back an estimated 25 percent to 30 percent of active U.S. data centers. As of December 2025, 78 private equity firms backed an estimated 13 to 17 gigawatts (GW) of active data center capacity across 670 data centers or campuses. - Private equity is backing half of the planned data center expansion. Private equity-owned or -financed companies have announced or initiated at least another 26.8 GW of U.S. data center capacity in development, under construction, or actively planned, amounting to over half of the total 50 GW of data centers in the pipeline by 2030. - In several states, private equity is backing large portions of data center capacity and expansion. Private equity firms own one third of the active center capacity in Texas. In Arizona, private equity controls almost half of current data center capacity and one third of planned expansion in the state. In Virginia, private equity controls nearly one quarter of online capacity and over 10 percent of projects in development. - The five largest private equity firms backing data centers control nearly 20 percent of existing capacity and 30 percent of planned capacity. The five largest private equity data center owners in the United States( by total active and planned capacity) are Brookfield Asset Management, Ares Management, Blue Owl Capital, DigitalBridge, and Pantheon Ventures. The interactive map provides a detailed overview of the over 79 companies and 670 unique data center sites that were analyzed. Texas, Arizona, and Virginia are among several key states where private equity is responsible for large amounts of data center capacity and expansion. Read the full report here. ###

artigo.texto: Chinese battery manufacturer Svolt Energy has begun mass production of its new 100-kWh Dragon Armor semi-solid-state battery, marking an important step toward bringing next-generation battery technology to more electric vehicles. The new battery supports a 900-volt electrical architecture and 6C fast charging, with Svolt claiming it can add up to 500 kilometers (311 miles) of driving range in just 12 minutes. The first battery packs have rolled off the production line at Svolt’s facility in Changzhou, Jiangsu province, China. The company says multiple automakers have already selected the battery for potential vehicle applications, although the first models to receive it have not yet been officially announced. The development comes as Chinese battery manufacturers accelerate efforts to improve EV charging speeds, battery safety, and long-term durability without waiting for fully solid-state batteries to become commercially widespread. Svolt Dragon Armor Battery Promises 500 km of Range in 12 Minutes The new 100-kWh Dragon Armor battery is designed around a 900-volt high-voltage system and supports a charging rate of up to 6C. According to Svolt chairman and CEO Yang Hongxin, the system can replenish enough energy for approximately 500 km (311 miles) of driving in 12 minutes. If achieved under suitable real-world conditions, that charging performance could make long-distance electric vehicle travel more convenient by significantly reducing charging stops. However, Svolt has not disclosed the specific testing conditions behind the 12-minute charging claim. Actual charging times and the amount of range recovered will depend on factors such as the vehicle’s efficiency, battery temperature, charger output, and the battery’s charging curve. The battery also uses liquid cooling on both its upper and lower surfaces to help manage heat during high-power charging. Effective thermal management is particularly important for batteries designed to accept large amounts of energy in a short period. Semi-Solid-State Technology Targets Better Safety and Durability Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries that rely on liquid electrolytes, semi-solid-state batteries combine solid and liquid components in their electrolyte systems. This hybrid approach aims to deliver some of the potential safety and performance advantages associated with solid-state technology while retaining a more practical route to commercial production. Svolt says its new battery uses a separator transfer-printing process at the cell level. The company claims this manufacturing technology improves battery safety while supporting fast charging and a longer service life. The pack also features six layers of protective material on its underside. According to Svolt, this construction provides impact resistance three times higher than the relevant Chinese national standard. These features are intended to improve protection against physical damage, an important consideration as automakers continue to increase battery capacity and charging power. Nevertheless, the reported safety advantages remain manufacturer claims. Independent testing and additional technical details will be needed to establish how the battery performs in different crash, thermal, and charging scenarios. Svolt Claims More Than 3,000 Charging Cycles Battery longevity is another major focus of the Dragon Armor pack. Svolt says its high-speed stacking technology helps the battery achieve a cycle life exceeding 3,000 charging cycles. The company also cites a theoretical lifetime driving distance of more than 1 million kilometers (621,000 miles). Such a figure would be significant if confirmed in long-term vehicle use, particularly for drivers who cover high annual mileage and for commercial fleets that depend on battery durability. However, a battery’s cycle life does not translate directly into a guaranteed vehicle lifespan. The outcome depends on factors including the definition of a charging cycle, operating temperatures, charging habits, depth of discharge, and the conditions under which the battery is tested. Svolt has not published enough test information to independently verify its claimed lifetime performance. Which Electric Cars Will Use Svolt’s New Battery? The battery’s connection to Great Wall Motor (GWM) makes future applications within the wider Chinese automotive industry worth watching. Svolt originated as GWM’s battery business before becoming an independent company in 2018, although it has continued to maintain close commercial ties with the automaker. The Wey V8X battery-electric crossover has been mentioned as a possible early application in industry reporting, but this has not been officially confirmed by Svolt. Further announcements should clarify which vehicles will use the battery, when those models will enter production, and whether the technology will initially be limited to premium EVs or expand into more affordable segments. The manufacturer has also argued that semi-solid-state batteries could become a long-term technology rather than simply a temporary step toward fully solid-state batteries. artigo.texto: Four years ago, central Michigan was promised a $2.36 billion battery-component plant and 2,350 jobs. What’s left is roughly 270 acres of farmland and a recalled township board. The lawsuit never reached a trial; it ended in settlement talks. What Michigan put on the table The Sixth Circuit’s February opinion lays out the history. - In September 2022, Gotion Inc., the U.S. subsidiary of Chinese battery maker Gotion High-Tech, secured state grants for land, infrastructure, permitting and wetland mitigation. - Green Charter Township, Mecosta County and the City of Big Rapids added a $540 million local tax incentive package. - In July 2023, Gotion picked the site from 56 candidates. State and local incentives combined totaled $715 million. - In August 2023, the township board signed a Development Agreement promising to help Gotion obtain permits. That same month, Gotion paid $24 million for nearly 270 acres. The court noted the timing: all of this followed the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, whose tax incentives set off a wave of clean-energy manufacturing investment. How it fell apart Voters recalled the township board in November 2023. All five replacement members had campaigned on blocking the project. According to the appeals court, the new board rescinded two resolutions the project needed. When Gotion took its site plan to the county instead, the township stripped Mecosta County of its zoning authority over the township. It then threatened to sue the county if it processed the application, and the county cancelled its review. Related Articles - Florida’s School-Zone Camera Law Waived One State Radar Rule. A Judge Says It Missed Another. - Auto Loan Fraud Is the New Car Theft, and It’s Hiding in Plain Sight Gotion sued in March 2024 and won a preliminary injunction that May. The court ordered the township to honor the agreement. The injunction didn’t save the project. Gotion’s grant agreements with the state required progress on infrastructure and site development by set deadlines. On September 17, 2025, the Michigan Strategic Fund declared Gotion in default because “no Eligible Activities” had happened on the property for more than 120 consecutive days. On January 30, 2026, the state demanded the $23.7 million back. The court noted that total state funding could have reached $175 million. Gotion then admitted in its own appellate brief that the project “is no longer viable.” The Sixth Circuit dismissed the township’s appeal as moot. The court pointed out that Gotion missed the state’s deadlines even with an injunction in hand and no stay in place. Gotion’s next step was to say it would seek monetary damages from the township. How it ended That damages fight went to settlement talks. The district court docket in Gotion, Inc. v. Green Charter Township (W.D. Mich., No. 1:24-cv-00275) shows settlement conferences before Magistrate Judge Phillip J. Green on September 25 and October 2. The proceedings were stayed while the parties negotiated. On October 23, U.S. Rep. John Moolenaar, who represents the area and led opposition to the plant, issued a statement celebrating the outcome. He also conceded the financial result: Michigan taxpayers “will not receive restitution from the state subsidies Gotion refused to pay back.” The state wanted its $23.7 million back. Moolenaar says it won’t get it. Why car people should care This wasn’t an assembly plant. It was a battery-component factory, the kind of upstream supplier that makes battery materials before anyone builds a cell or a car. That supply-chain gap is a big reason EVs still cost more than gas cars of similar size, and it’s why states were willing to pay so much to fill it. Gotion shows what goes wrong when the money moves before the building does. A development agreement signed by one township board held up in court. It still couldn’t make a plant viable once the politics turned and the state’s deadlines slid past. Moolenaar’s office says his “NO GOTION” policy, which became law in 2025, was meant to keep companies like Gotion from collecting federal clean-energy incentives. If a battery maker’s economics lean on those credits, ownership questions can sink a project before anyone pours concrete. The Jeeps It Supplied Aren’t Going Anywhere. The incentives were priced for a factory, and the $23.7 million the state demanded back isn’t coming. What happens next The parties still have to file the formal settlement. The public docket shown hadn’t been updated after October 15. The terms will matter for Green Charter Township, which spent more than two years in federal court over a contract a previous board signed. Announcing a battery plant is easy. Getting one built takes a township that stays put and deadlines a company can actually hit. artigo.texto: Morgan County ballot question seeks public input on data center rules The referendum asks voters whether restrictions should be placed on data center construction and operations JACKSONVILLE, Ill. (WAND) – We’ve seen data center debates play out in county board meetings across central Illinois. However, in Morgan County, that debate is headed to the ballot box. While the results won’t be binding, county leaders said they could help guide their next steps. “The goal is just to get the people’s voice in front of our local government leaders, so that people can take it seriously, that we do care about the construction and operation of data centers in our area,” said petitioner Colleen Flinn. Flinn and Khara Koffel gathered more than 1,100 signatures to put the question on the ballot, asking whether restrictions should be implemented for data center construction and operations. “Getting 1,100-plus signatures is not a small feat. I will say that there was a lot of legwork, with people going into restaurants and into businesses. We went to concerts on the square and parades everywhere that we possibly could to get a wide variety of input from people in our county,” Koffel said. Commissioner Michael Woods emphasized that the nonbinding question asks voters whether restrictions should be implemented — not whether they support data centers. “The reality is that if the majority says yes, what that does is give us a little bit more guidance to say, ‘What kind of restrictions should we be looking at? How should we look at the impact of data centers on our county?’ If the majority says no, then that also tells us a great deal,” Woods said. The county recently extended its moratorium by six months. Voters and county leaders say the ballot question gives residents a voice in decisions about what could be built in their communities. “We have three members on our commission, so that means there’s only three people. But behind those three people is a significant amount of 30-some-thousand people that really need to have a strong voice,” Woods said. Petitioners say placing the question on the ballot highlights the importance of civic engagement and shows how many people in the area care about the issue. Copyright 2026 WAND. All rights reserved.

TeraWulf, a Maryland-based company, first announced plans in August 2025 to convert a former coal-powered plant to a data center. The local law would rewrite Lansing’s zoning code to define “cryptocurrency,” “cryptocurrency data mine,” “data center,” and “general processing.” The aforementioned land uses are not permitted under the current zoning code, so by defining these facilities, the town would effectively ban them. In response to the proposed ban, TeraWulf CEO Paul Prager wrote an Oct. 2 letter to the Town Board urging it to allow the data center project to move forward. Otherwise, the letter suggests the company would take legal action. Prager recently took to the data center’s website landing page to share additional thoughts on the ban, attempting to address what he described as misinformation he feels residents and elected officials have about the project. “Consider the facts before deciding the outcome,” Prager wrote . At the October meeting, she said she never supported the ban. “There are a lot of other things I wanted to do on the town board and I didn’t,” she said. “I don’t want to waste any more time dealing with banning data centers when we need some investment in this town.” Montague then asked the town’s attorney, Noreena Chaudari, whether they would be able to begin the November public hearing with Lansing residents who did not speak during the September meeting. artigo.texto: DeSoto County Commission fails to approve 237-acre rezoning for data center project near Arcadia More than 100 people attended a DeSoto County Commission meeting Tuesday evening to oppose a proposed data center project near Arcadia, urging commissioners to reject the plan due to concerns about its impact on the community. The DeSoto County Board of County Commissioners denied the first of two additional rezoning applications for the DCIP Group's proposed 825-acre data center project. On Tuesday, commissioners' vote to approve the application failed in a 2-2 tie on the nearly 238-acre rezoning request, which could delay the proposed development. Commissioners heard presentations from county and developer experts, plus public comment, in the more-than-six-hour meeting ending after midnight Wednesday. The project, located on East Roan Street just outside of Arcadia, involves rezoning a nearly 238-acre site and a separate 554-acre site of agricultural land. On Wednesday, commissioners are expected to consider a different, larger rezoning request for the additional 554 acres by Swisher Properties. Back in March, commissioners approved the first 34 acres of the site, which was previously a power plant. However, the two additional applications for the project have alarmed residents. "Please don't tell me that those 55+ citizens won't be affected by a data center 500 feet from their homes," said Eloise Johnson, an Arcadia resident, in a previous meeting. Former DeSoto County Commissioner John Johnson shared his concerns in August, saying, "I think the place where they want to put it is not a good place. I think the impact on too many people is too great." The DCIP Group, the developer behind the project, stated that only 10.9% of the property—roughly 100 acres—is planned for data center buildings. They say approximately 75 percent of the property will remain open land, adding that landscape buffers and setbacks will be expanded to 200 to 500 feet from surrounding neighbors. The DCIP Group has also said that existing wetlands and floodplains will continue to be preserved and protected. However, earlier this month, the planning commission raised unresolved issues, including water use, wastewater, traffic, noise, wetlands, and whether the project fits the county's long-term growth plan. The county's own report indicated that the project could affect nearby living conditions because it would operate 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, with potential noise, lighting, and visual impacts. "We just don't know what's going to happen, you know, with the water consumption, with the noise pollution," said Jennifer, an Arcadia resident. "There's so many what-ifs. And we just don't feel that this is a good thing for this town, in this county." The debate over the DCIP project is not over. On Wednesday, commissioners are expected to consider a larger rezoning request for an additional 554 acres by Swisher Properties. artigo.texto: DeSoto County data center delay: Commission fails to approve 553-acre rezoning near Arcadia Around 100 people attended a DeSoto County Commission meeting Wednesday evening as commissioners considered a 553-acre rezoning request for a proposed 825-acre data center project near Arcadia. The DeSoto County Board of County Commissioners denied a rezoning request for approximately 554 acres of agricultural land proposed for the DCIP Group's larger data center campus. The vote prevents the property, known as Swisher Property, from moving forward under the current application after commissioners tied 2-2, failing to pass a motion to approve the rezoning request. Swisher Property is located along Northeast Roan Street, across from the original 34-acre site commissioners approved for DCIP in March. The Swisher application seeks to rezone about 554 acres from agricultural land to Planned Unit Development land for a large industrial data center project. The vote came one day after commissioners deadlocked 2-2 on a separate rezoning request for nearly 238 acres of the proposed campus. That application failed to gain enough votes for approval. DCIP Group CEO Jon Brown addressed commissioners Wednesday night, less than one day after the board's 2-2 vote failed to approve the company's nearly 238-acre 3F Ranch rezoning request. "I don't know if I like the result of that last night, but it wasn't a decision made in haste," Brown said."We heard what people said last night, we heard about their concerns." "Based on that, we went back and we reflected this morning and we made some serious changes to the application," Brown said. Brown said the failed rezoning vote led the company to downsize and modify its proposal for the larger Swisher property before Wednesday's vote. Under the proposed modifications, DCIP removed a planned power-generation facility from the Swisher property, reduced the proposed building footprint and increased proposed setbacks for noise-generating technology from up to 500 feet to up to 1,000 feet from nearby homes. Together with the original 34-acre site and the 3F Ranch and Swisher applications, the DCIP concept has involved 825 acres. Residents have repeatedly raised concerns about the project's potential water use, wastewater, noise, traffic, environmental impacts and compatibility with the county's long-term growth plans. The County's Planning Commission recommended denial of the Swisher rezoning in a 4-1 vote in early October. The DCIP Group has said its plans include significant open space and buffers and that the project would be designed to address environmental and community concerns. The original 34-acre DCIP project was approved in March on the site of a former power plant. The two larger rezoning applications were exempted from the county's one-year data center moratorium and therefore continued through the normal review process. The denial prevents the 554-acre Swisher property from being rezoned for the proposed data center under the current application. artigo.texto: Cal Poly brought together local leaders and industry experts Wednesday to discuss the growing debate over data centers and their potential impact on the Central Coast. The university’s Real Estate Day featured panels on data center demand, infrastructure needs, financing, site selection and industry trends. More than 5,200 data centers currently operate in the United States, with more than 2,000 planned, according to the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. The facilities support the internet and artificial intelligence but can require significant amounts of electricity and water. A recent Gallup Poll found 70% of Americans do not want data centers in their communities. “Residents think about electricity bills; who pays for grid expansion; water use; land consumption; construction activity; generator emissions; noise; and the character of the surrounding area,” said Hamed Ghoddusi, director of Cal Poly’s Real Estate Initiative. Ghoddusi said he does not expect data centers in San Luis Obispo County but said northern Santa Barbara County could be more receptive because of resource availability, historical energy facilities and its proximity to Vandenberg Space Force Base. Speakers included San Luis Obispo County District 3 Supervisor Dawn Ortiz-Legg, San Luis Obispo Assistant City Manager Scott Collins, Cal Poly faculty and representatives from the technology, real estate and construction industries.

artigo.texto: Uma nova onda de crimes direcionados a infraestruturas de tecnologia nos Estados Unidos tem intrigado autoridades e especialistas em segurança. Quadrilhas especializadas estão combinando ataques cibernéticos, falsificação de sinais de GPS e identidades geradas por inteligência artificial para desviar caminhões carregados com equipamentos de alto valor, acumulando prejuízos superiores a US$ 100 milhões — o equivalente a cerca de R$ 534 milhões. Como funciona o golpe digital O esquema criminoso começa com a invasão de contas legítimas de corretores de frete para a publicação de ofertas falsas de transporte. Quando as transportadoras respondem aos anúncios fraudulentos, acabam acessando links maliciosos. Com o roubo de credenciais, os criminosos passam a disputar fretes reais fingindo ser empresas idôneas. O transporte da carga pode ocorrer tanto com a contratação involuntária de motoristas legítimos quanto com o uso de cúmplices que se apresentam em depósitos portando documentos falsificados com o auxílio de IA. Táticas violentas e spoofing de GPS Além das fraudes no ambiente virtual, os criminosos recorrem a abordagens físicas e manipulação tecnológica durante os trajetos. Em uma das ocorrências envolvendo US$ 13 milhões em servidores destinados ao estado da Geórgia, um veículo colidiu propositalmente contra o carro da polícia que fazia a escolta da carga, forçando a parada enquanto o caminhão continuava o percurso e desaparecia. Em outra situação, os criminosos recorreram ao spoofing de GPS para transmitir coordenadas falsas à central de monitoramento, mascarando a rota real do veículo. Nos dois episódios, os produtos não foram recuperados. Desde 2025, autoridades registraram quase duas dezenas de roubos focados nesse segmento, impulsionados pela rápida expansão dos investimentos em data centers. Alvos e destino das peças roubadas A lista de materiais visados pelas quadrilhas engloba uma grande variedade de componentes essenciais para a infraestrutura de TI. Entre os itens subtraídos estão servidores, chips de memória RAM, cabos de fibra óptica, fios de cobre, equipamentos para racks e hardwares dedicados à mineração de criptomoedas. Diferente de eletrônicos tradicionais, boa parte desse material não é comercializada em plataformas abertas de e-commerce. As investigações apontam que as peças são desmontadas e comercializadas no mercado paralelo, muitas vezes com destino certo antes mesmo da execução do crime, incluindo compradores em países que sofrem restrições de exportação por parte dos Estados Unidos, como a China.

artigo.texto: A Hyperscale Data, Inc. (AMEX:GPUS) contratou a empresa de consultoria imobiliária comercial Newmark Group para identificar potenciais financiadores para o desenvolvimento e expansão de seu campus de data center de inteligência artificial em Michigan. A nomeação foi feita por meio da Alliance Cloud Services (ACS), uma subsidiária indireta integral da Hyperscale Data, que opera as instalações em Michigan. A empresa busca financiamento de longo prazo por meio de dívida para apoiar a construção e o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura, reduzindo, ao mesmo tempo, sua dependência da emissão de novas ações ordinárias. Nenhum acordo de financiamento foi garantido, e a Hyperscale Data não divulgou o montante que pretende angariar nem os termos do empréstimo proposto. Newmark irá avaliar opções de financiamento institucional A Newmark auxiliará a Hyperscale Data na identificação de potenciais financiadores institucionais e na avaliação de possíveis acordos de financiamento para o campus de Michigan. A empresa pretende avaliar estruturas de empréstimo que reflitam as necessidades de construção do projeto, os fluxos de caixa operacionais previstos e os planos de desenvolvimento a longo prazo. As condições potenciais de financiamento serão avaliadas considerando diversos fatores, incluindo custos de juros, cronogramas de pagamento, exigências de garantia e cláusulas contratuais do credor. A Newmark já intermediou financiamentos para grandes empreendimentos de data centers, incluindo um empréstimo de construção de US$ 7,1 bilhões para um projeto de data center de IA em Abilene, Texas, em 2025. A empresa também intermediou um financiamento de US$ 975 milhões para um novo centro de dados construído no norte da Virgínia durante 2026. A Hyperscale Data afirmou que a experiência de Newmark nos mercados de capitais de infraestrutura digital foi um fator determinante em sua nomeação. Empresa busca reduzir a dependência de financiamento por meio de ações A estratégia de financiamento da Hyperscale Data visa estabelecer uma estrutura de financiamento de longo prazo para as instalações em Michigan, à medida que estas progridem nas fases de construção, comissionamento e operação comercial. A administração acredita que o financiamento institucional por meio de dívida pode proporcionar maior certeza em relação às futuras necessidades de investimento de capital e reduzir a necessidade de emissão adicional de ações. O presidente executivo, Milton “Todd” Ault III, afirmou que a nomeação representa um passo importante para garantir o financiamento adequado à dimensão do projeto. “A contratação de Newmark é um passo importante para o financiamento do nosso campus em Michigan de forma institucional e a longo prazo”, disse Ault. “A obtenção do financiamento por meio de dívida que buscamos reduziria substancialmente nossa necessidade de captar capital adicional para este projeto. Acreditamos que a vasta experiência e conhecimento da Newmark podem nos ajudar a buscar uma estrutura de financiamento que reflita a dimensão do Campus de Michigan e seu perfil de receita previsto. Nosso objetivo é financiar o desenvolvimento de forma responsável, preservando ao máximo o valor de longo prazo do projeto para nossos acionistas.” O diretor executivo, William Horne, afirmou que a empresa se concentraria em condições de financiamento que apoiassem o desenvolvimento, mantendo, ao mesmo tempo, a flexibilidade financeira. “O financiamento de dívida de longo prazo, obtido com a assistência da Newmark, reduziria nossa dependência de capital externo e proporcionaria uma base financeira mais sólida para a construção e operação do Campus de Michigan a longo prazo”, disse Horne. A empresa reconheceu que a obtenção de financiamento por meio de dívida não eliminaria necessariamente a necessidade de capital próprio adicional. O Michigan AI Campus firmou um contrato inicial com um cliente para fornecimento de 20 MW O campus de Michigan é operado pela ACS, que anteriormente firmou um contrato de prestação de serviços com um provedor de nuvem digital (neocloud) com sede na Califórnia. O acordo abrange a colocation e os serviços de centro de dados relacionados, suportando uma capacidade inicial de computação crítica de IA de 20 megawatts (MW). O contrato tem um prazo inicial de 10 anos, com duas opções de prorrogação adicionais de cinco anos disponíveis para o cliente. O cliente também detém o direito de preferência para mais 32 MW de capacidade, sujeito à disponibilidade. Caso a capacidade adicional fosse desenvolvida e utilizada, a implantação total do cliente poderia atingir 52 MW. No entanto, os 32 MW adicionais não fazem parte da capacidade inicialmente contratada, e qualquer expansão permanece sujeita às disposições contratuais e aos requisitos de desenvolvimento pertinentes. A Hyperscale Data não divulgou o valor financeiro do contrato com o cliente. Os primeiros 10 MW deverão entrar em operação em dezembro de 2026 A Hyperscale Data continua a ter como meta dezembro de 2026 para energizar os primeiros 10 MW de capacidade computacional crítica de IA em suas instalações em Michigan. A empresa espera que as atividades geradoras de receita comecem em decorrência desse marco. Atingir a meta continua dependendo da conclusão das obras de infraestrutura necessárias e dos procedimentos de comissionamento. Os acordos de financiamento propostos têm como objetivo apoiar o desenvolvimento da instalação por meio de etapas sucessivas, incluindo a expansão da infraestrutura e a implantação junto aos clientes. A administração afirmou que uma estrutura de dívida de longo prazo adequada poderia melhorar sua capacidade de planejar investimentos à medida que o campus avança em direção a operações geradoras de receita. O financiamento continua sujeito à aprovação do credor Embora a Newmark tenha sido contratada para identificar potenciais financiadores, essa contratação não constitui um compromisso de financiamento. artigo.texto: Hybrid energy storage systems, which pair two storage technologies with complementary strengths such as a battery with a supercapacitor, are widely promoted as a way to cut losses and shrink system dimensions. Yet a new systematic study suggests that the celebrated benefits of these hybrids depend far less on the storage technologies themselves than on one deceptively simple property of the electricity demand they must serve: how much the load fluctuates. The dominant predictor of both loss savings and sizing gains, the researchers report, is the variation coefficient of the load profile, defined as its standard deviation divided by its mean, with Pearson correlation coefficients of approximately 0.9. The study, published in the journal Energy Informatics by Sebastian Günther, Astrid Bensmann and Richard Hanke-Rauschenbach, tackles a long-standing weakness in the hybrid storage literature. Previous case studies had reported loss savings mostly between 0 and 30 percent, and in some cases up to 70 percent, but those numbers are hard to generalize because each study used different applications, load profiles, dispatch strategies, reference systems and modeling assumptions. More importantly, the authors argue, case studies entangle two distinct mechanisms: the way a load is distributed across two storage units during operation, and the simple fact that one technology may have intrinsically better efficiency or lower self-discharge than the other. To disentangle these effects, the team employed the concept of loss-equivalent storage units. Two storage units are loss-equivalent if they produce the same total energy losses when operated independently over a given load profile, even if one loses more energy through conversion inefficiency and the other through self-discharge. By constructing hybrid pairs from parameter tuples that are individually equivalent to a reference single storage system, any advantage the hybrid shows can be attributed to its systemic operational behavior rather than to a trivially superior parameter set. The authors had previously shown theoretically that a hybrid cannot outperform a correctly sized single storage system when both units share identical efficiency and self-discharge parameters, and that outperformance requires distinct loss characteristics; the new study confirms this empirically, with gains exactly zero when the two units are parameterized identically. The technical machinery behind the results is a linear storage model formulated as a cascaded, bi-level quadratic programming problem. Each storage unit is characterized by constant rated power limits, an energy capacity, constant charge and discharge efficiencies, and a linear self-discharge rate. Conversion losses are proportional to instantaneous storage power, while self-discharge losses are proportional to the stored energy content. For each load profile, an inner optimization finds the minimal energy and power dimensions a single storage system needs, while an outer level searches for loss-equivalent parameter tuples that achieve defined total losses with a defined ratio of efficiency-related to self-discharge-related losses. A second optimization then minimizes the operational burden of the base storage while holding the hybrid’s dimensions fixed. Dispatch is determined by offline optimization rather than a real-time energy management system, which the authors note keeps the results untangled from the behavior of specific control strategies. The scale of the parameter study is considerable. The researchers drew on 1024 distinct load profiles from the n1024 dataset of the Energy Systems Time Series Suite, a collection derived from diverse real-world energy systems including photovoltaic installations, wind farms, residential, commercial and industrial loads, microgrids, machine tools, production plants, electric vehicles and rail transport, supplemented by semi-artificial profiles generated to increase diversity. Half of the profiles change sign, representing discharge with intermittent charging events. Varying the reference efficiency across three values, the reference loss ratio across six values, the deviation between the two storage units across five levels, and the specific power pairing across nine combinations produced 829,440 distinct hybrid optimizations, more than 800,000 parameter configurations in total, each recorded alongside 119 time-series features of the load profiles. The headline finding concerns what drives the gains. Across the densely populated range of variation coefficients up to approximately 5, the relationship between load variability and relative sizing gains is well represented by a linear trend, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.89. Higher variability means stronger differences between sustained and transient demands, giving the dispatch optimizer more room to allocate operating regimes to whichever storage unit has the more favorable loss characteristic. Low-variability profiles, by contrast, offer little potential, because there is simply not enough temporal structure to exploit. The strength of the loss-parameter deviation between the two units is the second key driver: sizing gains fall linearly as the deviation ratio decreases, vanishing entirely when both units are parameterized identically. Higher total reference losses also raise gains proportionally, since losses then contribute more to the installed capacity needed to meet the same load, but the internal composition of those losses, whether they stem from self-discharge or conversion inefficiency, turns out not to matter, and neither does the specific power pairing of the two units under ideal dispatch. Here the study delivers its most sobering practical message. artigo.texto: Bateria Gen6 da BMW ganha prêmio de inovação em tecnologia na China Tecnologia Gen6 equipa a linha Neue Klasse com arquitetura de 800 volts, carregamento bidirecional e ganho de até 30% em autonomia e velocidade de recarga O Grupo BMW foi reconhecido com o prêmio "Tecnologia Inovadora Global de Veículos de Nova Energia" durante o Congresso Mundial de Veículos de Nova Energia de 2026, realizado na China. A honraria premiou as inovações da sexta geração (Gen6) de baterias de alta tensão da montadora alemã, que se tornou a única fabricante automotiva estrangeira a receber a distinção no evento. A tecnologia serve como base técnica para a linha Neue Klasse, nova família de veículos 100% elétricos da marca alemã. A transição da quinta para a sexta geração da arquitetura eDrive envolveu o registro de mais de 500 registros de patente pelo grupo automotivo. "Ele confirma nossa abordagem de longo prazo, que combina inovação tecnológica com os mais altos padrões de qualidade e segurança. Com a Neue Klasse, estamos estabelecendo novos padrões nessa área", afirmou Jochen Goller, membro do Conselho de Administração da BMW AG. Células cilíndricas e arquitetura de 800 V Desenvolvida sobre uma arquitetura elétrica de 800 volts, a bateria Gen6 adota células cilíndricas com cátodo de alto teor de níquel e invólucro estrutural de aço. O conjunto elimina a necessidade de módulos intermediários — conceito conhecido como cell-to-pack —, permitindo que as células sejam integradas diretamente à carcaça do equipamento para elevar a densidade energética no mesmo espaço de instalação. Segundo dados da fabricante, o formato garante um ganho de densidade de energia superior a 20% em comparação à geração anterior, proporcionando um incremento de até 30% na autonomia do veículo e na velocidade de recarga. O sistema também foi projetado para permitir carregamento bidirecional (fornecendo energia da bateria de volta à rede ou a outros dispositivos) e suporte a infraestruturas de recarga de 400 V e 800 V. O gerenciamento do fluxo de energia e dos dados da bateria é realizado pela unidade de controle Energy Master, sistema com hardware e software desenvolvidos internamente pela própria BMW e instalado diretamente no conjunto da bateria de alta tensão. Produção global e estratégia industrial A revelação do prêmio ocorre em paralelo à consolidação da rede global de produção do componente. A BMW deu início à fabricação em série das baterias Gen6 no complexo de Shenyang, na China, que se somou às unidades de Debrecen (Hungria) e Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Alemanha). As fábricas de Woodruff (Estados Unidos) e San Luis Potosí (México) estão programadas para iniciar a montagem em série da tecnologia nas próximas etapas de expansão da rede. A estratégia industrial da montadora prevê a instalação das unidades de montagem de baterias próximas às linhas de produção dos veículos elétricos (conceito "local for local"), visando reduzir distâncias de transporte, mitigar gargalos de suprimento e padronizar o controle de qualidade por meio de inteligência artificial e inspeções automatizadas em tempo real.

artigo.texto: San Diego’s Congressional Democrats announced that they’ll introduce legislation to require local support of a controversial data center before it could be built on federal land downtown. Right now, San Diego definitely does not support such a project. Voice of San Diego revealed earlier this month that Manchester Financial Group was mulling a 400-megawatt data center on Navy land called NAVWAR. That triggered outrage from the community and the San Diego City Council passed an emergency ban on data centers on Tuesday (though that ban wouldn’t apply to federal land). During the vote, Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera called on Congress to help the city prevent the data center from coming to town. By Thursday, Reps. Sara Jacobs, Scott Peters, Mike Levin and Juan Vargas announced their bill. “The key thing for me is that wherever data centers are going, local communities should have a say,” Jacobs said. The Navy selected Manchester to build the military a new command center building in exchange for permission to redevelop the rest of the 70-acre site. Back in 2024, Manchester pitched plans to build thousands of apartments – possibly for military families or veterans – hotels and retail. Jacobs, who serves on the House Armed Services Committee, said the bill would only apply to the NAVWAR site. Congress returns for several weeks before the holidays after the midterms. If the bill doesn’t make it before recess and the new Congress is installed, Jacobs said she’ll attempt to introduce it in the next National Defense Authorization Act. That’s a yearly federal law that sets the budget and policies for the Department of Defense. President Donald Trump wants more data center development and signed an executive order to build them faster, especially on military land. Jacobs said that may not matter. “Politics on data centers in general has changed so dramatically that Republicans and Democrats both recognize the need for local support on these projects,” Jacobs said.

artigo.texto: South African commercial and industrial businesses are rethinking how they manage their energy costs. Instead of relying on solar panels alone, more companies are combining on-site solar PV, battery storage under a capable control system, and wheeled renewable energy from wind and solar farms. Wheeling lets a business buy energy generated elsewhere and have it credited to its facility through the existing grid. The goal is simple: lower the cost of every kilowatt-hour the facility consumes, with the added assurance that operations keep running when the grid fails. For years, the main concern for engineers and plant managers was keeping the lights on during load shedding or grid faults. That conversation has moved on. Now the bigger question is how to combine on-site solar with external renewable energy to get meaningful cost savings, not just backup power. Rooftops run out of space before demand runs out Most facilities that install solar panels quickly hit a ceiling. Even a factory or warehouse that covers its entire roof and all its available land with panels usually can't generate enough energy to meet its total annual electricity consumption. Solar might cover demand around midday, but across a full year, on-site solar rarely offsets more than about 30% of a facility's total electricity use, depending on the load profile. This is where wheeling comes in. Wheeling allows a business to buy renewable electricity from a wind or solar farm elsewhere in the country. It is a contractual and metering arrangement: the generator feeds energy into the grid, and that energy is credited against the facility's consumption, net of wheeling charges. It largely removes the rooftop constraint, although wheeling is currently most straightforward on the Eskom network and in a growing number of wheeling-ready municipalities. Wind is a particularly useful partner for solar in this setup. Wind farms often generate at night and during other times when solar isn't producing, which fills the gaps in a facility's renewable supply. Wind is not optional in this picture: it is what carries a facility's renewable offset past the solar ceiling. As a general example, a mix of roughly one-third solar and two-thirds wind typically gives a more stable renewable supply across the year than solar-heavy combinations, and can lift renewable electricity use from around 30% to as much as 80%. Batteries keep everything running smoothly Battery storage is what ties this all together. When on-site solar and grid supply, including wheeled energy, both feed a facility, the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) control system manages the interaction between them. It does more than switch between sources: it optimises behind-the-meter solar consumption and shifts energy use across time-of-use tariff periods, which compounds the savings that wheeling already delivers. The BESS needs to be sized correctly for the job: the inverter should be rated to carry the facility's full electrical load the instant the grid drops out, and the battery should hold enough energy to supply roughly two hours of the facility's load during peak tariff periods. During the load-shedding years, sizing a battery for essential loads only was common in homes and small commercial sites, but large operations needed full business continuity and never really had that option. Today, with the grid more stable, most large commercial and industrial battery systems in South Africa are justified primarily on time-of-use arbitrage, with backup as the built-in insurance. A battery is a significant capital investment with a finite cycle life, which is exactly why the business case has to be built on daily tariff savings rather than on the occasional outage. Wheeled energy can also make charging the battery cheaper, but this depends heavily on how the wheeling power purchase agreement (PPA) is priced. Where the PPA is structured at a discount to the Eskom wholesale tariff across all tariff periods, every kilowatt-hour used to charge the BESS costs less than it otherwise would, which improves the economics of time-of-use arbitrage even further. A flat-rate PPA, by contrast, can end up more expensive than the wholesale tariff during off-peak periods, which is exactly when a battery is typically charged. The pricing structure of the wheeling agreement is therefore not a side issue: it determines whether wheeled energy strengthens or weakens the battery business case. The bigger picture Solar was never going to solve the problem on its own, and the problem is no longer just keeping the lights on. It is the cost of every kilowatt-hour a facility consumes. For South African businesses serious about cutting that cost, the real opportunity lies in combining what they can generate on site with what they can bring in from elsewhere, and using a well-controlled battery system to make it all work together. Henri van Eetveldt, Head of Business Development at EXSA. **The views expressed do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Media Group.

Featured products include the AOZ73216QI and AOZ73104QI controllers and the AOZ57011QI and AOZ51316QI Dual Smart Power Stages, which improve reliability for high-current GPUs and SoCs in AI data centers. AI Data Center: AOS’ AI data center portfolio now includes AlphaSGT™ MOSFETs, αSiC, and GaN products for hot-swap, 48V/54V, and emerging 800VDC power architectures. These devices enable high-density DC/DC and AC/DC conversion with improved thermal performance and ultra-low switching losses in compact, cooling-efficient designs for AI servers and accelerators. New products offer double-sided cooling, efficient high-voltage conversion, high-frequency power delivery, and the ruggedness needed to meet reliability and efficiency requirements in demanding AI factory environments. Industrial Power: AOS’ latest MOSFETs and motor driver ICs are designed for BLDC motor applications ranging from power tools and outdoor equipment to e-mobility systems. The expanded portfolio features low-loss MOSFETs in a broad range of robust power packages, including DFN5x6, TOLL, GLPAK™, and GTPAK™ with topside cooling. artigo.texto: FORT WAYNE — The seemingly never-ending requests by the Google Data Center, 5801 Adams Center Road, for more generators and more land compelled the Protect Allen County Coalition (PACC) to act. On Oct. 25, PACC hosted a backyard community gathering near the giant data center. The official nonviolent and peaceful event was titled: “Not at Our Expense: Residents Fight for Clean Air, Protection of Local Lands, and Economic Stability.” Organizers shared Google updates, and residents shared their concerns. “Today’s community gathering is in direct response to Google’s new permit application for 228 additional diesel generators that they’d like on site,” Danielle Doepke, PACC organizer, said. Additionally, the destruction of wetlands also concerned the group. “We also have evidence of illegal destruction of wetlands violating an Endangered Species Act," Doepke said. PACC also had ongoing concerns about Google communications, transparency, and respect for the neighborhood. “We’ve had three years of very little communication and transparency from Google as well as from our local and state representatives,” Doepke said. “We’re hoping to get together with neighbors and the people who have been most directly impacted by Google’s presence in Allen County. We want to hear from them about what their experience has been,” she said. Organizers set up several tables and asked attendees to share their concerns and needs. The tables included one that was set up for residents to share what they wanted Google and various municipal representatives to know about their concerns. For example, Doepke cited both a data center moratorium and a local review commission that could have addressed resident concerns if both of the resolutions had not been recently shot down by a majority of Fort Wayne City Council members. Still another table was set up to recruit volunteers to help organizers moving forward on data center issues and other concerns. “There’s been an announcement of a potential nuclear facility coming to New Haven. And (talk of) an AEP transmission line. There is a lot coming at us all at once. So, that is a part of the reason we are here today. We want to stay connected and be able to talk about what is happening around us,” Doepke said. Back-to-back Neighbors The backyard chosen to host the gathering was a 1-acre property that backs up to the Google Data Center. A chain-link fence put up by the homeowner years ago and a new split rail fence installed by Google are all that separate the two properties. According to several neighbors living with the Google Data Center in your backyard is challenging. For example, currently, two giant red cranes on the data center campus dominate the sky-blue view. The high cranes contrast with the underground burrows that groundhogs and moles are carving throughout once inviting neighboring green lawns. According to homeowners Sue and Barry Dibble, the nearby construction and other land-use disruptions force moles and groundhogs into their backyard and other neighboring yards. The animals then create many underground tunnels that cause the grassy surface to become soft, squishy, and difficult to walk on safely. Both the homeowners and the event organizers cautioned attendees to be very careful and not to walk alone toward the fences separating the properties due to the unstable ground. To stay or to go Meanwhile, concerns about the environment and air pollution are top of mind for many. Some residents wonder about selling their respective properties while others dig their heels in and are determined to stay. For example, when asked what her most pressing concern was, homeowner Sue Dibble had a list of concerns. “I would say the air pollution, the noise, and the traffic. And I am not selling my house. So, I am really worried about them trying to take it,” she said. “My dad built this house in the 1950s,” she said. “It’s a homestead,” her husband, Barry Dibble, said. Likewise, a nearby neighbor is also concerned about the environment and what to do with her home. “My biggest concern is the environment. I have asthma and I am sure a lot of other people have health issues where the air quality is really going to make a big impact,” Amanda Scheitlin said. “I would love to move because I can’t imagine living with this for the rest of my life. I could see myself moving, but I do not have plans to move at this time,” she said. Respect and responsibility The community gathering highlighted the residents' desire that the nearby AI industry make environmentally responsible decisions and be a good neighbor. Scheitlin, who lives within a mile of the data center, said she wishes it would have been built somewhere else. “But now that they’re here, they should take responsibility for the environmental impact that they’re causing,” Scheitlin said. “They should have thought this through and did all the safeguards for the impact that it was going to make on the people and the animals. On our environment, and our wetlands,” she said. Meanwhile, Sue Dibble is looking for respect. “I want them to start paying respect to the people that live out here. I mean, it’s horrible. They pull out in front of you … the traffic is horrible. The dump trucks coming up and down constantly, the dirt is flying everywhere, and you normally can’t leave your windows open,” she said. Residents struggle with lights and noise Besides the cranes, and a risky trek across the lawn, three lights shine in the bedroom windows at night, Sue Dibble said. Additionally, she and others said they hear the humming during the week and on Saturdays. “I don’t know what it is. It comes all night long. It’s just a humming. I don’t know what’s causing it,” Scheitlin said. And then there’s the trucks According to Barry Dibble, truck traffic around his home is more than a little challenging. He shared several encounters. artigo.texto: Planning commission considering preemptive restrictions on data centers DRESDEN, Tenn. (WBBJ) - The Dresden Municipal-Regional Planning Commission met Thursday to continue discussing the proposed zoning regulations for data centers and hyperscale data centers within the city limits. Staff planner Donny Bunton presented the proposal to amend Dresden’s zoning regulations. “He had made similar recommendations to, I think he said today, 14 or 15 of the cities he deals with, and so he brought us a proposed ordinance that he thought we should look over,” said Tommy Moore, planning commission chairman. The planning commission proposed adopting zoning regulations that would be more restrictive than what Dresden already has. The proposed amendment to the Dresden municipal zoning ordinance adds definitions of data centers and hyperscale data centers, where they would be allowed, minimum lot sizes, sound and distance restrictions and more. “Now we’ve actually been studying for about three months and the mayor actually made some changes in the way the ordinance looked, but also added a few things that we considered today,” said Moore. If passed, the following would be required: - Data centers and hyperscale data centers will only be allowed in M-2 “heavy industrial” districts - A lot size of at least three acres, or 20 acres for a hyperscale center - A maximum build height of 90 feet, or 150 feet for a hyperscale center - A minimum distance from residential dwellings of 500 feet, or 1,000 feet for a hyperscale center - Setback 25 feet from property lines, or 100 feet away for a hyperscale center. - A noise level limit of 60 decibels measured from any nearby residential dwelling, roughly the volume of normal conversation - Mandatory electrical demand reduction during system stress “We’ve talked with the Weakley County Municipal Electric System, we’ve talked to the city public works director just to see what things we should be dealing with from their perspective,” said Moore. This comes as data center plans in the area have run into trouble in the planning stage. Gibson County Commissioner Jeff Morris confirmed that a data center proposed near Milan is no longer on the Gibson County Commission’s docket. The landowners withdrew from the deal, so it will not be on the agenda for the commission’s next meeting Nov. 9. Copyright 2026 WBBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Retiree Eileen Castle hasn't been able to enjoy her backyard since a data center moved in next door in Lowell, Massachusetts, bringing noise, fumes, dust and water mist. But a few streets away, contractor Louis Haas is grateful to Markley, the company running the facility, for redeveloping an abandoned site he says was rife with drug use. Dubbed "the Dungeon" by some locals for the imposing black silhouette it casts over a residential neighborhood of this old milling city, those opposing views encapsulate how data centers are polarizing communities across the United States. Republican-governed states, with their looser regulations, host most of the country's current AI build-out. But in liberal-leaning New England, some feel betrayed by their elected representatives, while others fear being left behind if the industry is curbed. - 'Nothing but noise' - Over the din of construction behind a spiked fence, Castle, 82, told AFP her great-great-grandparents bought the property. But since the data center moved into a disused pasta factory a decade ago, "We have had nothing but noise. We have dust, dirt. We have all kinds of mist" from the adjoining cooling towers, which she fears could carry Legionnaires' disease. Noxious fumes made a long interview outdoors impossible, and she lamented that her grandchildren can no longer swim in her small pool. "I think every once in a while that maybe I should sell my house," she says, but adds her property value has plummeted. "The Markley Group serves more than 600 clients in Massachusetts and connects the digital infrastructure that powers our economy, our schools, and the everyday needs of our community," Markley Group CEO Jeff Markley said in a statement to AFP. The company said its backup diesel generators run only for five minute tests each week and, thanks to abatement efforts, produce "about 44 decibels of sound, quieter than a soft conversation three feet away." It said it tests its water twice a year for Legionnaires', and has planted 2,000 trees. In 2015, the city council gave Markley a 20-year property and personal property tax break estimated at $77 million, the Lowell Sun newspaper reported at the time. Enthusiasm has since cooled. In March, the council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium on construction and expansion of commercial data centers, though Markley's 352,000-square-foot site was grandfathered in. Residents represented by the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) and others have sued to challenge its expansion, which included increasing the number of generators to 27, and won a temporary injunction in August. CLF attorney Adam Reynolds told AFP that it is the "compounding effect of pollution that's really significant" in a historically industrial area. - Community divisions - Markley has supporters. Haas, 50, who supplies coffee to a major tech company, said the boom had been good to contractors like him. "I'm a big liberal, I'm a Democrat. But I'm also pro-jobs and pro-economy," he told AFP. Markley said it employs more than 100 full-time staff in Lowell, a third of them local. On top of that, over 100 unionized trades workers work on campus. Another backer, Sarah Bibeau, a 43-year-old single mother of two who works in the defense sector, told AFP the company had been "kind and considerate," fixing roads and offering favors ranging from yard work to free Red Sox tickets. Detractors include Jake Fortes, a 44-year-old travel agent who founded the group "Honest Future for Lowell" and whose property sits on the fence line. "We're getting steamrolled by this company. So some of us have taken it to task," Fortes told AFP. Like Castle, he feels let down by Democrats, including state Governor Maura Healey -- who signed a sales tax break for data centers into law but then paused new applications this year, a reversal that illustrates the party's dilemma. Luz Marte, a 38-year-old lab technician, bought her house a year ago, without realizing the site was a data center. "It sounds very loud, like an airplane is going to take off," she told AFP as her three-year-old son played. Her home insurer recently moved to triple her premium, which she believes is linked to Markley buying a building even closer to her property. "This is a home I bought for my son, to grow up, feel alive, and have a future," she said. "Now I'm doubting that idea."

artigo.texto: Emerald Battery Labs to supply a 60-kWh sodium-ion storage system to Issaquah The Seattle-based manufacturer is partnering with the City of Issaquah to equip Pickering Barn with a sodium-ion system. A $671,000 grant partly funds the resilience project, which must obtain several UL certifications. Emerald Battery Labs, a Seattle-based manufacturer of sodium-ion batteries, has announced a partnership with the City of Issaquah, Washington. The company will supply a battery energy storage system (BESS) for the city's resiliency project at Pickering Barn. The municipal deployment adds to other U.S. projects, such as the two 10 MW plants completed by Uriel Renovables or the storage contracts won by Flatiron Energy in the Bronx. The project is supported in part by a $671,000 grant from TransAlta Centralia Generation LLC. A site designated as a resilience hub Pickering Barn is a historic landmark in the center of Issaquah. It is a designated Resilience Hub site under the city's initiative of the same name. According to the city, it provides warming and cooling centers, emergency services and community support during grid outages or natural disasters. The city's Solar + Storage Microgrid Feasibility Study identified the site as a priority for a community resilience microgrid. Earlier this year, the city completed installation of a 64.9 kW-DC solar photovoltaic array as the first step of the project. Integrating a storage system is required to let the facility "island" from the grid and support critical loads during extended outages. A 60-kWh sodium-ion system The grant will allow Emerald to develop and deploy a 60-kWh sodium-ion system, paired with the existing solar and hardware systems. The company says it will finalize the system design and obtain UL 9540, UL 9540A and UL 1973 certifications. It will also support the city through permitting and procurement. Its work will focus on sodium-ion integration, energy management, battery management system communication protocols and system-level safety validation. According to Emerald, sodium-ion chemistry offers improved thermal stability, improved safety, longer cycle life and no cobalt or lithium dependency. The company says a certified product at this scale would open a new segment of stationary storage, notably for resilience hubs, microgrids and backup power in the Pacific Northwest. Statements from officials "Issaquah is committed to investing in clean energy that also strengthens our community's resilience," said Mayor Mark Mullet. He said pairing solar power with battery storage at Pickering Barn will help keep essential services available during power outages while advancing the city's climate goals. David Bell, co-founder and CEO of Emerald Battery Labs, says sodium-ion batteries are more sustainable than lead-acid and safer than lithium-ion. He adds that they can be produced from abundant, low-cost materials sourced in the United States. In his view, Pickering Barn will show that sodium-ion systems can meet or exceed the safety, cost and performance standards required for municipal deployment. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 % A site already engaged in energy efficiency Pickering Barn has stood for more than 110 years. The city installed heat pumps there in 2025 and solar panels in 2026. It says these projects improve energy efficiency, generate clean electricity, help lower municipal energy costs and serve as an educational resource. The site hosts a weekly Farmers Market from May through October and welcomes more than 37,000 visitors a year, including 264 events in 2025. In 2023, the U.S. Green Building Council awarded Issaquah LEED Gold certification. Issaquah is the first city in Washington state to achieve it, and one of only five LEED-certified communities statewide.

artigo.texto: New Scotland residents packed a special Town Board meeting Wednesday night to demand stricter rules for battery energy storage systems, arguing the town's current law lets the facilities sit far too close to homes. Under existing regulations, battery storage systems can be built in residential zones of seven acres or more, as near as 135 feet from a property line — a distance several residents said leaves them exposed to fire and toxic gas risks. The pushback, first detailed by NEWS10 ABC, centers on a push to rewrite the town's battery-storage law so facilities are confined to industrial zones rather than allowed near residential property. Stacey DiMura, a New Scotland resident and member of the group Not In Our BESS-t Interest, told the board the systems should be kept well beyond 135 feet from homes. Residents at the meeting characterized battery energy storage systems as too loud and too dangerous to sit so close to where people live. Fire Risk and Gas Concerns Take Center Stage Much of Wednesday's discussion focused on what happens when something goes wrong inside a battery storage unit. The facilities store energy and release it back into the grid when demand is high, but the board acknowledged that lithium-ion batteries packed into large containers can release poisonous gas if they catch fire — and that such fires cannot be extinguished with water, per the same NEWS10 report. New York State recommends an evacuation zone of at least 300 feet around these systems. Town board member Dan Leinung said that if New Scotland imposes its own setback requirement, it would likely be significantly greater than that 300-foot state recommendation. The board signaled it is open to considering changes that would move battery systems farther from houses than current law allows. The Wormer Road Project in Limbo The debate comes as a specific project remains stalled. Massachusetts-based New Leaf Energy has proposed a five-megawatt battery energy storage system on Wormer Road in New Scotland. The company has said its proposal meets the 2025 New York State Fire Code, which it described as the country's most sophisticated fire code, according to NEWS10's report. Accounts differ on why the project is currently paused. NEWS10 reported the proposal is on hold for at least a few months pending a decision by the Planning Board, while The Altamont Enterprise reported the hold stems from New Leaf Energy's search for a viable water source to serve the site. The two outlets also differ on the project's exact address, with NEWS10 and other reporting citing Wormer Road generally, the Enterprise identifying the site as 37 Wormer Road on land owned by a town councilman, and the Daily Gazette identifying it as 39 Wormer Road, where New Leaf is seeking a special-use permit to build the system using Tesla Megapack 2XL units. New Scotland Weighs Its Options Without a Statewide Rulebook New Scotland isn't alone in grappling with these questions. The Altamont Enterprise reported that residents at the special session pointed to Guilderland, a draft law in Bethlehem limiting facilities to industrial zones, and the town of Tonawanda in western New York, which adopted its own battery storage law in March 2024. New York's statewide BESS guidelines currently include two tiers of regulation, though some municipalities like Tonawanda have created a third tier of their own, per the Enterprise. That patchwork approach reflects a broader tension described by Spectrum News: New Scotland is weighing the state's clean-energy goals against neighborhood safety concerns with no statewide rulebook yet in place to guide the decision. Supporters of battery storage, including developers and officials quoted by the Times Union, describe the systems as a tool to support and balance the electric grid rather than a neighborhood hazard. New Scotland has already granted at least one such project approval elsewhere in town. RIC Development LLC won permit approval for a five-megawatt facility at 1543 Indian Fields Road in Feura Bush, according to the Daily Gazette, with the Planning Board attaching 45 conditions covering emergency planning, landscaping, lighting and fire-protection measures. Town Officials Say They're Listening New Scotland Town Supervisor Douglas LaGrange told residents it was good to hear their research and suggestions during Wednesday's session. Leinung said the board would review what residents brought forward and determine what makes sense for the town going forward, though no changes to the law have yet been adopted and the outcome of Wednesday's special meeting was not immediately resolved.
