artigo.texto: Cushman & Wakefield Expands Southwest Data Center Platform with Returning Industry Veteran Mark Bauer and Team NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 29, 2026-- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK) has strengthened its data center capabilities with the addition of specialized advisory experts led by Mark Bauer, an industry veteran with nearly three decades of experience in data center real estate and digital infrastructure strategy. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261029885722/en/ Mark Bauer As Executive Vice Chairman, Bauer joins Cushman & Wakefield’s Phoenix office with Managing Director Clark Bauer, Senior Associate Valeria Galindo, and Brokerage Specialist Bridgette Kiefer, bringing together a team focused on serving data center tenants, landlords, developers, investors, and operators. The team specializes in multi-tenant data centers and advises clients on leasing, acquisition, investment, development and land transactions. Their collective experience spans work with Fortune 500 companies, hyperscale and enterprise data center operators, as well as many of the industry's leading developers. Leveraging deep technical knowledge and longstanding industry relationships, the team provides strategic guidance across the full lifecycle of data center projects and digital infrastructure portfolios. “As the data center sector continues to play a critical role in the digital economy, we are excited to welcome a team with such impressive experience and market credibility,” said Bryon Carney, Managing Principal for Cushman & Wakefield in Phoenix. “Their expertise expands our capabilities in a key growth area and reinforces our commitment to delivering best-in-class solutions for clients. We look forward to the impact they will bring and the continued success we will achieve together.” Mark Bauer’s data center career began at Cushman & Wakefield in the late 1990s, where he launched the firm's original Southwest data center platform. He later built up CBRE’s data center platform before joining JLL, where he consistently ranked in the top 2% of brokers globally for deal volume. Throughout a career spanning more than 28 years, focused exclusively on the data center and colocation industry, Bauer has negotiated more than $12 billion in transaction consideration and facilitated over 25 million square feet of transactions. His expertise includes advising tenants, landlords, buyers and sellers on complex leasing, investment, acquisition and development assignments. He also serves as a high-level consultant to enterprise clients, data center developers, and operators on a global scale, helping them optimize their digital infrastructure strategies and portfolios. Supporting the platform is Clark Bauer, who specializes in data center site selection and land development, and has experience advising developers, hyperscale users and enterprise tenants on site strategy, land acquisition and tenant representation assignments. Galindo supports clients in data center leasing, site selection, land acquisition, disposition and agency representation, and Kiefer supports transactions by managing site selection research, market analysis, and deal execution from initial materials through closing. “I’m extremely excited to return to Cushman & Wakefield with a deeply experienced and well-connected team that’s hyper-focused on data centers,” said Mark Bauer. “In this market, demand is driven less by location than by what a site can deliver: reliable power, municipal support, and a developing workforce. Sites that combine smart development with energy generation are positioned to become high-demand assets. Our team has the expertise to identify, secure, and deliver on all three.” About Cushman & Wakefield: Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK) is a leading global commercial real estate services firm for occupiers and investors with approximately 53,000 employees in over 350 offices and nearly 60 countries. In 2025, the firm reported revenue of $10.3 billion across its core service lines of Services, Leasing, Capital markets, and Valuation and other. Built around the belief that Better never settles, the firm receives numerous industry and business accolades for its award-winning culture. artigo.texto: NIPSCO to Deliver $57.5 Million in Savings to Electric Customers From Data Center Development - Average residential electric customer expected to receive approximately $90 total, or about$5 per month for 18 months - New credit builds on $1.75 billion in previously announced NIPSCO electric customer credits MERRILLVILLE, Ind.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 28, 2026-- NiSource Inc. (NYSE: NI) today announced that it will deliver $57.5 million in savings to its existing electric customers generated through data center development. Subject to regulatory approval, the average residential electric customer is expected to receive a monthly bill credit of approximately $5 for 18 months, beginning approximately 30 days after approval. The credit is an expansion of the value being driven through our NiSource GenCo model and is an early example of how the region’s growth can create meaningful benefits for existing NIPSCO electric customers. The new credit builds on $1.75 billion in customer credits expected from previously announced agreements with Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft. Under those agreements, large-load customers will fund the infrastructure needed to serve them, while a portion of the revenues generated through their contracts will be returned directly to existing NIPSCO electric customers. Electric customers can expect the first of these credits to begin in the first quarter of 2027 and ramp up over time. “When our region grows, our customers share in the benefits,” said Vince Parisi, NIPSCO President and Chief Operating Officer. “Putting the value from data center development directly back on customers’ bills is one more way we’re turning growth into real savings for families across northern Indiana.” Visit NIPSCO.com to learn more about NIPSCO’s efforts to support customer affordability. About NiSource NiSource Inc. (NYSE: NI) is one of the largest fully-regulated utility companies in the United States, serving approximately 3.3 million natural gas customers and 500,000 electric customers across six states through its local Columbia Gas and NIPSCO brands. The mission of our approximately 7,700 employees is to deliver safe, reliable energy that drives value to our customers. NiSource is a member of the Dow Jones Sustainability - North America Index and is on Forbes lists of America’s Best Employers for Women and Diversity. Learn more about NiSource’s record of leadership in sustainability, investments in the communities it serves and how we live our vision to be an innovative and trusted energy partner at www.NiSource.com. artigo.texto: "No data centers, no ICE, no Kings - the state of demonstrations days before the midterms Ahead of the US midterms, ACLED examines how protests over immigration, the No Kings movement, and data centre opposition could shape key congressional races. Kieran Doyle, US Analyst at ACLED, said: “Democrats seem poised to make gains in both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, an outcome that would significantly limit the Trump administration’s ability to legislate for the remainder of his term. Though the overall landscape of protests and political violence in the US appears relatively calm, several key issues have remained highly visible in recent weeks. "Among the top issues ahead of 3 November are immigration and concerns over AI, especially data center construction. Of the more than 12,600 protests recorded in the US by ACLED so far this year, over half – nearly 6,600 – have shown support for immigrants and opposition to Trump’s migration crackdown. Though much smaller in number, protests opposing data centers have emerged as part of a powerful grassroots movement that could be a deciding factor in key races. "The Migration Crackdown "With pro-immigration protests currently on pace to surpass last year’s record breaking figures, recent polls have shown that more voters now trust Democrats to handle immigration than they do Republicans. At the same time, ICE arrest figures surged to record levels over the summer. "Meanwhile, ICE agents have been involved in several violent incidents in the recent weeks. On at least two occasions, once in Woodland, California on 20 October, and once in Houston, Texas on 10 October, ICE agents struck people with their vehicles. In both cases, ICE claimed that the people struck had intentionally thrown themselves at official vehicles, but video footage appeared to contradict these accounts in both instances. In Houston, the struck man suffered two broken legs and was taken into ICE custody. Neither man has been charged with a crime. "In the days between these two incidents, on 17 October, ICE agents broke a US citizen‘s arm and tased him as they detained him in Long Beach, California. ICE claimed the man had smashed a government vehicle’s mirror. ICE agents did not render aid to the man before turning him over to the local police, who brought him to a hospital. He has not yet been charged with a crime. "These incidents add to the violent altercations involving law enforcement agents involved in the Trump administration’s migrant crackdown this year, including lethal shootings in Houston, Texas and Biddeford, Maine, as well as the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis. 'No Kings On 17 October, the fourth No Kings day of action was held in cities and towns across the country Unlike previous No Kings days, which aimed to stage the largest number of protests possible, organizers for No Kings 4 instead focused on making an impact at the ballot box, holding early voting and canvassing events. Even as they shifted energy away from demonstrations, nearly 300 protests were held across the country. Almost all of these showed opposition to Trump, who previously told voters, “Pretend I’m on the ballot.” "Data Centers "ACLED analysis shows that opposition to data centres has sparked nearly 330 demonstrations across the US in 2026, with activity concentrated in Texas and the Midwest- States where several key congressional races will be decided in the coming week. "The issue is becoming increasingly central ahead of the midterm elections, with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) targeting Republican candidates over their support for data centre development in the final days of campaigning. "ACLED has previously highlighted the growing political and commercial risks associated with grassroots opposition to data centres." Want to know more? Journalists can contact the ACLED Press Office to arrange interviews or request expert analysis. Explore the US Conflict Monitor for updates, or browse our specialized data tools. Not a member of the press? Speak to the team about subscription options and access.

(NYSE: BDC) (“Belden” or the “Company”), a global full-stack networking solutions company, today reported fiscal third quarter results for the period ended September 27, 2026. Third Quarter 2026 Highlights - Record revenues of $966 million , up 38% y/y and up 11% y/y organically - Record orders of $1,017 million , up 46% y/y and up 16% y/y organically, with a book-to-bill of 1.05x - GAAP EPS of ($0.29 ), including non-cash purchase accounting charges related to the Ruckus acquisition - Adjusted EPS of $2.26 , up 15% y/y - Reached agreement to supply $100 million of fiber solutions to major US data center customer in 2027 "Belden delivered another record quarter, with revenue of $966 million, up 38% year over year and 11% organically, and Adjusted EPS of $2.26, up 15% year over year. We also surpassed $1 billion in quarterly orders for the first time, with orders up 46% year over year and 16% organically, and a book-to-bill of 1.05x," said Ashish Chand, President and CEO of Belden Inc. "Demand remains robust across our key markets as AI and automation drive continued investment in networking infrastructure, from the data center to the factory floor. Our data center business reached an important milestone, with a signed agreement to supply $100 million of fiber assemblies in 2027. artigo.texto: Governor Josh Stein wants North Carolina to enact new rules requiring data centers to pay more for their electricity. He recommends the Utilities Commission should instate ‘large load’ tariffs on the companies that run data centers. Stein argues it's because they pull so much electricity. Some critics say their heavy power usage could raise bills for everyone else but that the large-load tariffs, if approved, could offset that. Other WRAL Top Stories WRAL asked the governor why North Carolina is behind other states who are receiving clean energy, for example, from their deals with tech companies that operate data centers. Stein said North Carolina does not have the framework in place to require the companies to provide the state those benefits. There is a proposed deal, between the tech companies building data centers and Duke Energy which provides most of North Carolina's electricity, that's currently before the state Utilities Commission for final approval. Stein indicated it's a step in the right direction but doesn't go far enough. He's urging the Utilities Commission to push for less industry-friendly rules, although he has little power to force such a change. The governor used to control the Utilities Commission, but after Stein was elected in 2024 the Republican-led state legislature stripped him of that power and gave Republican political appointees a majority on the commission. "There is no reason why the largest, wealthiest companies in the history of the world cannot be required to pay for the energy generation and transmission costs that they put onto the system. Let's create a world where regular North Carolinians actually benefit and not be harmed from these data centers," Stein said in a press conference in Raleigh. Other states have worked out contracts that require these tech companies to provide something in return for building and operating there. "For example, in Minnesota, Google agreed to pay for nearly 2,000 megawatts of wind, solar, and battery storage that will both power the data centers and strengthen the energy grid for all Minnesotans. In Indiana, Amazon is providing 960 megawatts of clean energy. In Ohio, Meta is paying for 1,200 megawatts of nuclear energy. North Carolina should be receiving these same kinds of commitments, but right now we're getting none of them," Stein said. Earlier this year, Duke reached an agreement with data centers that does include some protections. "Protections like making data center contracts use a public template, guaranteeing that long-term contracts have minimum purchase protections, requiring large energy users to reduce power when the grid is strained at the beginning of their contract. It only lasts for the first five years, but it's better than nothing, ensuring that data centers pay up front for the necessary improvements to the grids that are required, like substations and transmission lines. But there is still so much work to do, the governor said. WRAL reached out to Duke Energy for response to the governor's call for more benefits and protections to be placed in the current settlement. "Powering the demands of a growing state at the lowest possible cost requires balanced, diverse energy sources and is at the heart of the Carolinas Resource Plan and our recent settlement on a large load tariff. We look forward to continuing to work with Governor Stein, the North Carolina Utilities Commission, and other engaged partners on clean energy programs that can benefit all customers,”said Bill Norton with Duke Energy. In May, Duke Energy announced it was joining Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Nucor in signing onto agreements in North and South Carolina to accelerate clean energy options in response to growing demand. "In this new era of large-scale energy demand, Duke Energy is committed to working with our regulators and customers to find innovative and responsible ways to satisfy the growing need for more and cleaner energy. With the help of companies like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Nucor, we can accelerate our service of large customer needs and the transition to cleaner energy, while reducing financial risks and supporting economic development in our communities," said Lon Huber with Duke Energy. However, Governor Stein wants the Utilities Commission to go beyond the agreed-upon settlement with Duke Energy that proposes large load tariffs on data centers to also require the companies provide clean energy. "One other very important protection that the large load tariff gets at, but doesn't fully encompass, is a separate rate class ... We have residential, we have commercial, we have industrial, but really these data centers exist as a separate category because of the sheer amount of energy," said Attorney General Jeff Jackson. Jackson's office used to have more sway over the Utilities Commission as well but, like with Stein, state lawmakers took away some of the attorney general's authority after Jackson won election in 2024. Jackson said rate agreements need to be made, and then communicated to residents so they are not under the impression they have to pay for data center improvements. The current deal lays out data centers will have to pay for upgrades like transmission lines, Jackson said. But, it is not clear who will foot the bill for other improvements, to the grid for example. Jackson said the proposed agreement would require large power users to cover certain grid upgrades, including transmission lines But he said it is not clear who will foot the bill for other improvements – like power plants for example. The Utilities Commission is finalizing its settlement and both leaders say they want to see changes before it’s all said and done.

artigo.texto: BYD confirma marca Yangwang no Brasil em 2027 Atualizado Depois de trazer a divisão premium Denza ao Brasil, a BYD acaba de confirmar que terá mais uma submarca no país. É a Yangwang, focada no mercado de alto luxo e posicionada exatamente acima da Denza. A estreia está marcada para 2027, com a abertura das primeiras concessionárias. Os pontos de venda não serão compartilhados entre as duas marcas e serão pensados para atender clientes normalmente acostumados a comprar carros de marcas como McLaren, Aston Martin, Bentley e Rolls-Royce. Segundo Werner Schaal, diretor comercial da Denza no Brasil, há dois modelos confirmados. Um deles é o cupê U9, um superesportivo de mais de 1.300 cv. Outro, é o SUV gigante U8, conhecido não apenas pelo porte mastodôntico, mas por ter a capacidade de flutuar em trechos alagados ou de rios, como um barco. Vale lembrar que a BYD já trouxe exemplares de ambos para o Brasil para ações de marketing. Com a nova marca, a chinesa quer alcançar um novo patamar do mercado brasileiro, ainda mais exclusivo e restrito que o da Denza, que atualmente vende modelos entre R$ 400 mil e R$ 750 mil. Os Yangwang provavelmente custarão mais de R$ 1 milhão. Uma curiosidade é que a BYD não mudará o nome da marca de luxo para mercados fora da China, ainda que exista alguma dificuldade na pronúncia. No mandarim, Yangwang significa “olhar para cima” no sentido de ambição e de alcançar o ápice. Executivos da marca disseram que a questão foi definida pela própria matriz. O movimento é diferente daquele feito com a Fangchengbao, que teve os produtos colocados sob a marca Denza em mercados fora da China. A ofensiva em solo brasileiro terá dois carros grandes com muita potência e luxo. O U8 é um SUV gigantesco com 5,32 metros de comprimento, 3,05 m de entre-eixos, mais de dois metros de largura e cerca de 3.500 kg de peso em ordem de marcha. Mas o porte nem é a característica mais chamativa do U8. O SUV usa quatro motores elétricos (um em cada roda), combinados a um propulsor 2.0 turbo a gasolina que atua como gerador. Ao todo, são 1.197 cv 130 kgfm de torque, que fazem o gigante ir de 0 a 100 km/h em apenas 3,6 segundos. Com um motor em cada roda, além de poder girar sobre o próprio eixo, o U8 também é capaz de flutuar em trechos muito alagados por cerca de 30 minutos, permitindo ao motorista escapar de situações de emergência. Já o U9 busca roubar clientes dos superesportivos europeus. Para isso, repete a estratégia de usar um motor em cada roda. Porém, como é um veículo elétrico, dispensa o propulsor a combustão. Ainda assim, entrega até 1.306 cv de potência e incríveis 160 kgfm de torque, o suficiente para levar o modelo aos 100 km/h em apenas 2,4 segundos, superando os 300 km/h de velocidade máxima. Com a suspensão ativa DiSus-X, o U9 ainda tem uma curiosa função de saltar e rodar com apenas três rodas em contato com o solo. A viabilização do Yangwang U8 no Brasil era um desafio técnico-legal até pouco tempo. Pela regra anterior do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB), condutores com CNH de categoria B só podiam dirigir veículos com Peso Bruto Total (PBT) de até 3.500 kg - o que forçaria os proprietários do U8 (que beira os 4.000 kg com carga total) a tirarem carteira de habilitação de categoria C. A questão foi resolvida com a mudança na legislação que aumentou o PBT máximo para motoristas com CNH B. A novidade vale apenas para veículos elétricos e híbridos plug-in, aumentando o peso para 4.250 kg exatamente por conta do peso que as baterias trazem para o conjunto.

The transaction represents an enterprise value of approximately $320 million. EnerSys expects to realize $15 million to $20 million in annual run-rate cost synergies within the first 18 months, reflecting the unique benefits of combining Ultralife with EnerSys. Ultralife is a leading provider of rechargeable and non-rechargeable batteries, battery systems, and related accessories for military communications and other specialized applications. The company serves government, defense, and commercial customers globally and generated $191 million in revenue in fiscal 2025. Headquartered in Newark, New York, Ultralife employs more than 700 people, with principal operations across the U.S., Canada, U.K., and China. “This acquisition is a compelling strategic fit for EnerSys and directly advances our strategy to build a broader, more differentiated defense power platform,” said Shawn O'Connell, President and Chief Executive Officer of EnerSys. “Building on the success of our recent acquisitions, Ultralife expands our portfolio of advanced, reliable, high-performance power solutions. Together, we will be better positioned to support the U.S. Department of War (DoW) and allied forces with leading-edge, cost-effective technologies for the increasingly electrified battlefield of the future. We know the Ultralife business and its team well, and are confident that our shared commitment to engineering, problem solving, and customer focus will create a strong cultural fit. We look forward to combining our strengths to accelerate growth, enhance performance, and deliver greater value to our customers and shareholders.” Mark Matthews, Chief Technology Officer and President, Precision Power Solutions, added, “Ultralife complements our multi-chemistry expertise and our liquid reserve technologies with an impressive patent portfolio and strong, longstanding customer relationships. Ultralife’s products offer exceptional capabilities such as very high energy density, long shelf life, low self-discharge, useful pulse power, and cold-weather performance, which are ideally suited to the growing defense mission profiles of today and tomorrow.” “Combining with EnerSys is an exciting next step that will allow us to unlock value and growth opportunities for both companies, while delivering substantial and certain cash value to Ultralife shareholders,” said Michael Manna, President and Chief Executive Officer of Ultralife. “This transaction is a testament to the hard work and dedication of our entire organization, and now offers even greater opportunities for our valued employees. We look forward to partnering with the EnerSys team with the combined scale, resources, and shared vision to accelerate innovation and better serve our global customer base.” Acquisition Expected to Offer Compelling Strategic and Financial Benefits - Expands EnerSys’ advanced defense power technology portfolio with the addition of Ultralife’s differentiated multi-chemistry capabilities, purpose-built advanced manufacturing capacity with existing security and environmental permits, and operational expertise to scale production of EnerSys’ proprietary liquid reserve battery technology. - Increases scale and broadens exposure to the large and rapidly growing defense market with capabilities across mission-critical applications in munitions, soldier power, drones, counter drones, and autonomous systems accelerating EnerSys’ focused growth strategy. - Deepens customer relationships by creating a broader, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC)-compliant product portfolio for U.S . DoW and allied customers. - Supports an attractive financial profile. The transaction is expected to be accretive to adjusted diluted earnings per share within approximately 18 months after closing, excluding transaction and integration costs and other non-recurring items. Transaction Details and Timing The transaction will be funded through cash on hand. The transaction has been unanimously approved by the Boards of Directors of both companies. Under the terms of the merger agreement, EnerSys, through a subsidiary, will commence a tender offer to acquire all of the outstanding shares of Ultralife common stock at a price of $16.00 per share in cash at closing, representing a total enterprise value of approximately $320 million. The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including the tender of at least a majority of the outstanding shares of Ultralife’s common stock and receipt of applicable regulatory approvals, and is expected to close in the first quarter of calendar year 2027. Advisors XMS Capital Partners, LLC is serving as financial advisor to EnerSys, and Reed Smith LLP is serving as legal counsel to EnerSys in connection with the transaction. artigo.texto: [SMM Flash] CATL-Affiliated Jianxiawo Lithium Mining Project Receives EIA Approval October 30: The Yichun Municipal Ecology and Environment Bureau issued its approval for the Environmental Impact Assessment Report of the Zhenkouli–Jianxiawo lithium mining project operated by Yichun Times New Energy Mining Co., Ltd. From an environmental protection perspective, the bureau approved in principle the project’s proposed nature, location, scale, production process and environmental protection measures. According to the approval, the project is located at the border of Yifeng County and Fengxin County in Yichun, Jiangxi Province, with a total mining area of 2.5029 square kilometres. The project is classified as a new development, with a designed lithium ore mining recovery rate of 98%, usable ore resources of approximately 513.525 million tonnes, annual ore mining capacity of 30 million tonnes and a designed mine life of 18 years. The planned product output is 30 million tonnes of run-of-mine ore per year. The mining process includes topsoil stripping, drilling, blasting, loading and truck haulage. After crushing, ore will either be transported by conveyor to the concentrator or loaded directly for external sale. Total project investment is approximately RMB 4.35 billion, including around RMB 288 million in environmental protection investment, accounting for 6.61% of the total. The approval requires the project to implement the “three simultaneous” environmental protection system, under which environmental facilities must be designed, constructed and commissioned together with the main project. The company must also obtain the required pollutant discharge permit before starting production facilities or generating actual emissions, and the project may formally commence operations only after its supporting environmental protection facilities pass acceptance procedures.

artigo.texto: Voters in Wisconsin Rapids have elected a new alder to their local board, after the former District 7 representative sent a personal email to a local business over anti-data center signs. The challenger, Rusty W. Brown, brought in 172 votes. The sitting representative at the center of the recall, Michael Timm, received 144. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “Im very proud to accept the position of Alderman of District 7,” a post on the Brown for Alderman Facebook page reads. “I have lived in this district my entire life and I look forward to representing your voices in government.” On his official Facebook page, Timm congratulated Brown on his win, and offered his support. “The work continues.” Timm wrote. “Let’s move forward with respect for one another and for the process that gives every voice a say.” The recall for Alder Michael Timm came after a recall petition was filed against him over the email — which locals felt were trying to put pressure on the business. A data center proposal has been very controversial in the small central Wisconsin community, and local leaders have reevaluated proposals after public outcry. In a statement before the election, Timm said he didn’t do anything wrong by sending the email. Over 250 signatures were required to start the recall, and the Wisconsin Rapids city clerk ordered the recall election back on Sept. 23. artigo.texto: On Sept. 8, Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey issued an executive order requiring data centers in the state to receive local approval. The order also requires data centers to pay their own energy costs and establishes guardrails for environmental protection. In a September press conference, Healey claimed that data centers in other states — particularly Texas, Arizona and Virginia — have caused an array of issues. These include increased utility bills, environmental damage and public health risks, all while consuming large amounts of nonrenewable energy. “They consume massive amounts of energy, and that drives up utility bills, which truly no one can afford,” Healey said in the press conference. According to Healey, if left unchecked, data centers could consume more energy than is available on the grid. She argues that Massachusetts data centers should provide their own clean energy if they can; otherwise, they should pay ratepayers for the energy they consume until they have their own energy supply. The executive order creates a Ratepayer Protection Fund that will consist of fees paid by data centers that fail to provide their own clean energy. The fund will be returned to residents in an effort to offset costs associated with the data centers’ energy demand, and the exact mechanism of returns will be through the regulatory process. In the past, the Healey administration has returned Alternative Compliance Payments to ratepayers through bill offsets or direct credit bills. The order also explains that any project that exceeds 25 megawatts is subject to the administration’s siting and permitting reforms, which include community engagement and environmental protection. The reforms include the requirement of a Cumulative Impact Analysis. However, the guidelines outlined in Healey’s executive order could still leave ratepayers footing the bill. Barbara Kates-Garnick, a professor of practice in energy policy at the Fletcher School at Tufts University, explained that even if data centers pay their fair share of energy costs, utility rates could still increase. “Even though [the data centers are] paying quote-unquote ‘their fair share,’ they're going to require a lot of power, and we all pay for transmission in our rates,” she said. “So I definitely believe that that will be a place where prices will be higher for the customer, even though in theory that's something we’re trying to avoid.” Even so, Kates-Garnick recognized the challenge of balancing the state’s technology ambition with affordability and clean energy goals. “I think that’s important to the governor, too, and she was very careful in this to make sure that she stated the importance of technology while she’s still trying to protect the local customer and keep the costs down,” Kates-Garnick said. “It’s technology, affordability and clean energy all coming together. It’s a challenge.” Amid the AI arms race, Kates-Garnick noted the importance of making sure that technological development does not come at the expense of the local communities significantly impacted by the construction of data centers. “It’s really important that the community have a say and local control over the siting of the data center because it may use the resources of the community,” she said. The order also requires the Office of Environmental Justice and Equity to review the community benefit agreements under its established standards and guidelines. Audrey Hufnagel, an executive board member of the Tufts Climate Action Club, raised concerns about how data centers could contribute to environmental inequality. She stated that data centers “have a disproportionate impact on communities that are already suffering the worst effects of climate change.” Many critics like Hufnagel are concerned about whether communities have enough influence to prevent data center construction from being concentrated in lower-income and environmentally vulnerable areas. According to Hufnagel, it is often difficult for communities with fewer resources to organize and prevent the development of data centers, leaving them more vulnerable to its effects. Healey has made clear her intent to regulate the effects of data center construction and operation on local communities and the environment, all while keeping the state a hub for innovation. “[Tech companies] will not roll into a community, build a massive facility, dirty our water and leave ratepayers holding the bag,” Healey said. “If a company wants to do business here, they need to do it right, and they need to do it with community support.”

artigo.texto: Who will pay for data centers’ growing electricity demands in NJ? New state regulations could determine who shoulders the costs of grid upgrades, how developers guarantee payments, and what happens when projects fail. A New Jersey Board of Public Utilities stakeholder meeting is set for Nov. 4. As New Jersey residents grapple with rising electricity bills, state regulators are preparing rules that could determine whether households and small businesses end up paying part of the cost of powering massive data centers. The New Jersey Board of Public Utilities will hold a virtual stakeholder meeting Wednesday, Nov. 4, from 10 a.m. to noon to discuss how the state’s new Data Center Fair Share Act should be implemented. The public can also submit written comments through Nov. 13, according to a notice issued by the board. The board will establish rules for how the costs of power lines, substations, and other electrical infrastructure needed to serve data centers are calculated and paid for, with the goal of preventing those expenses from being passed along to other electricity customers. Data centers house the computer systems supporting artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and other digital services. Don’t miss the NJ stories that matter. Sign up for our free newsletter → All four of New Jersey’s electric distribution companies will be subject to the new rules: Public Service Electric & Gas, Jersey Central Power & Light, Atlantic City Electric, and Rockland Electric Co. Each utility will be required to develop special electricity rates and requirements for large data center customers based on statewide standards established by the board. Large data centers can consume enormous amounts of electricity, placing additional demands on the regional power grid. The New Jersey Board of Public Utilities has identified the risk that the costs of expanding electrical infrastructure to serve these facilities could be passed along to other customers, particularly if data centers close, abandon projects, or use less electricity than originally planned. The Data Center Fair Share Act, signed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on July 7, is designed to prevent utilities from passing those costs along to other customers. The law gives the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities 12 months to establish standards, including the specific rules utilities must follow to protect customers from additional costs. What the state is deciding Under the Data Center Fair Share Act, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities must establish standards for separate electricity rates for large data centers, with safeguards to prevent costs attributable to those facilities from being passed along to other customers. According to the board’s request for information, the law requires data center operators to cover costs attributable to their electricity use, including infrastructure investments, system upgrades, and potential stranded costs. Stranded costs are expenses for infrastructure and other investments that utilities may be unable to recover if a data center closes, abandons a project, or uses less electricity than anticipated. Under the law, data center customers must provide financial guarantees covering at least 85% of the electricity supply they request for 10 years, subject to standards developed by the Board of Public Utilities. The requirement is intended to protect other customers from paying for infrastructure built to serve projects that never reach their expected size. Regulators must also decide how to define a large data center, how to calculate financial guarantees, and what happens if developers abandon projects or fail to meet their electricity commitments. During electric grid emergencies, large data centers would be required to reduce their electricity use before residential customers face power reductions. The law allows exceptions for essential operations, but the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities must decide which operations qualify and how the requirements will be enforced. Another question is how to prevent developers from dividing projects into smaller facilities or using complex corporate structures to avoid the regulations. The board specifically raises those issues in its request for information. How other states are handling data center costs New Jersey is among dozens of states developing special electricity rates and financial protections for large data centers. A national database compiled by Metro Colo Advisory, a commercial data center consulting firm, has tracked 105 utility and regulatory filings involving special electricity rates for data centers and other large power users across 45 states. The database, updated Oct. 29, includes approved requirements, pending proposals, special agreements, and ongoing regulatory proceedings. Although states are taking different approaches, many are considering or adopting financial guarantees, long-term contracts, and minimum payment requirements to protect other electricity customers from data center-related costs. In Ohio, regulators approved a requirement for large data center customers served by AEP Ohio to pay for at least 85% of their contracted electricity capacity, even when they use less. The requirement is part of a special data center rate approved by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio in July 2025. Virginia regulators have approved a separate rate class for large electricity customers served by Dominion Energy, including data centers. Beginning in January 2027, qualifying new customers must make a minimum 14-year service commitment. Certain large customers must also pay minimum charges based on 85% of their contracted transmission and distribution demand and 60% of generation demand. In Michigan, the Michigan Public Service Commission approved a minimum 15-year contract for large customers served by Consumers Energy, along with minimum payments based on 80% of billing demand and penalties for ending contracts early. artigo.texto: ONU survey finds 55% of Ohioans oppose data center construction Data centers are a hot-button issue this election season, and a new Ohio Northern University survey finds most Ohioans oppose building them in the state. ADA, Ohio (WLIO) — A statewide survey by Ohio Northern University’s Institute for Civics and Public Policy (ICAPP), in partnership with SurveyUSA, found that 55% of Ohio adults oppose building data centers in the state. The survey included 1,650 Ohio adults and examined opinions on data center development, American pride and the country’s future. Researchers found three main concerns were among the leading reasons for opposition to data centers. “79% think that they’re going to drive up utility bills. That was probably the most obvious issue that we found. And then 66% think it’s going to have a negative impact on the environment. 50% think it’s going to have a negative impact on the economy,” said Aldon Edger, a sophomore statistics major who worked on the study. Student researchers said opposition to data center construction was consistent across nearly all major demographic groups and regions of Ohio. “Whether you’re a strong Republican or a strong Democrat, we found it’s pretty much the same findings through all demographics. Even throughout regions in Ohio, it all remains the same. We can be pretty confident in what we found,” said Evan Kimmel, a sophomore accounting major. The survey also asked Ohioans about their patriotism and views on the country’s future. 86% of respondents said they have moderate to extreme pride in being American, while 85% said they are proud of the country’s history, founding principles and cultural identity. However, 57% said they have little to no pride in the direction the United States is heading. “With the divisive issues like data centers, there’s a lot of fear out there of what’s going on. So, it wasn’t exactly a surprise to see that there was more pride in the past than the future,” said Curtis Ware, a criminal justice major. Students are working to share the findings with the public through educational projects designed to explain policy issues. “One of our main projects that we’re working on right now is ‘ICAPP Examines,’ and what we do with that is we really take relevant policy issues that people may not fully understand and we kind of explain them in a way that the general public is able to gather the information that they need to make informed voting decisions,” said Lauren Childs, a junior creative writing and English major. artigo.texto: CATL plans small-scale production of solid-state batteries in 2027 — Electrek Battery manufacturer CATL has reported pilot production of fully solid-state battery cells with a capacity of 20 Ah. The company expects to begin small-scale production of such batteries in 2027 and transition to mass production around 2030, Electrek reports. Target: 500 Wh/kg CATL uses a sulfide-based solid electrolyte. Such a system is characterized by high ionic conductivity and deformability, but stable contact between the battery's solid components remains a technical challenge. The company said that its sulfide batteries have entered pilot production of 20 Ah cells. CATL's target is to achieve an energy density of 500 Wh/kg. Fully solid-state batteries differ from semi-solid-state batteries in that they use a solid rather than liquid electrolyte to transfer lithium ions. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Limited volumes at the start CATL Chairman and CEO Robin Zeng said in June that, on a scale from one to nine, fully solid-state batteries are at the fourth level. CATL continues to invest in the technology but expects limited production volumes at the initial stage. Other automakers and battery manufacturers also cite 2027 as a target for launching such technologies. Toyota plans to release its first electric vehicle with a fully solid-state battery in 2027 or 2028. Samsung SDI intends to begin mass production of SolidStack batteries in the second half of 2027, while BYD's FinDreams division plans to produce sulfide fully solid-state batteries in limited batches from 2027 and ramp up production by 2030.

artigo.texto: Nevada regulators review NV Energy 2026 plan as data centers drive demand LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Nevada regulators are reviewing NV Energy’s long-term plan for meeting electricity demand as the state draws growing interest from power-hungry data centers and other large customers. The Public Utilities Commission is going over NV Energy’s 2026 Integrated Resource Plan this week in Carson City. Regulators are also considering a proposed “Large Load Electric Service Agreement,” aimed at ensuring reliable service and financial protections as Nevada becomes more appealing to new large-load customers such as data centers. RCG Economics, which does local economic forecasting and analysis, reports Nevada’s data center boom is outpacing the power grid. The firm says 39 data center projects interested in Nevada have requested nearly three times the amount of power generated by NV Energy during peak hours last year. NV Energy is building a framework intended to prevent potential growth from leading to cost shifts for existing customers. Sean Dalesandro, the developer proposing the Manse Technology Campus in Nye County, said data center developers are required to cover major infrastructure upgrades tied to their projects. “What can data center developers do? Well, what they have to do is pay for all the upgrades required for their project, and because data center projects are large loads, those costs can be substantial,” Dalesandro said. Dalesandro said adding large loads can require reinforcing major parts of the transmission system. “There’s all this equipment that goes into the transmission system, transmission lines, substations, and transformers and switching yards. All of that has to be reinforced if you add a large load to it,” he said. NV Energy said its guiding principle is that “growth should pay for growth.” The utility said that as Nevada continues to attract new businesses and large energy users, including data centers, “we believe the customers driving significant new demand should bear the costs associated with serving that demand, while existing residential and business customers should be protected from those costs.” Dalesandro said requiring developers to pay for upgrades can also strengthen the grid for others. “They have to be paid for by the developer, and that enhances the bulk electric system so that all of the residential and other users on the grid benefit,” he said. Beyond power costs and infrastructure, experts say Nevada’s climate and connectivity help make it a premium location for data centers. Greg Moody, an associate professor of information systems at UNLV, said data centers are expensive to build and operators want to protect that investment. “We have lots of fantastic stuff,” Moody said. Moody said Nevada avoids many severe weather risks seen elsewhere. “But we don’t get big tornadoes, we don’t get large floods, we do not get hurricanes, risk of lightning storms, ice storms, all that fun stuff that hits all different parts of the country; we simply don’t have,” he said. Moody also said Nevada provides humidity-free air conditioning, adding that “75% of the year it is 72 degrees or cooler.” He said another major advantage is internet backbone access through Las Vegas. “Almost every single major ISP backbone provider goes through Las Vegas, and so as a result, if you build a data center right next to essentially what would be the spine of the nervous system, you get a lot better access speed, and speed is very important when you’re dealing with large quantities of data,” Moody said. Electricity prices are also a key factor NV Energy wants to protect as demand grows. According to Electricity Cost Comparison.com, Nevada pays less than 13 cents per kilowatt hour, with an average power bill of $110 a month. By comparison, the site lists Texas at about 16 cents per kilowatt hour, California at almost 30 cents, and Hawaii at 47 cents per kilowatt hour, with an average power bill of $407 a month. The Integrated Resource Plan and the Large Load Electric Service Agreement are expected to receive approval from the Public Utilities Commission, with possible language changes. Nevada’s lower tax rates compared with neighboring states and significant tax abatements also add to the state’s appeal for data center developers. Qualified developers can receive a sales tax reduction on equipment and building materials for new projects.

artigo.texto: Oracle Cloud to Offer Google TPUs and New AI Chips Oracle is broadening OCI’s AI infrastructure with Google TPUs and other chips while deepening its Nvidia partnership to give customers more workload choice. Oracle is broadening the range of AI chips available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, saying it plans to deploy Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) as well as inference chips from OpenAI, Cerebras, SambaNova, and Positron AI. The move gives OCI customers more options for running AI workloads beyond Nvidia GPUs. Oracle said Tuesday, Oct. 27, that it will become the first hyperscaler to offer TPUs outside Google Cloud. The announcement, made at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, came alongside an expansion of Oracle’s partnership with Nvidia. Oracle said Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now generally available on OCI. The company also said it plans to expand OCI Superclusters to multi-gigawatt scale using Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. Industry analysts said Oracle’s adoption of the additional AI accelerators gives customers more flexibility to match infrastructure to specific workload requirements. While Oracle Cloud has relied primarily on Nvidia GPUs, it also has some AMD GPU deployments, according to analysts. “Oracle has been a leader in AI factory development using Nvidia systems, and their move today suggests that they’re aligning with the industry direction towards heterogeneous computing,” said Brendan Burke, research director at Futurum Group. “Oracle is working closely with partners like OpenAI to select the best-fit compute, including Cerebras for fast inference.” “The usage of alternative accelerators suggests that there are unique advantages to each, and that it’s worthwhile to offer choice to customers overall,” Burke added. Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said the announcement is an aggressive expansion by Oracle Cloud to support multiple AI chip architectures. “This is Oracle trying to be the open silicon cloud – something for everybody,” Kimball said. Burke noted that the challenge for Oracle will be proving that the new AI accelerators are competitive with Nvidia-based offerings and showing long-term commitment to them rather than treating them as limited experiments. OCI Expands Beyond Nvidia with New AI Accelerators Oracle said Google TPUs for training and inference will be available on OCI in 2027, with adoption ramping over a multi-year period. Oracle also said it will deploy the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine for high-speed AI inference in 2027, while Positron AI’s Positron Atlas inference chip is now generally available on OCI. Oracle also said Tuesday that it will deploy OpenAI’s Jalapeño inference accelerators, developed in partnership with Broadcom. OpenAI and Broadcom previously said they expect initial deployment of Jalapeño by the end of 2026, but Oracle did not specify when the chip will be available on OCI. SambaNova also announced Tuesday that it is collaborating with Oracle to deploy its SN50 inference chips in OCI, though no availability date was given in the press release. The SN50 is SambaNova’s fifth-generation Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit chip, designed for agentic AI workloads. SambaNova asserts that the chip delivers up to five times the speed of competing chips at a total cost of ownership that is three times lower. The company also said the SN50 draws an average of 20 kW per rack, which is low enough to scale in existing air-cooled data centers. Why Google Is Bringing TPUs to Oracle Cloud Burke said Google TPUs are highly competitive processors that have shown significant generational improvements. With its eighth-generation TPU family, Google introduced two versions of the processor: TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference. In a company blog post, Google said both versions deliver up to twice the performance per watt. Google also said TPU 8t provides up to 2.7x better performance per dollar, while TPU 8i provides up to 80% better performance per dollar than the previous generation. Hyperscalers such as Google and AWS have found strategic value in building custom AI chips for their own infrastructure and cloud services. Now they also appear to see an opportunity to commercialize those chips more broadly. AWS has reportedly considered selling its Trainium AI chip for use in third-party data centers. Oracle’s announcement suggests Google also sees a market for TPUs beyond its own cloud platform. After weighing whether to reserve its compute capacity for internal teams or make it more broadly available, Google appears to have shifted toward external deployment, Burke said. He attributed that move in part to continued tightness in the AI compute market. “There's higher value in making it available than using it all internally,” he said. Kimball said Google’s decision to make TPUs available on OCI allows customers to use them without migrating their data to Google Cloud. “This is about Google understanding the value that it’s delivering in its TPU and trying to bring that value to customers, regardless of where their data lives,” Kimball said. “Oracle Cloud has a lot of customer data and a lot of AI use cases being deployed in it, so it only makes sense that you would want to bring TPUs to where the data is.”

artigo.texto: A new report from the Common Sense Institute predicted that developing data center projects could give some relief to homeowner’s taxes by contributing approximately $3.1 billion by 2040. The report, titled “The Tax Impact of Data Centers in Iowa: New Revenue for Communities, Relief for Taxpayers,” examined the industry’s tax contributions as it continues to grow. Between 2014 and 2025, data centers paid about $319 million in property taxes. Annual payments on these data centers are expected to increase to $140 million by 2031 and $292 million by 2040, adding up to about $3.1 billion, with almost 90% of the revenue still to come in the years to come. According to the report, an acre of data center land was estimated to be worth $4,884 in property taxes. That some acre of land, under its previous use, would be worth $29 in property taxes. Available data center campuses in 2025 generated about 153 times more property tax revenue than the same land under its previous use. These increasing tax revenues are relieving homeowners, according to the report. “CSI estimates that approximately $3.4 million of data center property taxes in 2025 reduced homeowner tax bills, averaging about $15 per home,” said a CSI news release. Some communities have already begun to see property tax relief due to data center campuses. According to CSI, the Norwalk Community School District, south of Des Moines, has saved about $631 per household over the past three fiscal years. Similar savings were calculated for Waukee, at $269 saved over the past four fiscal years. Between 2015 and 2025, CSI calculated that taxable sales increased 50% in Iowa cities with data centers, suggesting a relationship between data center development and local economic activity. “Data centers are quickly becoming a major asset to Iowa’s local economies,” said CSI’s Vice President of Policy and Research Ben Murrey in the news release. “We’re talking about turning land that generated about $30 per acre in property taxes into data center campuses that generate millions in revenue for local communities. That’s a big deal, especially for homeowners who are feeling the squeeze of rising property taxes. The opportunity now is for local leaders to make the most of that investment, strengthening essential services while putting more money back into the pockets of Iowa taxpayers.”

Attendees are invited to see AOS' latest products, which meet growing demands for higher power delivery and performance, greater efficiency, smaller board space, and higher reliability in AI core power, AI data center, and industrial power designs. AOS will exhibit solutions in the following key application areas: AI Core Power: New AOS power management products meet the high-performance needs of AI computing, graphics, and next-generation notebook applications. These devices enable high-density DC/DC and AC/DC conversion with improved thermal performance and ultra-low switching losses in compact, cooling-efficient designs for AI servers and accelerators. New products offer double-sided cooling, efficient high-voltage conversion, high-frequency power delivery, and the ruggedness needed to meet reliability and efficiency requirements in demanding AI factory environments. Industrial Power: AOS' latest MOSFETs and motor driver ICs are designed for BLDC motor applications ranging from power tools and outdoor equipment to e-mobility systems. AOS has developed extensive intellectual property and technical knowledge that encompasses the latest advancements in the power semiconductor industry, which enables us to introduce innovative products to address the increasingly complex power requirements of advanced electronics. AOS differentiates itself by integrating its Discrete and IC semiconductor process technology, product design, and advanced packaging know-how to develop high-performance power management solutions. AOS' portfolio of products targets high-volume applications, including personal computers, graphics cards, data centers, AI servers, smartphones, consumer and industrial motor controls, TVs, lighting, automotive electronics, and power supply units for various equipment. artigo.texto: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa took aim at Gov. Greg Abbott’s record on data centers and campaign contributions while saying she would prioritize education funding and putting money back in Texans’ pockets during her campaign stop Wednesday evening in El Paso. The rally at the Epic Railyard Event Center marked her third stop in El Paso ahead of the Nov. 3 general election, where she hopes to unseat the Republican incumbent, who is seeking his fourth term in office. The rally kicked off with a performance by El Paso rapper Krystall Poppin, who had the crowd chanting “915,” “Go, Gina” and “Go, Poppin.” Hinojosa was introduced by New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, who urged attendees to bring people to the polls during the last two days of early voting and on Election Day. “Get her over the finish line,” Lujan Grisham said. Hinojosa, 52, is a civil rights lawyer and state representative from Austin. The rally followed a volunteer event and stop at the University of Texas at El Paso to mobilize supporters to hit the polls. “There’s one fight,” Hinojosa said. “Is this going to be a Texas for the people, or is this the billionaires’ world and we just live here?” Abbott, 68, has made two campaign stops in El Paso and has a third scheduled onThursday. Hinojosa and Abbott are among the slew of state candidates stopping in El Paso during the last week of the early voting. Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico visited on Monday, and his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, will come Sunday. Hinojosa said she wants to secure the American dream by reallocating state resources to save public schools and giving $1,500 to every Texas household through what she dubbed the Greg Abbott corruption tax refund. She also said she wanted to suspend the gas and diesel tax in the state and reign in health insurance companies. Hinojosa also took aim at Abbott’s email communications with tech billionaire Elon Musk, which the governor’s office withheld from release under state open records laws. “Hundreds of pages of redacted emails that he refuses to hand over. These are documents that, as a legislator, I am routinely given when I ask for them. Not this time – very suspicious, not this time,” Hinojosa said at the rally. “I think they’ll show he sold us out.” On Monday, a Travis County judge ruled that Abbott must allow Hinojosa to review unredacted communications between he and Musk. Abbott’s attorneys filed an appeal, according to Bloomberg Law. The 15th Court of Appeals on Tuesday issued a stay on the ruling which prevents Hinojosa from immediate access to the documents. Hinojosa after the rally said though she may not be able to publicly disclose the contents of the emails, she would use the information to create legislation to put a stop to potentially corrupt dealings. Her term as a state representative ends before the next Texas Legislature session begins. “As a legislator, I have power to take action, to be able to right the wrongs that are happening, and to ask questions to make sure the public gets the information that they need,” Hinojosa said. Abbott’s office did not respond to a request for comment. Musk has donated $5.5 million to Abbott’s reelection campaign, Texas Ethics Commission filings show. Hinojosa also said she wanted to put a moratorium on data center agreements. “When I am governor, we will put a pause – a moratorium on any agreements until we can pass laws to make sure that the people of El Paso and Texas have a seat at the table to decide if and how these data centers come into their communities,” Hinojosa said. Abbott promoted Texas as a destination for data centers before public backlash and concerns about how resources such as energy and water would be impacted by the operation of the facilities throughout the state. In early August, Abbott issued a series of guidelines for data center operations that, in part, aim to make the companies pay for their own electric infrastructure and eliminate incentives. Hinojosa said it was no shock that the permits were still being issued after the governor’s directives and said data centers are part of the reason the state is losing billions of dollars in revenue. “We are losing more than a billion dollars a year in this state because of it – that’s money the rest of us have to pick up the tab for,” she said, referring to sales tax breaks given to data centers.

artigo.texto: District 34 candidates discuss brain drain, data centers and child care GRAND ISLAND, Neb. (KSNB) - Ben Blodgett and incumbent Loren Lippincott, candidates for Legislative District 34, discussed brain drain, data centers and child care access in interviews less than a week before the midterm election. The district covers parts of Hall County as well as Hamilton, Nance and Merrick counties. The election is Nov. 3. Keeping young people in Nebraska Brain drain refers to young people leaving Nebraska for better opportunities. Blodgett said one solution is to create more opportunities in trades while students are in high school. “I’d like to see more programs put in the schools to offer trades to the younger kids and let them know that ... if you don’t feel you’re cut out for school, here’s an avenue, you know, plumbers, electricians, construction, all those aspects to where we can get younger kids good paying jobs and to stay local,” Blodgett said. Lippincott said making Nebraska more tax friendly will help young Nebraskans stay in the state. “We need to make this state more friendly toward citizens in terms of the taxes,” Lippincott said. “For instance, if we were to simply get rid of our inheritance tax, Nebraska is one of only five states in the union that has an inheritance tax. We’re the only state, this side, west of the Mississippi River, that has an inheritance tax.” Data centers Blodgett said companies building new data centers in Nebraska need to be more transparent and communities should have a big say in whether to allow them. “We need to have put in their guidelines and they need to be more transparent and with that, we also need to leave it up to the communities whether to allow data centers in there or not,” Blodgett said. “I don’t think that there should be any protections or anything for them, any kind of deals made with utilities as far as what they need to pay. It needs to be fair across the board.” Lippincott said there needs to be protection for the power grid and natural resources, but not all aspects of data centers are bad. “A lot of these data centers, instead of pulling on energy during the high load times, can instead flatten out that cyclical up and down by using power during times of low use for our electrical centers and that’s something that actually can be helpful, not harmful.“ Child care access Blodgett said funding needs to be created for child care. “We need to create money for childcare and we just need to have responsible spending and make cuts where necessary to allow and allocate those funds for childcare and make it to where working class people can afford to know that their kids are safe,” Blodgett said. Lippincott said working-class families need tax breaks to help them afford child care. “We need to cut back on the things that government is requiring the populace to pay for in terms of their taxes and then also help people who do need daycare for their children some tax breaks for them in order to be able to take care of their kids,” Lippincott said. artigo.texto: Publicidade WASHINGTON, 29 Out (Reuters) – Os eleitores de dez Estados dos EUA decidirão na próxima terça-feira se devem restringir a implantação de data centers em suas comunidades, à medida que a rápida expansão para impulsionar o boom da IA desperta oposição local. A resistência é especialmente visível em Ohio, um dos mercados de data centers que mais crescem no país. Nenhum outro Estado tem mais propostas eleitorais relacionadas a data centers, com eleitores em mais de uma dúzia de jurisdições prestes a avaliar 21 propostas paralelamente às eleições de meio de mandato da próxima terça-feira, de acordo com o grupo de pesquisa apartidário Ballotpedia. Alphabet lucra bilhões com chips de IA, mas formação de estoque aperta o caixa Venda de chips de IA exige que a Alphabet invista em hardware muito antes que os clientes paguem Samsung prevê que escassez de chips de IA se agrave A Samsung informou que seu estoque de HBM para o próximo ano já está esgotado Os eleitores em 38 jurisdições locais analisarão pelo menos 41 medidas que atrasariam, proibiriam ou imporiam novos requisitos aos data centers — as instalações de grande porte que fornecem o poder de computação necessário para executar aplicativos de IA. A maioria dos Estados exige campanhas de coleta de assinaturas ou outras demonstrações de apoio público antes que as medidas possam ser incluídas na cédula eleitoral, e sua presença reflete a crescente oposição aos data centers em todo o espectro político. O apoio à proibição da construção de certos data centers vem tanto de democratas quanto de republicanos, disse a organizadora local Jessica Baker. “Todos nós queremos a mesma coisa.” Baker, que faz parte do grupo de defesa Conserve Ohio, disse que as preocupações com o consumo de eletricidade e água dos data centers estão impulsionando a oposição. Mesmo que os desenvolvedores gerem sua própria energia por meio de turbinas a gás ou reatores nucleares, muitos moradores ainda não querem que as instalações sejam construídas perto de suas comunidades, porque estão preocupados com riscos à saúde de seus filhos, como a asma, disse ela. Se os eleitores de Ohio aprovarem restrições, é provável que os desenvolvedores redirecionem os projetos para outros locais, em vez de abandoná-los completamente, disse Baron Fung, que supervisiona pesquisas sobre infraestrutura de TI na empresa de pesquisa de mercado Dell’Oro Group. O setor já enfrenta grandes obstáculos, incluindo esperas de anos para conexões à rede elétrica e custos crescentes de construção. Continua depois da publicidade “Se houver um cancelamento ou atraso em determinados locais, (os desenvolvedores) podem, potencialmente, transferir parte dessa demanda para outro local”, disse Fung. A todo vapor O crescimento recente sugere que a oposição local não desacelerou significativamente o setor. A capacidade dos data centers em construção nos EUA aumentou 48% de dezembro de 2025 a junho de 2026, medida em gigawatts, de acordo com John McWilliams, chefe de análises de data centers da empresa de serviços imobiliários Cushman & Wakefield. “Embora existam regiões ou jurisdições em todo o país onde há algum atrito entre os desenvolvedores, ainda há áreas onde os projetos estão avançando”, disse McWilliams. Continua depois da publicidade As propostas de referendo chamaram a atenção de alguns dos maiores participantes do setor. Em Sunbury, perto de Columbus, uma proposta que proibiria data centers que consumissem mais de 25 megawatts de energia poderia inviabilizar o projeto de US$2 bilhões proposto pela Amazon. A diretora de políticas públicas da Amazon, Shannon Kellogg, apareceu na TV local em outubro para responder a perguntas sobre o projeto antes da votação. Um porta-voz da Amazon se recusou a dizer se as iniciativas eleitorais em todo o território dos EUA afetariam os planos de expansão dos data centers da empresa. “Estamos focados em trabalhar com os moradores e autoridades locais para construir data centers que gerem empregos, fortaleçam as economias locais por meio de milhões em pagamentos de impostos e alimentem as tecnologias nas quais os clientes confiam”, disse o porta-voz. Continua depois da publicidade “Independentemente do resultado de qualquer medida específica, nosso compromisso com as comunidades onde atuamos permanece o mesmo.”

artigo.texto: O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) ampliou de zero para até 50 MW a margem disponível para conexão de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias no barramento de 69 kV da subestação Milagres, no Ceará. A mudança está na primeira revisão da nota técnica sobre a capacidade remanescente do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) para os leilões de baterias de dezembro, divulgada nesta segunda-feira, 26 de outubro. A alteração ocorreu após a Axia Energia, responsável pela instalação, corrigir as informações encaminhadas à Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) sobre a disponibilidade física para novas conexões no local. Na versão original, publicada em 30 de setembro, o barramento havia sido classificado como sem disponibilidade física, o que levou o ONS a considerar margem nula para novos empreendimentos. Em ofício de 19 de outubro, a transmissora retificou a informação, reconhecendo a existência de espaço para novas conexões. Com a atualização, o ONS passou a considerar uma margem de até 50 MW no barramento, na subárea e na área correspondente, conforme a tabela de conclusões da nota técnica. A revisão também corrigiu a capacidade de interrupção de curto-circuito de um disjuntor da subestação Milagres, em 230 kV, de 40 kA para 50 kA. Segundo o operador, a alteração não modificou os resultados das análises de curto-circuito, porque a restrição permanece associada a outro disjuntor, cuja capacidade é de 40 kA. O documento também recebeu correções em tabelas, classificações de barramentos e referências internas, sem outras alterações nas margens de capacidade remanescente. Os estudos do ONS identificam a capacidade disponível para conexão dos projetos que disputarão os dois leilões de baterias, previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. O primeiro será destinado a equipamentos com conteúdo nacional, enquanto o segundo permitirá a participação de sistemas de armazenamento independentemente dessa exigência.

artigo.texto: Portugal está a reforçar a sua posição como mercado emergente de Data Centers na Europa, impulsionado pelo crescimento da procura associada à inteligência artificial (IA), pela forte conectividade internacional e pela expansão de projetos de grande escala. De acordo com o mais recente Data Centers Iberian Region Snapshot, elaborado pela Colliers, empresa global e diversificada de serviços profissionais e de gestão de investimentos, especializada em Imobiliário Comercial, Engenharia e Gestão de Investimento, Lisboa dispõe atualmente de 25 MW IT de capacidade operacional, mas apresenta um pipeline de desenvolvimento de aproximadamente 1.389 MW IT. Cerca de 91% da capacidade assegurada deverá estar operacional antes de 2030. Apesar de não terem sido identificados novos projetos ou aumentos de capacidade operacional em Lisboa durante o período analisado (abril a setembro de 2026), o mercado mantém uma dinâmica de desenvolvimento significativa. A Colliers destaca que a combinação entre uma base operacional ainda reduzida e um pipeline de grande dimensão coloca Portugal numa posição forte para captar uma nova vaga de procura por infraestrutura digital. “O mercado de centros de dados em Portugal ainda é pequeno quando comparado com o de outros países com maior tradição neste setor (FLAP-D). No entanto, apesar de contar com menos projetos, Portugal tem três projetos que já são, ou virão a ser, muito relevantes em termos de dimensão: o Start Campus, em Sines, o Merlin, em Lisboa, e o Covilhã DC (Asterion). Em conjunto, estes projetos representam um pipeline de desenvolvimento muito significativo”, diz José María Guilleuma, managing director de Data Centers da Colliers, ao Jornal Económico. “Portugal já conseguiu atrair grandes projetos de Inteligência Artificial, mas falta-lhe transformar Lisboa numa localização atrativa para os grandes operadores de hiperescala, à semelhança do que acontece em Barcelona”, acrescenta o responsável. A crescente relevância da inteligência artificial está a alterar os requisitos dos operadores e utilizadores de Data Centers, aumentando a necessidade de capacidade energética, conectividade e instalações preparadas para cargas computacionais de elevada densidade. Neste contexto, a construção do Lisbon AI Campus da Merlin Edged está em curso. A primeira fase prevê 80 MW IT, distribuídos por duas instalações de 40 MW, com entrega prevista para o quarto trimestre de 2027. Está ainda prevista uma capacidade adicional de 100 MW IT em três edifícios, elevando a capacidade planeada do campus para 180 MW IT. Para além desta capacidade, a Merlin Edged prevê desenvolver até mais 1.120 MW IT no seu pipeline futuro, incluindo 200 MW IT em Vila Franca de Xira e outros 920 MW IT numa localização ainda não divulgada. Sines ganha importância estratégica na corrida à IA Fora da região de Lisboa, o projeto de Sines assume uma relevância crescente na estratégia nacional de infraestrutura digital. Segundo a Colliers, a Start Campus, em parceria com a Nscale e a Microsoft, ampliou o seu projeto para implementar mais de 66.000 GPUs NVIDIA Rubin a partir do final de 2027, complementando as mais de 12.600 GPUs NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra previstas para o SIN01. A Start Campus mantém autorização para uma capacidade total de 1,2 GW, reforçando Sines como uma das localizações europeias com maior potencial para infraestrutura de IA de grande escala. Também fora de Lisboa, a entrada da NxN no mercado português, através da aquisição de um Data Center operacional de 1 MW IT em Évora, evidencia a expansão gradual do mercado para outros pontos do território. A atratividade de Lisboa enquanto localização para Data Centers é suportada pela sua forte conectividade internacional, nomeadamente pela rede de cabos submarinos e pela infraestrutura de fibra ótica. O mercado beneficia ainda de um enquadramento regulatório considerado favorável e de uma crescente valorização das infraestruturas digitais como setor estratégico. “Portugal é uma geografia ideal, graças à sua localização estratégica voltada para o Atlântico. É verdade que o novo enquadramento regulatório em Espanha poderá beneficiar Portugal, ao posicioná-lo como uma boa alternativa para a diversificação europeia dos países nórdicos”. “No entanto, Portugal já beneficia de previsibilidade regulatória, e o seu modelo e estrutura da rede elétrica estão alinhados com as orientações da União Europeia”, conclui José María Guilleuma. Fonte e crédito da imagem: O Jornal Económico / Portugal
