artigo.texto: A rápida expansão de grandes data centers nos Estados Unidos tem transformado esses empreendimentos em alvos de protestos e da oposição de diferentes segmentos da sociedade. Pesquisas mostram que a maioria da população se opõe à construção dessas infraestruturas em seus bairros, e a resistência virou uma rara bandeira que une republicanos e democratas. No Brasil, o setor ainda é muito menor. Os EUA concentram 58% da capacidade instalada no mundo, segundo a consultoria Data Center Hawk, enquanto o Brasil responde por pouco mais de 1%. Mas o país entrou na rota de investimentos do setor, e movimentos de oposição começam a aparecer, o que passa a preocupar as empresas. A resistência brasileira se materializa de diferentes formas: ações do Ministério Público pedem a paralisação ou explicações sobre grandes projetos; moradores pressionam por mais detalhes; nas redes sociais, postagens questionam os empreendimentos, algumas capitaneadas por políticos de esquerda; e nos estados, projetos de lei propõem restrições ao setor. Por trás dos movimentos nos dois países estão preocupações em comum, como o intenso consumo de energia, o uso de água, a poluição sonora e o excesso de calor. Em uma pesquisa recente do Fórum Econômico Mundial com economistas-chefes, a maioria avaliou que o avanço dos data centers de IA será um motor de tensão no mundo, por aumentar o custo de energia e água sem impacto positivo na criação de empregos. Um levantamento da consultoria Innova Assuntos Públicos mapeou pelo menos 20 projetos de lei sobre data centers em assembleias legislativas. Nove propõem restrições e exigências, sete focam em incentivos e quatro são neutros ou mistos. O tema ganhou relevância em 2026. Só quatro das propostas foram apresentadas no ano passado, e apenas uma era restritiva. Para Andriei Gutierrez, sócio da Innova, o cenário decorre de um “efeito EUA”, com movimentos sociais usando a experiência americana para alertar sobre os riscos do crescimento desenfreado do setor. Ele também avalia que grandes anúncios foram feitos com o poder público sem aproximação prévia com as comunidades afetadas, o que impulsionou a opinião negativa. “O cenário está mudando, e as empresas vão precisar ter uma nova abordagem a partir de agora. Não é um sinal vermelho como nos EUA, mas é um sinal amarelo. É bom porque nos obriga a avançar com mais cautela, mas há uma janela de oportunidade para investimentos”, diz Gutierrez. Luis Tossi, vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), observa empresas do setor tentando se aproximar de comunidades locais para negociar benfeitorias junto com a implementação de projetos. A americana Equinix, uma das maiores empresas do mundo em data centers e infraestrutura digital, que tem projetos no Brasil, vê a oposição como um fator a considerar. Segundo Eduardo Shuto, diretor de estratégia Latam da empresa, antes de anunciar projetos a companhia faz um trabalho nas comunidades, apresentando dados sobre uso de água e energia e estimativas de benefícios para a região. “Isso sempre foi um fator e agora vai ser mais do que nunca”, diz. Nos Estados Unidos, pelo menos 106 projetos de data centers foram bloqueados ou adiados por oposição de comunidades locais no primeiro semestre de 2026, segundo a consultoria 10a Labs. No Brasil, o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública pedem na Justiça a paralisação das obras de um data center em Pecém (CE), previsto para atender o TikTok, até que sejam feitos uma consulta a uma comunidade indígena e um estudo de impacto ambiental. A Omnia, responsável pelo projeto, diz manter diálogo com o poder público e as comunidades e ter todas as licenças exigidas. Uma ação parecida do Ministério Público Estadual afeta um projeto da Elea Data Center em Belém, ainda em desenvolvimento. A empresa afirma colaborar com o órgão e seguir todos os processos de licenciamento. Em Campinas, o Ministério Público Estadual abriu inquérito sobre um projeto da Terranova. O Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente havia levantado suspeitas sobre liberação antecipada de alvarás e riscos na ligação de energia. A prefeitura diz que o licenciamento está em andamento. A empresa afirma seguir os ritos legais e ter investido em uma subestação como reforço ao sistema elétrico. Setor em expansão e gargalo elétrico Mesmo pequeno, o setor brasileiro ficou seis vezes maior desde 2012, segundo a multinacional de serviços imobiliários JLL, e 2026 caminha para recorde de novas entregas, com investimentos previstos de US$ 8 bilhões. O tamanho do mercado consumidor, a demanda global puxada pela IA e a matriz elétrica majoritariamente limpa colocaram o Brasil como potencial polo de atração. O tema apareceu até no discurso de vitória do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, no domingo (25). A Brasscom, associação de empresas de tecnologia da informação, projeta que o mercado deve triplicar até 2031, com potencial de R$ 92 bilhões em investimentos. Aprovada recentemente, o Redata, legislação de incentivo ao setor, isenta de impostos federais a importação para equipamentos e exige uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. O setor cobra também a desoneração do ICMS pelos estados, mas ela depende da regulamentação federal, travada em parte por divergências sobre a inclusão do gás natural entre as fontes de energia que dão acesso ao incentivo tributário. Nos EUA, o setor é majoritariamente alimentado por combustíveis fósseis. Aqui, os empreendimentos são apresentados como solução para o excesso de energia solar e eólica nos horários de maior geração, que impõe cortes para proteger a rede, o chamado curtailment. Mas essas fontes não garantem energia 24 horas por dia, como esse tipo de operação exige. Os data centers já disputam espaço na rede com outras indústrias. No primeiro leilão da Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast), em outubro, três data centers em São Paulo levaram todos os 228 MW disponíveis. artigo.texto: Council, community members weigh in ahead of data center regulation vote SAN ANTONIO - City council will vote Thursday on how to regulate data centers within city limits. It's a divisive issue, with some wanting to keep them as far away as possible. Others tout their financial benefits. RELATED: Weighing the options: Council discusses data center regulation The council will vote on adjusting guidelines around what data centers in San Antonio will look like. Community members are asking for stronger regulations before more get here. A small protest formed at the steps of city hall ahead of Thursday's council meeting. "Everything that is going on in city council tomorrow with the vote on the Unified Development Code is absolutely necessary," one woman said. "It's about time that the city of San Antonio protect residents from this enormous growth of data centers that has happened and continues to happen." The conversation last came up during the October 15th meeting. City staff gave council the option to let data centers into San Antonio automatically with a list of rules: Restricting them to commercial and industrial areas. Keeping centers at least 500 ft away from buildings, homes and landscaping — and completely out of the Edwards Research Recharge zone. "There you see in the picture, those are diesel generators in the back there, and we were all of 650 ft from a playground," Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones said after visiting a center. A second option would involve all those same guidelines -- only each project would have to come before council. "It's been critical for my community and for myself to make sure that we are pushing on policies that can ensure that residents have the ability to communicate directly with the developers, ask the question they want to get to know, make sure they get the concessions they're looking for and the community benefits they're looking for and finally, making sure that council has their back," said District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan. Online data shows 89 data centers already exist in San Antonio. We asked Councilman Galvan where this effort comes from. "Because there hasn't been an opportunity before," he said. Councilman Galvan has led the effort of data center regulation, saying he wants each center to come to the council for approval. He hopes his colleagues will support him. "I think we need to look at responsible policy again that protects our people and says to the data centers, if you can meet 'a, b, c, d, e' qualifications. If you're willing to abide by these rules and we're willing to talk about you being here within our city," said District 10 Councilman Marc Whyte. He believes that while data centers should be regulated, they also come with financial benefits in the midst of the city's budget deficit. "The jobs that they create for our city, the revenue that they create for our city cannot be overlooked," Councilman Whyte said. "I hope my colleagues take that into account [Thursday]." Thursday's vote will change the city's Unified Development Code (UDC) which outlines rules for land use and development. We'll keep you updated on what the council decides.

artigo.texto: The Scoop PsiQuantum is building its first product. It isnât a quantum computer, but it could become a superpower for AI data centers. The company has been working for a decade on building quantum computers that use photons as âbitsâ of information and has built its own optical chips that control light particles with extreme precision. That ability to manipulate light could turn out to be a marketable tool in the next phase of the AI race, where data centers, bottlenecked by the limits of copper wiring, are switching to using fiber optics instead. PsiQuantum says it has been showing potential customers a prototype of a new âoptical circuit switchâ that could be used to route optical signals from GPUs across data centers much more efficiently. Customers were most focused on PsiQuantumâs ability to beat a benchmark known as âinsertion loss,â measured in decibels, that determines how many photons escape during transport, potentially leading to a degraded signal. To work in an AI datacenter, insertion loss needed to be less than two to three decibels, PsiQuantum said. Its prototype barreled through that requirement, reaching 1.2. Know More The AI boom wouldnât have happened without the ability to network hundreds of thousands of AI processors together. But all that networking is also the data centerâs weakest link. While GPUs can crunch numbers at blazing speeds, they are bottlenecked by the comparatively slow copper that carries the output of that math from GPU to GPU. Thatâs especially true during the training process of increasingly large AI models that require the most coordination between large numbers of GPUs. The next generation of data center racks are more often using optical cables to carry the data between GPUs. But optical information must be converted into an electrical signal in order to be routed to its destination, then converted back into light, before itâs converted once again when it reaches its destination. All those conversions happening billions of times per second in the largest data centers require optical switches that generate heat, energy and bulk. PsiQuantum says its new device can do that without ever having to convert the photons into electrical signals. It could be used to create speed-of-light connections between server racks in AI data centers that generate almost no heat and consume negligible energy. The only major hyperscaler currently using purely optical circuit switching in an AI data center today is Google, which built a system that uses tiny mirrors, known as MEMS, to direct the light signal. Robert Soderbery, executive vice president of PsiQuantum, said in an interview with Semafor that separate data center racks will effectively behave as one, using PsiQuantumâs device. Data could flow between GPUs in separate server racks at the same speed and latency as they would between GPUs interconnected inside a single rack. That would be a huge advantage because today server racks are reaching the limit of compute density, size and energy efficiency. PsiQuantum isnât alone. The battle to convert data center networking to photonics has been raging since the ChatGPT moment kicked off the AI race. Earlier this year, photonic computing company Lightmatter helped launch an initiative to standardize optics in the data center space. Nvidia has been spending billions on investments in optics computing companies like Lumentum and Coherent. For now, the GPU reigns supreme but data centers are seeing a lot more of the light.

artigo.texto: Sigenergy Launches SigenCube Commercial & Industrial Battery Energy Storage System Sigenergy has introduced the SigenCube Commercial & Industrial Battery Energy Storage System, a product aimed at the main obstacles facing commercial storage installations, according to pv magazine. The company says the system reaches an energy density above 220 kWh/m2, sharply reducing the space a project needs. In a 4 MWh project, conventional solutions generally occupy more than 80 m2 of land, while the SigenCube needs 54.5 m2, a footprint reduction of more than 30%. Its integrated architecture places the Power Conversion System, high-voltage components and distribution units in one cabinet. To simplify scaling of multi-megawatt projects, each cabinet carries an Energy Management System and can support up to 100 units in parallel without external data loggers. Automated failover is included to avoid single points of failure. Factory pre-commissioning and app-based setup allow technicians to finish basic configuration and diagnostics in three to five minutes. On performance, the system provides a 150% peak power overload for 10 seconds, supplying surge support for heavy industrial machinery. Sigenergy states that it prevents tripping and manages load spikes when handling inrush currents from industrial air compressors, conveyor drive systems or motor-driven centrifugal pumps. The SigenCube uses predictive smart thermal management that monitors real-time cell conditions and day-ahead load forecasts to optimize cooling. By adjusting coolant temperatures before load changes, it reduces auxiliary power consumption by as much as 20% and works to limit calendar aging, helping extend battery life. Noise levels stay below 60 dB at one meter, comparable to the ambient sound of a normal conversation, which the company says allows installation near office buildings, commercial centers and residential-adjacent areas. Inside the battery pack, the design uses high-temperature fire-resistant isolation and reinforced six-sided insulation, supported by 40 NTC temperature sensors monitoring 64 cells per pack, a density of 0.625 NTC per cell that the company describes as well above the industry average. Pack-level safeguards include pressure relief valves, electrical insulation sheets, crash frames, high-strength crossbeams, leakage detection and optional aerosol fire suppression in select regions. At system level, the SigenCube adds top explosion vents, smoke and heat detectors, emergency fans, cabinet-level aerosol suppression and a water firefighting interface, backed by eight layers of overcurrent protection. A sealed cooling loop provides a 10-year coolant life, reducing scheduled replacements. Pack-level active balancing delivers a 7A balancing current, keeping battery strings uniformly balanced and removing the need for periodic on-site state-of-charge calibration. The system offers grid-forming capabilities with 0ms load-side disruption to keep critical industrial loads running without interruption. It also provides 100% three-phase imbalance handling under complex load conditions, fault ride-through during voltage sags and swells, and MWh-level black start without external grid support. Additional grid-stabilizing features include rapid reactive power response for voltage regulation, virtual inertia support for grid frequency, active power oscillation damping and weak grid adaptation for stable operation in high-impedance environments. artigo.texto: Microsoft: lucro acima da expectativa (Divulgação/Getty Images) Editor de Invest Publicado em 28 de outubro de 2026 às 17h33. A Microsoft abriu o ano fiscal de 2027 com números acima do que Wall Street esperava. A empresa lucrou US$ 36,6 bilhões no trimestre encerrado em setembro, 32% a mais que no mesmo período de 2025. O lucro por ação ajustado ficou em US$ 4,89, contra consenso de US$ 4,71 compilado pela FactSet. A receita chegou a US$ 92,3 bilhões, alta de 19% e cerca de US$ 1,7 bilhão acima dos US$ 90,6 bilhões projetados pelos analistas. A alta de 32% no lucro é "inflada" por uma base de comparação fraca. Há um ano, a Microsoft registrou perdas de US$ 3,1 bilhões com seus investimentos na OpenAI, dona do ChatGPT. Agora, a participação gerou ganho de US$ 207 milhões. Excluído esse efeito, como a própria empresa faz no indicador ajustado, o lucro foi de US$ 36,4 bilhões, com crescimento de 18%. O Azure, plataforma que aluga capacidade de computação para empresas treinarem e rodarem modelos de inteligência artificial, faturou US$ 33,2 bilhões, alta de 48%. É o ritmo mais forte da série de cinco trimestres divulgada pela empresa e supera os 44,3% esperados pelos analistas, segundo a FactSet. Sozinho, o Azure já responde por mais de um terço da receita total da Microsoft. Somado ao Microsoft 365 e a outros serviços corporativos, o negócio de nuvem movimentou US$ 63,9 bilhões, com crescimento de 30%, acima dos 27% registrados no trimestre anterior. Na versão corporativa do pacote de escritório, a receita subiu 17%, puxada pela migração de clientes para planos mais caros, incluindo o assistente de IA Copilot. O número de licenças corporativas cresceu 5%. A demanda contratada dá a dimensão do que ainda está por vir. A carteira de contratos comerciais a reconhecer chegou a US$ 677 bilhões, alta de 73%. Cerca de 30% desse valor, algo próximo de US$ 200 bilhões, deve virar receita nos próximos 12 meses. Já o valor dos novos contratos assinados com empresas caíram 12% no trimestre, porque a base de comparação inclui um grande contrato do Azure fechado há um ano. Com isso, o segmento Agents and Infra, que reúne nuvem e softwares corporativos, faturou US$ 76,8 bilhões (alta de 25%) e teve lucro operacional de US$ 40,6 bilhões (alta de 24%). Para atender essa demanda, a Microsoft segue ampliando data centers, em linha com a aposta bilionária das big techs em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. Esses investimentos, incluindo arrendamentos, somaram US$ 45,2 bilhões no trimestre, 30% a mais que um ano antes e o equivalente a quase metade da receita do período. Cerca de três quartos foram para ativos de vida curta, principalmente processadores e chips gráficos (GPUs), usados em serviços de IA. O efeito aparece no caixa. A geração de caixa operacional cresceu 29%, para US$ 58 bilhões, mas os pagamentos por equipamentos e instalações dobraram, para US$ 39,4 bilhões. O fluxo de caixa livre, assim, caiu 27%, para US$ 18,6 bilhões. A empresa devolveu US$ 10,2 bilhões aos acionistas, sendo US$ 7,3 bilhões em dividendos e US$ 2,9 bilhões em recompra de ações. O crescimento acelerado também pesa na lucratividade da nuvem. De cada US$ 100 que a Microsoft fatura com o negócio, o que sobra depois dos custos diretos para entregar o serviço caiu de US$ 68 para US$ 66. Isso acontece porque o Azure, que é o produto que mais cresce, dá menos lucro que outros produtos da área. Ainda assim, a empresa como um todo ficou mais rentável, com a margem operacional passando de 49% para 50%. A Microsoft também segurou os gastos. As despesas operacionais subiram só 6%, e o número de funcionários caiu 2% em um ano. Nos negócios ligados a PCs, games e buscas, o desempenho foi mais fraco. A divisão Devices and Consumer faturou US$ 15,5 bilhões, queda de 3%. As vendas de licenças do Windows para fabricantes de computadores e de dispositivos próprios recuaram 22%, diante de uma base inflada pelo fim do suporte ao Windows 10 no ano passado, da redução de estoques por fabricantes e de um mercado de PCs mais fraco. No Xbox, a receita com conteúdo e serviços caiu 2% e a de consoles, 14%. A compensação veio da publicidade em buscas, que cresceu 12% sem considerar os custos de aquisição de tráfego, com Bing, Edge e LinkedIn. O lucro operacional da divisão subiu 2%, para US$ 5,4 bilhões, ajudado pela menor amortização de ativos da compra da Activision Blizzard. Após a divulgação do resultado, a ação da companhia, que havia fechado o pregão de hoje em queda, subia 4,4%.

artigo.texto: Franklin County residents urge planning commission to address data center concerns FRANKLIN COUNTY, Va. (WSET) — Franklin County residents continue to push back against proposed data centers as the county’s Planning Commission considers revisions to its zoning ordinances. At their work session Wednesday night, the commission reviewed proposed changes to Articles 2 and 3 of the county’s zoning ordinances. Discussions focused on whether community complaints should be allowed anonymously, how county officials can inspect land and structures, and how developers must submit permits and applications. SEE ALSO: Virginia voters decide whether to enshrine reproductive rights in state constitution But Christine Sizemore, vice chair of the Franklin County Community Coalition, urged commissioners to prioritize changes addressing data centers rather than waiting until the broader zoning rewrite is complete. “I would appreciate it if the Planning Commission would consider undertaking a discussion around how to amend either the current ordinance and also integrate data center requirements into the Berkeley draft rewrite at this point instead of waiting until we are all done and then do it,” Sizemore said. She added that residents are concerned about the county’s existing protections against data center development. “As you may have heard last week, we are absolutely not protected when it comes to data centers,” Sizemore said. Commission members did not comment on data centers during Wednesday’s meeting. However, they said they plan to address the issue at next week’s meeting.

artigo.texto: Addressing the Environmental Challenges of Wind, Solar, and Energy Storage in Texas Written by: Brent Bennett, Ph.D. and Cullen Neely Download the full paper here. Key Points - Using wind and solar to produce electricity requires 22 times more land for wind and roughly seven times more land for solar than comparable fossil fuel generation resources. - Most states around the country, including Texas, are just now catching up to crafting regulations to govern the siting and disposal of wind, solar, and energy storage, and gaps exist that will create billions of dollars in future unfunded liabilities. - Texas needs to enact more comprehensive siting and disposal regulations to protect landowners’ property rights and prevent future waste-disposal disasters. - Texas also must reform its electricity market to stop overbuilding distant wind and solar generation and the transmission needed to connect those resources to the grid. Executive Summary Texas has become the nation’s leading producer of both wind and solar energy, with over 15,000 wind turbines and rapid utility-scale solar growth transforming the state’s electricity landscape. However, the explosive growth of these resources—which require dozens of times more land per unit of energy produced than natural gas, coal, and nuclear—is imposing distinctive burdens on neighboring landowners and generating waste streams that existing regulations were not designed to handle. In many ways, electric grids across the country are trading the air emissions challenges associated with fossil fuel combustion for the land use and materials challenges of handling large amounts of wind, solar, and energy storage facilities. This paper examines the current state of electricity generation permitting in Texas as it applies to wind, solar, and energy storage facilities. It reviews the land and material intensity of renewable energy technologies, catalogs the siting and disposal challenges they create, surveys how other states have responded to these challenges, and traces the legislative history of relevant Texas permitting laws. The Texas Legislature has made meaningful progress in recent sessions on decommissioning and disposal requirements, but significant gaps remain—particularly in the area of siting and permitting, where no statewide framework yet exists for wind, solar, or battery facilities. Introduction In addition to being highly variable and weather-dependent, a fundamental challenge of wind and solar energy is their low power density. Wind turbines and solar panels require dozens of times more land and materials to produce equivalent amounts of energy as natural gas and coal power plants. This reality has profound implications for land use, property rights, and environmental stewardship in Texas and across the nation. Figure 1 illustrates the dramatic differences in land requirements across electricity generation technologies. For a 1,000 megawatt (MW) power plant, nuclear energy requires approximately 1 square mile, coal requires roughly 2 square miles, and natural gas about 3 square miles. By contrast, solar energy requires approximately 27 square miles, and wind energy demands about 89 square miles to produce the same amount of power. These figures account for the full land footprint required for fuel extraction and transportation for fossil fuels and nuclear, making the comparison especially striking. Importantly, they do not include the additional transmission infrastructure that wind and solar require, as these facilities are typically located far from the population centers they serve. Figure 1 Land Required to Produce 5,200 GWh of Power in One Year—Equal to the Average Annual Output of a 1,000 MW Power Plant Operating at a 60% Capacity Factor Note. The figure represents the amount of land required for 5,000 GWh of annual production, assuming a 60% capacity factor for nuclear, coal, and natural gas, 20% for solar, and 34% for wind. Capacity density for gas, coal, and nuclear derived from Smil, V., Power Density, MIT Press, 2015. Capacity density for wind and solar taken from Lopez, A. et al., Renewable energy technical potential and supply curves for the contiguous United States: 2024 edition, National Renewable Energy Laboratory, June 2025, pp. 4, 15 (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/2500362). Land requirements for wind include spacing between turbines. Values for wind and solar do not include land for transmission lines or energy storage to ensure equal reliability to dispatchable power. The implications of this low power density become even more dramatic when applied to real-world policy scenarios. Previous Life:Powered research calculated the land required if Texas were to transition to 100% wind and solar electricity generation and found that such a transition would require approximately 6 million more acres of land than the current electric grid—more than five times the area of Harris County, which is where Houston is located (Bennett, 2019, p. 3). The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region is currently on a path toward 50% wind and solar generation by 2030, which will require more than 1 million additional acres compared to what was required for electricity generation and delivery in 2018 (see Table 1 below). Texas consumes approximately 13% of the nation’s total electricity (EIA, 2025, Table 2.8), and other parts of the country, particularly the Northeast, will likely require a greater share of land to achieve high wind and solar penetration, given that Texas’s geography and climate are better suited to wind and solar generation than most other states. This enormous land footprint carries cascading consequences: displaced agricultural activity, fragmented wildlife habitats, altered rural landscapes, and the need for thousands of miles of new transmission lines. artigo.texto: Data center demand for electrical equipment soared over the past quarter while utility sales have slowed somewhat, company leaders said Tuesday during Hubbell's third-quarter earnings call. Hubbell's Electrical Solutions segment saw organic sales rise 22% year over- year, Chief Financial Officer Joe Capozzoli said. Sales to data centers rose more than 80% — exceeding the company's expectations for the year — while demand from light industrial and other nonresidential markets remained strong. The 2025 acquisition of NSI Industries drove another 29% increase on top of organic sales growth, according to slides released during the call. In the Utility Solutions segment of the company, organic sales rose just 5%, with an 8% increase in grid infrastructure sales offset by a 4% decline in sales by the company's grid automation division. Most of the decline, according to CEO Gerben Bakker, could be attributed to slowing sales of substation control houses and a temporary shortage of metering equipment. Bakker said the shortage, which occurred when one of the company's contract manufacturers was unable to source a key component from a supplier, should be resolved by the end of the year. “We continue to believe utility T&D markets are in the early stages of an attractive multiyear investment cycle, driven by aging infrastructure and bolstered by load growth and data center interconnections,” Bakker said. 15% Proportion of Hubbell electrical segment sales that now go to data centers. Net third-quarter sales in Hubbell's utility segment, up 8.9% over last year. Bakker said Hubbell continues to invest about $25 million per quarter in additional manufacturing capacity, and that the company plans to double that to $50 million per quarter next year. Most of the expansions, he said, involve adding machines and assembly lines to existing factories—though in some cases the company has begun adding square footage to existing factories as well. “You can only keep adding so many machines before you run out of roofline,” he said. Capozzoli noted that the majority of the new capacity will serve transmission, substation and data center markets. Despite the ongoing expansion and rising inflation, Capozzoli said the company continues to improve its operating margins in line with a long-term effort to cut costs. Hubbell has also secured higher prices for its products in recent quarters, which in tandem with growing demand and expanding productivity has allowed the company's margins to stay ahead of inflationary pressures. However, Capozzoli said Hubbell plans to implement 2027 price increases early, beginning this November, to address cost inflation and maintain the company's margins.

artigo.texto: O Santander aposta no armazenamento de energia em baterias para ampliar sua atuação no financiamento da transição energética no Brasil. No quinto leilão do Eco Invest, o banco levou a gestão da cadeia de beneficiamento de minerais críticos, baterias e mobilidade elétrica, que vai mobilizar R$ 6,5 bilhões. O programa do Tesouro Nacional para atrair capital privado para projetos verdes opera na modalidade blended finance, em que o capital subsidiado público entra para reduzir custos ou mitigar riscos, atraindo recursos privados em maior escala. O quinto leilão vai mobilizar até R$ 49,9 bilhões em seis cadeias produtivas ligadas à inovação. Esta edição busca conectar o capital produtivo e financeiro a universidades, centros de pesquisa e startups. Para isso, combina três mecanismos financeiros: fundos de investimento em inovação, uma linha de crédito corporativo e recursos não reembolsáveis para pesquisa aplicada e empreendedorismo de base tecnológica. O Tesouro vai aportar R$ 13,2 bilhões em capital catalítico nesta edição, com o custo de 1% ao ano para os bancos: R$ 9 bilhões para fundos de inovação investirem em dívida conversível em participação (equity) e R$ 4,2 bilhões para crédito corporativo. Os bancos vencedores terão que captar os outros R$ 36,7 bilhões de recursos privados. O principal critério de seleção do Eco Invest é a alavancagem. Para os recursos destinados ao fundo de inovação, o Santander ofereceu a alavancagem máxima de duas vezes: o Tesouro entra com R$ 1,5 bilhão e o banco capta outros R$ 3 bilhões. Na linha de crédito, a alavancagem ofertada foi de 20 vezes: o Tesouro vai colocar R$ 100 milhões e o Santander terá que captar outros R$ 1,9 bilhão para oferecer empréstimos para a cadeia de baterias, minerais críticos e mobilidade elétrica. O banco tem nas baterias sua estratégia principal por considerá-las a oportunidade mais madura entre as três frentes. Segundo Júlio Meirelles, responsável pela área de energia e project finance do Santander, o Brasil está passando por um movimento semelhante ao que aconteceu em outros mercados: após forte expansão das fontes de energia renováveis, cresceu a necessidade de soluções para armazenar energia e dar mais flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico. O executivo afirma que o Santander participou de cerca de 70 operações de financiamento de armazenamento nos últimos oito anos, em dez geografias, incluindo Europa, Estados Unidos e Chile. “O armazenamento é a próxima etapa da expansão renovável no Brasil. As baterias podem ajudar a aproveitar a energia que seria desperdiçada quando a geração solar e eólica supera a capacidade de absorção do sistema, além de viabilizar a continuidade da expansão das fontes renováveis”, afirma Meirelles. Apetite por baterias O governo federal prepara um leilão para contratar capacidade de armazenamento de energia, previsto para acontecer em dezembro. O Santander olhou para o certame para estimar o potencial de negócios do setor. “A expectativa é que a contratação de baterias crie demanda não apenas para os operadores dos sistemas, mas também para fabricantes e fornecedores”, diz Meirelles. Além dessa demanda, o banco também considerou os projetos de geração renovável que podem incorporar baterias independentemente da contratação pública e os investimentos necessários para desenvolver a cadeia de fornecimento. Outras fontes de financiamento da cadeia de valor das baterias também foram analisadas. Projetos que utilizam conteúdo local, por exemplo, podem ter acesso a linhas de financiamento subsidiadas, como a Finame, do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). Os importados ficam de fora dessa linha. “Mesmo quando há funding subsidiado, ele vai preencher um certo espaço. Existe um gap que pode gerar oportunidade para nós”, afirma Meirelles. “Essa análise de onde há espaço para o banco atuar com alternativas de financiamento foi o que fundamentou a estratégia do lance do Santander no Eco Invest.” Minerais e mobilidade elétrica Em minerais críticos, o executivo afirma que o banco está mapeando projetos com clientes. Embora reconheça a importância estratégica de terras raras no contexto geopolítico e de mercado, o banco pretende avaliar oportunidades com diferentes minerais, de acordo com os critérios de elegibilidade do leilão. O Santander também considera financiar empresas em estágio inicial, as chamadas mineradoras juniores. “O edital tem claramente um viés de atuar nos empreendimentos dentro da cadeia que são incipientes. Isso foi levado em consideração na nossa estratégia.” Isso abre espaço para avaliar empresas em fase pré-operacional, que hoje dependem de capital estrangeiro, sobretudo. Essas empresas costumam usar capital próprio na pré-operação e, em etapas seguintes, como a construção da mina em escala industrial, fazem novas captações via equity e se financiam também com contratos de venda antecipada (offtake). A mobilidade elétrica é a frente com menor expectativa de geração de volume de negócios entre as três, afirma Alex Sciacio, líder de finanças sustentáveis do Santander, “com a expectativa de ter tickets médios menores do que projetos de mineração e de armazenamento.” Há uma obrigação no edital do leilão do Eco Invest de que 10% dos recursos devem ser direcionados para mobilidade elétrica de duas rodas, como motos e bicicletas. Equity Os leilões do Eco Invest trabalharam, até agora, com instrumentos de dívida (no primeiro, segundo e quarto leilões) e de participação acionária (no terceiro). Nesta quinta concorrência, o modelo é híbrido, com a introdução de dívida conversível. Até agora, o Santander só havia vencido concorrências de dívida. Como este é o primeiro com operação de equity que o banco venceu, a estratégia para fazer os desembolsos ainda não está inteiramente definida. O banco considera tanto aportes diretos quanto estruturas de fundos, segundo Meirelles. artigo.texto: Pine Island settles Project Skyway lawsuit, clears way for state data center review PINE ISLAND, Minn. (KTTC) – The legal battle over Pine Island’s Project Skyway data center came to an end Wednesday night, as city leaders approved a settlement deal. It paves the way for a new state environmental review. Under the deal, state agencies will conduct a review of water, noise, light, energy and grid impacts, plus a mitigation plan to lessen any potential harm. That includes 90 days of public comment which will be 60 days at the state level and 30 days at the city with public meetings. City leaders will review and respond to those comments. The new state review will control future decisions, and no construction can start until the city approves that mitigation plan. According to Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy CEO Kathryn Hoffman, this is the first time state agencies will conduct an environmental review for a data center in Minnesota. “The city will have an opportunity to decide, does this make sense for us? Do we feel that our resources are protected, that this is a good deal for the city of Pine Island?” Hoffman said. “And they can decide whether to approve it, to modify it, maybe add some more conditions if they want, or reject it.” Developer Ryan Companies says all sides found common ground to settle, and while prior city approvals remain valid, the project welcomes state-level review describing an air-cooled system with no constant water use and major clean-energy investment. “We’ve worked really, really hard to lean into the community, but also create a project that meets Minnesota’s highest standards,” said Senior Vice President of Development Peter Fitzgerald. “Minnesota has some of the highest standards in the country. And the fact that we have a client that’s willing to meet or exceed those high standards is really remarkable.” Moving forward, the state will conduct a new environmental review as developers submit their paperwork, then the city will vote on any added protections. Wednesday’s vote came at a special council meeting with no public comment. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. Copyright 2026 KTTC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- HiTHIUM is showcasing the ARKVOLT F8S and HeroEE 16 at All Energy Australia 2026 on 28–29 October, offering distinct residential storage configurations. The F8S focuses on flexible high-voltage expansion, while the 16 kWh HeroEE 16 offers greater starting capacity for compatible low-voltage systems. Australia installed 276,011 home batteries in the first half of 2026, an increase of 52% compared with the preceding six months, according to the Clean Energy Council. The country also added 1.89 GW of rooftop solar capacity, with the federal Cheaper Home Batteries Program supporting battery uptake. The modular high-voltage F8S uses DC-BOOST technology to manage battery modules independently, allowing new and existing modules to work together. Its 8–32 kWh configurations enable households to expand storage in stages while retaining installed modules. It is rated for at least 11,000 cycles under specified test conditions, supporting long-term use. The HeroEE 16 combines a 16 kWh low-voltage lithium iron phosphate (LFP) design with a cycle-life rating of up to 11,000 cycles. Parallel connections allow expansion, while individual modules can be checked or replaced without dismantling the battery. It is designed for households seeking higher initial capacity and integration with compatible low-voltage inverters. With compatible inverters, both products can store rooftop solar power for later use. Backup functions require additional equipment. Ratel, General Manager at HiTHIUM Hero Energy, said: "As the global home energy transition deepens, the residential storage market is evolving to meet increasingly diverse and sophisticated customer needs. Leveraging HiTHIUM's deep expertise in cell R&D and smart manufacturing, we integrate inherent safety at the cell level into our system designs to deliver reliable, market-specific solutions for Australia. For us, global expansion is about more than geographic reach. We are dedicated to building long-term, sustainable value with our regional partners." HiTHIUM draws on its battery cell and system engineering expertise for residential storage. Cumulative global shipments exceeded 200 GWh as of October 2026. Its Australian utility-scale work includes its role in supplying 640 MWh of batteries for Lightsource bp's Woolooga BESS in Queensland, currently undergoing commissioning, and the supply of 500 MWh of batteries for FRV's Gnarwarre BESS in Victoria, under construction since August 2025. HiTHIUM aims to build ties with local installers, distributors and industry partners. artigo.texto: UCSB chemical engineer to develop low-cost technologies for renewable energy storage Coming with nearly $1 million in unrestricted research funding, a 2026 Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering has been awarded to UC Santa Barbara’s J. Tyler Mefford. The assistant professor of chemical engineering will use the support to pursue more affordable ways to store renewable energy for months at a time, a major challenge in the transition to cleaner energy sources. Mefford is one of 20 early-career researchers this year to receive the five-year fellowship. Established in 1988, it supports early-career scientists pursuing ambitious, potentially transformative ideas. Previous fellows have gone on to receive some of science’s highest honors, including Nobel Prizes and election to national academies. “These scientists, engineers and mathematicians are asking ambitious questions about our bodies, our planet, and the technologies shaping our future,” said Nancy Lindborg, president and CEO of the Packard Foundation. “At a time of significant uncertainty in the research landscape, flexible, long-term support for early-career researchers matters more than ever.” Storing renewable energy year-round Mefford’s research focuses on a promising idea to use renewable-generated energy to store hydrogen in inexpensive liquid organic molecules, then recover that energy when it is needed. “If we can figure out how to cycle hydrogen into liquids electrochemically, that should create very low-cost energy storage,” Mefford said. Although solar and wind power have become increasingly economical, storing the electricity they generate remains a challenge. “Renewables today are very affordable,” he said. “For the most part, it’s cheaper to build a solar farm or a wind farm than it is to install a new natural gas plant.” But the transient nature of renewable energy presents a problem, Mefford explained. “When the sun sets, or the wind stops blowing, where do we get our energy from?” In particular, Mefford wants to make the abundant solar energy generated in the summer available during the winter, when limited sunlight means a dropoff in solar energy production. “This project is focused on developing new energy storage technologies and chemistries that could do that at really low cost,” he said. “Basically, we want to make the lowest-cost energy storage technology that has ever existed.” Achieving that goal will require a better understanding of how different materials and catalysts influence the chemical reactions involved in storing and releasing hydrogen. Instead of studying one material at a time, Mefford and his team want to draw inspiration from fields that take a faster-paced approach to discovery. That means screening multiple materials simultaneously to understand the underlying principles of using hydrogen to store energy in liquid form. The approach could help accelerate the development of promising materials and catalysts. High risk, high reward The research is still in its early stages, and the scientific uncertainties make it particularly well suited to the Packard Fellowship’s funding model. “The Packard Foundation is very supportive of high-risk projects that have the potential to be high-reward,” Mefford said. “I am really excited to work on this, and thankful for the Packard Foundation for recognizing the potential impact of this work and for supporting research into renewable and clean energy.” Mefford will use the fellowship to bring on additional students and to support the work of designing and building the instruments that will help his team develop catalysts, improve experimental methods and better understand the chemical reactions involved with storing hydrogen. These resources could accelerate this research at a time when the need for affordable, reliable clean energy is growing. “We have a limited time to solve this problem,” he said. “If we really want a grid powered predominantly by renewable energy, we need to figure out how to mitigate the challenges.”

artigo.texto: Moura vai produzir grandes baterias de olho em leilão Empresa conhecida por baterias de veículos automotivos já atua com equipamentos de grande porte O Grupo Moura, conhecido por sua atuação com baterias automotivas, investirá R$ 200 milhões na ampliação de sua capacidade de produção no complexo fabril de Belo Jardim, no agreste pernambucano. A iniciativa visa implantar uma linha de fabricação para baterias de grande porte, conhecidas pelo jargão “utility scale”, e mira o leilão marcado pelo governo federal para dezembro deste ano. “A gente está se preparando tanto em nível de espaço físico quanto de equipamentos. A linha de produção já foi, inclusive, comprada”, afirmou ao Valor o diretor de operações de lítio da Moura, Spartacus Pedrosa. Segundo o executivo, a iniciativa gerará entre 150 a 200 empregos diretos. A intenção é dar conta da demanda que virá com o certame, que prevê a incorporação de baterias no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), com operação em agosto de 2028. O prazo, para Pedrosa, é desafiador e, por isso, a companhia tomou a decisão de realizar os aportes ainda que a iniciativa seja inédita e objeto de algumas incertezas regulatórias. “A gente está nesse negócio há mais de 10 anos, fomos a primeira empresa a fornecer um sistema 100% nacional para aplicação no Brasil. Então, esse é o contínuo dessa história. Estava muito nítida a necessidade de haver leilão há alguns anos por conta do avanço das energias intermitentes na rede”, afirmou. O executivo avaliou, no entanto, que essa frente de negócio não depende apenas do leilão e disse que a companhia conta com 40 sistemas de armazenamento de maior porte já instalados em clientes industriais e do agronegócio, por exemplo. Outra possível frente de atuação é a de data centers, lembrou. “A vantagem do leilão é que ele traz uma escala que até então se não via. Esse será um legado importante para outros negócios: com o volume, teremos acesso a melhores custos, escala para que se consiga, do ponto de vista industrial, reduzir o preço final para o cliente”, apontou. A companhia também está apostando numa agenda de continuidade de leilões para a tecnologia, completou. Para Pedrosa, porém, as baterias para veículos continuarão sendo o carro-chefe da companhia, mas a ideia é que os sistemas de grande porte ganhem tração com o certame. A expansão conta com parceria da Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL), fabricante chinesa de baterias, que fornecerá os módulos. A partir deles, a Moura atua como integradora, incorporando componentes como inversores, transformadores, além da parte de eletrônica embarcada. Segundo o Grupo Moura, que faturou R$ 5 bilhões no ano passado, o financiamento combina recursos próprios e de instituições como Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), Banco do Nordeste (BNB) e Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep). Ainda para participar do leilão, a Moura credenciou-se junto ao BNDES como fornecedora de sistemas de armazenamento de baterias junto a outras oito companhias e figura ainda na lista de fornecedora de desenvolvimento de projeto de software/firmware (EMS, na sigla em inglês) junto a outras duas concorrentes. O certame está marcado para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro deste ano.

artigo.texto: Publicidade O primeiro leilão de baterias do Brasil teve edital aprovado com mudanças para permitir maior competitividade entre as empresas participantes, além de uma redação mais genérica sobre a base pagadora dos custos da contratação, conforme deliberado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) na terça-feira. Os valores das garantias de proposta e de fiel cumprimento caíram quase 40%, acompanhando a atualização do investimento de referência para as baterias, que passou de R$9,8 milhões para R$6 milhões por megawatt (MW). Também foi aceita a possibilidade de formação de consórcios entre empresas do mesmo grupo econômico, ponto que vinha sendo pleiteado por empresas interessadas. O certame de baterias tem sido amplamente aguardado pelo setor elétrico, uma vez que ampliará o leque de recursos de segurança energética do Brasil em meio ao forte crescimento das fontes renováveis de energia, e já tem mobilizado diversos investidores, incluindo fabricantes estrangeiras e nacionais do segmento. As mudanças no edital devem ajudar a ampliar a disputa no certame inédito, que atraiu cadastramento recorde de mais de 296 gigawatts (GW) de empreendimentos, segundo a agência reguladora. Mas a Aneel manteve exigências para comprovação da capacidade financeira dos empreendedores, visando evitar a participação de ‘aventureiros’ no leilão. Continua depois da publicidade Para consórcios de empresas do mesmo grupo econômico, por exemplo, a comprovação do patrimônio líquido mínimo será feita apenas por meio da controladora, de forma a evitar distorções de dupla contagem de patrimônio, como a que teria ocorrido no leilão de térmicas realizado em março. No caso de fundos de investimento em participações (FIP) com projetos participantes do leilão, deverão ser identificados os cotistas cuja participação indireta seja superior a 5%. A ideia, segundo a Aneel, é exigir a identificação dos investidores que tenham exposição econômica relevante nos projetos vencedores. Os preços-teto do leilão foram fixados em R$1,76 milhão por MW ao ano para a disputa de baterias com conteúdo nacional, marcada para 2 de dezembro, e de R$1,58 milhão por MW ao ano para a concorrência de 4 de dezembro, que não tem exigência de nacionalização. Continua depois da publicidade Já com relação à discussão sobre os pagadores do custo associado ao leilão, tema que ameaça causar uma judicialização, a Aneel retirou do edital referências expressas aos geradores de energia como base pagante, substituindo pela expressão ‘usuários de reserva de capacidade’. No entanto, o regulador ressaltou que isso não muda o entendimento atual de quem são os pagadores — os geradores, conforme definido em lei –, e nem prepara o edital para uma eventual mudança da legislação. Os geradores de energia estão se mobilizando no Congresso para conseguir mudar, antes do leilão em dezembro, o trecho de uma lei que imputa a eles os custos da contratação das baterias para o setor elétrico brasileiro. Continua depois da publicidade Caso isso ocorra, a Aneel irá rediscutir os contratos associados ao leilão, afirmou o relator do processo, Gentil Nogueira. ‘É lógico, há o interesse legítimo na modificação legislativa, a gente compreende essa posição. Mas de qualquer forma, havendo a modificação legislativa, qualquer texto que fosse colocado traria invariavelmente a discussão para a Aneel sobre os efeitos sobre esse contrato’, destacou Nogueira, na véspera.

artigo.texto: District 38 candidates discuss data centers, school budgets, nursing homes HASTINGS, Neb. (KSNB) - Tim Anderson and Janelle Anderson-Ehrke are running against each other for the District 38 seat in the state legislature. The midterm election is Nov. 3. District 38 covers several counties along the Kansas-Nebraska line, from Red Willow County to Nuckolls County, as well as Clay County and part of Phelps County. Local4 discussed several topics with both candidates, including data centers, budget cuts and rural nursing homes. Data centers Tim Anderson said there are local regulations that new data centers should follow. “Data centers definitely need to use the energy and they need to use their own energy and pay their own way there,” Tim Anderson said. “And for water usage, they better have a good plan and information for us about how much water they are going to be using and the type of system that they’re going to be using.” Anderson-Ehrke said data centers need to be locally controlled and need to provide benefits to the state if they want to be located here. “If we put a data center in Nebraska, they need to pay an incentive, not get an incentive,” Anderson-Ehrke said. “Obviously, they want to be here, so we need to make them pay to play. It has to be local control, meaning that we do not put a data center unless that community or that area wants that data center.” Budget cuts and rural schools The candidates also discussed budget cuts and how to protect rural schools and small-town services. Tim Anderson said one of the keys is listening to residents. “I know if you talk about cutting or capping sale or like their taxes, you had better make sure that their services aren’t being cut as well,” Tim Anderson said. “So, like, for instance, Sutton here, like they may need more paras than maybe some, but other people don’t, but we have to listen to make sure that we’re not cutting those services from them by capping.” Anderson-Ehrke said more consistency and transparency in the budget will help protect rural schools and small-town services. “Right now, there’s no incentive to run a fiscally, not that they’re not, but there’s no incentive to run a fiscally responsible school district,” Anderson-Ehrke said. “If there was a bonus system for those districts that are running very efficiently, sharing costs, and most importantly, really focusing on the education component, I think everybody would be on the same page.” Rural nursing homes The candidates also discussed protecting rural nursing homes. Tim Anderson said a key to supporting the facilities as they age is through the pharmacists who supply medications. “We need to make sure that our pharmacists are close to each of us, so we have to protect the pharmacies that provide the medicines for those facilities,” Tim Anderson said. Anderson-Ehrke said she would like to see more funding to support Medicaid patients. “We’ve got to make sure that we’re getting them the funding they deserve because we’re getting more, instead of private pay, our Medicaid patients are becoming even, and that makes it unprofitable, so we’re going to have to look at that model and figure out ways that we can fund it properly,” Anderson-Ehrke said. Pillen says Nebraska’s infrastructure can handle current data center demand Governor spoke at a Fremont event on grid investments; Democratic opponent Lynne Walz criticizes Pillen’s timing on halting incentives FREMONT, Neb. (WOWT) - Gov. Jim Pillen said Thursday that Nebraska can currently handle its energy demands, including the strain from data centers on the state’s electric grid. Pillen was joined by state and federal leaders at an event in Fremont to highlight ongoing investments in Nebraska’s electric grid. The group announced a new round of funding. Grid investments In 2025, Nebraska was awarded nearly $14 million to modernize and strengthen Nebraska utilities. The funding is going toward items including stronger utility poles, additional power lines and modern substations to help keep power on in homes during storms. Pillen, Walz on data centers After the presentation, Pillen was asked about the strain data centers place on the grid. Pillen, who is running for reelection, said any future projects must protect Nebraska’s water supply, receive no tax incentives and provide community enhancements up front. Pillen said a state task force is set to meet in November to establish guardrails for future data centers. Lynne Walz, the Democratic candidate for governor — one of Pillen’s opponents in next week’s election — was asked about data center impacts. A spokesperson for the campaign responded with a statement. First Alert 6 also reached out to Brett Lindstrom, who is also running for governor, for comment and has not heard back. artigo.texto: Preparations are underway for repowering the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm, which was commissioned in 2006 near Šibenik. Croatia’s first wind power plant – Ravne 1 (5.95 MW) – began producing electricity two years earlier. After 20 years of operation, the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm in Croatia is entering reconstruction, and the comparison of technical details demonstrates how much wind energy technology has advanced during that period. The plant, built by Germany’s wpd, consists of 14 Enercon E-48 wind turbines with an individual capacity of 800 kW, mounted on 50-meter-high towers, with a rotor diameter of 48 meters. The total installed capacity is 11.2 MW. The battery’s role would be to optimize the wind farm’s production The makeover of the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm involves the replacement of the 14 existing wind turbines with no more than five new ones, of up to 6 MW each, according to the environmental impact report for the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm repowering project. The request for the assessment was submitted to the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition by Vjetroelektrana Trtar Krtolin, registered in Dubrovnik. The investor also plans to install a battery energy storage system (BESS) of up to 10 MW and 20 MWh. The battery would be used for the optimization of the wind farm’s production, namely storing energy from production when the plant is operating at full generating capacity, and delivering it to the grid when production within the electricity system is insufficient and the timing is most favorable, the report reads. Extension of operational lifespan The investor explained that the project’s objective is to repower the wind farm to allow for the extension of its operational lifespan, enabling energy generation in a safe, economically viable, and environmentally friendly manner, and the delivery of electricity into the Croatian power system. In line with the European Union’s directives on repowering renewable electricity plants, the EIA is limited to potential effects arising from changes or expansion versus the original project, the investor noted. Of note, wpd said in mid-2023 that it planned to build a solar power plant at the site of its existing wind farm Katuni in Croatia.

artigo.texto: Data center apologists on the Pulaski County Quorum Court pulled out all the stops on Tuesday night in a last-ditch effort to help AVAIO Digital build in Pulaski County sans any sort of regulations on noise, light pollution and energy and water consumption. Those efforts failed. County Judge Barry Hyde vetoed the ordinance last month, after the Sept. 22 vote to pass the regulations. At Tuesday night’s meeting, his vote was overridden in a 10-4 vote. Hoping to sway the vote, Justice of the Peace Douglas House, a Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders appointee and former Republican House member who joined the court last month, gave a lengthy invective about the threat of legal action from AVAIO, based on documents he claims to have received from AVAIO’s legal representation at Kutak Rock law firm. “These folks are fixin’ to go to court with us,” House said. “They have already told us they’re going to sue. I have asked them to wait and let this process work out and they have so far withheld the legal action at this time. They’re not going to wait any longer.” House attended the Pulaski County Planning Board meeting earlier on Tuesday, saying he had written an alternative piece of legislation to the one presented by Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood and finally passed. He said at the Quorum Court’s agenda meeting two weeks ago that he would pursue his proposed ordinance if the justices of the peace were unable to override Hyde’s veto, but that if the override was successful, he would discard his measure. He repeated that on Tuesday, telling planners his measure, at this point, still needed some revisions. The irony is that the Pulaski County Planning Board and Quorum Court have since May dragged out efforts to pass a moratorium to pause the incoming project, in order to get proper regulations in place, arguably giving AVAIO Digital a longer timeline to build what’s known as “vested rights” — legalese for more grounds to sue — in its massive $6 billion project outside of Wrightsville. AVAIO has had logging trucks at the site all summer, residents living on the edge of the project say, and the crews have been clearing trees on the site throughout the entire battle over regulations. In September, the company bought 300 adjoining acres next to its already-enormous project site, indicating it has no intentions to leave town. “I’m sympathetic. I wouldn’t want this thing in my backyard either,” House said. “But the fact is we can’t let emotion dictate how we’re going to vote. We have to follow the law.” Tina Ward, the justice of the peace who represents Ward 9 — the working-class, minority-heavy area where both the AVAIO and Google data centers are planned — shot back at House, “We were elected. You were selected.” Dominique Lane, the deputy county attorney, was also asked to read a freshly issued legal opinion by Attorney General Tim Griffin on the matter. Lane, reciting and paraphrasing sections of the opinion, which few in the room had read, said that the county “has limited authority to regulate a data center” without a zoning ordinance in place. On the matter of personal liability, the AG is of the opinion that the elected officials’ personal immunity from an AVAIO lawsuit would be covered “unless it is waived through applicable insurance coverage,” a point many JPs (and likely everyone in the audience) struggled to understand. The justices of the peace — who have heard variations of House’s argument about the threat of lawsuits for months — were unmoved. Those who voted in favor of overriding Hyde’s veto of the ordinance regulating data centers in Pulaski County included Julie Blackwood, Natalie Capps, Donna Massey, Luke McCoy, Kathy Lewison, Steven Person, Curtis Keith, Tina Ward, Patricia Young-Baker, and Staci Medlock. JPs Dianne Curry, Aaron Robinson, Douglas House and Paul Elliott voted against the override. Rebekah Davis was absent. The Quorum Court now faces the unenviable task of sorting out how to implement the ordinance on an emerging industry that has sizable impacts the public — and regulators — are scrambling to understand. The regulations have a sweeping and technical scope, dealing with matters as diverse as wastewater and fire prevention to keeping noise and light pollution to a minimum. Wendell Griffen, the Democratic candidate for county judge and drafter of the ordinance, spoke during a public comment period, noting that the regulations are not anti-industry or anti-development but an attempt to put the public back in the driver’s seat on a project many didn’t know about until years into its development. “Regulation is not destruction of development,” Griffen said. “It is not destruction of industry. It is the protection of the people that industry is supposed to serve.” Griffen beat Hyde in the Democratic primary in March, although Hyde’s political sympathies have been called into question. A September report on campaign contributions showed that Hyde had given to a number of Democratic causes, but he also contributed almost $2,100 to Sanders’ reelection effort. Byron Tate contributed additional reporting for this article.

artigo.texto: Como ISA Energia quer crescer no descompasso entre data centers e rede elétrica CEO Rui Chammas vê demanda por novas conexões em São Paulo, mas orienta empresas a antecipar pedidos diante do tempo necessário para construir a infraestrutura elétrica Pedro Gil Editor do Exame INSIGHT Publicado em 29 de outubro de 2026 às 07:00. RESUMO ＋ Rui Chammas, CEO da transmissora ISA Energia Brasil, alertou que a expansão dos data centers em São Paulo exigirá novos investimentos em transmissão, mas o prazo da infraestrutura elétrica não acompanha o ritmo dos projetos. Responsável por 30% da transmissão de energia do país e 95% em São Paulo, a companhia já possui conexões com data centers e prevê ampliar a rede. A expansão dos data centers em São Paulo deve exigir novos investimentos em transmissão de energia, mas há um descompasso entre o prazo de implantação desses empreendimentos e o de construção da infraestrutura elétrica. O alerta é de Rui Chammas, CEO da ISA Energia Brasil, que tem orientado empresários do setor a antecipar suas demandas para que as conexões estejam disponíveis quando os projetos precisarem delas. “A velocidade dos data centers é diferente da velocidade que a gente consegue desenvolver infraestrutura de transmissão”, afirmou o executivo em entrevista ao EXAME Insight. Atualmente, a ISA é responsável por transmitir 30% da energia do país e 95% da energia do estado de São Paulo. A companhia já possui conexões com data centers e vê no crescimento desses investimentos uma oportunidade para ampliar sua infraestrutura. “O que a gente tem percebido é que este crescimento demandará investimento em mais infraestrutura em São Paulo, onde a gente opera muito bem”, disse. A expansão da rede já aparece no balanço. No segundo trimestre de 2026, a ISA registrou receita líquida regulatória de R$ 1,24 bilhão, alta de 21% sobre o mesmo período do ano anterior, impulsionada pela entrada em operação de projetos e por reforços nas instalações existentes. O Ebitda, lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciação e amortização, somou R$ 966,9 milhões, avanço de 22%. Os investimentos chegaram a R$ 1,1 bilhão no trimestre. A necessidade de novas conexões aparece em um momento em que o setor elétrico enfrenta uma sobreoferta de geração. Para o executivo, o Brasil passou por um excesso de investimentos nessa atividade e precisará de tempo até que a demanda absorva a energia disponível. Ao mesmo tempo, serão necessários ajustes na rede para lidar com as oscilações da produção solar e eólica. É nessa frente que a ISA também busca oportunidades. A empresa estuda participar do leilão de reserva de capacidade com baterias, destinadas principalmente ao atendimento no fim do dia, quando a geração solar deixa de produzir. A companhia já investiu em baterias na divisa entre São Paulo e Paraná. Em Ribeirão Preto, instalou um equipamento conhecido pela sigla FACTS, que permite controlar o fluxo de energia nas linhas e contribui para a estabilidade da rede. “A transmissão está ajudando a minimizar os impactos dessa sobreoferta, ao mesmo tempo que garante estabilidade para a rede”, afirmou. Para financiar os projetos, a ISA tem recorrido a debêntures de infraestrutura. Segundo o executivo, as emissões permitem captar recursos com remuneração ligada ao IPCA, índice que também corrige suas receitas, acrescida de uma taxa de juros real. Onde falta energia O custo dessa expansão, porém, pesa no resultado. Apesar do crescimento operacional, o lucro líquido regulatório caiu 32% no segundo trimestre, para R$ 173,9 milhões, afetado pelo aumento das despesas financeiras relacionadas ao endividamento. No acumulado do primeiro semestre, o lucro nessa mesma base somou R$ 531,6 milhões, queda de 10%. A conta exige que a companhia estime o custo futuro da dívida ao decidir quanto pode oferecer nos leilões de transmissão. O objetivo é preservar uma rentabilidade superior ao custo de financiamento. Em julho, a ISA também reforçou sua estrutura de capital com uma oferta primária de ações de R$ 1,2 bilhão. Desde 2019, a ISA colocou em operação 17 projetos de transmissão. Segundo o CEO, esses empreendimentos apresentam, na média, taxa interna de retorno do acionista superior a 10%. Há mais dois projetos em construção. 'Perguntas frequentes' Por que a expansão dos data centers em São Paulo exige novos investimentos em energia? ＋ A expansão exige mais infraestrutura de transmissão para conectar os novos data centers à rede elétrica. Segundo Rui Chammas, CEO da ISA Energia Brasil, o prazo de implantação desses empreendimentos é menor que o necessário para construir a infraestrutura de transmissão. O que as empresas de data centers devem fazer para garantir conexão à rede elétrica? ＋ As empresas devem antecipar suas demandas de energia, segundo Rui Chammas. O CEO da ISA Energia Brasil afirma que esse planejamento permite disponibilizar as conexões quando os projetos precisarem delas. Qual é a participação da ISA Energia Brasil na transmissão de energia? ＋ A ISA Energia Brasil transmite 30% da energia do país e 95% da energia do estado de São Paulo. artigo.texto: MONTGOMERY COUNTY, Texas – Texas is becoming a hot spot for data centers. The Lone Star State is home to more than 300 data centers, according to ENOUGH previous reporting, with several proposed in Montgomery County. As Election Day approaches, some voters are questioning how the rapid growth of the industry could affect their daily lives — and their ballots. Data centers help power everything from artificial intelligence to the apps people use every day. They require enormous amounts of electricity and often water to keep machines running. For some Montgomery County residents, the connection between data centers and everyday life isn’t immediately clear. “It may or may not affect day to day, but honestly I don’t have enough research behind it to connect with what I’m dealing with on a day to day basis as far as what I’m spending money on,” said Ashley Morgan, a voter in Montgomery County. A new University of Houston survey shows many Texas voters are questioning whether the benefits of data centers are worth the cost. Jobs, growth, concerns over who pays the bill Not everyone sees the issue the same way. For those in industries tied to the real estate and development boom, data centers represent economic opportunity. “I’m in commercial real estate, so we got several deals just in our small office in The Woodlands that we’re working that, you know, are data center related,” said John Hornbuckle, a voter in Montgomery County. “I think it is bringing a lot of good paying jobs to Houston.” Others, however, are concerned about who shoulders the financial burden when large corporations move in. “I feel like the local people around the data centers are the ones paying the bill instead of the people that actually own these data centers,” said Jerry Lazo, a voter in Montgomery County. “I just don’t want any of my bills to go up more from where they are already at.” Ron Welsh, another Montgomery County voter, takes a more pragmatic view. “My thoughts are that data centers are coming. They are not going anywhere, we are going to live with it,” Welsh said. Voters call for limits, oversight According to the University of Houston’s Hobby School survey, 79% of Texas voters want limits on how many data centers can be built in the state. “I feel like it’s something that should be voter approved,” said Michelle Baker, a voter in Montgomery County. Some residents put the issue in even starker terms. “I rather have water than artificial intelligence,” said Teawana, a voter in Montgomery County. No matter which side of the debate voters fall on, this election could help shape Texas’ future on the data center issue.

artigo.texto: BYD diz que pediu a Lula acordo para transferência de tecnologia chinesa Alexandre Baldy afirmou que decisão depende mais de relação diplomática do que da iniciativa corporativa O vice-presidente do Grupo BYD Brasil, Alexandre Baldy, afirmou que pediu ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) que estabeleça um diálogo diplomático que possa permitir a transferência da tecnologia da China para a produção de baterias de lítio. Em entrevista a jornalistas neste 5ª feira (29.out.2026), o executivo explicou que a possibilidade seria uma forma de aproveitar as reservas do elemento na América do Sul. “Até disse ao próprio presidente Lula que a gente possa estabelecer essa relação diplomática com o governo chinês para que possa sonhar com uma transferência de tecnologia. Hoje nós fabricamos o pack da bateria, mas nós importamos a célula da China”, disse. Atualmente, a BYD está avança no processo de nacionalização da produção de veículos em sua fábrica de Camaçari, na Bahia. De acordo com Baldy, 85% das células de bateria usadas na produção são fabricadas na China. Pequim impõe regras restritas sobre a transferência de tecnologia por empresas chinesas em operações no exterior. As novas condições inviabilizam que empresas chinesas transfiram ativos considerados estratégicos para grupos estrangeiros. “É um sonho como esse que a fábrica da BYD idealiza, mas não depende de uma decisão corporativa. É muito mais uma decisão diplomática, em que nós poderíamos aproveitar que temos as maiores bacias de lítio do planeta aqui no cone sul do continente sul-americano”, afirmou. Desde a inauguração da unidade baiana, em outubro de 2025, a montadora chinesa opera no modelo SKD (semi-knocked down), sistema em que kits de peças chegam parcialmente desmontados para montagem final no Brasil. A mudança em curso busca ir além desse modelo, com a instalação de fábricas de estamparia, soldagem e pintura para produzir etapas importantes da carroceria localmente. A BYD estabeleceu como objetivo ultrapassar 50% de conteúdo local na montagem a partir de janeiro de 2027. A meta tem relação direta com as perspectivas de exportação para países do Mercosul, especialmente a Argentina, onde as exigências de conteúdo regional para a importação de veículos podem chegar a 35%. O modelo SKD difere do CKD (completely knock down), em que as peças chegam completamente desmontadas. No CKD, a fábrica local precisa executar praticamente todo o processo de montagem do veículo, incluindo soldagem, pintura e estamparia, o que exige uma estrutura industrial mais robusta. O SKD reduz os investimentos iniciais, acelera a entrada em novos mercados e facilita o treinamento da mão de obra local. O sistema também serve como estratégia para contornar impostos e tarifas de importação em determinados países.

artigo.texto: How neighbors say data center construction has affected Ahwatukee community PHOENIX (AZFamily) — A data center under construction in an Ahwatukee neighborhood is drawing criticism from people who live nearby. Critics of data centers are pointing to the project as an example of problems with data centers and the people building them. Homeowners say construction changed their view Annette Poleon’s home off South 48th Street in Ahwatukee was built in 1993. It was the first home she and her husband owned, and it is where they raised their family. “This would be our forever home,” Poleon said. Poleon said she was born and raised in the Caribbean and grew up with a single mother. “What we’ve been able to do here, the success that we’ve had, as homeowners, as residents of the area has meant so much to us,” she said. Her view started to change in April, when Menlo Digital began construction on a data center campus. The campus will have five two-story buildings totaling nearly 1 million square feet. Menlo Digital calls itself a “data center company … with a proven track record of developing specialized technology facilities.” Records show the company bought the 38-acre site north of Chandler Boulevard in 2015. About nine years later, it submitted plans for a data center, and Phoenix approved them. City says zoning allows data center Ana Marshall, another homeowner, questioned the location. “Why did you build it so close to residential area? There’s so much land and dirt around here. You are telling me the city of Phoenix could not negotiate moving this out a mile out?” Marshall said. In response to questions, a spokesperson for the city said the property was rezoned in 1996 and that a data center is allowed under its current zoning. The city said the project was approved before city leaders adopted a data center ordinance last year. The ordinance is not retroactive. Residents describe construction impacts Marshall provided video from Sept. 12 at 6:02 a.m. that shows construction. She said she hears the construction every morning and cannot escape it because she works from home. “The worst part became when they started digging. I can’t describe it. I mean, if you can picture a monsoon dust storm,” Marshall said. Between May and Oct. 15, building was allowed from 5 a.m. to 7 p.m. The city considers those summer hours. Phoenix confirmed it received complaints about work done earlier than those hours. Neighbors raise health and environmental concerns Neighbors said they are concerned about the noise the data center will emit and about health and environmental impacts. “I don’t know that there is a really a way to coexist this close. This makes sense. There’s just too much of industrial pollution, noise and diesel pollution that will be unavoidable,” Marshall said. The city confirmed no health and environmental impact studies were done. They were not required. “They need to be held accountable for the impact that it has on neighbors,” Poleon said. Poleon said she is not against data centers. “I am not against data centers. I am in IT. I do implementation of IT solutions. What I’m against are data centers in the middle of neighborhoods,” she said. Attorney general to investigate Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes held a town hall on data centers earlier this month. She announced her office would investigate the project and consider a nuisance lawsuit. Neighbors, including Poleon, are considering their options. “I’ve got a 90-year-old mom that lives with me. My husband and I are getting older. We’re about to retire,” Poleon said. “To even think about or consider moving was never on our radar.” Arizona’s Family Investigates reached out to Menlo Digital by phone and email for a response and has not heard back. Neighbors started a nonprofit called Stop the Data Center in Ahwatukee. The group continues to hold regular meetings. How the data center will be powered The company plans to build an electrical substation on site. The site will have more than 100 diesel generators to keep up with demand.
