artigo.texto: O Brasil precisará incorporar a geração de energia nuclear em sua matriz para conseguir atender à imensa demanda energética projetada para a instalação de novos data centers nas próximas décadas. A avaliação é de Celso Cunha, presidente da Abdan (Associação Brasileira para o Desenvolvimento de Atividades Nucleares). Em entrevista recente, o dirigente destacou que o interesse pela energia nuclear disparou em âmbito global, impulsionado justamente pela necessidade de alimentar centros de processamento de dados. A tecnologia é apontada como a alternativa mais eficiente para garantir o fornecimento contínuo e sem interrupções de eletricidade a essas estruturas. Especialistas dos setores de infraestrutura digital e energia elétrica apontam que o país possui plenas condições de se consolidar como o principal polo de data centers na América Latina. Esse otimismo ocorre em meio a uma onda de aportes globais voltados à inteligência artificial, computação em nuvem e expansão da capacidade computacional. Projeções da Moody’s indicam que o mercado brasileiro pode movimentar cifras de até US$ 3 trilhões nos próximos cinco anos. Na corrida por atrais investimentos estrangeiros para o segmento, o território brasileiro leva vantagem frente a outros países sul-americanos devido à sua matriz energética predominantemente renovável e à capacidade de mesclar diferentes fontes. Contudo, há um consenso no setor elétrico de que o apetite voraz por energia desses empreendimentos representa um desafio significativo. Como os data centers operam ininterruptamente — 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana —, eles exigem suprimento constante, seguro e com tarifas competitivas. “Alguns milissegundos sem energia em um data center custam mais caro do que uma usina nuclear inteira”, pontua Celso Cunha. O presidente da Abdan reforça que a geração atômica reúne todas as propriedades exigidas por essas instalações: trata-se de uma fonte firme, capaz de operar sem interrupções, e que apresenta baixos níveis de emissão, superando fontes renováveis intermitentes como a eólica e a solar no quesito estabilidade. Assista à entrevista de Celso Cunha: “O Brasil tem um potencial enorme para atrair data centers e se fala em até 70 gigawatts até 2050, mas é humanamente impossível atender uma demanda dessa sem considerar a energia nuclear. O mundo todo está usando”, declarou o executivo. Atualmente, o Brasil encerrou o primeiro semestre com aproximadamente 706 MW (megawatts) de capacidade instalada voltada a data centers. “É tanta energia que se precisa que nós vamos precisar de todas as fontes. Não vai ser só do gás ou só do nuclear. Se nós quisermos atender aos data centers, nós vamos precisar usar toda a nossa criatividade, nossa capacidade”, complementa. Para viabilizar a inserção da energia nuclear nesse ecossistema, a aposta recai sobre os SMRs (Pequenos Reatores Modulares, na sigla em inglês), tecnologia que ganha força no mercado internacional. Esses dispositivos contam com potências que variam de 50 MW a 300 MW por unidade, dimensões bem inferiores às das usinas tradicionais. O grande diferencial está na fabricação modular: os reatores são produzidos em série no ambiente fabril e montados diretamente no local de operação, o que diminui custos e encurta prazos de implantação. “Você pode comprar como se fossem geladeiras. Ele já sai certificado e você compra o primeiro, o segundo, o terceiro e vai colocando em paralelo no data center. Ele não entra todo de uma vez, você pode botar esses SMRs de forma fracionada, de acordo com a necessidade do cliente do projeto”, explica Cunha. Interface com o Redata O setor nuclear brasileiro demonstra forte interesse em suprir as demandas de projetos que venham a ser contemplados pelo Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), marco legal sancionado recentemente pelo governo federal com o intuito de conceder incentivos fiscais ao setor. A proposta aprovada pelo Congresso Nacional e promulgada pelo Executivo ainda demanda regulamentações específicas, sobretudo no que tange à definição exata das fontes energéticas exigidas dos empreendimentos beneficiados. Inicialmente, o texto previa que apenas centros abastecidos por energia 100% limpa teriam direito aos benefícios tributários. No entanto, uma emenda articulada no Senado abriu espaço para incluir fontes consideradas de “baixa emissão”. A modificação abriu caminho para o emprego de gás natural, modalidade amplamente defendida pela indústria e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia. Apesar do debate em torno do gás natural, Celso Cunha avalia o cenário com tranquilidade. Na visão da Abdan, o arcabouço legal contempla implicitamente a energia nuclear, mesmo sem citá-la de maneira explícita. A expectativa do setor é que uma portaria ministerial detalhando as matrizes energéticas autorizadas seja publicada pelas autoridades competentes nas próximas semanas. artigo.texto: Charlie Berens, state senator ask lawmakers to end data center sales tax exemptions Candidates for governor weigh in on bill that would repeal tax break for data center developers GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY) - Comedian Charlie Berens is among those asking state lawmakers to support a bill that would end sales and use tax exemptions for data centers. Berens recently recorded a video for social media with state Sen. Andre Jacque, R-New Franken, a co-sponsor of the bill. Jacque is not seeking re-election, but the issue will be a factor for some voters in closely contested races across the state, including the race for governor. Tax break tied to data center projects The tax break for data center developers is one reason Wisconsin is being considered for many projects. Recent estimates from the Legislative Fiscal Bureau indicate developers are saving more than $1.5 billion, and that is only the current estimate. In the video, Berens asked Jacque about the bill. “Cool, so Democrats can sign on, Republicans can sign on, but what does the bill say?” Berens asked. “It’s a very simple bill,” Jacque said. Jacque also explained his support for the bill in an interview. “It’s something we don’t give other businesses. It’s kind of reserved for charities, churches, schools, and there’s really no reason why you and I should pay sales tax on buying a computer or equipment for a building, and data centers don’t,” Jacque said. Exemption passed in 2023 budget The exemption was passed as part of the biennial budget approved by state lawmakers and signed into law by Gov. Tony Evers in July 2023. “Unfortunately, there was kind of a bipartisan deal during the budget back in 2023 that slipped this in there with a thousand other provisions,” Jacque said. “There had been a stand-alone bill that I had opposed in the Senate, and like I said, they slipped it in there. This is an opportunity to fix that mistake.” Jacque was also asked why he voted for a budget that included a tax break he says he does not support. “I opposed the tax break as a member of the Senate Ag and Revenue Committee,” Jacque said. “However, it was included in the budget which had support from both sides of the aisle, and Governor Evers did sign it, but again, it was certainly not anything that was drawing my support for the budget.” Candidates for governor respond The bill is still seeking co-sponsors. Both candidates for governor were asked to weigh in because the bill would likely be signed into law or vetoed during the next administration. The question came up during a Democratic Party town hall at the Appleton Public Library. Democratic candidate David Crowley addressed it. “I want to be very clear, me and Sarah Godlewski have been on the campaign trail to let people know that the free ride data centers have been getting, it ends with a Crowley-Godlewski administration,” Crowley said. In July, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel asked Crowley about rolling back tax incentives for data centers. Crowley said, “I do not believe Wisconsin should automatically roll back all data center tax incentives, but I do believe we need a more rigorous review of whether taxpayers are receiving sufficient value for the incentives being provided.” Crowley’s campaign recently said that he favors local communities making the decision on data centers that is right for them, with no back room deals or utility rate increases. In a statement about rolling back tax incentives, the campaign said, “While his focus has always been on reforming the system to hold Big Tech accountable, as governor, David will sign a repeal if one is passed in the legislature.” Republican candidate Tom Tiffany said in an interview he would support the bill. He also questioned Crowley’s stance. “Remember, these are some of the wealthiest companies in the world. They don’t need a subsidy from the taxpayers of Wisconsin, and this is where there’s a key difference between me and my opponent, David Crowley. David Crowley supports those subsidies; I do not, and I will eliminate them as governor,” Tiffany said. State Democrats point out that Tiffany, as a member of Congress, voted in favor of the SPEED Act. The act reformed federal permitting laws and accelerated the construction process for new data centers. Bill unlikely to advance this year The legislation is not likely to go anywhere this year without a special session being called. Jacque is leaving office in January. He said his intention is to hand off pursuit of the bill to others who have signed on. Copyright 2026 WBAY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: O primeiro leilão de sistemas de armazenamento de energia do Brasil, marcado para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, teve seu edital aprovado com alterações que visam ampliar a competitividade entre as empresas participantes. Além de uma redação mais genérica sobre a base pagadora dos custos da contratação, conforme deliberado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) na 3ª feira (27/10). O leilão atraiu mais de 6 mil projetos, somando 297 gigawatts (GW). Os valores das garantias de proposta e de fiel cumprimento caíram quase 40%, acompanhando a atualização do investimento de referência para as baterias, que passou de R$ 9,8 milhões para R$ 6 milhões por megawatt (MW). Também foi aceita a possibilidade de formação de consórcios por empresas do mesmo grupo econômico, ponto que vinha sendo pleiteado, explica o InfoMoney. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos e início em agosto de 2028. Os preços-teto foram definidos pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) em R$ 1,76 milhão por MW/ano para projetos com conteúdo nacional e R$ 1,58 milhão por MW/ano para projetos sem essa especificação, detalha o Capital Reset. Na avaliação da Associação Brasileira de Soluções em Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE), esses valores contribuem para tornar o leilão atrativo, destaca o Megawhat. O edital, aprovado por unanimidade pela diretoria da ANEEL, prevê que os custos sejam divididos entre as empresas geradoras de energia, conforme determina a lei vigente sobre o tema. A divisão exata entre os tipos de geradoras é tema de outra consulta pública, que ficará aberta até 6 de novembro. O rateio do valor é um dos principais pontos de discussão. As geradoras defendem que as baterias beneficiam todo o sistema e, por isso, o custo deve ser dividido com os consumidores, como ocorre hoje com as termelétricas, que têm função equivalente à de reserva. Já outros segmentos afirmam que a conta deve ficar com as geradoras, principalmente as renováveis, como eólica e solar, que inseriram a necessidade de armazenamento de energia no sistema ao produzirem mais energia do que a demanda em determinados períodos do dia. No Congresso, um projeto de lei do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) prevê a divisão da conta com os consumidores e teve a urgência aprovada em 13 de outubro. No entanto, o diretor-geral da ANEEL, Sandoval Feitosa, já alertou que se deputados e senadores alterarem a lei que determinou que os geradores de energia arquem com os custos, a agência terá de alterar o edital e também adiar o leilão, informa o Megawhat. O que atrasará ainda mais a instalação de grandes baterias no país. O leilão de baterias foi dividido em dois processos. O primeiro (LRCAP de 2026 — Armazenamento Nacional) destina-se a projetos com conteúdo nacional — peças e equipamentos fabricados no país — e ocorrerá em 2 de dezembro. O outro (LRCAP de 2026 – Armazenamento) é voltado a empreendimentos que não cumprem essa exigência e será realizado dois dias depois, em 4 de dezembro.

artigo.texto: Editors Note: More data and information regarding tax revenue and utilities will be part of a follow up data center related story on Oct. 29 Wired fences still line cow pastures along the county's back roads. Other WRAL Top Stories Even in an age of technology, much of Mecklenburg County, Virginia remains unspoiled. But even places that feel as though they'd never change, sometimes do. In Mecklenburg County, government officials say there are ten data center campuses in a county that's home to approximately 30,000 people, with additional undeveloped sites laying the groundwork for even more. There are approximately 700 active or planned data center projects in the state. That's more than five times the amount in North Carolina. Certain research suggests Americans have increasingly negative views about the data center industry. A recent Pew Research Center survey shows an increase in the number of surveyed adults who view data centers as bad for the environment, energy costs and quality of people living nearby. Polling conducted by WRAL itself also supports the sentiment that more people oppose them than support them. This comes as cities across North Carolina weigh and vote on data center moratoriums, including Raleigh, where leaders voted to pause developing new, larger data centers for six months. Government officials in Mecklenburg County, including some nearby residents, voiced support for the industry, citing the impacts from their tax revenue and the economic benefits they've brought to the rural county at the Virginia-North Carolina border. Meanwhile, not every neighbors is sold. "There's other places they could go besides right there" | Living with a new neighbor It only takes a couple seconds for Robert Bruce to welcome his new next-door neighbor. Once a day, Bruce makes the ten second walk behind his house to catch a glimpse of the progress being made. Even though he's within a stone's throw of the data center's construction, he's supportive of the industry in the county, even if it means they're built behind his house. "That's the sign of progress," Bruce chuckled. On the other side of the Chase City construction site live Katie and Sadie Snyder, a mother and daughter whose house sits at the end of a road leading directly into the upcoming data center. The noise is constant, they say. The traffic and noise from the project are loud enough that it's prompted them to look for new housing elsewhere. "I don't understand why they couldn't put that on Highway 58," Katie said. It's not difficult finding research supporting the notion that Americans are not overwhelmingly ecstatic about the idea of data centers in their community. Research from the University of Virginia showed two of every three surveyed Americans (in a sample of more than 3,000 people) opposed a data center being built in their community. "That figure is so well established that dozens of surveys could be cited for it," analysts wrote. In fact, fewer than half of respondents in a recent WRAL/ WSOC poll said they supported at least some data center development. "I live very close to Microsoft and have mixed feelings about its impact. While I understand the importance of economic growth, I've noticed significant changes in our neighborhood that concern me," one resident responded in a local Facebook group when asked by WRAL, regarding recent data center development. Where people live though, relative to the data center's location, may influence how they ultimately feel about them. Almost 2,000 adults were surveyed in separate research efforts from the University of Virginia, which found that people are more likely to be tolerant of a data center in their community if they already live near one. A smaller percentage of people living within five miles of a data center "strongly opposed" them, as well. Impacts to county and localities Most of the data center campuses in the county are run by Microsoft. As recently as the 2023 fiscal year, the company cites a 21 percent increase in regional economic activity, along with supporting job creation and adding to the region's labor income. Some local county and city leaders within Mecklenburg County have welcomed the industry, citing the financial flexibility they have provided. Alex Gottschalk, the County Administrator in Mecklenburg County, spoke to WRAL at length about the impacts data centers have had in the county. He says data centers account for roughly 45 percent of the county's general fund now, and can contribute as much as 25 to 30 percent of the county's overall budget. "When we're in a spot like we are, which is a rural county which has faced tremendous amount of economic pressure over the past 30 years-- and has a lot of service delivery demands that are the same that you would see in any urban or suburban community-- we need to be able to fund those things. There's only a limited number of ways that is possible for any local government," Gottschalk said. Gottschalk pointed to an additional $1.5 million in reductions that were made across the county that were a product of data center development: the reduction of personal property tax rates, and the elimination the vehicle registration fee and consumer utility tax. "Many of these sites, existed for 20 to 30 years and produced zero, and one of our sites in particular used to be a correctional institute of the Commonwealth of Virginia. So that site produced no direct revenue to the county. It is now a data center. It's one of our most valued properties in the county, one of the highest tax-producing ones. So all of that is an increase. In that location, we went, and many others, we went from zero to substantial, and so that's how we choose to view this as net gains. Alden Fahringer, Mayor of Chase City, also told WRAL the generated revenue has allowed localities to make improvements they otherwise could not make. "Life is slowly trickling back into small towns like mine," Fahringer said. What's next for North Caroli

artigo.texto: US Signal buys Hillsboro data center for $20M amid city moratorium Published 4:29 pm Tuesday, October 27, 2026 As Hillsboro remains under a moratorium on data center development and just approved its first phase of permanent restrictions, a national digital infrastructure company has purchased an existing facility in the city for $20 million. US Signal announced the acquisition Tuesday, Oct. 27, of a 63,000-square-foot data center in an industrial park at 3295 N.E. 83rd Ave. The facility has approximately 14,000 square feet of data hall space and 4.5 megawatts of power on site, according to the company. Washington County property records show US Signal purchased the property from Madrona Joes LLC and Watumull GI Joe’s LLC in a transaction recorded Oct. 14. In a release, the company said the facility offers opportunities to “expand capacity,” although it remains unclear whether that would involve physically expanding the building, increasing its electrical capacity or making greater use of the existing space. It is also unclear whether any potential expansion would be subject to the city’s moratorium or newly adopted regulations. What are Hillsboro’s restrictions? The Hillsboro City Council approved a 120-day moratorium July 27, temporarily halting new and expanded data center development while city officials worked on permanent changes to the city’s development code. The moratorium is scheduled to expire Nov. 24, although the council could extend it for an additional six months. On Oct. 20, councilors unanimously adopted the first phase of those permanent regulations, limiting new standalone data centers to the city’s Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones and capping the amount of land they can occupy. Washington County property records classify the 5.08-acre property as Industrial Park land, although its specific zoning designation under Hillsboro’s development code has not been confirmed by city officials. The new rules also require public hearings for proposed standalone data centers, establish a temporary 1,000-foot buffer between new data centers and schools and place additional limits on smaller accessory data centers operated by businesses. The regulations are scheduled to take effect Nov. 19, five days before the current moratorium expires. Neither the company nor the city immediately responded to requests for comment Tuesday. “Hillsboro gives us a way to grow in a market where available capacity is extremely limited,” John White, US Signal’s chief operating officer, said in a release. “We’re bringing an existing facility into our network and building on the approach we’ve taken in other communities: data centers sized for the markets they serve, with the connectivity and services customers need to grow.” According to US Signal, Hillsboro’s data center market had an estimated vacancy rate of just 0.2% during the first half of 2026. The acquisition marks US Signal’s first owned data center in the Portland metro area, adding to its existing Oregon presence in Bend and a nationwide network of 17 data centers. The company said the Hillsboro facility creates opportunities to expand its colocation services, which provide space and infrastructure for customers to house computing equipment, connect the site to its fiber network and deploy additional cloud infrastructure in the Pacific Northwest. The acquisition is part of a broader expansion effort supported by US Signal’s owner, Igneo Infrastructure Partners, an international infrastructure investment firm. Meanwhile, city officials are preparing a second phase of data center regulations, expected to address building heights, buffers, environmental protections and other development standards during winter and spring 2027.

artigo.texto: Data Center Divide: Virginia communities grapple with costs, benefits, unknowns (WSET) — Virginia is home to more data centers than anywhere else in the United States, according to Statista. While these massive campuses are powering the future from artificial intelligence to the cloud, they are creating a data center divide for many Commonwealth communities. NORTHERN VIRGINIA - LESSONS LEARNED A constant hum. Massive industrial buildings rising beside homes and schools. Billions of dollars flowing into local government budgets. Across Northern Virginia, the data center boom is bringing economic opportunity and a growing debate over what communities must give up to get it. As data centers spread across Virginia, the big questions are hitting closer to home, including who benefits, who pays, and what data centers could mean for your electric bill, your neighborhood and your quality of life. For our region, data centers are either being built, proposed or generating discussion about how to plan and regulate them in Amherst, Appomattox, Botetourt, Campbell, Franklin, Halifax, Pittsylvania and Roanoke counties, along with the City of Danville. DANVILLE-PITTSYLVANIA COUNTY – STACK DATA CENTER The $100 billion STACK data center development is moving forward at Berry Hill in Danville-Pittsylvania County. The project is raising concerns about its potential impact on the area. Protesters have voiced concerns about the effect on electricity costs, the environment and more. The STACK development is expected to include 21 buildings across roughly 3,00 acres off Berry Hill Road. The power demand is projected to reach up to 3,000 megawatts, which is enough to power two million homes. HALIFAX COUNTY – NAVIGATING DATA CENTER REGULATIONS Halifax County officials have been navigating the possibility of data center development. After voting in March to draft new data center regulations, the county is working to develop an ordinance. Halifax Industrial Development Authority Director Brian Brown said 10 developers reached out over the past year. He said he is actively speaking with three of them about small to mid-size projects. CAMPBELL COUNTY – CABIN FIELD ROAD DATA CENTER In Campbell County, a proposed data center is drawing pushback from residents. In 2025, Mesh Capital presented a proposal for a three-building, 450,000-square-foot data center off Cabin Field Road. In October of last year, county supervisors voted 5-2 against rezoning the property for the data center. Mesh Capital presented a new plan in January, and the site was approved. Since then, residents said they have heard nothing about the project. With the ongoing drought, they are worried about a data center’s impact on already low water levels. APPOMATTOX COUNTY – PROJECT HERCULES In Appomattox County, construction is about to begin on Project Hercules, a complex with seven data centers. Some residents are upset that such a large project was approved behind closed doors. County officials said the complex, which will be built in the Appomattox Center for Business and Commerce, will bring an investment of $8 billion to $10 billion to the county, along with 250 jobs. Community members said they did not find out about Project Hercules until after it was approved, when a public announcement was made in December 2024. County officials said much of the negotiation was subject to two non-disclosure agreements. AMHERST COUNTY – PREPARING FOR THE FUTURE While there is no data center project currently moving forward in Amherst County, the possibility is generating debate among residents. In August, the board of supervisors voted to require special use permits for future data centers. That gives the county more control and residents a chance to weigh in. BOTETOURT COUNTY – GOOGLE DATA CENTER PROJECT Work is underway on a major Google data center project in Botetourt County. Residents there said they lack full answers about the project and a meaningful voice in what happens next. Called Project Raspberry, the 312-acre site will be home to three Google data centers. Botetourt County Administrator Gary Larrow and Director of Economic Development Kyle Rosner declined an interview to answer our questions about the project. We also reached out to every member of the county board of supervisors. None were available to talk. Google said they want to be good stewards in the county and said the data centers will bring new jobs to the area. ROANOKE COUNTY – GOOGLE EYES ADDITIONAL DATA CENTER Google also has plans for another data center in Roanoke County. The data center is proposed for Wood Haven Technology Park. Residents said they are concerned about not having a voice in this project. County leaders responded to those concerns. FRANKLIN COUNTY – PROJECT FLASH Residents in Franklin County are questioning what comes next after a failed data center proposal called Project Flash. County officials said there are no data centers currently being considered. Some residents who opposed the project have called on the county to put more safeguards in place quickly. With 60% of the county unzoned, developers would have few restrictions on where to build. ELECTRIC GRID IMPACTS – VALLEY LINK PROJECT The amount of energy data centers use is among the top concerns of many Virginia residents opposed to the projects. Valley Link is working on a $1 billion transmission line project to power data centers in northern Virginia. The transmission line would stretch from Campbell County more than 100 miles north to Culpeper to feed electricity needs there. For some families in Campbell and Appomattox counties, the proposed transmission line would change their way of life. GOV. SPANBERGER’S RESPONSE In October, Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced plans to expand Virginia’s power supply as electricity demand rises. Her energy plan calls for more power from nuclear and renewable sources. Spanberger also backed a recent State Corporation Commission decision that requires data centers to pay

artigo.texto: CATL advances 20 Ah solid-state battery cells ahead of 2027 trial production CATL has advanced its all-solid-state battery development from a 10 Ah-class validation platform to 20 Ah sample trials, according to Y-Auto. It targets small-batch production in 2027, with large-scale manufacturing planned around 2030. The company provided an update on October 27 in response to investor questions on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange’s Hudongyi platform. Its development team has more than 1,000 people, and the programme targets an energy density of about 500 Wh/kg. CATL has not confirmed that figure as a production-cell specification or disclosed expected trial output, automotive customers or a vehicle launch date tied to these cells. What CATL’s solid-state cells still need to prove Energy density is only one measure of battery performance. Durability, manufacturing yield, cost, safety and performance under real operating conditions will also determine whether the cells are suitable for production vehicles. Chairman Robin Zeng previously rated CATL’s solid-state battery technology at Level 4 on a nine-level readiness scale. The assessment provides context for the development still required, but the more consequential test is whether the company can manufacture reliable cells at commercially viable cost. Sulfide cells face interface and durability hurdles. Sulfide electrolytes conduct lithium ions effectively, but maintaining stable contact between solid components remains a challenge. Electrodes expand and contract during charging and discharging, which can disrupt those interfaces. Cell design must manage contact pressure and interface resistance to maintain performance. Sulfide materials also require protection from moisture because reactions can release hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), a toxic gas. Material handling and manufacturing conditions therefore remain important considerations for commercial production. The 500 Wh/kg goal also raises questions about electrode design. Such high cell-level energy density can involve higher-capacity anode architectures, including lithium-metal or anode-less designs. For example, Samsung SDI has described an anode-less approach for its all-solid-state batteries. CATL has not disclosed the anode configuration used in the cells covered by its latest update. CATL, Toyota and Samsung SDI have different targets CATL is targeting small-batch production in 2027. Toyota and Idemitsu aim to commercialise sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries for battery-electric vehicles between 2027 and 2028, while Samsung SDI has targeted mass production in the second half of 2027. These milestones are not directly equivalent. Samsung SDI has also identified humanoid robots as a potential early application for its technology while continuing development for electric vehicles. These timelines do not mean the companies’ products will reach the market at the same time, in comparable volumes, or with equivalent performance. How all-solid-state batteries differ from semi-solid designs All-solid-state batteries use a solid electrolyte rather than relying on a liquid electrolyte within the cell. Semi-solid and hybrid designs retain some liquid electrolyte, although terminology and configurations vary by manufacturer. Progress with a semi-solid design does not, by itself, show that a company has overcome the interface, durability, and manufacturing challenges of an all-solid-state cell. For CATL, the central challenge is turning its current development work into repeatable, cost-competitive production.

artigo.texto: WASHINGTON – Global tech trade association ITI today issued new industry-led commitments for the development of new data centers. The roadmap details how industry is working with communities as it builds the computing capacity essential to economic growth and national security. Data centers power services Americans use every day, from hospitals and banks to schools and emergency services. As data centers deliver more essential services and demand grows, communities and policymakers are asking important questions about electricity costs, reliability, water use, and local benefits. ITI’s new roadmap addresses those questions and details what responsible, community-centered growth looks like from the industry’s perspective. “America does not have to choose between expanding its digital infrastructure and supporting communities. With strong partnership between industry and communities, we can do both,” said ITI Executive Vice President of Public Sector Gordon Bitko. “Responsible data center growth requires the technology industry, policymakers, utilities, communities, and other stakeholders to work together to protect ratepayers, modernize the grid, strengthen energy reliability, and ensure communities benefit from investments. ITI’s roadmap puts communities at the center of data center development.” In Responsible Growth: A Roadmap for Development of New Data Centers, the technology industry commits to: - Work with communities early and support benefits that reflect local needs; - Help to upgrade America’s energy infrastructure while protecting affordability for existing consumers; - Use water and energy responsibly and promote environmental stewardship; - Improve reliability, resilience, and security of data center facilities and the broader grid; and - Provide meaningful transparency through appropriate reporting. The roadmap also calls on policymakers to advance each of these principles through flexible, evidence-based policies that reflect local conditions rather than one-size-fits-all mandates. Clear and predictable rules can address public priorities, encourage long-term investment, and strengthen America’s economic competitiveness and national security.

artigo.texto: Marsh Advances Carbon Market Integrity Through Innovative Risk Management Solution for Carbon Project Developer Invert Press Release Date 10-27-2026 Invert and Marsh's 5-year partnership produced the first reversal insurance policy, replacing buffer pools to unlock capital and scale carbon markets. OTTAWA, ONTARIO, CANADA, October 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Invert Inc. (“Invert”), a leading carbon reduction and removal company, and Marsh, a global leader in insurance broking and risk advising, announce the successful placement of the first reversal insurance policy under Verra’s durability pilot. This landmark achievement is the culmination of more than five years of Invert and its broker, Marsh, pursuing specialized risk management solutions for the rapidly evolving carbon markets, with a dedicated focus on buffer pool replacement. Marsh successfully brokered the transaction, placing the policy with Oka, with underwriting by CarbonPool, whose innovative product offering finally delivered the exact solution required to bring this long-term vision to life. As carbon markets mature and transition toward compliance-grade standards, robust and regulated risk transfer mechanisms have become essential for scaling project finance. Over the past five years, Invert, acting as a carbon project developer and investor, has engaged Marsh to help procure and design insurance products specifically suited to the complex needs of project developers. These bespoke solutions (ranging from non-delivery coverage and buffer pool replacement insurance to parametric and alternative risk transfer products) are designed to unlock better project economics and provide greater certainty for offtakers and buyers. Ultimately, utilizing these tailored financial tools improves Invert's working capital, enabling the company to fund new initiatives, optimize existing projects, and maximize its positive environmental impact. This newly placed policy, structured by CarbonPool and underwritten by Oka, provides critical protection against the risk of reversal, which is the chance that carbon previously credited as stored is unexpectedly re-released into the atmosphere. Historically, developers managed this risk by contributing a large portion of their credits to a buffer pool, a requirement that ties up valuable inventory that cannot be sold or financed. By participating in Verra's durability pilot and substituting the traditional buffer pool contribution with regulated insurance, Invert transfers the reversal risk directly to an insurer. This allows the company to make a significantly greater proportion of its issued credits immediately available for sale, optimizing cash flows and investor returns while ensuring a robust financial mechanism remains in place. "Our work with Marsh isn't just about derisking Invert’s portfolio; it's about building the financial infrastructure the entire carbon market desperately needs," said Andre Fernandez, CEO of Invert Inc. "Because of our deep involvement in designing these mechanisms, we act as an introducer for Marsh, serving as a vital bridge, introducing our peers and clients to Marsh's specialized capabilities. Whether you are a developer looking to unlock working capital or a buyer seeking certainty, we are working with Marsh to solve the carbon markets risk transfer challenges." Hema Mistry, UK CEO, Financial and Professional Liability, Marsh Risk, said: “This landmark placement demonstrates how insurance can play a practical role in helping carbon projects manage reversal risk in a more capital efficient way. This is an important part of the wider evolution of how carbon markets are managing permanence risk, with insurance solutions emerging to support the growth and integrity of high-quality carbon projects.” This evolving financial infrastructure demonstrates tangible market benefits beyond the project developer. Crucially, this approach provides buyers with the institutional credibility required for corporate balance sheets, signaling a new standard of financial rigor in carbon credit procurement. Invert remains committed to advancing the financial maturity and capital efficiency of the carbon market, continuing to pursue solutions with industry leaders like Marsh to ensure that high-quality, nature-based carbon projects are bankable, investable, and scalable. About Marsh. Marsh (NYSE: MRSH) is a global leader in risk, reinsurance and capital, people and investments, and management consulting, advising clients in 130 countries. With annual revenue of $27 billion and more than 95,000 colleagues, Marsh helps build the confidence to thrive through the power of perspective. For more information, visit marsh.com or follow us on LinkedIn and X. About Invert. Invert is an award-winning carbon reduction and removal company committed to empowering organizations to take bold climate action. With a mission to drive global goals for decarbonization, Invert is dedicated to making a measurable impact on our planet’s future through carbon project origination and financing and sourcing high-integrity carbon credits for businesses. artigo.texto: Portugal está a reforçar a sua posição como mercado emergente de Data Centers na Europa, impulsionado pelo crescimento da procura associada à inteligência artificial (IA), pela forte conectividade internacional e pela expansão de projetos de grande escala. De acordo com o mais recente Data Centers Iberian Region Snapshot, elaborado pela Colliers, empresa global e diversificada de serviços profissionais e de gestão de investimentos, especializada em Imobiliário Comercial, Engenharia e Gestão de Investimento, Lisboa dispõe atualmente de 25 MW IT de capacidade operacional, mas apresenta um pipeline de desenvolvimento de aproximadamente 1.389 MW IT. Cerca de 91% da capacidade assegurada deverá estar operacional antes de 2030. Apesar de não terem sido identificados novos projetos ou aumentos de capacidade operacional em Lisboa durante o período analisado (abril a setembro de 2026), o mercado mantém uma dinâmica de desenvolvimento significativa. A Colliers destaca que a combinação entre uma base operacional ainda reduzida e um pipeline de grande dimensão coloca Portugal numa posição forte para captar uma nova vaga de procura por infraestrutura digital. “O mercado de centros de dados em Portugal ainda é pequeno quando comparado com o de outros países com maior tradição neste setor (FLAP-D). No entanto, apesar de contar com menos projetos, Portugal tem três projetos que já são, ou virão a ser, muito relevantes em termos de dimensão: o Start Campus, em Sines, o Merlin, em Lisboa, e o Covilhã DC (Asterion). Em conjunto, estes projetos representam um pipeline de desenvolvimento muito significativo”, diz José María Guilleuma, managing director de Data Centers da Colliers, ao Jornal Económico. “Portugal já conseguiu atrair grandes projetos de Inteligência Artificial, mas falta-lhe transformar Lisboa numa localização atrativa para os grandes operadores de hiperescala, à semelhança do que acontece em Barcelona”, acrescenta o responsável. A crescente relevância da inteligência artificial está a alterar os requisitos dos operadores e utilizadores de Data Centers, aumentando a necessidade de capacidade energética, conectividade e instalações preparadas para cargas computacionais de elevada densidade. Neste contexto, a construção do Lisbon AI Campus da Merlin Edged está em curso. A primeira fase prevê 80 MW IT, distribuídos por duas instalações de 40 MW, com entrega prevista para o quarto trimestre de 2027. Está ainda prevista uma capacidade adicional de 100 MW IT em três edifícios, elevando a capacidade planeada do campus para 180 MW IT. Para além desta capacidade, a Merlin Edged prevê desenvolver até mais 1.120 MW IT no seu pipeline futuro, incluindo 200 MW IT em Vila Franca de Xira e outros 920 MW IT numa localização ainda não divulgada. Sines ganha importância estratégica na corrida à IA Fora da região de Lisboa, o projeto de Sines assume uma relevância crescente na estratégia nacional de infraestrutura digital. Segundo a Colliers, a Start Campus, em parceria com a Nscale e a Microsoft, ampliou o seu projeto para implementar mais de 66.000 GPUs NVIDIA Rubin a partir do final de 2027, complementando as mais de 12.600 GPUs NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra previstas para o SIN01. A Start Campus mantém autorização para uma capacidade total de 1,2 GW, reforçando Sines como uma das localizações europeias com maior potencial para infraestrutura de IA de grande escala. Também fora de Lisboa, a entrada da NxN no mercado português, através da aquisição de um Data Center operacional de 1 MW IT em Évora, evidencia a expansão gradual do mercado para outros pontos do território. A atratividade de Lisboa enquanto localização para Data Centers é suportada pela sua forte conectividade internacional, nomeadamente pela rede de cabos submarinos e pela infraestrutura de fibra ótica. O mercado beneficia ainda de um enquadramento regulatório considerado favorável e de uma crescente valorização das infraestruturas digitais como setor estratégico. “Portugal é uma geografia ideal, graças à sua localização estratégica voltada para o Atlântico. É verdade que o novo enquadramento regulatório em Espanha poderá beneficiar Portugal, ao posicioná-lo como uma boa alternativa para a diversificação europeia dos países nórdicos. No entanto, Portugal já beneficia de previsibilidade regulatória, e o seu modelo e estrutura da rede elétrica estão alinhados com as orientações da União Europeia”, conclui José María Guilleuma. artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media The nation’s biggest grid operator is about to start working on a fix that would make it much easier to add batteries to existing power plants and solar and wind farms. PJM Interconnection is finally taking steps that could let a lot of new battery capacity connect to its grid without eons of delay. PJM is the biggest grid operator in the U.S., serving customers across 13 mid-Atlantic, Midwestern, and Southern states. Its grid is notoriously bogged down and congested, especially now that data centers are clamoring for more power, and that’s leading to high electricity prices in its territory. Among other shortcomings, it’s been falling behind its counterparts elsewhere in the country in pursuing a straightforward solution: allowing power plants to add batteries on-site in order to get more out of grid connections that aren’t always used to full capacity. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has directed grid operators to pave the way for these kinds of battery additions under Surplus Interconnection Service (SIS) rules. The idea is to let existing power plants — mainly solar and wind farms — add batteries that can soak up excess power when it’s not needed, and then inject it through existing grid connections when power plants aren’t generating at their full potential. That could be particularly valuable when region-wide demand for electricity spikes, usually on hot summer afternoons or cold winter mornings. PJM has seen the cost of capacity resources to keep the grid running during these times skyrocket over the past few years, largely due to pressures to supply power to proposed data centers. But PJM has been a laggard in reforming its SIS procedures, according to grid experts and clean energy groups that have been pushing for changes for years. It has approved very few such projects, even as grid operators in other regions have crafted regulations and processes that have opened the door to tens of gigawatts of SIS capacity. Now — better late than never — PJM has agreed to kick off a stakeholder process to reform its market rules to clear the way for SIS battery additions. Its Market Implementation Committee is set to consider the next steps at its Nov. 4 meeting, according to Jon Gordon, a senior director at clean-energy trade group Advanced Energy United. If a plan wins approval, PJM could complete work on the changes and seek FERC’s permission as early as April 2027 to enact them. Taking advantage of SIS opens up huge opportunities. “It’s clearly catching on” in other parts of the country, said Gavin Ahern, co-founder of Surplus Interconnection, which consults with power plant owners on adding capacity through these approaches. His company has tracked 44 gigawatts of historical SIS project requests as of mid-2026, about 80% of them in the form of proposals to add batteries to existing projects. Some notable projects that have been proposed or approved include the addition of batteries to North Dakota wind farms by NextEra Energy and Great River Energy and to gas power plants in California, and the addition of solar power to gas plants in Illinois. For clean energy developers looking to boost the value of their projects and supply capacity to meet booming data center demand, SIS is a no-brainer, Ahern said. “Renewable energy developers have been among the quickest to see the potential,” he said. “They’re looking to get more out of sites they’ve already paid to connect.” The lion’s share of this activity is in the territories of two Midwestern grid operators: Midcontinent Independent System Operator, with 14.8 GW proposed across 138 active requests, and Southwest Power Pool, with 14.3 GW proposed across 89 active requests. Another 6 GW across 51 active requests are pending across the U.S. West, and the Southeast has 1 GW proposed across 29 active requests. But in PJM, only 14 SIS requests have been submitted, and of those, only two have been approved, as of the grid operator’s most recent update in November 2025. That’s wasting an enormous amount of potential, according to data from Umed Paliwal, a principal scientific engineering associate in the Electricity Markets and Policy Department at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. His research indicates that PJM could add 24 GW of energy storage through surplus interconnection at existing power plant sites. (Paliwal also estimates that PJM could add 102 GW of solar and 28 GW of wind through SIS by building solar and wind farms that share the grid connections of gas peaker plants, which generally fire up only when demand peaks, leaving a lot of capacity for renewable energy to flow during the majority of the year.) Using SIS to get projects going could help developers save more than $31 billion in interconnection costs and grid upgrades, according to Paliwal. What’s more, since they’re riding on existing grid connections, SIS projects can add their capacity within one to two years — far faster than new power plants and battery installations, which face yearslong wait times in PJM’s backlogged interconnection queues. This chart from decarbonization think tank RMI shows how much more quickly SIS can bring new resources online than PJM’s standard interconnection process. “We have members who are really rip-roaring to go on this,” said Gordon of Advanced Energy United. “What I’ve learned is that the devil’s really in some of the wonky details that have become obstacles to solving this problem.” So what has been holding SIS back in PJM? The answer can be broken into two parts: First, PJM needs to fix its approach to studying SIS projects’ impacts on its grid. Then, it needs to fix its approach to how those projects operate in its energy and capacity markets. Clean energy groups got to work on the first part of the challenge back in 2024, asking FERC to force PJM to restructure how it studied the grid impacts of adding new resources to an existing generation or battery project. artigo.texto: Aneel aprova editais de leilões de baterias e conta fica com geradores Agência mantém obrigação de custeio para geradores, enquanto agentes do setor articulam no Congresso mudança na legislação A Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) aprovou nesta 3ª feira (27.out.2026) os editais dos 2 primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. A agência manteve os geradores de energia elétrica como responsáveis pelos custos da contratação, conforme determina a Lei nº 15.269 de 2025. Os certames estão marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro –um deles exige um mínimo de conteúdo nacional, o outro admite equipamentos importados. Durante o processo de consulta pública, agentes do setor elétrico propuseram à agência reguladora uma redação mais genérica. Queriam que a expressão “agentes de geração”, fosse substituída por “usuários de reserva de capacidade”. A ideia era acomodar eventuais mudanças na legislação. A Aneel acolheu parcialmente a sugestão no edital, mas manteve a referência explícita aos geradores na definição dos responsáveis pelo pagamento no contrato. A decisão se dá enquanto o Congresso discute uma mudança na lei para retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear as baterias. Em 13 de outubro, a Câmara aprovou o regime de urgência do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716 de 2026, apresentado pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). A proposta revoga o trecho da lei de 2025 e estabelece a aplicação da regra geral de divisão de custo. Caso seja aprovada antes da realização do leilão, o edital precisaria ser alterado, pois as despesas passariam a ser divididas entre os usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo consumidores. PONTOS-CHAVE Apesar da recusa quanto às regras de custeio, a agência acabou aceitando parte das contribuições do setor privado. Eis alguns pontos chave do edital: - exigências patrimoniais – a Aneel flexibilizou as regras para permitir consórcios entre empresas de um mesmo grupo econômico. Para evitar a contagem duplicada de recursos financeiros, determinou que o patrimônio líquido exigido seja comprovado exclusivamente pela controladora, sem somar o patrimônio das subsidiárias controladas; - baterias colocalizadas – a agência manteve a proibição de participação de sistemas de armazenamento colocalizados em usinas geradoras, apesar dos pedidos de flexibilização. A justificativa é que esses sistemas dependem operacionalmente da usina à qual estão vinculados, o que poderia comprometer o atendimento integral aos comandos de carga e descarga do ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico). - participação de transmissoras – a Aneel autorizou a participação de concessionárias de transmissão nos certames. A possibilidade foi analisada a partir de consulta da Taesa. Segundo parecer da Procuradoria Federal junto à agência, as transmissoras também poderão atuar por meio de subsidiárias ou sociedades de propósito específico, mediante autorização regulatória e separação contábil e financeira das atividades.

artigo.texto: The mid-term elections are next week. Here in Alabama, voters will choose a new Governor and decide races for the U.S. House, among others. Higher prices for groceries and gasoline appear to be a major issue with the public. Another is what to do about data centers. These big projects are supported by those who see them as a money maker or a way to harness artificial intelligence. There are those who hold a less positive view. Let’s take a look at the issue and how the two men running for Governor of Alabama are talking about it… Democrat Doug Jones and Republican Tommy Tuberville both want to be Alabama governor. Whoever wins the race to lead the state next week will have high profile problems to deal with, and data centers are one of them. The internet platform website Cleanview keeps an eye on data centers in Alabama. That website says there are thirteen in operation and fifteen more planned. It’s what’s not known about data centers, that’s one issue. “The misconceptions, I think, are just the fact that we don't have a lot of information because the facilities are fairly private and off the like off the grid," said Jonathan Frame. He’s an assistant professor of Geology at the University of Alabama. Frame studies the issue of data centers as an assistant professor of Geology at the University of Alabama. We’ll be talking with him a lot during this story. But, first let’s hit the campaign trail with Jones and Tuberville. Both candidates are talking about data centers and tying their opponents to the issue. Jones is taking direct aim at what he says are Tuberville’s ties to these projects. “Tuberville scare tax about China doesn't acknowledge the fact that on 14 different occasions, while a United States senator, Tommy Tuberville bought and sold stock and options in Alibaba," Jones said. Tuberville’s campaign responded to charges that the Senator bought stock in Ali Baba, which runs data centers. They claim these buys were made by the lawmaker's broker, not by Tuberville specifically. During a conference with reporters, Tuberville says he supports data centers and that social media critics are trying to turn the public against them. "Social media is good in some forms, but we have the Democrats and we have Chinese propaganda. Everybody out there is pushing against data centers for some reason," Tuberville said. APR news contacted both candidates to answer further questions on the subject of data centers, but neither camp responded. We then turned to Doctor Frame to address concerns about these mega projects one by one. First is the belief that data centers will soak up local water resources. "Well, I mean, everything is kind of interconnected. So, there's a lot. There's different regions and different states have different water rights. So there there's not one answer to that," he said. Here in Alabama, there’s also an apparent concern of sharing water resources with agriculture. Doctor Frame admits that might be an issue. "It depends on the state in which the water rights are granted, but in some states where you have basically free access to an aquifer's storage of water, and you're sharing that aquifer with other agricultural industries, then yes, it could," he said. Along with water use, residents are reportedly concerned that data centers will drive up utility rates by using more energy. Cynthia Almond is the president of the Alabama Public Service Commission. She says that recent legislation establishes safeguards to protect customers from higher utility rates associated with data centers. "These developments must not only pay their own way for the additional cost that they create, but they also must provide a benefit to the broader electric system and existing customers like you and me," she said. Alabama Senate Bill 270 took effect on Oct. 1 and requires data centers using more than 150 megawatts of electricity to sign large-load energy contracts with the APSC. Almond says the commission closely reviews these contracts and evaluates how a facility can affect residents. "The main thing is we want to make sure that existing customers are not left responsible for any of those investments if the development or the data center doesn't materialize as expected or later reduces its operations," she said. Data centers continue to remain a hot topic in the race for Alabama's governor. The issue may be that voters have to make their decision at the ballot box next Tuesday, with more concerns than answers.

artigo.texto: O Serviço Brasileiro de Apoio às Micro e Pequenas Empresas do Rio Grande do Norte (Sebrae-RN) inaugura nesta quinta-feira (29), às 18h30, seu segundo Data Center no Brasil. A estrutura funcionará na sede da instituição, em Natal, e receberá investimento de aproximadamente R$ 70 milhões para atender unidades do Sebrae em 12 estados das regiões Nordeste, Norte e Sudeste. Os recursos destinados ao projeto são provenientes do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais que utilizarão a infraestrutura tecnológica. Com a inauguração, o Rio Grande do Norte passará a integrar, ao lado do Distrito Federal, a lista de localidades que abrigam Data Centers do sistema. Data Center do Sebrae-RN homenageará Senador Fernando Bezerra A nova estrutura receberá o nome de Senador Fernando Bezerra, que presidiu o Conselho Deliberativo do Sebrae-RN na década de 1990. Ele também participou do processo de viabilização da compra do imóvel onde funciona a atual sede da instituição, na capital potiguar. Segundo Franklin Maux, gerente de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação do Sebrae-RN, a escolha do Rio Grande do Norte levou em consideração diferentes fatores, entre eles o potencial energético do estado. A disponibilidade de fontes renováveis de energia pode contribuir para a instalação de empreendimentos voltados à infraestrutura tecnológica. Estrutura deve padronizar sistemas e impulsionar o setor de tecnologia O Data Center terá a função de armazenar, processar, gerenciar e proteger informações utilizadas pelas unidades do Sebrae atendidas pelo projeto. A instalação reunirá servidores, equipamentos de rede e sistemas de armazenamento de dados. De acordo com o Sebrae-RN, a nova infraestrutura também deverá favorecer a padronização dos sistemas tecnológicos das unidades estaduais, que atualmente trabalham com diferentes tecnologias. Além disso, o empreendimento poderá estimular novos investimentos no setor de tecnologia do Rio Grande do Norte e contribuir para a formação de profissionais especializados na área. O que é um Data Center? Um Data Center é uma instalação que concentra equipamentos e sistemas responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento, gerenciamento e proteção de dados. Esse tipo de infraestrutura é utilizado por organizações para manter sistemas digitais e dar suporte às suas operações. No caso do Sebrae-RN, a unidade de Natal será responsável por atender às demandas das unidades da instituição contempladas pelo projeto, ampliando a estrutura tecnológica disponível para o funcionamento dos serviços.

artigo.texto: Fluidstack hosts open house on Wythe County data center as protesters voice frustration WYTHE COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - A Texas-based company that has broken ground on a data center project in Progress Park held an information session Wednesday with Wythe County residents. The company, Fluidstack, is building a computing campus on 99 acres in the park. The open house was meant to address community concerns about water use, energy demand and noise levels. Protesters gathered outside while company experts answered questions inside on water, power and taxes. Many residents said the event left them with more frustration than answers. Company responds to concerns Kate Franco, Fluidstack’s public affairs lead, said the company is building only closed-loop cooling. “People are usually concerned about water usage, and we’re only building closed-loop cooling, so it’s a one-time fill of a cooling tank,” Franco said. “People are often concerned about the impact of a data center on their energy bill, and we are paying for all our own energy with APCO and any upgrades or equipment that we need. People are concerned about noise, and we’re staying within the Progress Park noise limits, just like every other business in the park.” Franco also described the jobs the project will bring. “There are about 1,000 construction jobs at peak, and 75 full-time jobs once we’re operational,” she said. Fluidstack said it plans to be operational by the end of 2027. Protesters question format and timing Maranda Edwards said the format of the event did not address residents’ questions. “If they wanted to answer our questions, they’d host a town hall, not host a science fair,” Edwards said. Georgia Randall said the setup kept residents from speaking and listening as a group. “We don’t all have a chance to talk as one voice and listen as one voice. They’re breaking it up into little sections, so we can’t all hear at one time, speak at one time. I don’t like the way they’re doing it,” Randall said. Andy Kegley, a member of the group Preserve Wythe, said the meeting came too late. Ground at Progress Park is already leveled. “The Preserve Wythe group is really happy that this meeting is finally happening. But the problem is it’s after the fact,” Kegley said. “They’re answering a lot of questions. There’s still a bunch of questions they’re not going to answer.” Kegley said the company will not say who the end user of the data center is. Residents look to zoning Wythe County residents said their concerns extend beyond this project. Another data center project is already planned near the Pulaski County line. Neighbors who spoke with a reporter Wednesday said they hope to change Wythe County’s zoning rules to make it more difficult for data center developments to be built. Copyright 2026 WDBJ. artigo.texto: UPS Eyes $15 Billion AI Data Center Logistics Opportunity United Parcel Service Inc. (UPS, Financials), a logistics and package delivery provider, estimates that the surge in artificial intelligence data centers would create a $15 billion possibility for logistics each year. As businesses invest substantially in AI infrastructure, CEO Carol Tome predicted that the buildout would provide revenue for decades to come. UPS may be involved in every step of the supply chain, from transporting sophisticated chips to storing equipment and delivering components to operational facilities, as well as coordinating ocean freight. By focusing on more lucrative shipments rather to just increasing package volume, UPS is able to take advantage of this opportunity. Health care, returns, and data-center logistics are three high-value sectors that management has been focusing on developing while cutting lower-margin operations, including millions of Amazon deliveries. In comparison to $6 billion in 2020, UPS anticipates health care revenue alone to reach over $13 billion this year. In response to better-than-expected performance in the third quarter, the business increased its yearly projections. Data centers offer investors a new avenue for development beyond conventional package delivery, especially if expenditure on AI infrastructure stays high. The key concern is UPS's ability to really acquire a portion of the $15 billion industry. The next impetus will come from developments in data-center logistics and the sustainability of margin improvements from higher-value shipments.

artigo.texto: The Tennessee Valley Authority used to hire someone to travel to Silicon Valley and recruit data centers to the South. That era has completely ended, a TVA official said Wednesday. The new era is marked by data center companies coming to the region without incentives or recruitment. It’s also marked by data centers requiring so much electricity that TVA is charging them higher rates and special fees to protect other customers, said Jared Mitchem, principal of strategic energy initiatives at the federal agency. TVA once recruited data centers by offering a lower manufacturing electricity rate. Now it’s placed the computing facilities into their own higher rate class in August, a roughly 10% hike. While the nation’s largest power provider recruited data centers to buy its excess power in the 2010s, TVA no longer has excess power. “The tables are turned completely from us recruiting and offering incentives, to us raising the stakes, raising the costs, raising the performance requirements,” Mitchem said during a panel at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga. artigo.texto: Instalado na sede do Sebrae-RN, em Natal, o projeto conta com investimento de aproximadamente R$ 70 milhões, provenientes do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais que utilizarão a estrutura Publicado 28 de outubro de 2026 às 16:00 O Sebrae no Rio Grande do Norte inaugura, nesta quinta-feira (29), às 18h30, o segundo Data Center do Sistema Sebrae no país. A estrutura representa um dos principais investimentos da instituição nas áreas de tecnologia e segurança da informação e será responsável pelo armazenamento e processamento de dados de unidades do Sebrae em 12 estados das regiões Nordeste, Norte e Sudeste. Instalado na sede do Sebrae-RN, em Natal, o projeto conta com investimento de aproximadamente R$ 70 milhões, provenientes do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais que utilizarão a estrutura. O equipamento receberá o nome de Senador Fernando Bezerra, primeiro presidente do Conselho Deliberativo do Sebrae-RN, na década de 1990. Ele também teve atuação decisiva para viabilizar a aquisição do imóvel onde funciona a atual sede da instituição, em Natal. Com a implantação da estrutura, o Rio Grande do Norte será a segunda unidade do Sistema Sebrae no país a contar com um Data Center, juntando-se à unidade já existente no Distrito Federal. A iniciativa busca fortalecer a segurança das informações e ampliar a eficiência da infraestrutura tecnológica utilizada pela instituição. Um Data Center, ou centro de dados, é uma instalação que reúne servidores, sistemas de armazenamento, equipamentos de rede e outras tecnologias responsáveis pelo processamento, gerenciamento, proteção e distribuição de grandes volumes de informações. Segundo Franklin Maux, gerente de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação do Sebrae-RN, a escolha do estado está relacionada, entre outros fatores, ao potencial energético potiguar. A disponibilidade de fontes renováveis pode contribuir para tornar o Rio Grande do Norte mais competitivo na atração de investimentos em infraestrutura tecnológica. Franklin explica ainda que a implantação permitirá maior padronização da infraestrutura tecnológica das unidades estaduais. Atualmente, o Sistema Sebrae utiliza diferentes sistemas e tecnologias, o que aumenta a complexidade das operações. A expectativa é que o empreendimento também estimule o mercado local de tecnologia e contribua para a formação de profissionais especializados. “A ideia de termos esse Data Center no Rio Grande do Norte também é estimular que outros investimentos venham para o estado, aproveitando nossos recursos e, principalmente, a mão de obra local. Fazemos questão de fomentar a formação desses negócios”, afirmou. artigo.texto: The Jobs That Actually Exist Inside Data Centers Data centers create relatively few permanent jobs, but they still rely on a small, skilled on-site workforce to keep facilities secure, powered, cooled, and running. On the whole, data centers do not create large numbers of permanent jobs once construction is complete. But limited staffing is not the same as no staffing. To understand data centers’ true impact on employment, it is necessary to look at the roles they do create, the skills those positions require, and who typically fills them. With that in mind, here is a look at the jobs in a typical data center, focusing on roles that require in-person, on-site work. Data centers may also support a wider range of software development and IT jobs tied to the workloads they host, but those roles are rarely based inside the facilities where the hardware physically resides. Data Center Technicians: The Core of On-Site Operations “Data center technician” is a broad term for workers responsible for installing, maintaining, and troubleshooting IT equipment and supporting infrastructure inside a facility. Depending on the operator, technicians may rack and stack servers, run and label cables, replace failed hardware, monitor equipment health, and respond to incidents tied to physical infrastructure. In many facilities, technicians make up the largest share of the on-site workforce. Smaller data centers may operate with relatively lean teams, while hyperscale campuses can employ much larger technician teams spread across multiple buildings and shifts. Network Engineers: Building and Maintaining Connectivity In a data center environment, network engineers are responsible for designing, implementing, and supporting the network infrastructure that connects servers, storage, and external connectivity. In some facilities, technicians handle portions of this work as well. But operators with more complex or performance-sensitive environments may rely on network specialists to manage switching, routing, redundancy, and optimization. Because a data center’s core network architecture typically does not change dramatically once the facility is up and running, the permanent on-site footprint for network engineers is often fairly small. Some facilities may maintain only a limited number of network specialists on site, while others depend partly on centralized or remote teams. HVAC Specialists: Keeping Cooling Systems Running Cooling is fundamental to data center reliability, which makes HVAC expertise especially important. Whether a facility relies on chillers, evaporative cooling systems, CRAH units, or other thermal management technologies, it needs people who can maintain the equipment and respond to problems as they arise. Some operators outsource HVAC work to specialist firms. Even so, facilities with complex cooling systems or a very low tolerance for downtime are more likely to maintain dedicated on-site expertise or ensure regular on-site support from contracted specialists. Electricians: Supporting Mission-Critical Power Electrical infrastructure is another essential part of ongoing data center operations. Although the bulk of electrical work occurs during construction, operating facilities still need skilled electricians to inspect equipment, troubleshoot faults, support preventive maintenance, and perform repairs or upgrades to switchgear, UPS systems, backup power, and distribution infrastructure. As with HVAC work, some electrical support may be outsourced. However, because data center power environments are highly specialized and downtime is expensive, operators often prefer electricians who understand the demands of mission-critical facilities. Security Staff: Protecting the Physical Facility Physical security remains a core requirement in data centers. Hardened building design, surveillance systems, and access controls all help reduce risk, but they do not eliminate the need for trained personnel who can manage entry, monitor suspicious activity, and respond quickly to incidents. Security staffing levels vary based on a facility’s size, location, and risk profile. In general, however, data centers maintain a dedicated on-site security presence, with larger or more isolated sites often requiring broader coverage across shifts and access points. Data Center Managers: Overseeing Daily Operations Most data centers also employ a small number of managers responsible for overseeing day-to-day operations. These leaders coordinate staffing, maintenance planning, incident response, vendor relationships, compliance requirements, and overall facility performance. In effect, they translate business priorities into operational execution and ensure teams remain aligned around uptime, efficiency, and safety. Who Do Data Centers Hire? Understanding the employment impact of data centers also requires looking at who fills these roles. Available evidence suggests that many data center jobs are filled locally. The Brookings Institution, for example, has found that local employment rates tend to increase when data centers open in a community, even if the absolute number of permanent roles remains relatively modest. That pattern is not especially surprising. Many on-site data center jobs require technical skills and training, but they do not always demand rare expertise that would force operators to recruit exclusively from outside the region. The result is a more nuanced employment picture than either critics or boosters sometimes suggest. A typical data center does not create a hiring bonanza once it is operational, and construction jobs are generally more numerous than long-term facility roles. Still, most data centers do require a core on-site workforce with expertise in hardware support, networking, cooling, electrical systems, physical security, and facility operations.

artigo.texto: The San Diego City Council Tuesday unanimously backed a 45-day moratorium on the permitting, approval and development of data centers within city limits. The vote was prompted last week after a local developer floated the idea of building one near Old Town in the Naval Information Warfare Systems Command site, known as NAVWAR. Mayor Todd Gloria immediately issued and signed an executive order to temporarily pause data center development in San Diego until the city can develop regulations. Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7. "San Diego is a city of innovation, and I want us to continue leading in the technologies and jobs of the future," Gloria said. "But we cannot allow a rapidly expanding industry to get ahead of the rules needed to protect our residents. Data centers can place significant demands on our water supply, electricity grid and limited land, with consequences for utility bills, housing opportunities and neighborhoods." Dozens of San Diegans spoke at Tuesday's council meeting, including speakers dressed as Elmo from "Sesame Street" and Lord Farquaad from "Shrek," nearly unanimously opposed to the development of data centers in the city. "San Diegans were clear, unambiguous and passionate about why data centers don't belong in San Diego," Council President Joe LaCava said. Tuesday's action puts the pause on the development of data centers for 45 days while city staff develop a framework on how to proceed with such facilities, if at all, in the future. The moratorium could be extended for nearly two years if the council chooses to. City staff would have a deadline of 180 days to bring forward preliminary recommendations to the mayor and council. It would be guided by a Data Center Stakeholder Working Group, including representatives with expertise in fields ranging from technology, utilities, water, land use, housing and community advocacy, according to a statement from the mayor's office. The plan is to officially amend the city's land development code next year. Councilman Sean Elo-Rivera tacked on amendments to the moratorium intended to guide the creation of a framework, including: - Council notification of any proposed centers within seven days - No costs from data centers imposed upon city residents - Project labor agreements needing to use union labor during construction, clean, renewable energy only - A minimum distance from schools, parks and child care centers, among others The idea of a 400-megawatt data center by the San Diego-based Manchester Financial Group was being considered for the NAVWAR location. It would include enough energy to power around 300,000 homes annually and would be the largest in the state of California. Local "The costs dramatically outweigh any benefits in the current environment," Councilman Raul Campillo said. Ted Eldredge, president and CEO of that company, said the data center was one of several ideas and that nothing had been finalized. "Manchester Financial Group's priority for the Old Town Campus redevelopment is delivering modern facilities for NAVWAR, and we remain committed to working with the Navy and other community stakeholders to do so throughout this process," he wrote in a statement. "Several other project elements are being considered such as retail, commercial, industrial and hospitality uses. The possibilities of a medical center, university campus, defense industry campus, data center and life science facility are also being explored." This 70-acre, Navy-owned site has been the subject of redevelopment speculation for several years, including as a mixed-use site that could include affordable house as well as military housing. Since NAVWAR is federally owned, a city moratorium is more of a symbolic measure for that specific site, but several council members said the fight would continue. "The people asking the hardest questions and fighting the hardest are the ones who will live with it," said Elo-Rivera, referring to dozens of young people speaking at Tuesday's meeting. "The future does not belong to billionaires. Donald Trump wants data centers on federal land so he can dodge communities like ours." Trump has ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to find military property that could be used to house data centers. "San Diego needs more affordable housing, not more computer servers," Councilman Stephen Whitburn said. "Federal ownership does not mean San Diegans should be shut out of decisions which will impact us for generations to come." One of Elo-Rivera's amendments was to get Gloria's government affairs team to lobby lawmakers to take the issue up in Congress. "Working families and young people are being priced out of the city, struggling to afford rent, and wondering whether they can ever buy a home in San Diego," Council President Pro Tem Kent Lee said. "That includes countless service members who call San Diego home. NAVWAR should maximize its potential as a transit-oriented development with a vibrant residential neighborhood. The city should utilize the extent of our land use authority to regulate data centers and to protect the quality of life for all San Diegans."
