artigo.texto: Artificial intelligence — and the data centers needed to power it — are major political issues this midterm election. More than two-thirds of New Hampshire residents would oppose an AI data center being built in their town and 45% would support halting construction of any more data centers statewide, according to a University of New Hampshire poll from June. If policies about AI and data centers matter to your vote, we’ve compiled information on where the candidates for major offices this year stand. Gubernatorial: Republican Kelly Ayotte vs Democrat Cinde Warmington Both Republican incumbent Gov. Kelly Ayotte and her opponent Democrat Cinde Warmington are calling for a temporary moratorium on building new data centers in the state, but they differ on how they would do so. Ayotte plans to put a moratorium on new data centers in her state budget plan. Ayotte spoke out earlier this year against data center proposals in Bow and Nottingham. In an interview with NHPR, Ayotte said that based on her conversations with the head of the region’s electric grid operator, ISO New England, the state's energy infrastructure can’t support large data centers without ratepayers seeing their bills go up. “I don't want that to happen. I want to bring energy costs down,” she said. Ayotte said she plans to include a moratorium on new data center construction in her 2027 state budget proposal. The proposal, which will be introduced in February, would need approval by the state Legislature, and the state budget takes effect on July 1, meaning a moratorium enacted that way would not go into effect until next summer at the earliest. Warmington calls for an immediate executive order imposing a moratorium. Warmington criticized Ayotte’s plan and what she called the governor’s failure to take action sooner, telling NHPR that Ayotte “provided no leadership” on a doomed Democratic-led effort to enact a moratorium this spring in the Legislature. Warmington said that as governor she would issue an executive order banning the facilities, as opposed to putting the measure in her budget. “I want a moratorium and I want it now,” she told NHPR. “Kelly is proposing something in her budget into the future. By the time that's enacted, we will have data centers in our state.” Ayotte, for her part, said during an Oct. 22 NHPR candidate forum that a governor isn’t legally allowed to issue a moratorium via executive order, according to conversations she said she had with the state’s attorney general. During that same debate, Warmington criticized Ayotte for signing HB 672 into last year. The bill deregulated off-grid electricity providers, meaning facilities that supply their own power would not be subject to oversight from the Public Utilities Committee and could skirt certain regulations related to pricing and renewable energy. As the bill was being debated, its proponents said it would support energy-intensive facilities like data centers, while potentially protecting ratepayers from rising costs by preventing additional strain from being added to the grid. Ayotte pushed back against Warmington’s characterization of the bill. “HB 672 was signed to make it easier to drive down electric costs,” she said in a statement. U.S. Senate: Democrat Chris Pappas vs Republican John Sununu Both Democrat Rep. Chris Pappas and Republican John E. Sununu have said they support a state-level moratorium on data center construction. While U.S. senators do not oversee state policy, they could take a policy position on any federal legislation that could restrict or protect state-level moratoriums. Both Sununu and Pappas have called for more federal oversight of AI, though they named different priorities and strategies. In an interview, Pappas told NHPR that Congress should establish “guardrails that will regulate big tech," and a federal approval process for new AI models before they are made public. During a Oct. 13 debate, he said the US should embrace the positive aspects of AI and “outcompete China.” As a member of Congress, Pappas signed a bipartisan letter on Oct. 14 raising concerns about tech behemoth Meta using a federal tax credit to fund data center construction. Sununu has called for rules primarily around AI safety and security, saying he would advocate for legislation that protects children and seniors, and prioritizes cybersecurity and national security. 1st Congressional District: Democrat Stefany Shaheen vs Republican Anthony DiLorenzo In the race for Pappas’ seat in the U.S. House, the candidates disagree on how to address data center construction. Democrat Stefany Shaheen has called for a statewide moratorium. Republican Anthony DiLorenzo has said he is in favor of local communities making that decision themselves. “I support local control. If a local municipality wants to support a data center, they should be able to do so and along with a data center comes a lot of economic prosperity,” DiLorenzo said during an Oct.19 debate. When it comes to AI development, both have said there is a need for regulations at the Congressional level, but they differed on how they would like to see this accomplished. During an Oct. 6 NHPR candidate debate, DiLorenzo called for a “public-private partnership” for crafting these regulations, so that the U.S. “[wins] the AI race” but privacy, children and jobs are protected. “AI has the potential to devastate our labor markets, and if we are not proactive in addressing AI, it could be catastrophic,” he said. Shaheen said Congress should set AI regulations that prioritize safety and economic security. “We need a regulatory roadmap that gives control to the states to protect our economies here at home, and we need to be clear about where those threats exist, how we protect young people, how we protect the future of our economy,” she said during the same Oct. 6 debate. 2nd Congressional District: Democrat Maggie Goodlander vs Republican Lily Tang Williams Democratic Incumbent Rep. artigo.texto: Iowa could double data center tax revenue by reclassifying as manufacturers, study finds (We are Iowa)– A new economic study from Common Sense Institute Iowa (CSI) found that Iowa could be taking hundreds of millions of additional dollars from data centers if the state considers them as manufacturers. Recently, the city of Ames paused approval for a data center to allow for more research after community push back. Putting politics aside, CSI wants residents to look at the issue from an economic standpoint. In 2025, Iowa data centers paid $56.1 million in property taxes. Data center property tax is expected to reach $140 million by 2031 and $292 million by 2040. However, CSI said those numbers could double if Iowa would treat data centers as manufacturers. In Iowa, manufacturers are only taxed on their output. Data centers are taxed on their input, for example their servers, and then they are taxed again on their output. CSI said that if Iowa doesn’t change the law, the state could miss out big time. “At the end of the day what communities do is a political decision … what people need to understand in Iowa and Iowa’s communities is that, from an economic standpoint, you either take part in investment growth and economic growth and the buildout that’s going to happen anyway — or you can say I don’t care about the economics of it and forego economic opportunity and job growth and income growth,” said Ben Murrey, director of policy and research at Common Sense Institute Iowa. One of the big complaints against data centers is infrastructure strain on communities, leading to higher water and power bills. “What we’re seeing is quite the opposite [of putting high demands on energy resources] because the supply is responding to the increase in demand and companies like Google in Cedar Rapids are investing a lot of money in increasing the supply of energy,” Murrey said. CSI plans to conduct a larger study next year about increases to energy supplies, but Murrey points out that it’s not the case everywhere. Power bills are going down 20% after Google paid for investments to transmission and generators in Cedar Rapids, the study says. That led to energy supply increases, which lowered resident’s power bills. The CSI study also found that data center parcels generated roughly 153 times the property tax in 2025 compared to under its previous use. It’s projected to rise to about 505 times by 2040. Homeowners are also seeing property tax relief, according to the study. In Norwalk, residents reportedly saved $631 over three years, and in Waukee, homeowners saved $269 over four years. “It’s like the build out of the railroad over a century ago,” Murrey said. “You have two options: you can be part of investment and part of economic growth and jobs that come with it or you cannot be part of it. It’s happening either way.”

artigo.texto: PRICE —Valar Atomics and its proposed nuclear energy development in Carbon County drew considerable attention during the Price City Council meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 28. Council members also considered a battery energy storage project and several other city matters during the meeting. Harry Hanson, representing Valar Atomics, appeared before the council to address questions about the company’s plans in Carbon County and provide updates on its existing work in Emery County. Hanson explained that Valar has secured approximately 640 acres of state trust land for its proposed Carbon County development and is pursuing additional land through the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). He said the BLM process could take seven to 10 years, while the overall project could develop in phases over several decades. Council members questioned Hanson about property taxes, water use, grazing rights, public safety, waste disposal and the project’s timeline. Hanson said improvements and equipment built on the state land would generate local property tax revenue. According to preliminary estimates he shared, the initial development could produce revenue equivalent to approximately half of Carbon County’s current property tax collections. Council members pressed him on whether commitments to property tax relief would be formalized in writing. Hanson said he could not speak for county officials about how the money would be used. On water use, Hanson said Valar’s reactors are cooled with helium rather than water and that the company is working with potential data center customers using closed-loop cooling systems. He also said existing grazing permit holders would be able to continue using undeveloped portions of the property as the project progresses. Council members raised questions about environmental oversight and nuclear waste. Hanson said federal regulators oversee most aspects of nuclear operations, while spent fuel would be stored in protected dry casks on-site until a federal long-term storage facility becomes available. Hanson also discussed the company’s test reactor in Orangeville. He said the reactor was intentionally subjected to a failure scenario in July and shut down as designed. However, Valar has not yet obtained a commercial operating license, and Hanson said the company intends to refine its design before seeking one. When asked about the Carbon County project’s timeline, Hanson said the company would like to begin moving dirt in 2027, although commercial operations remain dependent on licensing and other approvals. The council also asked about local hiring and opportunities for residents to learn more about the proposal. Hanson said the Orangeville operation has approximately 102 employees and that many jobs draw on the region’s existing energy workforce. He also offered additional facility tours and small-group discussions. Following the presentation, Hanson and several other Valar employees moved into the hallway, where the majority of the crowd gathered to continue the conversation. For nearly two hours, residents had the opportunity to speak directly with company representatives, ask questions and voice concerns about the proposed development. Valar employees remained in the hallway throughout the discussions, listening to residents, providing information and addressing concerns as the council continued with the remainder of its meeting. The project returned to the discussion during the public comment portion of the meeting when residents questioned whether promised economic benefits would be guaranteed. Liz Trostle, chair of the Green Team of Carbon County, asked what assurances exist in writing for local jobs, tax revenue, infrastructure costs and possible cleanup responsibilities if the project does not move forward. Zena Robinson submitted questions for the public record concerning commercial licensing, potential agreements with Price City utilities, emergency response, water consumption and the Orangeville test facility. Other speakers raised concerns about potential electricity costs associated with data centers, the transportation of nuclear materials on city roads and opportunities for residents to provide input directly to elected officials. Marianne Lawrence suggested a public website tracking known facts, outstanding questions and project developments. Although the proposed site is outside Price City limits, council members emphasized that its impacts could extend into the city. In the end, no action was taken on Valar’s proposal as the company’s appearance was an informational presentation. Another significant discussion involved a proposed battery energy storage system presented by representatives of Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems (UAMPS). Scott Meadors and Alex Estejo outlined a potential 5.04-megawatt battery storage project that would provide approximately two hours of energy storage capacity for Price City. The battery would allow the city to store electricity when costs are lower and utilize that energy during periods of higher demand, reducing the need to purchase more expensive electricity during peak usage. UAMPS representatives estimated the project could save Price City approximately $5.4 million over 20 years, with the initial investment potentially recovered in less than six years. Council members questioned the system’s lifespan, safety, maintenance requirements and operational costs. Representatives explained that the system would have an anticipated lifespan of approximately 20 years and would include monitoring and fire suppression equipment. The proposed location is near the Price substation, although additional planning would be necessary before a final site is selected. The council approved continuing development work on the project. artigo.texto: SALEM TWP. — Supervisors paved the way for a potential $43 million community benefit agreement that includes a $12 million “micro-hospital” with their votes Tuesday to nearly triple the size of the township’s data center overlay district. Supervisor John Fogg and Chairman Rick Talanca voted to approve two ordinances to amend the township zoning map at a regular meeting that immediately followed a public hearing on the expansion issue. Supervisor Steven Fraind abstained from the vote because the house in which his mother resides and transferred into his name several years ago is part of a $1.2 billion land sale necessary for the establishment of 4,466-acre data center campus in the township. Jack Sordoni, principal of the 4-3 Consulting Group that negotiated that land deal, touted the hospital as one of the benefits the community would see with the establishment of a third data center campus in the township during a slide presentation that was part of his testimony at the public hearing. The supervisors also approved further expanding the data center district by 185 additional acres to accommodate a fourth data center campus as requested by Moores 109 LLC. Sordoni said 4-3 is proposing a “stabilize-and-transfer” micro-hospital with a full emergency department open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, on 42 acres along U.S. Route 11 (Salem Twp. Boulevard) at the intersection with Stone Church Road. The facility would be a welcome addition to the community, given that Berwick Hospital Center closed in 2022. The next-closest hospital to the township is Geisinger Bloomsburg Hospital, which Google Maps puts at a 22- to 40-minute drive, depending on where in the township the drive begins. Thirteen members of the public spoke about the Proposed data center district expansions, with eight supporting them and five opposed. The data center developers will have to come before the board of supervisors for approvals of land development plans and they will need state approvals, as well. Check back for an updated story with more details from the hearings and supervisors meeting.

artigo.texto: Alton residents pack open house about possible data center at former steel mill Developer Terrawatt has not yet submitted a proposal to the city ALTON, Ill. (First Alert 4) - Dozens of Alton residents attended an open house to learn about a possible data center at the former Alton Steel Mill. The project from developer Terrawatt is drawing mixed reactions. The line to get into the open house wrapped around the block, with many people waiting 45 minutes to an hour. Inside, the room was packed, with representatives speaking about the project. Protesters held up signs and banners, voicing their opposition. Residents share concerns and support Stacy Roquemore, who lives in Alton, said he is concerned about the project. “The noise, the pollution, it’s everything, the raising of costs of our bills and I mean as everyone knows here in Illinois, the costs of our electric, gas and water are already so high,” Roquemore said. Some attendees said they believe the project will bring opportunity. Russell Scott, a Local 218 union worker, said he supports it. “It helps the brothers and sisters out with more jobs and stuff like that. Just more jobs, that’s all,” Scott said. Steven Landreth, a local electrician who lives in Alton, also said he sees a benefit. “The city needs a place to bring in some cash, some local business and jobs,” Landreth said. Other attendees said they are keeping an open mind. One attendee said he wants to hear details about the project. “I just want to hear the time frame, and then what they say the impact is going to be on the public, what they will do to local power, the local water…” the attendee said. Christy Fritz-Parker, a homeowner in Alton, said she opposes the project. She was among several protestors who stayed outside the open house. “I think they were hoping that here in Alton, we’re maybe not as educated as maybe St. Louis or these other communities, but I want them to know that the word is out and people here in Alton do not want the data center,” Fritz-Parker said. Development consultant says project will benefit Alton Cecilia Dvorak, CEO of Steadfast City Economic and Community Partners, is from the development consultant firm working with Terrawatt. She said the open house provides a venue for people to learn about the proposal and its impacts. “We’re able to provide a venue for people to get a little bit of understanding of the proposal itself, also the impacts. And then the conversation also helps us inform what the proposal looks like,” Dvorak said. Dvorak said the project will be beneficial for Alton. “There’s a significant amount of benefit, particularly in tax revenues that can be generated by the project just by its presence,” Dvorak said. Project details and next steps The proposed data center would be called the Riverbend Technology Center. It would be housed at the former Alton Steel Mill, which closed at the start of the year. Some residents also expressed concern about Terrawatt because the company is behind the data center project at the Armory in Midtown St. Louis. Terrawatt sued the city several months ago over prerequisites for construction. Terrawatt has not yet submitted a proposal to the city of Alton on the data center. Reporter Raya Torres was told the goal is to submit the proposal by the end of the year, but that is not definite. The company said it was important to host the open house so it could inform people about its proposal. Copyright 2026 KMOV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: O Rio Grande do Norte vai receber o segundo Data Center do Sistema Sebrae no Brasil. A estrutura será inaugurada nesta quinta-feira (29), às 18h30, na sede do Sebrae-RN, em Natal, e ficará responsável pelo armazenamento e processamento de dados de unidades da instituição em 12 estados das regiões Nordeste, Norte e Sudeste. O investimento previsto é de aproximadamente R$ 70 milhões. Os recursos são provenientes do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais que utilizarão o equipamento. Com a inauguração, o Rio Grande do Norte passará a contar com uma estrutura desse tipo no sistema, ao lado do Distrito Federal, onde funciona o primeiro Data Center da instituição. O espaço receberá o nome de Senador Fernando Bezerra, que foi o primeiro presidente do Conselho Deliberativo do Sebrae-RN, na década de 1990. Ele também participou da viabilização da compra do imóvel onde funciona a atual sede da instituição, na capital potiguar. Segundo Franklin Maux, gerente de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação do Sebrae-RN, a escolha do estado levou em consideração, entre outros fatores, o potencial energético potiguar. A disponibilidade de fontes renováveis pode favorecer a instalação de empreendimentos de infraestrutura tecnológica. A nova estrutura também deve permitir maior padronização dos sistemas utilizados pelas unidades estaduais, que atualmente operam com diferentes tecnologias. De acordo com o Sebrae-RN, o projeto poderá estimular investimentos no setor de tecnologia no estado e contribuir para a formação de profissionais especializados. Um Data Center é uma instalação que concentra servidores, equipamentos de rede e sistemas de armazenamento responsáveis pelo processamento, gerenciamento e proteção de informações. A estrutura será utilizada para atender às operações das unidades do Sebrae contempladas pelo projeto.

artigo.texto: CASPER, Wyo. — The planned data center project at Falls Ranch will move forward under a new development company despite the sudden departure of Prometheus Hyperscale, ranch representatives announced Wednesday evening. The announcement came hours after local officials learned Prometheus backed out of its proposed $500 million computing center east of Casper. Falls Ranch representatives said the change in partners will not stall progress on the 940-acre site south of Interstate 25, with public meetings planned for 2027. “This has always been a Wyoming project, but today it represents something even greater: an opportunity for Natrona County to shape its own economic future,” Robert Hand, representative for Falls Ranch, said. Hand said the project will still pursue local filing deadlines, work to build community partnerships and bring construction jobs, long-term employment and tax revenue to the county. “This recent shift will expedite and elevate this project for Natrona County, and we couldn’t be more excited about it,” he said. “Falls Ranch will remain committed to agricultural stewardship and will continue to honor Wyoming’s ranching legacy.” The release did not name the incoming developer or explain why Prometheus exited the deal. Earlier Wednesday, Prometheus confirmed it had abandoned its proposal to build a 1.5-gigawatt campus on the ranch. The original plan called for data halls, closed-loop cooling systems and on-site natural gas generators supplied by Evansville-based Mesa Power Solutions. Company leaders had pitched the project as a source of 3,000 temporary construction jobs, 150 permanent positions and tens of millions of dollars in annual property tax revenue. The project drew pushback from nearby landowners along Hat Six Road and Meadow Acres. Neighbors raised issues during public meetings over round-the-clock generator noise, light pollution, air emissions, heavy truck traffic and state sales tax exemptions for data center equipment. Prometheus had not submitted applications to the Natrona County Planning and Zoning Commission before pulling out. County commissioners were shocked at the company’s departure, noting Prometheus gave no warning before walking away. “I have absolutely no clue of why they’ve decided to pull out or anything else at this point in time,” Natrona County Commissioner Dave North said earlier in the day. Justin Farley, CEO of Advance Casper, said earlier Wednesday that other tech developers currently hold land options in the county and that local industrial recruitment continues.

artigo.texto: RES has welcomed its first consent for a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Northern Ireland, after Mid and East Antrim Borough Council’s Planning Committee approved the Ballyross BESS. Located on land approximately 2 km south-west of Gleno and 8.5 km south-west of Larne, Ballyross is strategically positioned close to the existing Ballyvallagh substation. This will support the efficient operation of the system while minimising the need for additional grid infrastructure. As constraints on Northern Ireland's electricity system increase, clean, low-cost electricity capable of powering homes and businesses can sometimes be prevented from reaching consumers. Battery energy storage projects such as Ballyross can help make better use of this electricity by storing it when generation is high and releasing it when demand rises. By adding flexibility and supporting grid stability, Ballyross will help create a more efficient and resilient electricity system. Peter Deeney, Senior Development Project Manager at RES, said: "From our office in Larne, RES has been proud to contribute to Northern Ireland’s energy future and economic growth since the early 1990s. Securing consent for Ballyross, our first battery energy storage project to be consented in Northern Ireland, is an important milestone as we continue transforming the way energy is generated, stored, and supplied. “Battery storage is becoming increasingly important as Northern Ireland continues its transition to a low-carbon energy system. Projects such as Ballyross can help make the electricity network more flexible and resilient, so that more renewable energy can be stored and used when it is needed most.” The approved scheme also includes a substantial landscaping package. New native-species planting will help the development blend into the surrounding landscape while creating wildlife corridors and pollinator-friendly habitat that deliver additional biodiversity benefits. Peter continued: “Alongside its strategic location close to Ballyvallagh substation, the site was selected because it has limited visibility from local properties. The new planting will further reduce visibility while providing valuable resources for a wide range of flora and fauna. “We would particularly like to thank the local residents and stakeholders who engaged with us throughout the development of Ballyross. The feedback shared during consultation helped inform our landscaping plan and shape the project’s final design.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: The San Diego City Council, on a 9-0 vote Tuesday, passed an urgency ordinance that places a moratorium on the development of new data centers within the city. Coming days after an executive order from Mayor Todd Gloria, the moratorium is designed to give officials time to develop policies and recommendations to make sure that data centers align with the city’s General Plan and its Climate Action Plan. “I appreciate the City Council’s unanimous ratification of the temporary moratorium on data center development,” Gloria said in a statement. “This is a necessary and responsible step to make sure any development does not outpace our responsibility to protect San Diegans.” The temporary moratorium lasts 45 days but gives the City Council the power to extend the suspension for another 10 months and 15 days. No more than two extensions will be allowed and will require approval from four-fifths of the council. The pause “gives us time to start putting the right regulations in place,” Councilmember Marni von Wilpert said. “AI data centers must pay their own way without passing additional electricity or water costs onto our residents. It is already too expensive to live here.” The moratorium, however, does not figure to directly impact any possible construction of a data center that the Manchester Financial Group is exploring as part of its plans to redevelop the 70.3-acre Naval Base Point Loma Old Town Campus, which is home to Naval Information Warfare Systems Command (NAVWAR). That’s because NAVWAR is on federal land, beyond the city’s jurisdiction. Manchester Financial executives have looked at the possibility of a data center to make up a portion of the NAVWAR site, although the group says it is merely one of a range of options on the table. The current development plan already contemplates a number of definitive uses, including 8,900 residential units and two hotels totaling 480 rooms. The company has floated the idea of a 400-megawatt data center, which would be the largest in California, but Manchester president and CEO Ted Eldredge told the Union-Tribune last week, “We’re not married to that megawattage” and that any possible facility is dependent on market conditions and overall feasibility. After Tuesday’s vote, Eldredge said in a statement, “We continue to look at a variety of options for the site as we seek to build a best-in-class facility for the Navy,” adding that any proposed plans must go through environmental review before any decisions will be made. “The City and public will have (the) opportunity to review proposed plans and provide comment,” Eldredge said. “We remain committed to working with the Navy and community stakeholders throughout this process.” Essential toward driving the boom in artificial intelligence, data centers have drawn increasing scrutiny across the country in recent months. The facilities house racks of computer systems required to train generative AI models and chatbots. Supporters say data centers can drive cutting-edge technology and actually drive down overall energy costs through economies of scale. But critics worry the electricity needed to feed data centers will strain the grid and drive already steep power bills in San Diego Gas & Electric’s service territory — with rates at or the near the top of most expensive in the country — even higher. In addition, data centers, in order to stay cool, can suck up large amounts of water. The moratorium aims to set data center guidelines within the city’s purview. The pause passed Tuesday includes establishing a working group of as many as 15 stakeholders to develop recommendations for water and electricity demand and potential impacts on utility bills, housing and neighborhoods. “San Diego welcomes innovation, investment and the jobs that come with them,” Gloria said. “What we will not do is ask residents to absorb unnecessary costs or neighborhood impacts.” Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera called for, and the City Council accepted, a list of principles to guide the framework for what the Gloria administration and city staff may permanently put into place. They include policies seeking “no direct or indirect costs to San Diego residents or ratepayers;” data centers that use 100% renewable energy and no fossil fuels for backup generation; a plan for using recycled water at the facilities; and a “minimum separation” distance between any data centers and schools, parks and child care facilities. “People want quick, decisive action on this, not a long bureaucratic conversation,” Elo-Rivera said. “People don’t want data centers in their communities and the reasons are loud and clear.” Though not formally included within the moratorium, Elo-Rivera called for SDG&E to be excluded from the city’s proposed stakeholder group of up to 15 members. “In SDG&E’s eyes, no cost to San Diegans has ever been excessive,” said Elo-Rivera, a frequent critic of the utility. “They remind us of that every single month, and now they want even more,” referring to an upcoming SDG&E general rate case before the California Public Utilities Commission. Asked for a reaction, SDG&E spokesperson Anthony Wagner told the Union-Tribune that a working group examining data center issues “should include the relevant technical expertise, including SDG&E. artigo.texto: Is Dallas-Fort Worth on track to become the heart of America's largest data center market? To see what's happening, NBC 5 Investigates mapped the locations of DFW area data center projects under construction or in the planning pipeline, using data provided by two companies that closely track data center development. Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are The maps highlight the rapid pace of planned data center growth in the region, and they pinpoint communities - especially south of Dallas - that could see a data center boom. Development experts said the growth in that region is driven largely by access to power and fiber connections. And some believe the area's growing popularity with developers will propel Dallas to become the anchor of a Texas market with more data centers than any other state. Southern DFW's data center corridor Create a free account with NBC 5 DFW to save articles and videos. The development data illustrates how much of the current boom is clustering in three communities south of downtown Dallas running along Interstate 35, and then to the east toward Interstate 45. NBC 5 Investigates created maps using information provided by Cleanview and Datacenter Map, two leading groups that track data center development plans. In Lancaster, Red Oak and Wilmer, the development data showed 10 data centers currently operating and almost four times as many on the way. Some are under construction; others are proposed sites or projected additions to existing data center campuses. In Red Oak, NBC 5 Investigates' mapping of data from the two tracking organizations shows nine data centers currently operating and 14 more in planning or under construction. In Lancaster, three data centers are under construction and 11 more are in the pipeline, while in Wilmer, 11 new data centers are planned on top of one already there. Analysts who track data center construction told NBC 5 Investigates it's easy to see why so many developers are drawn to corridors south of downtown Dallas. They cite not only availability of power and major fiber connections, but also momentum created by an already established data center market. "Everybody wants to be where everybody already is, right? The market has proven to be successful for data center developers and operators. And so that attracts more as well," said John McWilliams, who studies data center development for commercial real estate giant Cushman & Wakefield. 'Dallas is the anchor' McWilliams said Dallas is now leading a Texas market that's on track to overtake Virginia as the nation's biggest data center location. "Texas is enormous. It's got the scale to grow, the room to grow, and facilitate that demand. And Dallas is just kind of the anchor of that," McWilliams said. McWilliams said, when measured by the amount of power consumed by data centers, the Dallas market is on pace to nearly double in size in the next three to five years, based on projects under construction. And the pipeline of future proposed projects is even larger, although it's not guaranteed that all of those projects will be built. McWilliams recently published a study that ranked the Dallas area as the No. 1 primary data center market, not just in America, but the world. The report considered factors like power and land availability and the current construction pipeline. 'No better place in the Western world for data centers' According to developers, several factors position the DFW area for explosive data center growth and explain why more companies have targeted locations in communities just south of Dallas. "Dallas has always been at the center of fiber connectivity between the West Coast and the East Coast," said Haynes Strader, chief development officer at Skybox, a Dallas-based data center company that's building a 100-acre data center campus in Lancaster. Strader explained early data centers preferred to be close to those major internet connection points. He said the area just south of Dallas also sits at a major electric power intersection between West Texas and North Texas. "A lot of that power connectivity sits in south Dallas, and so there was a lot of excess capacity for many, many years in south Dallas," Strader said. Skybox said it aimed to build in industrial areas, not near homes, and said its data centers contribute millions in tax revenue to cities like Lancaster, where the city council has welcomed data center construction. Strader believes the Southern Dallas boom will keep booming over the next five to 10 years. "There's no better place in the Western world for data centers to live than Texas. You've got a massive amount of generation capacity. Tremendously talented workforce," Strader said. Living through a boom In communities where data centers are rising from the ground, and more are in the works, some residents wonder what living through a boom will look like. Red Oak resident Chris Villegas told NBC 5 he had no idea he was living in a corridor that was on track for data center growth until he learned on social media about plans for a data center just on the other side of the fence line from his family's home. That's not what he expected when he moved to Red Oak, hoping for a country lifestyle not far from the city. "We saw tractors driving down the street, lots of just farmland," Villegas said. Villegas said he's not opposed to all data centers but doesn't think Red Oak needs more, especially near homes. Villegas and his wife helped launch a local group calling for "no more data centers," along with neighbors like Lacey Hammel, who worry the more data centers built there, the more may follow. "I feel like if they add all of this, then the land is going to be even more valuable in that regard. So, the growth would seem to just continue unchecked," Hammel said. artigo.texto: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore), through its Energy Research Institute @ NTU (ERI@N), and Singapore energy storage company VFT have launched a S$15 million joint research laboratory to develop safer, more durable and cost-effective batteries for storing renewable electricity and supporting future power grids. The NTU-VFT Joint Lab was launched at the Asia Clean Energy Summit, held as part of Singapore International Energy Week 2026. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, which store energy within battery cells themselves, VRFBs store energy in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks. Because their storage capacity can be increased simply by using larger tanks, they are well suited to storing and supplying electricity over extended periods, making them a candidate technology for large-scale, long-duration energy storage. A key safety advantage of the technology lies in its chemistry. VRFBs use non-flammable, aqueous-based liquids to store energy, significantly reducing the risk of battery fires compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries. This characteristic is becoming increasingly relevant as power grids incorporate more intermittent renewable energy sources such as solar and wind, requiring storage systems that can absorb electricity when renewable generation is high and release it when needed, helping to maintain a reliable power supply. Professor Madhavi Srinivasan, Executive Director of ERI@N, said: “As the global energy transition accelerates, safe and efficient energy storage will become increasingly important to keeping electricity supplies stable and reliable. By combining NTU’s deep expertise in materials science, AI, energy technologies and sustainability with VFT’s industry experience, we aim to develop safer, longer-lasting and sustainable batteries to power our future energy grid.” She added that VFT’s journey shows how NTU’s research can translate into real-world applications, noting that what began as a spin-off from NTU working on their first generation of energy storage systems has evolved into a company developing commercial energy-storage systems, and expressing that the university is glad to be working with VFT once again to develop the next generation of energy storage solutions and drive further innovation. Dr Vidal Bharath, Chief Executive Officer of VFT, framed the challenge facing modern power systems: “The challenge is no longer simply generating more renewable energy. Power systems also need safe, reliable and affordable ways to store that electricity for use when renewable generation falls or demand rises.” He said that by combining NTU’s research capabilities with VFT’s experience in developing and deploying flow batteries, the partners aim to overcome the technical and cost barriers to wider adoption of new energy-storage technologies and accelerate commercial deployment. The research programme at the Joint Lab will pursue several technical directions. Researchers will develop more powerful and efficient flow batteries, including improved battery stacks and cooling systems designed to manage heat and boost performance. Other areas of research include improving power conversion and control systems to increase energy efficiency, and using artificial intelligence to monitor battery performance, detect faults and predict maintenance needs. Sustainability and cost are also central to the collaboration. The researchers will explore ways to recover and recycle vanadium from industrial waste and alternative sources, an approach that could potentially reduce costs and improve the sustainability of the technology. The S$15 million collaboration is supported under Singapore’s Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 plans and aims to develop new intellectual property, prototypes and technologies that can be progressively validated and incorporated into future commercial energy-storage systems. Beyond technology development, the Joint Lab is intended to strengthen Singapore’s talent and R&D capabilities in long-duration energy storage, helping the country transition towards cleaner and more resilient power systems. VFT, founded in 2018, is an NTU spin-off based on technology developed at ERI@N. The company raised US$20.5 million in 2025 to expand manufacturing and deployment of its flow-battery systems. The renewed partnership between the university and its spin-off reflects a broader effort to move laboratory-scale advances in energy storage toward commercial systems capable of supporting grids that increasingly depend on variable renewable generation. artigo.texto: Arlington officials are exploring areas within the city’s boundaries where data centers could be located and standards regulating their operation, should developers show interest. In a Tuesday meeting, Arlington City Council members were for the first time presented with proposed ordinances that outlined the zoning districts where certain data centers would be based. The proposed ordinances detailed regulations for data centers that would operate primarily out of their own buildings, in shared spaces and those that act as accessories — or sit adjacent — to larger infrastructure. Council members first received a presentation in late September about the different types of data centers and which of these the city was most likely to see. Land development assistant director Kenneth Bloom explained that a set of ordinances was created for data centers across the three kinds of development based on the types of hubs most likely to operate in Arlington given the city’s limited land availability. For example, a data center operating in its own building with the most likelihood of setting up shop in Arlington would be an enterprise facility, according to city documents. These centers typically require 5 to 10 acres. An enterprise facility is often wholly operated by a single company to process internal data and operations. Homebuilder D.R. Horton’s facility, located off Interstate 30 in north Arlington, is an example of an enterprise data center. Data centers in stand-alone buildings would only be permitted in light industrial and industrial manufacturing-zoned districts, accompanied by a specific use permit. Stand-alone data centers would be allowed in planned development-zoned districts as long as the project is specifically identified, according to city documents. Additionally, these facilities would have to comply with further regulations, including maintaining a distance of at least 300 feet from homes and a building height of no more than 75 feet. Stand-alone centers would also be prohibited from using evaporative cooling. Enterprise or stand-alone data centers would be required to comply with limits on daytime and nighttime noise levels and conduct testing before and after construction, city staffers proposed. Edge data centers also have a high probability of being built in Arlington. These facilities would be what Bloom described as equipment box-accessories, operating either inside or near a larger building. Bloom compared these data centers to equipment boxes found directly next to cell towers. No cooling regulations were proposed for the equipment box-like data centers, but they would be limited to a surface area of 200 square feet and not measure more than 12 feet in height. Co-located data centers would likely operate as accessories in buildings with multiple tenants, according to a Sept. 29 council agenda, but these facilities have moderate chances of coming to Arlington. City staffers propose accessory-designated data centers to operate in any nonresidential zoning, but they must be tied to the building’s primary use. “A financial services company might have three stories in the building that they might use, one for their data center uses,” Bloom said, detailing a scenario in which a data center would act as an accessory. Accessory-designated data centers would be prohibited from equipping evaporate cooling and outdoor backup power generators, such as diesel-generated power sources, city documents show. However, depending on their size, the centers would be permitted battery energy storage systems. The technology is compared to that of a large battery, storing energy from the electric grid for later use in the event of a power outage. Council member Brittney Garcia-Dumas asked Bloom how proposed ordinances were crafted, later stating she wants data centers located “as far away” from homes and residents as possible. “These things kind of came about just from research and from other ordinances around the country and around the state,” Bloom said. “Again, kind of tailored to what Arlington’s needs really would be.” Garcia-Dumas said she supports the city’s proposed regulations on noise before granting permits, considering how residents’ quality of life can be affected. “I’m in favor of the modeling … so that we can really look out for our residents as we are also looking out for our economic future,” Garcia-Dumas said. Before Bloom addressed Garcia-Dumas’ questions, Bloom said regulations and ordinances are subject to change. “This is a work in progress. The technology changes every day,” Bloom said. artigo.texto: O projeto de energia solar fotovoltaica em telhados, combinado com um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang, é o primeiro projeto operado pela VinEnergo sob um contrato de compra de energia direta (DPPA). Os primeiros clientes a se beneficiarem da energia limpa e da tecnologia avançada de armazenamento de energia da VinEnergo são a Future Production, Investment and Development Joint Stock Company (proprietária e operadora da fábrica de carros e motocicletas elétricas VinFast em Ha Tinh) e a VinES Ha Tinh Energy Solutions Joint Stock Company (proprietária da fábrica de baterias VinES Ha Tinh). Além disso, o sistema solar fotovoltaico em telhados da VinEnergo também fornece eletricidade para a fábrica de baterias da joint venture VG, também localizada dentro do complexo de fabricação de baterias e veículos elétricos na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang. A VinEnergo opera um sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica em telhados, combinado com baterias de armazenamento de energia, em Ha Tinh. A VinEnergo Energy Joint Stock Company colocou oficialmente em operação um sistema de energia solar fotovoltaica em telhados, combinado com armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), para fornecer eletricidade limpa à fábrica de automóveis VinFast, à fábrica de baterias VinES e à joint venture de fabricação de baterias VG, na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang (província de Ha Tinh). Com uma capacidade total de até 22 MWp de energia solar e 45 MWh de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), a VinEnergo garante um fornecimento de energia estável a custos otimizados para seus parceiros, além de contribuir para a redução da sobrecarga na rede elétrica nacional. Segundo estimativas, em seu primeiro ano de operação, o sistema deverá gerar aproximadamente 39 milhões de kWh de energia limpa, contribuindo para a redução de mais de 25.000 toneladas de emissões de CO2 (o equivalente à absorção de mais de 1,13 milhão de árvores por ano). Em particular, a transição para a energia limpa da VinEnergo ajudará as unidades beneficiárias a reduzir a pressão sobre a rede elétrica e aumentar a autossuficiência energética, otimizando custos em cerca de 3,5 bilhões de VND por ano. O sucesso operacional e o fornecimento estável de energia às três usinas parceiras na fase inicial servem como base para que a VinEnergo continue desenvolvendo e promovendo a transição para energia verde nas fases subsequentes. Este modelo combina fontes de energia renováveis com um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) de grande escala, visando completar a infraestrutura de energia verde, a distribuição e a comercialização de eletricidade para os consumidores da região. A Sra. Nguyen Huong Giang, Vice-Diretora Geral da VinEnergo, declarou: “Por meio deste projeto, a VinEnergo irá gradualmente completar um ecossistema energético abrangente, desde fontes renováveis, sistemas de armazenamento e mecanismos de DPPA até infraestrutura de distribuição e varejo, capaz de atender à crescente demanda de eletricidade de projetos industriais emergentes na Zona Econômica de Vung Ang, em particular, e em todo o país, em geral. Temos orgulho de utilizar nossos próprios produtos, capacidades tecnológicas e plataforma de fabricação no Vietnã para solucionar os desafios energéticos de nossos parceiros comerciais, contribuindo para o aumento da competitividade e da participação de energia verde no setor industrial.” Atualmente, a VinEnergo fornece soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) para diversos grandes projetos da Hanoi Power Corporation e da Northern Power Corporation, totalizando mais de 1,1 GWh, o que comprova a capacidade das empresas vietnamitas de dominar tecnologias essenciais e implementar projetos de grande escala. No mercado internacional, a VinEnergo anunciou um portfólio de projetos de energia renovável totalizando 10 GW e está atualmente implementando seus primeiros projetos na Ásia e na Europa. Nos próximos três anos, a VinEnergo pretende desenvolver um portfólio de projetos com capacidade total de até 100 GW, tornando-se assim uma das empresas líderes mundiais em energia renovável.

artigo.texto: Meio Ambiente Greenline leva tecnologia de carbono a fórum em Campo Grande Empresa brasileira participa de evento em 3 de novembro e reúne 14 projetos no Centro-Oeste, com potencial estimado de sequestrar 12,6 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ Uma empresa brasileira de tecnologia voltada ao monitoramento ambiental vai apresentar soluções para o mercado de carbono em Campo Grande. A Greenline participa, no dia 3 de novembro, do II Fórum MS Sustentabilidade, com iniciativas voltadas à conservação do Cerrado e do Pantanal. A atuação da companhia no Centro-Oeste reúne 14 projetos, que abrangem cerca de 134 mil hectares e têm potencial estimado de sequestro de 12,6 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂), segundo dados divulgados pela empresa. O evento será realizado no Centro de Convenções Rubens Gil de Camillo e reunirá representantes de empresas, poder público, universidades e organizações da sociedade civil para discutir alternativas de desenvolvimento sustentável. Entre os temas da programação está o mercado de créditos de carbono. A Greenline desenvolve projetos com monitoramento digital que combina imagens de satélite, inteligência artificial e dados de vegetação. Segundo a empresa, a tecnologia permite acompanhar em tempo real toda a área das propriedades participantes. Os projetos e créditos emitidos passam por validação da certificadora independente Bureau Veritas, conforme informado pela companhia. Além da atuação regional, a empresa afirma desenvolver projetos que abrangem mais de 1,5 milhão de hectares no Brasil, com potencial estimado de geração de créditos equivalentes a mais de 25 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ por ano. A Greenline também integra um grupo de trabalho que discute metodologias para o mercado regulado de carbono no país. O fórum terá debates sobre recursos hídricos, agropecuária sustentável, energia, gestão de resíduos e economia regenerativa, com foco em soluções para os desafios ambientais e econômicos de Mato Grosso do Sul.

artigo.texto: Sierra Club Michigan launches online tracker of lawmakers’ and candidates’ data center stances LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - The Michigan chapter of the Sierra Club has launched an online “Data Center Position Tracker” that lists where state lawmakers and legislative candidates stand on data center policy. The Sierra Club said it’s asking whether lawmakers and candidates: - Support a temporary statewide moratorium on data centers - Would vote for strong regulations - Would vote to repeal the state’s data center tax incentives Marta Johnson of Sierra Club Michigan said the tracker is “intended to support advocacy and accountability efforts to accelerate data center legislative action.” Emily Woodcock, Michigan state director for Clean Water Action, a partner in the project, said the tracker is meant to put lawmakers on the record. “And so, this tool is a really important step that forces lawmakers to be on the record, stating something publicly that we can then hold them accountable to moving towards, you know, eventually having state laws that protect these communities.” Woodcock said. How the tracker works Each responding lawmaker or candidate is listed with a photo and an icon showing their stance on each of the three issues, with some entries including written statements. The Sierra Club says every legislator and candidate received at least two outreach attempts. The page also calls the list “crowdsourced” and invites people to ask their own lawmakers to write in with their position. Some responses are not yes or no Several officials and candidates offered answers that are more complicated than a simple “yes,” or “no.” Republican Sen. Michele Hoitenga said she would support a set of regulations, except for a requirement that data center projects use union labor, a regulation posed in the Sierra Club’s full questionnaire. “With regard to the question: Will you vote for permanent regulations to protect our water, energy grid, transparency, community benefits agreements, and require union labor, if put up for a vote? I would support all aspects of the bill with the exception of mandating union labor,” Hoitenga wrote. Democratic Sen. Jeff Irwin said he would vote to remove the sales tax reduction for large data center projects if protections for ratepayers and water use stay in law. He also wants to keep clean energy and efficiency standards that are in the same law. “I would vote to remove the sales tax reduction for large projects if we keep the provision protecting ratepayers by requiring MPSC to set rates such that residents are NOT subsidizing data centers and the provision requiring their water use to be provided and regulated by a municipal source. I wouldn’t want to lose local control and protections for water and ratepayers. We also have some clean energy and energy efficiency standards in the law granting sales tax exemptions, I would like to keep those standards as well,” Irwin wrote. Division on the data center issue Woodcock said Clean Water Action’s canvassers hear concerns “over affordability, what data centers will do to energy prices ... and what that could do to water across the state.” Johnson said the groups see a lack of transparency around data center projects, including nondisclosure agreements. Business groups see it differently. Mike Alaimo of the Michigan Chamber of Commerce told News 10 in September that hyperscale data centers provide a “massive opportunity” for the state, and that repealing incentives would show corporations that Michigan “is not open for business.” Concerns across party lines Woodcock said her group’s canvassers hear the same concern regardless of political affiliation. “It has been probably 20 years since there’s been an issue that has been like the number one issue for people that we talk to, regardless of location, political spectrum, background. This is something everyone is concerned with,” Woodcock said. “It is quite clear where the public stands on these issues. That is not the mystery. The mystery seems to be where their lawmakers stand,” said Nora Naughton with the Sierra Club. What’s next Johnson said the group expects to keep adding names. “We’re very optimistic that we’ll be able to continue to add lawmakers and decision makers onto this tracker. This is just our opening start for this effort,” she said. Bills on data center moratoriums, regulations and tax incentives have been introduced at the state Capitol this year, but so far, none have reached the Governor’s desk. artigo.texto: COMPANY NEWS: ENERGEE's Golden Brick Battery technology, used in the 75 kWh RWD version of the Australian-market ZEEKR 7X, is among the technologies the company is showcasing at All Energy Australia 2026, as the Geely Holding Group subsidiary makes its first appearance at the Melbourne clean-energy exhibition on 28–29 October. The Chinese battery developer is using the event to introduce Australian industry visitors to two parts of its business: Golden Brick Battery for vehicles and Matchless Battery for residential, commercial and industrial, and utility-scale energy storage. Together, the technologies span vehicle electrification and stationary energy storage applications. What the ZEEKR 7X shows The ZEEKR 7X offers visitors a familiar point of reference for the mobility technology. Its 75 kWh Golden Brick Battery adopts an 800V architecture, with a peak operating voltage of 735V, energy consumption of 13.9 kWh per 100 km, delivering up to 480 km range. With a maximum charging power of 450 kW, ZEEKR 7X can add 190 km of driving range in five minutes, and 330 km in 10 minutes. According to the official Australian specifications, the 75 kWh RWD version achieves a charge from 10% to 80% in approximately 10.5 minutes under specified conditions. ENERGEE also offers a high-performance battery system for battery electric vehicles (BEVs). This battery system balances performance and charging speed with a 900V architecture, supporting ultra-fast charging. Advanced battery capabilities enable a 10%-80% charge in 7.5 minutes. The wider Golden Brick Battery range extends beyond passenger EVs to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), light commercial vehicles and heavy trucks. Besides ZEEKR 7X, selected models of Geely and smart across the globe are also fitted with the Golden Brick Battery. Battery intelligence is part of the story Alongside its battery packs, ENERGEE offers its self-developed BMS. It monitors battery condition and temperature, supports cell balancing and manages aspects of charging and battery operation. ENERGEE says the platform performs hundreds of battery-state scans per second, with millisecond-level safety responses. The company describes its functional-safety design in terms of ASIL D and combines vehicle-cloud connectivity with intelligent management algorithms. For automotive customers, that integration matters because the BMS has to work with the chemistry, pack design and the vehicle’s controls over the battery’s operating life. Battery technology for residential, C&I, and utility-scale energy storage Stationary storage is represented by the Matchless Battery range of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic cells, serving residential energy storage, C&I and utility-scale applications. The CM100 is a 100 Ah cell with a stated energy density of 164 Wh/kg and a cycle-life rating of at least 6,000 cycles. The larger CM310 is rated at 314 Ah and 179 Wh/kg, with at least 9,000 cycles. ENERGEE also cites overcharge and full-penetration nail tests in which tested cells did not catch fire or explode. For vehicle manufacturers, fleet operators and storage integrators, the Melbourne appearance introduces ENERGEE's battery technologies across mobility and stationary storage. It brings together cell design and battery management within the same company, with potential applications across Australian vehicles and energy storage projects. It will become a trusted, full-scenario technology partner in the Australian new energy market, deeply empowering the construction of the local clean energy ecosystem. More information about the company and its products is available at https://energee.geely.com/.

artigo.texto: Meta toma uma dura do MPF A Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão do Ministério Público Federal (MPF) enviou à Meta uma lista de 12 recomendações para que adote "medidas urgentes" de transparência no período eleitoral para garantir "liberdade de expressão nas redes Facebook, Instagram, Threads e WhatsApp". Do site do MPF: A empresa têm prazo de 48 horas para responder se acatará as recomendações e para detalhar as providências que serão adotadas durante o segundo turno das eleições, além de 30 dias para apresentar relatório conclusivo. O MPF também apresentou à Justiça Federal de Porto Alegre (RS) ação civil pública para barrar bloqueios e restrições arbitrárias praticados pela Meta em redes sociais. A medida do MPF foi motivada pela representação das organizações Artigo 19, Conectas, Sleeping Giants e CTRL+Z, segundo as quais a Meta, em outubro e setembro deste ano, "aplicou número expressivo de sanções, como remoção de postagens, suspensão de perfis, restrição territorial e limitação de funcionalidade". [ATUALIZADO 22.out.2026 às 9h17] Em outra medida, o MPF também foi à Justiça para tentar forçar a Meta a restabelecer conteúdos e perfis derrubados arbitrariamente, em até 24 horas, sob pena de multa de R$500 mil por dia. De acordo com o jornal O Globo: Segundo o MPF, foram registrados mais de mil relatos de intervenções promovidas por plataformas digitais, especialmente a Meta e o X. A ação, no entanto, é direcionada apenas à Meta e à sua representante no Brasil. EIS A LISTA de recomendações propostas para os próximos cinco dias (até o segundo turno) enviada pela procuradoria do MPF. Os itens foram levemente editados pelo Núcleo para brevidade e clareza: - abstenha-se de remover publicações, suspender ou desativar contas, restringir territorialmente a visualização de conteúdos, reduzir alcance ou limitar funcionalidades sem fundamento jurídico ou contratual específico; - direcione recursos técnicos e recursos humanos para garantir prioritariamente as liberdades de opinião, de expressão e de manifestação, criando ajustes na moderação automática incidente sobre postagens com termos como “manifestação”, “convocação”, “ato público”, “passeata”, “marcha”, entre outros análogos, e submetendo-as, extraordinariamente, à revisão humana necessária; - aplique seus critérios de moderação de forma isonômica, sem distinção em razão da orientação política ou ideológica do conteúdo ou de seu autor; - direcione recursos técnicos e recursos humanos para para coibir o uso ilícito ou abusivo dos instrumentos de notificação submetendo necessariamente moderações decorrentes de denúncias em massa à revisão humana; - submeta à revisão humana a suspensão ou desativação de contas decorrentes de enquadramentos em infrações graves, como terrorismo e exploração sexual de crianças e adolescentes, sobretudo quando derivadas de reportes de outros usuários; - restabeleça imediatamente contas, publicações, alcance e funcionalidades quando reconhecido, por revisão humana, erro de moderação de conteúdo; - comunique, a cada usuário afetado, de forma individualizada, clara, acessível toda medida de moderação que lhe vier a ser imposta, inclusive a decorrente de sistema automatizado, informando a natureza e a duração da medida, a natureza da infração atribuída, a regra aplicada, os elementos que justificaram o enquadramento, a origem da decisão e os meios e prazos de contestação, e valendo-se, extraordinariamente, do recurso denominado “Megafone”, já empregado pela empresa, que permitiria informar aos usuários, em posição destacada de seus feed, quando forem alvo de uma dada restrição, sem necessidade de recorrerem ao Painel de Status da Conta - de modo a melhor cumprir com os deveres de transparência aqui delineados; - reconheça (no prazo máximo de 02 dias), valendo-se do mesmo recurso “Megafone” ou de outro análogo, as falhas de moderação de conteúdo apontadas pelo Comitê de Supervisão, e formule pedido público de desculpas; - assegure, em posição destacada do feed de cada usuário, um link de fácil acesso aos procedimentos de contestação gratuita para todas as modalidades de restrição; - comprometa-se (no prazo máximo de 03 dias) com a contratação de uma auditoria independente para analisar os algoritmos de moderação utilizados nas plataformas controladas pela Meta ao longo dos últimos dois meses; - comprometa-se (no prazo máximo de 03 dias), com a elaboração, sugerida pelo Comitê de Supervisão da Meta, de um arcabouço de métricas para avaliar os esforços da empresa em favor da integridade das eleições no Brasil, indo além das meras referências, hoje realizadas, a dados agregados de anúncios veiculados ou de número contas removidas; - preserve os registros técnicos, documentos e informações sobre os episódios, incluídas as decisões de moderação, seus fundamentos, as notificações recebidas e os pedidos de revisão, observados os limites legais de proteção de dados pessoais e de sigilo das comunicações. [ATUALIZAÇÃO 22.out.2026 às 9h16] A Meta informou que não irá comentar a um pedido de comentários feito pelo Núcleo por email. >> Íntegra do documento do MPF

artigo.texto: [SMM Flash] CATL-Affiliated Jianxiawo Lithium Mining Project Receives EIA Approval October 30: The Yichun Municipal Ecology and Environment Bureau issued its approval for the Environmental Impact Assessment Report of the Zhenkouli–Jianxiawo lithium mining project operated by Yichun Times New Energy Mining Co., Ltd. From an environmental protection perspective, the bureau approved in principle the project’s proposed nature, location, scale, production process and environmental protection measures. According to the approval, the project is located at the border of Yifeng County and Fengxin County in Yichun, Jiangxi Province, with a total mining area of 2.5029 square kilometres. The project is classified as a new development, with a designed lithium ore mining recovery rate of 98%, usable ore resources of approximately 513.525 million tonnes, annual ore mining capacity of 30 million tonnes and a designed mine life of 18 years. The planned product output is 30 million tonnes of run-of-mine ore per year. The mining process includes topsoil stripping, drilling, blasting, loading and truck haulage. After crushing, ore will either be transported by conveyor to the concentrator or loaded directly for external sale. Total project investment is approximately RMB 4.35 billion, including around RMB 288 million in environmental protection investment, accounting for 6.61% of the total. The approval requires the project to implement the “three simultaneous” environmental protection system, under which environmental facilities must be designed, constructed and commissioned together with the main project. The company must also obtain the required pollutant discharge permit before starting production facilities or generating actual emissions, and the project may formally commence operations only after its supporting environmental protection facilities pass acceptance procedures.

artigo.texto: MINERAL EXPLORADO NA BAHIA DEVE GANHAR FORÇA COM IA E DATA CENTERS A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) e dos data centers pode ampliar a demanda por vanádio produzido na Bahia, impulsionada pela necessidade de tecnologias de armazenamento de energia em larga escala. O mineral é utilizado na fabricação de baterias de fluxo de vanádio, que podem armazenar eletricidade por longos períodos e atender a instalações que exigem fornecimento contínuo de energia. A Bahia tem participação relevante no setor mineral nacional. O estado produz vanádio e urânio e responde pela extração de 47 das 93 tipologias minerais existentes no Brasil. A mineradora canadense Largo opera a mina Maracás Menchen, na Bahia, considerada uma das principais operações de vanádio do mundo. Além de liderar a produção de vanádio e urânio, o estado é responsável por produzir 47 das 93 tipologias minerais existentes no Brasil. Tradicionalmente, o vanádio é empregado na fabricação de aços de alta resistência e ligas metálicas especiais. Nos últimos anos, o mineral também ganhou espaço nas discussões sobre tecnologias de armazenamento de energia, especialmente diante da expansão das fontes renováveis e do aumento do consumo de eletricidade por instalações digitais. Eletricidade prolongada Diferentemente das baterias convencionais de íons de lítio, essa tecnologia armazena energia em soluções líquidas que contêm vanádio. Os líquidos circulam entre tanques e células eletroquímicas, permitindo o armazenamento de grandes volumes de eletricidade por períodos prolongados. Entre as características das baterias de fluxo estão a possibilidade de armazenamento por várias horas, a longa vida útil e o menor risco de incêndio em comparação com algumas tecnologias convencionais. Essas características podem tornar o sistema uma alternativa para aplicações industriais, redes elétricas e data centers, que precisam manter servidores e equipamentos de processamento em funcionamento contínuo. O avanço da inteligência artificial amplia a demanda por capacidade computacional e, consequentemente, por infraestrutura elétrica. Nesse cenário, soluções de armazenamento podem contribuir para a gestão do fornecimento de energia e para a estabilidade das redes. Mercado brasileiro de data centers Segundo a consultoria imobiliária JLL, o mercado brasileiro de data centers deve dobrar de tamanho até 2030. No primeiro semestre de 2026, o Brasil registrou 706 megawatts (MW) de capacidade instalada no segmento, de acordo com os dados apresentados no levantamento. O volume representa um crescimento superior a seis vezes em relação a 2012, equivalente a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual de 15%. A expansão dos centros de processamento de dados exige investimentos em geração, transmissão e sistemas de reserva de energia. Essa necessidade pode abrir espaço para tecnologias de armazenamento de longa duração, entre elas as baterias de fluxo de vanádio. Para a Largo, a ampliação desse mercado representa uma possibilidade de diversificação da demanda pelo mineral, atualmente utilizado sobretudo pela indústria siderúrgica. A concretização dessa oportunidade, porém, depende da evolução da adoção da tecnologia e dos investimentos em infraestrutura energética. Setores de defesa e aeroespacial Além das aplicações no armazenamento de eletricidade, o vanádio é utilizado na produção de aços de alta resistência e ligas metálicas destinadas a setores como defesa e indústria aeroespacial. A demanda norte-americana também integra a estratégia comercial da Largo. Em julho, a mineradora recebeu um aporte de US$ 60,1 milhões para fornecer pentóxido de vanádio de alta pureza aos Estados Unidos, com entregas previstas até janeiro de 2030. A empresa é fornecedora da Agência de Logística de Defesa dos Estados Unidos (DLA). Segundo a companhia canadense, o relacionamento comercial com os Estados Unidos também está associado ao interesse de países ocidentais em reduzir a dependência de fornecedores como China e Rússia. *Com informações do Portal A Tarde.

artigo.texto: Energy officials visits Georgia Tech as US seeks to expand battery manufacturing ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson visited the Georgia Tech Manufacturing Institute’s Advanced Manufacturing Pilot Facility Wednesday to introduce new initiatives and tour the facility. The Trump administration is attempting to put policies in place to increase U.S. battery production. The United States produces about 7% of the world’s batteries, according to the International Energy Agency. China manufactures about 80%. “The United States has led the world for the last 60 years in battery technology, but we have lagged the world in battery manufacturing,” Robertson said. Robertson and the Trump administration are working to address that gap. “Our mission: to have a fully integrated battery supply chain here in the United States by 2030,” Robertson said. The United States is relying on the South, including Georgia, to help close the gap. “Georgia and the Southeast are the battery belt,” said Tim Lieuwen, Georgia Tech’s incoming interim president. EV factories, battery plants and manufacturing facilities are popping up across Georgia, Tennessee, and into the Carolinas. Reaching a fully integrated supply chain will require teamwork from academia and the federal government. “Batteries are becoming increasingly important to both our economic security and our national security,” Lieuwen said. artigo.texto: Three months after leaders extended a moratorium on new data center development in Prince George’s County, Maryland, the county council passed legislation this week aimed at preventing an existing project from moving forward at the site of the old Landover Mall. Related stories - Prince George’s Co. Council wraps up 2026 session touting accomplishments, despite turmoil - Prince George’s County Council passes bills aimed at street vending - Prince George’s County gets the ball rolling on Sphere with final vote to approve concert venue “A loophole was created in 2021 that allowed the Brightseat Park (development) to go forward, almost putting a data center in Landover, which is very close to a residential community,” council member Shayla Adams Stafford, whose district includes the site, said as she explained her vote for the bill Tuesday. The council had voted in 2021 to take itself out of the approvals process, with a goal of speeding data center construction. Adams Stafford said the new law will require the Brightseat Park application to go before the county council again, essentially killing it since there’s so much opposition. Going forward, applications for data centers will have to go through a lengthier process that includes detailed site plans considering how surrounding land is being used. The bill also puts proposed facilities through a more in-depth public review, ensuring the council has a say on every application. The legislation was in response to bubbling public opposition to the Landover project, which prompted the county’s first data center development moratorium in 2025. At the time, council members said they were unaware of the plans until it was almost too late. Hiccups in other aspects of the pre-construction process have dragged out the project since 2021. artigo.texto: (Iowa) -- A new survey of registered voters in five battleground states, including Iowa, shows data centers are not a major priority for voters in this year's elections. The survey from Infrastructure for America finds only 3% of voters in Iowa, Michigan, Georgia, Ohio, and Texas mentioned data centers when asked to name the most important issue facing their state. In fact, data centers ranked near the bottom of voters' priority lists, with 6% of voters citing data centers being built in their community as one of the top two most important issues affecting their vote. More than two thirds of voters surveyed said they would still vote for a candidate they agree with on most issues but disagree with on data centers. Only 6% of voters said data centers are among the top two issues that matter most to their vote. The survey showed voters want more local control over the development of data centers. 72% of voters surveyed said local government should approve or deny the construction of new data centers in their community. The full survey is available on the Infrastructure for America website.

artigo.texto: Fact brief: Does NV Energy's Greenlink project include a data center in Yerington? No. The Greenlink transmission line and the Monarch data center campus planned for near Yerington are separate projects. Greenlink is NV Energy's two-part project. Greenlink West is a 350-mile-long transmission line that will run from Las Vegas to Yerington; it is expected to be in service next year. Greenlink North will be a 235-mile-long transmission line from Yerington to Ely. Originally slated to be operational by 2028, the federal Bureau of Land Management (BLM) sided with several groups' protests against the line and remanded portions of the project back to the state BLM office. Monarch is being developed by Copia Power. Operation of the first phase of the project depends on buildout of utility infrastructure including Greenlink and NV Energy's Walker River Substation. No data centers are part of Greenlink, although data centers could be powered by it. This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one. The Nevada Independent partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims. The Nevada Independent is always on the lookout for claims that could use a fact check. But we could use your eyes and ears too.
