artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – San Antonio is clamping down on data centers in city limits, limiting them to heavy commercial and industrial areas and requiring council approval. The 9-2 vote on Thursday afternoon came one year to the day after Councilman Ric Galvan (D6), who says his Northwest Side district has the majority of the city’s data centers, asked city staff to look into potential data center regulation. “Every single data center that’s proposed to come to San Antonio must come to council,” Galvan said after the meeting. “Must have a public meeting, must showcase the full site plan, must communicate on emergency plans and make sure that there is a clear coordination with the community and with council on how this data center will come to our city. That means that residents will be able to voice their opinion.” Misty Spears (D9) and Marc Whyte (D10) were the only votes against the new regulations, preferring a version in which at least some of the facilities wouldn’t need specific permission from council. The growing number of data centers has become a hot-button topic in Texas politics, raising concerns about issues from their power and water use to noise or air quality concerns to the AI technology the infrastructure enables. The Texas Tribune has tracked nearly 600 data centers operating or planned across the state. San Antonio’s previous current code didn’t have a standalone data center definition. Instead, it fell under office data processing and management, which had allowed the facilities in most non-residential areas. Multiple options Council members considered multiple regulatory approaches on Thursday. The differences came down to whether to allow data centers “by right” if they meet certain restrictions or to require council approval for each one. City staff recommended allowing data centers “by right” in heavy commercial and industrial areas as long as they are at least 500 feet away from certain areas like housing, schools, and daycares; have a certain type of landscaping; and all buildings and on-site power are at least 50 feet from the property line. They would not have been allowed over the recharge zone of the Edwards Aquifer. So long as a project met all of those requirements, it would have been allowed. Otherwise, it would have required approval from the city council. The second option, which council ultimately improved, would also restrict the facilities to heavy commercial and industrial areas. Instead of predetermined site plan requirements, such as setbacks or minimum distances from certain uses, the city council could impose restrictions and approve each project on a case-by-case basis. City staff say they still wouldn’t be allowed over the aquifer recharge zone. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones had pushed another set of requirements that would also require council approval for every project while also including numerous other requirements like certain landscaping, a 45-day prefiling notice, public engagement meetings, noise restrictions, a 1,000-foot setback from the edge of the property, enclosed backup generators, green space replacement, and local air quality monitoring and replacement. After an Oct. 14 council meeting where the first three options were discussed, the zoning commission developed its own option that blended different elements. Under that approach, data centers would have been allowed by right in heavier industrial areas if they met requirements for landscaping, screened generators, being at least 350 feet away from areas like housing and schools, downward-facing lighting, and noise limitations. If not, they’d need council approval. Council approval would also have been necessary for projects in areas zoned for general commercial, business parks, and light industrial uses. The zoning commission had also recommended existing locations still be allowed to get permits to repair, rebuild, or expand within their existing boundaries. Discussion Jones unsuccessfully pushed for the council to use her requirements, but it failed by a 5-6 vote. “The ‘S’ code is kind of where we landed today, but I think we’ll find, as other communities have found, that we’ll need stronger protections,” she told reporters after the vote. Councilman Marc Whyte (D10) also unsuccessfully pushed to use the zoning commission’s proposal, which he called a compromise. “If we tell companies that even on heavy industrial land — land we zoned exactly for this kind of use — that every project is going to get decided on a case-by-case basis, we’re telling them essentially that the rules are not written down. They get made in this room, one vote at a time,” Whyte said, warning the projects would just move out of city limits. That attempt also failed in a 5-6 vote. The council members did agree to add a minimum distance to the UNESCO World Heritage Site as an optional requirement. The council vote and discussion followed a two-hour parade of public comment, including people concerned about the data centers and workers who say the facilities provide good construction jobs. “What we heard the most from neighbors, besides they don’t want data centers, is ‘we never knew the data center was being built.’ We never had an opportunity to say, ‘we don’t want it here,’” said DeeDee Belmares, a clean energy advocate with Public Citizen. “Data centers have become so integral to society that they are going to be built either way,” said Jeremy Chavez, an electrician with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 60. “We should ensure that their construction benefits the people of San Antonio by building them here. Build them with strong labor agreements and ensure they get built responsibly.” Read also:

artigo.texto: Xcel Energy moves closer to opening battery storage facility at Blue Lake site Battery storage units arrived at Xcel Energyʻs Blue Lake site in Minnesota, marking a significant construction milestone for the facility being built in Scott County. The Blue Lake facility batteries will store energy generated across Xcel Energy’s Upper Midwest system, including energy from wind, solar, nuclear and natural gas resources. The 135.5-megawatt battery energy storage facility will include 132 battery units capable of storing energy and delivering electricity for up to four hours, enough energy to power approximately 125,000 homes when demand is highest. “For more than a century, energy companies have generated electricity when customers need it and delivered it almost immediately. Battery storage changes what’s possible. It allows us to store energy and dispatch it when it’s needed most, giving us a powerful new tool to maintain reliability, support growing energy needs and make the most of the diverse resources that power our system,” Bria Shea, president of Xcel Energy–Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota, said. Battery storage stores energy when it is available and dispatches it back to the grid when customer demand is higher. “The Blue Lake project demonstrates how battery storage is becoming an increasingly important part of grid operations,” Justin Meagher, Xcel Energy battery storage project manager, said. “These systems can respond quickly to changing conditions, store energy when it’s available and provide electricity when customer demand is high. That flexibility helps us operate the electric system more efficiently while continuing to deliver reliable service to customers.” The Blue Lake Battery Energy Storage System is expected to begin serving customers in 2027. Xcel Energy, headquartered in Minneapolis, distributes electricity and gas to customers across eight states: Minnesota, Colorado, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, New Mexico and Texas.

artigo.texto: JACKSONVILLE, Fla. – Data center companies scouting locations across the country have set their sights on Jacksonville — and the power demands they’re bringing with them are staggering. A full year of public records obtained by the News4Jax I-TEAM reveals just how much electricity these companies are requesting from JEA, and how the utility is responding. One request, enough power for 700,000 homes In September 2024, JEA received an inquiry from Cecil LMNO requesting 1,248 megawatts of power — enough electricity to light up approximately 700,000 Jacksonville homes, or more than 100 NFL stadiums the size of EverBank Field. That request was the highest single power demand uncovered in the year of records reviewed by the I-TEAM. While other data center proposals requested smaller amounts, many still exceeded JEA’s maximum single-customer power load. Jordan Pope, JEA’s interim Chief Administrative Officer, addressed the challenge head-on. “And here at JEA, while we’re investing in our future infrastructure and future energy needs, those loads are a bit too high right now for us to serve today,” Pope said. “So when we work with these companies who are making inquiries, we’re looking at the timeframe it would take to serve them. And many times that’s years down the road, which may not meet their requirements.” How Jacksonville’s current power customers compare Pope explains that one megawatt equals one million watts of power. JEA currently provides electricity to six local data centers, but they are relatively small operations — some housed in downtown buildings — requiring fewer than 10 megawatts each. The records paint a clear picture of how data center demands stack up against Jacksonville’s existing largest power users. The customer with the highest monthly peak electric usage in 2025 was a steel company, which drew a peak of nearly 64 megawatts for its plant’s furnace, plus an additional 18 megawatts for other portions of the facility. Paper and cardboard manufacturer WestRock recorded the third-highest annual consumption rate, with a peak draw of 40 megawatts. Infrastructure hurdles stand in the way Even if JEA wanted to accommodate the largest requests, major infrastructure challenges remain. “Each of these sites would need their own dedicated substation or potentially multiple substations in order for JEA to serve them,” Pope said. “With supply chain constraints being a concern, especially because of the growth of data centers, long lead items such as substation transformers can take years to acquire and then install.” JEA officials also say they suspect some of the inquiries didn’t come from companies seriously looking to relocate to Jacksonville, but rather from those evaluating the broader energy market — essentially testing the waters by comparing available electricity, costs and infrastructure across multiple cities. What it means for Jacksonville residents For residents concerned about large data centers moving into their neighborhoods, Pope says the public will have a voice in the process. “We discuss these things in our board meetings,” Pope said. “The city council currently has had some discussions about data centers as far as planning and zoning requirements.” To protect existing ratepayers, JEA is also implementing what’s called a large load tariff, designed to ensure current customers aren’t subsidizing new, high-demand users — making sure every customer pays their fair share.

artigo.texto: Oct. 29, 2026 NBC News and ‘Today’ feature VCU’s Stephen Fong in report on data centers and public health Share this story This week, Virginia Commonwealth University professor and environmental researcher Stephen S. Fong spoke with NBC News correspondent Stephanie Gosk about the impact of data centers on the environment and community health. In Northern Virginia’s Loudoun County, about an hour west of the nation’s capital, Discovery Elementary School is located within a half-mile of 11 data centers. With as many as 264 backup diesel generators helping to power the massive facilities, community members have expressed concern about the effects on the school’s students and residents in the surrounding neighborhood. Fong, Ph.D., a professor of chemical and biomolecular engineering in VCU’s College of Engineering and associate director of research and graduate studies in the School of Life Sciences and Sustainability, part of the College of Humanities and Sciences, has been studying air pollution and the environment for years. According to Fong’s calculations, just one generator running at full capacity emits more pollution than 100 18-wheelers. With the quantity and size of the diesel generators being installed for data centers, “they’re producing enough air pollution that there are concerns about what kind of health impacts this would have on students,” he told Gosk. When asked if the state should be continuously monitoring the air quality near Discovery Elementary School, Fong said, “Personally, I think they should." Fong added to VCU News that the number of backup generators and the frequency with which they're turned on is not publicly known, so "having some instruments that continuously measure air pollutants would give students and residents some real-time information on the air quality," he said. Recently, Fong and an interdisciplinary team of VCU researchers were awarded a VCU Breakthroughs grant. Their project, titled “Understanding the Environmental and Community Impacts of Data Centers in Virginia through Modeling, Measurement and Participatory Research,” will test air quality around data centers in the Richmond region. Fong and Damian Pitt, Ph.D., an associate professor in the L. Douglas Wilder School of Government and Public Affairs, are co-principal investigators on the project, which also includes Wilder School associate professor I-Shian (Ivan) Suen, Ph.D.; Beth Kreydatus, a professor in the Department of Focused Inquiry in the College of Humanities and Sciences; and Carly Muir, an assistant professor in the School of Life Sciences and Sustainability. Watch Fong’s NBC News and “Today” appearance on “Elementary school in middle of 11 data centers.” Subscribe to VCU News Subscribe to VCU News at newsletter.vcu.edu and receive a selection of stories, videos, photos, news clips and event listings in your inbox.

artigo.texto: Columbia County chair candidates discuss data centers, growth, traffic at library forum COLUMBIA COUNTY, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - Democrat Cambrey Wood and Republican Alison Couch addressed data centers, traffic and growth in front of a room of voters as they run to lead Columbia County for the next four years. A forum at the Columbia County Library brought the candidates together to discuss the big issues facing the county. Both candidates said Columbia County should slow residential growth. Both said public safety is their top budget priority. Couch has served as Appling Harlem’s commissioner while the county voted to bring a 3,000-acre data center to that area and developed the data center zoning ordinance. She said the county did it for property tax relief for citizens. Couch said she voted for the White Oak data center because it is in an industrial park. Augusta airport targets holiday parking, hangar completion while TSA checkpoint timeline Airport Executive Director Herbert Judon said much of the work remains on track for holiday travel. She said she voted against the project in Pumpkin Center, which is across the street from a neighborhood. “I do not see the need for any more data centers in Columbia County,” Couch said. “The goal was property tax relief and that will be achieved with the funding from the data centers that we currently have. I worked diligently on the data center ordinances to provide guardrails for our citizens and protect them.” Wood has been critical of the project. Wood said the tax relief deal still gives data centers a tax break and that the community is not getting enough in return. “I think that $40 million a year is a pretty short-sighted and low payoff solution when you’re leaving 2 plus billion dollars on the table over the next 25 years that could have been used to offset costs for other things like capital improvement projects or road projects or safety upgrades or law enforcement equipment,” Wood said. Traffic was also a topic of discussion. Wood brought up rural, underdeveloped roads that need to be redeveloped. Couch said the area near the Interstate 20 Grovetown exit is where she has heard the most concern. She said the county is putting a lot of work into that area now. Wood advocated for a zoning overhaul to spread development into rural parts of the county while keeping their character. “I would definitely support an overhaul of our existing planning, zoning, and development ordinances, targeting specific areas within the county as appropriate for increasing density, which would allow us to then plan our growth out into the more rural areas of the county and maintain the county character that we have in the various areas,” Wood said. Halloween candy prices vary across Augusta stores Bag prices range from under $9 to about $30 at Kroger, Walmart, Target and Costco as Halloween falls on a Saturday. Couch said bringing business is important but that expanding county services into areas of growth is the top priority. “An important part of growth also is to be able to provide services for the residents that are joining our community,” Couch said. “So responsible growth means providing sheriff’s department, providing fire services, providing quality of life projects and providing traffic infrastructure.” District 1 candidates Michael Jordan and Alex Griffin also answered questions about how they would lead in the seat Connie Melear is termed out of. Griffin said he’d like to see work put into the stretch of Washington Road around Bobby Jones Expressway to redevelop aging infrastructure. Jordan said the growth in Columbia County is good, but he wants to ensure the County can afford that growth. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- Electric vehicles have gone mainstream, yet fears of battery fires and inflated range claims still linger. While spec sheets for new models often look impressive, consumers remain unsure whether safety guarantees and real-world range can actually be trusted. To address these market concerns, IM Motors recently teamed up with CATL for a factory tour—skipping the PowerPoint slides to lay bare the manufacturing process, safety protocols, and the reality behind range estimates. Image Source: IM Motors What Ultimately Underpins Battery Safety? The tour took place at one of CATL’s “Lighthouse Factories” in Ningde. As site officials explained, the “lighthouse” designation isn't about automation for its own sake, but upgrading quality judgment from human intuition to systematic standards. AI-powered defect identification works three times faster than manual checks, reducing rework by roughly 70%. From raw materials to recycling, every step is digitally recorded and fully traceable—meaning the batch, materials, and processing history of any cell can be retrieved instantly. Image Source: CATL According to the briefing, a single battery cell passes through roughly 200 processes and 700 quality control nodes from raw material to finished product. The target defect rate on the manufacturing line is set at the PPB level—one part per billion. Behind that number lies a philosophy: safety isn't a matter of luck during spot checks; it’s written into the production line as an input condition from the very first step. Image Source: CATL “Safety relies not just on manufacturing, but on design redundancy,” noted Tang Guocheng, CATL’s product manager for domestic passenger vehicles. The upcoming IM LS8 NEO pure electric model, for instance, features a Pyrofuse active fuse: it actively cuts the high-voltage circuit within milliseconds if a collision or thermal runaway risk is detected. The logic is simple—cut the power before the fire starts—adding a critical layer of redundancy for user safety. Starting July 1, the mandatory national standard GB38031—2025 imposes stricter requirements on battery thermal propagation. “The national standard sets the passing grade, but CATL and IM Motors are building in a buffer above that line,” Tang said. But that’s far from enough. IM Motors engineers conduct rigorous real-world validation before batteries are installed. From the bitter cold of minus 30 °C in Hailaer to scorching surface temperatures exceeding 50 °C in Turpan, and the continuous uphill climbs of Yulong Snow Mountain, they repeatedly test the stability and adaptability of the thermal management system. This ensures the product is delivered with confidence. IM LS8 NEO BEV (Image Source: IM Motors) There’s another dimension to safety: IM Motors announced that the new LS8 NEO will exclusively use CATL batteries rather than “self-developed” alternatives. The rationale? Power batteries are patent-intensive and require long validation cycles. Instead of reinventing the cell, it’s better to specialize and collaborate, delivering mature technology directly to users. That may sound like posturing, but combined with the processes and validation data mentioned earlier, it clarifies who is underwriting safety—the deep vehicle expertise of SAIC combined with CATL’s high-precision R&D team creates a dual technical shield. How Can Displayed Range Match Real-World Data? Beyond safety, consumer anxiety stems more from daily use: battery degradation, inflated range claims, incompatible chargers, and winter power loss. Without solving these, even the most impressive spec sheets are meaningless. Nothing frustrates drivers quite like range estimates that suddenly plummet. On the highway, watching five kilometers of range disappear for every two traveled creates constant anxiety about whether you’ll make it to the next charger. Asked about the solution, Tang explained that CATL’s new BMS achieves battery estimation accuracy within ±3%, covering over 200 real-world driving scenarios. With that precision, users have a stable expectation of remaining range—no more guessing on every trip. This system is already deployed in the IM LS8 NEO. Meanwhile, the new BMS employs an industry-first polarization model for power control, predicting available battery power in real time. This boosts discharge power by roughly 20% at low charge levels. In practical terms, even with just 20% charge left, the vehicle retains punch for overtaking and climbing hills—it won't go “soft.” The BMS also features an “all-weather” design: even after the car is turned off, it continues to collect battery status data at low power, waking up early to issue warnings if anomalies are detected. For users, this means many potential faults are intercepted before they escalate into accidents. Beyond the new BMS, IM Motors representatives noted that under its NEXT·2028 strategy, the IM NEO tri-electric architecture extends its pursuit of quality to the entire power and energy management system. The NEO Hurricane motor, the new Efficiency Master Management System 3.0, and a full-domain thermal management system together form the core tri-electric technology suite of the IM LS8 NEO. What Other “Invisible Efforts” Exist Beyond Batteries? Batteries are just the entry point. The processes, validation, and precision discussed earlier all boil down to one thing: mastering the “invisible work” to earn consumer trust. Can this logic extend from the battery to the entire vehicle? Judging by IM Motors’ recent launches—especially the upcoming LS8 NEO—the answer is yes. On the powertrain front, the IM LS8 NEO offers two battery systems: a 103 kWh ternary lithium battery optimized for performance and cold-weather adaptation, and a 93 kWh lithium iron phosphate battery focused on extended range and balance. artigo.texto: A Motorola lançou hoje (27) o Moto G47 Power, versão com melhorias na bateria do modelo que estreou no primeiro semestre, prometendo autonomia superior a 78 horas com uma carga graças ao tanque de energia de 7.000 mAh. A novidade chega primeiro ao mercado europeu, mas com preço acima do especulado anteriormente. O mais recente integrante da série Moto G também tem, entre os destaques, a câmera de 108 MP liderando o conjunto fotográfico com abertura f/1,7 e zoom de 3x sem perda de qualidade da imagem, segundo a fabricante. A certificação IP64 é outro atrativo, oferecendo resistência contra água e poeira. Quanto custa o Moto G47 Power? Com ficha técnica semelhante à do Moto G47 convencional, o lançamento possui tela LCD de 6,67 polegadas com resolução HD (1604 x 720 pixels) e taxa de atualização de 120 Hz. O chip também é o mesmo MediaTek Dimensity 6300, acompanhado de 4 GB de RAM expansível até 12 GB por meio da função RAM Boost. - Ele tem 128 GB de armazenamento interno, com possibilidade de expansão via cartão microSD de até 1 TB; - Voltando à parte de câmeras, há o sensor macro de 2 MP junto à lente de 108 MP na traseira, enquanto a câmera de selfie tem 8 MP; - Alto-falantes estéreo com Dolby Atmos, 5G, NFC, Bluetooth 5.4, porta USB-C, entrada P2 para fone e proteção de tela Corning Gorilla Glass 7i também estão presentes; - Carregamento rápido de 30W e carregamento reverso de 6W são outros destaques do modelo que vem com Android 16 instalado de fábrica. Já à venda em alguns países europeus, o Moto G47 Power custa entre 309 e 369 euros, dependendo do mercado, o que dá entre R$ 1.836 e R$ 2.193 pela cotação do dia, sem considerar impostos e taxas. Ele pode ser encontrado nas cores azul, preto e capri. Os valores ficaram acima do que havia sido especulado por informantes, recentemente, como observa o site PhoneArena. Por enquanto, o novo intermediário da Motorola não tem previsão de lançamento no Brasil. Trabalhando em novidades para a sua linha de dobráveis, a empresa estaria preparando a estreia do Razr Flex. Saiba mais sobre o dispositivo nesta matéria. Com informações de PhoneArena.

This includes facilities owned by Hyundai, the factory recently inaugurated in Halmahera with investment from China, as well as the CATL and Antam collaboration factory. According to him, this development indicates the growing integration of the electric vehicle battery ecosystem in Indonesia, encompassing mining, mineral processing, and battery cell production. artigo.texto: Long before much of Maryland knew what a data center was, Frederick County looked like it could be the industry’s next hub. A Washington, D.C. exurb of rolling farmland, Frederick sits just across the Potomac River from Northern Virginia’s “Data Center Alley” and boasts fiber-optic connection to the industry capital. When County Executive Jessica Fitzwater was elected four years ago, she promised policies and regulations to make Frederick “a national leader” in responsible data center development. Today, Frederick is home to Maryland’s only large-scale data center development, and its leaders are learning the hard way about the hazards of navigating the charged and changing politics of the industry, which critics decry for devouring energy, water and land. The divide over data centers has all but consumed Frederick politics. Fitzwater, a Democrat, faces a surprisingly strong challenge from the former Frederick Mayor Jeff Holtzinger, and the race has turned into a reckoning over her handling of the industry. Over two weeks last month, Fitzwater touted — then spiked — a $110 million agreement with the county’s lead data center developer, and she has extended the county’s data center moratorium from the end of this year to next summer. Next week’s election could help shape the county’s — and Maryland’s — longer-term approach to data centers. While most of the state lives under a data center freeze, the outcome in Frederick will be an early test of just how resilient the state’s grassroots backlash will be. Read More A secret courtship Four years ago, developers broke ground on a sprawling campus at the site of an old aluminum smelting plant outside Adamstown, a quaint village in southern Frederick. Known today as Quantum Maryland, the data center complex spans hundreds of acres and draws busloads of construction workers a day. County leaders once flirted with an even bigger vision. In 2019, Frederick officials entered a nondisclosure agreement with Amazon. The county then held closed-door meetings for close to a year with the company on a proposal they called “Project Holiday,” which would have set aside three areas of southern Frederick County for a $30 billion venture with as many as 15 data centers. The extent of these exchanges is public because the Sugarloaf Alliance, a group dedicated to preserving Frederick’s rural character, successfully sued over access to the records. “Everybody [was] looking at us like we’re wearing tinfoil hats,” Steve Black, a southern Frederick farmer and president of the alliance, said about the early days of his anti-data center advocacy. Black said he knows many loyal Democrats who are torn over whether to support Fitzwater in the general election. At the time of Project Holiday, Fitzwater served on the County Council and was briefed on the Amazon talks months after they happened. She was elected county executive in 2022 and is quick to point out that her administration hasn’t approved any new data centers. Instead, she appointed a task force to study the industry and has imposed a series of moratoriums, the latest of which expires in July 2027. Nevertheless, Fitzwater has drawn the ire of the county’s anti-data center coalition in part because of zoning changes enacted by the county council. The changes, similar to a proposal introduced by Fitzwater, expanded a designated data center zone from roughly 1,600 acres to 2,600, including several hundred acres of farmland. In an August interview, Fitzwater said her job is to ensure the industry is strictly regulated and brings benefits to her constituents. Frederick has collected more than $55 million in property and land transfer taxes from the Quantum campus, and industry boosters say the project could eventually net over $200 million annually for the county. For some neighbors near the Quantum campus, the upside is hard to see. Where Hope Green once looked out over mountains and deer from her yard, she now sees a hulking warehouse and stacks of diesel generators. She says construction on the Quantum site has tarnished her well water, and Maryland environmental regulators have cited developers there for repeated discharges into a local creek and other violations. A spokesperson for the site’s master developer, Catellus Development Corporation, declined to comment on environmental issues but said in a statement that the company remains committed to the project. “For years, we have operated in good faith through the County’s legally established land-use process,” a Quantum Maryland spokesperson said. Born and raised on an Adamstown farm, Green had hoped to spend her retirement in her house. Now she insists the county or developer should buy her and her neighbors out of their homes. “What’s left of my family is here. My church is here. My friends are here,” she said. But “if I want to have peace of mind for the rest of my life, I have to leave.” A political landmine Last month, Frederick County officials announced a proposal they said would squeeze the local data center industry for a transformative infusion of cash. The agreement with Catellus, valued at $110 million, would pay for renovations to an elementary school near the county’s sole data center campus; a new community recreation building; a jobs-training facility; and protections for farmland. It would also freeze parts of the county’s rezoning and bar changes to noise and environmental regulations for at least eight years. Fitzwater called the agreement “unprecedented” and touted it as among the largest commitments of its kind in the country. But instead of plaudits, the county’s anti-data center faction condemned the package for provisions that threatened to lock in some of the project’s most controversial aspects. The announcement inflamed a debate that had dominated the primary contests in June. artigo.texto: Franklin County residents remain concerned about data centers after Project Flash FRANKLIN COUNTY, Va. (WSET) — Public opposition to data centers in Franklin County continues even after Project Flash was rejected, with residents raising concerns about property values, noise pollution and the county’s lack of zoning restrictions. On Oct. 21, Board of Supervisors Chair Lorie Smith said the board had no active data center proposals under consideration. “We as a board, don't have any current proposals in front of us or anything,” Smith said. But some residents say the rejection of Project Flash has not put their concerns to rest. Penny Hodges, a Franklin County resident and real estate agent, questioned whether the project was permanently abandoned or simply put on hold. She also expressed concern about the potential impact of a data center on nearby property values. “Do you really want to live within arm’s reach of a data center? No, who would?” Hodges said. “The noise. The noise pollution, the vibration.” Hodges said she does not want residents to bear the burden of living near a development whose potential effects remain a concern. “I wouldn’t want to be their guinea pig, would you?” she said. SEE ALSO: Botetourt officials decline interviews as protests target Google data center plan Christine Sizemore, vice chair of the Franklin County Community Coalition, opposed the proposal and said the county needs stronger guidelines governing data center development. “One thing Franklin County does not have is appropriate guidelines and restrictions in place right now,” Sizemore said. “Data centers are allowed by right.” Nearly 60% of Franklin County is unzoned, according to information presented in the report. The lack of zoning restrictions in those areas could leave developers with fewer land-use limitations, depending on other applicable regulations. The issue has raised questions about whether county officials will take steps to establish additional zoning rules before another data center proposal emerges. Supervisor Dan Quinn said there isn't much that can be done to bring the county’s unzoned areas under zoning regulations. “I’m not working to get them zoned in,” Quinn said. “I would say that the citizens in those areas are fiercely independent, and they appreciate being unzoned. They like it that the government is not controlling what they can do there.” Quinn also raised concerns about the use of a referendum to change zoning in those areas. His comments underscore a divide between residents seeking additional development restrictions and those who value the limited government oversight associated with unzoned land. Although county officials say no data center proposals are currently before the Board of Supervisors, opponents of Project Flash say they intend to keep pressing for safeguards. Hodges said residents should continue to voice their concerns rather than assume the issue has been resolved. “This is not the time to back down and back off,” she said. “I mean, we just have to keep the heat on.”

artigo.texto: The Tampa City Council has moved to restrict development of new artificial intelligence data centers, directing city staff to prepare a temporary moratorium and immediately stop accepting applications for such facilities. The motion, introduced by Chair Alan Clendenin, passed without opposition during the closing minutes of a special meeting primarily devoted to the Tampa Bay Rays’ community benefits agreement. Clendenin called on staff to “immediately cease accepting (and) processing land development applications for data centers,” while the city develops regulations governing the facilities. The proposal also directed staff to prepare a resolution for the Council’s Nov. 5 meeting invoking the pending ordinance and declaring the city’s intent to amend its comprehensive plan, land development code and city code. Staff would also draft an ordinance establishing temporary development restrictions while the city considers longer-term regulations. Clendenin requested public hearings in December and January, including one scheduled for Jan. 7. The motion did not specify how long the proposed moratorium would remain in place. The proposal comes months after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed SB 484, which affirmed local governments’ authority to regulate data centers through comprehensive planning and land development rules. The law also requires large-load electric customers to cover their own utility and infrastructure costs rather than shifting those expenses to other ratepayers. The move follows similar action by Hillsborough County Commissioners in August, when the Board voted unanimously to draft a moratorium on AI data centers in unincorporated areas and explore restrictions on their use of county drinking water for cooling. At the time, Hillsborough County residents raised concerns about the facilities’ electricity and water demands, potential impacts on utility bills, noise and development pressure in rural neighborhoods. However, county attorneys advised Hillsborough Commissioners that the county’s proposed moratorium cannot take effect until after Oct. 1, 2027, unless a court overturns restrictions imposed by SB 180. Clendenin’s motion goes further by seeking an immediate halt to new applications within Tampa city limits, although the Council has not yet adopted the moratorium ordinance.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia A Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) apresentou hoje o TENER+ em seu lançamento global na All Energy Australia 2026, onde também exibiu o TENER Sodium. A empresa 29 de outubro de 2026, às 11:27 MELBOURNE, Austrália, 29 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) apresentou hoje o TENER+ em seu lançamento global na All Energy Australia 2026, onde também exibiu o TENER Sodium. A empresa assinou memorandos de entendimento (MoUs) com a Hitachi Energy, o EPEC Group e a UNSW Sydney para reforçar a execução e a conexão à rede elétrica de projetos de baterias de grande escala na Austrália. TENER: projetado para oferecer desempenho de longo prazo e atender aos rigorosos requisitos de conexão à rede elétrica da Austrália Os sistemas de armazenamento de energia TENER+ e TENER Sodium da CATL foram projetados para oferecer a confiabilidade e o desempenho de longo prazo exigidos pelos projetos australianos de armazenamento de energia em escala de serviços públicos. Projetados para condições climáticas extremas, elas visam atender aos rigorosos requisitos de conexão à rede elétrica da Austrália e dar aos financiadores do projeto a confiança necessária na confiabilidade e no desempenho a longo prazo que sustentam as receitas das baterias. O TENER+ é um sistema de armazenamento de energia de capacidade ultr elevada, com 9 MWh, que ajuda os desenvolvedores a gerar valor para os projetos no longo prazo e maximizar sua capacidade de armazenamento. O TENER+ reduz em até 40% o número de contêineres necessários e em 12% a área ocupada pelo projeto, sendo ideal para empreendimentos com restrições de espaço. Seu sistema inteligente de gerenciamento térmico proporciona maior eficiência de ciclo e menor consumo de energia auxiliar. Várias baterias TENER+ podem ser comissionadas simultaneamente com um único clique para agilizar a implantação do projeto. Projetado para uma vida útil de 25 anos, o TENER+ oferece resfriamento a líquido e proteção para ambientes úmidos e costeiros. Os níveis de ruído permanecem abaixo de 65 dBA a 1 metro de distância. Seu design de exaustão superior com tecnologia “sem ilha de calor” direciona o ar quente verticalmente para cima, afastando-o das unidades adjacentes. Isso evita a dissipação horizontal do calor e minimiza o impacto térmico sobre as unidades PCS adjacentes, permitindo que operem à potência nominal máxima mesmo nas condições extremas do verão. O TENER Sodium é o primeiro sistema de armazenamento de energia com baterias de íons de sódio produzido em massa e validado em campo do mundo. Ele fornece mais de 30 MWh através de sua arquitetura de gabinete modular. Projetado para o calor da Austrália, ele opera em temperaturas de até 55 °C e oferece mais de 10.000 ciclos a 45 °C. Oferece 95% de eficiência de ida e volta, com uma vida útil de mais de 20 anos. Em conjunto, esses sistemas de armazenamento de energia oferecem aos desenvolvedores e proprietários de ativos a possibilidade de escolher entre as tecnologias de íons de lítio e de sódio. O sódio é muito mais abundante e está distribuído geograficamente de forma mais ampla do que o lítio, oferecendo uma alternativa para diversificar as cadeias de suprimentos de baterias. “O valor de uma bateria é medido ao longo de toda a sua vida útil de um projeto e não apenas no dia em que ela é colocada em funcionamento”, disse Zane Zhou, gerente-geral da CATL Austrália e Nova Zelândia. “Os desenvolvedores precisam ter confiança de que suas baterias suportarão os ciclos de operação previstos para comercialização no Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade e manterão um bom desempenho durante toda a vida útil dos sistemas instalados em projetos de grande escala. É para isso que o TENER+ e o TENER Sódio foram desenvolvidos. Estamos oferecendo tecnologias de íon-sódio e íon-lítio para dar aos proprietários e desenvolvedores de ativos a flexibilidade de escolher a tecnologia certa para o seu sucesso.” Parcerias da CATL com a indústria local para acelerar a transição energética da Austrália para fontes de energia limpa Os sistemas de armazenamento de energia TENER ajudam a superar os desafios da rede elétrica australiana diante da crescente participação das fontes renováveis na matriz energética. As fontes renováveis responderam por um recorde de 44,3% da geração de eletricidade do Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade (NEM) no trimestre encerrado em setembro de 2026. As baterias em escala de rede responderam por 8% da geração de eletricidade no pico da demanda noturna, superando pela primeira vez as usinas a gás, segundo o Operador do Mercado de Energia Australiano (AEMO). Com a desativação das usinas a carvão, a rede elétrica necessita cada vez mais de sistemas de armazenamento de energia com capacidade de formação de rede para garantir suporte de tensão e frequência. Para ajudar a fornecer mais armazenamento na Austrália, os três memorandos de entendimento da CATL visam abordar os desafios de uma rede elétrica movida a fontes renováveis usando a experiência e a inovação australianas. Os produtos de baterias CC da CATL e os sistemas de conversão de energia da Hitachi Energy formarão a base de uma oferta integrada proposta para a Austrália e para a região da Ásia-Pacífico. Por meio dessa parceria, a empresa busca ampliar a compatibilidade entre os sistemas, padronizar a implementação dos projetos e reduzir os riscos de integração. Na Austrália, a CATL colaborará com o EPEC Group e o Instituto de Pesquisa e Validação de Armazenamento de Energia de Xiamen (ESVL) para combinar sua tecnologia de armazenamento de energia com a experiência do EPEC em integração à rede elétrica e execução de projetos de engenharia, além de aproveitar a capacidade do ESVL de validar sistemas em escala real. artigo.texto: SHAKOPEE, Minn. (Oct. 27, 2026) -- Xcel Energy advanced its battery storage strategy Monday with the arrival of battery units at its Blue Lake site, a significant construction achievement that supports the company's efforts to build a more flexible, resilient energy system for customers across Minnesota. The Blue Lake project is part of a broader plan to diversify the resources that power Minnesota while maintaining the reliable service customers depend on and keeping bills as low as possible. Together with two planned projects in Becker, Minnesota, Xcel Energy expects to operate more than 735 megawatts of battery energy storage in Minnesota by the end of 2027, creating the largest battery portfolio in the Upper Midwest. "For more than a century, energy companies have generated electricity when customers need it and delivered it almost immediately. Battery storage changes what's possible. It allows us to store energy and dispatch it when it's needed most, giving us a powerful new tool to maintain reliability, support growing energy needs and make the most of the diverse resources that power our system," said Bria Shea, president of Xcel Energy–Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota. Battery storage helps strengthen grid reliability by storing energy when it is available and dispatching it back to the grid when customer demand is higher. The evolution of energy storage systems over the years means they can be deployed more broadly at existing energy sites such as Blue Lake, allowing Xcel Energy to leverage existing infrastructure while integrating new technologies. The Blue Lake batteries will store energy generated across Xcel Energy's Upper Midwest system, including energy from wind, solar, nuclear and natural gas resources. The 135.5-megawatt battery energy storage facility will include 132 battery units capable of storing energy and delivering electricity for up to four hours, enough energy to power approximately 125,000 homes when demand is highest. "The Blue Lake project demonstrates how battery storage is becoming an increasingly important part of grid operations," said Justin Meagher, Xcel Energy battery storage project manager. "These systems can respond quickly to changing conditions, store energy when it's available and provide electricity when customer demand is high. That flexibility helps us operate the electric system more efficiently while continuing to deliver reliable service to customers." The Blue Lake Battery Energy Storage System is expected to begin serving customers in 2027. # # # About Xcel Energy Xcel Energy (NASDAQ: XEL) is a leading energy provider, dedicated to serving millions of customers with excellence. We make energy work better for customers, helping them thrive every day. That means always raising the bar — delivering better service and providing more reliable, resilient and sustainable energy. Headquartered in Minneapolis, we work every day to generate and distribute electricity and gas to customers across eight states: Minnesota, Colorado, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, New Mexico and Texas. For more information, visit xcelenergy.com or follow us on X and Facebook.

artigo.texto: Gov. Kelly talks property taxes, AI, data centers in conference on Kansas economy The term-limited governor also offered some advice for her replacement photo by: Dmitry Martirosov/Journal-World As she prepares to leave office after eight years, Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly on Thursday reflected on her tenure and offered advice on some the most pressing issues facing not only The Sunflower State, but the nation. Property taxes, data centers, artificial intelligence and the current political climate were all top of mind for Kelly, who delivered her remarks at the 2026 Kansas Economic Policy Conference at the University of Kansas, where about 100 people were present. Kelly, who is term-limited, echoed many of the same concerns others have about AI, property taxes and what the future holds for younger generations. She said people are “petrified” of the technology because of its uncertainty, and advised college graduates who are entering the workforce to embrace patience. Kelly was elected governor in 2018 and reelected in 2022. Two state senators are vying to replace her in Tuesday’s election — Ty Masterson, a Republican, and Cindy Holscher, his Democratic opponent. Property taxes — and how high they have gotten — were a major talking point on Thursday. Kelly, a Democrat, said one way to address the issue is through better partnerships between state and local governments. She said the state should pick up some of the burden that local governments are paying, such as corrections, mental health and public health services, and added that putting a law in place might also help alleviate the problem. Property taxes are the largest combined state and local revenue source in Kansas, accounting for more than 30% of the total share, according to the Kansas Legislative Research Department. Kansas collected $6.6 billion in revenue from property taxes in fiscal year 2025, which is roughly one third of all local and state tax revenues collected that year. In 2025, Kansas brought in $323 million more in local tax revenue than it did during the previous year, an increase that was largely driven by higher revenues from property tax. Annual property tax revenues continue to rise year over year, according to the legislative research department. In 2025, revenues rose 3.8% from 2024 and were about $1 billion more than three years prior. photo by: Dmitry Martirosov/Journal-World photo by: Dmitry Martirosov/Journal-World Jim McLean, a correspondent at Kansas Public Radio and one of Thursday’s moderators, asked Kelly whether combining local districts into larger government units would be a good idea to grow their tax base. It would be difficult, Kelly said, and instead pushed for more incentives. She said lawmakers in those areas will likely receive pushback and will never vote to approve it. “There has to be some structure (where) there is the burden on the state, but then also the responsibility on the local unit government to actually at least flatten, if not decrease, property taxes,” Kelly said. Kelly on Thursday also acknowledged concerns around data centers. Their water and energy consumption should be considered, she said, and the cost generated by powering them should not be placed on everyday citizens, who should be the final arbiters on whether to allow them into their communities or not. She said data centers have become more of a political issue than anything else, and once the midterm elections are over things will hopefully slow down. Speaking of the current political climate, Kelly didn’t mince words, calling it “polarized,” “ugly” and “nasty.” Responding to an audience member question about what would she advice the next governor, Kelly kept it simple: Be kind, she said. “Whatever you’re doing is going to impact people in their real lives,” Kelly said. “Just be kind — and choose good.”

artigo.texto: Economic leaders announce plan for possible data center in Delhi Township: Here’s what you need to know Possible data center site planned at Holt Economic Opportunity Park LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - The Lansing Economic Area Partnership and Lighthouse Sustainability want to build a data center on 423 acres off College Road that was set aside for future economic development in 2003. The site is known as the Holt Economic Opportunity Park. It is west of US-127 and south of Holt Road. The two organizations announced the effort Tuesday. What LEAP and Lighthouse are proposing According to the announcement, a strategic plan “will define what a data center project should look like before an application is filed.” The framework is “intended to change how those larger projects work” and will “begin with the community, establish expectations and propose projects that can meet rigorous environmental standards and provide meaningful community investment.” Bob Trezise, president and CEO of LEAP, said the announcement describes a process and not a project. “What we actually announced today is a process, not a project,” Trezise said. “We are basically flipping the script on how to introduce a major economic development project. We want to do community engagement first.” The pitch includes a fully funded residential solar and battery program estimated to cut participating homeowners’ energy costs by 50%. It also includes a required community benefits agreement and a separate $20 million community investment fund. “It’s kind of a Goldilocks. It’s not a big thousand acre site in a farm field. It’s not in an urban area. It’s in an industrial area. And we also believe that the data center itself is going to be very unique in being a clean, green data center,” Trezise said. In a press release, Trezise said: “Delhi Township had a vision for the property before we sought a development partner. We chose Lighthouse because they bring deep renewable energy expertise and a commitment to making development work for the people who live here. That combination matters. Smart growth means attracting investment that strengthens our economy while protecting the natural resources and way of life that make this community home.” No application filed, no end user named No formal application has been filed, and no end user has been identified. Delhi Township has had a moratorium on data center reviews since April. Township Manager Tracy Miller said the board approved a 12-month moratorium. LEAP and Lighthouse said they will “respect that moratorium and focus on community engagement strategy.” The engagement process gives residents time to examine studies, question the project team and provide input before the township is asked to consider future development. Trezise said community input will be the ultimate decision maker. “It’s definitely up to the community. Delhi Township has a moratorium in place. We welcome that. It provides great space to have a non-pressure conversation,” Trezise said. A community engagement webinar is scheduled for Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. Delhi Township responds Miller released a statement Tuesday afternoon: “Delhi Township is committed to being a great place for residents to live, work and raise a family. As the state and federal government have continued to consider rules and regulations for data centers, and they have continued to be a significant issue for those communities currently considering proposals, our Township Board approved a 12-month moratorium on data centers last April,” Miller said. “The Township is learning about the LEAP/Lighthouse Sustainability announcement at the same time as members of the media. Township Board members have not received any kind of land use application or proposal from a data center developer. There is no data center proposal being considered or discussed. Board members have not communicated with a data center developer and they have not, and will not, sign any non-disclosure agreements,” Miller said. “To be very clear, this topic has not been discussed at Township Board meetings. The Township and its staff are not involved in this. The LEAP/Lighthouse effort is independent from the Delhi Township Board, Planning Commission or administration and the Township was not at all aware of this announcement before receiving a press release on Tuesday,” Miller said. Neighbors push back Neighbors who back up to the land, including Nicole Blumhart, disagree with the description of the area as industrial. “This is a residential community with 112 homes, and it’s not industrial whatsoever,” said Blumhart, who lives next to the proposed site. “You don’t hear anything. I cannot imagine living here with a 24-7 hum. It would be a living nightmare.” “I really hope that they hear our concerns,” Blumhart said. This is a developing story. artigo.texto: Emergent technologies raise concerns about natural resources, exploitation and education in Montana From mining to timber to tourism, Montana’s natural resources have been the bedrock of economic opportunity and industrial extraction for more than a century. Now that data center developers have descended on the Treasure State, some local tribes are outlawing these projects to safeguard sovereignty, land and water. There’s a lot to like about Montana for companies seeking to site data centers, according to energy industry veteran Bob Morris with Montana Technological University. Reliable, affordable electricity, he said, is a draw for data center builders — and Montana boasts the seventh-lowest electricity rates in the country. Plus, he said, the northern climate makes for economical cooling of the machinery used in these facilities. “We’ve got great infrastructure,” he added. “We’ve got a good fiber-optic network. We’ve got good highways, good rail transport, and then there’s us. Montana’s got a great workforce, hardworking and a thriving business environment.” The attraction doesn’t necessarily go both ways between potential developers and the communities in their crosshairs. In 2026, the Fort Peck Tribes and the Northern Cheyenne Tribal Council both made official policies to keep data centers out. Leaders for both groups said they wanted to avoid risks to their natural environment, and the long history of outside exploitation didn’t endear the developers to Native community members. But technological developments like AI will still be a part of Montana’s digital landscape, no matter where the infrastructure to power them ends up being built. Some Indigenous technology leaders from across the region have advocated for tribes to embrace AI so community members avoid being left out of a major trend shaping education and career possibilities. Software engineer Michael Running Wolf from Birney, Montana, on the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation, travels North America promoting AI use as an avenue to address pressing Native community needs. His work with a team of “Indigenous technologists” from the Crow Tribe and the Little Shell Chippewa in Montana focuses on language revitalization using AI. He cautions against the impulse to turn away from innovative technologies altogether. Similarly, Caitlin Bordeaux, a director at the computer science group Indigitize, is a Sicangu Lakota educator who works across Montana and South Dakota engaging Indigenous communities in culturally relevant digital education. Indigitize helps expand computer science opportunities for underserved students in Indian Country, rooted in the hope that emerging technologies can support Native priorities rather than exacerbating existing disparities. Ready for the future Access issues for high-tech tools disproportionately hinder small, rural schools, according to Montana Digital Academy Executive Director Jason Neiffer. To level the playing field, the academy’s new Frontier Learning Lab offers resources for Montana teachers to navigate AI and other digital tools while sharing insights and best practices for implementation. Neiffer told Buffalo’s Fire he understands the hesitations around joining the AI bandwagon, and he hopes the lab can inform thoughtful approaches to adoption. “Education has to prepare students for the world in which they’re going to live,” Neiffer said. Grant funding for the Frontier Learning Lab came from the nonprofit aiEDU, which equips teachers with an understanding of AI readiness and AI literacy so they can effectively support students and families encountering new technology on the ground. The organization’s national programs lead, Connor Mulvaney, lives in Polson on the Flathead Reservation, where he’s collaborated with the local community to boost knowledge around using AI and deploying it responsibly. “I think we need to be informed decisionmakers,” he told Buffalo’s Fire. He said his goal with aiEDU in Montana is to give individual communities the foundations for determining their own preferred approaches to new technology. Since AI is hardly a singular, static piece of new technology, Mulvaney added, the decisions being made today will likely need to be revisited and built upon as these concepts evolve over time. It’s important, he said, to make sure Indigenous communities have what they need to navigate current conversations and prepare for what might come next. And research by the Montana Afterschool Alliance, another grantee supported by aiEDU, demonstrates the important role young people have to play in guiding and informing these discussions. In 2025, the alliance piloted community conversations in parts of Montana that rarely see themselves considered the vanguard of change and innovation. The team deliberately began their work with convenings in Harlem on the Fort Belknap Reservation, Poplar on the Fort Peck Reservation and in the Flathead Reservation communities of Pablo and Ronan. The alliance focused heavily on incorporating input from younger community members into these conversations, revealing noteworthy ways Indigenous youth are interacting with AI. “Through our conversations we heard the sentiment that unlike prior technology rollouts, generative AI was already in use from within communities,” Heather Jameson from the afterschool alliance told Buffalo’s Fire. “And in many cases youth are outpacing adults in adoption.” The findings in the alliance’s landscape review from these sessions showed Montana Native youth have a healthy skepticism of AI and they recognize its limitations for providing factually accurate answers to specific questions. They’re highly exposed to AI-generated multimedia via social channels, less versed in using large language model chatbots, and good at identifying AI content in ways that often far surpass their elders’ ability to recognize such media. artigo.texto: WUXI, China, Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solid-state batteries are at a critical stage of transition from pilot production to large-scale manufacturing. To address key challenges in densification and solid-solid interface contact, Lead Intelligent has developed a horizontal warm isostatic pressing machine that delivers uniform three-dimensional pressure of up to 600 MPa across a wide temperature range from room temperature (RT) to 150°C. The machine achieves temperature control accuracy of ±2°C and pressure control accuracy of ±2%. Integrating automatic loading and unloading with precise, coordinated temperature and pressure control, the machine can increase cell density to over 95%, accelerating the industrialization of solid-state batteries. As solid-state batteries move toward mass production, two major challenges remain: high impedance caused by insufficient solid-solid interface contact, and the limitations of conventional unidirectional pressing, including uneven density and pronounced edge effects. Based on Pascal's principle, isostatic pressing applies isotropic pressurization within a sealed chamber to achieve multidimensional material compaction and densification. It is a key processing route for addressing solid-solid interface contact challenges in solid-state batteries. For the practical requirements of large-scale solid-state battery manufacturing, warm isostatic pressing offers an effective balance between densification performance, production efficiency, and manufacturing cost, making it a highly cost-effective option for mass production. As construction of solid-state battery capacity accelerates, warm isostatic pressing machines are becoming core incremental machines for battery manufacturers' next-generation solid-state production lines. Core Technology: Precise Temperature-Pressure Coordination for High-Precision Process Control Building on its R&D system, Lead Intelligent's horizontal warm isostatic pressing machine overcomes the "black box" limitations of traditional warm isostatic pressing process by enabling real-time monitoring of temperature and pressure inside the chamber. The machine upgrades from conventional unidirectional pressing to precise temperature-pressure coordination to promote closer contact between electrodes and electrolytes, making it well suited for solid-state battery mass production. - Pressure system: It delivers uniform three-dimensional pressure of up to 600 MPa, with pressure control accuracy ≤±2%. Automatic pressure compensation and emergency depressurization functions keep pressure fluctuations within ±2% during a 30-minute pressure holding period, ensuring process stability and repeatability. - Temperature system: The working temperatures can reach up to 150°C, and can be adjusted within a wide operating range from room temperature (RT) to 150°C, with temperature control accuracy of ±2°C. The initial heating time to 150°C takes no more than three hours, balancing process adaptability with mass production cycle-time requirements. - Chamber specifications: The working chamber inner diameter is ≥400 mm, the effective length is ≥4,000 mm, and the volume is around 500 L. It accommodates batch processing of workpieces in various sizes and meets the capacity requirements of GWh-scale production lines. Designed for Mass Production: Comprehensive Optimization for Large-Scale Manufacturing For GWh-scale manufacturing, warm isostatic pressing machines must do more than meet core process specifications. They shall also coordinate with whole line cycle time, logistics systems, and upstream and downstream processes. To meet these requirements, Lead Intelligent has optimized machine structure, automatic operation, and safety systems in parallel. Horizontal Design for Continuous Production Lines The horizontal working chamber and automatic loading and unloading design significantly reduce factory height requirements while seamlessly integrating with automatic logistics systems to meet the needs of continuous production and material transfer between upstream and downstream processes, adapting to takt-based operation on large-scale production lines. Electrodes and solid electrolytes can be stacked and assembled before being loaded into the chamber for pressing and densification, simplifying process flow. Full-process Automation to Minimize Manual Intervention The machine enables unmanned operation throughout cell pretreatment and material box circulation. It integrates four key functions: cell hot air preheating, cold air drying and cooling, automatic fixture loading and unloading, and material box automatic circulation. The machine covers the entire workflow including loading, pretreatment, isostatic pressing and unloading, minimizing manual intervention and improving production efficiency and process consistency within each batch. Multi-Layered Safety Controls for Reliable Operation The machine incorporates a comprehensive multi-layered safety assurance system. At the foundational level, the machine is equipped with dual pressure and temperature monitoring for the chamber, together with pipeline pressure-relief ports to safeguard machine operation. In addition, an innovative triple deformation monitoring system provides real-time monitoring to enhance operational safety and maintain process precision. As a world-leading provider of intelligent manufacturing solutions for the new energy industry, Lead Intelligent has completed the full-process layout for solid-state battery manufacturing, covering key stages including dry electrode processing, high-precision stacking, warm isostatic pressing, and formation and grading. The company has the capacity for batch delivery of GWh-level solid-state battery whole line solutions. artigo.texto: [SMM Flash] CATL-Affiliated Jianxiawo Lithium Mining Project Receives EIA Approval October 30: The Yichun Municipal Ecology and Environment Bureau issued its approval for the Environmental Impact Assessment Report of the Zhenkouli–Jianxiawo lithium mining project operated by Yichun Times New Energy Mining Co., Ltd. From an environmental protection perspective, the bureau approved in principle the project’s proposed nature, location, scale, production process and environmental protection measures. According to the approval, the project is located at the border of Yifeng County and Fengxin County in Yichun, Jiangxi Province, with a total mining area of 2.5029 square kilometres. The project is classified as a new development, with a designed lithium ore mining recovery rate of 98%, usable ore resources of approximately 513.525 million tonnes, annual ore mining capacity of 30 million tonnes and a designed mine life of 18 years. The planned product output is 30 million tonnes of run-of-mine ore per year. The mining process includes topsoil stripping, drilling, blasting, loading and truck haulage. After crushing, ore will either be transported by conveyor to the concentrator or loaded directly for external sale. Total project investment is approximately RMB 4.35 billion, including around RMB 288 million in environmental protection investment, accounting for 6.61% of the total. The approval requires the project to implement the “three simultaneous” environmental protection system, under which environmental facilities must be designed, constructed and commissioned together with the main project. The company must also obtain the required pollutant discharge permit before starting production facilities or generating actual emissions, and the project may formally commence operations only after its supporting environmental protection facilities pass acceptance procedures.

artigo.texto: Regra exige relato de emissões para 600 grandes companhias Ministério da Fazenda fixa normas e cronograma para adoção gradativa das medidas O Ministério da Fazenda publicou nesta quinta-feira (29) portaria que define a cobertura setorial do mercado regulado de carbono brasileiro. A norma estabelece os segmentos enquadrados nas obrigações de Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação (MRV) de emissões de gases de efeito estufa e o cronograma para implementação gradual. As regras começam a valer a partir de 2027 para empresas com emissões anuais acima de 10 mil toneladas. A Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono estima que menos de 600 grandes empresas terão de iniciar os processos de relato de emissões, ou seja, informar de forma precisa a quantidade de CO2 emitida. O objetivo do governo é construir uma base oficial de dados antes do início do funcionamento do mercado regulado de carbono no Brasil, a partir 2030. O texto final traz mudanças em relação à proposta submetida à consulta pública em 28 de julho, após diferentes setores pedirem alterações na distribuição entre as três etapas de implementação. Em entrevista ao Valor, a secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis, avaliou o resultado da consulta pública como positivo. Sem a inclusão de novos segmentos, o plano mantém o total de 17 setores, mas redistribui algumas atividades entre as etapas do cronograma. Para Reis, a manutenção do escopo confirma o acerto da proposta original do governo federal. Sobre a antecipação de alguns segmentos para a primeira fase, a secretária afirmou que o movimento demonstra que “os setores já se consideram maduros, preparados e entendem o valor da regulamentação”. O mercado regulado prevê que as emissões de gases de efeito estufa passem a ser medidas, reportadas e limitadas por lei. Empresas que emitem mais de 10 mil toneladas por ano deverão monitorar e reportar suas emissões. Para aquelas com emissões superiores a 25 mil toneladas anuais, haverá limites de emissão. A política busca reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa e estimular o desenvolvimento de tecnologias de baixo carbono. O teto global de emissões e as regras para a distribuição das Cotas Brasileiras de Emissão (CBEs) estão previstos para 2030, com o início do Plano Nacional de Alocação (PNA). A portaria não exige a apresentação imediata de relatórios nem estabelece limites de emissão ou custos para as empresas. Até o início do PNA, a Fazenda recomenda o acompanhamento da regulamentação. Para o secretário-adjunto José Pedro Bastos Neves, a regulamentação também pode abrir oportunidades para soluções nacionais de descarbonização. Neves afirmou que a pauta traz uma oportunidade para valorizar tecnologias e rotas de descarbonização que são desenvolvidas no Brasil. A primeira etapa de MRV começa em 2027 e abrange as indústrias de alumínio, ferro e aço em usinas integradas, cimento, exploração e produção de petróleo e gás natural, papel e celulose, vidro, além de alguns segmentos da indústria química e da mineração de minério de ferro e de bauxita. Em relação ao desenho preliminar, foram antecipados para a etapa inicial o vidro, a mineração de minério de ferro e bauxita e alguns segmentos da indústria química. Já o refino de petróleo e o transporte aéreo deixaram de integrar essa fase. A segunda etapa, prevista para começar até 2029, abrangerá cerâmica, ferro e aço em usinas semi-integradas, atividades da indústria química não incluídas na primeira etapa, indústria de alimentos e bebidas, mineração das demais substâncias minerais, refino de petróleo e setor elétrico. Deixam a segunda fase os segmentos de alumínio reciclado, vidro, resíduos sólidos e tratamento de esgoto. A terceira etapa permanece prevista para 2031 e inclui os transportes rodoviário, ferroviário e aquaviário, sem alterações em relação à proposta original. Cada etapa prevê um período de preparação e adaptação de quatro anos antes da consolidação dos dados. No primeiro ano, as empresas devem elaborar o plano de monitoramento e submetê-lo à aprovação do órgão gestor do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). No segundo e no terceiro anos, começa o monitoramento efetivo, com a medição e a coleta de dados sobre emissões e remoções de gases de efeito estufa. No quarto ano, ocorre a consolidação dos dados e o envio do relato de emissões no âmbito do PNA. A retirada dos setores de resíduos sólidos e tratamento de esgoto do cronograma geral decorre, segundo Reis, do entendimento de que a própria legislação afasta obrigações diretas para atividades que comprovadamente apresentam atributos de produção sustentáveis. “Para incentivar a descarbonização, e aqui a gente está falando principalmente da emissão de metano no setor de resíduos, o melhor é que eles atuem pelo lado do voluntário, gerando crédito de carbono”, explicou ela. Segundo Reis, o mecanismo também pode contribuir para ampliar o tratamento de resíduos e estimular o fim dos lixões. A Fazenda também atendeu a um pedido do setor aéreo para alinhar o cronograma de MRV. “Ao invés de fixar o transporte aéreo na etapa 1, definimos que a exigência ocorrerá no momento em que o ProBioQAV (programa voltado ao mercado de combustível sustentável de aviação) for regulamentado”, resumiu. Para Taciana Stec, especialista do Instituto Talanoa, a alteração do cronograma da primeira etapa é positiva. Ela ressalta, porém, que ainda não há clareza sobre como será a integração dos créditos florestais ao mercado regulado. Marta Salomon, especialista sênior do Talanoa, afirma que, quando os tetos de emissão entrarem em vigor, o sistema começará a cumprir seu objetivo de reduzir as emissões dos setores intensivos de carbono.

artigo.texto: - English News - Tech science - NASA Artemis Moon Mission | Extreme Cold Battery Technology Development Why NASA develops extreme-cold batteries to power future missions?:Technology could power NASA’s Artemis missions to return humans to the Moon - Copy link The Moon’s South Pole experiences extremely cold temperatures, making it difficult for batteries to work reliably. To address this challenge, NASA is developing a new type of battery that could help astronauts and robotic vehicles operate in the Moon’s harsh environment. The project, called Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space (SPEARS), aims to develop batteries that can withstand extreme temperatures, remain safe, and provide reliable power for future lunar missions. The technology could support NASA’s Artemis campaign, which aims to return humans to the Moon and establish a sustained presence there. How does NASA’s new battery work? Conventional lithium-ion batteries, commonly used in smartphones and laptops, contain liquid electrolytes. These liquids can freeze in extreme cold, affecting battery performance and potentially damaging the cells. High temperatures can also create problems. NASA’s SPEARS project aims to overcome these limitations by replacing liquid electrolytes with solid materials made from ceramics or polymers. These solid electrolytes do not freeze like liquids, helping the batteries withstand extreme temperature changes. During thermal vacuum tests at NASA’s Langley Research Center, prototype battery cells operated at temperatures as high as 80 degrees Celsius and as low as minus 60 degrees Celsius. They also showed reduced performance at minus 80 degrees Celsius. The batteries were further exposed to temperatures ranging from 100 degrees Celsius to minus 170 degrees Celsius without sustaining damage. However, the batteries cannot operate immediately at the coldest temperatures. Small heaters would be used to warm them to their operating range when needed. How could these batteries help astronauts on the Moon? Reliable batteries will be essential for future lunar missions, particularly in areas near the Moon’s South Pole that receive little or no sunlight. NASA’s solid-state batteries could power a range of equipment, including: - Lunar rovers: Vehicles exploring the Moon’s surface and dark, shadowed craters. - Astronaut tools: Equipment such as drills used to explore the lunar surface. - Emergency power supplies: Portable batteries for astronauts during critical situations. - Scientific instruments: Devices that collect data during long-duration lunar missions. Because the batteries would not need to be kept warm continuously, they could also reduce the need for heavy heating and temperature-control systems. This could help make spacecraft and lunar equipment lighter and more efficient. Could the technology be used on Earth? Although SPEARS is being developed for space exploration, the technology could also have applications on Earth. Solid-state batteries may eventually be useful in electric vehicles, smartphones, drones, and other portable electronic devices. The project began in 2026 and is currently focused on developing and testing the technology. NASA’s Ames Research Center is also working on hardware and electronics to help prepare the batteries for future spaceflight testing. If development progresses successfully, SPEARS could become an important part of the technology needed to support longer and more sustainable human missions to the Moon. - Instagram tests 90-minute long-form videos: Know whether it could challenge YouTube's dominance in India - 7 WhatsApp scams that can empty your bank account: Beware of fake rewards, challans & other surprises fraudsters use - India's Sarvam to build AI tools for Army and Navy: Project will develop technology for military operations and training under a 5-year deal
