artigo.texto: Pelo menos nove empresas estão em processo de credenciamento pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) para se tornarem fornecedoras nacionais para o leilão de reserva de capacidade de baterias de grande porte. O governo prepara dois certames, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. O primeiro exigirá pelo menos 15% de conteúdo nacional e terá um preço-teto de R$ 1,76 milhão por MW/ano (megawatt por ano), 11% maior do que para projetos sem essa exigência. O processo de aprovação do BNDES tem duas etapas: primeiro, a empresa é credenciada como fornecedora; depois, precisa ter o seu sistema de baterias credenciado — etapa em que o banco verifica se o produto tem os requisitos de conteúdo nacional. Até agora, apenas uma companhia obteve o credenciamento completo do BNDES para seu modelo de bateria, a brasileira You.On. As outras companhias que já iniciaram o processo são as brasileiras Moura, WEG e SecPower; as chinesas BYD, Gotion, TBEA e Trina; e a canadense Canadian Solar. Os sistemas de armazenamento foram tema do evento “Reset Conecta: Transição Energética — Baterias em grande escala: o Brasil entra no jogo” realizado nesta quinta-feira (29), em São Paulo, e patrocinado pelo Bradesco. Alexandre Esposito, chefe da área de transição energética e clima do BNDES, diz ver um “compromisso firme” das participantes e ter a expectativa de que todas cumpram as exigências, com diferentes níveis de conteúdo local. O banco faz a comprovação de cada componente e avalia a capacidade produtiva das companhias diante do cronograma de entrega, que prevê o início da operação dos sistemas em agosto de 2028. O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) vê risco de o Brasil enfrentar déficit de potência além do limite regulatório a partir de 2027. Outras empresas ainda planejam fazer o processo de habilitação, como já anunciou a brasileira UCB Power. “A resposta de industrialização foi muito forte”, disse Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). “Quando a gente olha o quadro de componentes estratégicos e auxiliares de um sistema, vê quão longa é a cadeia. Ela pode ser semelhante à automotiva em nível de complexidade.” Três companhias — Moura, Automa e Reivax — também estão no processo de credenciamento para serem fornecedoras de software. Rotas tecnológicas Há quatro “rotas” de credenciamento no BNDES que as empresas podem seguir: junto ao mínimo de 15% de conteúdo nacional nos sistemas de armazenamento (formados pela bateria em si e outros equipamentos), a primeira exige pelo menos três componentes produzidos no Brasil, sendo um considerado estratégico. As demais rotas exigem que as baterias em si tenham um mínimo de conteúdo local. A rota 1 deve concentrar o maior número de empresas, uma vez que todas precisam se adaptar a esse patamar mínimo, mas Esposito vê potencial para companhias alcançarem a rota 4, com maior parcela de produção local. A ideia é que o leilão atue como um indutor de uma indústria que ainda está começando no Brasil — para isso, as regras seguem um modelo desenvolvido pelo BNDES no passado para a indústria de fabricantes de componentes para energia eólica. “No longo prazo, o objetivo é a gente conseguir fazer uma convergência de capex e de preço final entre os projetos com conteúdo nacional e aqueles sem”, diz Esposito, do BNDES. Embora o país tenha players importantes de baterias para outros fins, como a pernambucana Moura, a cadeia de produção dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia (conhecidos pela sigla em inglês BESS) é dominada pela China, que concentra a capacidade de fabricação do componente fundamental, as células. Crédito mais barato O credenciamento no BNDES habilita as empresas a participarem do leilão de conteúdo nacional e também a buscarem financiamento do próprio banco. Quanto maior for a parcela de conteúdo nacional, melhores as condições ofertadas. Para a empresa que se credenciar da rota 2 em diante, o financiamento do BNDES obtido pela empresa virá todo do Fundo Clima, um dos principais instrumentos de financiamento climático do país, que abastece as linhas de crédito subsidiadas do BNDES e do Eco Invest. O custo nominal do crédito do Fundo Clima é de 6,5% ao ano. Na rota 1, a empresa terá acesso a 80% de crédito do Fundo Clima e o resto via outras linhas do próprio BNDES. Como os projetos têm grandes dimensões e valores, a tendência é que as empresas componham o financiamento com recursos de outros mecanismos, como linhas de bancos públicos, bancos privados e mercado de capitais. Para Fabiana Costa, superintendente de sustentabilidade do Bradesco, a natureza do setor de baterias vai exigir que os bancos trabalhem com múltiplos produtos, de debêntures incentivadas a fiança e crédito. “Não há necessariamente um produto específico de prateleira, mas um portfólio que a gente precisa endereçar”, disse. O quinto leilão do Eco Invest, voltado para cadeias produtivas ligadas à inovação, incluiu um fundo temático para minerais críticos, mobilidade elétrica e baterias. A cadeia foi arrematada pelo Santander, que vai mobilizar R$ 6,5 bilhões e aposta no segmento de armazenamento de energia por considerar o setor o mais maduro entre as três frentes. Os leilões de bateria são esperados há anos no Brasil para dar mais flexibilidade e potência ao setor elétrico, que viu a geração por fontes intermitentes — como solar e eólica — crescer de forma acelerada na última década. Players ainda aguardam definições sobre regras importantes, como o rateio dos custos dos sistemas, hoje previstos para serem repassados para as empresas geradoras de energia.

artigo.texto: Preparations are underway for repowering the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm, which was commissioned in 2006 near Šibenik. Croatia’s first wind power plant – Ravne 1 (5.95 MW) – began producing electricity two years earlier. After 20 years of operation, the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm in Croatia is entering reconstruction, and the comparison of technical details demonstrates how much wind energy technology has advanced during that period. The plant, built by Germany’s wpd, consists of 14 Enercon E-48 wind turbines with an individual capacity of 800 kW, mounted on 50-meter-high towers, with a rotor diameter of 48 meters. The total installed capacity is 11.2 MW. The battery’s role would be to optimize the wind farm’s production The makeover of the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm involves the replacement of the 14 existing wind turbines with no more than five new ones, of up to 6 MW each, according to the environmental impact report for the Trtar-Krtolin wind farm repowering project. The request for the assessment was submitted to the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition by Vjetroelektrana Trtar Krtolin, registered in Dubrovnik. The investor also plans to install a battery energy storage system (BESS) of up to 10 MW and 20 MWh. The battery would be used for the optimization of the wind farm’s production, namely storing energy from production when the plant is operating at full generating capacity, and delivering it to the grid when production within the electricity system is insufficient and the timing is most favorable, the report reads. Extension of operational lifespan The investor explained that the project’s objective is to repower the wind farm to allow for the extension of its operational lifespan, enabling energy generation in a safe, economically viable, and environmentally friendly manner, and the delivery of electricity into the Croatian power system. In line with the European Union’s directives on repowering renewable electricity plants, the EIA is limited to potential effects arising from changes or expansion versus the original project, the investor noted. Of note, wpd said in mid-2023 that it planned to build a solar power plant at the site of its existing wind farm Katuni in Croatia.

artigo.texto: O deputado federal Danilo Forte (PP-CE) foi designado na quarta-feira, 28 de outubro, relator do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3.716/2026, que propõe retirar dos geradores de energia elétrica a obrigação exclusiva de custear a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias como reserva de capacidade. A proposta está pronta para inclusão na pauta do plenário da Câmara dos Deputados. Forte também foi o autor do requerimento de urgência aprovado pela Câmara em 13 de outubro, que permite a votação do projeto diretamente pelo plenário, sem necessidade de passar pelas comissões. O texto é de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). Apresentado em julho, o PL revoga um dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que estabeleceu o rateio dos custos da contratação de reserva de capacidade com baterias exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Se o projeto de lei for aprovado, as baterias passarão a seguir a regra geral de rateio dos custos da reserva de capacidade, com cobrança dos consumidores de energia elétrica. A tramitação ocorre faltando pouco mais de um mês para os primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade com baterias, previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Aneel aprovou os editais na terça-feira, 27 de outubro, mas indicou que uma eventual alteração legislativa poderá exigir a revisão das regras. O diretor-geral da agência, Sandoval Feitosa, afirmou que, caso a legislação seja modificada antes dos certames, será necessário republicar os editais e remarcar as sessões públicas. Isso pode acontecer porque a Aneel trabalha com antecedência mínima de 30 dias entre a publicação dos editais e a realização dos leilões, prazo que precisaria ser considerado caso a mudança na legislação exigisse alterações nas regras da disputa. Em paralelo aos editais, a Aneel conduz outro processo para regulamentar o rateio do encargo entre os geradores. O tema está em consulta pública, e recebe contribuições até 9 de novembro.

artigo.texto: CATL secures major Australian battery deal as sodium-ion technology draws industry interest Chinese energy giant CATL will supply a major 400MW Victorian battery project, expanding its Australian footprint while unveiling new sodium-ion technology. Chinese energy storage giant CATL has been selected to supply a major 400-megawatt battery project in Victoria, marking a significant expansion of its footprint in Australia’s National Electricity Market while unveiling new sodium-ion technology tailored for extreme heat. Strategic Grid Integration The Baranduda Electrical Energy Reserve, a 400-megawatt facility with 1.86 gigawatt-hours of storage, is being developed by Birdwood Energy near Wodonga. The project sits adjacent to the existing Victoria-New South Wales electricity interconnector, positioning it as a critical node for grid stability during peak demand periods. The State Electricity Commission, a publicly owned entity revived by the Carroll Labor government, recently injected $43 million to acquire a minority stake in the development. This investment finalizes the capital stack required for construction and represents the first public-private partnership between the state government and a superannuation fund, specifically Aware Super, to deliver a renewable energy asset. Birdwood Energy managing director Alex Marriott-Smith confirmed that CATL was chosen following a rigorous procurement process evaluating cost, technical capability, and deliverability. The selection underscores CATL’s dominance in utility-scale storage, leveraging its global manufacturing scale to secure large-scale contracts in competitive markets. Sodium-Ion Alternative At the All Energy Australia conference in Melbourne, CATL showcased its new utility-scale Tener+ system, which the company claims reduces the required physical footprint by 35 per cent compared to legacy models. More significantly, the company highlighted its Tener Sodium battery, a modular grid-scale system utilizing sodium-ion chemistry rather than traditional lithium iron phosphate. Sodium-ion technology has emerged as a vital alternative amid persistent supply chain constraints and geopolitical tensions surrounding lithium and cobalt extraction. CATL asserts that its sodium-ion modules are specifically engineered for Australia’s harsh climate, maintaining operational integrity at temperatures up to 55 degrees Celsius. Zane Zhou, general manager of CATL Australia and New Zealand, noted that the sodium-ion offering has generated substantial interest across the National Electricity Market and the off-grid mining sector. Mining operators are increasingly seeking to electrify heavy machinery and reduce diesel consumption, requiring robust storage solutions that can withstand remote, high-temperature environments. Market and Policy Implications The Baranduda project claims the longest storage duration in Victoria at 4.65 hours, allowing it to absorb excess daytime solar generation and dispatch power during the evening peak. This duration is essential for managing the rapid influx of rooftop solar and the scheduled retirement of legacy coal-fired power stations. Industry analysts note that while lithium-ion remains the standard for grid storage, sodium-ion technology offers a lower total installation cost and eliminates reliance on critical minerals that face export restrictions. The commercial validation of sodium-ion at Baranduda could accelerate its adoption across the Asia-Pacific region. The Victorian government’s revival of the State Electricity Commission was explicitly designed to intervene in a market where private capital has occasionally hesitated to underwrite long-duration storage projects. By taking a minority stake, the SEC de-risks the investment for private partners like Aware Super, bridging the gap between ambitious climate targets and the actual deployment of firming capacity. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, which rely on expensive and geographically concentrated minerals, sodium-ion cells utilize abundant, low-cost materials. This structural advantage insulates developers from the volatile price swings that have periodically disrupted the global battery supply chain over the past three years. Furthermore, the thermal stability of sodium-ion chemistry reduces the need for energy-intensive liquid cooling systems. In outback mining operations and regional grid nodes, where ambient temperatures regularly exceed 40 degrees Celsius, the ability to operate safely at 55 degrees Celsius without derating capacity provides a distinct engineering advantage. The integration of the Baranduda facility into the National Electricity Market will also test the regulatory frameworks governing long-duration storage. Current market mechanisms were primarily designed around two-hour discharge cycles, and operators are lobbying for updated capacity value metrics that properly remunerate four-hour and six-hour systems for their extended grid-support capabilities. As Australia accelerates its transition away from coal, the deployment of diverse storage chemistries is viewed as a critical hedge against technological lock-in. Grid operators require a heterogeneous mix of assets to manage frequency, voltage, and seasonal energy shifting, ensuring that the failure or degradation of one technology class does not compromise overall system security. Construction timelines and final grid connection dates for the Baranduda reserve are expected to be finalized following the completion of remaining environmental and planning approvals. artigo.texto: Data center boom: What Virginia communities should ask before saying yes LOUDOUN COUNTY, Va. (WSET) — A constant hum. Massive industrial buildings rising beside homes and schools. Billions of dollars flowing into local government budgets. Across Northern Virginia, the data center boom is bringing economic opportunity and a growing debate over what communities must give up to get it. As data centers spread across Virginia, the decisions local leaders make today could affect residents’ electric bills, neighborhoods and quality of life for years to come. For Greg Pirio in Loudoun County, the problem is difficult to ignore. “Yeah, it’s just a constant irritation,” Pirio said. His neighbor, Jessica Medeiros, shares his frustration. “It increases my anxiety. I’m like, uuuuuggggh,” Medeiros said. Their common neighbor is a Vantage data center in Loudoun County, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world. According to Loudoun County government figures for 2026, the county has 233 data center buildings in operation, with another 171 planned. Medeiros said she understands the need for data centers but questions how close some facilities are allowed to come to residential neighborhoods. “I don’t have a problem with data centers. Yes, we need them, but they should not be in such close proximity to residents to affect their daily lives,” she said. The noise from the Vantage facility comes from an on-site power plant operated by eight gas turbine engines. “If I stay out here too long, I’ll get a headache. It’s just awful,” Pirio said. At a recent town hall meeting, a Vantage representative promised changes to address concerns about the noise. “So we’re changing the complete design of the generators or the turbines,” the representative said. Whether those changes will resolve the neighbors’ concerns remains to be seen. Billions in revenue, but at what cost? Despite complaints from some residents, the demand for data centers continues to grow. Nicole Riley, director of the Data Center Coalition, said the industry is responding to increased demand for artificial intelligence and cloud storage. “I think we’re going to need more of them or we’re certainly going to need what we’re building,” Riley said. For Loudoun County, the economic impact is substantial. Data centers contributed $1.2 billion to the county government’s budget this year, accounting for 39% of the total, according to figures provided for the investigation. That revenue helps pay for schools, law enforcement and other public services. “So that’s a significant amount of money that they can put towards schools, that they can put towards law enforcement and other priorities,” Riley said. The industry is also credited with helping reduce Loudoun County’s real estate tax rate by 30% between 2016 and 2026. But Pirio said lower property taxes do not erase the effects of living near a noisy industrial facility. “Even if there’s been a reduction in our property taxes, having to live with this noise and the health effects and the destruction of the natural environment. There are no regulations,” he said. His comments reflect his concerns about the effects of noise and development. The investigation did not establish that the facility caused specific health problems. The concerns extend beyond Loudoun County. Prince William County had 57 data center buildings in operation, with another 100 under construction or planned, according to county government figures for 2026. Some facilities are rising near existing neighborhoods and schools. Jessica Creech said the area near her home was wooded when she moved in. Construction changed the landscape, and she now hears a steady hum from the nearby data center. “Before the sun comes up, you can hear it a lot more clearly, but it’s just like a constant hum or buzz,” Creech said. A few miles away, Roger Yackel takes local leaders and reporters on tours to show them the scale of the development. During one stop near Yung Elementary School, the group viewed construction of a Microsoft data center next to the school. “This is an elementary school that was built 13 years before the data center,” Yackel said. “And I think that’s important. You choose a site with an elementary school close by, you made a mistake.” For residents, the issue is not necessarily whether data centers should exist. It is where they should be built and what protections should be in place for nearby communities. Donna Gallant has spent years fighting development near her Prince William County neighborhood. Her battle began in 2022, when she challenged the county in court over rezoning plans that allowed heavy industrial development, including data centers, near homes and schools. She lost the legal battle. “I’m not anti-data. I’m anti-data when you drop them into residential areas, schools, homes and national parks. They don’t belong there,” Gallant said. Now, Google is constructing a data center campus with buildings reaching about 75 feet tall near her neighborhood. A Google spokesman said the company works to limit the effects of construction on nearby residents. “There will be construction activities during the night, but we will limit the ones that are the loudest to the daylight hours,” said Clay Allsop, a Google spokesman. The company expects to apply similar noise mitigation practices to its planned development in Botetourt County near Roanoke. Gallant worries that more development could further change the character of her neighborhood. “Your home is your sanctuary. When you can no longer sit out and enjoy because the noise is so loud, and it’s going to get worse,” she said. “I have friends in Loudoun. They say it’s horrible. artigo.texto: Rwanda uses CMAS 2026 to advance Carbon Markets, Climate Finance and Green Growth Hosting CMAS 2026 reflects confidence in Rwanda’s progress in developing carbon market regulations and its ambition to help shape Africa’s climate finance future. Since launching its National Carbon Market Framework in 2023, Rwanda has established procedures for implementing Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, developed a national carbon registry and introduced independent verification requirements. Ministerial instructions issued in January 2026 further clarified fees and benefit-sharing arrangements. The summit brings together governments, project developers, investors, carbon credit buyers and development finance institutions to strengthen partnerships and move projects towards implementation. It is hosted with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the African Development Bank, with the Development Bank of Southern Africa and AUDA-NEPAD as partners. For Rwanda, the goal is clear: translate carbon market opportunities into measurable climate and economic benefits. Carbon markets and Rwanda’s green growth agenda Carbon markets support Rwanda’s climate commitments and green growth ambitions under Vision 2050. However, their value extends beyond emissions reductions. The country wants projects to deliver wider benefits, including land restoration, job creation, stronger community resilience and improved livelihoods. Although Rwanda contributes relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions, it remains vulnerable to climate-related disasters. In May 2023, floods and landslides in the Western, Northern and Southern provinces claimed more than 130 lives and destroyed homes, roads and crops. Investments in restored hillsides, protected wetlands and improved drainage can help communities withstand future climate shocks. Carbon finance can also support cleaner economic growth. Electric mobility can reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and improve urban air quality, while clean cooking and renewable energy can lower household costs and ease pressure on forests. Mobilizing investment and creating green jobs Carbon credits can generate revenue from verified emissions reductions or removals, helping finance projects that might otherwise struggle to attract investment. According to figures provided for this article, Rwanda’s Environment Management Authority (REMA) has registered 29 carbon market projects covering land restoration, agriculture, forestry, electric mobility, waste management and renewable energy. Carbon credit sales have generated approximately US$1.5 million. Rwanda’s Article 6 cooperation agreement with Singapore also provides a framework for authorized projects to access international buyers. The opportunities extend to employment. Carbon projects can create jobs in tree planting, land restoration, clean cooking, electric mobility, waste management and the measurement and verification of emissions reductions. These activities can build local skills and expand economic opportunities in rural communities as well as urban centres. Across Africa, the African Union’s Action Plan on Carbon Markets provides a shared direction, while institutions such as the African Development Bank and the Development Bank of Southern Africa are working to support investment and mobilize private capital. Ensuring communities share the benefits For carbon markets to deliver lasting value, communities hosting projects must benefit directly. Rwanda’s January 2026 Ministerial Instructions provide for 30 per cent of carbon market revenues from qualifying land-based projects on farmers’ or public land to go to communities and landowners. Beyond revenue, projects can deliver practical improvements. Clean cooking reduces household smoke and firewood collection, while land restoration can improve soil quality, protect water resources and strengthen resilience to climate change. Transparent benefit-sharing arrangements are therefore essential to ensuring that carbon finance supports local development rather than benefiting only investors and project developers. Protecting carbon market integrity Strong safeguards are critical to ensuring that carbon markets deliver genuine climate benefits. Under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, authorized international transfers of mitigation outcomes are subject to government approval, tracking and corresponding adjustments where applicable. These measures help prevent emissions reductions from being counted more than once towards national climate targets. Article 6 also includes provisions to support overall mitigation of global emissions. Carbon credits should complement, not replace, efforts by countries and companies to reduce their own emissions. Reliable verification, transparent registries and effective government oversight are essential to maintaining market confidence. For African countries, clear regulations and fair contractual terms can also strengthen negotiating power and help ensure that more of the value generated by carbon projects benefits local economies. From dialogue to delivery CMAS 2026 aims to turn discussions into practical outcomes in four key areas: - Project development: Connect credible projects with investors and buyers to accelerate implementation and carbon credit issuance. - Climate finance: Secure investment commitments and expand blended finance to help early-stage projects attract private capital. - Policy alignment: Strengthen cooperation on Article 6, national registries and emissions measurement and verification. - Community benefits: Advance commitments on revenue-sharing, local employment and skills development. Achieving these outcomes will require transparent regulations, predictable fees, reliable registries and investment in African technical expertise. artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 27 de outubro de 2026, às 18:34 A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou nesta terça-feira, 27, os editais dos leilões para a inédita contratação de baterias, que irão contribuir para a segurança do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Para o certame com conteúdo local, o preço-teto foi fixado em R$ 1.760.000,00/MW ao ano, enquanto o certame sem a restrição terá preço-teto de R$ 1.580.000,00/MW ao ano. O relator é o diretor Gentil Nogueira. Conforme lei de 2025, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, na forma de baterias, terão custos de contratação rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia. Isso gerou críticas do setor, e um dos argumentos é a falta de tratamento isonômico. No início de outubro, a Câmara dos Deputados aprovou o requerimento de urgência do projeto de lei que abre margem para o custo da contratação de baterias ser arcado pelos usuários finais de energia elétrica do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), incluídos os consumidores. A votação do mérito do texto (PL 3716/2026) deve ocorrer em breve. Tendo em vista eventual mudança, o Diretor-Geral da Aneel, Sandoval Feitosa, reforçou que eventual mudança legislativa será recepcionada “com a maior agilidade possível”. Nos processos de hoje, a Aneel faz um ajuste de redação para substituir a expressão “gerador de energia” por “usuário de reserva de capacidade”, tanto no edital quanto no Contrato de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (CRCAP). A nova redação permite melhor adequação à proposta de regulamentação do rateio dos custos dos Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (LRCAPs) de baterias. A norma está em discussão na consulta pública, com prazo de contribuição até 6 de novembro. O titular do empreendimento fará jus à receita fixa (em R$/ano), a ser paga em 12 parcelas mensais. Em geral, os contratos terão 15 anos de duração, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. A área técnica da Aneel propôs uma mudança nos editais dos leilões para a contratação de baterias, que pode levar à inclusão dos consumidores no rateio do custo de contratação. Os certames estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. As baterias serão contratadas na modalidade de “reserva de capacidade”. Em geral, os custos administrativos e financeiros e os encargos tributários precisam ser rateados entre todos os usuários finais de energia elétrica do SIN, incluídos os consumidores. A exceção, contudo, foi dada aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Daí a alegação de falta de isonomia. Contato: renan.monteiro@broadcast.com.br Veja também

artigo.texto: O Motorola Edge 70 Neo deve ser o novo lançamento da Motorola para as próximas semanas ou meses. Um novo vazamento revela algumas especificações desse aparelho, como sua bateria massiva de 7.000 mAh e até mesmo o visual do produto, que não é muito diferente do restante da linha. Segundo o vazamento, o novo Edge 70 Neo deve entregar uma tela de 6,78 polegadas na resolução 1.5K com taxa de atualização de 144 Hz, além da proteção Gorilla Glass 7i. Mas o que realmente chama a atenção é essa bateria com capacidade de 7.000 mAh, que possivelmente será compatível com recarga de 45W. No segmento interno, a fabricante deve inserir o chip Snapdragon 7s Gen 3, introduzido ao mercado em 2024 para celulares intermediários. Para memória RAM, há uma expectativa para versões de 6 GB ou 8 GB, que é o padrão nesse tipo de produto. No armazenamento é bem provável que o Motorola Edge 70 Neo seja vendido com 128 GB e 256 GB. Em relação ao conjunto de câmeras, a região traseira desse smartphone deve entregar um sensor primário Sony Lytia Y710 de 50 MP, com abertura de f/1.8. Ele se juntará a uma câmera macro de 2 MP e um sensor de luz 3 em 1. Já na câmera frontal, utilizada para as selfies, a resolução é de 32 MP, sugere o rumor. Motorola já confirmou o celular sem querer Em agosto, um funcionário da Motorola acidentalmente revelou esse smartphone ao publicar sobre testes do Android 17 Beta em um fórum da Lenovo. Tanto na postagem do fórum quanto no formulário de inscrição para os testes, o nome do Motorola Edge 70 Neo foi repetido algumas vezes. A fabricante já lançou os modelos Edge 70 padrão, Edge 70 Max, Edge 70 Pro, Edge 70 Pro+, Edge 70 Fusion, Edge 70 Fusion+ e anunciou o super Signature 27 recentemente. Historicamente, essa linha da Motorola possui um modelo Neo, mas neste ano isso ainda não aconteceu. Havia a esperança que esse Edge 70 Neo fosse lançado em setembro ou ainda em outubro, mas parece que esse produto ficará cozinhando no forno por mais algumas semanas. Vale notar que os vazamentos são rumores e é necessário aguardar pela revelação oficial da Motorola. Por falar na Motorola, a empresa lançou o novo Moto G47 Power com uma bateria gigantesca e uma câmera bem parruda de 108 MP. artigo.texto: Despite her own hard times, a Maryland woman became a leading data center activist Despite her hard financial times, a Maryland woman became a leading local data center activist — an example of the way the issue has prompted people to get involved. SCOTT DETROW, HOST: The backlash against data centers has inspired newcomers to get involved in civic activism, like one woman in Prince George's County, Maryland, who got more involved despite facing a lot of challenges in her own life. Jenny Abamu of member station WAMU in Washington, D.C., reports. JENNY ABAMU, BYLINE: The overgrown grass and weeds seem to stretch into the horizon, nearly 90 acres of empty land in Landover, Maryland, in a predominantly Black community. It had been Landover Mall, which closed in 2002. Then, in 2024, the same developer that built the mall won approval from county planners for a $5 billion data center campus. Taylor Frazier McCollum, who lived less than a mile away, described the moment she learned about the development. TAYLOR FRAZIER MCCOLLUM: I was like, oh, hell, no. Why would you want to bring water-polluting, diesel-generating, like, data centers right down the street from where people live, work, play? Like, it just - it didn't make sense to me. ABAMU: Frazier McCollum isn't the typical land use protester, the not in my backyard homeowner. She doesn't own a home. In fact, in 2024, as a single mother, her and her young daughter were evicted from their rental. She worked at a waxing center that reduced its wages, and she fell behind on her rent. Since then, they've moved around. FRAZIER MCCOLLUM: It was difficult. It was just hard for me because I created this ideal life, paying for us to live in this apartment and have our own space. And then to have it taken away, it felt like something that wasn't ever going to end. ABAMU: They lived in her grandfather's home when she learned about the proposed project. She created a petition, gaining over 25,000 signatures, leading to widely attended protests and culminating with moratoriums on data centers throughout the county, blocking the $5 billion project. She went to county meetings, testified at the state capitol and endorsed political candidates. Along the way, she found herself an unusual coalition, socialists, environmentalists, neighbors angry about their electricity bills. Staci Hartwell, a long-term environmental activist, said she struggled to get traction on the data centers until Frazier McCollum came along. STACI HARTWELL: This is something that was happening in her neighborhood. And it was really like her awakening. ABAMU: But this all comes as Prince George's County needs revenue. It lost several major economic anchors. The NFL Washington Commanders are moving back to D.C. A Six Flags closed. Federal workers have lost their jobs. There's a county budget deficit. For local officials, data centers were supposed to help stem the hemorrhaging. When Frazier McCollum went to a county council meeting in September to ask for a public fund to help residents repair their roofs, something her grandfather needs, council member Wanika Fisher reminded her that the data center pause didn't help. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) WANIKA FISHER: I don't see where the money's coming from. I think we have to have a real conversation. And I'm not saying that a data center is the answer, but I'm saying it's worth the hard discussion. ABAMU: But Frazier McCollum has put the data center fight before everything. She's lost jobs to show up at county hearings or knock on doors. She's become the face of data center activism, featured in local media. Activists like Hartwell helped her find grants to travel to other Black communities, fighting data center growth in Atlanta, Memphis and even across the globe in Zambia. FRAZIER MCCOLLUM: I feel like so many people are depending on this fight to be successful, not just for myself, but even, like, across the country to, like, set precedence for other people that are fighting against hyperscale data centers. ABAMU: Her father, Lacy McCollum Jr., sees the data center fight rooted in civil rights. LACY MCCOLLUM JR: While I'm afraid for her, we need those people. We needed the Medgar Evers. We needed the Martin Luther King. We needed the Malcolm X, people like Taylor. And they jump out there. Then people behind them get to make progress. ABAMU: She's been encouraged to run for office. She says she wants to pay off debt and traffic tickets first. FRAZIER MCCOLLUM: Like, I didn't want to have to focus on housing and the campaign and doing everything else. Now is not maybe the moment for it, but I do have aspirations to run for something. ABAMU: In the meantime, she's pitching to turn the old Landover site into a sports complex, affordable housing or a heritage tourism site. But she acknowledges that wouldn't be as lucrative as a data center campus. For NPR News, I'm Jenny Abamu in Landover, Maryland. artigo.texto: Peugeot has unveiled the RCZ Vision, an electric sports coupe concept powered by a 500-horsepower drivetrain and a solid-state battery that the company says is 4.3 inches thick. The battery was developed with US manufacturer Factorial Energy. It can recharge from 10 to 80 percent in as little as 10 minutes, according to Peugeot. The car uses a 1,000-volt electrical system that supports rapid charging. Peugeot says the battery's high energy density allows it to store more electricity in a smaller space. Peugeot quotes a driving range of up to 373 miles on a single charge and a target energy consumption of 11.5 kilowatt-hours per 62 miles. These are manufacturer figures for a concept vehicle. The concept sits on Stellantis' STLA One architecture, which is scheduled to launch in 2027. Peugeot says the architecture supports modern electronics and various battery types, and describes the concept as lightweight and aerodynamic. The design draws on the RCZ coupe that Peugeot produced between 2009 and 2015. It introduces the company's Feline Future styling philosophy, which Peugeot says will define the look of its future cars. Styling features sculpted surfaces, muscular shoulders, and a glass-bubble cabin that stretches across much of the vehicle. Feline Future rests on five principles: freedom, courage, elegance, inner force, and instinct. The concept replaces a conventional steering wheel with Peugeot's square-shaped Hypersquare system. It relies on steer-by-wire technology and has no mechanical connection to the wheels. At low speeds, drivers can manoeuvre the car with less than one full turn. Peugeot also says the RCZ Vision is the first model to carry brake-by-wire technology. This replaces the hydraulic link between pedal and brakes with electronic controls. The company expects more precise braking and better energy recovery. The cockpit carries a new version of Peugeot's i-Cockpit with transparent Micro LED displays. One screen above the steering wheel shows driving information, while a floating central display handles navigation, entertainment, and vehicle settings and can be switched off. The concept also features Level 2++ driver assistance, which allows hands-free driving on city streets and highways under certain conditions. Despite its sporty proportions, it has a four-seat cabin that can carry two adults in the rear. Interior materials include Alcantara, recycled leather, and aluminium details. The rear seatbacks fold down to increase luggage space. The car rides on forged aluminium wheels measuring 21 inches at the front and 22 inches at the rear. Peugeot chief executive Alain Favey said the company was setting out its vision with a car firmly focused on the future, dedicated to delivering the ultimate driving pleasure. Design director Matthias Hossann said the car gives the Feline Future language a new expression.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- on Oct. 27, CATL addressed investor queries on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange's interactive platform regarding the progress of its Hefei sulfide solid-state pilot base. The battery giant remains firmly committed to all-solid-state technology — which it describes as industry-leading — and expects small-scale production by 2027. That timeline tracks with earlier disclosures: small-scale trial production in 2027, followed by mass production around 2030. Image credit: CATL On the technology front, CATL is betting heavily on the sulfide route. It has built a 10Ah-level verification platform and moved its sulfide solid-state battery into 20Ah sample prototyping, targeting an energy density of roughly 500Wh/kg. The company's 2025 annual report shows R&D spending of 22.147 billion yuan — a 19.02% annual jump — with the solid-state R&D team swelling to over 1,000 people. Even so, Chairman Zeng Yuqun struck a cautious note at the Summer Davos Forum. If technology maturity is scored on a 1-to-9 scale, he said, solid-state batteries are currently only at level 4. Commercialization still faces steep engineering and cost hurdles. CATL isn't alone in eyeing 2027. Samsung SDI has pegged its mass-production target for the second half of that year, while Toyota's sulfide-route preparations point to the same window. BYD, for its part, has explicitly targeted 2027 for small-scale output. With top players from China, Japan, and South Korea converging on the same rollout timeline, the engineering race for next-generation battery technology has entered a critical phase.

artigo.texto: Google vira alvo de investigação criminal na Finlândia por derrubar floresta para data center Desmatamento de 330 hectares expulsou espécies nativas e moradores relatam contaminação de riachos; projeto de 13 bilhões de euros é paralisado A polícia da Finlândia deu início a uma investigação criminal nesta quinta-feira, 29, para apurar infrações às leis ambientais do país no terreno onde o Google pretende construir um data center, em uma área rural do norte finlandês. Segundo as autoridades locais, a Tuike Finland, subsidiária do Google, derrubou 330 hectares de floresta, ou cerca de 400 mil árvores, em Muhos, antes que fossem concluídas as avaliações de impacto ambiental exigidas pela legislação da Finlândia. “Com base em informações preliminares, houve ambiguidades e deficiências na drenagem e na gestão da água no canteiro de obras do projeto de datacenter da Tuike Finland Oy”, disse a polícia finlandesa em comunicado. “A investigação criminal irá examinar, entre outras coisas, circunstâncias relacionadas a essas questões”, acrescentou a nota. Proliferação de data centers Como seus vizinhos nórdicos, a Finlândia atrai empresas de tecnologia interessadas em instalar data centers pela estabilidade geopolítica e pela grande disponibilidade de terrenos, além do clima frio, que tende a reduzir os gastos com energia. As autoridades do país analisam pedidos referentes a um total de 145 novos data centers, em diferentes etapas de planejamento. Entre eles está um projeto de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) avaliado em 13 bilhões de euros. Este é o maior investimento do Google na Europa. Agora, com o caso do desmatamento, a Autoridade Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão ordenou que a empresa americana interrompa imediatamente as obras de dois novos data centers no país, em Muhos e Otanmäki, onde outras 150 mil árvores foram removidas. Antti Järvinen, gerente nacional do Google na Finlândia, pediu desculpas pela derrubada das árvores, mas sustentou que a empresa seguiu o “melhor entendimento que tínhamos da legislação na época”. Debate nacional Os projetos da big tech contaram com o apoio do governo finlandês. Em setembro, quando os planos do Google foram divulgados, o primeiro-ministro Petteri Orpo afirmou que atrair investimentos era uma “prioridade máxima” e que o acordo “traria benefícios duradouros”. As denúncias sobre a suposta conduta irregular da empresa americana, porém, provocaram um debate nacional sobre o impacto desses acordos para as comunidades locais, o meio ambiente e os galopantes preços da energia. O tema pode influenciar as eleições parlamentares previstas para abril. Mais de 93 mil pessoas assinaram uma petição que pede maior regulamentação dos data centers e indenização por danos ambientais. Especialistas apontam que essas instalações criam poucos empregos locais e que os ganhos para o país como um todo são mínimos. A retirada da vegetação e da camada superficial do solo em Muhos e Otanmäki deixou muitas áreas cobertas por lama, causando o vazamento de água contaminada para riachos e para o rio Oulujoki. A destruição das florestas já afeta diretamente os animais e as comunidades locais: o desmatamento expulsou espécies nativas, como o pica-pau-de-três-dedos, e fez com que lobos da região passassem a invadir áreas urbanas de alguns vilarejos. Além disso, moradores relatam contaminação dos riachos locais e transtornos pelo barulho das máquinas. Posicionamentos Em resposta à decisão, o Google confirmou a paralisação das atividades e declarou que cumprirá rigorosamente as exigências das autoridades finlandesas. A multinacional comprometeu-se a plantar árvores em 130 hectares na região de Muhos, medida classificada por ecologistas como insuficiente para reparar os danos causados. Porta-vozes da Associação Finlandesa para a Conservação da Natureza (SLL), por sua vez, criticaram duramente a conduta da empresa, classificando a ação como “pura arrogância”. E mesmo com Orpo priorizando investimentos em IA, o incidente foi descrito por ele como um “banho de água fria”.

artigo.texto: Adani Green Bets On Battery Storage To Boost Earnings And Power Sales The renewable energy company plans to expand battery storage capacity to 50 GWh over five years as it seeks to reduce power curtailment, address transmission constraints and strengthen earnings Adani Green Energy is stepping up investment in battery energy storage as it seeks to improve renewable power utilisation, mitigate transmission bottlenecks and build a more reliable clean energy business. The company has set a target of 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage capacity over the next five years, positioning energy storage as a potential driver of future growth. The strategy comes as India expands renewable energy generation while grappling with the challenge of delivering intermittent solar and wind power when and where electricity is needed. Storage systems can help bridge this gap by retaining surplus electricity and releasing it during periods of higher demand or limited transmission availability. Adani Green had 6.63 GWh of operational battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity at its Khavda project in Gujarat, accounting for more than half of India's operational battery storage capacity, according to company disclosures in October 2026. It aims to exceed 10 GWh of battery storage capacity in the financial year 2026–27. Storage Expansion Targets Grid Constraints The expansion reflects a broader shift in India's renewable energy industry, where developers are increasingly looking beyond installed generation capacity towards the ability to supply power when required. Transmission congestion can prevent electricity generated at renewable energy sites from reaching consumers, resulting in curtailment and potential revenue losses. Adani Green is developing a 30-gigawatt renewable energy project across 538 square kilometres at Khavda. Integrating battery storage with generation assets could help the company manage constraints on power evacuation and improve the utilisation of its renewable energy portfolio. During the company's second-quarter earnings discussions for FY27, its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) stood at Rs 8,276 crore. Management indicated that the figure could have approached Rs 9,000 crore in the absence of curtailment, highlighting the potential financial impact of transmission-related constraints. Industry analysts note that storage is becoming increasingly important to the economics of renewable energy projects, although the benefits depend on battery costs, utilisation rates, project financing and the availability of grid infrastructure. Earnings Potential Drives Investment Adani Green's storage ambitions reflect a wider industry trend towards combining solar, wind and storage to provide more dependable electricity. Battery systems can also help manage peak demand, improve grid flexibility and reduce the need to curtail renewable generation. However, the expansion of battery storage requires significant capital investment. Developers must balance the cost of batteries, financing conditions and long-term project returns against the commercial benefits of storing and dispatching electricity. The company is also pursuing pumped-storage projects to complement battery installations. Its strategy signals a move towards an integrated renewable energy model in which generation and storage work together to improve power delivery and operational flexibility. For India's clean energy transition, the challenge will be to scale storage capacity while ensuring projects remain financially viable. As renewable generation grows, the ability to store and deliver electricity efficiently is likely to become an increasingly important factor in investment decisions and the sector's long-term economics.

artigo.texto: New BESS in Portugal will be required to form the grid and to supply synthetic inertia, under an ordinance that the Portuguese Government, a Portugal-based national government, has issued. The requirement applies in full to plants of 45 MW or more, and also to those that are connected at 110 kV or above. Plants of 10 MW to 45 MW will have to form the grid as well, but on terms that the grid operator is yet to set. Every plant that is covered must keep an energy reserve, so that it can answer frequency swings between 47.0 Hz and 52.5 Hz. The ordinance also requires every plant of 500 kW or more to switch automatically from charging to discharging when the frequency falls. It came into force on 23 October 2026, and it applies to the connection requests that have been filed since that day. Portugal makes grid forming mandatory for BESS of 45 MW or more An ordinance of the Portuguese Government has made grid forming and synthetic inertia mandatory for every BESS of 45 MW or more that seeks a connection in Portugal. artigo.texto: Strategic Value Partners Backs NewEdge Power With Joint Venture for Utility-Scale Battery Storage Strategic Value Partners, L.P. and NewEdge Power have unveiled a partnership in which funds managed by the investment firm will commit initial capital to form a joint venture centered on utility-scale power while also backing the growth of NewEdge's development platform, the companies said in a joint announcement dated Oct. 29, 2026. The deal rests on NewEdge's prior support from SJF Ventures, which led its Series A round in 2025, and from original investment partners Segue Sustainable Infrastructure and North Sky Capital. Financial terms were not made public. NewEdge's project pipeline covers utility-scale battery storage and solar as well as distributed power assets in multiple U.S. power markets. The joint venture's seed portfolio will aim for as much as 1.2 GW of capacity in PJM, which operates the grid across 13 states and Washington, D.C. With SVP's backing, NewEdge intends to move that portfolio forward and chase further opportunities within PJM and elsewhere in the United States. The tie-up arrives as PJM and other American power markets confront escalating electricity needs. Growth in manufacturing, electrification and data centers is driving demand for additional capacity that can be commissioned swiftly. Battery storage is one option that can address that requirement quickly and at reasonable cost. Joe Nano, NewEdge's Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder, said power availability had for decades been assumed while demand held steady. He pointed to extraordinary demand growth from data centers and the return of manufacturing to the U.S. as creating a need for new resources, calling battery storage a crucial element of the answer that can be deployed fast. According to Nano, SVP supplies the scale, know-how and confidence to extend NewEdge's platform record and broaden its ability to serve the U.S. power market at this moment of opportunity. Mike Ungari, SVP's Global Head of Real Estate, said rising electricity demand and the imperative to add capacity quickly are transforming power markets. He noted that demand tells only part of the story, since in markets such as PJM obtaining well-positioned sites and a workable route to the grid accounts for a substantial share of the opportunity. Ungari said the partnership merges NewEdge's skill at finding and advancing such sites with SVP's experience investing in power and infrastructure. NewEdge will oversee development within the joint venture, and SVP will provide funding for chosen projects as they advance. SVP's platform investment in NewEdge will likewise be disbursed across the investment period to bolster and grow the company's development team and capabilities. Steve Barna, NewEdge's Chief Development Officer and Co-Founder, said the company was established around locking in premium sites and interconnection positions in the markets that most need new capacity. He said SVP's capital should let the seed portfolio and pipeline advance through development at the speed the market demands. Andrew Shore, a Managing Director on SVP's North American Investment Team, will join NewEdge's Board of Directors as an observer under the transaction. He will sit alongside NewEdge's Joe Nano and Steve Barna, SJF Ventures' Dave Kirkpatrick and Alan Kelley, and independent director Brent Beerley. The board carries substantial power-sector experience, including SJF Ventures' clean energy stakes in Terabase Energy, Nextpower (NASDAQ: NXT, previously Nextracker), Community Energy (sold to AES) and groSolar (sold to EDF), plus two renewable company exits by Beerley to Iberdrola Renewables and AES. Ackman-Ziff Real Estate Group LLC was financial advisor to NewEdge, and Verdonck Partners LLC was buy-side advisor to SVP. Amis, Patel & Brewer, LLP provided transaction counsel to NewEdge, while Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP provided transaction counsel to SVP. NewEdge Power is a utility-scale and distributed power development platform operating in several major U.S. power markets, with projects spanning utility-scale battery storage, utility-scale solar and distributed power. Its leadership team has together worked on and delivered over 48 GW of power projects involving solar, battery storage, wind, geothermal, hydroelectric and conventional power. SVP is a global alternative investment firm that pursues opportunistic strategies spanning performing and event-driven debt, hybrid solutions, hard assets such as infrastructure, real estate, power and airplanes, and special situations private equity. The firm reports roughly $22 billion in assets under management and over $60 billion of capital invested since Victor Khosla founded it in 2001. artigo.texto: O Google derrubou cerca de 400 mil árvores no norte da Finlândia para construir dois data centers, estruturas que processam dados e sustentam serviços de internet e de inteligência artificial. As obras começaram sem as avaliações de impacto ambiental exigidas pela legislação finlandesa, segundo reportagem do The Guardian. Os dois projetos somam € 13 bilhões (cerca de R$ 72,38 bilhões) em infraestrutura de IA, o maior investimento do tipo já feito no país. A escala do desmatamento e o início das obras sem avaliação ambiental geraram revolta entre moradores e organizações ambientais finlandesas. Dimensão da área desmatada Em Muhos, uma faixa de floresta de 3 quilômetros por 2 quilômetros foi derrubada, totalizando 330 hectares e cerca de 250 mil árvores. A empresa retirou até a camada superficial do solo, deixando um lamaçal a 400 metros do rio Oulujoki. Na vila de Otanmäki, a ecologista Mari Annala, da Associação Finlandesa para a Conservação da Natureza, calcula que outras 150 mil árvores foram cortadas. A água dos riachos da região ganhou coloração marrom, e a madeira retirada de forma irregular não pôde ser comercializada com serrarias. Suspensão das obras pela Autoridade local A Autoridade Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão enviou notificações ao Google e determinou a paralisação temporária dos dois canteiros de obras no dia 6 de outubro. A empresa havia avançado com o desmatamento antes de concluir os estudos de impacto ambiental previstos em lei. O diretor do Google na Finlândia, Antti Järvinen, reconheceu o erro publicamente, mas justificou que a companhia seguiu a interpretação que tinha da legislação até aquele momento. A empresa afirmou que vai atender todas as exigências pendentes e vai replantar vegetação em 130 hectares em Muhos. Revolta e pressão popular Mais de 93 mil pessoas assinaram uma petição exigindo regras mais duras para data centers e uma taxa de compensação às comunidades atingidas. O primeiro-ministro Petteri Orpo, que considerava a atração desses investimentos uma prioridade máxima, descreveu o episódio como um banho de água fria para o governo. Impacto no cotidiano de Otanmäki A antiga vila mineira de Otanmäki viu o dia a dia mudar com a chegada das obras. A moradora Anni Ranta, de 53 anos, cuja família vive na região há gerações, relatou que lobos passaram a entrar na aldeia depois que animais silvestres deixaram a floresta. Ela também expressou receio quanto ao barulho constante das obras e à possibilidade de o data center tornar a vila um alvo estratégico, dada a fronteira extensa que a Finlândia compartilha com a Rússia. O biólogo Vesa Hyyryläinen, da mesma associação ambiental, constatou que pica-paus que nidificavam na área foram afastados pelo desmatamento. Atração das big techs pelo país A Finlândia se tornou um dos destinos preferidos para esse tipo de instalação, com 145 projetos em diferentes estágios de planejamento espalhados pelo território. O clima frio favorece o resfriamento dos servidores e reduz os custos com energia, um dos maiores gastos operacionais desses complexos. Estabilidade política, disponibilidade de terras e matriz energética renovável completam os atrativos que colocaram o país no radar da corrida global por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. O Ministério do Meio Ambiente deve avaliar os próximos passos do licenciamento, enquanto o episódio reacende o debate sobre os limites da expansão desses projetos no território finlandês. Como funciona a avaliação de impacto ambiental que o Google pulou - A empresa deve apresentar um relatório técnico descrevendo como o projeto afetará florestas, rios, animais e comunidades locais; - A agência governamental de supervisão analisa esse relatório antes de qualquer trabalho começar. - Se houver riscos significativos, a agência pode exigir mudanças no projeto ou negar a aprovação; - Somente após essa avaliação ser concluída e aprovada a empresa pode iniciar as obras de desmatamento e construção.

artigo.texto: A diretoria da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou na noite desta terça-feira (27) os editais para os dois leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratar baterias de grande porte no Brasil, previstos para dezembro. As regras foram aprovadas por unanimidade e acataram algumas mudanças propostas pela equipe técnica após uma consulta pública que recebeu quase 2.500 sugestões. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos e início em agosto de 2028. Os preços-tetos foram definidos pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia em R$ 1,76 milhão por MW/ano (megawatt/ano) para projetos com conteúdo nacional e R$ 1,58 milhão por MW/ano para projetos sem essa especificação. Os editais preveem que os custos sejam divididos entre empresas geradoras de energia, como determina a lei atual sobre o tema. A divisão exata entre os tipos de geradoras é tema de outra consulta pública aberta até 6 de novembro. O rateio do valor é um dos principais pontos de discussão no setor: as geradoras defendem que as baterias beneficiam todo o sistema e por isso o custo deve ser dividido com consumidores, como acontece hoje com termelétricas, que têm função equivalente à de reserva. Já outros segmentos afirmam que a conta deve ficar com as geradoras, principalmente as renováveis como eólica e solar, que inseriram a necessidade de armazenamento no sistema ao produzir mais energia do que a demanda em determinados períodos do dia. No Congresso, um projeto de lei do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) prevê dividir a conta com consumidores, e teve a urgência aprovada em 13 de outubro. Agentes do mercado pediram que os editais acomodem eventuais mudanças de legislação. Em resposta, a Aneel fez algumas mudanças de termos técnicos na redação dos editais, mas afirmou que qualquer mudança vai exigir nova análise da agência. A jornalistas, o diretor-geral da Aneel, Sandoval Feitosa, disse que uma mudança na lei antes das datas do leilão faria a agência republicar editais e adiar a data dos certames. No caso de uma mudança posterior aos leilões e anterior à assinatura dos contratos, ele disse esperar que a legislação traga provisões para a mudança O primeiro leilão, para projetos com conteúdo nacional, está marcado para 2 de dezembro, enquanto o segundo, sem essa exigência, acontece em 4 de dezembro. Na semana passada, a empresa You.On se tornou a primeira credenciada pelo BNDES para participar do certame com requisito de nacionalização. Flexibilização de garantias Para se adaptar a novas projeções do Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2035, publicado recentemente pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), a Aneel reduziu o investimento de referência de R$ 9,8 milhões por MW para R$ 6,0 milhões/MW. Isso também reduziu as garantias e o patrimônio líquido mínimo exigidos, o que a agência considera que aumenta a competitividade dos leilões. Os empreendimentos deverão ter potência mínima de 30 MW, com compromisso de fornecer carga máxima por quatro horas — o que permite entrar em campo no período mais crítico do dia, quando o sol se põe e não há mais geração solar, mas a demanda por energia aumenta — e tempo de recarga completa de até seis horas. É exigida a capacidade de cumprir dois ciclos de descarga e recarga por dia, com limite de 366 ciclos por ano (os ciclos desgastam a bateria). O pagamento será feito por receita fixa anual, com parcelas mensais, que poderá ser ajustada conforme o desempenho. Entre as mudanças acatadas após a consulta pública estão a permissão para formação de consórcio por empresas do mesmo grupo econômico, com comprovação de patrimônio líquido apenas pela controladora. A identificação de cotistas de fundos de investimentos, antes prevista para a etapa de inscrição, poderá ser feita na etapa de habilitação dos projetos, para cotistas com participação acima de 5%. Também foi incluída a possibilidade de empresas de transmissão que têm contratos no mercado regulado participarem do leilão, contanto que não haja prejuízo para as entregas previstas.

artigo.texto: [Solid-state battery: Solid Power’s MOBIUS pilot line for continuous production of sulphide electrolyte begins commissioning, capacity to increase by 150%] [Solid-state battery: Solid Power's MOBIUS pilot line for continuous sulphide electrolyte manufacturing begins commissioning, capacity to increase by 150%] On October 26, 2026, US solid-state battery enterprise Solid Power announced on its official website that its MOBIUS™ pilot line for continuous sulphide solid-state electrolyte manufacturing at its Thornton, Colorado facility has entered the commissioning phase, with materials beginning to be introduced into the line. The line has a designed annual capacity of 45 mt, and once operational, total electrolyte capacity at the SP2 plant is expected to reach approximately 75 mt/year, a 150% increase from the previous level. Site acceptance testing (SAT) for the primary powder processing has been completed, with full SAT expected to be completed by month-end October, and the line is planned to officially commence operations in Q4 2026. Solid Power is positioned as a supplier of electrolyte materials to Tier 1 battery manufacturers and automakers, and continuous manufacturing is the core pathway for achieving its commercial-scale, consistency, and cost targets.

artigo.texto: ARCADIA, Fla (WINK) — It took about 30 minutes longer, but the result was the same. After nearly seven hours of presentations, negotiations, and public comment, DeSoto County commissioners effectively killed plans for what might have been one of the world’s largest data centers. Commissioners deadlocked 2-2 on a request to rezone almost 554 acres of agricultural land to pave the way for an artificial intelligence data center. The tie vote means the motion failed. It came almost 24 hours after commissioners voted the same way on a separate re-zoning request from the same company, DeSoto County Industrial Park Group (DCIP). Commissioner Elton Langford and J.C. Deriso voted in favor of the project. Commissioner Jerod Gross and Judy Schaefer voted against it. The Florida Commission on Ethics ordered Commissioner Steven Hickox to sit out the vote. Hickox said a step-family member was involved in a possible land deal with DCIP. He was not present at Wednesday's meeting. The company proposed building a data center that could have grown to more than 1,000 acres, centered around a decommissioned natural gas plant off Roan Street, just east of Arcadia. DCIP submitted three separate applications. Commissioners approved the first phase of the project, which is 34 acres, back in March. But the project faced fierce opposition from some neighbors who argued that developers didn't provide enough information about the project, while raising concerns about it's possible impact on property values, the environment, and DeSoto County's rural way of life. That included several elderly residents from Arcadia Village, a mobile home retirement community located just west of the property. The land stretches from south of Northeast Roan Street to State Road 70 and Northeast Hansel Drive, roughly one mile east of Turner Avenue. "Arcadia may not have the wealth of Sarasota or Naples. We don't have luxury waterfront developments or sprawling corporate campuses," said Ashwani Soin, who owns the Arcadia Oaks assisted living facility. "But what we do have is something increasingly difficult to find a genuine sense of community. People recognize one another." Developers offered several concessions after Wednesday's loss, including doubling the buffer between residential areas to 1,000 feet and eliminating plans for an on-site power plant. Developers agreed to 82 conditions imposed by the county, including two last second requests that came after midnight. The county limited noise to between 50 and 60 decibels and required the company to install a closed loop system, which reduces the amount of water needed to support a data center. "We want to be good neighbors," DCIP CEO Jon Brown said. "I ask that you guys vote yes. I think this is good for the county. I think it's not just about tax dollars, it's about jobs, it's about adding benefits without consuming too much property." DCIP said the project would create about 150 full-time employees that include maintenance workers and technical staff. The company said it would also generate significant tax revenue for one of Florida's poorest counties, which has seen revenue loss tied to the decimation of Florida's citrus industry. "Takes money to do anything. Takes money to run a county," Commissioner Elton Langford said. "I don't want to have to reach into y'all's pocket every time we need something. But there are things that has to be done that we're statutorily tied to, we have to have some kind of funds to operate and do the business of this county." Ultimately, uncertainty helped sink the project. A report from county staff said that developers did not provide an operational analysis identifying the full scope of the project’s activities, including equipment, emissions, noise, or other operational impacts. Representatives for the company pointed out that operational details are not required at this point in the process, and that commissioners would have future opportunities to vote on the project. "I'm not real comfortable with it," Commissioner Judy Schaefer said. "I think there's a lot of the unknowns that are still there. Do I think it could be fixed? Yes, I do. But that's not the point we're voting at right now." After the vote, DCIP CEO Jon Brown offered a short response. "You lick your wounds and move on," Brown said.

artigo.texto: A leading UK renewables developer, OnPath Energy, has achieved financial close on the Common Farm solar park in South Yorkshire, which is its first co-located solar energy and battery storage project. OnPath Energy is currently building the 49 MW solar and 50 MW two-hour battery energy storage system (BESS) close to the Todwick Road Industrial Estate in Dinnington, to the east of Sheffield, which will be able to generate enough homegrown electricity to meet the average annual requirements of up to 18 800 family homes. The project has a subsidy free, long-term route-to-market contract with a global technology company for the solar asset and a third-party optimisation agreement to support the BESS. NatWest provided project financing for the combined asset, with the long-term agreement including a term loan and other ancillary facilities to support the project throughout its construction and operational life. Construction work on the Common Farm co-located solar and BESS, is set to be completed by mid-2027. Local consultation work is continuing around how the annual community benefits package of around £50 000, which could equate to around £2 000 000 through the project’s lifetime, can best be used to build community value by supporting local community and environmental priorities. Infrastructure consultancy, AECOM, is acting as lead consultant for the project, with specialist engineering contractor, Grupotec, delivering the required design, engineering, procurement, and construction work, as well as operational maintenance and management work, once green electricity generation begins. Burges Salmon provided legal advice to OnPath Energy on the deal, with AECOM providing technical advice. Oliver Hartley, Finance Director at OnPath Energy, commented: “While there are currently few co-located sites across the UK, especially at this scale, it makes technical and operational sense to place solar and battery technologies in the same location and allows for efficient use to be made of the available grid connections. Reaching financial close on our first co-located solar and battery site demonstrates the confidence that all parties have in the project’s commercial potential, the effectiveness of the different technologies we’re utilising, and the strength of our relationships with our lenders, advisors, and suppliers.” Hartley added: “Work is progressing well on the Common Farm solar and BESS park, which we’ve been able to deliver thanks in part to our revolving credit facility, enabling us to deliver our project plans with maximum efficiency. Delivering this project will further enhance OnPath Energy’s contribution towards reducing the UK’s dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthening its energy security while also delivering a wide range of direct environmental, economic, and community benefits to the local area.” Kristofer Gibson, Director, Infrastructure & Project Finance, NatWest, commented: “We are pleased to support OnPath Energy on this bilateral financing of Common Farm solar park, OnPath’s first UK solar and BESS co-location project. The project reflects NatWest’s ongoing commitment to financing the infrastructure required for UK’s energy transition, while further strengthening our longstanding relationship with OnPath Energy.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: A demora na expansão da rede de transmissão, que pode levar cerca de sete anos, ameaça a capacidade do Brasil de atrair investimentos em data centers, especialmente em regiões com alta demanda como o interior de São Paulo. O alerta foi feito por Gustavo Estrella, diretor presidente da CPFL Energia, que defende um modelo diferenciado de conexão para atender ao crescimento acelerado da demanda por energia desses empreendimentos e evitar que os pedidos sejam feitos de forma duplicada, entre transmissão e distribuição. Durante participação no BrazilWind Power nesta terça-feira, 27 de outubro, Estrella ressaltou que, tradicionalmente, a expansão da transmissão acompanha o crescimento do consumo de energia. No caso dos data centers, porém, a demanda pode surgir rapidamente e em grandes blocos, exigindo que a infraestrutura seja ampliada antes mesmo da instalação dos empreendimentos. Os pedidos individuais de conexão podem variar de 100 MW a 200 MW e, como exemplo, Estrella citou Campinas, que tem cerca de 1,2 milhão de habitantes e uma capacidade de atendimento de aproximadamente 350 MW. Dois data centers com pedidos de 200 MW cada representariam uma demanda superior a esse volume. Para viabilizar a conexão dos empreendimentos, o executivo defendeu um regime específico que permita distinguir a demanda real de solicitações duplicadas ou especulativas e estabelecer garantias de compromisso dos investidores com os custos da infraestrutura necessária. Ele afirmou que, atualmente, entre 70% e 80% do consumo de energia dos data centers no Brasil está na área de concessão da CPFL, com concentração na região de Campinas. Nos últimos 12 meses, a distribuidora negou pedidos de conexão que somavam 8 GW de capacidade. Embora parte desse volume possa corresponder a solicitações duplicadas ou especulativas, o executivo destacou que há uma demanda expressiva por novos projetos. Como o prazo médio de planejamento e construção de uma linha de transmissão é de sete anos, o executivo vê risco de os investimentos serem direcionados a outros países, como Chile, Argentina e Paraguai. Estrella também ressaltou que a localização dos data centers depende de fatores como latência, telecomunicações, segurança e acesso a outras infraestruturas. Por isso, cabe ao setor elétrico criar condições para atender aos empreendimentos nas regiões escolhidas pelos investidores. A CPFL projeta crescimento de aproximadamente 40% no consumo de energia dos data centers em sua área de atuação em 2026, seguido de uma expansão próxima de 100% em 2027, segundo o executivo. Investimentos bilionários Estrella destacou o potencial econômico da expansão dos data centers no Brasil. Segundo ele, cada gigawatt de capacidade instalada pode representar cerca de US$ 10 bilhões em investimentos na infraestrutura física do empreendimento, além de US$ 30 bilhões a US$ 50 bilhões em equipamentos, dependendo do perfil da instalação, como serviços de computação em nuvem ou aplicações de inteligência artificial (IA). O executivo mencionou um potencial de expansão da capacidade instalada para a faixa de 13 GW a 15 GW, cenário que poderia representar investimentos de centenas de bilhões de dólares. Na avaliação do executivo, a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) pode ajudar a enfrentar a questão tributária para os data centers, enquanto a expansão da transmissão permanece como um desafio estrutural. O executivo também chamou atenção para as mudanças nas condições de operação das redes de distribuição, diante dos eventos climáticos extremos, da intermitência da geração renovável e do surgimento de novas cargas em regiões rurais e remotas. Esses fatores podem exigir investimentos adicionais para adequar a infraestrutura elétrica. Nesse contexto, defendeu que as decisões regulatórias equilibrem o impacto dos custos sobre os consumidores e a necessidade de oferecer segurança aos investidores, especialmente em projetos com horizonte de retorno de 20 a 30 anos. “É fundamental que a gente tenha uma regulação que seja previsível, que seja robusta e que, de alguma forma, garanta o retorno desse investimento em um prazo tão longo”, afirmou.
